IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0001)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, on the petition of Ashley Colby for dissolution of her marriage to Sarah Colby. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. The marriage has suffered an irremediable breakdown due to persistent financial conflicts and fundamentally incompatible parenting philosophies. Ashley Colby, as petitioner, respectfully submits this brief in support of her proposed parenting plan, child support calculation, and property division. The issues before the Court involve the physical custody arrangement for the two minor children, the calculation of child support pursuant to Alaska Civil Rule 90.3, and the equitable distribution of the marital estate, including the allocation of marital debt. Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court enter a judgment of dissolution consistent with the terms set forth herein, all of which are grounded in applicable Alaska law and designed to serve the best interests of the children and fairly allocate the economic consequences of this dissolution.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Colby and Sarah Colby were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The marriage produced two children, currently ages six and nine, both of whom are minors within the meaning of Alaska law. The couple's marriage deteriorated over the course of approximately two years preceding the filing of this petition, as a result of ongoing and unresolved conflicts regarding financial decision-making and deeply incompatible approaches to parenting. These conflicts have proven irremediable, and incompatibility of temperament has caused the breakdown of the marital relationship.
Ashley Colby is employed as a registered nurse and earns approximately $62,000 annually. Sarah Colby is employed as a petroleum engineer and earns approximately $95,000 annually. The parties' respective incomes are relevant both to the child support calculation and to the equitable allocation of marital debt.
The marital estate consists of the jointly owned family home in Anchorage with an estimated equity of $140,000, two vehicles, a shared savings account, and approximately $28,000 in credit card debt. The family home has served as the primary residence of the children throughout the marriage.
Ashley proposes a custody arrangement in which the two minor children reside primarily with her during the school week. Sarah would have alternating weekend visitation and an extended summer parenting period of six consecutive weeks. The parties have agreed to share legal custody and to make all major decisions jointly concerning the children's education, healthcare, and general well-being.
Ashley requests that child support be calculated pursuant to Alaska Civil Rule 90.3, based on Sarah's income as the non-custodial parent under the proposed primary physical custody arrangement. Ashley further requests an equal division of marital assets and asks that Sarah assume primary responsibility for the approximately $28,000 in credit card debt, given her substantially greater earning capacity.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts resolve dissolution proceedings pursuant to AS 25.24.946 and related statutes. A petition for dissolution may be granted where incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and where the parties have reached agreement, or where the court determines after examination, on the terms of custody, support, property division, and debt allocation. AS 25.24.200; AS 25.24.220.
The paramount consideration in all custody matters is the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.070 establishes that, unless detrimental to the child's welfare, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the pendency of custody proceedings. Courts examine parenting agreements with particular care when minor children are involved. AS 25.24.220(h).
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, child support is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage under Civil Rule 907(a)(2). For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). The definitions of physical custody arrangements are set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(f).
The division of marital property at dissolution is governed by AS 25.24.160, which requires the court to divide marital property in a just manner, without regard to fault, and to fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce by considering enumerated statutory factors. AS 25.24.160(a)(4). Spousal maintenance, if awarded, must also fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution based on the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(2). Courts in Alaska have expressed a preference for resolving the financial consequences of divorce through property division rather than maintenance awards. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE MINOR CHILDREN
The proposed parenting plan provides that the two minor children will reside primarily with Ashley Colby during the school week, with Sarah Colby exercising alternating weekend visitation and a six-consecutive-week extended summer parenting period. The parties have agreed to joint legal custody, under which all major decisions regarding the children's education, health, and general welfare will be made jointly. This arrangement serves the best interests of the children and should be approved by the Court.
Alaska law requires the Court to examine whether proposed custody agreements are just and in the best interests of the children of the marriage. AS 25.24.220(d)(2). The proposed arrangement provides stability and continuity of care during the school year by maintaining a consistent primary residence, while simultaneously ensuring that the children have meaningful and substantial time with both parents. AS 25.20.070 reflects Alaska's strong policy that children shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents.
The six-week summer parenting period afforded to Sarah is substantial and meaningful. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) acknowledges that an obligor parent may receive a credit for extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days, though the Court retains discretion in applying that credit. The summer period proposed here, at six consecutive weeks, approaches but does not reach the 30-percent threshold that would convert the arrangement from primary physical custody to shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2). Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), primary physical custody exists where the children reside with the non-custodial parent for less than 30 percent of the year. Six weeks represents approximately 11.5 percent of the calendar year, well within the primary custody definition.
Joint legal custody is appropriate here because both parties have demonstrated an ongoing commitment to the children's education, healthcare, and general welfare, and because the parties have agreed to this arrangement. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a court must independently assess whether custody arrangements serve the children's interests. Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002). The arrangement proposed by Ashley accomplishes this goal by preserving meaningful parental relationships with both parents while providing the children with a stable primary home environment.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED PURSUANT TO CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON SARAH COLBY'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS THE NON-CUSTODIAL PARENT
Because the children will reside primarily with Ashley Colby under the proposed parenting plan, Sarah Colby is the non-custodial parent for purposes of child support calculation. Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that in a case where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, child support "will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2) under all circumstances." For two children, that multiplier is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Sarah Colby earns approximately $95,000 annually as a petroleum engineer. Her adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) is determined by reducing her gross income by mandatory deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A). Voluntary contributions to tax-deferred retirement accounts are also deductible, subject to the 7.5-percent cap established by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B). Health insurance premiums paid by Sarah for her own coverage are deductible up to 10 percent of total income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(F). Work-related childcare expenses for the children who are the subject of this order are also deductible. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E).
Ashley Colby respectfully requests that the Court require both parties to submit Civil Rule 90.3 affidavits disclosing income and applicable deductions so that the Court may determine Sarah's adjusted annual income with precision. Based on a gross annual income of $95,000 and applying applicable deductions, Sarah's adjusted annual income is estimated to be in the range that, when multiplied by 27 percent for two children, will produce a monthly support obligation substantially greater than what Ashley earns in comparable disposable income.
The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed that the purpose of child support is to serve the needs of the children, and that the Rule 90.3 formula is designed to produce a realistic estimate of the non-custodial parent's capacity to contribute to those needs. Ronny M. v. Nanette H., 303 P.3d 392 (Alaska 2013). The Court further recognized in Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), that the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 913(b) is distinct and applicable only when the threshold custody time requirements are met. Because the proposed arrangement here falls within primary physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), the straightforward primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) applies.
Should the Court find that Sarah's summer parenting time, combined with alternating weekends, approaches a level of physical custody that more accurately reflects shared responsibility for the children's direct expenses, the Court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(b) to apply the shared custody formula. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), shared physical custody support is calculated by determining what each parent would owe under Civil Rule 90.3(a), multiplying each figure by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and computing the net difference multiplied by 1.5. Rowen v. Rowen, 963 P.2d 249 (Alaska 1998). However, because the proposed parenting plan does not grant Sarah at least 30 percent of overnights per year, the primary custody formula controls at this time.
The Court also has authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to impute potential income to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. No such imputation is sought here, as both parties are employed in professional capacities.
C. THE MARITAL ESTATE SHOULD BE DIVIDED EQUALLY, AND SARAH COLBY SHOULD ASSUME PRIMARY RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE MARITAL CREDIT CARD DEBT
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires the Court to divide marital property in a just manner without regard to fault, fairly allocating the economic effect of divorce based on enumerated statutory factors. Those factors include: the length of the marriage and station in life of the parties during the marriage; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties, including their educational backgrounds, training, employment skills, and custodial responsibilities; the financial condition of the parties, including the availability and cost of health insurance; the conduct of the parties, including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home or the right to live in it to the party with primary physical custody of the children; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property; and the income-producing capacity of the property and the value of the property at the time of division. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(A)-(I).
The marital estate here consists of the jointly owned family home with approximately $140,000 in equity, two vehicles, a shared savings account, and approximately $28,000 in credit card debt. Ashley requests an equal division of the positive marital assets, which is the presumptive starting point under Alaska law. Marine v. Marine, 957 P.2d 314 (Alaska 1998).
With respect to the family home, the Court should consider the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period, to the party who has primary physical custody of the children. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F). Ashley, as the proposed primary physical custodian of the two minor children ages six and nine, has a compelling interest in maintaining the stability of the family home environment for the children during the school year. The Court may award Ashley the right to reside in the home for a reasonable period or, in the alternative, order that the home be sold and the equity divided equally. Either approach produces a just result consistent with the statutory framework.
With respect to the $28,000 in credit card debt, Ashley requests that the Court assign primary responsibility for this debt to Sarah. This request is grounded in the statutory factors of earning capacity and financial condition. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(A), (C), (D). Sarah earns approximately $95,000 per year as a petroleum engineer, compared to Ashley's approximately $62,000 per year as a registered nurse. The disparity of approximately $33,000 in annual gross income represents a significant difference in financial capacity. Requiring Sarah to assume the marital debt is consistent with a just allocation of the economic effect of dissolution, as required by AS 25.24.160, and does not constitute a penalty for fault but rather a recognition of the parties' differing financial circumstances and capacities.
The Court should also note that the allocation of debt to Sarah, in conjunction with an equal division of marital assets, results in an overall distribution that fairly reflects the statutory factors and does not leave Ashley without the financial resources to meet her own needs and the needs of the children in her primary care. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), reinforces that property division and support serve distinct purposes, and that courts should seek to resolve the financial consequences of divorce through the property division to the greatest extent practicable. Assigning the debt to Sarah in light of her greater earning capacity accomplishes precisely this objective.
D. THE DISSOLUTION PETITION SATISFIES THE STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS OF AS 25.24.200 AND AS 25.24.220
The petition for dissolution satisfies the conditions of AS 25.24.200. Incompatibility of temperament, evidenced by two years of unresolved conflict over financial management and parenting philosophy, has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. The parties have agreed on joint legal custody, and Ashley's proposed primary physical custody arrangement addresses the children's care comprehensively. The petition sets forth the proposed distribution of real and personal property, the allocation of marital debt, and the terms of child support. AS 25.24.200(a)(2)-(4).
At the hearing required by AS 25.24.220, the Court will examine the petitioner and assess whether both parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action, whether the child custody and support agreements are just and in the best interests of the children, and whether the property and debt allocation agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. AS 25.24.220(d)(1)-(3). The Court must apply heightened scrutiny where minor children are involved. AS 25.24.220(h)(3). Ashley welcomes that scrutiny, as the arrangements proposed herein are designed, in their totality, to protect the children's interests and to produce a fair economic outcome for both parties.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Ashley Colby respectfully requests that the Court:
1. Grant the petition for dissolution of the marriage of Ashley Colby and Sarah Colby;
2. Approve the proposed parenting plan granting Ashley Colby primary physical custody of the two minor children during the school week, with Sarah Colby receiving alternating weekend visitation and a six-week extended summer parenting period, and with both parties sharing joint legal custody;
3. Order Sarah Colby to pay child support calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on her adjusted annual income as the non-custodial parent, with application of the 27-percent multiplier applicable to two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), upon submission and review of both parties' Civil Rule 90.3 affidavits;
4. Order an equal division of the marital estate, including the equity in the family home, the two vehicles, and the shared savings account, with appropriate consideration given to the desirability of awarding Ashley Colby the right to reside in the family home during the period of the children's minority pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F); and
5. Order Sarah Colby to assume primary responsibility for the approximately $28,000 in marital credit card debt, in light of her substantially greater earning capacity and the requirements of AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
A just and proper resolution of this matter will serve the best interests of the two minor children and fairly allocate the economic consequences of this dissolution between the parties.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0002)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Alaska Superior Court on the petition of Priya Larsen (hereinafter "Petitioner") for dissolution of her marriage to Colin Larsen (hereinafter "Respondent"). The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and have two minor children, currently ages six and nine. The marriage broke down in early 2023 due to Colin Larsen's prolonged absences for remote work on the North Slope, financial stress, and irreconcilable differences between the parties. Petitioner submits this brief in support of the proposed dissolution agreement, addressing child custody, child support calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3, and equitable distribution of the marital estate, including the family home in Eagle River, joint savings, vehicles, and outstanding marital debts. The parties have reached a tentative agreement on all material terms, and Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court enter a final decree of dissolution consistent with those terms and the requirements of Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Larsen and Colin Larsen were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. Two children were born of the marriage: a nine-year-old child and a six-year-old child, both of whom are minors for purposes of this proceeding. In early 2023, the marriage experienced an irremediable breakdown caused by Colin Larsen's extended and repeated absences from the family home due to remote employment on the North Slope, compounding financial stress, and irreconcilable differences that rendered the continuation of the marital relationship impossible. No reconciliation is anticipated, and both parties acknowledge that incompatibility of temperament has caused the permanent breakdown of the marriage.
Following separation, Priya Larsen has remained in the former marital home located in Eagle River, Alaska, where she has been the primary caregiver for the couple's two children. Colin Larsen now resides in a rented apartment in Wasilla, Alaska. The parties have engaged in good-faith negotiations and have reached a tentative agreement on the major issues of custody, child support, property division, and debt allocation, as described below.
With respect to custody, the parties have agreed to joint legal custody of both minor children. The children will reside primarily with Priya Larsen at the Eagle River home during the school year. Colin Larsen will have parenting time on alternating weekends and for six consecutive weeks during each summer. This arrangement is designed to serve the best interests of the children by maintaining stability in their school environment while preserving a meaningful and consistent relationship with their father.
With respect to child support, Colin Larsen earns approximately $7,800 in gross monthly income. Based on his adjusted annual income and the applicable guidelines, the parties have agreed that Colin Larsen will pay $1,450 per month in child support for the two minor children.
The marital estate consists of the following assets: the Eagle River family home, currently valued at approximately $295,000 with a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, yielding roughly $85,000 in equity; a joint savings account containing approximately $18,000; and two vehicles. Priya Larsen seeks to retain the family home and one vehicle. Colin Larsen will retain the second vehicle and receive an equalized share of the home equity through a deferred buyout arrangement. Outstanding marital debts include approximately $24,000 in combined credit card balances and a personal loan of approximately $9,500, for a total marital debt of approximately $33,500. The parties have agreed to divide these debts equally, with each spouse assuming responsibility for specific accounts to be itemized in the final dissolution decree.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska law provides a streamlined process for the dissolution of marriage by mutual petition. Under AS 25.24.200, a husband and wife together may petition the superior court for dissolution of their marriage if, among other conditions, incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, the parties have agreed on child custody, visitation, and support, and the parties have agreed as to the distribution of all property and the payment of all unpaid obligations. When minor children are involved, the court applies a heightened level of scrutiny to ensure that the agreements reached are just and serve the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.220(h).
For a dissolution petition filed by both spouses, the court may grant a final decree only upon finding, among other things, that the written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are in the best interests of the children and just as between the spouses; that the division of property and allocation of debts are fair and just; and that the spousal maintenance and property division fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution by considering the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). AS 25.24.230(a); AS 25.24.230(b).
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. In cases of primary physical custody, the support award is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources minus certain mandatory and voluntary deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1). Where shared physical custody applies, Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides an alternative formula accounting for each parent's income and the proportion of time each parent has physical custody of the children.
Property division in divorce and dissolution proceedings is governed by AS 25.24.160. The court must divide property in a just manner, considering factors including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity of the property. AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
The Alaska Supreme Court has addressed property division and spousal support in the dissolution context in a line of decisions. In Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), the court addressed the relationship between property division and spousal maintenance and emphasized that these two forms of economic relief serve distinct purposes in fairly allocating the economic effect of dissolution. In Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014), the court examined the degree of scrutiny applicable to pro se dissolution proceedings, particularly where one party appears without counsel, and underscored the importance of ensuring that agreements are voluntary and fair. In Hockema v. Hockema, 403 P.3d 1080 (Alaska 2017), the court affirmed a superior court's discretionary approach to structuring property equalization payments over time where immediate payment would have caused hardship. In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the court affirmed the methodology for calculating adjusted annual income for child support purposes under Civil Rule 90.3, including the treatment of fluctuating income. In Laughlin v. Laughlin, 229 P.3d 1002 (Alaska 2010), the court reaffirmed that child support must be calculated in conformity with Rule 90.3 and that departures from the formula require express findings of unusual circumstances. In Osterkamp v. Stiles, 235 P.3d 178 (Alaska 2010), the court examined equitable considerations in property division, including the treatment of debts and the allocation of credit for contributions made by one party during the marriage.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE DISSOLUTION PETITION SATISFIES ALL STATUTORY PREREQUISITES UNDER AS 25.24.200.
The petition for dissolution in this case satisfies each of the conditions required by AS 25.24.200(a). First, incompatibility of temperament, manifested through Colin Larsen's extended North Slope absences, financial strain, and irreconcilable differences, has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. No prospect of reconciliation exists, and both parties acknowledge the finality of the marital breakdown.
Second, because there are two unmarried minor children of the marriage, both under the age of nineteen, the statute requires that the parties have agreed on custody, visitation, and child support. AS 25.24.200(a)(2). The parties have reached such an agreement: joint legal custody with primary physical residence at the Eagle River home during the school year, alternating weekend parenting time for Colin Larsen, and six weeks of summer parenting time each year. Colin Larsen will pay $1,450 per month in child support. This agreement is consistent with the statutory framework and with the best interests of the children, as further discussed in Section IV.B below.
Third, the parties have agreed on the distribution of all real and personal property, including the family home, the joint savings account, and the two vehicles. The agreement takes into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4), as required by AS 25.24.200(a)(3). The economic effect of dissolution is fairly allocated through the deferred equity buyout, the equal division of the savings account, and the respective vehicle assignments, as further discussed in Section IV.C.
Fourth, the parties have agreed as to the payment of all unpaid marital obligations, including the credit card balances and personal loan totaling approximately $33,500, which are to be divided equally with each party assuming specific accounts to be itemized in the decree. AS 25.24.200(a)(4). This satisfies the final prerequisite for a jointly filed petition.
B. THE PROPOSED CUSTODY AND PARENTING TIME ARRANGEMENT SERVES THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND SATISFIES THE REQUIREMENTS OF AS 25.24.220 AND AS 25.24.230.
When a dissolution petition involves minor children, the court is required to examine whether the written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the spouses and in the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.220(d)(2); AS 25.24.230(b)(2). Where, as here, there is a minor child of the marriage, the court must also apply a heightened level of scrutiny to its review of the parties' agreements. AS 25.24.220(h)(3).
The proposed custody arrangement satisfies this standard. Joint legal custody ensures that both parents will participate in major decisions affecting their children's education, health care, and general welfare. Primary physical residence with Priya Larsen during the school year maintains continuity and stability for the children, who have been residing in the Eagle River home throughout the period of marital discord. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of stability in children's living arrangements, particularly during the school year, as a key component of any custody analysis. Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014).
The alternating weekend parenting schedule and the six-week summer visitation block are consistent with Colin Larsen's current employment situation and geographic location in Wasilla. This schedule ensures that the children maintain a meaningful and consistent bond with their father without disrupting their school schedules or primary caregiving arrangement. The agreement adequately accounts for both parents' circumstances and represents a balanced and child-focused resolution.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically recognizes the desirability of awarding the family home or the right to reside in it to the parent with primary physical custody of the children. The proposed arrangement honors this statutory preference by allowing Priya Larsen and the children to remain in the Eagle River home during the school year, thereby avoiding the disruption and harm that a forced relocation or home sale would cause to the minor children.
AS 25.24.230(b)(2) requires that the agreements on custody, support, and visitation constitute the entire agreement of the parties on those subjects. Petitioner represents that the terms set forth in the dissolution petition and this brief constitute the complete agreement of the parties on all custody, visitation, and support matters. The court is asked to incorporate these terms fully and specifically in the final decree as required by AS 25.24.230(f).
C. THE PROPOSED CHILD SUPPORT AMOUNT IS CONSISTENT WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3 AND IS SUPPORTED BY THE RECORD.
Child support in this case is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Because the children will reside primarily with Priya Larsen during the school year, with Colin Larsen exercising alternating weekend and summer parenting time, this matter is appropriately analyzed under the primary physical custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), adjusted annual income is "the parent's total income from all sources minus" certain enumerated deductions, including mandatory taxes, retirement contributions within specified limits, work-related child care expenses, and health insurance premiums. Colin Larsen's gross monthly income is approximately $7,800, yielding a gross annual income of approximately $93,600. After applicable deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), the adjusted annual income figure serves as the basis for the support calculation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), the applicable support percentage for two children is 27 percent of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), that adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) must be calculated based on the parent's total income from all sources, reduced by the listed deductions, and that this calculation drives the resulting support obligation. The proposed monthly support amount of $1,450 is consistent with the application of Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to Colin Larsen's income, accounting for reasonable deductions, and Petitioner submits that this figure accurately reflects the applicable formula.
Departures from the Civil Rule 90.3 formula are permitted only upon a finding of unusual circumstances and require express written findings. Laughlin v. Laughlin, 229 P.3d 1002 (Alaska 2010). The proposed support amount of $1,450 per month does not represent a departure from the formula; rather, it reflects a straightforward application of the guidelines to Colin Larsen's income. No unusual circumstances exist that would justify deviation from the formula amount.
The court should also be aware that Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) permits an extended visitation credit of up to 75 percent for periods of extended visitation exceeding 27 consecutive days. Colin Larsen's six-week summer parenting block may qualify for such a credit, and Petitioner requests that if any credit is applied, it be reflected expressly in the dissolution decree. Civil Rule 90.3(b) would govern the child support calculation if the court were to determine that the parenting time arrangement constitutes shared physical custody; however, Petitioner submits that the primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) is the applicable framework given that the children's principal residence during the school year is with Priya Larsen.
The child support provisions in the dissolution petition have been reviewed in light of the policy goals articulated by the Alaska Supreme Court in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), which recognized that the Civil Rule 90.3 formula is designed to ensure adequate support for children consistent with each parent's ability to pay and to produce predictable and consistent outcomes. The proposed support amount serves both of these purposes.
D. THE PROPOSED DIVISION OF MARITAL PROPERTY AND ALLOCATION OF DEBTS IS FAIR, JUST, AND CONSISTENT WITH AS 25.24.160 AND AS 25.24.230.
The division of marital property must be "in a just manner" and must "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" by being based on consideration of the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The proposed property division satisfies this standard.
The marital estate consists of the following assets:
1. The Eagle River family home, valued at approximately $295,000, subject to a mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, yielding net equity of approximately $85,000;
2. A joint savings account containing approximately $18,000; and
3. Two vehicles.
Priya Larsen will retain the family home and one vehicle. She will assume the existing mortgage obligation. Colin Larsen will retain the second vehicle. To equalize the parties' respective shares of the home equity, Colin Larsen will receive a deferred buyout payment representing his equitable share of the approximately $85,000 in home equity. The timing and structure of the buyout are to be set forth in the dissolution decree, consistent with the court's equitable discretion to structure payments over time where immediate payment would cause hardship. Hockema v. Hockema, 403 P.3d 1080 (Alaska 2017).
The joint savings account of approximately $18,000 is to be divided equally between the parties, with each receiving approximately $9,000. This equal division is straightforward and appropriate given that the savings account represents liquid marital assets accumulated during the marriage without any significant separate property contribution by either party.
With respect to marital debts, the approximately $24,000 in credit card balances and the $9,500 personal loan, totaling approximately $33,500, are to be divided equally, with each party assuming approximately $16,750 in obligations through responsibility for specific accounts to be itemized in the final decree. This equal division of debt is consistent with the statutory requirement that the parties agree to the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred during the marriage. AS 25.24.200(a)(4). It is also consistent with the principle, affirmed in Osterkamp v. Stiles, 235 P.3d 178 (Alaska 2010), that equitable considerations govern the allocation of marital debts and that the court should credit each party appropriately for debts assumed in the division.
The factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4) support the proposed division. The parties were married for approximately nine years, a marriage of moderate length during which both parties contributed to the marital estate. The parties are of similar age and general health. While Colin Larsen's North Slope employment provides a higher current income, Priya Larsen has assumed the primary caregiving role for the minor children, which has affected her earning capacity and employment flexibility. The Eagle River home is the children's primary residence, and AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly recognizes the desirability of awarding the family home to the parent with primary physical custody. The deferred buyout structure is appropriate given the current mortgage balance and the practical impossibility of a forced sale, which would be contrary to the children's best interests.
AS 25.24.230(a)(3) requires that the division of property "fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution" and take into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). The proposed division accomplishes this objective. Priya Larsen receives the family home, stability for herself and the children, and one vehicle. Colin Larsen receives the second vehicle, an equal share of the joint savings account, and a deferred equalization payment representing his share of the home equity. The equal allocation of marital debts ensures that neither party is disproportionately burdened by obligations incurred during the marriage. The overall arrangement represents a fair and equitable distribution of the marital estate and fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution between the parties.
Because no spousal maintenance is sought by either party, the court need not conduct a separate analysis of the factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(2). Petitioner notes, however, that the property division has been structured with awareness of those factors, including the parties' earning capacities, the length of the marriage, and the custodial responsibilities Priya Larsen will carry going forward. The Alaska Supreme Court in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), observed the preference in Alaska courts for resolving financial concerns through property division where possible, and the proposed arrangement is consistent with that preference.
E. THE COURT SHOULD APPLY HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY AND FIND THAT THE AGREEMENTS ARE JUST AND VOLUNTARILY ENTERED.
Because minor children are involved in this dissolution proceeding, AS 25.24.220(h)(3) requires the court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny in examining the parties' written agreements. Under AS 25.24.220(i), upon applying heightened scrutiny the court must determine that the agreements are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that the agreements concerning custody, support, and visitation are in the best interests of the children.
Petitioner respectfully submits that the agreements in this case satisfy that standard. The custody and parenting time arrangement prioritizes the children's stability, educational continuity, and relationship with both parents. The child support amount has been calculated in conformity with Civil Rule 90.3. The property division fairly allocates the marital estate in a manner that accounts for the children's need to remain in the family home, Colin Larsen's equitable interest in the accumulated home equity, and the equal sharing of marital debts. All agreements were reached voluntarily through good-faith negotiation, without coercion or duress, and each party understands the nature and consequences of the dissolution.
AS 25.24.230(b)(4) requires a finding that the spousal maintenance and division of property fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. AS 25.24.230(b)(5) requires a finding that each spouse entered the agreement voluntarily and free from the coercion of another person. Petitioner affirms both conditions. The written agreements constitute the entire agreement between the parties on all subjects addressed therein, as required by AS 25.24.230(b)(2) and (b)(3).
The court is asked to incorporate all terms of the parties' agreement fully and specifically in the final decree of dissolution, consistent with AS 25.24.230(f), which requires the court to "fully and specifically set out in the decree the written agreements of the spouses and shall order the performance of those written agreements." The decree should also specify whether child support payments are to be made through the child support services agency.
F. THE PROPOSED DISSOLUTION IS PROCEDURALLY PROPER UNDER AS 25.24.220 AND AS 25.24.250.
The Department of Law, in cooperation with the Alaska Court System, is required by AS 25.24.250 to prepare forms and instructions for use by persons seeking dissolution of their marriage. Petitioner has utilized the appropriate forms and has endeavored to ensure that the petition and supporting materials conform to all applicable requirements of the Alaska Rules of Civil Procedure. The dissolution petition constitutes the entire agreement between the parties, as required by AS 25.24.250(c).
The hearing required by AS 25.24.220(a) should be scheduled in accordance with the Alaska Rules of Civil Procedure. Both parties are prepared to attend the hearing personally, as required by AS 25.24.220(b) for a jointly filed petition. Petitioner requests that the court conduct its examination of the parties in compliance with AS 25.24.220(d) and, given the presence of minor children, with the heightened scrutiny required by AS 25.24.220(h) and (i).
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Priya Larsen respectfully requests that the Alaska Superior Court:
1. Find that the conditions for dissolution under AS 25.24.200(a) have been met, including the irremediable breakdown of the marriage due to incompatibility of temperament;
2. Find that the written agreements concerning joint legal custody, primary physical residence with Priya Larsen, alternating weekend and summer parenting time for Colin Larsen, and child support of $1,450 per month are just between the parties and in the best interests of the two minor children;
3. Find that the proposed division of the marital estate, including the deferred equity buyout of the Eagle River home, equal division of the joint savings account, respective vehicle assignments, and equal allocation of marital debts, fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution in accordance with AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and AS 25.24.230;
4. Find that all agreements were entered into voluntarily, without coercion or duress, and constitute the entire agreement between the parties;
5. Apply the heightened level of scrutiny required by AS 25.24.220(h) and (i) and find that all agreements satisfy that standard; and
6. Enter a final decree of dissolution that fully and specifically sets out all written agreements of the parties, designates responsibility for specific marital debt accounts, and specifies the child support payment mechanism, consistent with AS 25.24.230(f).
Petitioner submits that the proposed dissolution agreement is fair, just, and fully consistent with Alaska law, and respectfully requests that the Court grant the petition and enter the final decree of dissolution.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0003)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Nakamura respectfully petitions this Court to establish a formal custody and parenting plan order governing the care of his four-year-old daughter, Lily Nakamura. Marcus and Michael Nakamura were in a committed romantic relationship for approximately three years before separating in early 2023. The parties never married. Since the separation, Lily has resided primarily with Marcus in Anchorage, while Michael exercises informal, unscheduled parenting time on a rotating basis. No court order currently governs custody, legal decision-making authority, or any parenting schedule for Lily.
The absence of a formal custody order has created increasing instability in Lily's day-to-day life. Without clear, enforceable rights and responsibilities, both parents are left without guidance on scheduling, decision-making, medical care, education, and a host of other matters that directly affect Lily's well-being. Marcus brings this petition not to deprive Michael of a relationship with Lily, but to ensure that Lily enjoys the stability, consistency, and security that a child her age requires. A formal parenting plan will provide both parents with defined rights and will protect Lily's long-term interests.
This Court has jurisdiction and authority under AS 25.20.060 to resolve this custody dispute and to enter an order based on the best interests of the child. Marcus respectfully requests that the Court award him primary physical custody of Lily, with a structured and predictable schedule of parenting time for Michael, and that the Court address legal custody in a manner consistent with the parties' demonstrated ability, or inability, to communicate and cooperate.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Nakamura and Michael Nakamura began a committed romantic relationship in approximately 2020. Their daughter, Lily Nakamura, was born during the relationship and is presently four years old. The parties were never married. Their relationship broke down due to irreconcilable differences, and they separated in early 2023.
Following the separation, Lily remained in the primary care of Marcus at his residence in Anchorage, Alaska. Marcus has been the consistent, day-to-day caregiver for Lily since the separation. He arranges and attends Lily's medical appointments, manages her daily routines, and provides her with a stable home environment. Marcus has fostered a relationship between Lily and Michael throughout the post-separation period and does not seek to eliminate Michael's involvement in Lily's life.
Michael exercises parenting time with Lily on an informal, unscheduled, and rotating basis. There is no written agreement, court order, or parenting plan in place to govern when Michael may have parenting time, for how long, or under what conditions. This arrangement has become increasingly unpredictable. The lack of structure has made it difficult for Marcus to plan consistently for Lily's care, education, and medical needs. Lily is approaching school age, and the absence of a stable, court-ordered schedule poses a growing risk to her educational continuity and overall well-being.
No prior court has entered any order addressing custody, legal decision-making authority, parenting time, or child support for Lily. Marcus now petitions this Court to enter a comprehensive custody order that will provide Lily with the stability and predictability she needs and that will give both parents clear, enforceable rights and responsibilities.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska Statute AS 25.20.060 grants the superior court authority to resolve custody disputes between parents and directs that custody be awarded on the basis of the best interests of the child. In determining the best interests of the child, the court is required to consider all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Neither parent is entitled to a preference in the awarding of custody under AS 25.20.060(b).
Alaska Statute AS 25.24.150(c) sets forth a non-exhaustive list of factors the court must consider when determining a child's best interests. Those factors include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form one; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence of substance abuse; and other pertinent factors.
During the pendency of a custody proceeding, AS 25.20.070 provides that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents, unless such access is shown to be detrimental to the child's welfare or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) applies.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that stability and continuity in a child's living arrangement are paramount considerations in custody proceedings. In West v. Lawson, 951 P.2d 1200 (Alaska 1998), the court emphasized a strong preference for preserving stability in children's lives and avoiding repeated custody disruptions. Similarly, in Havel v. Havel, 216 P.3d 1148 (Alaska 2009), the court recognized that the child's need for stability and continuity is a central concern in custody determinations. The Alaska Supreme Court has further recognized that unnecessary litigation and conflict are counterproductive for all parties, particularly for children, and that arrangements providing consistency of care best serve a child's interests. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011).
Joint legal custody is generally preferred under Alaska law, but it is appropriate only when the parents can communicate and cooperate in the child's best interest. Peterson v. Swarthout, 214 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2009). Where the parents demonstrate difficulty cooperating on major decisions, sole legal custody may be warranted.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THIS COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH A FORMAL CUSTODY ORDER BECAUSE THE CURRENT INFORMAL ARRANGEMENT FAILS TO PROTECT LILY'S BEST INTERESTS.
The absence of any court order governing Lily's custody is itself a source of instability that undermines her best interests. Alaska Statute AS 25.20.060 directs that when there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. The current arrangement, characterized by unscheduled, rotating, and informal parenting time, provides no enforceable framework for either parent and no predictable structure for Lily.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(5), the court is required to consider "the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity." Lily has now lived primarily with Marcus in Anchorage for over two years since the separation. That continuity of care is a significant factor weighing in favor of confirming Marcus as the primary physical custodian. The Alaska Supreme Court in West v. Lawson, 951 P.2d 1200 (Alaska 1998), articulated a strong judicial preference for maintaining stability in children's lives and avoiding disruptions to established arrangements. Formalizing the current primary care arrangement through a court order is the most direct means of preserving the stability Lily has known since the separation.
Moreover, Lily is approaching school age, and the absence of a defined parenting schedule will soon create concrete logistical problems related to enrollment, attendance, and educational continuity. A court-ordered parenting plan that addresses the school year, holidays, vacations, and weekday and weekend time with each parent is necessary to prevent future conflict and to give Lily the routine she needs to thrive.
B. THE BEST INTERESTS FACTORS UNDER AS 25.24.150(c) SUPPORT AWARDING PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY TO MARCUS.
The factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) collectively support awarding primary physical custody of Lily to Marcus, with a structured schedule of parenting time for Michael.
1. Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs of the Child.
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) requires the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Lily is a four-year-old child at a formative stage of development. Children of her age benefit most from consistent caregiving, predictable daily routines, and a stable home environment. Marcus has provided exactly that environment since the separation. He has managed Lily's daily physical care, arranged her medical appointments, and ensured that her social and emotional needs have been met in a consistent setting.
2. Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Child's Needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) directs the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. Marcus has demonstrated both the capability and the commitment to serve as Lily's primary caregiver over the more than two years since separation. He has been the constant, day-to-day presence in her life. Michael's parenting time, while meaningful, has been informal and unscheduled, reflecting a pattern that has not provided the same degree of sustained, predictable involvement. This distinction does not diminish the importance of Michael's relationship with Lily, but it does bear on which parent has demonstrated the sustained capacity to serve as primary caregiver.
3. Love and Affection Between the Child and Each Parent.
AS 25.24.150(c)(4) requires the court to consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. Both Marcus and Michael share a loving relationship with Lily, and Marcus does not dispute that Lily loves her father Michael and benefits from time with him. This factor supports structuring a parenting plan that preserves and nurtures Lily's bond with both parents, rather than eliminating or sharply limiting either parent's involvement. The court should award Marcus primary physical custody while providing Michael with regular, structured, and meaningful parenting time.
4. Length of Time in a Stable Environment and Continuity.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) instructs the court to weigh the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. As discussed above, Lily has resided primarily with Marcus for over two years. Disrupting that arrangement without a compelling countervailing reason would be contrary to the weight of Alaska authority emphasizing the value of continuity. In Havel v. Havel, 216 P.3d 1148 (Alaska 2009), the Alaska Supreme Court emphasized this principle in reviewing a custody schedule modification. In West v. Lawson, 951 P.2d 1200 (Alaska 1998), the court similarly recognized the importance of avoiding disruption to established care arrangements.
5. Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Child.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the court to consider each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. Marcus has consistently facilitated Michael's informal parenting time since the separation, demonstrating his commitment to ensuring that Lily maintains a relationship with Michael. Marcus's decision to petition for a formal order, rather than seek to limit Michael's access, reflects his understanding that Lily benefits from both parents' involvement. The court should credit this demonstrated willingness when evaluating the best interests factors.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Andrea C. v. Marcus K., 355 P.3d 521 (Alaska 2015), noted that the willingness of each parent to support the child's relationship with the other parent is a significant consideration in custody determinations, particularly where the children benefit from stability and both parental relationships.
6. Other Pertinent Factors.
AS 25.24.150(c)(9) permits the court to consider other factors it deems pertinent. Lily's approaching school age is a pertinent consideration. The transition to formal schooling will require consistent attendance, a defined primary residence for enrollment purposes, and a structured parenting schedule that minimizes disruption to school days and routines. A formal primary custody designation with Marcus is necessary to facilitate that transition in the most stable and child-centered manner possible.
C. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY IF THE PARENTS CAN COOPERATE, OR SOLE LEGAL CUSTODY TO MARCUS IF COOPERATION IS NOT FEASIBLE.
Legal custody governs major decision-making for the child on matters including education, healthcare, and religious upbringing. Joint legal custody is the preferred outcome under Alaska law when both parents can communicate and cooperate effectively in the child's best interest. Peterson v. Swarthout, 214 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2009). Marcus does not presently oppose joint legal custody if the parties can establish a workable framework for communication and cooperation.
However, if the record at hearing demonstrates that the parties' communication has broken down to a degree that makes joint decision-making unworkable, the court should award sole legal custody to Marcus as the parent who has been the consistent primary caregiver and decision-maker for Lily since the separation. The focus of the legal custody determination must remain on what arrangement best serves Lily's interests rather than on vindicating either parent's preferences. AS 25.20.060(b) confirms that neither parent is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody.
D. THE COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH A STRUCTURED PARENTING SCHEDULE THAT PROVIDES LILY WITH FREQUENT AND CONTINUING CONTACT WITH MICHAEL.
Alaska Statute AS 25.20.060(c) provides that the court may award shared custody if it is in the best interests of the child, and that any such award shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Even if this Court determines that primary physical custody with Marcus is most appropriate, the parenting plan should include a regular and predictable schedule of parenting time for Michael that gives Lily meaningful, ongoing contact with him.
A well-structured parenting schedule, specifying regular weekday or weekend time, holiday allocations, vacation periods, and a mechanism for resolving scheduling conflicts, will serve Lily's interests far better than continued reliance on an informal, unscheduled arrangement. In Rooney v. Rooney, 914 P.2d 212 (Alaska 1996), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized the importance of structured arrangements that give both parents defined, predictable access to the child, particularly when the parents have demonstrated difficulty reaching voluntary agreements.
AS 25.20.070 reinforces that during the pendency of these proceedings, Lily should have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents, absent a showing of detriment to her welfare. Marcus does not seek to limit Michael's access during the proceedings. Rather, Marcus seeks to formalize and make predictable the access that Michael already exercises, so that Lily is not subject to the uncertainty and instability of an ad hoc arrangement.
E. THE COURT SHOULD ADDRESS CHILD SUPPORT IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3.
Because this proceeding will establish a formal custody arrangement, the Court should also address child support. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), where one parent has primary physical custody, child support is calculated based on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage for the number of children. If the Court were to determine that a shared physical custody arrangement is appropriate, Civil Rule 90.3(b) would govern the calculation, using each parent's income and the percentage of time each parent exercises physical custody.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), shared physical custody exists for purposes of the rule when a child resides with a parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30, but no more than 70, percent of the year. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), primary physical custody exists when the child resides with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. The court's custody determination will directly govern which support calculation methodology applies.
Marcus respectfully requests that the Court order child support in an amount consistent with Civil Rule 90.3 based on the custody arrangement established at hearing and each parent's verified income.
V. CONCLUSION
The present informal custody arrangement for four-year-old Lily Nakamura is inadequate to protect her long-term well-being and provides neither parent with clear, enforceable rights or responsibilities. Marcus Nakamura has served as Lily's consistent primary caregiver since the parties' separation in early 2023 and now petitions this Court to formalize that arrangement through a comprehensive custody and parenting plan order.
For the foregoing reasons, Marcus Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Enter an order awarding Marcus Nakamura primary physical custody of Lily Nakamura, consistent with her best interests under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150(c);
2. Award joint legal custody to both parents if the Court finds that cooperation is feasible, or sole legal custody to Marcus if cooperation is not feasible, consistent with Lily's best interests;
3. Establish a detailed, written parenting plan specifying Michael's regular parenting time, holiday schedule, and vacation periods, ensuring Lily has frequent and continuing contact with Michael consistent with AS 25.20.060(c);
4. Order child support in an amount calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a), based on the primary physical custody arrangement and verified income of both parties; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the best interests of Lily Nakamura.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0004)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Nakamura ("Father") brings this petition to establish legal and physical custody of his four-year-old daughter, Lily Nakamura ("Lily"), born during his relationship with Sarah Nakamura ("Mother"). The parties were never married and have no existing custody, visitation, or child support order from any court. Since the parties' separation in February 2024, Lily has resided primarily with Mother at her Anchorage apartment while Father has exercised informal weekend parenting time. Mother has now notified Father of her intention to relocate Lily to Juneau within 60 days for employment purposes. Because no formal order governs Lily's custody, Father has no legal mechanism to prevent or challenge that relocation, to enforce his parenting time, or to ensure his continued meaningful involvement in Lily's life.
Father respectfully requests that this Court exercise its jurisdiction under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.30.300, make an initial determination of legal and physical custody of Lily in the best interests of the child, and issue an order that preserves Lily's relationship with both parents to the greatest degree practical. Given the urgency created by Mother's intended relocation, Father further requests expedited consideration of this matter.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
A. The Parties and the Child
Marcus Nakamura and Sarah Nakamura were never married. They cohabited in Anchorage, Alaska, for approximately three years and are the biological parents of Lily Nakamura, who is approximately four years of age. Lily was born in Anchorage and has resided in Anchorage for the entirety of her life.
B. The Separation and Informal Custody Arrangement
The parties ended their relationship in February 2024 following a period of mutual conflict and a breakdown in communication that rendered continued cohabitation untenable. Following the separation, Lily began residing primarily with Mother at Mother's apartment in Anchorage. Father has exercised parenting time on weekends on an informal, cooperative basis. No written parenting plan, no court order, and no administrative agreement of any kind has been executed governing legal custody, physical custody, visitation, or child support with respect to Lily. The arrangement that has existed since February 2024 is entirely voluntary and has no legal force.
C. Father's Relationship with Lily
Throughout Lily's life, Father has been an engaged and loving parent. He has maintained consistent contact with Lily and has exercised his informal weekend parenting time reliably since the separation. Lily shares a close bond with Father and has benefited from his regular presence. Father is capable of and desires to meet Lily's physical, emotional, mental, and social needs.
D. Mother's Announced Relocation
Mother has recently informed Father that she intends to relocate with Lily to Juneau, Alaska, within 60 days to pursue a new employment opportunity. She has made this announcement without any agreement from Father and without any court order authorizing such relocation. Because no formal custody order exists, Father currently has no legal mechanism to prevent the relocation, to enforce his parenting time, or to seek modification of any prior order. If the relocation occurs before a custody order is entered, Father faces the prospect of losing the close, frequent contact with Lily that Lily has enjoyed throughout her life. Father therefore petitions this Court to establish custody on an expedited basis.
E. Jurisdiction
Lily has resided in Anchorage, Alaska, continuously since her birth. Alaska is therefore Lily's home state within the meaning of AS 25.30.300. No other court has issued a custody determination concerning Lily, and no proceeding is pending in any other state.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060, when there is a dispute over child custody between parents who have never been married, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the custody matter. The court is required to award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child, considering all relevant factors including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Under AS 25.20.060(b), neither parent is entitled to any preference in the awarding of custody, regardless of the question of the child's legitimacy. The court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined to be in the best interests of the child, and any such award must assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c).
The factors the court must consider in determining the best interests of the child under AS 25.24.150(c) include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference, if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse directly affects the child's well-being; and any other factors the court considers pertinent.
Under AS 25.20.070, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child considering the factors under AS 25.24.150(c), or unless the rebuttable presumption of AS 25.24.150(g) is present, "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody under AS 25.20.060 - 25.20.130."
This Court has jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination because Alaska is Lily's home state on the date of commencement of this proceeding. AS 25.30.300(a)(1). No other court has made or is positioned to make a custody determination concerning Lily.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THIS COURT HAS JURISDICTION TO MAKE AN INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION CONCERNING LILY
Before reaching the merits of a custody dispute, a court must confirm that it has subject matter jurisdiction to act. AS 25.30.300 governs jurisdiction for initial child custody determinations. Under AS 25.30.300(a)(1), a court of this state has jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination if "this state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding." The statute further provides that the provisions of AS 25.30.300(a) "are the exclusive jurisdictional bases for making a child custody determination by a court of this state," and that physical presence of a party or a child is neither necessary nor sufficient to make such a determination, though it is relevant to the home state analysis. AS 25.30.300(b)-(c).
Lily has lived in Anchorage, Alaska, for the entirety of her life. She was born in Anchorage and has resided there continuously through the date of this filing. Alaska is unquestionably Lily's home state. No other court has issued any custody order or has a proceeding pending with respect to Lily. Accordingly, this Court has jurisdiction under AS 25.30.300(a)(1) to make the initial custody determination that the parties have not previously sought and that is now urgently required by the circumstances.
B. BECAUSE THIS IS AN INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION, THE COURT MUST DECIDE CUSTODY SOLELY ON THE BASIS OF LILY'S BEST INTERESTS, WITH NO PRESUMPTION IN FAVOR OF EITHER PARENT
Under AS 25.20.060(a), in a dispute over child custody, the court "shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child." Critically, AS 25.20.060(b) expressly provides that neither parent is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody, regardless of the question of the child's legitimacy. This provision eliminates any presumption in favor of the parent who currently has de facto primary custody by virtue of an informal post-separation arrangement. The fact that Lily has resided primarily with Mother since February 2024 is not a reason to award Mother primary custody going forward; it is one circumstance among many that the Court must weigh.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that custody determinations must be grounded in the totality of the best interests factors rather than in any threshold presumption favoring one parent. In Carle v. Carle, 503 P.2d 1050 (Alaska 1972), the court recognized the foundational principle that custody must be governed by the child's best interests, not by status or default arrangements. In Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), the court affirmed that a trial court must undertake a thorough best interests analysis before settling on a custody arrangement, even where one parent has exercised greater day-to-day care. In Jaymot v. Skillings-Donat, 216 P.3d 534 (Alaska 2009), the court reaffirmed that the trial court is charged with weighing all relevant factors and that its role includes judging the credibility of witnesses and weighing conflicting evidence in light of the child's welfare. Father respectfully submits that a careful application of those principles here supports the relief he seeks.
C. THE STATUTORY BEST INTERESTS FACTORS SUPPORT AN AWARD OF JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY AND A MEANINGFUL PHYSICAL CUSTODY SCHEDULE FOR FATHER
1. Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs of the Child (AS 25.24.150(c)(1))
Lily is four years old, an age at which her developmental well-being depends on stability, predictability, and the reliable presence of both parents in her life. Her physical and emotional needs are best served by a custody arrangement that provides consistent routines and meaningful contact with Father, who has been a present and engaged parent throughout her life. A formal custody order providing Father with regular, protected parenting time will serve Lily's developmental needs far better than the current informal arrangement, which provides no protection against disruption.
2. Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet Lily's Needs (AS 25.24.150(c)(2))
Father has demonstrated both the capability and the desire to meet Lily's needs. He has exercised his informal weekend parenting time consistently since the February 2024 separation. He has maintained a close relationship with Lily and has shown commitment to her well-being. Under AS 25.20.060(b), his status as an unmarried father creates no disadvantage. The statute is clear that neither parent is entitled to preference, and Father's engagement with Lily over her lifetime demonstrates that he is fully capable of sharing legal and physical custody.
3. Love and Affection Between Lily and Each Parent (AS 25.24.150(c)(4))
Lily shares a close, loving bond with Father. He has been a consistent presence in her life, and her emotional attachment to him is a product of the regular contact they have maintained since her birth. The preservation of this bond is a key consideration in any best interests analysis. In Jayda Roman v. Cleveland Karren, 461 P.3d 1252 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized the importance of a child's emotional attachment to a parent who has maintained meaningful involvement in the child's life. Awarding Father a structured, court-ordered parenting schedule will protect this bond and ensure that Lily continues to benefit from Father's love and involvement.
4. Stability and Continuity (AS 25.24.150(c)(5))
Lily has lived her entire life in Anchorage, Alaska. She has established connections in Anchorage, including her relationship with Father and with members of Father's family and community. Allowing Mother to relocate Lily to Juneau without a court order and without Father's consent would sever these connections abruptly and deprive Lily of the continuity and stability that this factor is designed to protect. Alaska courts have recognized continuity of environment as an important consideration. In Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011), the court acknowledged the importance of stability and continuity in custody arrangements to a child's welfare. A formal custody order entered before any relocation occurs will provide the structure needed to protect Lily's stability regardless of where each parent ultimately resides.
5. Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Child (AS 25.24.150(c)(6))
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the court must consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. Mother's unilateral announcement of an imminent relocation, made without consulting Father and without any legal process, raises concerns about her willingness to prioritize Lily's relationship with Father. Father, by contrast, has cooperated with the informal custody arrangement since the separation and has not sought to exclude Mother from Lily's life. This factor weighs in favor of Father receiving meaningful legal authority over decisions affecting Lily's residence and education.
In Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed the significance of a parent's willingness to foster the other parent's relationship with the child, noting that a parent who is manipulative or places emotional priorities above the child's best interests may warrant less deference on this factor. Father submits that Mother's unilateral relocation announcement, without any discussion with Father or any effort to preserve Lily's relationship with him, is relevant evidence on this factor.
6. Absence of Domestic Violence, Substance Abuse, or Child Neglect (AS 25.24.150(c)(7) and (c)(8))
There is no history of domestic violence by Father against Mother or Lily, no history of child abuse or neglect by Father, and no evidence of substance abuse by Father that affects Lily's well-being. The rebuttable presumption in AS 25.24.150(g) therefore does not apply to Father, and no restriction on his custodial rights is warranted on those grounds. Father's home is a safe and appropriate environment for Lily.
D. FATHER IS ENTITLED TO JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY AND A MEANINGFUL PHYSICAL CUSTODY SCHEDULE UNDER AS 25.20.060(c)
Father seeks an award of joint legal custody, giving both parents equal authority over major decisions affecting Lily's health, education, and welfare. He further seeks a physical custody schedule that provides him with a substantial and regular share of parenting time. AS 25.20.060(c) authorizes the court to award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined to be in the best interests of the child, and requires that any such award "assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible."
Alaska courts have recognized that shared physical custody arrangements serve the best interests of children when both parents are capable and willing to participate in the child's upbringing. In Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court examined the proper framework for custody modification where parties had previously exercised a shared arrangement, reaffirming that frequent and continuing contact with each parent is a goal embedded in Alaska's custody statutes. In Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), the court affirmed a week-on, week-off shared physical custody arrangement as consistent with the child's best interests where both parents were capable and engaged. Father submits that a similar arrangement, or at minimum a schedule providing him with substantial parenting time, is appropriate here.
Under AS 25.20.070, during the pendency of proceedings the child "shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents" unless such access is shown to be detrimental to the child's welfare or unless the domestic violence presumption of AS 25.24.150(g) is present. Neither condition applies here. Father therefore requests that the Court enter an interim order during the pendency of this proceeding ensuring Lily's continued equal access to both parents.
E. THE COURT SHOULD ENTER AN INTERIM PROTECTIVE ORDER PRESERVING THE STATUS QUO AND PROHIBITING RELOCATION PENDING RESOLUTION OF THIS PETITION
Mother's announced intention to relocate Lily to Juneau within 60 days creates an urgent circumstance that requires the Court's prompt attention. Because no custody order currently exists, there is no legal mechanism preventing Mother from relocating Lily and effectively extinguishing Father's parenting time before this Court can act. The equities strongly favor the entry of an interim order restraining any relocation of Lily outside the Anchorage area until a formal custody order has been entered.
