Requiring Brandon to pay $1,400 per month is consistent with his elevated income, consistent with the children's needs, and consistent with the equitable sharing of financial responsibility that Alaska law requires.
As the court recognized in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the primary purpose of Rule 90.3 is to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay. That purpose would be disserved by leaving in place a support order premised on income and circumstances that no longer reflect reality. The requested modification is a straightforward application of the guideline to current facts, supported by the additional equitable considerations arising from the child's diagnosis.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Tomas Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court enter an order modifying the existing child support obligation to reflect Brandon Nakamura's current annual income of $89,000, the children's increased financial needs arising from the younger child's developmental disability, and the applicable Alaska child support guidelines, resulting in a revised monthly support obligation of approximately $1,400. Tomas further requests that the Court make any additional findings necessary to support a variance under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) to address the therapeutic and specialized care expenses not captured by the standard guideline calculation, and that the modified order take effect as of the date of filing of this petition.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0010)
I. INTRODUCTION
Jacob Bergstrom, the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children, moves this Court for an upward modification of the existing child support order. The current order requires Michael Bergstrom to pay $850 per month, an amount based on his 2021 annual income of approximately $62,000. Since the entry of that order, Michael's income has increased substantially, to approximately $94,000 per year, representing a change of more than 15 percent from the income figure underlying the existing order. Jacob's income and custodial responsibilities have remained materially unchanged. Applying the formula set forth in Civil Rule 901(a), the current support obligation is now significantly lower than the amount Michael would be required to pay based on his present income, and upward modification is warranted as a matter of both law and equity.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jacob Bergstrom and Michael Bergstrom were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the court entered a child support order requiring Michael to pay $850 per month. That figure was calculated based on Michael's annual salary of approximately $62,000 as a commercial electrician and Jacob's part-time income of approximately $24,000 per year. The order reflected the parties' custody arrangement, under which Jacob serves as the primary physical custodian of the two minor children.
Since entry of the 2021 order, Michael received a substantial promotion and his annual salary has increased to approximately $94,000. Jacob remains the primary physical custodian of the parties' two children, providing care for approximately 280 out of 365 overnights per year. Jacob's income has remained at approximately $24,000 per year. No modification to the child support order has been sought or granted since its entry in 2021. The current monthly obligation of $850 no longer reflects Michael's financial capacity to support the children, and the discrepancy between the existing order and the amount required under Civil Rule 90.3 is substantial.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170, after entry of a final judgment, the court may, upon motion of either party, modify so much of the judgment as provides for the maintenance of minor children. A modification of child support requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). Civil Rule 988(a) governs the calculation of child support when one parent holds primary physical custody, and provides that a material change of circumstances is presumed when the support obligation as calculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 536 P.3d 438 (Alaska 2017).
A significant increase in the income of the non-custodial parent is a recognized basis for modification. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018); Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989). Courts have consistently held that child support calculations must reflect actual income, and a trial court presumptively does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. MICHAEL'S SUBSTANTIAL INCOME INCREASE CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES.
Since the entry of the 2021 child support order, Michael's annual income has increased from approximately $62,000 to approximately $94,000, an increase of roughly $32,000, or approximately 52 percent. This income change plainly satisfies the threshold for a presumptive material change in circumstances. As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), a material change of circumstances is presumed when child support as recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3 differs from the outstanding order by more than 15 percent. Here, that threshold is exceeded by a considerable margin.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a change in one or both parents' level of income constitutes a material change of circumstances sufficient to justify modification of a child support order. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). Similarly, in Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989), the court affirmed that an increase in the non-custodial parent's income justified upward modification of child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3. The facts here squarely support the same conclusion.
B. THE CORRECT CHILD SUPPORT AMOUNT MUST BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON MICHAEL'S CURRENT ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) sets forth the method for calculating child support when one parent holds primary physical custody. The rule provides that the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which for two children is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Adjusted annual income under the rule means the parent's total income from all sources, reduced by mandatory deductions including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A).
Michael's gross annual income is now approximately $94,000. After accounting for applicable mandatory deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), Michael's adjusted annual income will be determined by the Court based on documentation of his actual withholdings and deductions. Applying the 27 percent multiplier from Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to his adjusted annual income will yield a monthly child support obligation substantially higher than the current order of $850 per month. As the Alaska Supreme Court stated in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), a court presumptively does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3. Jacob respectfully submits that the Court should calculate the new obligation in strict accordance with the rule.
C. JACOB'S CUSTODIAL ROLE AS PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODIAN IS UNCHANGED AND SUPPORTS APPLICATION OF CIVIL RULE 90.3(a).
Jacob has continuously served as the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children throughout the period since the entry of the divorce decree. Jacob provides care for approximately 280 out of 365 overnights per year, well above the threshold required for primary custody status under Civil Rule 90.3(f). This custodial arrangement has not changed since the original order was entered in 2021. Because Jacob holds primary physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(a) directly governs calculation of Michael's child support obligation, and the 27 percent multiplier for two children applies.
The existing support award of $850 per month was calculated when Michael earned $62,000 annually. It does not account for his current earning capacity. Continuing to hold Michael to an obligation calibrated to a salary that is now more than 50 percent lower than his actual income fails to reflect the children's entitlement to support commensurate with both parents' current financial circumstances. This Court has both the authority and the responsibility under AS 25.24.170 to modify the order to reflect current realities.
D. MODIFICATION IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND IS REQUIRED BY STATUTE.
The Alaska Legislature has expressly authorized courts to modify child support orders upon a showing of material changed circumstances. AS 25.24.170. The purpose of this authority is to ensure that support obligations remain responsive to actual parental income and the ongoing needs of the children. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that shifts in the needs of the children and changes in a parent's income are precisely the kinds of circumstances that justify modification. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
Here, the two minor children continue to reside primarily with Jacob, who bears the day-to-day financial burden of their care. Michael's significantly increased income means he has a correspondingly greater capacity to contribute to the children's support. The modification Jacob seeks does not seek a windfall: it seeks only to bring Michael's obligation into conformity with the amounts required by Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on his actual current earnings. Such a modification is both legally required and consistent with the children's best interests. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997) (affirming that child support must be just and proper, taking into account the needs of the children, the standard of living of the children, and the supporting parent's ability to pay).
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Jacob Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court find that Michael Bergstrom's income increase from approximately $62,000 to approximately $94,000 constitutes a material change in circumstances under AS 25.24.170 and Civil Rule 90.3(a), and that the Court enter an upward modification of the child support order consistent with the formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) as applied to Michael's current adjusted annual income. The modified obligation should be made effective as of the date of Jacob's motion, and the Court should order appropriate documentation to be submitted by Michael to allow precise calculation of his adjusted annual income under the rule.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0011)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Superior Court, Third Judicial District, on Ashley Okafor's petition for dissolution of marriage from Maria Okafor. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2016 and are the parents of two minor children, ages five and eight. The central disputes before this Court involve the appropriate residential custody schedule, the calculation and allocation of child support, the equitable division of the marital estate, and the proper allocation of the children's unreimbursed medical and childcare expenses. Both parties agree that a guardian ad litem should be appointed to evaluate the children's best interests in light of the ongoing custody disagreement. Ashley Okafor respectfully requests that this Court enter a dissolution decree establishing joint legal custody with primary residential placement of the children with Ashley during the school week, with alternating weekends and summer holidays with Maria, and that child support be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3 based on both parties' verified incomes. Ashley further requests an equitable division of all marital assets and liabilities pursuant to AS 25.24.160, and proportionate contribution by Maria to unreimbursed medical and childcare costs.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Okafor and Maria Okafor were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2016. Two minor children were born of the marriage, currently ages five and eight. Over the course of approximately two years preceding this filing, the marriage deteriorated due to persistent conflicts over financial management and fundamentally differing parenting philosophies. These irreconcilable differences caused an irremediable breakdown of the marital relationship, satisfying the statutory predicate for dissolution under AS 25.24.200.
Ashley filed a petition for dissolution in the Superior Court, Third Judicial District, in accordance with AS 25.24.210. Ashley proposes a joint legal custody arrangement under which the children would reside primarily with her during the school week and spend alternating weekends and designated summer holiday periods with Maria. Maria disputes this proposal and seeks equal physical custody on a week-on, week-off schedule.
The marital estate consists of the following assets and liabilities: a jointly owned home in Anchorage carrying approximately $85,000 in equity; two motor vehicles; and a shared savings account. Against these assets, the parties carry approximately $42,000 in combined credit card and personal loan debt, all of which was accumulated during the marriage. The parties dispute the equitable allocation of both assets and liabilities.
Ashley requests that the Court order Maria to contribute proportionately to her income to the children's unreimbursed medical expenses and work-related childcare costs. Both parties have agreed on the record that appointment of a guardian ad litem is appropriate given the depth and persistence of their disagreement over the residential custody schedule.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A petition for dissolution of marriage in Alaska must be filed with the Superior Court and must satisfy the conditions set forth in AS 25.24.200. Where a petition is filed by one spouse, AS 25.24.210 prescribes the required contents, including disclosure of each party's income, assets, liabilities, the date and place of the marriage, and information regarding each minor child of the marriage.
Upon filing, the Court must examine the petitioner and consider whether the statutory conditions have been met. AS 25.24.220 further directs the Court to evaluate whether written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children. Where a minor child's interests are at stake and the parties disagree over custody, AS 25.24.310 authorizes and, in appropriate circumstances, requires the Court to appoint a guardian ad litem or attorney to represent the child's best interests.
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3, which establishes the methodology for calculating support based on each parent's adjusted annual income and the custody arrangement in place. The division of marital property is governed by AS 25.24.160, which requires the Court to divide property in a just manner and to fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution by considering enumerated statutory factors. Spousal maintenance, if sought, must also fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution pursuant to AS 25.24.969(2).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY WITH PRIMARY RESIDENTIAL PLACEMENT OF THE CHILDREN WITH ASHLEY OKAFOR DURING THE SCHOOL WEEK.
The best interests of the children are the paramount consideration in any custody determination. Ashley's proposed arrangement, under which the children reside with her during the school week and spend alternating weekends and summer holidays with Maria, is designed to provide the children with stability and continuity during the school year while preserving a meaningful and ongoing relationship with Maria.
Under AS 25.24.220(d)(2), the Court must examine whether any written custody agreement is just between the parties and in the best interests of the children of the marriage. In performing this analysis, the Court must also consider whether the arrangement should include visitation by grandparents and other persons.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that residential continuity during the school year is a significant factor in serving the long-term well-being of minor children. In Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006), the court affirmed a primary custody award to the parent who had functioned as the primary caregiver, recognizing that such arrangements promote emotional stability and continuity. Similarly, in Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004), the court emphasized that the stability of the child's living environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity are central considerations in custody decisions.
Ashley has functioned as the primary caregiver during the school week throughout the parties' separation. Disrupting the children's school-week routine by shifting to a strict week-on, week-off schedule, as Maria proposes, risks introducing instability into the children's academic and social lives at a critical developmental period, particularly for the eight-year-old who is fully enrolled in school. Maria's week-on, week-off proposal, while providing equal parenting time, does not adequately account for the school-week continuity that serves these particular children's best interests.
Joint legal custody, however, is appropriate and is supported by both parties' acknowledgment that each parent has a meaningful role in the children's lives. Joint legal custody ensures that both Ashley and Maria participate in major decisions affecting the children's health, education, and welfare.
B. THE COURT SHOULD APPOINT A GUARDIAN AD LITEM TO REPRESENT THE CHILDREN'S BEST INTERESTS.
Both parties have agreed that the appointment of a guardian ad litem is appropriate given the nature and persistence of their custody dispute. The Court is authorized, and in the circumstances of this case should be required, to make such an appointment.
AS 25.24.310 provides that in an action involving a question of custody, support, or visitation, the Court may upon the motion of a party or upon its own motion appoint an attorney or the Office of Public Advocacy to represent a minor with respect to custody, support, and visitation. AS 25.24.310 further requires the Court to make a finding on the record before trial as to whether the minor should have legal representation or other services. AS 25.24.220(f) independently authorizes the Court to appoint a guardian ad litem to represent the best interests of the child, with appointment to be made under the terms of AS 25.24.310.
Restol v. Manshen, 530 P.3d 812 (Alaska 2007), the Alaska Supreme Court held that where a motion for appointment of a guardian ad litem is before the court, the court must make findings on the record explaining any denial of such a motion. Given that both parties here affirmatively seek a guardian ad litem appointment, no basis for denial exists, and the Court should appoint a qualified guardian ad litem promptly to investigate and report on the children's best interests, particularly regarding the disputed residential schedule.
The guardian ad litem's investigation and report will assist the Court in determining whether Ashley's proposed primary placement arrangement or Maria's week-on, week-off proposal better serves the children's day-to-day needs, emotional well-being, and long-term development. The appointment should be made under AS 25.24.310, and the Court should enter an order for costs and fees in accordance with that statute, allocating responsibility between the parties based on their respective financial circumstances.
C. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON EACH PARTY'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AND THE APPLICABLE CUSTODY FORMULA.
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. The applicable formula and percentage depend on the custody arrangement the Court ultimately orders.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), a parent has primary physical custody for purposes of the rule if the children reside with the other parent for a period specified in the custody order of less than 30 percent of the year. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), a parent has shared physical custody if the children reside with that parent for a period of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, the child support award is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: 27 percent for two children, pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources minus the mandatory and permissible deductions specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including federal, state, and local income taxes; Social Security tax; Medicare tax; mandatory union dues; mandatory retirement contributions; and certain voluntary retirement contributions up to the limits prescribed by the rule.
Ashley's proposed residential schedule, in which the children primarily reside with her during the school week and spend alternating weekends with Maria, may result in Maria having the children for less than 30 percent of the year, placing the arrangement within the primary physical custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(a). The parties should submit verified financial disclosures, including W-2 forms, tax returns, and documentation of all permissible deductions, to allow the Court to perform an accurate adjusted annual income calculation for each party.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that Civil Rule 90.3's formula produces a presumptive support figure that serves the children's financial needs, including housing, food, and clothing. In Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), the court explained that the formula in Civil Rule 90.3 does not anticipate a support order that would leave children with insufficient support for their basic needs. The Court should apply the formula as written based on verified incomes and the custody arrangement ultimately ordered.
If the Court determines that the children reside with Maria for 30 percent or more of the year, the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3 would govern. The Court should make this determination after receiving the guardian ad litem's report and entering final custody orders, at which point the precise percentage of time each child spends with each parent will be known.
D. THE COURT SHOULD ORDER EACH PARTY TO CONTRIBUTE TO UNREIMBURSED HEALTH CARE AND CHILDCARE EXPENSES PROPORTIONATELY, AND SHOULD REQUIRE HEALTH INSURANCE COVERAGE FOR THE CHILDREN.
Civil Rule 994(d)(1) requires the Court to address coverage of the children's health care needs and to require health insurance for the children if insurance is available to either parent at a reasonable cost and accessible to the children. Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(i) establishes a rebuttable presumption that the cost of health insurance is reasonable if the cost does not exceed five percent of the adjusted annual income of the parent who may be required to purchase the insurance. Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(ii) provides that health insurance is accessible to the children if the plan pays for health care services reasonably available to the children.
Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(B) provides that the Court shall allocate equally the cost of the children's health insurance between the parties unless the Court orders otherwise for good cause. Ashley requests that the Court order each party to maintain or obtain health insurance for the children if available at reasonable cost, with the premium cost allocated between the parties in accordance with the rule, subject to adjustment based on the relative incomes of the parties if good cause so warrants.
Regarding unreimbursed health care expenses, Civil Rule 90.3(d)(2) provides that the Court shall allocate equally between the parties the cost of reasonable health care expenses not covered by insurance unless the Court orders otherwise for good cause, and that a party shall reimburse the other party for that party's share of uncovered expenses within 30 days of receipt of the bill, payment verification, and insurance statement. Ashley requests that the Court enter an order consistent with this rule, requiring Maria to reimburse Ashley for Maria's proportionate share of all unreimbursed health care expenses within 30 days of receiving proper documentation.
Ashley further requests that work-related childcare expenses be taken into account in the child support calculation as a permissible deduction under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E), which allows deduction of work-related child care expenses for the children who are the subject of the child support order from the custodial parent's adjusted annual income.
E. THE COURT SHOULD DIVIDE THE MARITAL ESTATE EQUITABLY IN ACCORDANCE WITH AS 25.24.160, GIVING APPROPRIATE WEIGHT TO ALL STATUTORY FACTORS.
The division of marital property in an Alaska dissolution is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires the Court to divide property in a just manner without regard to fault, considering an enumerated list of factors. These factors include the length of the marriage and station in life of the parties during the marriage; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties; the financial condition of the parties; the conduct of the parties, including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home or the right to live in it to the party who has primary physical custody of the children; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question; and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
The marital estate consists of the Anchorage home with approximately $85,000 in equity, two vehicles, and a shared savings account, offset by approximately $42,000 in combined marital debt. All property described above was acquired during the marriage and constitutes marital property subject to equitable division.
With respect to the family home, AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically identifies the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of the children as a factor the Court must consider. In Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed an award of the family home to the parent with primary physical custody of the children, holding that such an award was not an abuse of discretion. Ashley, as the proposed primary residential parent during the school week, has a strong interest in remaining in the family home to provide continuity for the children's schooling and social connections.
Ashley proposes that the home be awarded to her, with Maria receiving an offsetting share of other marital assets, or that the home be sold and the equity divided equitably after accounting for the allocation of marital debt. The Court should also ensure that the $42,000 in marital debt is allocated in a just manner consistent with the equities of the division, considering each party's income, ability to pay, and the source of the underlying obligations.
In Siggelkow v. Siggelkow, 643 P.2d 985 (Alaska 1982), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that a spouse's failure to satisfy marital debts or preserve marital property is a relevant consideration in equitable division. To the extent that either party has unreasonably depleted marital assets or failed to contribute to the satisfaction of marital obligations during the pendency of this proceeding, the Court should weigh that conduct under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(E).
Civil Rule 90.1(e) requires that in divorce cases involving property division disputes, the parties file and serve, at least five days before trial, a list of all assets and liabilities with brief descriptions, characterization of each as marital or separate, the value of each, and the proposed disposition of each. Ashley will comply with this requirement and respectfully requests that the Court direct Maria to do the same, so that the Court has a complete and accurate picture of the marital estate before entering its division order.
Additionally, AS 25.24.155 limits the Court's ability to reserve or delay a property division decision. Under AS 25.24.155(a), the Court may not delay or reserve an issue of property division unless each party expressly agrees on the record to the delay or reservation, or a party who moves for delay shows good cause and the Court finds that the opposing party's interests will not be jeopardized. Ashley does not consent to any reservation of the property division issue and respectfully requests a complete and final division at the time of the dissolution decree.
V. CONCLUSION
For all of the reasons set forth above, Ashley Okafor respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Enter a dissolution decree dissolving the marriage of Ashley Okafor and Maria Okafor pursuant to AS 25.24.200 and AS 25.24.220;
2. Award joint legal custody of the two minor children to both parties, with primary residential placement of the children with Ashley Okafor during the school week and alternating weekends and designated summer holidays with Maria Okafor;

4. Calculate child support pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3 based on each party's verified adjusted annual income and the custody arrangement ordered by the Court, applying the primary physical custody formula at Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) for two children if the residential schedule results in Maria having the children less than 30 percent of the year;
5. Order both parties to maintain health insurance for the children if available at reasonable cost, allocate the premium cost between the parties pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(B), and require each party to contribute to unreimbursed health care expenses within 30 days of receiving proper documentation pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(d)(2);
