IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0012)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter arises from a petition for dissolution of marriage filed by Petitioner David Okafor in Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, following the irretrievable breakdown of his marriage to Respondent Colin Okafor. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. The central issues before the Court are: (1) the proper physical custody arrangement and corresponding parenting time schedule for the minor children; (2) the appropriate calculation of child support under the Alaska Child Support Guidelines; and (3) a just and equitable division of the marital estate, including the family home in Eagle River, a joint savings account, two vehicles, and a shared credit card debt.
David respectfully submits this brief in support of his proposed dissolution terms. He seeks primary physical custody of the children during the school year, with Colin exercising parenting time every other weekend and six weeks in the summer, child support calculated on Colin's gross oil field income of approximately $140,000 per year, and retention of the marital home to provide stability and continuity for the children. David is prepared to address Colin's request for an offsetting cash payment and proposes that the remaining assets and liabilities be divided in a manner that fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution consistent with Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Okafor and Colin Okafor were married in Anchorage, Alaska on or about 2015. The marriage produced two minor children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old (hereinafter "the children"). Throughout the marriage, David served as the children's primary caregiver, managing the household, arranging schooling and medical care, and attending to the children's daily needs. Colin has worked on the North Slope in the oil and gas industry under a rotational schedule that requires him to be away from the family home for two-week intervals at a time, earning approximately $140,000 per year in gross income.
Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to Colin's extended work absences and ongoing disputes over finances and parenting responsibilities. David filed a petition for dissolution in Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, seeking, among other things, primary physical custody of the children, appropriate child support, and an equitable division of the marital estate.
The marital estate consists of: (1) the family home located in Eagle River, Alaska; (2) a jointly held savings account of approximately $85,000; (3) two motor vehicles; and (4) a shared credit card balance of approximately $22,000.
David proposes that the children reside primarily with him during the school year, with Colin having parenting time every other weekend and six full weeks during the summer. Colin counters that he should share equal legal custody and receive additional parenting time structured around his two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off North Slope work rotation. Regarding property, David seeks to retain the family home to provide continuity and stability for the children. Colin requests an offsetting cash payment to equalize the asset division. As to child support, David contends that Colin's annual income of approximately $140,000 should yield a support obligation consistent with the applicable Alaska Child Support Guidelines, while Colin argues that his out-of-pocket travel costs and irregular pay periods warrant a downward adjustment.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts dissolving a marriage must address four principal areas: child custody and visitation, child support, property division, and allocation of debts. Each area is governed by specific statutory authority and court rules.
Under AS 25.20.110(a), an award of custody may be made or modified when the court determines that such an arrangement is in the best interests of the child. The court must consider all relevant circumstances, including the history of each parent's involvement with the children and compliance with prior orders.
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which establishes that a support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by a specified percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27% under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). The rule defines "adjusted annual income" as the parent's total income from all sources minus certain enumerated deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(b) governs shared and divided custody arrangements and provides an alternative calculation method.
Property division in a dissolution proceeding is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires that the division of property "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" based on consideration of specific statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the custodial parent, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property. Spousal maintenance, if any, is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and requires a similar multi-factor analysis.
The overall dissolution process for a jointly filed petition is governed by AS 25.24.200 and AS 25.24.210, which require the parties to present written agreements on custody, support, visitation, and property division for the court's review. Under AS 25.24.220(d), the court must examine whether the agreements are just, whether they reflect the best interests of the children, and whether they constitute the entire agreement between the parties. Where heightened scrutiny is warranted, AS 25.24.220(h) and (i) provide that the court must conduct a more searching examination of the terms.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. The Court Should Award David Primary Physical Custody of the Minor Children During the School Year Because That Arrangement Is in the Children's Best Interests.
The paramount consideration in any custody determination is the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.110(a) provides that a custody award shall be made based on what "is in the best interests of the child," and the court must enter its reasons on the record if a parent opposes the arrangement and the proposed order is granted.
In this case, the evidence overwhelmingly supports placing primary physical custody with David during the school year. David has been the children's consistent, day-to-day caregiver throughout the marriage. He has managed schooling, medical appointments, extracurricular activities, and daily routines. Colin, by contrast, is absent from the family home on a regular basis for two-week periods due to his North Slope work schedule, making it structurally difficult for him to serve as the primary residential parent during the school year.
David's proposal provides each child with a stable, consistent home environment during the academic year, which serves their educational and emotional needs. Colin would retain meaningful parenting time: alternating weekends during the school year and a full six-week block during the summer. This schedule accommodates Colin's work rotation while ensuring that the children maintain a close relationship with both parents.
Colin's counter-proposal of a custody schedule tied to his two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off work rotation presents significant practical difficulties. Because Colin is physically unavailable during his two-week North Slope shifts, the children would necessarily be in David's care during those periods regardless. Structuring a nominally equal custody schedule around Colin's absence does not serve the children's stability and would require frequent transitions between households even during the school year. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized, in cases such as Dragseth v. Dragseth, 210 P.3d 1206 (Alaska 2009), that trial courts have broad discretion in determining child custody and that the totality of circumstances must guide the analysis. Here, the totality of circumstances favors David's proposal.
Furthermore, as the court recognized in Helen S.K. v. Samuel M.K., 288 P.3d 463 (Alaska 2012), courts may look to the practical realities of each parent's schedule and earning patterns when structuring custody arrangements, and may impute parental responsibilities based on actual availability. Colin's regular and extended absences from Anchorage are a structural feature of his employment, not a temporary condition, and the Court should fashion a custody arrangement that reflects this reality.
AS 25.24.220(d)(2) requires the court to determine whether the custody agreement "is just as between the spouses and in the best interests of the children of the marriage." David's proposed arrangement satisfies both prongs of this test. It provides the children with a settled home base while preserving Colin's substantial parenting time, particularly during summer when his availability is greatest and the school schedule does not impose competing demands.
B. Child Support Should Be Calculated Based on Colin's Full Adjusted Annual Income Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), and a Downward Deviation Is Not Warranted.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that a child support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated "as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." For two children, the applicable percentage is 27%. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines "adjusted annual income" as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" certain specific deductions, including mandatory tax obligations, union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and limited voluntary retirement contributions, as well as work-related child care expenses and health insurance premiums subject to stated caps.
Colin earns approximately $140,000 per year in gross income from his North Slope employment. This figure forms the starting point for the adjusted annual income calculation. Colin has argued that his out-of-pocket travel costs and irregular pay periods warrant a downward adjustment. Neither argument supports a deviation from the guidelines.
First, travel expenses are not listed among the deductions permitted by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1). The rule's enumerated deductions are exclusive: only mandatory tax obligations, mandatory retirement and union contributions, limited voluntary retirement contributions, child or spousal support obligations from other relationships, in-kind support for prior children, work-related child care expenses, and health insurance premiums may reduce gross income. Commute and travel costs, even when substantial, are not recognized deductions under the rule. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), that adjusted annual income is calculated by applying the specific deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), and no others.
Second, Colin's irregular pay periods do not justify a downward adjustment. Civil Rule 90.3(a) is designed to address annualized income, and the rule expressly contemplates parents whose income varies by season or pay cycle. The court is required to assess total income from all sources on an annual basis and may, in appropriate cases, order unequal monthly payments to account for income seasonality under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(D)(ii), but irregularity in pay timing does not reduce the income base itself.
The court should also be aware that Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits the court to calculate child support based on a parent's potential income if that parent "voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed." While David does not assert at this time that Colin is underemployed, this provision reinforces that the guideline is designed to hold parents accountable for their actual earning capacity, not to reward departures from that capacity through selective expense claims.
Applying the 27% rate for two children to Colin's adjusted annual income, after only those deductions expressly authorized by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), will yield a support obligation that appropriately reflects Colin's financial capacity and the children's needs. David urges the Court to compute support accordingly and to decline any invitation to deviate downward based on unenumerated expense claims.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized in Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996) that the child support guidelines must be applied faithfully and that deviations require clear justification grounded in the text of the rule. Colin has offered no such justification here.
C. David Is Entitled to Retain the Marital Home in Eagle River, and the Division of Remaining Marital Assets and Liabilities Should Fairly Allocate the Economic Effect of Dissolution.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) directs the court to divide the parties' property "in a just manner" and requires that "the division of property must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" by considering a comprehensive list of statutory factors. Among those factors, AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically identifies "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children" as a relevant consideration.
This factor strongly favors David's retention of the Eagle River home. David will serve as the children's primary residential parent during the school year. The children are currently six and nine years old, and continuity of their home environment, school district, neighborhood relationships, and community ties directly serves their well-being. Uprooting them from the family home would compound the disruption already caused by the dissolution and is contrary to the children's best interests.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized the importance of this factor in property division. In Day v. Williams, 285 P.3d 256 (Alaska 2012), the court affirmed that equal division of property is the general presumption, but that the statutory factors, including the desirability of awarding the family home to the custodial parent, may support a deviation from strict equality. Similarly, in Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010), the court upheld a property distribution that gave weight to the parties' respective circumstances and necessities, consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(G). Green v. Green, 29 P.3d 854 (Alaska 2001) further confirms that the trial court has discretion to weigh these factors and reach a result that is equitable given the particular circumstances of the parties.
David acknowledges that Colin holds an interest in the marital home and is entitled to fair compensation for that interest. David proposes that the parties obtain an independent appraisal of the home's fair market value and that Colin receive an equalizing payment drawn from the parties' joint savings account of approximately $85,000. The savings account balance, after payment of the equalizing amount, would be divided between the parties. This approach achieves the twin goals of stability for the children and fair economic allocation between the spouses.
The two vehicles should be awarded one to each party based on current use and need, with any difference in value addressed through the overall offset calculation. The shared credit card balance of approximately $22,000 should be allocated equitably, taking into account each party's contributions to that balance and their respective abilities to service the debt going forward. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C) and (D) require the court to consider the earning capacity and financial condition of each party, including the availability and cost of health insurance. Colin earns approximately $140,000 per year; David, as the primary caregiver throughout the marriage, may have a reduced current earning capacity as a result of his custodial responsibilities during the marriage. These facts support placing a greater portion of the shared debt burden on Colin, or at minimum dividing it equally, while allowing David to retain the home with an appropriate offset.
AS 25.24.200(a)(3) requires that any property agreement "be fair and just and take into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4) so that the economic effect of dissolution is fairly allocated." The framework David proposes satisfies this standard. It honors the statutory preference for awarding the family home to the custodial parent, compensates Colin equitably from existing liquid assets, and allocates debts in proportion to the parties' respective financial capacities.
D. The Court Should Apply Heightened Scrutiny to the Written Agreements If Any Imbalance of Bargaining Power Is Present.
AS 25.24.220(h) requires the court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the parties' written agreements in dissolution proceedings under specified circumstances, including when one party is represented by counsel and the other is not, when there is a minor child of the marriage, or when there is a patently inequitable division of the marital estate. In this case, the presence of two minor children triggers the heightened scrutiny provision under AS 25.24.220(h)(3). The Court is therefore obligated under AS 25.24.220(i) to "examine the written agreements between the spouses to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that the agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are in the best interest of the children of the marriage."
David welcomes this heightened review. His proposed terms are designed precisely to withstand close judicial scrutiny: the custody arrangement is child-centered and practically workable, the child support calculation is grounded in the mandatory guidelines, and the property division fairly compensates both parties while recognizing the children's need for a stable home. David requests that the Court conduct the required examination and enter a dissolution decree that reflects the statutory mandate of fairness, both as between the parties and, most importantly, in the best interests of the children.
AS 25.24.250(c) further provides that dissolution forms and instructions "must specify that the dissolution petition constitutes the entire agreement between the parties." David confirms that all agreements and proposals set forth in the dissolution petition and in this brief represent his complete position, and that no side agreements or informal understandings exist that are not reflected in the record before the Court.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, David Okafor respectfully requests that the Court:
1. Award David primary physical custody of the two minor children during the school year, with Colin exercising parenting time every other weekend and six consecutive weeks during the summer, consistent with AS 25.20.110(a) and the children's best interests;
2. Calculate Colin's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using his full adjusted annual income of approximately $140,000 per year at the 27% rate applicable to two children, without downward deviation based on unenumerated travel costs or pay irregularities;
3. Award David the marital home in Eagle River pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), with Colin receiving an equalizing offset drawn from the joint savings account;
4. Divide the remaining marital assets, including the two vehicles and the joint savings account balance after the home offset, and allocate the shared credit card debt equitably between the parties based on the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4);
5. Apply the heightened scrutiny required by AS 25.24.220(h) and (i) in reviewing all written agreements, consistent with the presence of minor children; and
6. Enter a final decree of dissolution that fairly allocates the economic effect of the dissolution consistent with AS 25.24.160(a), AS 25.24.200(a)(3), and all applicable Alaska law.
David Okafor respectfully submits that the proposals set forth herein serve the best interests of the children, reflect a fair and just allocation of marital assets and liabilities, and comport with all requirements of Alaska dissolution law.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0013)
I. INTRODUCTION
This brief is submitted on behalf of Ashley Bergstrom, Petitioner, in the above-captioned dissolution proceeding. Ashley and Wesley Bergstrom were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. After years of marital deterioration attributable in significant part to Wesley's extended work absences on the North Slope and persistent financial disputes, Ashley filed for dissolution in the Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, in 2024. Three core issues are before the Court: (1) the proper physical custody arrangement and parenting schedule for the parties' two minor children; (2) the correct calculation of child support under Civil Rule 90.3, including whether Wesley's overtime and hazard pay must be included in his income base; and (3) the equitable division of the parties' jointly owned Eagle River home, which carries approximately $100,000 in net equity, and roughly $45,000 in shared marital debt. Ashley respectfully submits that the evidence and applicable Alaska law support a primary physical custody arrangement in her favor, a child support award calculated on Wesley's total income from all sources including overtime and hazard pay, and an equitable distribution of marital assets and liabilities that accounts for the economic realities facing each party following dissolution.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Bergstrom and Wesley Bergstrom were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. The marriage produced two minor children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old, both of whom have resided primarily with Ashley in Eagle River throughout the marriage. Wesley works as a pipeline technician on the North Slope, operating on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation that requires him to be physically absent from the family home for extended and recurring periods. His employment generates a substantially higher income than Ashley's, and that income includes not only a base salary but also overtime pay and hazard pay associated with the demanding conditions of North Slope work.
Over the course of the marriage, the parties accumulated marital property and debt. Their primary marital asset is the jointly owned family home in Eagle River, currently valued at approximately $310,000 with a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, yielding net equity of approximately $100,000. The parties also accumulated approximately $45,000 in shared credit card and vehicle loan debt during the marriage.
Ashley has been the primary caregiver for the children throughout their lives, managing their day-to-day needs, schooling, medical appointments, and extracurricular activities, particularly during Wesley's recurring two-week absences. She now proposes a custody arrangement in which the children reside with her during the school year, with Wesley receiving visitation on alternating weekends and for six weeks during the summer. Wesley counters that he seeks a 50/50 shared custody schedule aligned with his two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off work rotation. Both parties agree that Wesley shall pay child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3, but dispute whether his overtime and hazard pay should be counted toward the income base used in that calculation.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.150(c), the court shall determine custody in accordance with the best interests of the child, considering factors including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship with the other parent; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence of substance abuse affecting the child's well-being; and other pertinent factors.
When the court considers whether to award shared custody specifically, AS 25.20.090 sets forth additional factors, including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the education of the child, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child currently resides, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, accounting for actual time spent, proximity to school, and the willingness of each parent to facilitate the other parent's relationship with the child.
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 908(a), which provides that a child support award in a primary physical custody case equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, specifically 27% for two children. Adjusted annual income is defined as the parent's total income from all sources minus certain enumerated deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(b) governs shared custody calculations using a different formula that accounts for each parent's income and the time each parent exercises physical custody.
The division of marital property is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires that property acquired during the marriage be divided in a just manner and without regard to fault, with the division fairly allocating the economic effect of dissolution based on enumerated factors including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party under all circumstances, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD ASHLEY PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF THE CHILDREN BECAUSE THAT ARRANGEMENT BEST SERVES THEIR INTERESTS UNDER AS 25.24.150 AND AS 25.20.090.
The paramount consideration in any custody determination is the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.150(c) directs the court to weigh a comprehensive set of factors focused entirely on the well-being of the minor children. Applied here, those factors strongly support the primary physical custody arrangement Ashley proposes.
First, continuity of care and stability weigh heavily in Ashley's favor. AS 25.24.150(c)(5) expressly directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Throughout their lives, the children have resided primarily with Ashley in the Eagle River family home, attending school and building friendships in that community. Their routines, schooling, and social relationships are anchored there. Disrupting that stability by imposing a rigid 50/50 rotation would require the children to alternate between homes on a schedule that may not align with school calendars, extracurricular obligations, or the children's own emotional needs. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that preserving established, stable home environments serves children's best interests. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996).
Second, the practical realities of Wesley's work schedule counsel against a 50/50 arrangement. Wesley's North Slope rotation means he is physically unavailable to care for the children for two weeks at a time, on a recurring basis. Although his two-weeks-off periods do provide meaningful time, a 50/50 schedule premised on that rotation would subject the children to significant disruption whenever Wesley's shift schedule shifts or overlaps with school obligations. AS 25.20.969 directs the court to consider the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, including the actual time spent with each parent, the proximity of each parent to school, and the feasibility of travel. Wesley's employment location on the North Slope during his on-rotation weeks is fundamentally incompatible with day-to-day parental responsibility during those periods. A primary custody arrangement with Ashley, supplemented by substantial visitation during Wesley's off-rotation periods, more accurately reflects the actual parenting time each parent can reliably provide.
Third, AS 25.20.090(3) directs the court to consider the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent. Ashley has maintained a stable, continuous home environment for the children throughout the marriage. Her consistent presence, as opposed to Wesley's recurring two-week absences, demonstrates that her home provides the greater degree of stability. This is not a criticism of Wesley's dedication as a father; rather, it is a recognition that the structural demands of his employment have placed the primary caregiving burden on Ashley, and that the children's interests are best served by formalizing what has been their lived reality.
Fourth, the children's educational needs support Ashley's proposed arrangement. AS 25.20.090(4) identifies the education of the child as a relevant factor. Both children are of school age, and their academic schedules are fixed and predictable. Ashley's proposed arrangement, with the children residing primarily with her during the school year, directly aligns the custody schedule with the academic calendar, promoting consistency and educational stability. A rotating 50/50 schedule built around Wesley's shift work may not consistently align with school schedules and could introduce unnecessary uncertainty into the children's academic routines.
Ashley does not seek to exclude Wesley from his children's lives. She supports a meaningful visitation schedule, including alternating weekends and six full weeks during the summer, which will allow Wesley to maintain a close and loving relationship with the children during his off-rotation periods. AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Ashley's proposed parenting plan reflects her commitment to supporting that relationship.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that custody determinations must focus on the actual needs and circumstances of the children rather than on the preferences or convenience of the parents. Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002). Here, the children's needs for stability, educational consistency, and a reliable primary caregiver point clearly to an award of primary physical custody to Ashley, with generous and structured visitation for Wesley.
B. WESLEY'S CHILD SUPPORT OBLIGATION MUST BE CALCULATED ON HIS TOTAL INCOME FROM ALL SOURCES, INCLUDING OVERTIME AND HAZARD PAY, UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a).
The parties agree that Wesley is obligated to pay child support under Civil Rule 90.3. The dispute is whether his overtime pay and hazard pay should be included in the income base used to calculate that support. Alaska law is clear: they must be included.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus certain enumerated deductions. The rule's definition is broad and unambiguous. Overtime pay and hazard pay are components of Wesley's compensation for his work as a pipeline technician on the North Slope. They are income from his employment, and nothing in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) excludes them. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently interpreted this income definition broadly, in keeping with the rule's purpose of ensuring that child support reflects the parent's actual financial capacity. State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999). The primary beneficiary of support is the child, and the support calculation must capture the obligor parent's true earning capacity. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
Wesley may argue that his overtime and hazard pay are irregular or uncertain and therefore should not be included. Alaska courts have not recognized irregularity alone as a basis for excluding documented income from the support calculation. The court has the authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to consider a parent's potential income when a parent is voluntarily underemployed, and more generally, courts look to the realistic earning picture the obligor parent's work history presents. Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019) (affirming a child support calculation based on a parent's actual work history and earning pattern). Wesley's employment records will demonstrate that overtime and hazard pay are not occasional windfalls but are regular and predictable features of North Slope pipeline work. Accordingly, they must be reflected in his adjusted annual income.
Once Wesley's total income from all sources is properly calculated, the applicable multiplier under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) for two children is 27% (.27) of his adjusted annual income. If the Court awards primary physical custody to Ashley as argued above, the primary custody formula in Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs. If, contrary to Ashley's position, the Court were to award shared physical custody, the more complex formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b) would apply, but even under that formula Wesley's total income, including overtime and hazard pay, would remain the proper starting point for the calculation on his side of the ledger.
Ashley respectfully requests that the Court order Wesley to provide complete documentation of his earnings, including base wages, overtime pay, hazard pay, and any other compensation, for the preceding three years, so that the Court can make an accurate determination of his adjusted annual income for purposes of Civil Rule 90.3. Bergstrom v. Lindback, 779 P.2d 1235 (Alaska 1989) (emphasizing the importance of accurate income determination in child support calculations).
C. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD ASHLEY THE FAMILY HOME AND EQUITABLY DIVIDE THE MARITAL DEBT IN A MANNER THAT FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION.
The division of marital property is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires the court to divide property acquired during the marriage in a just manner, without regard to fault, based on enumerated factors designed to fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. The parties' primary asset is the Eagle River family home, with a net equity of approximately $100,000. Their primary liabilities are approximately $45,000 in shared credit card and vehicle loan debt accumulated during the marriage.
1. Ashley Should Be Awarded the Family Home or Its Equivalent Equity.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically identifies the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children as a factor the court must consider. This provision reflects the legislature's recognition that continuity of the home environment is closely linked to the children's well-being and that requiring the custodial parent and children to move unnecessarily compounds the disruption already caused by dissolution.
Here, the children have grown up in the Eagle River home. Their school, friends, and community connections are rooted in that neighborhood. Awarding the home to Ashley, or at minimum awarding her sufficient equity to secure equivalent housing in the same community, directly serves the children's best interests and the statutory mandate of AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F). The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed the importance of this factor in equitable property division. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996).
In addition to the home-award preference, the court must consider the earning capacity of each party under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C). Wesley's income as a pipeline technician substantially exceeds Ashley's earning capacity. That disparity means that Wesley is far better positioned to secure alternative housing following dissolution. Awarding Ashley the family home, or its equivalent equity, is just and equitable when the parties' respective earning capacities and financial conditions are weighed against one another. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(D) also directs the court to consider the financial condition of the parties, including the availability and cost of health insurance, which further underscores the economic vulnerability Ashley faces relative to Wesley.
The court should consider three potential approaches: (a) award Ashley the home and require her to refinance the mortgage in her name alone, compensating Wesley for his share of net equity through a property settlement note or other mechanism; (b) order the home sold and divide the net proceeds equitably with a greater share to Ashley in light of the statutory factors; or (c) allow Ashley the right to remain in the home for a defined period sufficient to minimize disruption to the children's schooling, with a deferred sale thereafter. Any of these approaches is consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4). Ashley submits that option (a), outright award of the home to her with a corresponding payment to Wesley for his equitable share, best serves the children's need for stability and is achievable given the available equity.
2. The Marital Debt Should Be Divided Equitably, with Responsibility Allocated in Proportion to Each Party's Financial Capacity.
The approximately $45,000 in shared credit card and vehicle loan debt was accumulated during the marriage and constitutes a marital obligation subject to equitable division. AS 25.24.160(a)(4) does not limit the court's authority to property alone; the court's equitable mandate encompasses the allocation of marital liabilities as well. The court must consider the circumstances and necessities of each party under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(G) and the earning capacity of each party under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C).
Because Wesley's income substantially exceeds Ashley's, a strictly equal 50/50 division of the marital debt would impose a disproportionate financial burden on Ashley relative to her capacity to absorb it. A just allocation would assign Wesley a greater share of the marital debt, proportionate to the disparity in their earning capacities, while ensuring that Ashley is not left with obligations she cannot reasonably service following dissolution. This approach is consistent with the statutory requirement that property division fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
Ashley further requests that any debt allocation order include provisions protecting her credit from default in the event Wesley fails to pay debts allocated to him. The court has authority under AS 25.24.160 to fashion a just order, and that authority encompasses protective provisions designed to prevent one party's non-compliance from harming the other party financially.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that both property division and support awards must be viewed together as part of a comprehensive effort to achieve a fair economic outcome following dissolution. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). Viewed holistically, awarding Ashley primary physical custody, a child support order based on Wesley's full income, and a favorable allocation of the family home and marital debt produces a result that fairly accounts for the length of the marriage, the parties' respective earning capacities, Ashley's role as primary caregiver, and the children's need for stability and continuity.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Ashley Bergstrom respectfully requests that the Court:
1. Award Ashley primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, with Wesley receiving visitation on alternating weekends and for six weeks during the summer, consistent with AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.090;
2. Order Wesley to pay child support calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on his adjusted annual income from all sources, including base wages, overtime pay, and hazard pay, at the applicable rate of 27% for two children;
3. Award Ashley the family home located in Eagle River or, in the alternative, award her sufficient equity from the sale of that home to secure comparable housing in the same community, consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F);
4. Allocate the parties' approximately $45,000 in shared marital debt in a manner proportionate to their respective earning capacities, with Wesley bearing a greater share consistent with his substantially higher income, pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4); and
5. Grant such other relief as the Court deems just and proper under AS 25.24.160.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0014)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Superior Court, Third Judicial District, on the petition for dissolution of marriage filed by Petitioner David Bergstrom. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. The marriage has irretrievably broken down due to irreconcilable differences, including persistent conflict over financial management and differing parenting philosophies. The central disputes before the court concern the appropriate physical custody schedule for the minor children, the proper calculation of child support under Alaska's guidelines, and the equitable division of the marital estate, which includes the family home, two vehicles, joint savings and retirement accounts, and substantial marital debt.
David Bergstrom respectfully requests that the court award him primary physical custody of the children during the school week, with Michael Bergstrom exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and during an extended summer period; that the court calculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 935 based on Michael's income as a petroleum engineer; and that the court divide the marital estate in a just and equitable manner consistent with Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Bergstrom and Michael Bergstrom were married in Anchorage, Alaska on or about 2015. Two children were born of the marriage: one child currently age nine and one child currently age six, both of whom are minors and residents of Alaska. The parties have resided in the family home located in Eagle River, Alaska throughout the marriage.
Over the past two years, the marriage has experienced an irremediable breakdown attributable to irreconcilable differences, including persistent disagreement over household financial management and fundamentally differing philosophies regarding parenting. These conflicts have proven impossible to resolve, and David Bergstrom filed a petition for dissolution in the Superior Court, Third Judicial District.
Regarding the children, David proposes that the children reside with him during the school week and that Michael exercise parenting time on alternating weekends as well as for an extended period each summer. Both parties agree to share legal custody and to make all major decisions concerning the children's education, health care, and general well-being jointly. Michael disputes the proposed residential schedule and seeks a week-on, week-off shared physical custody arrangement.
Michael Bergstrom is employed as a petroleum engineer and earns a substantially higher income than David Bergstrom. The parties have not yet reached an agreement on child support, and David contends that Michael's income warrants application of the Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines in a manner that accounts for Michael's superior earning capacity.
The marital estate consists of the family home in Eagle River, which carries a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $280,000 against an estimated market value of $410,000, yielding approximately $130,000 in equity. The marital estate also includes two vehicles, joint savings accounts, and retirement accounts accumulated during the marriage. The parties share approximately $45,000 in credit card debt. None of these assets or liabilities has been divided, and each remains subject to equitable distribution by the court.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts adjudicating dissolution proceedings are guided by a framework of statutes and rules designed to protect the best interests of minor children and to achieve a fair and equitable resolution of financial matters between the parties.
Under AS 25.24.200, a petition for dissolution may be filed when incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and when the parties have addressed, or the court will address, matters of child custody, support, visitation, property division, and debt allocation. Where the parties have not fully agreed, the court retains authority to resolve open issues at hearing.
With respect to custody, AS 25.20.090 sets forth the factors a court must consider in determining whether to award shared custody, including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the educational needs of the child, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the child's school, the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close relationship between the child and the other parent, any evidence of domestic violence or substance abuse, and any other factors the court considers pertinent.
Property division in a dissolution proceeding is governed by AS 25.24.160, which requires the court to divide marital property in a just manner by considering factors including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the time and manner of acquisition of property.
Child support is calculated under Civil Rule 932(a), which provides that in cases of primary physical custody, the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a percentage set forth in the rule: twenty percent for one child and twenty-seven percent for two children. Where shared physical custody is awarded, Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies a different calculation methodology that accounts for the percentage of time each parent has physical custody and each parent's respective income. The court retains discretion to vary the guideline amount upon a showing of unusual circumstances.
At the dissolution hearing, the court examines the parties and evaluates whether the conditions for dissolution have been met and whether any agreements are just, pursuant to AS 25.24.220. Where a minor child is involved, the court applies a heightened level of scrutiny to the agreements presented.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF THE MINOR CHILDREN TO DAVID BERGSTROM, WITH MICHAEL BERGSTROM EXERCISING ALTERNATING WEEKEND PARENTING TIME AND EXTENDED SUMMER VISITATION.
The best interests of the children are the paramount consideration in any custody determination. AS 25.20.090 enumerates the factors a court must weigh in assessing whether to award shared custody. Applying those factors to the circumstances of this case, primary physical custody with David Bergstrom during the school week is the arrangement best suited to serve the children's needs.
First, the stability of the home environment is a critical factor under AS 25.20.908. David Bergstrom has been the primary caregiver for the children during the school week throughout the period of marital conflict. Awarding primary physical custody to David preserves the existing routines, school relationships, and community ties the children have established, thereby minimizing disruption to their daily lives. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of maintaining continuity in a child's environment when assessing competing custody proposals. Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004).
Second, AS 25.20.090(4) requires the court to consider the children's educational needs. The children are ages six and nine, both enrolled in school in the Eagle River community. A primary custody arrangement with David ensures a consistent weekday schedule aligned with school attendance, homework routines, and extracurricular activities. A week-on, week-off schedule, as proposed by Michael, risks disrupting the children's educational continuity depending on each parent's proximity to the children's school.
Third, AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (C) require the court to consider the proximity of each parent to the other and to the children's school, and the feasibility of travel between the parents. The parties' respective residential locations and commuting logistics must be evaluated to ensure that the chosen schedule does not burden the children with excessive travel or logistical stress during the school week.
Fourth, AS 25.20.090(6)(E) requires the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the children and the other parent. David's proposed schedule preserves meaningful contact between the children and Michael through alternating weekends and an extended summer period, demonstrating David's good-faith commitment to Michael's continued involvement in the children's lives.
Fifth, AS 25.20.090(2) requires the court to consider the needs of the children. The children, ages six and nine, are at developmental stages that benefit greatly from predictability, routine, and parental availability during the school week. David's proposal provides those benefits while ensuring that Michael maintains a substantial and meaningful parenting role.
Taken together, these factors weigh in favor of awarding primary physical custody to David Bergstrom, with Michael exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and during an extended summer period, and with both parents sharing legal custody and joint decision-making authority over education, health care, and general well-being.
The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that custody agreements reached by the parties do not bind the court, which must independently determine what arrangement serves the children's best interests. Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002). The court must therefore evaluate Michael's counter-proposal for a week-on, week-off schedule against each of the statutory factors rather than treating equal time-sharing as a default outcome. On the facts presented, the statutory analysis supports David's proposed arrangement.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON MICHAEL BERGSTROM'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS A PETROLEUM ENGINEER.
Because David Bergstrom is seeking primary physical custody, child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides that "a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody as defined by paragraph (f) will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." For two children, that percentage is twenty-seven percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Michael Bergstrom is employed as a petroleum engineer, a profession that carries a substantially higher income than David's. The adjusted annual income calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) requires the court to begin with Michael's total income from all sources and to subtract only those deductions the rule expressly authorizes, including federal, state, and local income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and certain voluntary retirement contributions within the limits prescribed by the rule, as well as work-related child care expenses and health insurance premiums within the capped amounts.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the goal of the Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines is to obtain a realistic estimate of the obligor parent's adjusted annual income, and that deductions from income must be limited to those the rule specifically authorizes. Bergstrom v. Lindback, 779 P.2d 1235 (Alaska 1989). David therefore urges the court to scrutinize any claimed deductions Michael presents and to disallow any that fall outside the enumerated categories in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized that child support and property division are distinct issues that must be treated separately and must not be traded off against each other. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997). David Bergstrom does not seek any deviation from the Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines through property concessions; rather, he asks the court to apply the guidelines faithfully to Michael's income, ensuring that the children receive the level of support to which they are entitled based on Michael's actual earning capacity.
If, alternatively, the court determines that a shared physical custody arrangement is appropriate, child support would be recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which requires computing the amount each parent would owe the other assuming the other had primary custody, multiplying each figure by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and then awarding to the parent with the larger figure the difference between the two figures multiplied by 1.5. Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(A)-(C). Even under that scenario, Michael's significantly higher income as a petroleum engineer would result in a meaningful support obligation to David, given the disparity in the parties' respective earnings.
The court should further be alert to any attempt by Michael to understate his income or claim excessive deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes the court to impute potential income to a parent who voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed. While David does not presently allege that Michael is underemployed, the court should require full and transparent financial disclosure from Michael so that his adjusted annual income can be computed accurately.
C. THE MARITAL ESTATE SHOULD BE DIVIDED IN A JUST AND EQUITABLE MANNER CONSISTENT WITH AS 25.24.160.
The division of the marital estate, including the family home, two vehicles, joint savings and retirement accounts, and shared credit card debt, must be accomplished in accordance with AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires the court to divide marital property "in a just manner" based on a consideration of multiple enumerated factors.
The marital estate's most significant asset is the family home in Eagle River, which carries an estimated market value of $410,000 against a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $280,000, yielding approximately $130,000 in equity. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), the court must consider "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has sole physical custody of children." Because David is seeking primary physical custody, and because stability of the home environment is a recognized factor in the children's best interests, David respectfully requests that the court award him the family home, or at a minimum the right to remain in the home with the children for a reasonable period, with appropriate credit to Michael for his share of the equity.
In addition to the home, the court must consider the length of the marriage under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(A). The parties were married in 2015, and the dissolution is being sought approximately nine to ten years later. This is a marriage of meaningful duration, and the court should treat the property accumulated during that period as presumptively marital, subject to equitable division.
The court must also consider the earning capacity of each party under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C). Michael's substantially higher earning capacity as a petroleum engineer is a relevant factor in fashioning a property division that fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that equitable distribution does not require a precisely equal split but rather a division that is just in light of all relevant circumstances. Beal v. Beal, 209 P.3d 1012 (Alaska 2009).
The financial condition of the parties, including the availability and cost of health insurance, must also be considered under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(D). David, as the parent who will bear primary day-to-day caregiving responsibilities, will face increased household expenses associated with raising the children. The court should account for this reality in fashioning the property division.
The parties' joint savings and retirement accounts were accumulated during the marriage and are subject to division as marital property. The court is authorized under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) to require the assignment, delivery, or conveyance of any real or personal property, including retirement benefits, to achieve a just division. David requests that retirement accounts be divided in a manner that reflects the parties' respective contributions and the overall equities of the division.
The approximately $45,000 in shared credit card debt must also be allocated between the parties. The court's authority to address debt allocation in dissolution proceedings is established by AS 25.24.200(a)(4), which requires that petitioners have agreed, or the court will determine, the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both of them. David requests that the court allocate the marital debt in proportion to each party's ability to pay, taking into account the disparity in income.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that courts should carefully examine property settlements in dissolution proceedings, particularly where the parties' positions are not fully aligned and where one spouse has substantially greater economic resources. Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014). The court's review under AS 25.24.220(d) must confirm that the overall property division fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution in accordance with the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4).
D. THE COURT SHOULD CONDUCT A THOROUGH EXAMINATION AT THE DISSOLUTION HEARING CONSISTENT WITH AS 25.24.220.
At the dissolution hearing, the court is required by AS 25.24.220(d) to examine the petitioners and consider whether the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action, whether any written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children, and whether any property division agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4).
Because minor children are involved in this proceeding, AS 25.24.220(h)(3) requires the court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to all agreements presented. This heightened scrutiny is warranted and appropriate here, and David Bergstrom welcomes the court's thorough examination of all proposed terms. David respectfully submits that the custody, support, and property proposals he advances in this brief are just, fair, and fully consistent with the children's best interests and the equitable principles Alaska law requires.
Furthermore, AS 25.24.220(g) provides that the court may amend the written agreements between the spouses relating to child custody, child support, visitation, division of property, and allocation of obligations, but only if both petitioners concur in the amendment in writing or on the record. David is prepared to engage constructively with any amendments the court may propose, provided they serve the children's best interests and achieve a fair economic outcome.
V. CONCLUSION
For the reasons stated above, David Bergstrom respectfully requests that the court:
1. Award David Bergstrom primary physical custody of the two minor children, with Michael Bergstrom exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and during an extended summer period, and with both parents sharing legal custody and joint decision-making authority;
