IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0015)
I. INTRODUCTION
This brief is submitted on behalf of Petitioner Renee Larsen in support of her petition for dissolution of marriage from Respondent Wesley Larsen. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and have two minor children, ages six and nine. After years of marital conflict stemming from Wesley's extended North Slope work absences and persistent disagreements over finances and parenting, Renee filed this petition for dissolution in Alaska Superior Court pursuant to AS 25.24.200 and AS 25.24.210.
Three primary disputes require resolution by this Court. First, the parties disagree about physical custody of the two minor children, with Renee proposing a primary physical custody arrangement during the school year and Wesley proposing a 50/50 shared schedule built around his industrial rotation. Second, the parties dispute the proper calculation and amount of child support, with Renee asking the Court to apply the Civil Rule 90.3 formula to Wesley's substantially higher income and Wesley seeking credits for travel costs and a secondary residence. Third, the parties cannot agree on disposition of the marital home, which holds approximately $85,000 in equity, and responsibility for a $22,000 joint credit card debt incurred during the marriage.
Renee's proposed resolution on each issue is grounded in Alaska law, serves the best interests of the children, and fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution. This Court should grant the relief she requests.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Larsen and Wesley Larsen were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. Two children were born of the marriage: a daughter currently age nine and a son currently age six. Both children are enrolled in Anchorage schools and reside in the marital home with Renee.
Over approximately the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to two primary sources of conflict. First, Wesley's employment as a pipeline technician required him to work on the North Slope on a recurring two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation. His extended absences placed the burden of day-to-day parenting, school coordination, medical appointments, and household management squarely on Renee. Second, the parties experienced persistent and unresolved conflict over financial decisions and parenting choices, which eroded the foundation of the marriage beyond repair.
Renee filed this petition for dissolution based on the irremediable breakdown of the marriage due to incompatibility of temperament, as authorized by AS 25.24.200. The parties agree that the marriage has irretrievably broken down; the contested issues concern child custody, child support, and property division.
Regarding custody, Renee proposes that the children remain with her in Anchorage as their primary residence throughout the school year. Wesley would exercise visitation on alternating weekends when he is off rotation and would have the children for four weeks during the summer. Wesley counters with a 50/50 shared schedule structured around his North Slope rotation.
Regarding child support, Wesley works as a pipeline technician and earns substantially more than Renee. Wesley does not dispute his income figure but argues that his work-related travel costs and the expense of maintaining a second residence near the job site should reduce his child support obligation. Renee requests that the Court apply the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula straightforwardly to Wesley's adjusted annual income.
Regarding property, the parties jointly own a home in Anchorage with approximately $85,000 in equity. They also accumulated $22,000 in joint credit card debt during the marriage. Renee proposes that she receive the home in exchange for assuming the full $22,000 credit card obligation, thereby keeping the children in their established residence. Wesley requests an immediate sale of the home and an equal division of the net proceeds, as well as some sharing of the credit card debt.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Dissolution Generally
Alaska authorizes the dissolution of a marriage by petition to the superior court when incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and the conditions of AS 25.24.200 are satisfied. Under AS 25.24.210, the petition must be filed with the superior court, must recite the relevant conditions, must be signed and verified by the petitioner, and must state in detail the terms of the agreement between the spouses, or the positions of the parties, concerning custody, child support, visitation, spousal maintenance, and the division of property. AS 25.24.220 governs the hearing, at which the court examines the petitioner and considers whether the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action and whether the terms of any proposed agreements are just, fair, and in the best interests of the children.
B. Child Custody Modification
Under AS 25.20.110, an existing custody award may be modified when a change of circumstances requires modification and modification is in the best interests of the child. Where a parent opposes modification and modification is nonetheless granted, the court must enter its reasons on the record. The statute also establishes that a finding of domestic violence occurring since the last custody determination constitutes a change of circumstances as a matter of law.
C. Child Support
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), when one parent has primary physical custody, the support obligation equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a percentage that depends on the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27%. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), when parents share physical custody, a different formula applies that accounts for the percentage of time each parent has physical custody. The court retains authority to impute income to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably underemployed, and may vary from the formula only for good cause, upon clear and convincing evidence that a strict application would result in manifest injustice.
D. Property Division
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the court shall divide marital property in a just manner, based on consideration of multiple factors including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, earning capacity, financial condition, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the time and manner of acquisition of the property. Agreements on property division and spousal maintenance must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution and must take into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). AS 25.24.200(a)(3).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD RENEE PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF THE CHILDREN DURING THE SCHOOL YEAR BECAUSE THAT ARRANGEMENT BEST SERVES THE CHILDREN'S INTERESTS AND REFLECTS THE REALITY OF THEIR ESTABLISHED ROUTINES.
The paramount consideration in any child custody determination is the best interests of the children. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that continuity and stability in a child's living environment are critical factors in any custody analysis. See Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004). The court must also consider each parent's ability and desire to allow a loving, frequent relationship between the child and the other parent, as well as the practical realities of each parent's schedule and availability.
Renee has been the primary day-to-day caregiver for the children throughout the marriage, and particularly during the approximately two years of escalating conflict when Wesley's North Slope rotation kept him away from Anchorage for two-week intervals at a time. The children attend school in Anchorage, have established friendships, and are rooted in their community. Granting primary physical custody to Renee during the school year preserves that continuity. It ensures that the children have a stable, consistent home base with a parent who is present and available throughout the school week, rather than a rotating schedule that requires them to adapt to a different custodial structure every two weeks.
Wesley's proposed 50/50 schedule, structured around his two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off North Slope rotation, is logistically problematic and not in the children's best interests. When Wesley is on the North Slope, he is not available to exercise physical custody at all. A 50/50 schedule nominally assigned to Wesley would therefore, in practice, require either a third-party caregiver to cover his two-week absences or repeated disruption to the children's schedule. Neither outcome serves the children.
Renee's proposal, by contrast, is honest and workable. Wesley would have alternating-weekend visitation when he is off rotation and four weeks of summer parenting time, giving him meaningful, consistent contact with the children during periods when he is actually available to parent. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002) that custody agreements are not binding on the court and that the court must independently determine the arrangement that best serves the child's interests. Renee's proposal reflects the children's best interests in light of the actual realities of both parents' schedules and the children's established lives in Anchorage.
Furthermore, AS 25.24.220(d)(2) requires the court to consider whether any written agreements concerning child custody and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.220(h) calls for heightened scrutiny when there is a minor child of the marriage, and the children here are both minors. Under that heightened scrutiny, the Court should carefully examine whether Wesley's proposed schedule, which is structured around his employment rotation rather than the children's needs, truly serves those children. It does not. The Court should award Renee primary physical custody during the school year, with meaningful visitation to Wesley consistent with his actual availability.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON WESLEY'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME, AND HIS PROPOSED DEDUCTIONS FOR TRAVEL AND A SECOND RESIDENCE ARE NOT AUTHORIZED BY THE RULE.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) establishes a straightforward formula for child support when one parent holds primary physical custody. The non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income is multiplied by a set percentage: for two children, that figure is 27%. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999) that variation from this formula is permitted only for good cause, upon clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result from strict application of the rule, and that such variation must focus first and foremost on the needs of the children.
Wesley's income as a pipeline technician is not in dispute. He earns substantially more than Renee. The Rule 90.3(a)(1) framework specifies the categories of deductions that are authorized in calculating adjusted annual income, including mandatory taxes, Social Security and Medicare contributions, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and certain other enumerated items. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1). Work-related travel costs and the voluntary expense of maintaining a second personal residence near a job site are not among the authorized deductions. Wesley cannot reduce his child support obligation simply because his employment requires him to travel to the North Slope or because he has chosen to lease housing near the Slope for personal convenience.
The Alaska Supreme Court addressed the importance of the Rule 90.3 formula's predictability and adequacy in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), noting that two primary purposes of the formula are to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children and to make awards predictable and consistent. Allowing Wesley to reduce his obligation based on voluntary lifestyle expenses associated with his employment would undermine both of those purposes and would shift financial burden onto Renee and, ultimately, the children.
The Court should also consider that Wesley's higher earning capacity is itself a relevant factor. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4), the court may impute potential income to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably underemployed. The inverse principle is equally important: the court should not artificially deflate a high-earning parent's actual income through non-authorized deductions. If the Court applies the 27% formula to Wesley's properly calculated adjusted annual income, the result will be a fair and lawful child support award. If the parties cannot agree on the exact income figure, Renee requests that the Court require full financial disclosure and calculate adjusted annual income strictly in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Should the Court instead accept Wesley's proposed 50/50 custody schedule, which Renee opposes for the reasons stated in Section IV.A above, the shared physical custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b) would apply. Under that formula, each parent's hypothetical obligation to the other is calculated under paragraph (a), each figure is then multiplied by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and the parent with the larger resulting figure becomes the obligor parent. Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(A)-(C). Even under that calculation, given the significant disparity in the parties' incomes, Wesley would owe a meaningful child support obligation to Renee. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Rowen v. Rowen, 963 P.2d 249 (Alaska 1998) that the Rule 90.3(b) formula is applied flexibly but that conclusory claims of unfairness do not overcome a properly structured award.
C. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD RENEE THE MARITAL HOME IN EXCHANGE FOR HER ASSUMPTION OF THE JOINT CREDIT CARD DEBT BECAUSE THAT ARRANGEMENT IS JUST, ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION FAIRLY, AND SERVES THE CHILDREN'S INTEREST IN STABILITY.
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the court divides marital property in a just manner, taking into consideration a list of enumerated factors. Among those factors is the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of the children. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F). This factor is directly applicable here. If the Court awards primary physical custody to Renee, as Renee requests and as is in the children's best interests, then the family home should follow the children. Disrupting the children from their home, their neighborhood, and their community would compound the already significant upheaval of their parents' dissolution.
The property division Renee proposes is straightforward and fair. The marital home carries approximately $85,000 in equity. The joint credit card debt, incurred during the marriage, totals $22,000. Renee proposes to receive the home and to assume the entire $22,000 credit card obligation, netting her approximately $63,000 in value after subtracting the debt she would absorb. Wesley would be relieved of the $22,000 obligation entirely. The effective allocation would give Renee approximately $63,000 in net value and Wesley approximately $22,000 in debt relief, plus whatever other marital assets exist and are distributed separately. This is a reasonable and equitable arrangement given the factors in AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
The Alaska Supreme Court addressed the multi-factor property division framework in Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996), recognizing the full scope of considerations the court must weigh, including the time and manner of acquisition, the financial condition of the parties, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division. Applying those factors here: the home was acquired during the marriage and is unquestionably marital property; Renee's financial condition is materially weaker than Wesley's given the income disparity; and Wesley's higher earning capacity means he can replace housing value over time in a way that Renee, who earns significantly less and will bear the primary cost of raising the children, cannot.
AS 25.24.200(a)(3) requires that property division agreements be fair and just and take into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4) so that the economic effect of dissolution is fairly allocated. The Alaska Supreme Court in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019) affirmed that courts properly consider disparities in earning capacity when dividing property, recognizing that a party with lower earning capacity is at a structural economic disadvantage following dissolution. Renee is in precisely that position. Her proposal gives the children a stable home, gives Wesley a clean financial break from the mortgage and the credit card debt, and distributes the economic consequences of dissolution in a manner that accounts for the parties' very different financial positions going forward.
Wesley's proposal of an immediate sale and equal division of proceeds would net each party approximately $31,500 in equity before transaction costs, but would force Renee and the children out of their home, expose Renee to half of the $22,000 credit card debt with less income to service it, and leave the children without a stable residential anchor during an already difficult transition. That outcome is neither just nor consistent with the AS 25.24.160(a)(4) factors, particularly subparagraph (F) regarding the desirability of awarding the home to the primary custodial parent.
D. THE DISSOLUTION PETITION SATISFIES THE STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS AND THE COURT SHOULD CONDUCT THE HEARING WITH THE HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY WARRANTED BY THE PRESENCE OF MINOR CHILDREN.
AS 25.24.210 requires that the petition state in detail the terms of the parties' positions concerning custody, child support, visitation, and property division, as well as specified background information about the parties and children. AS 25.24.210(e). The petition filed in this matter satisfies those requirements.
At the hearing, AS 25.24.220(d) directs the court to consider, among other things, whether the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action and whether written agreements concerning child custody, support, and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children. Because the parties have minor children, AS 25.24.220(h)(3) mandates that the court apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the parties' agreements. Under that heightened scrutiny, AS 25.24.220(i) directs the court to examine the written agreements to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that custody, support, and visitation arrangements are in the best interests of the children of the marriage.
Renee submits that her proposed resolution on all three contested issues satisfies that heightened standard. The custody arrangement she proposes is grounded in the children's actual day-to-day needs and their established lives in Anchorage. The child support calculation she requests follows the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula without deviation and without unauthorized reductions. The property settlement she proposes fairly allocates the economic consequences of dissolution in light of the parties' income disparity and the children's need for residential stability.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Larsen respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Award Renee primary physical custody of the two minor children during the school year, with Wesley receiving alternating-weekend visitation when he is off his North Slope rotation and four weeks of summer parenting time, consistent with the children's best interests under AS 25.24.220(d)(2) and AS 25.20.110;
2. Calculate child support pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on Wesley's adjusted annual income as properly calculated under the Rule, applying the 27% multiplier for two children, and reject Wesley's proposed deductions for travel costs and a secondary residence as not authorized by the Rule;
3. Award Renee the marital home and its approximately $85,000 in equity, with Renee assuming the full $22,000 joint credit card obligation, as a just and equitable division of the marital estate consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and AS 25.24.200(a)(3); and
4. Apply heightened scrutiny at the dissolution hearing as required by AS 25.24.220(h)(3) and (i) given the presence of minor children, and enter findings that the proposed custody, support, and property arrangements are just and in the best interests of the children.
Renee Larsen respectfully submits that the relief requested herein is supported by Alaska law, consistent with the facts of this case, and in the best interests of the parties' children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0016)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, on the petition for dissolution of marriage filed by David Bergstrom. The parties, David Bergstrom and Danielle Bergstrom, were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. After approximately ten years of marriage, the parties have experienced an irremediable breakdown of their marriage due to irreconcilable differences arising from financial stress and sustained conflict over parenting decisions.
The parties have reached a tentative agreement on the major issues presented by this dissolution, including physical and legal custody of the minor children, child support, division of the marital home located in Eagle River, and allocation of marital debt. This brief is submitted to assist the Court in evaluating whether the proposed agreements satisfy the requirements of Alaska law and to provide a framework for the Court's analysis of the relevant statutory factors and applicable case law.
As set forth herein, the proposed custody arrangement serves the best interests of the children, the proposed child support amount is consistent with the Alaska Civil Rules, the proposed property division fairly allocates the economic effect of this dissolution, and the proposed debt allocation is just under the circumstances.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Bergstrom and Danielle Bergstrom were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. The parties are the parents of two minor children born of the marriage, currently ages six and nine. The marriage has deteriorated over the past two years due to financial stress and prolonged conflict over parenting decisions, resulting in an irremediable breakdown of the marital relationship. David filed a petition for dissolution in the Alaska Superior Court, Family Division.
David is employed as a commercial electrician and earns approximately $82,000 per year. Danielle works part-time as a dental hygienist and earns approximately $36,000 per year. During the marriage, the parties jointly acquired a residential home located in Eagle River, Alaska. The home carries an estimated market value of approximately $295,000 and is encumbered by a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, yielding an estimated equity of approximately $85,000. The parties also accumulated approximately $28,000 in shared credit card debt during the marriage.
The parties have reached a tentative agreement on the following terms. Danielle would receive primary physical custody of both minor children. David would exercise parenting time on alternating weekends and one evening per week. The parties would share joint legal custody, conferring jointly on major decisions regarding the children's education, healthcare, and general well-being. David proposes to pay $1,400 per month in child support. David further proposes to retain the Eagle River home by refinancing it solely in his own name and to compensate Danielle for her share of the equity through a cash payment at closing. The parties have yet to finalize allocation of the approximately $28,000 in marital credit card debt.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.200, a petition for dissolution may be granted where, among other conditions, the parties establish that incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, that they have agreed on custody, support, and visitation of their minor children, and that they have agreed on a fair and just distribution of all real and personal property, spousal maintenance if any, and allocation of debts. The agreement on property division must take into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.908(a)(2) and (4) so that the economic effect of dissolution is fairly allocated.
At the dissolution hearing, the Court is required under AS 25.24.220 to examine the petitioners and consider whether: the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action; the written agreements on child custody, child support, and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children; the written agreements relating to property division, spousal maintenance, and allocation of obligations are just; and the written agreements constitute the entire agreement between the parties.
With respect to child support, Civil Rule 90.3(a) establishes the method for calculating support in cases where one parent has primary physical custody, providing that the award shall be calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which is 27% for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(b) addresses cases of shared, divided, or hybrid custody and provides an alternative calculation methodology where applicable.
With respect to property division, AS 25.24.986(4) requires that the division of property be just and fairly allocate the economic effect of the dissolution based on consideration of enumerated statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, their earning capacities, their financial conditions, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
Under Civil Rule 90.1(e), in divorce cases involving property division disputes, the parties are required to file and serve a property division table not fewer than five days before trial, including a list of all assets and liabilities, their characterization as marital or separate property, their values, and each party's proposed disposition.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that trial courts have broad discretion in fashioning property divisions and will not disturb such a division unless it is clearly unjust. Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010). Similarly, the Court has recognized that equitable division does not require mathematical equality but rather a fair allocation of the economic consequences of the dissolution. Green v. Green, 29 P.3d 854 (Alaska 2001).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT SERVES THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE MINOR CHILDREN AND SATISFIES THE REQUIREMENTS OF ALASKA LAW.
Under AS 25.24.905(2), the Court must determine whether the written agreements between the spouses concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the spouses and in the best interests of the children of the marriage. The proposed arrangement designates Danielle as the primary physical custodian of both minor children, with David exercising parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week, and the parties sharing joint legal custody with joint decision-making authority over education, healthcare, and general well-being. This arrangement is consistent with the children's best interests and should be approved.
Alaska courts consider a range of factors when evaluating custody arrangements. AS 25.20.090 identifies the relevant considerations for shared custody determinations, including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the education of the child, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
The proposed arrangement addresses these concerns appropriately. Danielle, as primary physical custodian, will provide a stable and continuous home environment for the children in the Eagle River community where they currently reside. David's regular parenting time on alternating weekends and one evening per week maintains a meaningful and ongoing relationship between the children and their father. The joint legal custody provision ensures that both parents remain actively involved in the most significant decisions affecting their children's lives, including those concerning education and healthcare. This structure reflects a genuine commitment on the part of both parties to cooperative co-parenting and serves the developmental needs of children ages six and nine.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized the importance of stability and continuity in custody arrangements, as well as the value of maintaining children in familiar community settings. Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004). The proposed plan reflects these principles by keeping both children in their current community and school environment while providing regular, predictable contact with both parents.
B. THE PROPOSED CHILD SUPPORT AMOUNT OF $1,400 PER MONTH IS CONSISTENT WITH THE ALASKA CIVIL RULES AND SHOULD BE APPROVED.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of child support in cases involving primary physical custody. Under that rule, the child support award is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27%.
David earns approximately $82,000 per year as a commercial electrician. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), adjusted annual income is calculated by subtracting from total income mandatory deductions such as federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, and other qualifying deductions. A reasonable estimate of David's mandatory deductions, including federal income tax, Social Security tax at 6.2%, and Medicare tax at 1.45%, would reduce his gross income to an adjusted annual income in the approximate range of $62,000 to $66,000, depending on his specific filing status and applicable deductions. Applying the 27% multiplier for two children to an adjusted annual income of approximately $62,400 yields an annual child support obligation of approximately $16,848, or roughly $1,404 per month. The parties' proposed monthly support figure of $1,400 is therefore consistent with the guidelines calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) and should be approved.
Danielle's income of approximately $36,000 per year as a part-time dental hygienist does not reduce David's obligation under the primary custody formula, but it is a relevant consideration in confirming that the proposed support amount appropriately accounts for each parent's financial capacity to contribute to the children's needs. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that child support awards must be grounded in a realistic assessment of each parent's financial circumstances. Barnett v. Barnett, 238 P.3d 594 (Alaska 2010).
To the extent any question arises regarding whether David may be voluntarily underemployed or whether Danielle's part-time employment warrants imputation of additional income, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits the court to calculate support based on potential income of a parent who voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed. There is no indication in this case that either parent's income reflects anything other than their actual employment circumstances, and no imputation of income appears warranted.
C. THE PROPOSED DIVISION OF THE MARITAL HOME FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF THIS DISSOLUTION UNDER AS 25.24.160.
The parties acquired the Eagle River home jointly during the marriage. It represents the most significant marital asset subject to division. David proposes to retain the home by refinancing it solely in his name and to compensate Danielle for her proportionate share of the equity through a cash payment at closing. With an estimated market value of $295,000 and a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, the estimated equity is approximately $85,000. A cash payment to Danielle representing her equal share, approximately $42,500, would provide each party with an equal division of the marital equity.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires that the division of property fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce and directs the court to consider, among other factors: the length of the marriage and the station in life of the parties during the marriage; the age and health of the parties; their earning capacities; their financial conditions; the desirability of awarding the family home or the right to live in it for a reasonable period to the party who has primary physical custody of the children; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property; and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
Applying these factors to the present case supports approval of the proposed arrangement. First, the parties were married for approximately ten years, a moderate-length marriage that supports an approximately equal division of marital assets. Second, David's earning capacity as a commercial electrician at $82,000 per year is substantially greater than Danielle's current part-time income of $36,000 per year, which is relevant to his ability to refinance the home on his own and to make a cash equity payment to Danielle at closing. Third, Danielle will be the primary physical custodian of both minor children. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), the court is directed to consider the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody. Although this factor would ordinarily suggest awarding the home to Danielle, the parties have reached a mutual agreement that David will retain the home and compensate Danielle with a cash payment. Provided the cash payment is fair and sufficient to allow Danielle to secure alternative housing appropriate for herself and the children, this deviation from the default preference is permissible. Fourth, both parties acquired the home jointly during the marriage, and no claim of separate property in the residence has been asserted.
The Alaska Supreme Court has upheld property divisions that employ cash equalization payments as a mechanism to balance the allocation of a major asset retained by one spouse, provided the overall division is just and the economic consequences are fairly allocated. Beal v. Beal, 209 P.3d 1012 (Alaska 2009); Green v. Green, 29 P.3d 854 (Alaska 2001). The proposed arrangement accomplishes this objective here, so long as the cash payment to Danielle is sufficient to represent her actual equity share and is tendered at or before the closing of the refinancing.
The Court should further ensure, consistent with Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014), that the home is properly and independently valued before the cash equalization payment is fixed. The estimated market value of $295,000 appears to be an informal estimate. The Court should require confirmation of the home's market value, ideally through an independent appraisal, to ensure that Danielle's equity payment is grounded in an accurate figure and not a speculative or understated valuation.
D. THE ALLOCATION OF MARITAL CREDIT CARD DEBT MUST FAIRLY DISTRIBUTE THE ECONOMIC BURDEN OF OBLIGATIONS INCURRED DURING THE MARRIAGE.
The parties accumulated approximately $28,000 in shared credit card debt during the marriage. Under AS 25.24.200(a)(4), the spouses must agree as to the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both of them as a condition of obtaining a dissolution decree. The proposed agreement must address this debt with specificity.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires that the division of property, which encompasses the allocation of liabilities as well as assets, fairly allocate the economic effect of the dissolution. In evaluating a just allocation of the marital debt, the Court should consider each party's earning capacity, financial condition, and ability to service the debt obligations. David's gross annual income of $82,000 is substantially greater than Danielle's $36,000 annual income. Equalizing the parties' overall economic positions at dissolution favors assigning a proportionately greater share of the marital debt to David, particularly if David is retaining the home and its associated benefits.
One approach that is fair under the circumstances would be to divide the $28,000 in credit card debt equally, with each party assuming $14,000, and to treat each party's assumption of debt as an offset against their respective shares of the marital estate. Alternatively, if the parties agree that David will assume the entire debt balance, that assumption could be treated as an additional offset reducing the cash equity payment owed to Danielle at closing. Any allocation must be reflected clearly in the written dissolution agreement to ensure compliance with AS 25.24.200(a)(4) and to provide the Court a sufficient basis for its review under AS 25.24.220(d)(3).
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that trial courts must address debt allocation explicitly and that inequitable assignments of marital debt may render a property division clearly unjust. Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010). The parties should be prepared to present a clear and final agreed allocation of the credit card debt at the dissolution hearing.
E. THE COURT SHOULD APPLY HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY AS APPROPRIATE AND CONFIRM THAT THE PARTIES FULLY UNDERSTAND THE NATURE AND CONSEQUENCES OF THEIR AGREEMENT.
Under AS 25.24.220(d), the Court is required to examine the petitioners and consider whether the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action and whether the written agreements constitute the entire agreement between the parties. Under AS 25.24.220(h), the Court must apply heightened scrutiny if one party is unrepresented, if there is a minor child of the marriage, or if the division of the marital estate is patently inequitable.
Because this dissolution involves two minor children, the Court is required by AS 25.24.220(h)(3) to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the parties' agreements. That scrutiny requires the Court to confirm that the agreements are just, that they constitute the entire agreement, and that the custody, support, and visitation provisions are in the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.220(i).
The petitioner respectfully submits that the proposed agreements, as presented in this brief, satisfy this standard. The custody arrangement promotes the children's stability and maintains meaningful contact with both parents. The support amount is consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a). The property division provides for an equitable split of marital equity through a cash payment mechanism, and the debt allocation, once finalized, should be expressly reflected in the written agreement. The parties should be prepared at the dissolution hearing to confirm on the record their full understanding of each term and their voluntary consent to the agreement in its entirety, consistent with the requirements of AS 25.24.200(c).
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the proposed dissolution agreement between David Bergstrom and Danielle Bergstrom satisfies the requirements of Alaska law governing dissolution proceedings, child custody, child support, and property division. The proposed primary physical custody arrangement with Danielle and regular parenting time for David serves the best interests of the minor children and reflects the statutory factors set forth in AS 25.20.090. The proposed child support amount of $1,400 per month is consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) as applied to David's adjusted annual income. The proposed cash equalization payment to compensate Danielle for her equity in the marital home represents a just division of marital property under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), provided the home's value is confirmed by an independent appraisal. The parties must finalize and expressly state the allocation of the $28,000 in marital credit card debt in the written dissolution agreement to satisfy AS 25.24.200(a)(4).
Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court approve the dissolution petition and enter a final decree of dissolution incorporating the terms of the parties' agreement as refined and confirmed at the hearing.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0017)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Petrova ("Petitioner") respectfully submits this brief in support of the parties' petition for dissolution of marriage filed pursuant to AS 25.24.200. Marcus and Jennifer Petrova ("Respondent") have been married since June 14, 2014, and are the parents of two minor children. After approximately two years of marital deterioration marked by chronic communication breakdown, financial stress, and irreconcilable differences in parenting philosophy, the parties have reached a tentative agreement addressing all material issues required under Alaska law, including child custody, child support, and the division of marital property and debt.
The proposed agreement reflects the parties' good-faith effort to reach a resolution that serves the best interests of their children, equitably distributes the marital estate, and fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution. The parties submit this brief to assist the Court in evaluating whether the conditions of AS 25.24.200 have been satisfied and whether the proposed terms meet the statutory standards for a final decree of dissolution under AS 25.24.230.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Petrova, age 38, and Jennifer Petrova, age 35, were married on June 14, 2014, in Anchorage, Alaska. The marriage produced two minor children: a daughter, age 8, and a son, age 6. Both children currently reside in the family home located in Eagle River, Alaska.
Over approximately the past two years, the marriage suffered an irremediable breakdown caused by chronic communication difficulties, financial pressures arising from Marcus's reduced work hours in the oil and gas sector, and persistent disagreements concerning parenting decisions. These combined circumstances rendered the marriage irretrievably broken due to incompatibility of temperament, satisfying the threshold condition set forth in AS 25.24.987(1).
The parties have reached a tentative settlement agreement addressing all issues required for dissolution. With respect to the minor children, the parties have agreed to joint legal custody of both children, with Jennifer serving as the primary physical custodian during the school week at the Eagle River family home. Marcus will exercise parenting time every other weekend and one weeknight per week. Marcus agrees to pay $1,200 per month in child support, a figure the parties represent is consistent with the guidelines established under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
The marital estate consists of the following assets and liabilities:
(1) The family home in Eagle River, valued at approximately $385,000, with a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, reflecting a net equity of approximately $175,000.
(2) Two vehicles, including a truck retained by Marcus and a vehicle retained by Jennifer.
(3) A joint savings account holding approximately $18,000.
(4) Approximately $24,000 in shared credit card debt.
Under the proposed property division, Jennifer will retain the family home and assume sole responsibility for the outstanding mortgage. Marcus will retain his truck and will receive a negotiated portion of the joint savings account designed to offset his share of the home equity, thereby achieving a roughly equitable distribution of the net marital estate. The parties have also allocated responsibility for the shared credit card debt as part of the overall agreement.
Marcus filed the dissolution petition with the Superior Court for the Third Judicial District. The parties submit that the proposed agreement satisfies all substantive requirements of Alaska law governing dissolution and respectfully request that the Court approve the agreement and enter a final decree of dissolution.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Governing Dissolution Statute
Under AS 25.24.200(a), a husband and wife may jointly petition for dissolution of their marriage if, at the time of filing: (1) incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage; (2) if there are unmarried children of the marriage under age 19, the spouses have agreed on custody, visitation, and child support; (3) the spouses have agreed as to the distribution of all real and personal property and spousal maintenance, with the agreement being fair and just and taking into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4); and (4) the spouses have agreed as to the payment of all unpaid obligations.
B. Standards for Entry of Decree
Under AS 25.24.230(a), the Court may grant a final decree of dissolution upon finding that: the spouses fully understand the nature and consequences of their action; the written agreements on property division and obligations are fair and just and constitute the entire agreement; the property division fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution and takes into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4); each spouse entered into the agreement voluntarily and free from coercion; and the conditions of AS 25.24.200(a) have been met.
Because the parties have a minor child of the marriage, AS 25.24.905(3) requires the Court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny when examining the written agreements. Under AS 25.24.220(i), where heightened scrutiny applies, the Court shall examine the agreements to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that the child custody, support, and visitation agreements are in the best interest of the children of the marriage.
Under AS 25.24.949, where the petition is subject to AS 25.24.220(h), the Court may grant a final decree upon finding, among other requirements, that the written agreements on child custody, child support, and visitation are in the best interest of the children of the marriage, are just as between the spouses, and constitute the entire agreement of the parties on those subjects.
C. Child Support Guidelines
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs child support awards in cases of primary physical custody. Under that rule, the child support award is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a specified percentage, which is 27% for two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). "Adjusted annual income" as used in this rule means "the parent's total income from all sources minus under all circumstances" certain enumerated deductions.
D. Property Division Factors
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) directs the Court to divide property in a just manner, based on consideration of factors including: the length of the marriage; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties; the financial condition of the parties; the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property; and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a property division need not be precisely equal to be lawful; rather, the division must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution based on the totality of relevant statutory factors. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996). Courts retain broad discretion in fashioning a just division, and agreements reached by the parties are entitled to careful consideration, though the Court must independently satisfy itself that the terms are just. Richard v. Boggs, 162 P.3d 629 (Alaska 2007). The valuation of marital property, including the family home, is properly assessed at the time of the relevant proceedings. Beals v. Beals, 303 P.3d 453 (Alaska 2013).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PARTIES HAVE SATISFIED THE THRESHOLD CONDITIONS FOR DISSOLUTION UNDER AS 25.24.200(a)
The parties satisfy all threshold conditions for a joint petition for dissolution under AS 25.24.200(a). First, incompatibility of temperament, manifested through two years of chronic communication breakdown, financial strain, and irreconcilable parenting differences, has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. This satisfies the foundational requirement of AS 25.24.200(a)(1).
Second, the parties have reached a written agreement addressing custody, visitation, and child support for both minor children, satisfying AS 25.24.200(a)(2). The agreement provides for joint legal custody, primary physical placement with Jennifer during the school week, and a defined parenting time schedule for Marcus.
Third, the parties have agreed as to the distribution of all real and personal property, including the family home, vehicles, savings account, and credit card debt, satisfying AS 25.24.200(a)(3). The agreement takes into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4) and is designed to fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution, as required by AS 25.24.200(e).
Fourth, the parties have agreed as to the allocation of all unpaid obligations, including the mortgage and shared credit card debt, satisfying AS 25.24.200(a)(4).
B. THE PROPOSED CHILD SUPPORT AMOUNT IS CONSISTENT WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) AND SHOULD BE APPROVED
The parties have agreed that Marcus will pay $1,200 per month in child support. Because Jennifer has primary physical custody of both children, Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of the support obligation. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), the applicable percentage for two children is 27% of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. The agreed monthly support figure of $1,200, representing $14,400 annually, is consistent with this guideline framework.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that child support calculations under Civil Rule 90.3 must be grounded in an accurate determination of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income, taking into account all permissible deductions. Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019). Marcus's reduced work hours in the oil and gas sector have affected his income, and the agreed support amount reflects the parties' good-faith effort to apply the Rule 90.3(a) framework to the financial realities of this family. If the Court finds it necessary to independently verify the support calculation, Marcus is prepared to provide a completed Rule 90.3 child support schedule and supporting income documentation.
Courts may also consider whether a parent is voluntarily underemployed under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). Marcus's reduced hours stem from conditions in the oil and gas sector rather than a voluntary personal choice to reduce earnings, and therefore imputation of higher potential income is not appropriate in this case.
Because the parties have agreed on primary physical custody with Jennifer, Civil Rule 90.3(b), which governs shared, divided, or hybrid custody arrangements, does not apply to the base child support calculation here. However, the parties' agreement also provides Marcus with parenting time every other weekend and one weeknight per week. This parenting schedule does not rise to the level of shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(b), so the primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) correctly governs.
C. THE PROPOSED PROPERTY DIVISION FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION AND SATISFIES AS 25.24.160(a)(4)
The proposed property division is designed to fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution in accordance with AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and the factors identified therein. The marital estate, reduced to its net value, consists primarily of the family home equity of approximately $175,000, two vehicles, approximately $18,000 in savings, and approximately $24,000 in shared debt. The parties' total net marital estate is therefore approximately $169,000 after subtracting the credit card debt from other liquid and real property assets.
Under the proposed agreement, Jennifer retains the family home and assumes sole responsibility for the existing mortgage. This allocation serves the factor set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), which calls for consideration of "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." Jennifer is the primary physical custodian of both minor children during the school week, and continuity of the children's residence in the Eagle River home promotes their stability and well-being.
To offset Marcus's equity share in the home, Marcus will receive his truck and a negotiated portion of the joint savings account. This approach is consistent with the principle that courts should fashion a just division based on the totality of the statutory factors rather than demanding mathematical equality. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that parties may reach agreements that depart from a strict 50/50 split of the marital estate when they provide a reasonable explanation for the allocation and the overall result is just. Richard v. Boggs, 162 P.3d 629 (Alaska 2007).
In assessing the fairness of the division, the Court should also consider the following factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4):
(A) Length and station of the marriage. The parties were married for approximately ten years. This is a mid-length marriage in which both parties contributed to the acquisition of marital assets, including the family home purchased during the marriage.
(B) Age and health of the parties. Marcus is 38 and Jennifer is 35. Both are relatively young and do not present health factors that would significantly skew the equitable division in either direction.
(C) Earning capacity. Marcus has historically worked in the oil and gas sector, an industry subject to cyclical employment volatility. His reduced hours have constrained his near-term income. Jennifer's earning capacity must also be considered in the context of her primary custodial responsibilities for the two minor children. The Alaska Supreme Court has acknowledged that disparities in earning capacity between spouses are a legitimate consideration in property division. Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019).
(D) Financial condition of the parties. Jennifer will bear the ongoing cost of the mortgage on the family home, reducing her available financial resources. Marcus will not carry mortgage debt following dissolution. The allocation of the savings account portion to Marcus is intended to provide him with capital to establish a separate household and address near-term financial needs.
(E) Circumstances and necessities of each party. Jennifer's primary custodial role requires stable housing for the children. Marcus requires sufficient resources to secure alternative housing and resume financial stability following job market challenges in his sector.
(F) Time and manner of acquisition. The family home was acquired during the marriage and constitutes marital property subject to equitable division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
(G) Income-producing capacity and value at time of division. The home is valued at approximately $385,000 at the time of the dissolution proceeding. Beals v. Beals, 303 P.3d 453 (Alaska 2013), confirms that the time of the relevant proceeding is the appropriate valuation date.
The allocation of the $24,000 in shared credit card debt must also be addressed as part of the overall settlement. The parties have agreed on responsibility for these obligations as part of the comprehensive dissolution agreement, consistent with AS 25.24.200(a)(4). The Court should confirm that the debt allocation, when considered alongside the asset division, results in a distribution that fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution across both parties.
D. THE HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY STANDARD UNDER AS 25.24.220(h) IS SATISFIED
Because the parties have minor children, the Court is required by AS 25.24.220(h)(3) to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the written agreements. Under AS 25.24.220(i), the Court must examine whether the agreements are just, constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and whether the child-related terms are in the best interests of the children.
The parties submit that the proposed agreement satisfies this standard. The child custody arrangement provides both parents with meaningful involvement in the lives of the children. Jennifer's role as primary physical custodian during the school week provides the children with residential stability and continuity of schooling. Marcus's parenting schedule, consisting of alternating weekends and one weeknight per week, ensures that the children maintain a regular and predictable relationship with their father.
Joint legal custody reflects the parties' shared commitment to cooperative parenting and their recognition that both parents should participate in major decisions affecting the children's education, health care, and general welfare. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that arrangements preserving both parents' involvement in a child's life, when agreed to voluntarily and in good faith, warrant approval. Barnett v. Barnett, 238 P.3d 594 (Alaska 2010).
The child support obligation of $1,200 per month ensures that Marcus continues to contribute materially to the children's nurture and education, consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(1). F. THE AGREEMENT WAS ENTERED INTO VOLUNTARILY AND FREE FROM COERCION
AS 25.24.230(a)(4) requires that each spouse entered into the agreement voluntarily and free from the coercion of another person. THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN

I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Okafor ("Petitioner") respectfully submits this brief in support of her requests for child custody, child support, and equitable division of the marital estate following the irretrievable breakdown of her marriage to Danielle Okafor ("Respondent"). II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Okafor and Danielle Okafor were married on or about 2015 in Anchorage, Alaska. The parties have two minor children born of the marriage: one child currently age nine and one child currently age six. Throughout the marriage, the parties resided together in Eagle River, Alaska and jointly managed their household finances and parenting responsibilities.
Beginning in early 2023, the marriage suffered an irretrievable breakdown caused by prolonged and irreconcilable conflict over finances and fundamentally divergent parenting priorities. The parties have been unable to reconcile their differences. Petitioner now seeks dissolution of the marriage and appropriate orders governing the welfare of the minor children and the disposition of marital property.
Petitioner Ashley Okafor is the primary caregiver for the two children and proposes a parenting arrangement under which the children reside with her during the school week. She proposes that Respondent Danielle Okafor have parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week, with holidays alternating annually between the parties.
Respondent Danielle Okafor is employed as a licensed electrician with a reported annual income of approximately $72,000. The parties' marital estate includes the following:
1. The family home located in Eagle River, Alaska, purchased in 2017. The home carries a mortgage balance of approximately $210,000 against an estimated fair market value of $310,000, representing an estimated equity of approximately $100,000.
2. Two motor vehicles, the specific values and encumbrances of which the parties have not agreed upon.
3. A joint savings account holding approximately $18,000.
4. Shared credit card debt of approximately $9,500.
The parties have been unable to resolve any of these financial issues through informal negotiation, and they submit these matters to the Court for equitable resolution.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.160, in a divorce action the Court may provide for the payment of child support, the award of spousal maintenance, and the division of marital property between the parties. The statute directs that a division of property must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce based on consideration of enumerated statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, and the desirability of awarding the family home to the party who has primary physical custody of the children.
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3, which establishes a formula for calculating support based on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that a child support award in a case in which one parent has primary physical custody shall equal the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a specified percentage: twenty percent for one child, twenty-seven percent for two children, and thirty-three percent for three children. Where parents share physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies an alternate calculation methodology.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the Rule 90.3 formula exists to ensure consistency and adequacy in child support awards, and that agreements deviating from the formula warrant careful judicial scrutiny. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Court affirmed a trial court's income determination for child support purposes based on a parent's work history, educational background, and current employment status. The Court has further held that child support must be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3 and that any deviation from the formula must be grounded in the specific circumstances of the case. Laughlin v. Laughlin, 229 P.3d 1002 (Alaska 2010); Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002).
With respect to property division, AS 25.24.160(a)(4) directs the Court to divide property acquired during the marriage in a just manner without regard to fault, and authorizes the Court to invade premarital property when the equities so require. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the Court must carefully scrutinize proposed property divisions to ensure they fairly allocate the economic consequences of the divorce. Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY WITH PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY IN PETITIONER, CONSISTENT WITH THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
The best interests of the two minor children support the custody arrangement proposed by Petitioner. Ashley Okafor has served as the primary caregiver throughout the children's lives and is best positioned to maintain the stability and continuity of care that children of ages six and nine require. Petitioner proposes that Respondent enjoy parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week, which provides meaningful and regular contact with both parents while centering the children's school-week routine in Petitioner's home.
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(1), the Court may provide for child support contributions as may be just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children. The proposed custody schedule awards primary physical custody to Petitioner while preserving Respondent's parenting relationship with the children. The proposed holiday alternation arrangement further supports the children's ongoing relationship with both parents throughout the year.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that custody agreements, including those presented by the parties, do not bind the Court, which must independently determine what arrangement best serves the children's interests. Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002). Here, Petitioner's proposed arrangement is firmly grounded in the children's demonstrated needs and the existing parental roles within the household.
B. THE COURT SHOULD CALCULATE DANIELLE OKAFOR'S CHILD SUPPORT OBLIGATION UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON HER ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME.
Because Petitioner proposes primary physical custody in her favor, Respondent's child support obligation is properly calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a). Civil Rule 90.3(a) directs that the award equal the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which is "27% (.27) for two children." Respondent Danielle Okafor reports gross annual income of approximately $72,000 as a licensed electrician. Her adjusted annual income for purposes of Rule 90.3 is her total income from all sources minus the mandatory and permissible deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including federal income tax, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory retirement contributions, and any qualifying health insurance premiums.
Applying the twenty-seven percent figure for two children to Respondent's adjusted annual income, Petitioner requests that the Court determine the precise adjusted annual income figure based on financial disclosures provided by Respondent and enter a child support order accordingly.
In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that a court's income determination for Rule 90.3 purposes based on the parent's work history, credentials, and current employment is appropriate. Respondent's status as a licensed electrician with a stable reported income of approximately $72,000 provides a clear factual basis for the Court's determination.
Where Respondent's income suggests financial capacity, the Court is also authorized under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to consider whether a parent is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed, and may impute potential income if the facts support such a finding. No such finding is requested at this time, as Respondent appears to be employed consistent with her qualifications. However, Petitioner reserves the right to request imputation should circumstances change.
The Alaska Supreme Court held in Laughlin v. Laughlin, 229 P.3d 1002 (Alaska 2010) that child support must be computed in accordance with Rule 90.3, and in Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002) that deviations from the formula require careful justification. No deviation is sought here. Petitioner simply requests that the Court apply the formula as written and order Respondent to pay the resulting amount in monthly installments.
Petitioner further requests that the Court order Respondent to contribute to the children's documented medical and extracurricular expenses on a pro-rata basis, consistent with the parties' respective adjusted annual incomes as determined by the Court. AS 25.24.160(a)(1) provides authority for the Court to require contributions toward the nurture and education of the children as may be just and proper.
C. THE COURT SHOULD EQUITABLY DIVIDE THE MARITAL ESTATE IN ACCORDANCE WITH AS 25.24.160(a)(4), AWARDING THE FAMILY HOME TO PETITIONER AS PRIMARY CUSTODIAL PARENT.
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the Court shall divide property acquired during the marriage in a just manner, giving consideration to all relevant statutory factors. Those factors include: the length of the marriage and station in life of the parties; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties; the financial condition of the parties, including the availability and cost of health insurance; the conduct of the parties, including any unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property; and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
1. The Family Home
The family home in Eagle River was purchased in 2017, during the marriage. It carries an estimated fair market value of $310,000 against a mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, yielding an equity interest of approximately $100,000. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically identifies as a relevant factor "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." Because Petitioner is the primary physical custodian of the parties' two school-age children, this factor weighs strongly in favor of awarding the family home to Petitioner, subject to an equalization payment or credit to Respondent for her share of the equity as the Court deems just.
The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed in Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014) that property division must be grounded in a fair and thorough analysis of the marital estate, and that courts must scrutinize agreements and proposed divisions to ensure they fairly allocate the economic consequences of divorce. Petitioner does not seek to deprive Respondent of her equitable share in the home but asks the Court to recognize the primacy of the children's interest in stability when allocating the home to the primary custodial parent.
2. The Vehicles
The parties own two vehicles acquired during the marriage. Petitioner requests that the Court assign each vehicle to the party currently in possession or best situated by need, and offset any difference in value against the parties' other equitable adjustments. The Court should apply the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the circumstances and necessities of each party and the value of the property at the time of division.
3. The Joint Savings Account
The parties hold a joint savings account with approximately $18,000. Petitioner proposes that these funds be divided equally between the parties, subject to any equitable adjustments the Court deems appropriate upon consideration of the factors in AS 25.24.160(a)(4). An equal division of liquid marital assets is consistent with the general presumption of equitable distribution and would allow both parties to address immediate post-dissolution financial needs.
4. Shared Credit Card Debt
The parties carry shared credit card debt of approximately $9,500. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the Court may allocate marital liabilities as part of a just division of the marital estate. Petitioner requests that the Court divide this debt equally between the parties, or in such proportion as the Court determines is just after consideration of each party's financial condition and earning capacity. Petitioner specifically requests that the Court include indemnification provisions in any order to protect each party from liability for the other's assigned share of the debt.
D. THE PROPOSED PROPERTY DIVISION FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF THE DIVORCE CONSISTENT WITH AS 25.24.160.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) directs that the division of property must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce based on consideration of the enumerated factors. Here, the parties were married for approximately eight years, a period of moderate length during which they jointly acquired the family home, vehicles, savings, and marital debt. Petitioner has served as primary caregiver for two young children, which has affected her professional opportunities and earning trajectory. Respondent has maintained steady employment as a licensed electrician with a reported annual income of approximately $72,000, reflecting a stronger current earning capacity than Petitioner.
These facts, considered alongside the statutory factors including earning capacity, financial condition, length of the marriage, and the necessities of each party, support the division Petitioner proposes. The family home should be awarded to Petitioner, as primary custodial parent of two school-age children, with appropriate credit to Respondent. Liquid assets should be equitably divided. Marital debt should be allocated proportionally or equally, with appropriate protections for each party.
In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed a trial court's property division that accounted for differences in the parties' earning capacity and the value of separate versus marital contributions. Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012) similarly illustrates the Court's approach of applying the Rule 90.3 framework and related financial analysis to ensure that custody and support orders, taken together with the property division, produce an economically fair outcome for both parties and, most importantly, for the children.
Petitioner respectfully submits that the overall division she proposes is just, grounded in the statutory factors, consistent with Alaska Supreme Court precedent, and carefully tailored to protect the well-being of the two minor children at the center of this proceeding.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Ashley Okafor respectfully requests that this Court enter orders:

2. Calculating Respondent Danielle Okafor's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on her adjusted annual income derived from her reported earnings of approximately $72,000, and ordering Respondent to pay support in monthly installments accordingly;
3. Ordering Respondent to contribute to the children's documented medical and extracurricular expenses on a pro-rata basis consistent with the parties' respective adjusted annual incomes;
4. Awarding the family home in Eagle River to Petitioner as primary custodial parent, subject to an equitable credit to Respondent for her share of the marital equity, consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4);
5. Dividing the joint savings account and two vehicles equitably between the parties;
6. Allocating the shared credit card debt of approximately $9,500 equally, or as the Court deems just, with mutual indemnification provisions; and
7. Granting such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper under AS 25.24.160.

THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN

II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
