III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska law provides that a superior court presiding over a dissolution proceeding shall examine the parties' agreements and the evidence to determine whether those agreements are just, whether they fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution, and whether child-related agreements serve the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.230. In making a property division, the court is authorized under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) to divide property "whether joint or separate, acquired only during marriage, in a just manner," and may apply a set of enumerated statutory factors in determining what division is equitable.
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Where one parent has primary physical custody, support is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the percentage specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). In a case where the parents share physical custody as defined by the rule, the formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies. The court retains the authority under Civil Rule 90.3(k) to allocate the dependent tax deduction for each child between the parties as is just and proper and in the child's best interests, with any such allocation being consistent with applicable federal law.
Regarding spousal maintenance, AS 25.24.160(a)(2) requires that any maintenance award "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" by reference to the factors enumerated in that section. Because no spousal maintenance is at issue here, the primary economic dispute centers on the equitable division of the marital retirement asset.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that property division and spousal support serve distinct purposes and are analyzed under separate statutory frameworks. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). Courts must independently assess each issue rather than use one to offset the other. Id. Courts are further guided by the principle that a just property division begins with a presumptively equal division of marital assets, subject to departure based on the statutory factors. Fletcher v. Fletcher, 433 P.3d 1148 (Alaska 2018).
In dissolution proceedings involving a pro se party and a represented party, AS 25.24.220(h) directs the court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the parties' agreements.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD ALLOCATE THE DEPENDENT TAX EXEMPTION FOR BOTH CHILDREN TO DAVID FOR ALTERNATING TAX YEARS, AS THIS ALLOCATION IS JUST AND IN THE CHILDREN'S BEST INTERESTS.
Civil Rule 90.3(k) provides that "the court may allocate the dependent tax deduction for each child between the parties as is just and proper and in the child's best interests." The allocation must also be consistent with applicable federal law. Civil Rule 90.3(k).
In this case, David will be paying child support and will bear sole responsibility for the approximately $8,400 joint credit card balance. He will also be responsible for maintaining adequate insurance coverage during the periods he has physical custody. An allocation of the dependent tax deduction to David for alternating tax years would partially offset these financial obligations and would ensure that the economic benefit of the deduction inures to the party who bears the heavier direct financial burden in those years. By contrast, Danielle's retention of the family home will afford her substantial financial benefits, including access to the mortgage interest deduction and any future equity appreciation. Awarding Danielle both tax exemptions in addition to the family home would create a disparity that does not fairly reflect each party's respective financial contributions to the children's support.
An alternating-year allocation is a recognized and practical approach consistent with the equitable principles underlying Civil Rule 90.3(k). Courts routinely employ this mechanism where, as here, both parents are actively involved in the children's lives and each parent bears meaningful financial responsibility. Because David's employment income as a pipeline technician is likely to place him in a tax bracket where the exemption produces a meaningful reduction in tax liability, an alternating allocation would produce a real economic benefit that advances the children's overall financial well-being by preserving more net income in the household of the parent who is the support obligor.
Accordingly, David respectfully requests that the court allocate the dependent tax deduction for both children to David in odd-numbered tax years and to Danielle in even-numbered tax years, or in such alternating fashion as the court determines to be just and consistent with federal law.
B. DAVID'S UNION PENSION CONTRIBUTIONS ACCRUED DURING THE MARRIAGE ARE MARITAL PROPERTY SUBJECT TO EQUITABLE DIVISION UNDER AS 25.24.160, AND THE COURT SHOULD ORDER A QUALIFIED DOMESTIC RELATIONS ORDER TO ACCOMPLISH THE DIVISION.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) authorizes the court to provide "for the division between the parties of their property, including retirement benefits, whether joint or separate, acquired only during marriage, in a just manner." The statute expressly includes retirement benefits within the category of divisible marital property. The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that pension and retirement accounts accrued during the marriage are properly included in the marital estate and subject to equitable division. Gallant v. Gallant, 882 P.2d 1252 (Alaska 1994); Ogden v. Ogden, 39 P.3d 513 (Alaska 2001).
David's union pension contributions were accrued entirely during the period of the marriage, which began in 2014. No portion of the pension benefit appears to have been earned prior to the marriage. Accordingly, the full present value of the vested accrued benefit is marital property. The parties have not yet agreed on a valuation, and this dispute is squarely before the court.
In determining a just division of the pension, the court is directed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4) to consider the following factors, among others: the length of the marriage and station in life of the parties; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties; the financial condition of the parties; the conduct of the parties, including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question; and the income-producing capacity of the property and the value of the property at the time of division.
Several of these factors weigh in favor of providing Danielle with a meaningful share of the pension. The parties were married for approximately ten years, during which Danielle bore primary custodial responsibilities for the two children. David's earning capacity as a pipeline technician substantially exceeds what would be available to Danielle in the near term, particularly given her custodial role during the school week. The pension was earned entirely during the marriage. At the same time, Danielle is receiving the family home, the most significant single marital asset, which provides her with both a residence and long-term equity. This property award is a substantial benefit that should be weighed against any pension division in order to achieve an overall equitable result.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must carefully analyze retirement assets to ensure that all such assets are identified and appropriately valued before any division is ordered. Ogden v. Ogden, 39 P.3d 513 (Alaska 2001). Similarly, in cases involving significant marital assets on both sides of the ledger, a court is not required to divide every asset equally so long as the overall distribution is equitable. Fletcher v. Fletcher, 433 P.3d 1148 (Alaska 2018).
David proposes that the court order a formal actuarial valuation of the vested pension benefit accrued from the date of the marriage through the date of the dissolution decree. Following valuation, the court should determine the equitable share of that benefit to be awarded to Danielle in light of the full picture of the property division, including her receipt of the family home. If the court determines that Danielle is entitled to a portion of the pension, any distribution should be effectuated through a qualified domestic relations order consistent with AS 25.24.160(b), which requires that any judgment distributing retirement benefits to an alternate payee under the applicable plan provisions meet the requirements of a qualified domestic relations order as defined therein.
This mechanism protects both parties. It ensures that Danielle receives whatever share the court determines is equitable without subjecting David to early withdrawal penalties or tax consequences that would diminish the overall marital estate. Gallant v. Gallant, 882 P.2d 1252 (Alaska 1994).
C. THE COURT SHOULD DESIGNATE DAVID AS THE FINAL DECISION-MAKER FOR THE CHILDREN'S MEDICAL CARE IN THE EVENT THE PARTIES CANNOT REACH AGREEMENT, SUBJECT TO PROCEDURAL PROTECTIONS THAT PROTECT DANIELLE'S MEANINGFUL PARTICIPATION.
The parties have agreed to share legal custody of the two minor children. Shared legal custody means that both parents will ordinarily participate in making major decisions about the children's welfare, education, and medical care. However, when parents share legal custody and cannot agree, a practical mechanism must exist to resolve impasses, particularly in the context of time-sensitive medical decisions.
AS 25.24.160(a)(1) authorizes the court to provide for the nurture and education of the children in such manner as may be just and proper. AS 25.24.220(d)(2) directs the court to examine whether the written agreements of the parties concerning child custody and related arrangements "are just as between the spouses and in the best interests of the children of the marriage." AS 25.24.230(b)(2) similarly requires the court to find, before granting a dissolution decree under a heightened scrutiny regime, that the child-related agreements "are in the best interest of the children of the marriage" and are just as between the parties.
In this case, designating a final decision-maker for medical matters does not eliminate Danielle's participation. Rather, it ensures that in the rare circumstance where the parties cannot reach agreement, a decision can be made promptly and without requiring the children or their treating physicians to wait for judicial intervention. The parties' own history of chronic communication difficulties, cited as a contributing cause of the marriage's breakdown, underscores the practical necessity of such a mechanism.
David's rotating schedule as a pipeline technician in Kenai creates a factual asymmetry. During his work rotations, David may be difficult to reach in real time. Because Danielle will have primary physical custody during the school week and will therefore be more consistently present in the children's daily lives, and because the children's primary pediatric care providers are geographically proximate to the Eagle River family home, David concedes that designating Danielle as the final medical decision-maker in the event of an impasse is a practical and appropriate arrangement. David raises this issue not to oppose Danielle's authority, but to ensure that the final decree expressly defines the scope of that authority, including appropriate consultation requirements before any major elective medical procedure is scheduled, so that David's meaningful participation in legal custody is preserved.
The court should therefore order that: (1) both parents are obligated to confer in good faith before any major non-emergency medical decision is made; (2) in the event of a genuine impasse on a non-emergency medical matter, Danielle holds the authority to make the final decision; (3) emergency medical decisions may be made by whichever parent is present with the child at the time of the emergency, without prior consultation being required; and (4) the parent making any unilateral emergency decision must notify the other parent as soon as practicable thereafter.
This framework is consistent with the best-interests standard and with the practical realities of the parties' custodial arrangement. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that child custody and related legal authority decisions must be anchored in what actually serves the children's welfare, assessed from a practical standpoint. Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014); Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996).
D. THE PROPOSED CHILD SUPPORT AMOUNT OF $1,200 PER MONTH IS CONSISTENT WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3 AND SHOULD BE CONFIRMED IN THE FINAL DECREE, WITH ANY ADJUSTMENT FOR DAVID'S EXTENDED SUMMER PARENTING TIME AS THE RULE PERMITS.
David has proposed paying $1,200 per month in child support. The parties' custodial arrangement, under which the children reside primarily with Danielle during the school week and spend alternating weekends, school holidays, and four weeks each summer with David, will determine the applicable support formula.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides the primary framework for child support where one parent holds primary physical custody. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2), the support amount for two children is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by 27 percent. The adjusted annual income is determined by subtracting mandatory deductions specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) from David's total income from all sources.
David's four-week consecutive summer parenting block is significant. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) provides that "the court may allow the obligor parent to reduce child support payments by up to 75% for any period in which the obligor parent has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days." Because David's proposed four-week summer parenting period is exactly 28 days, the court has discretion to allow a reduction in support payments during that period. The final decree should specify the amount of the permitted reduction so that David may plan his financial obligations accordingly.
The court should confirm that $1,200 per month reflects a proper application of the Rule 90.3(a)(2) formula to David's adjusted annual income, or, if the calculation does not align with the formula, the court should adjust the amount to bring it into compliance. The primary objective is that the support award be "adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay," which is among the express purposes of the Rule 90.3 formula, as recognized in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), and that it be predictable and consistent for both parties.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, David Colby respectfully requests that the court:
1. Enter a final decree of dissolution confirming the agreed-upon custodial arrangement, property division, vehicle assignment, and credit card responsibility as set forth in the parties' petition.
2. Confirm the child support obligation at $1,200 per month or at such amount as a proper Civil Rule 90.3(a) calculation of David's adjusted annual income requires for two children, with a specified extended-visitation reduction credit for the four-week summer parenting period pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3).
3. Allocate the dependent tax deduction for the two minor children in alternating tax years between the parties, consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(k) and applicable federal law, with David receiving the deduction in odd-numbered years and Danielle receiving the deduction in even-numbered years.
4. Order a formal actuarial valuation of David's vested union pension benefit accrued during the marriage, and thereafter determine and order an equitable division of that benefit by means of a qualified domestic relations order consistent with AS 25.24.160(b), taking into account the full property division including Danielle's receipt of the family home.
5. Designate Danielle as the final decision-maker for the children's non-emergency medical care in the event of a parental impasse, subject to a good-faith prior consultation requirement and to David's right to make unilateral decisions during genuine medical emergencies when Danielle is unavailable, with prompt notification to follow.
6. Grant such other and further relief as the court determines to be just and proper under AS 25.24.160 and the related dissolution statutes.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0020)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Sutter ("Petitioner") respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for dissolution of marriage filed pursuant to AS 25.24.200. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and have two minor children together, currently ages six and nine. The marriage has irretrievably broken down due to irreconcilable differences, including persistent financial disputes and Michael Sutter's ("Respondent") extended North Slope work rotations, which left Petitioner as the de facto sole caregiver for the children throughout the marriage. Petitioner seeks an order establishing primary physical custody of the two minor children in her favor, setting child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3 based on Respondent's substantially higher income, awarding Petitioner the marital home in Eagle River subject to its existing mortgage obligation, equitably dividing Respondent's pension contributions accrued during the marriage, and equitably allocating the parties' joint credit card debt. The relief sought is firmly grounded in Alaska statutory and case law governing dissolution proceedings, property division, spousal maintenance, and child support. This Court has full authority under AS 25.24.160 and AS 25.24.200 to grant the requested relief.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Petitioner Elena Sutter, age 34, and Respondent Michael Sutter, age 37, were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. The marriage has lasted approximately ten years and produced two minor children, now ages six and nine. Throughout the marriage, Respondent was employed as an oil field technician, working extended rotations on the North Slope that frequently kept him away from the family home for prolonged periods. During those extended absences, Petitioner bore the full weight of child-rearing responsibilities for both children, managing the household, supervising schooling, providing emotional support, and attending to all day-to-day needs of the children without meaningful assistance from Respondent.
The marital home is located in Eagle River, Alaska. It carries an estimated current market value of approximately $410,000 against a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $280,000, leaving an estimated equity of $130,000. The parties also hold a joint credit card balance of approximately $18,000, which accumulated largely during the final year of the marriage and is believed to reflect household and family expenses incurred during a period of financial strain. In addition, Respondent has accumulated pension contributions through his employment during the marriage, which constitute marital property subject to equitable division.
Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated significantly. Ongoing disputes concerning finances and the imbalance of parenting responsibilities contributed to an irremediable breakdown of the marital relationship. Petitioner has filed for dissolution of marriage in the Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, and proposes that the children reside primarily in the Eagle River home with her, with Respondent exercising visitation on alternating weekends and for two weeks each summer. Child support is to be calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3 based on Respondent's substantially higher income as compared to Petitioner's income as a primary caregiver. The parties remain in dispute regarding the disposition of the marital home, the allocation of Respondent's pension contributions, and responsibility for the joint credit card debt.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts adjudicating dissolution petitions are governed by AS 25.24.200 through AS 25.24.230. Under AS 25.24.160(a), the superior court is empowered to provide for the nurture and education of minor children, award spousal maintenance, divide marital property justly, and assign marital obligations. Property division must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution and must be based on the statutory factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of each party, the conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary custody, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity of the property at the time of division.
Child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides that the support award is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by a percentage tied to the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27% of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources, reduced by mandatory deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A) through (G).
Under AS 25.24.230, the court may grant a final decree of dissolution if it finds, among other things, that the written agreements between the parties concerning custody, child support, visitation, property division, and allocation of obligations are just, that the spousal maintenance and property division fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution, that the agreements were entered into voluntarily and free from coercion, and that the conditions of AS 25.24.200(a) have been met. Where the court applies heightened scrutiny under AS 25.24.220(h), as may be warranted when there are minor children of the marriage, the court shall examine the agreements to ensure they are just and in the best interests of the children.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PETITIONER IS ENTITLED TO PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF THE MINOR CHILDREN BECAUSE SHE HAS SERVED AS THE CHILDREN'S PRIMARY CAREGIVER THROUGHOUT THE MARRIAGE.
The superior court must evaluate any custody arrangement in light of what arrangement will best serve the interests of the minor children. Alaska courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court in Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004), have recognized that the court must consider the totality of relevant circumstances bearing on the welfare of children, including each parent's demonstrated ability to provide care, stability, and continuity of environment for the children. In this case, those circumstances overwhelmingly favor primary custody in Petitioner's favor.
Respondent's employment on the North Slope required him to be absent from the family home for extended rotations throughout the marriage. During those absences, which were frequent and prolonged, Petitioner served as the sole caregiver for both children. She managed the household, supervised the children's education, addressed their medical and emotional needs, and provided the consistent, stable presence that young children require. The children, ages six and nine, have spent the majority of their lives in the Eagle River home under Petitioner's primary care. Disrupting that arrangement would undermine the stability and continuity that serves the children's best interests.
Petitioner does not seek to eliminate Respondent's relationship with the children. To the contrary, Petitioner proposes that Respondent exercise visitation on alternating weekends and for two consecutive weeks each summer, which allows for a meaningful ongoing parental relationship while preserving the consistency and routine that the children rely upon. This arrangement reflects a practical and equitable approach, particularly given that Respondent's continued employment on the North Slope will likely subject the children to ongoing periods of his absence regardless of the custody structure.
AS 25.24.160(a)(1) authorizes the court to provide for payments by either or both parties toward the nurture and education of their children. The proposed custody arrangement is consistent with the policy of AS 25.24.230(b)(2), which requires that the written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation be in the best interest of the children of the marriage. Petitioner submits that an award of primary physical custody to her, with defined and reasonable visitation for Respondent, satisfies this standard.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED PURSUANT TO CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON RESPONDENT'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS AN OIL FIELD TECHNICIAN, AND SHOULD REFLECT THE 27 PERCENT GUIDELINE FOR TWO CHILDREN.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides the governing framework for child support calculation in a primary physical custody arrangement. The rule requires the court to multiply the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage for the number of children subject to the order. For two children, that percentage is 27% (.27) of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Respondent earns a substantially higher income than Petitioner as an oil field technician on the North Slope. His adjusted annual income must be calculated by subtracting from his total income from all sources the mandatory deductions set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A) through (G), including federal and state income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory retirement contributions, and any other qualifying deductions. Voluntary contributions to tax-deferred retirement accounts are also deductible, but only to the extent that total voluntary and mandatory retirement contributions do not exceed 7.5% of total income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B).
The Alaska Supreme Court, in its discussion in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), confirmed that the Civil Rule 90.3 formula reflects a considered approach designed to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of the obligor parent to pay, and that awards are predictable and consistent. The guidelines are not advisory; they represent the baseline from which the court begins its analysis. The court in Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002) similarly affirmed that the rule is designed to obtain a realistic estimate of the obligor's adjusted annual income, and that departures from the guideline amount require good cause.
Petitioner requests that the court order Respondent to pay child support consistent with the Civil Rule 90.3(a) guidelines, calculated at 27% of his adjusted annual income for the two children. Given the disparity in the parties' incomes and Petitioner's substantially greater custodial responsibilities, a full guideline award is both warranted and necessary. Additionally, because Respondent's North Slope rotation schedule may at times result in extended periods of physical custody with the children during designated vacation time, the court should make clear in any support order that any adjustment for extended visitation is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3), which permits a reduction of child support payments by up to 75% only for periods in which the obligor parent has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days.
C. PETITIONER SHOULD BE AWARDED THE MARITAL HOME BECAUSE SHE HAS PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF THE CHILDREN AND EQUITY STRONGLY FAVORS THIS RESULT.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly identifies as a factor in property division "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." This factor directly supports an award of the Eagle River marital home to Petitioner.
The marital home has an estimated current market value of approximately $410,000 and carries a remaining mortgage balance of approximately $280,000, representing approximately $130,000 in equity. The children have grown up in this home and attend school in the Eagle River area. Uprooting them from the family home at the same time as the dissolution would compound the disruption they already face. Awarding the home to Petitioner, who will be the custodial parent, preserves the children's stability and continuity of environment. This result is consistent with the Alaska Supreme Court's recognition in Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996) that property division is the preferred mechanism for addressing the financial needs of the parties following dissolution, and that property awards should be crafted to serve the parties' practical circumstances.
A review of the full range of factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) further supports this award. The parties have been married approximately ten years, satisfying the length-of-marriage factor. Petitioner, at age 34, has reduced her career development by serving as primary caregiver throughout the marriage, affecting her earning capacity relative to Respondent's, who has accumulated a significantly higher income through his oil field employment. The financial condition of the parties, including the disparity in their earning capacities, weighs in favor of awarding Petitioner the asset that will provide her and the children with housing stability. The family home was acquired during the marriage and constitutes marital property subject to equitable division. The desirability of awarding the home to the custodial parent is explicitly recognized in the statute.
Petitioner proposes to assume the remaining mortgage obligation of approximately $280,000 as part of any order awarding her the home, thereby reducing the net benefit she receives and crediting Respondent with a corresponding portion of the marital estate to be offset through the allocation of other assets or by recognizing his reduced share of remaining marital debt. This approach is consistent with AS 25.24.200(a)(3), which requires that any agreement on property division be fair and just and take into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(4) so that the economic effect of dissolution is fairly allocated. The Alaska Supreme Court in Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010) has confirmed that property division must be evaluated in light of all statutory factors and that courts retain broad discretion to fashion a division that is equitable under the totality of the circumstances.
D. RESPONDENT'S PENSION CONTRIBUTIONS ACCRUED DURING THE MARRIAGE CONSTITUTE MARITAL PROPERTY AND SHOULD BE EQUITABLY DIVIDED.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) authorizes the court to divide "property, including retirement benefits, whether joint or separate, acquired only during marriage." Respondent's pension contributions accrued through his oil field employment during the marriage fall squarely within the definition of marital property subject to division under this provision. The statute further authorizes the court to require one or both parties to "assign, deliver, or convey any of their real or personal property, including retirement benefits, to the other party" in order to accomplish an equitable division.
In Young v. Lowery, 221 P.3d 1006 (Alaska 2009), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed the framework under which marital property, including retirement assets, must be divided, emphasizing that the division must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce by reference to the full set of statutory factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The length of the marriage, the relative earning capacities of the parties, and the financial condition of each party are all relevant to determining what share of the pension Petitioner should receive. Given that the marriage lasted approximately ten years and that Petitioner's reduced workforce participation enabled Respondent to advance in his career and accumulate these retirement benefits, Petitioner is entitled to a proportionate share of the marital portion of the pension.
Any order distributing benefits from a qualifying retirement plan must satisfy the requirements of a qualified domestic relations order as contemplated under AS 25.24.160(b). Petitioner respectfully requests that the court enter an appropriate order dividing the marital portion of Respondent's pension on an equitable basis, taking into account all relevant statutory factors, and that the court include the necessary provisions to ensure compliance with any applicable plan requirements for such a distribution.
E. THE JOINT CREDIT CARD DEBT SHOULD BE ALLOCATED EQUITABLY BETWEEN THE PARTIES, WITH RESPONDENT BEARING A GREATER SHARE GIVEN THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF ITS ACCUMULATION.
AS 25.24.160(a) authorizes the court to provide for the division of the parties' property and their obligations in a just manner. AS 25.24.200(a)(4) requires that the parties agree as to the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both of them. The joint credit card debt of approximately $18,000 accumulated largely during the final year of the marriage. Petitioner submits that this debt was incurred predominantly for household and family expenses during a period when the family was under financial strain due in significant part to Respondent's absence and the imbalance in financial contributions to the household.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(E) requires the court to consider the conduct of the parties, including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets, when dividing property and obligations. In Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that courts must consider the full financial picture of the parties, including liabilities, when fashioning a just resolution. While Petitioner does not allege deliberate waste, the concentration of the debt in the final year of the marriage, combined with the significant income disparity between the parties, supports allocating a proportionately greater share of this debt to Respondent. Respondent's substantially higher income as an oil field technician gives him significantly greater capacity to service this debt, and fairness requires that the allocation reflect that disparity.
Petitioner proposes that Respondent be responsible for no less than two-thirds of the joint credit card balance, with Petitioner assuming the remaining one-third. This allocation reflects the parties' relative financial capacities, the circumstances under which the debt was incurred, and the statutory directive that division of obligations must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. AS 25.24.230(a)(3) requires that the division of obligations be just, and a two-thirds allocation to the higher-earning party who was frequently absent while the household expenses accumulated is consistent with that standard.
F. THE COURT SHOULD APPLY HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY TO ANY AGREEMENTS GIVEN THE PRESENCE OF MINOR CHILDREN.
AS 25.24.220(h)(3) provides that the court shall use a heightened level of scrutiny of any agreements if there is a minor child of the marriage. Both of the Sutter children are minors. Accordingly, the court must examine the written agreements between the parties to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that the agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are in the best interests of the children of the marriage. AS 25.24.220(i). Petitioner submits that the proposed terms satisfy this heightened standard. The custody arrangement places the children with their established primary caregiver in the home where they have resided. The child support calculation follows the mandatory guidelines of Civil Rule 90.3(a). The property and debt allocations reflect a careful and balanced application of the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Elena Sutter respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Grant the petition for dissolution of marriage pursuant to AS 25.24.200 and AS 25.24.230;
2. Award Petitioner primary physical custody of the two minor children, with Respondent exercising visitation on alternating weekends and for two consecutive weeks each summer, consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(1) and the best interests of the children;
3. Order Respondent to pay child support calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) at 27% of his adjusted annual income for two children, with any extended visitation reduction governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3);
4. Award Petitioner the marital home in Eagle River, subject to her assumption of the remaining mortgage obligation, pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) and the equitable factors therein;
5. Enter an order equitably dividing the marital portion of Respondent's pension contributions accrued during the marriage, with such order satisfying the requirements of AS 25.24.160(b);
6. Allocate no less than two-thirds of the joint credit card debt of approximately $18,000 to Respondent and the remaining balance to Petitioner, pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and AS 25.24.230(a)(3);
7. Apply the heightened scrutiny required by AS 25.24.220(h)(3) and AS 25.24.220(i) to ensure all agreements are just and in the best interests of the minor children; and
8. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and equitable under the circumstances.

THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN

This matter comes before the Court on the parties' petition for dissolution of marriage. Petitioner David Sutter and Respondent Danielle Sutter were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and have two minor children together, ages six and nine. After years of marital strain attributable to David's extended work absences on the North Slope and persistent communication difficulties, David filed for dissolution in Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, in March 2025. The parties have reached a tentative agreement addressing the primary issues incident to dissolution, including physical custody and parenting time, child support, division of real and personal property, and allocation of marital debts. This brief is submitted to assist the Court in evaluating the agreement against the applicable statutory and rule-based standards and to demonstrate that the proposed terms are fair, just, and in the best interests of the minor children.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Sutter and Danielle Sutter were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. The marriage produced two minor children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old, both of whom reside in the family home located in Eagle River, Alaska. Over the course of the marriage, David worked as an oilfield technician on the North Slope, a position requiring extended rotational absences, typically in two-week-on and two-week-off cycles. Danielle has been the primary caregiver for the children during David's work rotations. The parties agree that the combination of David's prolonged absences and resulting communication breakdowns caused an irremediable breakdown of the marriage due to incompatibility of temperament.
David filed a petition for dissolution in March 2025. The parties have negotiated in good faith and reached a tentative agreement on all material issues. With respect to the children, the parties propose that Danielle have primary physical custody during the school year, with David exercising parenting time during his two-week off-rotation periods, alternating major holidays, and extended parenting time each summer. Both parties shall share legal custody of the children.
Regarding child support, David, as the parent with substantially higher income from his oilfield employment, agrees to pay support calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3. As to the marital estate, Danielle will retain the marital home in Eagle River, subject to her refinancing the existing mortgage solely in her name within a reasonable period. David will retain his personal savings account and his 401(k) account, both of which accrued value during the marriage. To account for the disparity in asset values between the marital home on one side and David's retained financial accounts on the other, David will make an equalization payment to Danielle. The parties further agree that the joint credit card balance of approximately $14,000 and the vehicle loan on the automobile in Danielle's possession will be allocated between the parties in proportion to respective use and ability to pay, subject to the Court's review and final decree.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.200, spouses may jointly petition the superior court for dissolution of their marriage upon a showing, among other things, that incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, that they have agreed on the custody, support, and visitation of their minor children, and that they have reached a fair and just agreement on the division of property and the allocation of debts. The petition must be filed and verified in conformity with AS 25.24.210.
Following filing, AS 25.24.220 requires the court to conduct a hearing and examine the petitioners to determine, among other things, whether the spouses fully understand the nature and consequences of the action, whether the custody and support agreements are just and in the best interests of the children, and whether the property and debt agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution taking into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). Where circumstances exist that require heightened scrutiny, such as the presence of minor children, the court must examine the agreements with greater care under AS 25.24.220(h) and (i).
Child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides a formula-based calculation using the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a specified percentage based on the number of children. The right to adequate child support belongs to the children, and the court is not bound by any parental agreement that falls below guideline levels absent a written finding that the children's needs will be otherwise met.
Property division in a dissolution proceeding must conform to AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires the court to divide property in a just manner based on enumerated factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, earning capacity, financial condition, and the desirability of awarding the family home to the parent with primary physical custody of the children. Spousal maintenance, if awarded, must comply with AS 25.24.160(a)(2). Debt allocation is similarly subject to the court's equitable authority and must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. These standards have been consistently applied and elaborated upon by the Alaska Supreme Court. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015); Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010); Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PARTIES' CUSTODY AND PARENTING TIME AGREEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND SHOULD BE APPROVED
The proposed custody arrangement places primary physical custody of both children with Danielle during the school year, while preserving David's meaningful and regular parenting time consistent with his North Slope work rotation. This arrangement reflects the realities of David's employment schedule and serves the continuity and stability interests of both children.
Under AS 25.20.090, when the court considers shared or primary custody arrangements, it must evaluate a range of factors including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent considering the actual time spent with each parent and the proximity of each parent to the school, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
Each of these factors supports the proposed arrangement. Danielle has served as the primary caregiver throughout the marriage, providing the children with a stable home environment in Eagle River where both children are enrolled in school. Retaining the children in this community minimizes disruption to their educational and social development. David's parenting time, structured around his predictable two-week off-rotation periods, is tailored to reflect the actual time he is available and present in Anchorage. This arrangement ensures that the children will have regular, meaningful contact with both parents throughout the year.
Furthermore, both parties have demonstrated a willingness to cooperate in facilitating the children's relationship with the other parent. The alternating holiday schedule and extended summer parenting time reflect a balanced and thoughtful agreement that serves the children's best interests. The court in Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002), recognized that parental agreements on custody, while not binding on the court, are relevant considerations and that courts must independently evaluate what arrangement best serves the children. The proposed arrangement withstands that independent scrutiny.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON DAVID'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS THE NON-CUSTODIAL PARENT
Because Danielle will have primary physical custody of both children during the school year, child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a). That rule requires the court to calculate support as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a specified percentage: 20% for one child and 27% for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A), (B).
David's adjusted annual income is derived from his total income as an oilfield technician, reduced by the mandatory deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including federal and state income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and any mandatory contributions to a retirement or pension plan, as well as permissible voluntary retirement contributions, health insurance premiums within the applicable cap, and other allowable deductions. The parties agree that David's income is substantially higher than Danielle's, and that David is properly designated the obligor parent.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently emphasized that Civil Rule 90.3 is designed to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children while remaining predictable and consistent. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015); Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012). In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the court confirmed that a parent's adjusted annual income for Rule 90.3(a)(1) purposes is calculated from total income across all sources, reduced by the deductions enumerated in the rule.
The parties request that the Court order David to pay child support in an amount calculated in strict conformity with the Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) percentage guidelines applied to his verified adjusted annual income, with appropriate provision for the children's health insurance and any work-related childcare expenses consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E) and (F). The Court should also note that during the summer period when David exercises extended parenting time, any reduction or credit mechanism must comport with the requirements of Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3), which permits reduction only for extended visitation exceeding 27 consecutive days and only up to the 75% limit specified in the rule.
C. THE PROPOSED PROPERTY DIVISION FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION AND SHOULD BE APPROVED
The proposed division of marital property satisfies the requirements of AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which mandates that the court divide the parties' property acquired during the marriage in a just manner, without regard to fault, and based on consideration of the statutory factors. The agreement as structured achieves an equitable result when measured against those factors.
The relevant statutory factors include the length of the marriage and the station in life of the parties during the marriage; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties, including their educational backgrounds, training, employment skills, work experiences, length of absence from the job market, and custodial responsibilities for children during the marriage; the financial condition of the parties, including the availability and cost of health insurance; the conduct of the parties, including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question; and the income-producing capacity of the property and the value of the property at the time of division. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(A)-(I).
Application of these factors strongly supports the proposed division. First, as to the marital home: AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly identifies the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children as a relevant consideration. Because the children will reside primarily with Danielle in Eagle River during the school year, awarding Danielle the family home directly serves the stability and continuity interests of both minor children and is squarely consistent with statutory policy. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized this principle in Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010), which highlighted the court's obligation to weigh all enumerated statutory factors in reaching a just result. Danielle's obligation to refinance the mortgage solely in her name protects David from ongoing liability on a debt secured by property he will no longer own.
Second, David retains his personal savings account and his 401(k) accrued during the marriage, both of which represent significant marital assets. The equalization payment from David to Danielle is designed to account for any disparity between the net equity in the marital home and the value of David's retained financial accounts. This mechanism ensures that neither party receives a windfall and that the division fairly allocates the marital estate. The Alaska Supreme Court in Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014), reaffirmed that the court must critically evaluate agreements between the parties to confirm that the property division is genuinely just, particularly where one party has significantly greater earning capacity, as is the case here given David's higher income as an oilfield technician.
Third, the agreement appropriately accounts for the disparity in the parties' earning capacities. David's long-established employment as an oilfield technician gives him substantially greater earning capacity and financial security going forward, while Danielle, who bore significant custodial responsibilities during the marriage and will continue to do so as primary custodial parent, may face reduced earning capacity in the short term. These facts weigh in favor of ensuring that Danielle receives a fair share of the marital estate through both the home award and the equalization payment. See Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019) (affirming courts' consideration of disparity in earning capacity and separate property status in structuring a just property division).
D. THE PROPOSED DEBT ALLOCATION IS EQUITABLE AND SHOULD BE INCORPORATED INTO THE FINAL DECREE
The parties' agreement allocates the joint credit card balance of approximately $14,000 and the vehicle loan on the automobile in Danielle's possession between the parties in proportion to respective use and ability to pay. This approach is consistent with the court's broad equitable authority under AS 25.24.160(a) to provide for a just division of marital obligations as part of the dissolution decree.
The factors that guide property division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) apply equally to the allocation of marital debts. David's substantially greater income and earning capacity support his assumption of a proportionately larger share of the joint credit card balance. Danielle's retention and continued use of the vehicle support her responsibility for the vehicle loan, which is secured by an asset she will continue to possess and use. At the same time, her reduced earning capacity during the period following dissolution warrants the Court's scrutiny to ensure that the debt allocation does not impose an undue burden that undermines the other equitable provisions of the dissolution decree.
The Court is respectfully requested to review and confirm that the debt allocation, as agreed by the parties, fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution and does not result in an inequitable outcome for either party or the children.
E. THE DISSOLUTION PETITION SATISFIES ALL PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS UNDER AS 25.24.200, AS 25.24.210, AND AS 25.24.220
The petition for dissolution meets the threshold requirements of AS 25.24.200(a). Incompatibility of temperament, as evidenced by David's prolonged North Slope absences and the persistent communication breakdown between the parties, has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. The parties have agreed on custody, support, and visitation for their two minor children. They have also reached a fair and just agreement on the division of property, including the marital home and all financial accounts, as well as the allocation of marital debts.
The petition has been filed and verified in the superior court in conformity with AS 25.24.210, which requires the petition to state in detail the terms of the custody, support, visitation, spousal maintenance, and property division agreements, as well as to identify the respective occupations, income, assets, and liabilities of the parties, the date and place of the marriage, and information concerning each minor child of the marriage.
At the scheduled hearing under AS 25.24.220, both parties will be present to be examined by the Court. The Court will be asked to determine that the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of the dissolution, that the custody and support agreements are in the best interests of the children, and that the property and debt agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution in conformity with AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). Because the parties have a minor child of the marriage, AS 25.24.220(h)(3) requires that the Court apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the agreements. The parties welcome this review and submit that the agreements, taken as a whole, satisfy the heightened standard imposed by AS 25.24.220(i).
The required forms and accompanying instructions, as prepared under AS 25.24.250, have been obtained and completed. The petition constitutes the entire agreement between the parties as required by AS 25.24.200(a) and AS 25.24.210(e)(10).
V. CONCLUSION
For all the foregoing reasons, the parties respectfully request that the Court:
1. Find that the conditions for dissolution under AS 25.24.200(a) are satisfied;
2. Approve the proposed primary physical custody arrangement placing the children with Danielle during the school year, with David's parenting time during his off-rotation periods, alternating holidays, and extended summer time, as being in the best interests of the minor children under AS 25.20.090;
3. Order child support from David to Danielle calculated in strict conformity with Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on David's verified adjusted annual income, for two children;
4. Approve the property division awarding the marital home to Danielle subject to refinancing, David's retention of his savings and 401(k) accounts, and an equalization payment to Danielle, as a just division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4);
5. Approve the proposed debt allocation assigning the joint credit card balance and vehicle loan between the parties in proportion to use and ability to pay, as a fair and equitable resolution of marital obligations under AS 25.24.160(a); and
6. Enter a final decree of dissolution incorporating all agreed terms.
Respectfully submitted.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0022)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Court in an action for divorce between Elena Colby, Petitioner, and Colin Colby, Respondent, married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The parties have two minor children, ages six and nine, and have accumulated marital assets and liabilities that require equitable resolution. The central disputes concern the physical custody schedule and visitation arrangement for the children, the proper calculation of child support, and the just division of the marital estate, including the Eagle River family home, two jointly held vehicles, and Colin's vested 401(k) retirement account accumulated during the marriage. Elena respectfully requests that this Court award her primary physical custody of both children, set Colin's visitation in accordance with his actual availability during off-rotation weeks, calculate child support pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3 based on Colin's substantially higher income as an oilfield technician, and divide the marital estate equitably under AS 25.24.160, rejecting Colin's attempt to offset marital home equity against Elena's student loan debt.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Colby and Colin Colby were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The parties have two minor children together, ages six and nine. Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to Colin's extended and repeated work absences on the North Slope and the parties' persistent disagreements regarding communication and financial management. The breakdown of the marriage has been irremediable, and Elena now seeks a dissolution of the marriage with appropriate orders regarding custody, support, and property.
Elena works part-time as a dental hygienist. Her income, while meaningful, is substantially lower than Colin's income as an oilfield technician employed on the North Slope. Colin works on a rotating schedule of fourteen days on and fourteen days off. During his on-rotation periods, Colin is physically absent from the Anchorage area and is therefore unavailable to exercise regular parenting responsibilities. Elena has served as the primary caregiver for both children throughout the marriage, managing the children's daily needs, schooling, medical appointments, and general welfare, particularly during Colin's extended North Slope absences.
The parties own a family home in Eagle River, Alaska, which carries an estimated current market value of $310,000 and an outstanding mortgage balance of approximately $180,000, resulting in net equity of approximately $130,000. The parties also jointly own two vehicles. Colin accumulated a vested portion of a 401(k) retirement account during the marriage. Elena incurred student loan debt during the marriage.
The parties agree that Elena should have primary physical custody of the children. They dispute the structure of Colin's visitation schedule. Elena proposes that Colin receive visitation on alternating weekends during his off-rotation weeks. Colin contends that his fourteen-days-on, fourteen-days-off rotation should be incorporated into the visitation schedule to provide him with extended blocks of time with the children during his off-rotation periods. The parties further dispute the division of the marital estate, particularly whether Elena's student loan debt should be used to offset Colin's proportionate share of the home equity award.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts have broad authority to enter orders governing child custody, child support, and property division in divorce proceedings. Under AS 25.24.160, in any judgment for divorce the court may provide for child support, spousal maintenance, delivery of personal property, and division of marital property in a just manner. Property division must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce based on the statutory factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which include the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, and the circumstances and necessities of each party.
Child custody may be modified or established in accordance with AS 25.20.110, which provides that any award of custody shall be entered based upon the best interests of the child. Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3, which establishes a formula based on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent and the number of children subject to the order.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that property division determinations rest within the sound discretion of the trial court and must be grounded in the statutory factors. Hooper v. Hooper, 188 P.3d 681 (Alaska 2008). Courts must consider each factor individually and reach a division that is just and equitable in light of all relevant circumstances. Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010). With respect to child support, the Rule 90.3 formula is designed to produce predictable and consistent results and to ensure that support orders are adequate to meet the needs of the children. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD ELENA PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF BOTH CHILDREN WITH VISITATION FOR COLIN STRUCTURED AROUND HIS ACTUAL AVAILABILITY DURING OFF-ROTATION WEEKS.
Both parties agree that Elena should be awarded primary physical custody of the two minor children. Because Colin's employment requires him to be physically present on the North Slope for fourteen consecutive days at a time, he is structurally unavailable to exercise regular daily parenting responsibilities during his on-rotation periods. The visitation arrangement must therefore be crafted to reflect this reality while still serving the best interests of the children.
Under AS 25.20.110(a), any award of custody or visitation may be structured or modified when the court determines that the arrangement serves the best interests of the child. The statute is clear that if a parent opposes a modification and the court grants it, the court shall enter its reason on the record. Here, the Court is not modifying a prior order but rather entering an initial custody arrangement. The children's best interests are best served by a visitation schedule that provides them with consistency, stability, and meaningful time with Colin during the periods he is actually available in the Anchorage area.
Elena proposes that Colin receive visitation on alternating weekends during his off-rotation weeks. This proposal is practical and appropriately tailored to Colin's schedule, because it avoids situations in which a scheduled visitation period would fall entirely or partially during an on-rotation period when Colin is on the North Slope. Guaranteeing visitation only during confirmed off-rotation windows gives the children reliability and prevents disruption to their school schedules and routines.
Colin's counter-proposal, which would build extended blocks of time into the schedule based on his fourteen-day rotation cycle, carries significant risks for the children. Extended blocks of fourteen-day visitation, while potentially available under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) for purposes of an extended visitation credit, are not required and must be evaluated in light of the children's ages, six and nine, and their need for stable routines. The Court has discretion to decline to order extended consecutive visitation blocks if such an arrangement is not in the children's best interests. Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002) (recognizing courts' independent obligation to determine arrangements that serve children's interests).
Structuring visitation on alternating weekends during Colin's confirmed off-rotation periods best balances his legitimate interest in parenting time with the children's need for stability, consistency, and a dependable residential schedule with their primary caregiver.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED PURSUANT TO CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON COLIN'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS AN OILFIELD TECHNICIAN, WITH ELENA RECEIVING PRIMARY CUSTODY CREDIT.
Because Elena will have primary physical custody of both children, child support must be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which governs support in cases of primary physical custody. Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that a child support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a percentage specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). For two children, that percentage is 27% of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" certain enumerated deductions, including mandatory federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, voluntary retirement contributions subject to a 7.5% cap, work-related child care expenses for the subject children, and health insurance premiums for the parent only up to 10% of total income.
Colin's income as an oilfield technician on the North Slope is substantially higher than Elena's part-time income as a dental hygienist. The Court must calculate Colin's adjusted annual income in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), taking into account all authorized deductions, and then apply the 27% figure applicable to two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). The resulting figure will represent the annual child support obligation, to be paid in equal monthly installments.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the Rule 90.3 formula is intended to produce predictable and consistent child support awards adequate to meet children's needs, subject to the parents' ability to pay. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). The formula serves a protective function for children and must be faithfully applied.
If Colin seeks any reduction in support based on extended visitation, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) authorizes the court to allow the obligor parent to reduce child support payments by up to 75% for any period in which the obligor parent has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days. However, any such reduction is discretionary and requires a court order specifying the allowable reduction. Elena does not concede that Colin's proposed visitation schedule, as described above, would qualify for this credit, and the Court should not presume eligibility absent a specific finding regarding the number of consecutive days actually exercised.
The Court should also note that if Colin is found to be voluntarily underemployed or if his income fluctuates significantly between rotation periods, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes the court to calculate support based on potential income. The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed the court's authority to consider a parent's full earning capacity in setting an appropriate support level. Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019). Colin's employment is established and his income from the North Slope is well-documented; there is no basis to reduce his support obligation below the formula-calculated amount.
C. THE MARITAL HOME SHOULD BE AWARDED TO ELENA AS THE PRIMARY CUSTODIAL PARENT, WITH EQUITABLE DIVISION OF THE NET EQUITY.
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the Court must divide marital property in a just manner, taking into account the enumerated statutory factors. Among those factors, AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly recognizes "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." This factor strongly supports awarding the Eagle River family home to Elena, who will serve as the primary custodial parent for the children aged six and nine.
The family home in Eagle River has an estimated market value of $310,000 and an outstanding mortgage balance of approximately $180,000, producing net equity of approximately $130,000. This equity represents a significant marital asset accumulated during the marriage and must be divided equitably. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that an unequal division of marital property may be appropriate where the statutory factors support such an outcome. Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002). Here, the desirability of maintaining residential stability for the two minor children in the family home weighs heavily in favor of awarding the home to Elena.
Additional statutory factors further support awarding Elena a substantial share of the home equity. The length of the marriage, though not exceedingly long, overlapped with the primary child-rearing years for both parties. Elena's earning capacity as a part-time dental hygienist is materially lower than Colin's earning capacity as a full-time oilfield technician. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C). Colin's financial condition, supported by his North Slope salary, is substantially stronger than Elena's. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(D). The circumstances and necessities of each party, particularly Elena's need to maintain stable housing for two young children on a part-time income, also weigh in her favor. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(G). These factors collectively support awarding the family home to Elena or, at a minimum, awarding her a disproportionate share of the net equity.
The Court should note that Hooper v. Hooper, 188 P.3d 681 (Alaska 2008), and Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010), both confirm that courts must weigh each statutory factor and reach a division that is just under the totality of circumstances. A division that preserves the children's home environment while accounting for the significant disparity in earning capacity between the parties is consistent with Alaska law.
D. COLIN'S REQUEST TO OFFSET ELENA'S STUDENT LOAN DEBT AGAINST HER HOME EQUITY AWARD SHOULD BE REJECTED AS INCONSISTENT WITH THE STATUTORY FRAMEWORK AND EQUITABLE PRINCIPLES.
Colin proposes that the Court offset any equity award to Elena against his proportionate share of her student loan debt incurred during the marriage. This request should be rejected. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the Court is charged with dividing marital property in a just manner, considering the statutory factors. Student loan debt incurred during the marriage may be addressed as part of the overall allocation of marital obligations, but it does not serve as an automatic offset against a property equity award.
Elena's student loan debt, incurred during the marriage, was an investment in her earning capacity that benefits the entire family unit by enabling her to contribute financially to the household. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C) directs the court to consider the earning capacity of each party, including educational backgrounds and training. To the extent Elena's education enhanced her employability and earning capacity, that factor is already built into the Court's overall analysis of earning capacity and financial condition. Requiring Elena to offset that debt directly against her home equity award would essentially penalize her twice: once by reducing her equity share and again by leaving her responsible for loan obligations that enhanced a capacity the Court is already considering.
Furthermore, the factor under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(H), which directs the court to consider the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question, supports treating the student loan as a marital obligation to be allocated separately and equitably, not as a mathematical reduction of Elena's home equity award. The Court has broad discretion under AS 25.24.160 to allocate marital debts in a manner it finds just. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996) (recognizing the court's broad discretion in property division under the statutory factors). Mechanically offsetting Elena's student loan debt against her equity award, without independent analysis of the debt's nature, purpose, and benefit to the marital estate, would not constitute the "just" division required by the statute.
E. THE JOINTLY HELD VEHICLES AND RETIREMENT ACCOUNT SHOULD BE DIVIDED EQUITABLY UNDER AS 25.24.160.
In addition to the family home, the parties jointly own two vehicles and Colin holds a vested portion of a 401(k) retirement account accumulated during the marriage. Both the vehicles and the retirement account are marital assets subject to division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which provides that marital property acquired during the marriage must be divided in a just manner.
With respect to the vehicles, the Court should consider the practical needs of each party. Elena, as the primary custodial parent responsible for transporting the children to school, medical appointments, and activities, has a strong practical need for reliable transportation. Colin's employment on the North Slope provides him with transportation to and from the job site. The Court should allocate one vehicle to each party in a manner that reflects these practical circumstances and the respective values of the vehicles, with any disparity in value addressed through an offsetting equalization payment.
With respect to Colin's 401(k) account, the portion accumulated during the marriage is marital property subject to division. AS 25.24.160(a)(4) expressly includes retirement benefits within the scope of marital property subject to division. The Court should determine the marital portion of the account as of the date of separation and divide it equitably, taking into account the overall property division and the statutory factors. As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002), retirement accounts accumulated during the marriage are properly included in the marital estate and may be divided through a qualified domestic relations order or other appropriate mechanism. The Court should ensure that any division of the retirement account is structured to comply with AS 25.24.160(b), which requires that any judgment distributing retirement benefits meet the requirements of a qualified domestic relations order under the applicable statutory provisions.
V. CONCLUSION
For all of the foregoing reasons, Elena Colby respectfully requests that this Court enter an order: (1) awarding Elena primary physical custody of both minor children, with visitation for Colin structured on alternating weekends during his confirmed off-rotation weeks; (2) calculating Colin's child support obligation pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on his adjusted annual income as an oilfield technician, applying the 27% rate applicable to two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B); (3) awarding Elena the family home in Eagle River or, at minimum, a disproportionate share of the net equity in recognition of her role as primary custodial parent and her substantially lower earning capacity; (4) rejecting Colin's request to offset Elena's student loan debt against her home equity award; and (5) dividing the jointly held vehicles and Colin's marital portion of the 401(k) retirement account equitably in accordance with AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The requested relief is consistent with Alaska law, supported by the statutory factors, and necessary to protect the best interests of the parties' two minor children and to fairly allocate the economic effects of this divorce.
