II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Nakamura and Colin Nakamura were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. The marriage produced two children, currently ages six and nine, both of whom reside with Renee at the marital home on Huffman Road in Anchorage. Throughout the marriage, Colin was employed as a pipeline technician on the North Slope, a position that required him to be away from the family home for extended and recurring periods. His employment in this capacity generated income substantially greater than Renee's earnings.
Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to the practical and emotional strains caused by Colin's absences and the parties' divergence on fundamental issues within the relationship. The parties participated in a course of marital counseling but were unable to reconcile their differences, ultimately rendering the marriage irremediably broken.
The marital estate consists primarily of the family home located on Huffman Road in Anchorage and Colin's employer-sponsored 401(k) retirement account. The parties agree that the marital home should be sold and the net equity divided equally. However, they dispute the treatment of the 401(k) account. Renee contends that the portion of the account accumulated during the marriage constitutes marital property subject to division by qualified domestic relations order. Colin argues that a pre-marital contribution balance exists within the account and should be excluded from the marital estate.
In addition to these assets, the parties carry approximately $28,000 in joint credit card debt. Renee asks the Court to assign the majority of this obligation to Colin in light of the significant disparity between the parties' earning capacities. Renee also proposes that she retain primary physical custody of the two children during the school year at the Huffman Road residence, with Colin receiving parenting time on alternating weekends and for six weeks each summer, and that the parties share joint legal custody. Renee further requests that the Court order Colin to pay monthly child support calculated in accordance with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3, based on his substantially higher income.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.160, the superior court is empowered, in a divorce or dissolution proceeding, to provide for the division of property, whether joint or separate, acquired during the marriage in a just manner, to order the payment of child support, and to award spousal maintenance as may be just and necessary. Property division must fairly allocate the economic effect of the divorce based on the statutory factors enumerated in AS 25.24.919(4), which include the length of the marriage and station in life of the parties, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of the parties, the conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
Child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 925(a), which provides that the award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a percentage determined by the number of children. Adjusted annual income is defined under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) as the parent's total income from all sources minus specified mandatory and permissible deductions. For shared physical custody arrangements, the calculation follows Civil Rule 90.3(b).
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that a trial court must begin its property division analysis with the presumption that an equal division of marital property is the most equitable starting point, and must then consider the statutory factors to determine whether deviation from equality is warranted. Onslow v. Brackeen, 557 P.3d 717 (Alaska 2002). Courts must make adequate factual findings and demonstrate that those facts were weighed in reaching a property division conclusion. Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010). Where one spouse has a substantially lower earning capacity, an unequal division of the marital estate may be appropriate. Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. The Portion of Colin's 401(k) Account Accumulated During the Marriage Is Marital Property Subject to Division by Qualified Domestic Relations Order
The central property dispute in this case concerns the proper treatment of Colin's employer-sponsored 401(k) account. Renee's position is straightforward: the portion of the account accumulated during the marriage, from 2014 through the date of separation, constitutes marital property subject to an equal division by qualified domestic relations order. Colin's pre-marital contributions, if properly documented, may be treated as his separate property, but the marital increment must be allocated equitably.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) directs the Court to divide "property, including retirement benefits, whether joint or separate, acquired only during marriage, in a just manner." The statute further provides that the Court may "invade the property, including retirement benefits, of either spouse acquired before marriage when the balancing of the equities between the parties requires it." This framework makes plain that retirement account contributions made during the marriage are presumptively marital, while pre-marital contributions occupy a separate category that may nonetheless be reached when equity demands it.
AS 25.24.160(b) specifically addresses retirement account distributions, providing that where a judgment distributes benefits to an alternate payee under the applicable state retirement provisions, "the judgment must meet the requirements of a qualified domestic relations order under the definition of that phrase that is applicable to those provisions." This provision confirms that dividing Colin's 401(k) by qualified domestic relations order is not only appropriate but is the procedurally correct mechanism for effectuating the Court's distribution of retirement benefits.
In Ogden v. Ogden, 39 P.3d 513 (Alaska 2001), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed the proper division of retirement accounts in dissolution proceedings, recognizing that courts must carefully distinguish between different types of retirement vehicles and the availability of present-value approaches versus deferred distribution by qualified domestic relations order. The Court's analysis in that case confirms that the trial court retains flexibility in structuring the division of retirement benefits, but that the division must accurately reflect the marital and non-marital components of the account.
Here, Renee does not seek to invade Colin's pre-marital contribution balance. She asks only that the Court identify the marital portion of the 401(k) using Colin's account statements and employer records, and allocate that marital increment equally by qualified domestic relations order. Colin bears the burden of documenting the claimed pre-marital balance with reliable evidence. Absent such documentation, the entire account should be treated as marital property. The statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) further support an equal division of the marital portion, given the ten-year marriage, the parties' respective earning capacities, and Renee's custodial responsibilities for the two children throughout the marriage.
In Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014), the Alaska Supreme Court examined a property division in which a 401(k) account was at the center of the marital estate, and the Court scrutinized the trial court's allocation of that asset in light of the disparity between the parties' positions. The case reinforces the principle that retirement assets must be valued and divided with precision, particularly in proceedings where one party proceeds without counsel or where the parties' financial circumstances are markedly unequal. Renee respectfully urges this Court to apply the same careful analysis here and to order division of the marital increment of Colin's 401(k) by qualified domestic relations order.
B. The Court Should Allocate the Majority of the Joint Credit Card Debt to Colin in Light of the Substantial Disparity in Earning Capacity
The parties carry approximately $28,000 in joint credit card debt. Renee requests that the Court assign the majority of this obligation to Colin. This request is firmly grounded in the statutory factors governing property and debt division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
The relevant statutory factors support Renee's position. First, AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C) directs the Court to consider "the earning capacity of the parties, including their educational backgrounds, training, employment skills, work experiences, length of absence from the job market, and custodial responsibilities for children during the marriage." Colin's employment as a pipeline technician on the North Slope generates income substantially higher than Renee's. Renee's earning capacity has been further constrained by her custodial responsibilities for the parties' two children throughout the marriage, particularly during Colin's extended North Slope work rotations.
Second, AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(G) requires the Court to consider "the circumstances and necessities of each party." Following the dissolution, Renee will be the primary custodial parent for two school-age children. Her financial circumstances and day-to-day necessities will be materially more demanding than Colin's, given the costs associated with maintaining a stable household for the children during the school year.
Third, AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(D) calls for consideration of "the financial condition of the parties, including the availability and cost of health insurance." Colin's substantially higher income places him in a far stronger position to absorb the joint debt obligations without jeopardizing his financial stability. Assigning the majority of the $28,000 debt to Colin is therefore consistent with the statutory framework and with the equitable principles underlying Alaska's property division law.
The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006), that an unequal division of marital assets and obligations is appropriate when the relevant statutory factors, particularly earning capacity and financial condition, support such an allocation. Similarly, in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed a property division that took into account the disparity in earning capacity between the parties and the custodial parent's greater post-dissolution financial burdens. These authorities confirm that this Court may and should allocate the preponderance of the joint credit card debt to Colin.
Renee does not seek to escape all responsibility for the jointly incurred obligations. She is prepared to assume a reasonable share of the $28,000 balance. However, fairness and the statutory command to "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" require that the larger portion of this debt be assigned to Colin, who possesses the financial capacity to service it without compromising the welfare of the children or his own basic needs.
C. Child Support Should Be Calculated Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Based on Colin's Adjusted Annual Income as a Pipeline Technician
Renee proposes a primary physical custody arrangement in which the two children reside with her at the Anchorage family residence during the school year. Under this arrangement, child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides that the award in a primary physical custody case equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines "adjusted annual income" as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" certain enumerated deductions, including mandatory federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and certain voluntary retirement contributions subject to a cap. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) specifies that the applicable percentage for two children is 27% (.27) of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income.
Colin's employment as a pipeline technician on the North Slope generates a substantially higher income than Renee's. The child support calculation should therefore begin with a full and accurate accounting of Colin's gross income from all sources, including any bonuses, hazard pay, or other supplemental compensation attributable to his North Slope position, reduced only by the deductions expressly authorized under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that courts must carefully assess each parent's income from all sources and apply the Rule 90.3 framework accurately, including the proper calculation of adjusted annual income for child support purposes. The Court's analysis in that case reinforces the importance of a thorough income review and the application of the correct percentage multiplier based on the number of children subject to the support order.
Renee acknowledges that Colin is entitled to claim the deductions authorized under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including mandatory tax withholdings and mandatory retirement contributions. However, any voluntary retirement contributions claimed as a deduction are subject to the combined cap of 7.5% of total income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B). Colin should not be permitted to inflate voluntary retirement deferrals to artificially reduce his adjusted annual income and thereby diminish his child support obligation.
Additionally, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) permits the Court to allow the obligor parent to reduce child support payments by up to 75% for any period in which the obligor has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days. Renee acknowledges that Colin's proposed six-week summer parenting block may qualify for this credit, and she does not object to its application to the summer months, provided that the credit is expressly conditioned on Colin's actual exercise of that parenting time. The child support order should specify the amount of the reduction allowable if extended visitation is exercised, consistent with the rule's requirements.
D. The Proposed Custody Arrangement Serves the Best Interests of the Children and Should Be Adopted by the Court
Renee proposes that the two minor children reside with her at the Anchorage family home during the school year, with Colin exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and for a six-week block each summer, and that the parties share joint legal custody. This arrangement reflects the practical realities of the parties' circumstances and places the children's best interests at the center of the custody framework.
AS 25.24.160(a)(1) authorizes the Court to provide for contributions toward "the nurture and education" of the children in a manner that is just and proper. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly identifies as a relevant factor "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." Although the parties have agreed to sell the marital home, this factor underscores the legislative policy favoring stability in the children's primary residential arrangements, a consideration that supports Renee's retention of primary physical custody and her ability to maintain a stable school-year residence for the children in Anchorage.
Colin's North Slope work schedule, which involves extended periods of absence from Anchorage, further supports this arrangement. The children are school-age, and their educational continuity, extracurricular activities, and peer relationships are anchored in Anchorage. Disruption to these connections would not serve their best interests. The alternating weekend schedule when Colin is in Anchorage and the six-week summer block provide Colin with meaningful, regular parenting time while preserving the children's stability during the school year.
Joint legal custody ensures that both parents remain engaged in major decisions concerning the children's education, health care, and general welfare. This arrangement reflects the parties' shared commitment to co-parenting and avoids the marginalization of either parent from significant decisions affecting the children's upbringing.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Order division of the marital portion of Colin's employer-sponsored 401(k) account, defined as contributions and earnings accumulated from the date of marriage through the date of separation, equally between the parties by qualified domestic relations order consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and AS 25.24.160(b), while excluding any documented pre-marital contribution balance as Colin's separate property;
2. Allocate the majority of the approximately $28,000 in joint credit card debt to Colin, based on the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the substantial disparity in the parties' earning capacities, Renee's post-dissolution custodial responsibilities, and the respective financial conditions of the parties;
3. Calculate Colin's monthly child support obligation pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on his adjusted annual income from all sources as a pipeline technician, applying the 27% multiplier applicable to two children, with a potential extended-visitation credit for the six-week summer parenting block conditioned on actual exercise of that parenting time; and
4. Enter a custody order consistent with Renee's proposed primary physical custody arrangement, with joint legal custody, alternating weekend parenting time for Colin, and a six-week summer parenting block, as this arrangement best serves the children's interests in stability, continuity, and meaningful relationships with both parents.
Renee Nakamura respectfully submits that the proposed terms, taken together, fairly allocate the economic effect of this dissolution consistent with AS 25.24.160, the Alaska Civil Rules, and the governing case law of the Alaska Supreme Court.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0024)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Colby respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for dissolution of the marriage between herself and Respondent Maria Colby. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and have two minor children, ages six and nine. The marriage has suffered an irremediable breakdown due to incompatibility of temperament, including persistent financial disagreements and extended periods of emotional estrangement. Priya now seeks a final decree of dissolution that establishes a primary physical custody arrangement, a properly calculated child support obligation, a fair and just division of marital property, and a resolution of the parties' shared debts. This brief addresses the applicable legal standards governing each of these issues and demonstrates that the proposed resolution is consistent with Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Colby and Maria Colby were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The couple has two minor children born of the marriage: one child age nine and one child age six. Over the past two years, the marriage has deteriorated due to irreconcilable differences, manifesting primarily as persistent disagreements regarding marital finances and extended periods of emotional estrangement between the parties. These circumstances constitute an irremediable breakdown of the marriage.
Priya works as a hospital administrator and earns approximately $72,000 per year. Maria works as a commercial fisheries contractor and earns approximately $48,000 per year. Priya proposes that the children reside primarily with her during the school week. Maria would exercise parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. Both parties agree to share joint legal custody and to consult each other on major decisions affecting the children's education, healthcare, and general well-being.
The marital estate consists of the following assets and liabilities: the marital home in Anchorage, which carries an estimated equity of $140,000 and a remaining mortgage balance of $210,000; a joint savings account; two vehicles; and approximately $35,000 in shared credit card debt accumulated during the marriage. The parties dispute the calculation of child support and disagree over which parent should be entitled to claim the children as dependents for federal income tax purposes.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska Superior Court has jurisdiction over dissolution proceedings pursuant to AS 25.24.200, which authorizes the court to grant a decree of dissolution where incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. Under that statute, the parties must reach agreement on child custody and support, division of property, and allocation of debts for a joint petition to proceed.
In adjudicating the issues presented by this dissolution, the court must apply several interrelated standards. With respect to property division and spousal maintenance, AS 25.24.922 requires that any division of marital property and any award of maintenance fairly allocate the economic effect of the dissolution, taking into consideration a series of enumerated statutory factors. With respect to child support, Civil Rule 934(a) establishes the formula governing support awards in primary physical custody cases, and Civil Rule 90.3(f) provides the definitions that determine which custody designation applies for purposes of the support calculation. Finally, AS 25.24.152 governs the allocation of dependent tax exemptions, prohibiting the court from unconditionally granting a noncustodial parent the right to claim a child as a dependent under federal income tax laws.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT SERVES THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND IS CONSISTENT WITH ALASKA LAW.
Priya proposes that the children reside with her during the school week, with Maria exercising parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. Both parties agree to share joint legal custody and to jointly consult on decisions regarding the children's education, healthcare, and general well-being.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), a parent has primary physical custody for purposes of the child support rule "if the children reside with the other parent for a period specified in the custody order of less than 30 percent of the year." Under the proposed schedule, the children would reside with Maria for approximately two days every two weeks plus one evening per week, which amounts to significantly less than thirty percent of the year. Accordingly, Priya holds primary physical custody as defined by the rule, and Maria is the noncustodial parent for child support purposes.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that custody determinations must be rooted in the specific circumstances of the children involved. In Helen S.K. v. Samuel M.K., 288 P.3d 463 (Alaska 2012), the court affirmed a custody arrangement that divided parenting time based on a careful examination of each child's needs and each parent's capabilities. Similarly, in Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006), the court upheld a primary custody award to one parent paired with structured visitation rights for the other, finding that arrangement served the children's best interests. The proposed parenting plan here reflects those same principles: it provides the children with a stable, school-week home base with Priya while preserving a meaningful and regular relationship with Maria through biweekly weekend visits and a weekly evening.
The joint legal custody arrangement, under which both parents share decision-making authority over education, healthcare, and general well-being, is likewise appropriate. Joint legal custody preserves both parents' meaningful participation in the children's lives without disrupting the stability the primary physical custody arrangement provides.
B. CHILD SUPPORT MUST BE CALCULATED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON MARIA'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME.
Because the children will reside primarily with Priya, Maria is the noncustodial parent obligated to pay child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a). That rule provides that a child support award in a primary physical custody case "will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage" specified in the rule. For two children, the applicable percentage is twenty-seven percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" a series of enumerated mandatory and permitted deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, voluntary retirement contributions up to the applicable cap, work-related child care expenses for the children subject to the order, and health insurance premiums paid by the parent for the parent only, subject to the ten percent income cap stated in the rule.
Maria earns approximately $48,000 per year as a commercial fisheries contractor. Because Maria is a contractor, she may also be subject to self-employment tax, which is itself a mandatory deduction under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A)(ii). Priya respectfully requests that the court require Maria to provide a complete financial disclosure so that the adjusted annual income calculation can be performed accurately and in compliance with Rule 90.3.
In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that the adjusted annual income calculation under Rule 90.3 must be performed with careful attention to each allowable deduction and that courts may not depart from the formula without basis. That principle applies with equal force here. The court should calculate Maria's child support obligation strictly in accordance with Rule 90.3(a), applying the twenty-seven percent multiplier for two children to her properly computed adjusted annual income.
If at any time Maria voluntarily reduces her income or becomes underemployed without reasonable justification, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes the court to calculate support based on a determination of Maria's potential income, taking into account factors including her employment and earnings history, job skills, educational attainment, the local job market, and other relevant circumstances.
C. THE NONCUSTODIAL PARENT MAY NOT BE UNCONDITIONALLY GRANTED THE RIGHT TO CLAIM THE CHILDREN AS DEPENDENTS FOR FEDERAL INCOME TAX PURPOSES.
Alaska law imposes strict limitations on the allocation of federal dependent tax exemptions in dissolution proceedings. AS 25.24.152(a) provides that in an action for divorce, dissolution, or to declare a marriage void, "the court may not unconditionally grant to a noncustodial parent the right to claim a child as a dependent under federal income tax laws." The court may permit a noncustodial parent to claim a child as a dependent for a given tax year only if that parent satisfies the requirements of federal law and was not in arrears at the end of the tax year in an amount more than four times the monthly child support obligation.
This same protection is codified in the dissolution-specific context under AS 25.24.232, which prohibits the court from incorporating into a final decree of dissolution any agreement that "unconditionally entitles a noncustodial parent to claim a child as a dependent under federal income tax laws."
Applying these statutes here, Maria, as the noncustodial parent, may not receive an unconditional right to claim either child as a dependent. Any allocation of the tax exemption to Maria for any given year must be conditioned upon her compliance with her child support obligation and upon her satisfaction of applicable federal tax law requirements. Priya, as the custodial parent, is entitled to retain the default tax exemption unless and until a conditional allocation to Maria is ordered by the court and the statutory conditions are satisfied for that particular tax year.
D. THE MARITAL PROPERTY MUST BE DIVIDED IN A MANNER THAT FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF THE DISSOLUTION.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires that the division of marital property be "just" and that it "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" by being based on a consideration of the enumerated statutory factors. Those factors include the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, their financial conditions, any unreasonable depletion of marital assets, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party who has primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity of the property.
The parties have been married since 2015, a marriage of approximately ten years. Both parties are working adults with meaningful earning capacity: Priya earns $72,000 per year and Maria earns $48,000 per year. The following principles should guide the court's division of each marital asset.
1. The Marital Home.
The marital home in Anchorage carries an estimated equity of $140,000 and a remaining mortgage balance of $210,000. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically identifies "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children" as an express factor in the property division analysis. Because the children will reside primarily with Priya during the school week, awarding Priya the right to remain in the family home directly supports the children's stability and continuity of environment.
In Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed the allocation of the family home in a dissolution involving minor children and primary custody, recognizing the significance of that asset to the custodial household. Consistent with that principle and with AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), Priya requests that the court award her the marital home, with Maria receiving an equalization payment or offset against other marital assets in recognition of her proportional equity interest.
2. The Joint Savings Account and Vehicles.
The joint savings account and two vehicles are marital assets subject to equitable division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). In Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that marital assets should be divided in a manner that accounts for each party's earning capacity and post-dissolution financial circumstances. The court should divide the savings account and vehicles in a manner that reflects both the relative earning capacity of the parties and their respective needs following dissolution. Priya proposes that each party retain one vehicle and that the savings account be divided equitably, with the precise allocation to be determined after full financial disclosure by both parties.
3. The Shared Credit Card Debt.
Approximately $35,000 in shared credit card debt was accumulated during the marriage. AS 25.24.200(a)(4) requires that the parties reach agreement as to "the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both of them." Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(E), the court may consider whether there has been any unreasonable depletion of marital assets in connection with the allocation of debt. Absent evidence of such depletion by either party, the debt should be allocated proportionally between the parties in a manner consistent with their respective financial circumstances and earning capacities. Priya proposes that the debt be divided equitably, with each party responsible for approximately half, subject to the court's review of each party's financial condition as disclosed in the proceedings.
In Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that a trial court's allocation of marital property, including debt, must be grounded in the statutory factors and must result in a division that fairly allocates the economic consequences of dissolution between the parties. That standard is satisfied here by the proposed equitable distribution of the credit card debt.
E. PROPERTY DIVISION AND ANY MAINTENANCE AWARD MUST FAIRLY ALLOCATE THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION UNDER AS 25.24.160.
AS 25.24.160(a)(2) authorizes the court to award maintenance to either party "as may be just and necessary without regard to which of the parties is in fault" and requires that any such award "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" by being based on a consideration of the factors enumerated in that subsection. Those factors include the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, their earning capacities, their financial conditions, the division of property under subsection (a)(4), and other relevant factors.
Priya does not presently seek spousal maintenance; however, she reserves the right to request such relief if the property division does not fairly allocate the economic effect of the dissolution in light of the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(2). The significant disparity in the parties' incomes, with Priya earning $72,000 and Maria earning $48,000, and the fact that Priya will bear the primary day-to-day costs of raising the children, are factors that the court should weigh carefully in fashioning the overall resolution. Teale v. Wysocki, 589 P.3d 625 (Alaska 2013), illustrates that the Alaska Supreme Court reviews property division and support determinations holistically to ensure that the combined economic effect of all orders is equitable as between the parties.
F. THE DISSOLUTION PETITION SATISFIES THE PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS OF AS 25.24.210.
AS 25.24.210 prescribes the required contents of a petition for dissolution of marriage. The petition must state the respective occupations and incomes of the petitioners, the date and place of the marriage, the name, date of birth, and current status of each minor child, whether the wife is pregnant, whether either petitioner requires medical care, whether any protective orders or domestic violence charges have been issued or filed during the marriage, whether either petitioner has received legal counsel, and that the petition constitutes the entire agreement between the parties.
Priya's petition satisfies each of these requirements. The petition discloses both parties' occupations and approximate incomes, identifies the marriage date and place as Anchorage, Alaska in 2015, identifies the two minor children by their ages, confirms that no pregnancy is present, and addresses the remaining required disclosures. The petition further states the terms of the parties' agreement on custody, parenting time, and proposed property division consistent with AS 25.24.210(e).
AS 25.24.155 governs the reservation of custody and property division issues and provides that the court may not delay or reserve such issues unless each party expressly agrees on the record or a moving party demonstrates good cause and the court finds that the opposing party's interests will not be jeopardized. Priya does not seek to reserve any issue; she requests that all matters be resolved in the final decree.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Priya Colby respectfully requests that this Court enter a final decree of dissolution of marriage granting the following relief: (1) a finding that the marriage has suffered an irremediable breakdown due to incompatibility of temperament; (2) an award of primary physical custody of the two minor children to Priya, with Maria exercising parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week, and joint legal custody shared by both parties; (3) a child support order requiring Maria, as the noncustodial parent, to pay support calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), applying the twenty-seven percent multiplier to Maria's properly computed adjusted annual income for two children; (4) a tax dependency allocation consistent with AS 25.24.152 and AS 25.24.232, conditioning any allocation of the federal dependent exemption to Maria upon her timely satisfaction of her child support obligation and compliance with federal law requirements; (5) an award of the marital home to Priya, with an equitable offset to Maria from other marital assets; (6) an equitable division of the joint savings account and vehicles; and (7) an equitable allocation of the $35,000 in shared marital credit card debt between the parties based on their respective financial circumstances.
Priya Colby respectfully submits that the proposed resolution fairly allocates the economic effect of this dissolution and serves the best interests of the parties' two minor children, consistent with Alaska law.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0025)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Bergstrom brings this action for dissolution of her marriage to Michael Bergstrom pursuant to AS 25.24.160 and AS 25.24.200. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and have two minor children, ages six and nine. After a decade of marriage marked by Michael's extended absences for North Slope employment and persistent disputes over financial management, the marriage has irretrievably broken down. Elena now seeks a final decree of dissolution that addresses physical and legal custody of the children, child support calculated in accordance with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3, allocation of marital property including the family home and Michael's PERS retirement account, and equitable distribution of the parties' joint debt. The relief requested is consistent with Alaska law and serves both the best interests of the minor children and the equitable treatment of both parties.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena and Michael Bergstrom were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. During the ten years of the marriage, the couple had two children, now ages six and nine. Throughout the marriage, Elena served as the children's primary caregiver while Michael worked as a petroleum technician on the North Slope, requiring extended absences from the family home located in Eagle River, Alaska.
Michael earns approximately $95,000 per year as a petroleum technician. Elena earns approximately $38,000 per year as a dental hygienist. The significant disparity in the parties' incomes, combined with Michael's recurring work-related absences and recurring disputes over financial management, caused the marriage to deteriorate over the past two years. The breakdown of the marital relationship is irremediable.
The marital estate consists of the Eagle River family home encumbered by a mortgage of approximately $220,000, two motor vehicles, a joint savings account, and Michael's PERS retirement account accumulated during the marriage. The parties have also incurred approximately $18,000 in shared credit card debt that has not yet been allocated between them.
Elena proposes that the children reside primarily with her during the school year, with Michael exercising alternating weekend visits and extended parenting time during summers and school breaks. The parties agree to share joint legal custody for major decisions affecting the children's health, education, and general well-being. Elena requests that child support be set according to Civil Rule 90.3, and that Michael contribute to unreimbursed medical and childcare expenses on a pro-rata income basis.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
In an action for dissolution of marriage, the superior court has broad authority to address child support, child custody, spousal maintenance, and property division. AS 25.24.160 authorizes the court to order payment for the nurture and education of children, award maintenance, and divide property acquired during the marriage in a just manner. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the division of property must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce based on a consideration of enumerated statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, their respective earning capacities, and the financial condition of each party. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(2), any maintenance award must be based on similar factors and must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce.
Child support is calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a), which sets support as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage for the number of children. Civil Rule 90.3(f) defines primary physical custody for purposes of applying the correct child support formula.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must carefully assess the best interests of the children in any custody determination, and has held that property division must reflect an equitable balancing of the parties' respective circumstances. Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004); Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND SHOULD BE APPROVED BY THE COURT.
The paramount consideration in any child custody determination is the best interests of the children. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(1), the court may provide for the nurture and education of the children as may be just and proper. Elena has served as the primary caregiver for both children throughout the marriage. The children, ages six and nine, are enrolled in school in the Eagle River area where Elena resides and intends to continue residing. Stability and continuity of environment are essential to their well-being.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a child's established living environment and the quality of the relationship with each parent are central factors in custody determinations. Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004). Elena's continuous role as primary caregiver, the children's established school placement, and the children's need for stable daily routines during the school year all support placing primary physical custody with Elena.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), a parent has primary physical custody for purposes of child support calculations when the children reside with the other parent for less than thirty percent of the year. The custody schedule proposed here, under which Michael exercises alternating weekends plus extended summer and school-break parenting time, may result in Michael having the children between approximately twenty-five and thirty percent of the year depending on the specific schedule ultimately ordered. The court should confirm the applicable custody category at the time of entry of the final decree so that child support is properly calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) or Civil Rule 90.3(f), as appropriate.
The proposed joint legal custody arrangement is equally consistent with the children's best interests. Sharing major decisions about health, education, and well-being ensures that both parents remain meaningfully involved in the children's lives despite the physical custody arrangement. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that joint legal custody can serve children's interests even when one parent holds primary physical custody. Helen S.K. v. Samuel M.K., 288 P.3d 463 (Alaska 2012).
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED PURSUANT TO CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON MICHAEL'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME.
The parties agree that child support shall be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. That rule provides that child support in a primary physical custody case equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage based on the number of children. Civil Rule 90.3(a). For two children, that percentage is twenty-seven percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Michael's gross annual income is approximately $95,000. His adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) is calculated by subtracting mandatory deductions, including federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and other qualifying deductions set forth in the rule, from his total income. After applying the applicable statutory deductions, Michael's adjusted annual income will be determined by the court. At twenty-seven percent of adjusted annual income, the resulting child support obligation will provide meaningful support for both children while remaining consistent with Michael's actual ability to pay.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that the Rule 90.3 formula must be applied rigorously and that a parent's earning capacity, including actual income, work history, and professional qualifications, forms the foundation of the child support calculation. Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019); Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002). Michael is an employed petroleum technician with a consistent and documented annual income. There is no basis for deviating from the guideline amount. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
In addition to the base child support obligation, Elena requests that Michael contribute to unreimbursed medical expenses and work-related childcare expenses on a pro-rata income basis. This approach is consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E), which allows work-related child care expenses to be deducted from a parent's income in calculating adjusted annual income, and with the broader framework of Civil Rule 90.3 ensuring that child-related costs are shared in proportion to each parent's financial capacity. Given that Michael earns approximately $95,000 and Elena earns approximately $38,000, Michael's pro-rata share of the combined income is approximately seventy-one percent, making his proportionate contribution to these additional costs equitable and appropriate.
C. THE MARITAL PROPERTY MUST BE DIVIDED EQUITABLY BASED ON THE FACTORS SET FORTH IN AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the court must divide property acquired during the marriage in a just manner, taking into account the factors enumerated in the statute. Those factors include the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each spouse, the financial condition of each party, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity of the property.
The parties' marital estate consists of the Eagle River family home with a $220,000 mortgage, two vehicles, a joint savings account, and Michael's PERS retirement account accumulated during the marriage. The division of this estate must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
1. The Family Home.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically identifies the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period, to the party who has primary physical custody of the children. Elena is the proposed primary physical custodian. Both children attend school in the Eagle River community. Awarding Elena the right to remain in the family home during the children's minority, or awarding her the home outright subject to assumption of the associated mortgage obligation, serves both this statutory preference and the children's need for stability.
The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed that awarding the family home to the primary custodial parent is appropriate where doing so serves the children's continuity of environment and the equities otherwise support such an award. Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002). Given Elena's role as primary caregiver and the children's established ties to the Eagle River community, the family home should be awarded to Elena, with the parties' equity in the home considered in the overall balancing of the marital estate.
2. Michael's PERS Retirement Account.
Michael's PERS retirement account accumulated during the marriage constitutes marital property subject to division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). AS 25.24.160(a)(1) expressly contemplates that the court may provide for the payment of amounts including retirement benefits in addressing the parties' respective contributions and needs. AS 25.24.160(b) further addresses the distribution of retirement benefits through a qualified domestic relations order where applicable.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that retirement benefits accumulated during a marriage are a significant component of the marital estate and must be valued and divided consistent with the statutory equitable factors. Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019). Given the length of the marriage, the parties' disparate incomes, and Elena's reduced earning capacity stemming from her years of primary caregiving, Elena is entitled to an equitable share of the marital portion of Michael's PERS account. The precise division should be accomplished through a qualified domestic relations order as required by AS 25.24.160(b).
3. Vehicles and Joint Savings Account.
The two vehicles and joint savings account should be divided equitably between the parties. Elena requires reliable transportation to fulfill her employment responsibilities and to transport the children to school, medical appointments, and other activities. The court should award each party one vehicle, with any difference in value between the vehicles treated as an offset within the overall property division. The joint savings account should be divided based on the overall equities of the property settlement, taking into account any offsetting adjustments made with respect to the family home, retirement account, and debt allocation.
4. Shared Credit Card Debt.
The parties have accumulated approximately $18,000 in shared credit card debt that remains unallocated. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the allocation of marital obligations is an element of the just division of the marital estate. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that equitable distribution of marital debt follows principles analogous to those governing property division, with courts considering the circumstances of each party, the nature of the obligations, and each party's ability to service the debt. Laughlin v. Laughlin, 229 P.3d 1002 (Alaska 2010).
Given the significant income disparity between the parties, and the fact that the debt was incurred jointly during the marriage, the court should allocate the shared credit card debt proportionately to the parties' respective incomes or in conjunction with the overall property settlement, ensuring that Elena is not unduly burdened by obligations she cannot realistically service on her $38,000 annual income.
D. THE DISSOLUTION PETITION MEETS THE STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS OF AS 25.24.200 AND AS 25.24.230.
For a dissolution petition to be granted under AS 25.24.200(a), the parties must demonstrate, among other conditions, that incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, that agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just and in the children's best interests, and that the property and debt agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. AS 25.24.230(a) requires the court to find that the spouses fully understand the nature and consequences of their action, that written agreements are fair and just and constitute the entire agreement, and that each spouse entered into the agreements voluntarily and free from coercion.
The circumstances of this case satisfy each of these requirements. Michael's recurring extended absences and the parties' ongoing financial disputes have created an irremediable breakdown of the marriage. Elena's proposed arrangements for custody, child support, and property division reflect fair and considered positions that account for the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4) as required by AS 25.24.200(e) and AS 25.24.230(a)(3). The petition should contain the specific information required by AS 25.24.210(e), including the parties' respective incomes, assets, liabilities, the terms of the custody agreement, and child support provisions.
Where the petition involves minor children and one party is the primary caregiver, the court should apply the heightened scrutiny directed by AS 25.24.220(h) to ensure that the child custody and property agreements are truly just and in the children's best interests. Elena welcomes such scrutiny as the proposed arrangements reflect both the children's developmental needs and the economic realities of the parties' circumstances.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Elena Bergstrom respectfully requests that the court:
1. Approve the proposed primary physical custody arrangement placing the children with Elena during the school year, with Michael exercising alternating weekend visits and extended parenting time during summers and school breaks, and grant the parties joint legal custody for major decisions;
2. Calculate and order Michael's child support obligation pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on his adjusted annual income of approximately $95,000, at the rate of twenty-seven percent applicable to two children, and further order that Michael contribute to unreimbursed medical and childcare expenses on a pro-rata income basis;
3. Divide the marital estate in a just and equitable manner consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including awarding Elena the family home given her primary custodial role, distributing Michael's PERS retirement account through a qualified domestic relations order as contemplated by AS 25.24.160(b), assigning one vehicle to each party, dividing the joint savings account equitably, and allocating the $18,000 in shared credit card debt in a manner proportionate to the parties' respective incomes; and
4. Grant such other relief as the court finds just and proper in furtherance of the best interests of the minor children and the equitable resolution of the parties' marital estate.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0026)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Colby ("Petitioner") respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for dissolution of marriage and proposed parenting plan. Ashley and Jennifer Colby were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, ages five and eight. The marriage has irretrievably broken down due to persistent financial conflict and irreconcilable differences in parenting approaches, and the parties have been unable to reach a negotiated resolution on custody, child support, or property division.
This brief addresses three principal issues: (1) the appropriate physical custody arrangement for the parties' two minor children; (2) the proper calculation of Jennifer Colby's child support obligation under Alaska Civil Rule 90.3; and (3) the equitable division of the marital home, joint savings account, and shared vehicle debt under AS 25.24.160. Ashley respectfully requests that this Court enter a dissolution decree awarding her primary physical custody of the children, ordering child support consistent with Alaska's guidelines, and dividing the marital estate in a just and equitable manner as outlined herein.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Colby and Jennifer Colby were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The marriage produced two minor children: a child currently age eight and a child currently age five. Both children have been raised in the Eagle River community, where they attend school and participate in extracurricular activities. Over the course of the marriage, persistent disagreements over finances and fundamentally incompatible approaches to child-rearing have caused the irretrievable breakdown of the marriage. Ashley filed a petition for dissolution in the Superior Court, Third Judicial District, pursuant to AS 25.24.200.
Ashley proposes a primary physical custody arrangement under which the children reside with her during the school week, with Jennifer exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and one weekday evening per week. Both parties agree to share joint legal custody. Jennifer, employed as a petroleum engineer, earns a substantially higher income than Ashley, and Ashley requests that child support be calculated in accordance with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 based on Jennifer's adjusted annual income.
The marital estate consists of the parties' home in Eagle River, which carries an outstanding mortgage balance of approximately $310,000 against a current estimated market value of approximately $375,000, yielding net equity of approximately $65,000. The parties also hold a joint savings account containing approximately $42,000 and a shared vehicle loan with an outstanding balance of approximately $18,000. The parties dispute both the custody schedule and the division of these marital assets and liabilities.
Jennifer contests the proposed parenting plan and instead requests a week-on, week-off shared physical custody schedule, asserting that an equal residential arrangement better serves the children's well-being and reflects her historically active involvement in their daily care.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts have broad equitable authority to resolve issues of custody, child support, and property division in dissolution proceedings. AS 25.24.160 authorizes the court to provide for child support, spousal maintenance, and the division of marital property in a manner that is "just and proper" and that "fairly allocate[s] the economic effect of divorce" by considering an enumerated list of factors. AS 25.24.200 sets forth the conditions governing joint petitions for dissolution, and requires that agreements on custody and property division be fair, just, and in the best interests of the children.
With respect to physical custody, where parents dispute a shared versus primary custody arrangement, the court must consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the child's continuity in the community, and any evidence bearing on domestic circumstances and parental cooperation. The Alaska Supreme Court has held that the trial court must make individualized findings based on these statutory factors. Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004).
Child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which sets the award as a percentage of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income: twenty percent for one child and twenty-seven percent for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2) defines primary physical custody as existing when the children reside with the other parent for less than thirty percent of the year. Shared physical custody, as defined in Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), requires that the children reside with the parent claiming that status for at least thirty but no more than seventy percent of the year. The distinction between primary and shared custody has significant consequences for the child support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(b).
Property division is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which directs the court to divide marital property "in a just manner" based on numerous factors including the length of the marriage, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of each party, and the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that the trial court retains broad discretion in dividing the marital estate, and will not disturb a property division unless it is clearly unjust. Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT SERVES THE CHILDREN'S BEST INTERESTS UNDER AS 25.20.090
The central question in any custody dispute is the best interests of the children. Under AS 25.20.090, the court must evaluate a range of factors when determining whether to award shared custody, including the children's needs, the stability of each parent's home environment, the children's educational continuity, the advantages of keeping the children in their current community, and each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate the other parent's relationship with the children. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that these factors must be evaluated in light of the particular facts of each case, and that custody arrangements must serve the children's actual developmental and emotional needs. Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004).
Here, the children are ages five and eight, both enrolled in the Eagle River school community. The eight-year-old in particular is at a critical developmental stage where academic consistency and the stability of a predictable weekly routine are paramount. A primary physical custody arrangement, in which the children reside with Ashley during the school week, best protects the children's educational continuity and daily stability. Under Ashley's proposed plan, Jennifer retains meaningful, regular contact through alternating weekends and a weekly evening visit, preserving the children's bond with both parents without subjecting them to the logistical disruptions of a week-on, week-off schedule.
Jennifer's request for a week-on, week-off arrangement, while reflecting her desire for equal residential time, does not automatically serve the children's best interests. AS 25.20.090(3) directs the court to assess the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent. Given the ongoing conflict between the parties that precipitated this dissolution, a schedule requiring weekly transitions may expose the children to repeated disruptions and the stress of frequent environmental changes. The five-year-old child, in particular, is at an age at which attachment and routine are critical to healthy development, and the court should weigh this factor heavily.
AS 25.20.090(6) requires the court to consider the optimal time each parent will spend with the children, including the feasibility of travel between the parents, special needs unique to each child, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate the other's relationship with the children. Jennifer's employment as a petroleum engineer may involve irregular work schedules or travel demands that are less compatible with the rigid alternating-week structure she proposes. Ashley's proposed schedule accommodates Jennifer's parenting role while providing the children with a stable residential anchor during the school week.
AS 25.20.090(5) also directs the court to consider the advantages of keeping the children in the community where they presently reside. Both children are embedded in the Eagle River community, and maintaining their school enrollment, peer relationships, and community ties argues in favor of a schedule that does not require the children to manage dual primary residences. Ashley's proposed primary custody arrangement achieves this goal.
For all of these reasons, the proposed primary physical custody arrangement, with Jennifer exercising meaningful parenting time on alternating weekends and one weekly evening, best serves the children's needs under AS 25.20.090 and should be adopted by this Court.
B. JENNIFER'S CHILD SUPPORT OBLIGATION SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON HER ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS A PETROLEUM ENGINEER
Because Ashley proposes primary physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), Jennifer's child support obligation must be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a). Under that provision, the annual child support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage: twenty percent for one child and twenty-seven percent for two children. For two children, Jennifer's obligation would equal twenty-seven percent of her adjusted annual income as calculated under the deductions specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus mandatory deductions such as federal, state, and local income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, as well as permissible deductions for voluntary retirement contributions within specified limits, health insurance premiums for the parent only within specified limits, and work-related child care expenses for the children who are the subject of the support order. Jennifer's income as a petroleum engineer is substantial and will govern the calculation. Ashley respectfully requests that this Court order Jennifer to provide complete documentation of her income and permissible deductions so that the Court may accurately determine her adjusted annual income and set support accordingly.
If this Court were instead to accept Jennifer's proposal of a week-on, week-off shared physical custody arrangement, child support would be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), which uses a more complex formula that partially offsets each parent's theoretical obligation against the other and multiplies the difference by a factor of 1.5. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1) defines shared physical custody as existing when children reside with a parent for at least thirty but no more than seventy percent of the year. The shared custody formula would reduce Jennifer's net child support obligation compared to a primary custody calculation, which would be inequitable given the parties' significant income disparity and Ashley's status as the primary residential parent. The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that the paramount focus of child support is the welfare of the children, not the financial interests of the parents, and that the support formula is intended to ensure children are adequately provided for across all their needs. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) also authorizes the court to calculate child support based on a parent's potential income where that parent is voluntarily and unreasonably underemployed. While Ashley does not allege that Jennifer is currently underemployed, this provision confirms that the court must assess each parent's true earning capacity in setting support. Ashley's income, which is lower than Jennifer's, and her status as the primary residential parent justify the primary custody support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
C. THE MARITAL ESTATE SHOULD BE DIVIDED EQUITABLY UNDER AS 25.24.160, WITH PARTICULAR ATTENTION TO THE FAMILY HOME AND THE PARTIES' FINANCIAL CIRCUMSTANCES
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires the court to divide marital property "in a just manner" based on enumerated factors including the length of the marriage, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of each party including availability of health insurance, whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the trial court must make individualized findings on these statutory factors and exercise its broad discretion to achieve a just result. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996); Green v. Green, 29 P.3d 854 (Alaska 2001).
1. The Family Home
The marital home in Eagle River has an estimated market value of approximately $375,000, subject to an outstanding mortgage of approximately $310,000, yielding net equity of approximately $65,000. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), the court is directed to consider the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period, to the party who has primary physical custody of the children. Where, as here, Ashley is the proposed primary residential parent of two school-age children embedded in the Eagle River community, this factor strongly supports awarding Ashley the right to remain in the family home, at minimum for a reasonable period sufficient to allow the children to complete their schooling without displacement.
The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019) that the family home may be treated as separate or marital property depending on its acquisition history, and that the court must consider each party's earning capacity and financial circumstances in allocating the home and its associated equity. Here, the home was acquired during the marriage and is unquestionably marital property. Ashley requests that the Court award her the family home, with the equity to be accounted for in the overall property division. Jennifer's higher income as a petroleum engineer makes her better positioned to establish alternative housing than Ashley, who would be the primary caregiver for two young children.
The court should also take into account the factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C) and (G), namely the earning capacity and circumstances and necessities of each party. Ashley's comparatively lower income and her primary custodial role make her need for stable housing more acute. An equitable division does not require an equal numerical split where the statutory factors support a different result. Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002) (court may award a greater percentage of the marital estate to the party with lower earning capacity and greater financial need). If the home is awarded to Ashley, Jennifer's share of the equity may be satisfied through an offset from other marital assets or through a deferred buyout arrangement.
2. The Joint Savings Account
The parties' joint savings account contains approximately $42,000. As a marital asset accumulated during the marriage, this account is subject to equitable division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). Ashley requests an equal division of this account, resulting in each party receiving approximately $21,000. This equal split is appropriate given that the savings account represents liquid funds without the complications of an underlying debt, and an equal division reflects the parties' joint contributions to accumulating this asset over the course of the marriage.
If, however, the Court determines that awarding Ashley the family home results in a disproportionate share of the net marital estate, the Court may allocate a larger portion of the savings account to Jennifer as an offset, so long as the overall division fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution as required by AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The Court has discretion to fashion a division that achieves overall equity across all assets and liabilities rather than applying a rigid equal-split rule to each item individually. Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010).
3. The Shared Vehicle Loan
The parties have a shared vehicle loan with an outstanding balance of approximately $18,000. This joint debt is a marital liability subject to allocation by the Court. Ashley requests that the Court assign responsibility for this debt to the party who retains the vehicle, and that the allocation of this liability be factored into the overall property division. If Jennifer retains the vehicle, she should bear responsibility for the loan balance. If Ashley retains the vehicle, the loan balance should be reflected as a liability offsetting her share of the marital estate, with any resulting imbalance adjusted through the savings account division or other means available to the Court.
The statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) support a holistic approach to asset and debt allocation that takes into account each party's financial condition and ability to service debt. Jennifer's higher income renders her better positioned to absorb debt service obligations where the division of assets and liabilities is otherwise equitable.
D. THE OVERALL PROPERTY DIVISION MUST FAIRLY ALLOCATE THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires that the division of property "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" based on the enumerated factors. Alaska courts have construed this provision to require individualized factual findings and a reasoned balancing of all relevant considerations, not mechanical equal division. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996); Green v. Green, 29 P.3d 854 (Alaska 2001). The length of this marriage (approximately ten years at the time of filing), the parties' differential earning capacity, Ashley's primary custodial role, and the children's need for residential stability all support the division Ashley proposes.
Alaska courts have also recognized that the preference in Alaska is to resolve post-dissolution financial needs through property division rather than spousal maintenance where possible. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015); Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002). Ashley does not seek spousal maintenance at this time, but requests that the property division be structured in a manner that fairly accounts for the economic disparity between the parties and provides Ashley with the financial foundation necessary to support herself and the two children as the primary residential parent.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Ashley Colby respectfully requests that this Court:
(1) Enter a dissolution decree finding that the marriage has irretrievably broken down and granting the petition for dissolution;
(2) Award Ashley Colby primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, with Jennifer Colby exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and one weekday evening per week, and with both parties sharing joint legal custody;
(3) Calculate Jennifer Colby's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on her adjusted annual income as a petroleum engineer, at twenty-seven percent of her adjusted annual income for two children;
(4) Award Ashley Colby the marital home in Eagle River, with the net equity of approximately $65,000 accounted for in the overall property division, in light of her status as the primary residential parent of two school-age children;
(5) Divide the joint savings account equally, subject to any offset required to equalize the overall property division;
(6) Allocate the vehicle loan balance to the party who retains the vehicle, with appropriate adjustment to the overall property division; and
(7) Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and equitable under the circumstances.
