Tomas Whitfield and Sarah Whitfield were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The marriage produced two minor children, currently ages five and eight. Throughout the marriage, Tomas worked extended rotations on the North Slope, which required him to be absent from the family home for substantial and recurring periods. During those periods of absence, Sarah served as the sole caregiver for both children, managing their daily educational, medical, and developmental needs without regular assistance from Tomas.
Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to ongoing financial conflict and irreconcilable differences arising from the demands of Tomas's work schedule and the resulting strain on the family unit. The parties now seek to formalize the dissolution of their marriage and to resolve the outstanding issues of custody, child support, and property division.
The parties have reached a tentative agreement that Sarah will retain primary physical custody of both minor children. Tomas will exercise parenting time every other weekend, during his off-rotation periods, and pursuant to a structured holiday schedule to be incorporated into the final parenting plan. Tomas has proposed paying $1,800 per month in child support, which he represents is consistent with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines.
The marital estate consists of the family home in Anchorage, valued at approximately $420,000 with an outstanding mortgage balance of approximately $280,000, leaving net equity of approximately $140,000. The estate also includes two vehicles, a joint savings account holding approximately $34,000, and approximately $22,000 in shared credit card debt accumulated during a period of reduced household income. Tomas proposes an immediate sale of the family home and an equal division of the net equity. Sarah requests the right to remain in the family home with the children for a minimum of two years to preserve stability for the children's education and well-being, with a deferred sale or buyout negotiation to occur at the conclusion of that period.
The parties have not yet completed mandatory initial financial disclosures as required by Civil Rule 26.1(b), and the property division table required by Civil Rule 90.1(e) has not yet been filed. Full compliance with those disclosure obligations is necessary before any property division order can be entered.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
In any divorce proceeding, the superior court is vested with broad discretion to divide marital property in a just manner, taking into account the statutory factors set forth in AS 25.24.160. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized that the trial court's discretion in allocating marital assets is broad, and that decisions regarding the family home occupy a place of particular importance when minor children are involved. Hanlon v. Hanlon, 871 P.2d 229 (Alaska 1994); Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006).
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which establishes guidelines for calculating support based on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent. Compliance with Civil Rule 90.3 is mandatory absent extraordinary circumstances, and any deviation from the guideline amount must be supported by findings on the record. Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014).
Property division must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce based on a consideration of the statutory factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the desirability of awarding the family home or the right to remain in it for a reasonable period to the party with primary physical custody of the children. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Sarah Is Entitled to the Right to Remain in the Family Home for a Reasonable Period Because She Will Have Primary Physical Custody of the Minor Children.
Alaska Statute 25.24.160(a)(4) directs the Court to consider, among the statutory factors for property division, "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." This provision is not discretionary in the sense of permitting a court to ignore the inquiry; the Alaska Supreme Court has held that a trial court commits reversible error when it fails to address the second component of this provision, which concerns the right to remain in the home for a reasonable period even when outright award of the home is not ordered. Hanlon v. Hanlon, 871 P.2d 229 (Alaska 1994).
The parties have tentatively agreed that Sarah will have primary physical custody of both minor children, ages five and eight. Both children are currently enrolled in or approaching enrollment in Anchorage schools. The family home is the only residence either child has known during their formative years. Uprooting both children from that home immediately upon dissolution would impose a significant disruption to their educational continuity and emotional stability at a time when their lives are already undergoing substantial change as a result of the divorce.
The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed an award of the family home to the custodial parent in Odom v. Odom, 141 P.3d 324 (Alaska 2006), emphasizing that the children had lived in the family home their entire lives and that the trial court acted well within its discretion in making that award. While Sarah does not at this stage demand the permanent award of the home to her, she does request the right to remain in the home for a minimum of two years, with a deferred sale or buyout arrangement to be negotiated at that time. This approach serves the children's best interests while preserving Tomas's financial stake in the equity, which will remain intact and subject to court order at the conclusion of the deferred period.
The Court in Silvan v. Alcina, 105 P.3d 117 (Alaska 2005), affirmed a trial court's order that the family home be sold and that the custodial parent receive a proportionate share of its value, while also ordering interim monthly payments to compensate the custodial parent during the transition period. The flexibility inherent in that approach underscores that the Court has wide latitude to craft property remedies that protect the children's stability while preserving both parties' economic interests. A two-year deferred sale or buyout arrangement is precisely the kind of equitable remedy contemplated by AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) and sanctioned by Alaska Supreme Court precedent.
The factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4) further support Sarah's position. The parties have been married since 2015. Sarah has been the primary caregiver throughout the marriage due to Tomas's extended North Slope rotations. Her earning capacity has been affected by that caregiving role. The financial condition of the parties includes approximately $22,000 in joint credit card debt, which will affect both parties' immediate liquidity. The family home is the most significant asset in the marital estate, with net equity of approximately $140,000. Forcing an immediate sale would deprive the children of their stable residence without a corresponding benefit to Tomas that could not equally be achieved through a deferred arrangement. The circumstances and necessities of Sarah and the children, as a statutory factor under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(G), weigh decisively in favor of a deferred sale or buyout.
Furthermore, the Court in Hooper v. Hooper, 188 P.3d 681 (Alaska 2008), recognized that the interplay between custody decisions and property division is significant, and that the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) must be considered together. When a court awards primary physical custody to one parent, it is the clear intent of AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) that the residential stability of the children be weighted heavily in the property division calculus.
The Court should therefore deny Tomas's request for an immediate sale and instead enter an order permitting Sarah to remain in the family home for a minimum of two years, with the parties to negotiate a buyout arrangement or deferred sale at the end of that period. In the event the parties cannot agree on a buyout price or terms at that time, the Court should retain jurisdiction to order a sale and divide the proceeds in a just manner consistent with the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
B. The Proposed Child Support Amount Must Be Verified Against Civil Rule 90.3(a) Guidelines Before the Court Enters a Final Order.
Tomas has proposed paying $1,800 per month in child support, which he represents is consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) guidelines. The Court may not simply accept a represented figure without verifying that it is, in fact, consistent with the applicable guidelines. Civil Rule 90.3(a) requires that child support for primary physical custody cases be calculated as an amount equal to the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage: 27% for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
The adjusted annual income calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) requires deduction of mandatory items including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, as well as voluntary retirement contributions up to 7.5% of total income, work-related child care expenses for the subject children, and health insurance premiums paid by the parent for the parent only, subject to a cap of 10% of total income.
Given Tomas's employment on the North Slope, his income is likely subject to specific deductions and benefits that must be accurately reflected in the Rule 90.3(a)(1) calculation. The Court should require Tomas to provide full financial disclosure pursuant to Civil Rule 26.1(b) before any child support order is entered. Civil Rule 26.1(b)(1)(J) requires production of pay stubs and proof of income from all sources for the past two months, and Civil Rule 26.1(b)(1)(I) requires production of federal tax returns for the past three years. Without these disclosures, neither Sarah nor the Court can verify whether the proposed $1,800 monthly figure accurately reflects the Civil Rule 90.3(a) calculation.
Sarah does not concede at this stage that $1,800 per month is the correct figure. She reserves the right to challenge that figure after full financial disclosure has been completed. The Court should condition entry of any child support order on compliance with Civil Rule 26.1(b) disclosure requirements and independent verification of the Rule 90.3(a) calculation.
Additionally, if the evidence shows that Tomas is voluntarily underemployed or underreporting income, the Court has authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to impute potential income to him based on his assets, earning history, job skills, educational attainment, and prevailing earnings levels in the local community. While Sarah does not presently allege deliberate underreporting, she reserves that argument pending receipt of complete financial disclosures.
C. The Court Must Require Full Financial Disclosure Before Entering Any Property Division Order.
Civil Rule 90.1(e) requires each party to file and serve a property division table at least five days before trial, listing all assets and liabilities, their characterization as marital or separate property, their values, and each party's proposed disposition. Civil Rule 26.1(b) requires initial financial disclosures to be made within 45 days after the filing of the answer, including real property information, financial account records, pension and retirement plan releases, debt documentation, and income verification.
The parties have not yet completed these mandatory disclosures. The values assigned to the family home, the vehicles, and the savings account are approximations. The credit card debt has been described generally but not documented by account statements as required by Civil Rule 26.1(b)(1)(F). No formal appraisal of the family home has been disclosed, and no tax assessment or broker's opinion has been provided as required by Civil Rule 26.1(b)(1)(A).
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a fair and just property division under AS 25.24.160 depends on an accurate and complete record of the marital estate. Barnett v. Barnett, 238 P.3d 594 (Alaska 2010). Entry of a final property division order based on approximate figures and incomplete disclosures would risk an unjust outcome for either party. Sarah respectfully requests that the Court require full compliance with Civil Rule 26.1(b) and Civil Rule 90.1(e) before scheduling any hearing on final property division.
D. Any Agreement Regarding Custody and Child Support Is Subject to Court Review for the Best Interests of the Children.
The parties' tentative agreement regarding primary physical custody and parenting time is subject to court approval. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(1), the Court may provide for child support in a just and proper amount to contribute toward the nurture and education of the children. The Court is not bound by the parties' proposed arrangement and must independently assess whether the custody and support terms are in the best interests of the minor children.
In reviewing the parties' agreement, the Court should consider the history of Sarah as the primary caregiver during Tomas's extended North Slope absences. That history is a significant factor in confirming that primary physical custody with Sarah is in the children's best interests. Tomas's proposed parenting time, consisting of every other weekend and off-rotation periods, should be structured in a manner that accounts for the irregular nature of his work schedule and provides the children with predictable and consistent contact with both parents.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized in Cox v. Floreske, 288 P.3d 1289 (Alaska 2012), that the trial court's discretion in matters of custody and property is broad, and that agreements reached by the parties are subject to the court's independent review to ensure fairness and compliance with applicable statutory standards. Sarah supports Tomas's involvement in the children's lives and does not oppose the proposed parenting time structure in principle, but she requests that any final parenting plan be reduced to a detailed written order that specifies parenting time during Tomas's off-rotation periods, a holiday schedule, and a procedure for addressing schedule modifications when Tomas's work rotation changes.
E. Sarah's Request for Deferred Property Division Is Consistent with Alaska Law Governing Reservation of Property Issues.
To the extent the Court treats the deferred sale or buyout arrangement as a reservation of the property division issue, the Court should note that AS 25.24.155 governs the circumstances under which a court may delay or reserve a property division decision. Under AS 25.24.155(a), the Court may reserve the issue of property division if each party expressly agrees on the record, or if the moving party shows good cause and the Court finds that the interests of the opposing party will not be jeopardized by the delay.
Sarah's request is not, strictly speaking, a request to reserve the property division issue; she requests that the Court enter a final order now that grants her the right to remain in the home for two years and defers only the buyout or sale mechanism to a date certain. This approach resolves the property division issue as to all other assets immediately, while providing a structured framework for the family home. It avoids the statutory concerns raised by AS 25.24.155(b), because Sarah's proposal does not put Tomas's interest substantially at risk: his equity stake in the family home is preserved, the home will be maintained by Sarah throughout the deferred period, and the Court retains jurisdiction to enforce the buyout or sale at the conclusion of the two-year term.
This structure is consistent with the approach affirmed in Silvan v. Alcina, 105 P.3d 117 (Alaska 2005), where the Alaska Supreme Court upheld a trial court's arrangement that allowed one party to remain in the family home pending a defined resolution mechanism, while protecting the other party's financial interest through specific court-ordered terms.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Sarah Whitfield respectfully requests that the Court enter an order:
1. Granting Sarah the right to remain in the family home located in Anchorage for a minimum of two years from the date of the final dissolution decree, consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) and the children's best interests;
2. Deferring the buyout or sale of the family home until the conclusion of the two-year period, with the parties to negotiate terms at that time, and the Court retaining jurisdiction to order a sale and just division of net equity if the parties cannot agree;
3. Requiring full financial disclosure from both parties pursuant to Civil Rule 26.1(b) and Civil Rule 90.1(e) before any final child support or property division order is entered;
4. Independently verifying any proposed child support figure against the Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) and (a)(2)(B) guidelines based on Tomas's verified adjusted annual income;
5. Entering a detailed parenting plan that incorporates Tomas's off-rotation schedule, a structured holiday calendar, and a procedure for addressing schedule modifications; and
6. Dividing all remaining marital assets and debts, including the joint savings account and shared credit card debt, in a just manner consistent with the statutory factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
Sarah remains committed to a fair and cooperative resolution of all outstanding issues and requests only that the Court ensure that any final orders are grounded in complete financial disclosures, verified guideline calculations, and a property division that accounts for the children's need for residential stability during this difficult transition.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0028)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Alaska Superior Court, Third Judicial District, Family Division, on Petitioner Renee Sutter's petition for dissolution of marriage from Respondent Danielle Sutter. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. The marriage has irretrievably broken down due to prolonged conflict over finances and differing parenting philosophies, and reconciliation is not possible.
Renee Sutter respectfully requests that this Court enter a dissolution decree that: (1) establishes a primary physical custody arrangement in favor of Renee with defined parenting time for Danielle; (2) orders child support calculated in accordance with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3; (3) requires Danielle to contribute proportionally to out-of-pocket medical and extracurricular expenses for the children; and (4) divides the marital home and joint credit card debt in a manner that fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution. As set forth below, applicable Alaska statutes and court rules fully support the relief Renee seeks.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Sutter and Danielle Sutter were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The marriage produced two minor children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old. The family resided in Eagle River, Alaska, and in 2017 purchased a home there, subject to a joint mortgage with an approximate remaining balance of $210,000. Over the course of the marriage, the parties also accumulated joint credit card debt of approximately $18,000.
Beginning in early 2024, the marriage broke down irretrievably due to irreconcilable differences arising from prolonged financial conflict and fundamentally differing parenting philosophies. Renee filed a petition for dissolution in the Alaska Superior Court, Third Judicial District, Family Division, seeking resolution of all outstanding issues including custody, child support, and property division.
With respect to the children, the parties have proposed a joint legal custody arrangement under which the children reside primarily with Renee during the school week. Danielle would have the children on alternating weekends, during school holidays, and for six weeks each summer. Both parties would share decision-making authority regarding the children's education, healthcare, and general well-being.
Danielle is employed as a licensed electrician and earns a consistent gross monthly income. Renee requests that child support be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3 based on Danielle's adjusted annual income and the primary physical custody arrangement proposed herein, and further requests that Danielle contribute proportionally to the children's out-of-pocket medical and extracurricular costs.
As to property, Renee proposes that the Eagle River marital home be listed for sale and that the net proceeds, after satisfying the mortgage and costs of sale, be divided equally between the parties. Danielle requests the right to buy out Renee's share and retain the property. With respect to the joint credit card debt of approximately $18,000 accumulated during the marriage, Renee requests that the debt be allocated equitably between the parties in connection with the overall property division.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska law vests the superior court with broad authority to resolve all incidents of a dissolution, including custody, child support, and property division. Under AS 25.24.160, the court may provide for the payment of child support, the award of spousal maintenance, and the division of marital property in a manner that is just and proper. Property division must "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" by consideration of the statutory factors enumerated in AS 25.24.905(4), including the length of the marriage, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of each party, and the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question.
The dissolution process itself is governed by AS 25.24.200 through AS 25.24.250. A joint petition for dissolution may be filed where incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and the parties have reached agreement on custody, support, property division, and debt allocation. AS 25.24.200(a). The petition must state in detail all terms of agreement concerning the custody of children, child support, visitation, and division of property, and must also state the income, assets, and liabilities of the respective petitioners at the time of filing. AS 25.24.210(e).
Upon filing, the court will hold a hearing pursuant to AS 25.24.220 and will examine the petitioners to determine whether they fully understand the nature and consequences of their action, whether agreements concerning child custody, support, and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children, and whether agreements relating to property division are just and fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. AS 25.24.220(d).
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3, which establishes a formula for calculating support based on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent and the custody arrangement. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), where one parent has primary physical custody, the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage: 20% for one child and 27% for two children. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that these guidelines are designed to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay, and to make awards predictable and consistent. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND SHOULD BE APPROVED BY THE COURT.
The primary concern in any custody determination is the best interests of the children. The arrangement proposed here, under which the children reside primarily with Renee during the school week and spend alternating weekends, school holidays, and six weeks each summer with Danielle, appropriately balances stability and continuity for the children with meaningful parenting time for both parties.
Under AS 25.24.200(a)(2), a joint petition for dissolution may include an agreement on custody only if the spouses have agreed on which spouse is to be awarded custody of each minor child and the extent of visitation, including the support to be provided on the children's behalf. The proposed arrangement satisfies each of these requirements. The children will maintain their established school-week routine with Renee, providing stability in their academic and social lives, while Danielle will exercise substantial parenting time during alternating weekends, holidays, and an extended summer period. Both parents will share decision-making authority regarding education, healthcare, and general well-being, reflecting a commitment to cooperative co-parenting.
When the court examines the petition at the dissolution hearing, it will consider whether the written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the parties and in the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.220(d)(2). The proposed custody terms meet this standard. The children will benefit from the continuity of their primary residence with Renee, from regular and meaningful contact with Danielle, and from the cooperative joint legal custody structure the parties have proposed.
B. CHILD SUPPORT MUST BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON DANIELLE'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME.
Because the children will reside primarily with Renee, this is a primary physical custody case for purposes of child support calculation, and the award must be calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a). Under that provision, "a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody as defined by paragraph (f) will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." For two children, the applicable percentage is 27% of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) is defined as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" mandatory deductions including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory contributions to a retirement or pension plan, as well as certain other allowable deductions. Danielle's adjusted annual income must be calculated by reference to her gross income as a licensed electrician, reduced by all applicable mandatory deductions set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A).
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the Rule 90.3 formula is intended to ensure that child support is adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay, and to produce predictable and consistent results. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). Accordingly, this Court should order Danielle to pay child support calculated in strict accordance with the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula, based on her documented adjusted annual income, for the benefit of both minor children.
In addition to base child support, Danielle should be required to contribute proportionally to the children's out-of-pocket medical expenses and extracurricular costs. Such contributions are expressly contemplated under AS 25.24.930(1), which authorizes the court to provide for payments "as may be just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children." The petition must also state the parties' agreement on health care expenses for the children as part of the child support terms. AS 25.24.210(e). Proportional allocation of these expenses, based on the relative incomes of the parties, is a fair and just approach consistent with Alaska law.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that child support calculations under Rule 90.3 must realistically reflect the financial circumstances of both parents. Halvers v. Pruitt, 404 P.3d 837 (Alaska 1999). Danielle's consistent employment as a licensed electrician indicates a stable, ascertainable income from which a child support obligation can be reliably calculated. Should this Court find at any point that Danielle is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed, the Court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to impute potential income to her based on her skills, employment history, and the local job market.
The child support award should further take into account the extended summer visitation period. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) provides that the court may allow the obligor parent to reduce child support payments by up to 75% for any period in which the obligor parent has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days. Because Danielle will have six weeks of consecutive summer parenting time, the order should specify the amount of any allowable reduction during that period consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3).
C. THE MARITAL HOME AND JOINT DEBT SHOULD BE DIVIDED IN A MANNER THAT FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION.
The division of the marital home and the joint credit card debt must be governed by the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which directs the court to divide marital property "in a just manner" by consideration of all statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of each party, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the income-producing capacity of the property.
The Eagle River home was purchased in 2017 and is encumbered by a joint mortgage with an approximate remaining balance of $210,000. It is therefore marital property subject to division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The applicable statutory factors favor a sale of the property and equal division of the net proceeds for the following reasons.
First, the length of the marriage, approximately nine years, suggests that both parties have contributed to the marital estate over a substantial period. Second, Danielle, as a licensed electrician, has a stronger earning capacity and is better positioned to qualify independently for new financing if she wishes to purchase a different residence. Third, with respect to the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody, AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) specifically identifies this as a factor the court must consider. While Renee does have primary physical custody, a sale and equal division of net proceeds would provide Renee with the capital necessary to secure appropriate housing for herself and the children, which equally serves this statutory purpose.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently required that property division fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution after considering all relevant statutory factors. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). Here, an equal split of net sale proceeds accomplishes this goal by giving each party a fair share of the equity accumulated during the marriage while avoiding the complications of a contested buyout valuation.
Renee does not oppose Danielle's interest in retaining the home, but Danielle's buyout proposal must be evaluated carefully. If the Court considers allowing Danielle to buy out Renee's share, it must ensure that the buyout amount is based on a current, professionally conducted appraisal of fair market value; that the buyout is completed within a defined period; that Renee is fully released from the joint mortgage obligation as a condition of any buyout; and that the agreed-upon division "fairly allocate[s] the economic effect of divorce" as required by AS 25.24.160(a)(4). If Danielle cannot satisfy these conditions within a reasonable period, the Court should order the home sold and the net proceeds divided equally.
With respect to the approximately $18,000 in joint credit card debt accumulated during the marriage, this debt constitutes a marital obligation subject to equitable allocation. Under AS 25.24.200(a)(4), the parties to a dissolution must agree "as to the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both of them." Because this debt was incurred jointly during the marriage, it should be allocated equally between the parties. Alternatively, the Court may allocate debt in a manner that offsets any disparity in the net property award, consistent with the overall goal of a just division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the division of marital debts, like the division of assets, must reflect all relevant circumstances of the parties. Laughlin v. Laughlin, 229 P.3d 1002 (Alaska 2010).
Any delay or reservation of the property division issue is strictly limited by AS 25.24.155, which provides that the court may not delay or reserve an issue of property division unless each party expressly agrees on the record or a party moving for delay demonstrates good cause and the court finds the opposing party's interests will not be jeopardized. Renee does not consent to any such reservation, and prompt resolution of the property issues is necessary to protect her ability to secure housing for herself and the children.
D. THE DISSOLUTION PETITION MEETS ALL STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS AND SHOULD BE APPROVED.
The petition for dissolution satisfies the requirements of AS 25.24.200(a). Incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. The parties are parents of minor children and have reached agreement on custody, visitation, and support. The parties have addressed the distribution of the marital home and joint debt. The petition constitutes the entire agreement between the parties as required by AS 25.24.200(a) and AS 25.24.210(e).
Under AS 25.24.210(e), the petition must state in detail the terms of the agreement on custody, child support including periodic payments and health care expenses, visitation, any spousal maintenance, and the fair and just division of property. The petition filed in this matter includes all of these required components. At the hearing scheduled under AS 25.24.220, the Court will examine the parties to ensure they understand the nature and consequences of their action, that the custody and support terms are just and in the best interests of the children, and that the property division fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution.
The Court should also note that AS 25.24.220(h) requires heightened scrutiny of agreements where there is a minor child of the marriage. Because the parties have two minor children, this standard applies, and the Court must carefully examine whether the written agreements are just and in the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.220(i). The proposed custody, support, and property terms presented here withstand this level of scrutiny, as they are transparently negotiated, based on disclosed incomes and assets, and designed to serve the children's stability and well-being.
Finally, the forms and instructions for dissolution proceedings are made available to the public as required by AS 25.24.250, and Renee has endeavored to comply fully with all procedural requirements of the Alaska Rules of Civil Procedure and the applicable statutes in preparing and filing this petition.
V. CONCLUSION
For all of the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Sutter respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Grant the petition for dissolution of the marriage of Renee Sutter and Danielle Sutter on the grounds that incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage;
2. Enter a custody order establishing primary physical custody of the two minor children with Renee Sutter, with parenting time for Danielle Sutter as set forth in the proposed parenting plan, including alternating weekends, school holidays, and six consecutive weeks each summer;
3. Order Danielle Sutter to pay child support calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on her adjusted annual income, at the 27% rate applicable for two children, with any extended visitation credit for the summer period determined under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3), and with proportional contribution to the children's out-of-pocket medical and extracurricular expenses;
4. Order the marital home in Eagle River to be sold and the net proceeds, after satisfaction of the mortgage and reasonable costs of sale, to be divided equally between the parties, unless Danielle Sutter completes a buyout of Renee Sutter's equity interest at fair market value within a court-ordered period and provides Renee Sutter with a full release from the joint mortgage obligation;
5. Allocate the approximately $18,000 in joint marital credit card debt equitably between the parties, consistent with the overall property division; and
6. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper under the circumstances.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0029)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Tomas Whitfield respectfully submits this brief in support of his petition for dissolution of marriage from Respondent Danielle Whitfield. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014 and have two minor children together, currently aged six and nine. After approximately ten years of marriage, the relationship has broken down irretrievably due to irreconcilable differences arising from financial stress and prolonged periods of separation attributable to Tomas's seasonal employment on the North Slope. The parties agree on the general framework for custody and legal decision-making authority but dispute the proper calculation and amount of child support, the disposition of the jointly owned marital home, and the allocation of marital debt. Tomas asks this Court to enter a dissolution decree that serves the best interests of the children, establishes a fair and workable child support obligation consistent with Civil Rule 90.3, and equitably divides the marital estate, including the family home equity and outstanding credit card obligations, in accordance with AS 25.24.160.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Whitfield and Danielle Whitfield were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2014. The marriage produced two minor children, now aged six and nine. For much of the marriage, Tomas has worked in seasonal employment on the North Slope of Alaska, which provided the family's primary source of income but also required extended periods of physical absence from the family home in Anchorage.
Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to a combination of financial pressures and the strains caused by Tomas's recurring absences. The parties have reached incompatibility of temperament that has caused the irremediable breakdown of their marriage, satisfying the foundational requirement for dissolution under AS 25.24.200.
Regarding the children, the parties have agreed in principle that the minor children will reside primarily with Danielle during the school year. Tomas will exercise alternating weekend visitation and will have extended parenting time during summer months and major holidays. Both parties agree to share legal custody and to make joint decisions regarding the children's education, health care, and general well-being. Both children currently receive speech therapy services that are not fully covered by insurance, generating ongoing out-of-pocket costs that Danielle contends should be factored into the child support determination.
The parties jointly own a home in Anchorage with an estimated fair market value of approximately $265,000 and an outstanding mortgage balance of approximately $210,000, leaving estimated equity of approximately $55,000. Danielle wishes to retain the marital home and refinance the mortgage solely in her name, thereby relieving Tomas of the mortgage obligation. Tomas does not object to Danielle retaining the home but requests an offsetting cash payment representing his proportionate share of the existing equity.
The parties also accumulated approximately $34,000 in credit card debt during the marriage. The allocation of this debt between the parties remains in dispute.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Dissolution of Marriage
Under AS 25.24.200, a husband and wife may jointly petition the superior court for dissolution of their marriage when incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, the parties have agreed on custody, support, and visitation for any minor children, and the parties have agreed as to the distribution of property and payment of obligations. The court is required under AS 25.24.220 to examine the petitioners and determine whether the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action, whether agreements regarding children are just and in the children's best interests, and whether agreements regarding property and debt allocation are just and fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution.
B. Child Support
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by a specified percentage, which is 27% for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus specified mandatory deductions and other enumerated items. The court retains discretion to deviate from the guideline amount in unusual circumstances, provided it makes specific findings on the record.
C. Division of Marital Property
Under AS 25.24.160, the court is authorized to provide for the division of property, whether joint or separate, acquired during the marriage, in a just manner and without regard to fault. The division must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce and must be based on consideration of multiple statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, their respective earning capacities, the financial condition of each party, the conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized in Hockema v. Hockema, 403 P.3d 1080 (Alaska 2017), that these statutory factors, often called the Merrill factors, guide trial courts in equitably allocating the economic effects of a divorce. The court in Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996), similarly recognized the broad statutory framework governing property division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
D. Modification and Best Interests of the Children
When custody and visitation are at issue, the overarching standard is the best interests of the children. Under AS 25.20.110, any subsequent modification of a custody or visitation award requires a showing of a change in circumstances and a finding that the modification would be in the child's best interests.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED PRIMARY CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND SHOULD BE APPROVED BY THE COURT.
The parties have agreed that the two minor children will reside primarily with Danielle during the school year, with Tomas exercising alternating weekend visitation and extended parenting time during summer months and major holidays. Both parties will share legal custody and joint decision-making authority regarding education, health care, and general well-being. This arrangement reflects the practical realities of Tomas's seasonal employment schedule while ensuring that the children maintain a meaningful and continuing relationship with both parents.
Under AS 25.24.220, the court must examine whether the written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the parties and in the best interests of the children. The proposed arrangement satisfies this standard. The children will have a stable primary residence with Danielle during the school year, promoting continuity in their education and daily routines. Tomas's extended summer parenting time ensures that the parent-child relationship is preserved and enriched during the periods when his employment schedule permits sustained involvement.
The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in Silvan v. Alcina, 105 P.3d 117 (Alaska 2005), illustrates that courts have approved shared and primary custody arrangements tailored to the specific circumstances of the parties, including employment obligations, so long as the children's best interests are served. The proposed arrangement here is similarly tailored to the realities of this family's circumstances and merits the court's approval.
Both parties' agreement to joint legal custody and joint decision-making regarding education, health care, and well-being reinforces the children's connection to both parents and reflects the kind of cooperative co-parenting arrangement courts in Alaska are encouraged to support. This Court should approve the proposed custody and visitation framework as just, workable, and in the best interests of the six- and nine-year-old children.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON TOMAS'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME, AND THE COURT SHOULD CONSIDER AN UPWARD DEVIATION TO ADDRESS THE CHILDREN'S UNINSURED SPEECH THERAPY EXPENSES.
1. The Guideline Calculation Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)
Because the proposed arrangement places the children in Danielle's primary physical custody during the school year, child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a). Under that rule, the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27% (.27). Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources, reduced by mandatory deductions such as federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, as well as certain voluntary retirement contributions, work-related child care expenses for the subject children, and health insurance premiums paid for the parent only.
Tomas's income derives primarily from his seasonal employment on the North Slope. Because that income is higher than a typical year-round salary and may fluctuate from season to season, the court should carefully evaluate Tomas's total income from all sources in calculating his adjusted annual income. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002), that the goal of the Rule 90.3 guidelines is to obtain a realistic estimate of an obligor's adjusted annual income. Similarly, the court in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), emphasized that the primary beneficiary of child support is the child, and that the formula is designed to contribute to the child's multiple needs, including food, housing, and clothing.
Tomas does not dispute his obligation to pay child support calculated on his actual adjusted annual income. He asks only that the calculation faithfully apply Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) by accounting for all permissible deductions, including mandatory payroll deductions associated with his North Slope employment, so that the resulting support obligation reflects his true ability to pay while adequately providing for the children's needs.
2. An Upward Deviation to Address Uninsured Speech Therapy Costs Is Appropriate
Danielle has requested that the court deviate upward from the guideline amount to address the children's ongoing speech therapy expenses that are not covered by their health insurance. This request has merit and should be considered by the court as part of a comprehensive support determination.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) identifies work-related child care expenses for the subject children as a permissible deduction from the obligor parent's adjusted annual income. However, extraordinary medical and therapeutic expenses that fall outside the scope of ordinary child-rearing costs and are not reflected in the standard guideline calculation may warrant a deviation. The court has authority to consider such unusual circumstances in fashioning a just support order. An upward deviation to account for the children's uninsured speech therapy costs would ensure that the guideline award does not leave the custodial parent bearing an inequitable share of these necessary therapeutic expenses.
Tomas does not oppose a reasonable contribution toward the children's uninsured speech therapy costs. He asks the court to establish a clear, specific framework, either through a percentage-based sharing arrangement or a defined monthly addition to the base guideline amount, to ensure transparency, predictability, and fairness for both parties. Any deviation from the guideline amount should be supported by documentation of the actual therapy costs and should be adjusted as those costs change over time.
C. THE MARITAL HOME SHOULD BE AWARDED TO DANIELLE SUBJECT TO A PROMPT, EQUITABLE CASH PAYMENT TO TOMAS REPRESENTING HIS PROPORTIONATE SHARE OF THE NET EQUITY.
1. The Statutory Framework Favors Awarding the Family Home to the Primary Custodial Parent
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), the court must consider "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." This factor reflects the Legislature's recognition that residential continuity and stability serve the children's best interests, and that uprooting children from their home in the wake of a divorce can compound the disruption they already face.
Here, the children have lived in the Anchorage home throughout their lives. Danielle will be their primary residential parent during the school year. Awarding her the right to remain in the home promotes continuity in the children's schooling, social relationships, and daily environment. The court in Hockema v. Hockema, 403 P.3d 1080 (Alaska 2017), confirmed that the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) guide equitable allocation of the economic effects of a divorce, including the disposition of the family home. Consistent with that guidance, this Court should award the family home to Danielle.
2. Tomas Is Entitled to an Offsetting Cash Payment Representing His Proportionate Share of the Equity
While the policy favoring award of the family home to the custodial parent is well established, a just division of property does not permit one party to receive the entirety of the marital equity without accounting for the other spouse's interest. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the division of property must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce, and the court must consider the financial condition of the parties, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the value of the property at the time of division.
The Anchorage home has an estimated market value of $265,000 with an outstanding mortgage of approximately $210,000, producing estimated net equity of approximately $55,000. If Danielle retains the home and refinances the mortgage in her name, she will receive the full benefit of that equity. Fairness and the statutory mandate of AS 25.24.160 require that Tomas receive an offsetting payment representing his proportionate share of the net equity.
The parties should agree, or the court should determine, the precise percentage of equity to which each party is entitled, taking into account the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the length of the marriage, the contributions of each party to the acquisition and maintenance of the home, and the overall structure of the property division. Tomas proposes that the equity be divided equally, resulting in a payment to him of approximately $27,500, to be made at the time of refinancing or within a judicially specified period thereafter. The court in Silvan v. Alcina, 105 P.3d 117 (Alaska 2005), approved a similar mechanism in which the court ordered a sale or buyout of the family home and required one spouse to pay the other a specified share of the home's stipulated value, confirming that this approach is an established and workable method of equitable property division in Alaska.
3. The Court Must Also Consider the Desirability of Awarding the Home in Light of Danielle's Ability to Refinance
The Court should condition any award of the family home to Danielle upon her demonstrated ability to refinance the mortgage within a reasonable and specified period. D. THE MARITAL CREDIT CARD DEBT SHOULD BE ALLOCATED EQUITABLY BETWEEN THE PARTIES IN ACCORDANCE WITH AS 25.24.160.
The parties accumulated approximately $34,000 in credit card debt during the marriage. Under AS 25.24.200(a)(4), a petition for dissolution must address the parties' agreement as to the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both of them. In allocating marital debt, the court should apply the same statutory factors that govern property division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the financial condition of each party, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the conduct of the parties in incurring and managing the debt. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Osterkamp v. Stiles, 235 P.3d 178 (Alaska 2010), that courts evaluate marital debts with careful attention to the specific circumstances surrounding their incurrence and the equities as between the parties.
Tomas proposes that the credit card debt be allocated in proportion to the overall property division. IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0030)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter arises from a petition for dissolution of marriage filed by Priya Whitfield in the Superior Court for the State of Alaska. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, currently ages six and nine. The marriage has broken down irreparably due to Brandon Whitfield's extended work absences on the North Slope and fundamental disagreements regarding financial management. Priya Whitfield's proposals are grounded in the best interests of the children, consistent with Alaska law governing dissolution proceedings, and supported by a fair allocation of the economic consequences of dissolution.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Whitfield and Brandon Whitfield were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The parties are the parents of two minor children born of the marriage, currently ages six and nine. Over the course of the marriage, Brandon Whitfield has been employed as a pipeline technician on the North Slope, a position that has required frequent and extended absences from the family home located in Eagle River, Alaska. Priya proposes that she serve as the primary physical custodian of the two minor children. Under her plan, the children would reside at the family home in Eagle River during the school year, maintaining continuity in their schooling, community, and established routines. Brandon would have parenting time every other weekend and a continuous block of six weeks during the summer.
