Brandon contests this arrangement and instead requests a 50/50 residential schedule during school breaks. With respect to financial matters, Brandon proposes that child support be calculated under Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 based on his higher income as a pipeline technician, that Priya retain the family home subject to a buyout of Brandon's equity interest, and that the parties divide the remaining marital debts equally, including a joint vehicle loan and approximately $28,000 in credit card balances accumulated during the marriage.
The marital home is located in Eagle River and serves as the primary residence for Priya and the children. Brandon's earning capacity as a pipeline technician substantially exceeds Priya's income. The parties accumulated approximately $28,000 in joint credit card debt and share a vehicle loan over the course of the marriage.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Dissolution Proceedings Generally
Alaska law establishes a specific statutory framework for dissolution of marriage. Under AS 25.24.200(a), a husband and wife may jointly petition for dissolution if incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, and if the parties have reached agreement regarding child custody, support, visitation, property division, and allocation of debts. The petition must comply with the requirements set forth in AS 25.24.210, which mandates that the petition state the terms of any custody, support, and visitation agreement in detail, as well as disclose the income, assets, and liabilities of each petitioner at the time of filing.
Under AS 25.24.220(d), the court is required to examine whether the parties' agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the spouses and in the best interests of the children of the marriage. The court must also examine whether the agreements relating to property and obligations are just and whether they fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution.
B. Custody Determinations
Alaska law requires that any custody arrangement be evaluated according to the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.090 identifies the factors a court must consider when determining whether to award shared custody, including the child's preference if of sufficient age and capacity, the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment each parent can offer, the child's education, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent. Courts have consistently recognized that stability and continuity in a child's living situation are paramount considerations.
C. Child Support
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 906(a), where one parent holds primary physical custody, the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a specified percentage based on the number of children. For two children, the applicable percentage is 27%. Civil Rule 90.3(f) defines primary physical custody as a situation in which the children reside with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. Shared physical custody is defined under Civil Rule 90.3(f) as a situation in which the children reside with each parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. Where shared physical custody applies, the support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(b) takes into account both parents' incomes and the respective percentages of time each parent has physical custody of the children. The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that these formulas are designed to ensure child support awards are adequate to meet the needs of children while remaining predictable and consistent. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
D. Property Division
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the court is authorized to divide between the parties all property, whether joint or separate, acquired during the marriage in a just manner, without regard to fault. The division must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution and must take into consideration factors including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, each party's earning capacity, the financial condition of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the income-producing capacity of the property. Spousal maintenance, if any, and property division together must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. AS 25.24.160(a)(2).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PRIYA WHITFIELD'S PROPOSED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT SERVES THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE MINOR CHILDREN AND SHOULD BE ADOPTED BY THE COURT.
The custody arrangement proposed by Priya Whitfield reflects the day-to-day realities of this family's life and is firmly grounded in the statutory factors set forth in AS 25.20.090. Priya has been the primary caregiver for the two minor children throughout the marriage, a role made necessary by Brandon's repeated and extended absences while working on the North Slope. The children have established roots in Eagle River, attend school in that community, and depend upon the stability and consistency that Priya's primary custody arrangement would preserve.
1. Stability of Home Environment and Community Continuity
Among the factors courts must weigh under AS 25.20.090 are the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the education of the child, and the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides. Priya's proposed plan directly advances each of these interests. The children attend school in Eagle River and reside in the family home. Maintaining primary residence with Priya during the school year ensures continuity of education, established peer relationships, and the stability of a home environment that the children have known throughout their lives.
Brandon's employment as a North Slope pipeline technician inherently involves unpredictable and extended periods of absence. A 50/50 residential schedule during school breaks, as Brandon proposes, fails to account for the practical limitations his work schedule imposes and could expose the children to disruption and instability during critical periods of the academic calendar. AS 25.20.090(3) requires the court to consider the stability of the home environment each parent can realistically offer, and Priya's consistent physical presence in Eagle River renders her home the more stable residential setting.
2. Optimal Parenting Time Allocation
AS 25.20.090(6) directs the court to consider the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, accounting for the actual time spent with each parent historically, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the school in which the child is enrolled, the feasibility of travel between parents, and any special needs of the child that one parent may be better positioned to address. Brandon's North Slope employment, which requires extended on-site rotations, significantly limits his practical availability. By contrast, Priya has been present and available in Eagle River to meet the children's daily educational, medical, and emotional needs.
Priya's proposal does not eliminate Brandon from the children's lives. To the contrary, it provides him with parenting time every other weekend and a full six consecutive weeks during the summer, a meaningful and substantial block of time that supports the father-child relationship without disrupting the children's school year schedule. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that meaningful parenting time arrangements must be grounded in the realistic circumstances of each family, not abstract formulas that fail to reflect how a family actually functions. Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002).
3. Willingness to Facilitate the Parent-Child Relationship
AS 25.20.090(6)(E) requires consideration of each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Priya's proposal, which affords Brandon regular weekend contact and an extended summer period, demonstrates her genuine commitment to ensuring that the children maintain a meaningful relationship with their father despite the breakdown of the marriage. This approach reflects good faith and a child-centered perspective that the Court should recognize.
4. Brandon's Proposed 50/50 Schedule During School Breaks Is Not Supported by the Statutory Factors.
Brandon's request for a 50/50 residential schedule during school breaks does not align with the statutory framework of AS 25.20.090. A rigid equal-time arrangement during school breaks ignores the practical realities of Brandon's work schedule, the distance between the North Slope and Eagle River, and the disruption that frequent residential transitions would impose on children ages six and nine. The court is directed by AS 25.20.090(6)(C) to consider the feasibility of travel between parents, and by AS 25.20.090(6)(B) to consider each parent's proximity to the school in which the children are enrolled. Brandon's North Slope employment makes consistent availability during school breaks uncertain. An arrangement predicated on Brandon being available for half of every school break period is speculative and potentially harmful to the children's well-being.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON BRANDON'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS THE NON-CUSTODIAL PARENT.
Because Priya Whitfield's proposed custody arrangement places the children in her primary physical custody, child support must be calculated under Civil Rule 994(a). Under that provision, "a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody as defined by paragraph (f) will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." For two children, that percentage is 27%. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2) defines primary physical custody for purposes of the rule as a situation in which "the children reside with the other parent for a period specified in the custody order of less than 30 percent of the year." Under Priya's proposed arrangement, Brandon would exercise parenting time every other weekend during the school year plus six weeks in the summer. This schedule, calculated on an annual basis, results in residential time for Brandon that falls below the 30-percent threshold required for shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1). Accordingly, the primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs.
The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018) that the classification of custody as primary or shared for purposes of Rule 90.3 is determined by the percentage of residential time specified in the custody order, not by informal arrangements or anticipated conduct. Here, the proposed parenting plan, as written, would not give Brandon 30 percent or more of annual residential time, placing this squarely within the Civil Rule 90.3(a) primary custody formula.
Brandon's adjusted annual income, as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), is his total income from all sources minus authorized deductions, including mandatory federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and permissible voluntary retirement contributions not exceeding the applicable cap. As a pipeline technician earning substantially more than Priya, Brandon's adjusted annual income will serve as the basis for a support award of 27% of that figure to reflect support for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019) that adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) encompasses total income from all sources and that courts must carefully calculate the applicable deductions before arriving at the figure used to compute the support award. Priya requests that the Court require Brandon to produce complete and verified documentation of his pipeline technician income, including any shift differentials, bonuses, or other compensation, so that adjusted annual income may be accurately determined.
Additionally, pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3), if Brandon exercises the six-week consecutive summer parenting period proposed by Priya, the Court may, in its discretion, allow an extended visitation credit of up to 75% of the child support amount for that period. Any such credit should be expressly stated in the support order and conditioned upon actual exercise of the extended visitation period.
C. THE FAMILY HOME SHOULD BE AWARDED TO PRIYA WHITFIELD AS PRIMARY CUSTODIAN, SUBJECT TO A BUYOUT OF BRANDON'S EQUITY INTEREST, AND THE MARITAL DEBTS SHOULD BE ALLOCATED EQUITABLY.
1. The Family Home Should Be Awarded to Priya.
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the court must divide the parties' property in a just manner, taking into consideration all relevant factors, including "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." This factor weighs strongly in Priya's favor. The Eagle River family home is the residence in which the minor children have been raised and in which they have established their educational and community lives. Awarding the home to Priya preserves residential continuity for the children and supports the overall custody arrangement proposed herein.
Priya does not seek to deprive Brandon of his equity interest. Rather, she proposes a buyout arrangement under which she would compensate Brandon for his proportionate share of the equity accumulated in the family home during the marriage. This approach is consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which authorizes the court to require one party to assign, deliver, or convey real or personal property to the other party to accomplish a just division. The buyout reflects a practical solution that fairly allocates the economic consequences of dissolution while keeping the children in a stable home environment.
In determining the buyout amount, the Court should consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the length of the marriage, the parties' respective earning capacities, the financial condition of each party, and the time and manner of acquisition of the property. Brandon's substantially higher income as a pipeline technician enhances his capacity to absorb the economic adjustment associated with vacating the family home. Priya's lower earning capacity and primary custodial responsibilities counsel in favor of minimizing the financial burden placed on her by the buyout obligation, including structuring the payment over a reasonable period of time.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that property division and spousal maintenance awards together must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce, and that each is a distinct instrument directed at achieving overall economic justice between the parties. Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). The proposed home buyout, evaluated alongside the allocation of marital debt addressed below, is designed to achieve precisely that fair allocation.
2. The Marital Debts Should Be Divided Equitably in Light of the Parties' Respective Financial Circumstances.
The parties accumulated approximately $28,000 in joint credit card balances and share a vehicle loan incurred during the marriage. Under AS 25.24.200(a)(4), the parties must agree as to the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both of them during the marriage. Where the parties cannot reach agreement, the Court has authority under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) to allocate those obligations in a just manner that fairly distributes the economic effect of dissolution.
Priya does not oppose an equitable division of the marital credit card debt. However, because the proposed custody arrangement places primary caregiving responsibilities on Priya, and because Brandon's income as a pipeline technician is substantially higher than Priya's, the Court should consider the financial condition and earning capacity of each party, as directed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C) and (D), when determining the precise allocation of debt. An equal 50/50 split of the $28,000 credit card balance may not be equitable if it places a disproportionate financial strain on Priya relative to her income and her role as primary custodian.
With respect to the joint vehicle loan, the Court should allocate responsibility for that obligation to the party who retains the vehicle. If Priya retains the vehicle for purposes of transporting the minor children during the school year, responsibility for the vehicle loan should be assigned to her, with appropriate credit given in the overall property division calculation. If Brandon retains the vehicle, the loan obligation should follow accordingly. In either case, the remaining marital estate should be adjusted to reflect the allocation of debt so that the overall division fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution as required by AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
The court in Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012) recognized that courts applying Civil Rule 90.3 must conduct a careful and particularized analysis of each parent's financial circumstances, a principle that applies with equal force to the equitable allocation of marital debts. The Court should likewise conduct a thorough examination of the parties' respective financial positions before imposing a debt allocation that could undermine Priya's ability to maintain a stable home for the minor children.
D. THE COURT SHOULD APPLY HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY TO ANY PROPOSED AGREEMENT WHERE THE PARTIES ARE UNREPRESENTED OR WHERE THE DIVISION IS INEQUITABLE.
Under AS 25.24.220(h), the court is required to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the parties' agreements if one party is represented by counsel and the other is not, if there is a minor child of the marriage, or if there is a patently inequitable division of the marital estate. Both minor children of the marriage are directly affected by the proposed custody and support arrangements, triggering the heightened scrutiny requirement of AS 25.24.220(h)(3). If either party is unrepresented at the dissolution hearing, AS 25.24.220(h)(1) provides an additional basis for the Court to look more carefully at the terms of any proposed agreement.
Where heightened scrutiny applies, AS 25.24.220(i) directs the court to "examine the written agreements between the spouses to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that the agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are in the best interest of the children of the marriage." Priya respectfully requests that the Court undertake that examination with care, ensuring that the custody arrangement, support calculation, and property division proposed herein comport with the statutory standards for fairness and the best interests of the children.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Priya Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Adopt her proposed primary physical custody arrangement, which places the children in her primary residential care in Eagle River during the school year, provides Brandon with parenting time every other weekend and six consecutive weeks during the summer, and preserves joint legal custody with shared decision-making authority on major issues;
2. Calculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on Brandon Whitfield's adjusted annual income as the non-custodial parent, applying the 27% multiplier applicable to two children, with a permissible extended visitation credit under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3) for the six-week summer parenting period if actually exercised;
3. Award the family home to Priya Whitfield as primary physical custodian, subject to a fair buyout of Brandon Whitfield's equity interest structured in a manner consistent with Priya's financial capacity;
4. Divide the marital credit card debt and vehicle loan in a manner that fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution in accordance with AS 25.24.160(a)(4), taking into account the parties' substantially different earning capacities and Priya's primary caregiving role; and
5. Apply the heightened scrutiny required by AS 25.24.220(h) and (i) to all written agreements in light of the presence of minor children of the marriage.
The arrangements proposed by Priya Whitfield are just, child-centered, and consistent with the letter and spirit of Alaska law governing dissolution of marriage. The Court should adopt them in their entirety.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0031)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Court in a dissolution of marriage proceeding between Elena Colby, Petitioner, and Colin Colby, Respondent. The parties were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. The marriage has irretrievably broken down due to Colin's prolonged work absences on the North Slope and irreconcilable differences concerning parenting and finances. Elena Colby respectfully requests that this Court enter a decree of divorce that awards her primary physical custody of the minor children, establishes joint legal custody consistent with Colin's own request, sets child support in accordance with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3, and divides the marital estate in a fair and equitable manner pursuant to AS 25.24.160.
Elena has served as the primary caregiver for the parties' children throughout the marriage. Colin's employment requires extended absences from the family home, and Elena has accordingly assumed the dominant role in the children's daily lives, schooling, healthcare, and emotional development. The proposed custody arrangement reflects these established parenting roles and serves the best interests of the children. The proposed property division addresses the marital home located in Eagle River, a joint savings account of approximately $42,000, two vehicles, and a joint credit card debt of approximately $18,500.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Colby and Colin Colby married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The marriage produced two children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old, both of whom currently reside in the family home in Eagle River with Elena. Throughout the marriage, Colin has worked on the North Slope in the oilfield industry, which requires him to be away from home for extended consecutive periods. These prolonged absences have meant that Elena has, as a practical matter, functioned as the sole caregiver during Colin's rotations away from home.
Elena has been responsible for enrolling the children in school, attending parent-teacher conferences, scheduling and attending medical and dental appointments, arranging extracurricular activities, and providing day-to-day emotional support. The children are currently enrolled in the Eagle River school district and have developed stable friendships, routines, and connections within their community.
Over the past two years, the marriage has deteriorated due to Colin's extended absences and irreconcilable disagreements regarding parenting decisions and financial management. The parties have agreed that Colin will not contest primary physical custody. Colin does, however, request joint legal custody so that he may continue to participate in major decisions concerning the children's education, healthcare, and general welfare. Elena does not oppose joint legal custody provided that it is structured in a way that preserves the children's stability and accounts for the practical difficulties posed by Colin's work schedule.
The marital estate subject to division consists of the family home located in Eagle River, a joint savings account containing approximately $42,000, two vehicles used by the respective parties, and a joint credit card debt of approximately $18,500 incurred during the marriage. The parties have not reached a final written agreement on the division of these assets and debts, and the Court's guidance is therefore required.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts are guided by a comprehensive statutory and rules-based framework when resolving disputes involving child custody, child support, and property division in divorce proceedings.
Regarding custody, AS 25.24.953 directs that the court shall determine custody in accordance with the best interests of the child. The statute enumerates specific factors the court must consider, including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable and satisfactory environment; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or neglect; and evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the child's well-being.
When shared custody is at issue, AS 25.20.090 sets forth additional factors the court shall consider, including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the child's educational situation, the advantages of maintaining the child in the community where the child presently resides, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent.
With respect to child support, Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides the primary custody formula under which the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income is multiplied by a set percentage based on the number of children. For two children, the applicable percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(f) defines primary physical custody as existing when the children reside with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. Civil Rule 90.3(f) further defines shared physical custody as existing when the children reside with a parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year.
Regarding property division, AS 25.24.987(4) requires the court to divide property acquired during the marriage in a just manner, without regard to fault, and based on a series of enumerated factors. Those factors include the length of the marriage and the parties' station in life, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of the parties, the conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division. AS 25.24.929(2) governs spousal maintenance and directs the court to fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce based on analogous factors.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY WITH ELENA IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN
The Court should award Elena Colby primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children pursuant to AS 25.24.150. The statutory best-interests analysis strongly supports placing primary physical custody with Elena, who has served as the children's day-to-day caregiver throughout the marriage.
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) directs the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. The children are ages six and nine and are enrolled in the Eagle River school district. Maintaining their current enrollment, routines, friendships, and community connections serves these needs directly. AS 25.24.150(c)(5) specifically identifies the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity as a factor for the court's consideration. The children have lived in the Eagle River home throughout their lives. Disrupting that stability would not serve their interests.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the children's needs. Elena has demonstrated her capability by managing the children's schooling, healthcare, and emotional well-being single-handedly during Colin's North Slope rotations. Colin's continued employment on the North Slope requires him to be physically absent from Eagle River for extended consecutive periods, which as a practical matter limits his ability to provide consistent daily care during those times.
AS 25.24.150(c)(4) identifies the love and affection existing between the child and each parent as a relevant factor. Elena does not dispute that Colin loves his children, and the proposed arrangement provides him with meaningful parenting time, including alternating weekends during the school year and extended time during summers and holidays. This structure preserves and reinforces the bond between Colin and his children while protecting the stability the children have known.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) directs the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Elena supports Colin's involvement in the children's lives and agrees to joint legal custody, which itself reflects her commitment to preserving his parental role. The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed that the best-interests framework is the controlling standard for all custody determinations, and that stability and the practical history of caregiving are central considerations in that analysis. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015); Helen S.K. v. Samuel M.K., 288 P.3d 463 (Alaska 2012).
The proposed parenting schedule awards Colin alternating weekends during the school year, extended parenting time over the summer, and additional time during school holidays. This schedule meaningfully incorporates AS 25.20.090(6), which directs the court to consider the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent by taking into account the actual time spent with each parent, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the school in which the child is enrolled, and the feasibility of travel. Because Colin's North Slope work schedule is defined by consecutive days on and off, the proposed arrangement can be structured around his rotation in a way that maximizes his time with the children when he is actually present in the Anchorage area. This flexibility honors the spirit of AS 25.20.090 without compromising the children's schooling or continuity.
B. JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY SHOULD BE AWARDED TO BOTH PARENTS
Elena does not oppose Colin's request for joint legal custody. Joint legal custody will allow both parents to participate in major decisions concerning the children's education, healthcare, and general welfare. AS 25.24.150(c)(2) recognizes the desire of each parent to meet the children's needs as a relevant factor, and joint legal custody is a direct mechanism for giving effect to that desire. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that joint legal custody can serve a child's best interests where both parents demonstrate a commitment to the children's welfare and the ability to communicate. See Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012).
Elena requests only that the joint legal custody order include a clear tie-breaking procedure or dispute resolution mechanism to address situations where the parties cannot reach agreement promptly, given the practical communication challenges posed by Colin's work rotations. This safeguard will ensure that the children's urgent healthcare and educational needs are not delayed by disagreements that cannot be resolved while Colin is working on the Slope.
C. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED PURSUANT TO CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON COLIN'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME
The Court should order Colin to pay child support calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which governs cases in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody. Under that rule, "a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody as defined by paragraph (f) will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." For two children, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) specifies a percentage of 27 percent.
Colin's employment in the oilfield industry on the North Slope generates substantially higher income than Elena's. His adjusted annual income must be calculated consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), which defines adjusted annual income as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" certain enumerated deductions, including mandatory tax withholdings, Social Security contributions, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions. Colin should be required to provide complete and verified income documentation, including recent pay stubs, tax returns, and any applicable employment contracts, so that the Court can accurately determine his adjusted annual income and calculate the appropriate support obligation.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the Rule 90.3 formula exists to ensure that child support awards are adequate to meet the needs of children and are predictable and consistent. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). The formula reflects the Legislature's policy judgment that children are entitled to financial support commensurate with their parents' earnings, and Colin's oilfield wages make a Rule 90.3(a) calculation particularly important to the children's well-being.
If the Court were to find that Colin's parenting time during summers and extended holidays qualifies as shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), meaning the children reside with Colin for at least 30 percent of the year, then the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b) would apply. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), the court would calculate the annual amount each parent would pay the other assuming the other parent had primary custody, multiply each amount by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and then identify the parent with the larger figure as the obligor, with the annual award equal to 1.5 times the difference between the two figures. Elena respectfully submits that the proposed parenting schedule, which places the children primarily with her during the school year, is more likely to yield a primary custody calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a), but she is prepared to present evidence as to the actual percentage of time the children will spend with each parent should the Court need to make that determination.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits the court to calculate child support based on a determination of a parent's potential income if that parent is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. That provision does not apply to Colin here, as he is fully and gainfully employed. However, should Colin reduce his income voluntarily between the filing of this action and the support hearing, Elena reserves the right to request that the Court impute potential income to him consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4).
The Alaska Supreme Court's decisions in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), and Helen S.K. v. Samuel M.K., 288 P.3d 463 (Alaska 2012), confirm that courts may consider the totality of a parent's employment history, earning capacity, and actual income in establishing the adjusted annual income figure used for child support calculations. These decisions reinforce that Elena is entitled to an accurate and fully documented accounting of Colin's oilfield earnings before the Court sets the support amount.
D. THE MARITAL ESTATE SHOULD BE DIVIDED EQUITABLY PURSUANT TO AS 25.24.160
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires the Court to divide property acquired during the marriage in a just manner, based on the enumerated statutory factors, and without regard to fault. Elena requests that the Court apply these factors to the marital estate, which consists of the Eagle River family home, the joint savings account of approximately $42,000, two vehicles, and the joint credit card debt of approximately $18,500.
1. The Eagle River Family Home
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) identifies as a relevant factor "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." This factor strongly favors Elena. The children are enrolled in the Eagle River school district and have established friendships and routines connected to their neighborhood and community. Disrupting their living situation by requiring the sale of the home or a change of residence would undermine the very stability that AS 25.24.150(c)(5) instructs the Court to preserve.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(G) directs the Court to consider the circumstances and necessities of each party. Elena, as the primary caregiver with lower earning capacity relative to Colin's oilfield income, has a greater necessity for stable housing. Colin, by contrast, spends significant portions of the year working on the North Slope, where employer-provided housing is customarily included in employment arrangements, reducing his immediate need for the family home.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(C) requires the Court to consider the earning capacity of the parties, including their employment skills, work experience, and custodial responsibilities during the marriage. Elena's extended absence from full-time employment due to her primary caregiving role may have affected her earning capacity and her ability to independently finance comparable housing if the family home were sold. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts may award a disproportionate share of the marital estate to compensate a party whose earning capacity was reduced by caregiving responsibilities assumed during the marriage. See Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002).
Elena requests either that the family home be awarded to her, with an equitable offset from other marital assets, or that she be granted the right to continue residing in the home for a reasonable period to allow the children to complete their schooling at their current schools without disruption.
2. The Joint Savings Account
The joint savings account currently holds approximately $42,000. This account is marital property subject to division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). Elena requests an equitable share of this account, with any division accounting for the offset applied in connection with the family home. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(A) directs the Court to consider the length of the marriage and the station of life of the parties. The marriage spanned ten years during which both parties contributed to the accumulation of savings, Elena through her caregiving labor and Colin through his financial contributions. An equal division of the savings account, subject to any offset, is appropriate in the first instance, though Elena recognizes the Court's discretion to adjust this figure in light of the overall equitable balance.
3. The Two Vehicles
Each party currently uses one of the two vehicles. Elena requests that each party be awarded the vehicle in his or her possession, with any difference in value addressed through equitable offset. This outcome minimizes disruption and serves the practical needs of each party going forward. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(I) instructs the Court to consider the value of property at the time of division. The parties should be required to provide current valuations of both vehicles so that any disparity in value can be properly accounted for in the overall division.
4. The Joint Credit Card Debt
The joint credit card debt of approximately $18,500 was incurred during the marriage and is therefore a marital obligation subject to allocation under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(E) identifies as a relevant factor the conduct of the parties, including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets. Elena requests that the Court inquire into the nature of the charges comprising this debt and allocate responsibility in proportion to each party's use of the credit account for personal versus family purposes. To the extent the debt was incurred for legitimate marital and family expenses, an equal division is appropriate. If, however, any portion of the debt was incurred by Colin for purposes unrelated to the marriage or family, Elena requests that he bear a greater share of that portion.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that marital debt is subject to equitable allocation under the same framework governing marital property, and that the Court must consider all relevant statutory factors in reaching a just result. See Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996); Rowen v. Rowen, 963 P.2d 249 (Alaska 1998).
E. THE COURT SHOULD APPOINT A GUARDIAN AD LITEM IF THE CHILDREN'S INTERESTS REQUIRE INDEPENDENT REPRESENTATION
AS 25.24.310(c) authorizes the Court to appoint a guardian ad litem on its own motion or upon the motion of either party to represent the best interests of the children in proceedings affecting their welfare. AS 25.24.150(b) specifies that any such appointment shall be made under the terms of AS 25.24.310(c). Elena does not affirmatively request a guardian ad litem appointment at this time, as the parties have substantially agreed on the custody framework. However, Elena brings this provision to the Court's attention and invites the Court to make the finding on the record required under AS 25.24.310(a) as to whether independent legal representation or other services for the minor children would serve their welfare. Should any dispute arise in the course of these proceedings that places the children's interests in tension with the positions of either party, Elena would support the appointment of a guardian ad litem to ensure those interests are independently represented.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Elena Colby respectfully requests that this Court enter a decree of divorce that:
1. Awards Elena Colby primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, with Colin Colby receiving alternating weekends during the school year and extended parenting time during summers and holidays, consistent with the best-interests framework of AS 25.24.150(c) and the shared custody factors of AS 25.20.090;
2. Awards joint legal custody to both parents so that each participates in major decisions regarding the children's education, healthcare, and general welfare, with a clear dispute resolution mechanism to address disagreements during Colin's work rotations;
3. Orders Colin Colby to pay child support calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on his fully documented adjusted annual income from his North Slope oilfield employment, applying the 27 percent rate applicable to two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), or, alternatively, calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b) if the Court determines the parenting schedule qualifies as shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1);
4. Awards Elena Colby the Eagle River family home, or grants her the right to reside therein for a reasonable period, with an equitable offset from other marital assets, pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) and (G);
5. Divides the joint savings account of approximately $42,000 equitably, subject to any offset applied in connection with the family home;
6. Awards each party the vehicle currently in his or her possession, subject to equitable adjustment for any disparity in vehicle values;
7. Allocates the joint credit card debt of approximately $18,500 equitably, with any disproportionate allocation reflecting the purposes for which the debt was incurred; and
8. Makes the findings required under AS 25.24.310(a) as to whether a guardian ad litem appointment is warranted for the minor children.
Elena Colby respectfully submits that the relief requested herein serves the best interests of the parties' children, fairly allocates the economic effects of the dissolution of this marriage, and is fully consistent with the applicable statutes and rules governing Alaska family law proceedings.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0032)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Court on the parties' petition for dissolution of marriage filed pursuant to AS 25.24.200. Jacob Larsen and Danielle Larsen, having been married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015, seek a final decree of dissolution on grounds of incompatibility of temperament that has caused the irremediable breakdown of their marriage. The parties have two minor children, ages six and nine, and have reached agreement on the central custody arrangement, a proposed child support figure, and the sale and division of the family home and joint savings account. The sole contested matter before the Court concerns the allocation of approximately $34,000 in credit card debt accumulated during the marriage.
This brief is submitted to assist the Court in understanding the applicable legal framework, to demonstrate that the proposed agreements concerning custody, child support, and property division satisfy the statutory requirements of Alaska law, and to present the factual and legal basis for an equitable allocation of the disputed marital debt. Jacob Larsen respectfully requests that the Court enter a final decree of dissolution incorporating the agreed-upon terms and resolve the credit card debt dispute in a manner that fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution, as required by AS 25.24.931 and AS 25.24.230.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jacob Larsen and Danielle Larsen were married on or about 2015 in Anchorage, Alaska. The marriage produced two minor children: one child currently age nine and one child currently age six. The parties enjoyed a stable family life for several years but, beginning in early 2024, experienced persistent and irremediable conflict stemming from fundamental disagreements over finances and divergent parenting values. These differences have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marital relationship. The parties agree that incompatibility of temperament is the basis for dissolution, satisfying the threshold requirement under AS 25.24.917(1).
Jacob has relocated to Fairbanks, Alaska, for employment purposes. Danielle remains in Anchorage, which is where the minor children reside and attend school. The parties have negotiated a joint legal custody arrangement under which the children reside primarily with Danielle during the school week. Jacob exercises parenting time on alternating weekends, during school holidays, and for six weeks each summer. This schedule accounts for the geographic distance between the parties and is designed to preserve each parent's meaningful relationship with the children.
The marital estate consists primarily of the family home located in Anchorage, Alaska, which the parties purchased in 2017. The home carries an outstanding mortgage balance of approximately $210,000 and is estimated to have a current market value of approximately $295,000, yielding gross equity of approximately $85,000. The parties have agreed to list the home for sale and to divide the net proceeds equally after payment of the outstanding mortgage and customary closing costs. Additionally, the parties hold a joint savings account with a balance of $18,500, which they have agreed to divide equally, each receiving $9,250.
The remaining disputed matter is the allocation of approximately $34,000 in credit card debt. The credit card accounts were opened and used during the marriage. Jacob contends that a substantial portion of the debt was incurred by Danielle for purposes unrelated to the family's shared needs or that constituted unreasonable depletion of marital assets. Danielle contends that the debt was incurred for household and family expenses and that Jacob bears equal or greater responsibility. Neither party has accepted primary liability for the debt, and the Court is asked to resolve this dispute based on the purpose and timing of the expenditures charged to the accounts.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A petition for dissolution of marriage filed by both spouses requires the Court to make specific findings before a final decree may enter. Under AS 25.24.220(d), the Court shall examine the petitioners and consider whether the spouses fully understand the nature and consequences of their action, whether the written agreements concerning custody, support, and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children, whether the property and debt agreements are just, and whether those agreements constitute the entire agreement between the parties. Under AS 25.24.230(a), the Court may grant a final decree of dissolution only upon finding, among other things, that the property and debt agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution, taking into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4), and that each spouse entered the agreement voluntarily and free from coercion.
With respect to child support, Civil Rule 915(a) provides the governing formula. A child support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: twenty percent for one child and twenty-seven percent for two children. The rule further defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus specified mandatory and permissible deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(b) addresses shared and divided physical custody calculations, applicable where the court finds that parents exercise shared physical custody as defined under the rule.
With respect to property and debt division, AS 25.24.160(a)(4) directs the Court to divide marital property, whether joint or separate, acquired during the marriage in a just manner. The division must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce based on a consideration of multiple factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the conduct of the parties including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that property division and spousal support serve distinct purposes and that courts are to strive for divisions that fairly allocate the economic consequences of dissolution as between the spouses. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). The court in Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014), emphasized the importance of scrutinizing the fairness of property division agreements, particularly where one spouse proceeds without counsel. Similarly, Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004) and Beal v. Beal, 88 P.3d 104 (Alaska 2004) confirm that the trial court retains broad equitable authority to fashion a property division that accounts for the actual conduct of each party during the marriage with respect to marital assets.
Where questions of property valuation and asset allocation are in dispute, Civil Rule 90.1(e) requires the parties to file, no later than five days before trial, a list including a brief description of all assets and liabilities of the parties, a designation of whether each is marital or separate property, the value of each asset and liability, and the proposed disposition of each.
IV. ARGUMENT

The parties have represented that Jacob's income, when subjected to the adjusted annual income calculation set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), yields a monthly support obligation consistent with the agreed figure of $1,200 per month.

Everett Thompson, the court reaffirmed that a parent's adjusted annual income is calculated from total income from all sources minus the deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), and that support awards grounded in that formula are presumed to satisfy the children's multiple needs, including housing, food, and clothing.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0033)
I. INTRODUCTION
This brief is submitted on behalf of Petitioner Priya Bergstrom in support of the proposed parenting plan, child support award, and equitable division of the marital estate in the above-captioned dissolution proceeding. Priya Bergstrom and Jennifer Bergstrom were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. Following a period of marital deterioration marked by communication breakdowns and divergent parenting philosophies, Priya filed for dissolution in Alaska Superior Court. The central disputes before the Court concern: (1) the appropriate physical custody arrangement and parenting schedule for the two minor children; (2) the calculation of child support consistent with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3; and (3) the equitable division of the marital estate, including the Eagle River family home, two vehicles, a joint savings account, and outstanding shared debt.
Priya respectfully requests that the Court enter orders establishing primary physical custody in her favor, with Jennifer exercising parenting time on alternating weekends, school holidays, and six weeks each summer. Priya further requests that the Court calculate Jennifer's child support obligation pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on her income as a licensed electrician. Finally, Priya requests that the Court divide the marital estate in a manner that is just and equitable under AS 25.24.160, including awarding Priya the family home in recognition of her role as the children's primary residential parent.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Bergstrom and Jennifer Bergstrom were married on or about 2015 in Anchorage, Alaska. The parties have two minor children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old, both of whom have resided with Priya at the family home in Eagle River throughout their lives and throughout the period of separation. The marriage broke down over approximately the past two years due to irreconcilable differences arising from communication failures between the parties and fundamentally incompatible parenting philosophies.
Priya filed for dissolution in Alaska Superior Court. The parties have reached a tentative agreement on joint legal custody but have not resolved the question of physical custody or parenting time. Priya proposes that the children reside primarily with her at the Eagle River family home during the school week, with Jennifer exercising parenting time on alternating weekends, school holidays, and six weeks each summer. Jennifer, who has relocated to Fairbanks following the separation, contests this schedule and seeks a more equal physical custody division. Jennifer has represented that she intends to return to the Anchorage area within approximately six months, though no such relocation has yet occurred.
The marital estate consists of the Eagle River family home valued at approximately $380,000 with a remaining mortgage balance of $210,000, yielding an approximate equity of $170,000; two vehicles; a joint savings account containing approximately $14,000; and approximately $28,000 in shared credit card debt. No agreement on the division of these marital assets and liabilities has been reached.
Jennifer is a licensed electrician whose income forms the basis of the proposed child support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3. Priya is the children's primary caregiver and has been their consistent residential parent during the period of separation.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts resolve dissolution proceedings involving minor children by applying a best interests of the child standard. Under AS 25.24.150(c), the court shall determine custody in accordance with the best interests of the child, considering a non-exhaustive list of statutory factors. These factors include the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the well-being of the child; and other factors the court considers pertinent.
In determining whether to award shared custody, the court looks to the additional factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the child's education, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child currently resides, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, including consideration of each parent's proximity to the child's school, the feasibility of travel between the parents, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate the other parent's relationship with the child.
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, support is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which is 27% for two children. Where the parents share physical custody, support is calculated under the more complex shared custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b). The determination of which formula applies depends on the physical custody arrangement ultimately ordered by the Court.
Division of the marital estate is governed by AS 25.24.160, which requires the court to divide marital property in a just manner, taking into account a range of enumerated factors including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party who has primary physical custody of children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the time, manner, and manner of acquisition of the property. The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that property division must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015); Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019).
The dissolution process itself is governed by AS 25.24.200 and AS 25.24.220, which require the court to examine the parties' agreements for justness and fairness, to consider whether agreements concerning child custody and child support are in the best interests of the children, and to apply heightened scrutiny where minor children are involved.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. The Court Should Award Priya Primary Physical Custody of the Two Minor Children.
The best interests of the two minor children strongly favor awarding primary physical custody to Priya Bergstrom. The children, ages six and nine, have resided with Priya continuously at the Eagle River family home before and throughout the separation. Awarding primary physical custody to Priya preserves the stable residential environment the children have known their entire lives and protects the continuity of care that Alaska law specifically values.
Under AS 25.24.150(c), the court must consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child and the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs. Priya has served as the children's primary caregiver throughout the marriage and the separation. Her continued role as the primary residential parent is the arrangement best suited to meeting the children's daily developmental, educational, and emotional needs.
The statute also requires the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Disrupting this environment by imposing a more equal physical custody split, particularly while Jennifer resides in Fairbanks, would undermine precisely the stability and continuity Alaska law directs courts to protect.
Under AS 25.20.090, the court must also consider the proximity of each parent to the school in which the child is enrolled and the feasibility of travel between the parents. Jennifer currently resides in Fairbanks, a distance of several hundred miles from Eagle River. This distance makes a equal-time shared physical custody arrangement logistically unworkable during the school year. Jennifer's representation that she intends to return to the Anchorage area within six months is speculative and unverified; no such relocation has occurred. Courts must make custody decisions based on present circumstances, not anticipated future events. Priya respectfully submits that Jennifer's future plans should not form the basis for an order that would immediately disrupt the children's school attendance, daily routines, and stable home environment.
AS 25.20.090 further instructs the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Priya is not seeking to limit the children's relationship with Jennifer. The proposed parenting schedule provides Jennifer with alternating weekends, all school holidays, and six weeks of summer parenting time. This schedule ensures that Jennifer maintains a meaningful and ongoing relationship with the children while preserving the children's day-to-day stability in Eagle River.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently emphasized that custody determinations must serve the children's best interests as their primary and overriding consideration. See Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002); Bergstrom v. Lindback, 779 P.2d 1235 (Alaska 1989). Under the facts presented, the primary physical custody arrangement proposed by Priya best serves the children's interests in stability, continuity, education, and consistent caregiving.
B. The Court Should Calculate Child Support Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Based on Jennifer's Income as a Licensed Electrician.
Because Priya seeks primary physical custody of the two minor children, child support should be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which governs awards in cases where one parent is awarded primary physical custody. Under that rule, the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable statutory percentage. For two children, the applicable percentage is 27%.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" certain enumerated deductions, including mandatory tax withholdings, Social Security and Medicare contributions, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, limited voluntary retirement contributions, work-related child care expenses for the children at issue, and qualifying health insurance premiums.
Jennifer is a licensed electrician and is capable of earning income commensurate with that profession. The Court should calculate Jennifer's adjusted annual income based on her actual earnings or, if the Court finds that Jennifer is voluntarily and unreasonably underemployed, based on her earning potential in the electrician trade. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes the court to calculate child support based on a determination of potential income for a parent who voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the Rule 90.3 formula is designed to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay, and to produce predictable and consistent awards. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). The formula reflects the children's need for financial support consistent with the non-custodial parent's means. Jennifer, as a licensed trades professional, has a demonstrated earning capacity, and Priya respectfully requests that the Court apply the Rule 90.3(a) formula based on a thorough examination of Jennifer's income documentation.
Should the Court ultimately award shared physical custody rather than primary physical custody to Priya, the support calculation would proceed instead under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which applies a different formula accounting for each parent's adjusted annual income and the percentage of time each parent has physical custody. See Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012); Rowen v. Rowen, 963 P.2d 249 (Alaska 1998). Under the shared custody formula, the parent with the larger calculated obligation becomes the obligor, and the annual award equals the difference between the two figures multiplied by 1.5. See Civil Rule 90.3(b). Priya submits that the primary custody formula is the appropriate one under the proposed parenting plan, but acknowledges the Court's authority to apply the shared custody formula if circumstances warrant.
Regardless of which formula applies, any child support order should be consistent with the statutory authority under AS 25.24.160(a)(1), which provides that the court may require payment of an amount of money, in gross or installments, as may be just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children.
C. The Court Should Award Priya the Eagle River Family Home and Divide the Remaining Marital Estate Equitably.
The division of marital property in a dissolution proceeding is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires the court to divide the parties' property acquired during marriage in a just manner, taking into account all relevant statutory factors. The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that property division must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce and that courts have broad discretion in doing so. See Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019); Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
Among the factors the court must consider under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) is the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children. This factor directly and powerfully supports awarding the Eagle River family home to Priya. The two minor children have lived in that home their entire lives. Their schools and community connections are rooted in Eagle River. Allowing Priya to remain in the home with the children preserves the continuity and stability that serve both the children's best interests and the equitable goals of property division under Alaska law.
The Eagle River home is valued at approximately $380,000 with a remaining mortgage of approximately $210,000, yielding equity of approximately $170,000. Priya proposes that she be awarded the home, assume responsibility for the remaining mortgage, and that Jennifer receive an offset of approximately $85,000 representing her proportionate share of the equity, either through a cash payment, an offset against other marital assets, or a deferred equity payment structured to protect both parties' interests.
The marital estate also includes two vehicles, a joint savings account of approximately $14,000, and approximately $28,000 in shared credit card debt. Priya requests that the Court divide these assets and liabilities equitably, considering the statutory factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the length of the marriage, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of each party, and the circumstances and necessities of each party. The marriage lasted approximately nine years, a period of moderate duration. Jennifer, as a licensed electrician, has a stronger immediate earning capacity than Priya, who has served as the primary caregiver during the marriage and whose earning capacity has been affected by the time spent in that role.
The court should also consider the availability and cost of health insurance for both parties and the financial obligations each will carry going forward, including the mortgage and ongoing child-rearing expenses. See AS 25.24.160(a)(4). An equitable division of the remaining liquid assets and shared debt should account for the disproportionate financial burden Priya will carry as the primary residential parent responsible for the children's day-to-day expenses.
Finally, under AS 25.24.220(d)(3), the court is required to examine whether written agreements relating to division of property are just and that the spousal maintenance and division of property fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution, taking into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). Because the parties have not reached agreement on property division, Priya respectfully requests that the Court make findings and enter orders consistent with these statutory standards.
D. Any Modification of Custody or Child Support in the Future Must Be Based on a Material Change in Circumstances.
Jennifer has represented her intention to return to the Anchorage area within six months. If Jennifer does relocate, she may seek modification of the parenting schedule at that time by demonstrating a material change in circumstances. Under AS 25.24.170, the court may modify provisions of a judgment relating to custody, visitation, or child support upon a showing of changed circumstances. Similarly, under AS 25.24.150, the court retains continuing jurisdiction to modify custody orders throughout the minority of the children.
Any modification of child support would also require a material change in circumstances. Under AS 25.24.170(b), for purposes of a motion to modify child support, the adoption of guidelines or a significant amendment to guidelines constitutes a material change in circumstances. A future relocation by Jennifer, if it results in a custody modification, could also trigger a recalculation of child support under the appropriate formula at that time. See Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997).
Priya respectfully submits that future contingencies should not govern the present custody order. The Court should enter a custody and support order based on present circumstances, preserving the right of either party to seek modification upon a genuine and verified material change.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Priya Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court enter orders:
1. Awarding joint legal custody to both parties, with primary physical custody to Priya Bergstrom, and parenting time to Jennifer Bergstrom consisting of alternating weekends, school holidays, and six weeks each summer, consistent with AS 25.24.150 and AS 25.20.090;

Priya Bergstrom respectfully urges the Court to enter these orders in the best interests of the minor children and in accordance with Alaska law governing dissolution proceedings.

II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Larsen and Wesley Larsen were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The marriage produced two children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old, both of whom currently reside with Elena at the family home in Eagle River, Alaska. Over the course of the marriage, the parties experienced persistent and unresolved conflict stemming from disagreements about finances, Wesley's extended and repeated absences for work on the North Slope, and a progressive breakdown of communication between the parties. The marital debts include approximately $34,000 in joint credit card obligations and a personal loan Wesley obtained during the marriage to fund a small business venture that ultimately failed. Elena contends that the personal business loan is Wesley's separate obligation, as it was incurred for his individual entrepreneurial undertaking and did not benefit the marital household. Wesley disputes this characterization and argues the loan should be treated as a joint marital liability subject to equal division.
Elena proposes that the marital assets be divided equally after each party's pre-marital separate assets are properly identified and offset. She further requests that the court award her primary physical custody of the children during the school year, with alternating weekend parenting time for Wesley and an extended six-week summer block. Wesley's North Slope work schedule, which commonly involves rotations of two weeks on the Slope followed by two weeks off, has historically limited his availability for consistent daily parenting during the school year.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Dissolution of Marriage
Under AS 25.24.200, a petition for dissolution of marriage may be filed when incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage under all circumstances. The statute requires, among other conditions, that the parties have reached agreements as to custody, visitation, child support, property division, and debt allocation, or that the court resolve those disputes in a just manner consistent with Alaska law.
B. Property Division
Pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the court shall provide for the division of the parties' property, whether joint or separate, acquired during the marriage, in a just manner and without regard to fault. The division must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution by being based on consideration of the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(A) through (I), including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, each party's earning capacity, the financial condition of the parties, the conduct of the parties including any unreasonable depletion of marital assets, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity of the property.
Spousal maintenance, if any, must likewise fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution based on the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(2). As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), spousal maintenance and property division serve distinct purposes and are not interchangeable, and courts in Alaska have expressed a preference for resolving financial concerns through property division where possible.
C. Child Custody
The court's paramount concern in any custody determination is the best interests of the children. When the court considers whether to award shared physical custody, AS 25.20.090 requires consideration of numerous factors, including the children's needs, the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the advantages of maintaining the children's established community ties, the feasibility of travel between the parents, each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate a close relationship between the children and the other parent, any evidence of domestic violence or substance abuse, and such other factors as the court finds pertinent.
D. Child Support
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, child support is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: 20% for one child and 27% for two children. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), where parents share physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f), a different formula applies that accounts for each parent's income and the proportion of custodial time each parent exercises. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1) defines shared physical custody as a period specified in the custody order of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year.
E. Petition Requirements
Under AS 25.24.210, the petition must state in detail the terms of the parties' agreements or proposed resolution concerning custody, child support, visitation, spousal maintenance, and property division, and must demonstrate that such agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution by taking into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4).
Under AS 25.24.220, the court shall examine the petitioners and consider whether the agreements are just and in the best interests of the children, whether the spousal maintenance and property division fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution, and whether the agreements constitute the entire agreement between the parties.
IV. ARGUMENT

AS 25.20.090(5) directs the court to consider the advantages of keeping the children in the community where they presently reside. Both children are enrolled in Eagle River schools, have established friendships and community connections there, and have an interest in maintaining those relationships. Awarding primary physical custody to Elena preserves those advantages.
AS 25.20.953 requires the court to consider the optimal time for each child to spend with each parent, accounting for the actual time spent with each parent, the proximity of each parent to the children's school, the feasibility of travel between the parents, and any special needs unique to the children. Wesley's North Slope rotations create significant logistical barriers to a week-on, week-off schedule. On his two-week work rotations, Wesley would be unavailable to exercise custody, necessarily requiring emergency adjustments to the schedule, which would be destabilizing for children ages six and nine.
AS 25.20.090(6)(E) further requires the court to consider each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. In Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that custody arrangements must be independently evaluated by the court to ensure they serve the children's best interests, and that the contractual intent of the parties is not determinative. Here, the court's independent evaluation of the children's circumstances strongly favors the stability and continuity that Elena's proposed arrangement provides.
2. Wesley's Proposed Week-On, Week-Off Schedule Is Not Workable Given His Employment Pattern.
A week-on, week-off shared physical custody arrangement presupposes that both parents are reliably available for their designated weeks. B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) BASED ON WESLEY'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME AS THE NON-CUSTODIAL PARENT.
