For two children, that percentage is 27% of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as "the parent's total income from all sources minus" mandatory deductions such as federal, state, and local income tax, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, as well as allowable deductions for voluntary retirement contributions within the stated cap, work-related child care expenses for the subject children, and health insurance premiums paid by the parent for the parent only within the 10% cap.

The Alaska Supreme Court in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), confirmed that adjusted annual income for child support purposes is determined by reference to the parent's actual work history, current employment status, and income from all sources, with the court drawing on all available evidence of a parent's earning capacity where that is relevant. Similarly, in Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012), the court applied the Rule 90.3 formula by reference to each parent's actual and documented income and the specified custody percentages.
In Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), the Alaska Supreme Court emphasized that the Rule 90.3 formula is designed to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children subject to the ability of parents to pay, and to produce predictable and consistent results. Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(E) makes clear that failure to exercise sufficient physical custody to qualify as shared physical custody is grounds for modification of any shared custody support order. Given the documented likelihood that Wesley will be unable to consistently exercise a week-on, week-off schedule due to his North Slope rotation, an order premised on shared physical custody support calculations would be subject to immediate challenge and modification, making the primary custody framework under Civil Rule 90.3(a) the more stable and appropriate basis for the court's support calculation.

2. The Remaining Marital Assets Should Be Divided Equally After Offset of Separate Pre-Marital Property.
Elena proposes equal division of the remaining marital assets: the joint savings account of approximately $18,000, the two vehicles, and Wesley's vested PERS retirement contributions accumulated during the marriage.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0035)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter concerns a petition for dissolution of marriage filed by Petitioner Elena Sutter in the Third Judicial District Superior Court, Anchorage, Alaska. The parties, Elena Sutter and Jennifer Sutter, were married in Anchorage in 2015 and are the parents of two minor children, currently ages six and nine. The marriage broke down irretrievably over the course of the past two years due to irreconcilable differences, including prolonged conflict over finances and differing parenting philosophies. The parties have been physically separated for approximately eight months, during which time the children have experienced significant residential instability.
Three principal disputes remain unresolved: (1) the appropriate physical custody arrangement for the two minor children; (2) the proper calculation of child support under the Alaska Child Support Guidelines; and (3) the division of the marital estate, including the family home located in Eagle River, a shared vehicle, and jointly accumulated marital debt. Petitioner Elena Sutter respectfully submits this brief to address each dispute in turn, explaining why the evidence and governing Alaska law support her proposed custody arrangement, her position on child support, and her request to retain the family home by buying out Respondent Jennifer Sutter's interest.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Sutter and Jennifer Sutter were married on or about 2015 in Anchorage, Alaska. Two children were born of the marriage: one currently age nine and one currently age six. Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to irreconcilable differences encompassing persistent financial conflict and fundamentally incompatible parenting philosophies. The parties have been physically separated for approximately eight months. During this period, the children's residential schedule has been unstable, causing disruption to their daily routines, schooling, and overall well-being. Both parties agree that an expedited custody evaluation is in the best interests of the children, given the ongoing residential instability the children have experienced since the separation.

Jennifer contends the home should be sold and the net proceeds divided equally, and further argues that each party should bear responsibility for debts incurred in her own name during the final year of the marriage.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts evaluating petitions for dissolution must examine the written agreements and disputed issues between the parties under AS 25.24.220. Where both spouses have retained counsel and minor children are involved, the court applies a heightened level of scrutiny to all agreements pursuant to AS 25.24.220(h), specifically reviewing whether agreements are just, constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and are in the best interests of the children.
Physical custody determinations, including whether to award shared custody, are governed by AS 25.20.090, which directs the court to consider the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity, the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, educational considerations, the advantages of keeping the child in the current community, the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, evidence of domestic violence or substance abuse, and any other pertinent factors.
Child support is calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), in cases involving primary physical custody, the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income is multiplied by the applicable percentage: 27% for two children. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), if the parents exercise shared physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f), a different formula applies. Civil Rule 90.3(f) defines shared physical custody as the children residing with a parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year.
The division of marital property is governed by AS 25.24.160(a)(4), which requires a just division of property acquired during the marriage based on consideration of multiple statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, earning capacity, financial condition of the parties, conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
Financial disclosure obligations in dissolution proceedings are governed by Civil Rule 26.1(b), which requires each party to provide comprehensive financial documentation without awaiting a discovery request, including tax returns, pay stubs, bank account statements, debt documentation, and employment benefit information.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PROPOSED PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AND SHOULD BE ADOPTED BY THE COURT.
Alaska law directs the court, when evaluating whether to award shared custody, to consider the full constellation of factors set forth in AS 25.20.090. Taken together, those factors support Elena's proposed custody arrangement, under which the children reside with Elena during the school week and spend parenting time with Jennifer every other weekend and one weeknight per week, with both parents sharing joint legal custody.
1. The Children's Need for Stability Strongly Favors a School-Week Primary Placement with Elena.
AS 25.20.090(2) directs the court to consider the needs of the child, and AS 25.20.090(3) requires consideration of the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent. The children, ages six and nine, are at formative educational and developmental stages. They have already experienced approximately eight months of residential instability since the parties' physical separation. Elena's proposed arrangement centers the children's weekdays and schooling around a consistent primary residence, which directly addresses the instability the children have experienced.
AS 25.20.090(4) calls for consideration of the education of the child. Frequent residential transitions on a week-on, week-off basis, as Jennifer proposes, risk disrupting these routines and may compound the educational and emotional difficulties the children are already navigating.
AS 25.20.090(5) instructs the court to consider the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides. Elena's proposed arrangement allows the children to remain rooted in their current school and community setting without the week-long absences from their primary support networks that a strictly equal alternating-week schedule would entail.
2. The Optimal Time Each Child Spends with Each Parent Favors Elena's Proposed Schedule.
AS 25.20.090(6) requires the court to evaluate the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, taking into account the actual time spent with each parent, proximity of each parent to the other and to the children's school, feasibility of travel between households, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Elena's proposal affords Jennifer meaningful and regular contact, including every other weekend and a mid-week visit, preserving Jennifer's parental relationship while prioritizing continuity for the children during the school week.
3. Both Parties Agree an Expedited Custody Evaluation Is Warranted.
Both Elena and Jennifer agree that an expedited custody evaluation is in the best interests of the children. The court should direct that any evaluation be completed on an expedited basis in light of the residential instability the children have already endured, and should consider the evaluator's findings and recommendations in accordance with AS 25.20.090(7).
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that custody determinations require careful, individualized analysis of all relevant factors, and that a child's well-being must remain the paramount consideration. See Helen S.K. v. Samuel M.K., 288 P.3d 463 (Alaska 2012). The weight of the statutory factors, applied to the facts of this case, supports primary physical placement with Elena during the school week as in the children's best interests.
B. CHILD SUPPORT MUST BE CALCULATED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3 USING ACCURATE, FULLY DISCLOSED INCOME INFORMATION FROM BOTH PARTIES.
The child support obligation between the parties depends first on the custody arrangement adopted by the court, because the formula differs depending on whether the children are in primary physical custody or shared physical custody as defined under Civil Rule 90.3(f).
1. If the Court Adopts Elena's Proposed Primary Physical Custody Arrangement, Child Support Is Calculated Under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27% (.27). "Adjusted annual income as used in this rule means the parent's total income from all sources minus" the deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including mandatory taxes, Social Security contributions, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, voluntary retirement contributions within specified limits, child or spousal support from different relationships, work-related child care expenses for the subject children, and health insurance premiums.
Jennifer's argument that Elena's recent promotion should reduce Jennifer's child support obligation misunderstands the operation of Civil Rule 90.3(a). Under the primary physical custody formula, it is the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income that drives the calculation. Elena's income is relevant as an independent factor only in certain limited contexts, such as the low-income adjustment under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(5) or an argument that deviation from the guidelines is warranted under the unusual circumstances provision. Jennifer has not articulated a valid basis for departure from the standard calculation. Her obligation must be computed based on her own adjusted annual income, not reduced simply because Elena has received a promotion.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits the court to calculate child support based on potential income if a parent "voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed." No such allegation has been made with respect to either party at this time. The court should compute support based on each party's actual adjusted annual income as disclosed pursuant to Civil Rule 26.1(b).
2. If the Court Were to Adopt a Shared Physical Custody Arrangement, Child Support Would Be Calculated Under Civil Rule 90.3(b).
Should the court instead adopt Jennifer's proposed week-on, week-off schedule, child support would be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), the shared physical custody formula. Under that provision, the court first calculates what each parent would owe the other assuming the other had primary custody, then multiplies each figure by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and determines the net obligation based on the difference between those two figures, multiplied by 1.5. In that scenario, both parties' incomes would directly affect the support calculation, and Elena's promotion would be a factor. However, as argued above, the facts of this case do not support a shared physical custody arrangement, and this alternative calculation should not apply.
3. Both Parties Must Fulfill Their Financial Disclosure Obligations Before Child Support Is Finalized.
Civil Rule 26.1(b) imposes mandatory initial disclosure obligations on each party in a dissolution action without awaiting a discovery request. Each party must provide, among other things, federal tax returns for the past three years including all schedules and attachments, pay stubs or other proof of income from all sources for the past two months, and signed releases authorizing the other party to obtain earnings and employee benefit information from the party's current employer. The disclosure obligation under Civil Rule 26.1(b)(1)(J) expressly includes "pay stubs, vouchers, or other similar proof of income from all sources for the past two months," encompassing the income from Elena's promoted position. Neither party may calculate or contest a support figure until both have fully complied with these disclosure requirements.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that accurate income information is essential to a proper support determination. See Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996). Elena respectfully requests that the court order both parties to complete their Civil Rule 26.1(b) disclosures on an expedited schedule so that accurate child support may be determined promptly.
C. THE MARITAL ESTATE MUST BE DIVIDED JUSTLY UNDER AS 25.24.160, AND ELENA SHOULD BE AWARDED THE FAMILY HOME OR, AT MINIMUM, THE RIGHT TO REMAIN IN IT FOR A REASONABLE PERIOD.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires the court to divide marital property "in a just manner" based on consideration of a comprehensive set of statutory factors. The court must consider: the length of the marriage and station in life of the parties; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties; the financial condition of the parties; the conduct of the parties, including unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of the children; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property; and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
1. Elena Should Be Awarded the Family Home in Light of Her Proposed Primary Physical Custody of the Children.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly directs the court to consider "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." This statutory factor is directly applicable here. Elena seeks primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, ages six and nine. The four-bedroom family home in Eagle River is the children's established residence and provides the spatial and environmental stability the children require, particularly given the residential disruption they have experienced during the eight months since the parties' separation.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that this statutory factor carries genuine weight in property division analysis. In Hanlon v. Hanlon, 871 P.2d 229 (Alaska 1994), the court held that a trial court is required not only to consider whether to award the family home outright to the primary custodial parent, but also to consider whether that parent should at minimum be permitted to remain in the home for a reasonable period of time. In Silvan v. Alcina, 105 P.3d 117 (Alaska 2005), the court explained that where shared physical custody applies, the statutory preference for awarding the family home to the primary custodian may not be triggered in the same way; by contrast, where one parent has clear primary physical custody, the factor applies with full force.
Awarding the family home to Elena supports the continuity and stability that the children urgently need. The children's school is in the Eagle River community. Displacing them from the family home would add further disruption to lives already marked by residential instability. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) and the interests of the children weigh clearly in favor of awarding the home to Elena.
2. Elena's Proposed Buyout of Jennifer's Interest Provides Jennifer with Fair Compensation While Preserving the Children's Home.
Elena proposes to purchase Jennifer's interest in the family home, thereby providing Jennifer with her equitable share of the approximately $120,000 in existing equity, while avoiding the expense and disruption of a forced sale. This approach serves both the statutory mandate of a just property division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and the children's need for residential stability.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that trial courts possess broad discretion in structuring property divisions in ways that achieve equitable outcomes, including awarding one party a buyout of the other's interest rather than ordering a forced sale. See Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002); Partridge v. Partridge, 239 P.3d 680 (Alaska 2010). The court should consider the financial condition of each party, including the availability of financing for the buyout, in determining whether Elena can effectuate the buyout within a reasonable time frame.
Jennifer's position, that the home must be sold and proceeds divided equally, disregards the statutory preference for awarding the family home to the primary custodial parent and fails to account for the harm that a forced sale and relocation would cause the children. While an equal division of proceeds may be just in some circumstances, it is not the only just result, and the statutory factors in AS 25.24.160(a)(4) make clear that equal division is not required. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that an unequal property division may be warranted where the circumstances of the parties and the needs of the children support it. See Green v. Green, 29 P.3d 854 (Alaska 2001); Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002).
3. The Allocation of Marital Debt Must Be Determined Based on the Totality of Statutory Factors, Not Solely on Which Party Incurred Each Debt.
The parties have approximately $34,000 in combined credit card and personal loan debt accumulated during the marriage. Jennifer proposes that each party bear responsibility for debts incurred in her own name during the final year of the marriage. Elena does not concede that this approach is equitable under Alaska law.
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires a just division of all marital property, including the allocation of marital obligations. The statute does not limit the analysis to debts incurred in the final year or to debts in each party's name. Rather, the court must consider the totality of factors, including the financial condition of each party, the circumstances and necessities of each party, and the conduct of the parties. Debts incurred during the marriage for joint household purposes are marital obligations regardless of whose name appears on the account. See Green v. Green, 29 P.3d 854 (Alaska 2001).
The court should evaluate the nature and purpose of each debt, the ability of each party to service debt obligations post-dissolution given their respective incomes and financial circumstances, and the overall equity of the division in light of the complete property and debt picture. Elena reserves the right to present detailed evidence regarding the purpose and circumstances of each debt obligation at the evidentiary hearing.
D. THE COURT MUST APPLY HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY BECAUSE BOTH PARTIES ARE REPRESENTED BY COUNSEL AND MINOR CHILDREN ARE INVOLVED.
AS 25.24.220(h) directs the court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny in its examination of any agreements submitted in connection with a dissolution petition when, among other circumstances, both parties are represented by counsel and the other is not, or when there is a minor child of the marriage. In this case, both parties have retained separate legal counsel and there are two minor children. Pursuant to AS 25.24.220(h)(3), the court is required to apply heightened scrutiny to all written agreements between the parties concerning child custody, child support, visitation, and property division, examining whether those agreements are just, constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and are in the best interests of the children. The court should therefore carefully examine any proposed parenting plan or property settlement to confirm that it satisfies these heightened requirements before approving it.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Elena Sutter respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Adopt Elena's proposed custody arrangement, awarding Elena primary physical custody of the two minor children with the children residing with her during the school week, Jennifer exercising parenting time every other weekend and one weeknight per week, and both parties sharing joint legal custody;
2. Order an expedited custody evaluation in accordance with the parties' joint agreement and the best interests of the children, and consider the evaluator's findings and recommendations pursuant to AS 25.20.090;
3. Order both parties to complete their mandatory financial disclosures under Civil Rule 26.1(b) on an expedited schedule, and thereafter calculate Jennifer's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on Jennifer's adjusted annual income with the applicable 27% percentage for two children;
4. Award Elena the family home in Eagle River, subject to Elena's payment of a buyout to Jennifer reflecting Jennifer's equitable share of the approximately $120,000 in equity, pursuant to AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) and the children's established interest in residential stability;
5. Allocate marital debt equitably based on the totality of the statutory factors under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), without restricting the analysis to debts incurred in each party's name during the final year of the marriage; and
6. Apply the heightened level of scrutiny required by AS 25.24.220(h) to all agreements submitted by the parties in connection with this dissolution.
Respectfully submitted.

III. LEGAL STANDARD
A petition for dissolution of marriage may be filed jointly by both spouses under AS 25.24.200, provided that certain enumerated conditions are satisfied at the time of filing. These conditions include: that incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage; that the parties have agreed on custody, visitation, and child support where minor children are involved; that the parties have agreed on the division of all real and personal property, spousal maintenance, and allocation of debts; and that the agreement fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution consistent with the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). See AS 25.24.983.
Under AS 25.24.210, the petition must be filed with the superior court, signed and verified by both petitioners, and must state in detail the terms of the parties' agreements on all required subjects, including custody, child support, visitation, spousal maintenance, and property division. See AS 25.24.210(b)(1), (e).
A hearing is required under AS 25.24.220, at which the court must examine the petitioners and determine, among other things, whether the parties fully understand the nature and consequences of their action; whether the written agreements on child custody, support, and visitation are just and in the best interests of the children; and whether the agreements on property division and maintenance fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution. See AS 25.24.220(d).
Because one party is represented by counsel and the other may not be, and because there are minor children of the marriage, the court is required by AS 25.24.985 to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the parties' agreements. Under that heightened scrutiny, the court must examine the agreements to ensure they are just, constitute the entire agreement of the parties, and that provisions regarding child custody, support, and visitation are in the best interests of the children. See AS 25.24.220(i).
The court may grant a final decree of dissolution if, upon consideration of the petition and testimony, it makes the requisite findings set forth in AS 25.24.230. For a joint petition subject to heightened scrutiny, those findings include that the parties fully understand the consequences of their action; that the child-related agreements are in the children's best interests and just between the parties; that the property and maintenance agreements are just and fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution; that each party entered the agreement voluntarily; and that the conditions of AS 25.24.200(a) have been met. See AS 25.24.230(b).
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, the support award is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: 20% for one child, and 27% for two children. See Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A), (B). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the Rule 90.3 formula is designed to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet children's needs and produce predictable, consistent awards. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).
Property division in a dissolution must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution by considering the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4), including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, earning capacity, financial condition, conduct of the parties, and the desirability of awarding the family home to the party who has primary physical custody of the children. See AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
Spousal maintenance must also fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution and must be based on the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(2), including the length of the marriage, the station in life of the parties, their respective earning capacities, and their financial conditions. See AS 25.24.160(a)(2). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that spousal maintenance and property division serve distinct purposes and are not interchangeable. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015).

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0037)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter arises from the dissolution of the marriage of Tomas Sutter and Maria Sutter, who were married in Anchorage, Alaska, in 2015. The parties have two minor children, aged five and eight, and the marriage has irretrievably broken down due to irreconcilable differences stemming from financial stress and extended periods of separation caused by Tomas's seasonal commercial fishing employment in Bristol Bay. The parties seek judicial resolution of four interrelated issues: (1) the establishment of a joint legal custody arrangement with primary physical custody in Maria; (2) calculation of child support in conformity with Alaska Civil Rule 947; (3) an equitable division of the marital estate, including the Eagle River family residence, joint savings, the commercial fishing vessel, and shared credit card debt; and (4) an order requiring Tomas to maintain health insurance coverage for the minor children as a condition of the final dissolution decree. This brief addresses each of those issues and demonstrates that the relief Maria requests is firmly grounded in Alaska statutory and case law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Sutter and Maria Sutter were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2015. The marriage produced two minor children, now aged five and eight. Over the course of approximately the past two years, the marriage deteriorated due to irreconcilable differences arising from financial stress and the parties' extended periods of physical separation while Tomas fulfilled seasonal commercial fishing contracts in Bristol Bay, Alaska.
The parties' principal marital assets consist of the following: (1) the Eagle River family residence, purchased in 2017 during the marriage, currently carrying an estimated $80,000 in equity; (2) a joint savings account holding approximately $14,000; and (3) a commercial fishing vessel that Tomas values at $45,000 and which he uses as his primary income-generating tool during Bristol Bay fishing seasons. The parties also carry approximately $22,000 in combined credit card debt. Tomas maintains access to group health insurance coverage for dependents through his commercial fishing employer.
The parties have reached a tentative agreement on a general custody framework. Tomas proposes joint legal custody, with the children residing primarily with Maria at the Eagle River family residence during the school year. He would exercise parenting time on alternating weekends and for six consecutive weeks during the summer. Both parties acknowledge that child support must be calculated under Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 based on each parent's respective income and allowable deductions. Maria requests, as a condition of the final dissolution decree, that Tomas be required to maintain health insurance coverage for the children through his employer's group plan.
The parties dispute the characterization and distribution of the fishing vessel. Tomas contends it should be awarded to him in full because it is his primary source of livelihood. Maria contends that the vessel, acquired or substantially appreciated during the marriage, must be included in the overall calculation of equitable distribution of marital assets.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.160, upon a judgment of divorce or dissolution, the court is authorized to provide for child support, spousal maintenance, division of marital property, and related relief. The division of marital property under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) must be made "in a just manner and without regard to which of the parties is in fault," and must "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce" by considering a series of enumerated statutory factors, including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of each party, the financial condition of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the primary custodial parent, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity of the property at the time of division.
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides that a child support award in a case where one parent holds primary physical custody shall be calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage based on the number of children. Civil Rule 90.3(d) governs health insurance coverage for the children and provides that the court shall require health insurance if coverage is available to either parent at a reasonable cost and accessible to the children.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently reviewed property division decisions for abuse of discretion, affirming awards that reflect a thorough and properly weighted consideration of the statutory factors. Hooper v. Hooper, 188 P.3d 681 (Alaska 2008). The court in Zimin v. Zimin, 837 P.2d 118 (Alaska 1992), recognized that fluctuating income from commercial fishing must be carefully analyzed when determining a parent's adjusted annual income for child support purposes. The court in Dragseth v. Dragseth, 210 P.3d 1206 (Alaska 2009), and Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), further confirmed the court's broad discretion in assessing income from commercial fishing enterprises, including business income, in setting child support obligations.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY WITH PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY IN MARIA AND A DEFINED PARENTING SCHEDULE FOR TOMAS
The parties have reached a tentative agreement on the general framework of a custody arrangement that serves the best interests of the two minor children. Under that framework, the children would remain in the Eagle River family home with Maria during the school year, Tomas would exercise parenting time on alternating weekends, and he would have six consecutive weeks of summer parenting time. Joint legal custody allows both parents to participate meaningfully in decisions affecting the children's welfare, education, and health, while the primary residential placement with Maria ensures continuity of schooling and daily routine for children aged five and eight.
AS 25.24.160(a)(1) authorizes the court to provide "for the payment by either or both parties of an amount of money or goods, in gross or installments that may include cost-of-living adjustments, as may be just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children." The statute also reflects the legislature's broader concern that any court order following divorce or dissolution serve the welfare of the children affected. The proposed custody arrangement respects the children's need for stability while preserving a meaningful and ongoing parenting relationship with Tomas during periods when his fishing schedule permits.
Under AS 25.24.200(a)(2), a dissolution petition filed by both spouses must include the spouses' agreement as to which spouse is to be awarded custody and the extent of visitation and support. The tentative custody framework articulated here satisfies those requirements and is consistent with the requirements for a valid dissolution agreement under AS 25.24.220(d)(2), which directs the court to examine whether "the written agreements between the spouses concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the spouses and in the best interests of the children of the marriage."
The Alaska Supreme Court in Dragseth v. Dragseth, 210 P.3d 1206 (Alaska 2009), affirmed trial court discretion in structuring parenting time arrangements that account for a parent's occupational unavailability during work seasons, precisely the situation presented here by Tomas's Bristol Bay fishing contracts. The proposed arrangement providing Tomas with alternating weekend parenting during the school year and six weeks of summer parenting time reasonably accommodates the seasonal nature of his work while protecting the children's educational stability.
B. CHILD SUPPORT MUST BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON EACH PARENT'S ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME, WITH CAREFUL ATTENTION TO TOMAS'S FLUCTUATING FISHING INCOME
Civil Rule 90.3(a) establishes the formula for child support in cases of primary physical custody. The non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income, calculated as total income from all sources minus the allowable deductions specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A) through (G), is multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) sets that percentage at 27% (.27). Accordingly, Tomas's child support obligation must be calculated by determining his adjusted annual income from all sources, including his commercial fishing earnings, and applying the 27% multiplier.
Civil Rule 90.3(e)(1) requires each parent to file a sworn affidavit stating adjusted annual income and its components, accompanied by documentation verifying income and deductions, at the time of the initial pleading or dissolution petition. Both Tomas and Maria are therefore required to submit compliant financial affidavits along with their dissolution filings.
A particular complexity in this case is the seasonal and fluctuating nature of Tomas's income from Bristol Bay fishing contracts. The Alaska Supreme Court addressed this precise issue in Zimin v. Zimin, 837 P.2d 118 (Alaska 1992), where the court examined how a commercial fisherman's variable annual earnings should be treated for child support calculation purposes. The holding in that case supports averaging a fisherman's income over multiple years to arrive at a representative adjusted annual income figure, rather than relying solely on any single year's earnings. Similarly, in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that a parent's income from a combination of commercial fishing, contract work, and other sources may be averaged across years to produce a fair and reliable adjusted annual income figure for Rule 90.3 purposes.
If the court finds that Tomas is voluntarily underreporting income or structuring his fishing business affairs to minimize his apparent earnings, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes the court to impute potential income based on the parent's assets, employment history, job skills, educational attainment, and prevailing earnings in the local community. The court should apply that provision if the evidence reveals a pattern of underreporting consistent with a strategy to minimize his child support obligation.
Maria respectfully requests that the court set child support at the amount produced by applying the 27% multiplier under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to Tomas's properly calculated adjusted annual income, using multi-year averaging where appropriate to reflect the fluctuating nature of Bristol Bay fishing earnings.
C. THE COURT SHOULD REQUIRE TOMAS TO MAINTAIN HEALTH INSURANCE COVERAGE FOR THE CHILDREN AS A CONDITION OF THE DISSOLUTION DECREE
Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(A) provides that "the court shall address coverage of the children's health care needs and require health insurance for the children if insurance is available to either parent at a reasonable cost and accessible to the children." Tomas maintains access to a group health insurance plan through his commercial fishing employer that covers dependents. A group employer plan by its nature offers more affordable per-member coverage than individual market plans and, unless the record demonstrates otherwise, is presumptively available at a reasonable cost.
Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(A)(i) establishes a rebuttable presumption that health insurance costs are reasonable if the cost of coverage does not exceed five percent of the adjusted annual income of the parent required to purchase the insurance. Given that Tomas earns income from Bristol Bay commercial fishing during productive seasons, there is no basis on the current record to conclude that the cost of extending dependent coverage through his employer's group plan would exceed that five-percent threshold. Tomas has not presented any evidence rebutting the reasonableness presumption.
Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(A)(ii) requires that the insurance be accessible, meaning the plan pays for health care services reasonably available to the children. Because the children reside in Eagle River, Alaska, and Tomas's employer group plan covers services within Alaska, the plan satisfies the accessibility requirement.
Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(B) further provides that "the court shall allocate equally the cost of this insurance between the parties unless the court orders otherwise for good cause." If Tomas pays the full premium attributable to the children's share of coverage, his child support obligation will be decreased by Maria's allocated share of those premiums. Conversely, if Maria is ordered to obtain alternative coverage, Tomas's obligation will be increased accordingly.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), acknowledged the relevance of health insurance availability when distributing marital obligations following divorce, noting that disparities in access to coverage are a proper factor in both property division and support determinations. In that case, the court took into account that one party had access to coverage through a specialized program while the other did not, and adjusted the overall distribution accordingly. Here, Tomas's access to employer-sponsored group coverage for the children is an asset of the dissolution proceeding that should be leveraged to serve the children's health care needs.
Maria respectfully requests that the court order Tomas to maintain the children on his employer's group health insurance plan as a condition of the dissolution decree, with the cost allocated equally between the parties pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(d)(1)(B), and that uncovered health care expenses be divided equally pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(d)(2).
D. THE MARITAL ESTATE MUST BE EQUITABLY DIVIDED UNDER AS 25.24.160, INCLUDING THE FISHING VESSEL, THE FAMILY RESIDENCE, THE JOINT SAVINGS ACCOUNT, AND THE SHARED DEBT
1. General Framework for Property Division
AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires the court to divide the parties' marital property in a just manner, without regard to fault, and to fairly allocate the economic effect of the divorce by weighing the factors enumerated in subsections (A) through (I). Those factors include: the length of the marriage and the station in life of the parties during the marriage; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties; the financial condition of the parties; the conduct of the parties, including any unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home to the primary custodial parent; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question; and the income-producing capacity of the property at the time of division.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Hooper v. Hooper, 188 P.3d 681 (Alaska 2008), confirmed that a trial court must address each of these statutory factors when dividing the marital estate, and that a division producing a substantial disparity between the parties' net awards requires a clear record justifying that result. The court in Ogden v. Ogden, 898 P.3d 379 (Alaska 2001), similarly emphasized that property division must rest on findings that are supported by the record and that fairly account for each party's economic position at the time of divorce. The court in Mahan v. Mahan, 719 P.3d 787 (Alaska 2015), affirmed that dissolution agreements addressing the disposition of income-producing assets such as commercial fishing vessels are scrutinized by the court to ensure they are just and that they fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution.
2. The Eagle River Family Residence
The Eagle River home was purchased in 2017, two years after the parties' marriage, and therefore constitutes marital property subject to division under AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The home currently carries an estimated $80,000 in equity. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly identifies as a relevant factor "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." Because Maria will serve as the primary custodial parent during the school year, and the children aged five and eight are enrolled in or approaching enrollment in Eagle River schools, a strong statutory basis exists for awarding Maria either title to the home or the right to remain in it for a reasonable period to avoid disrupting the children's schooling and established community ties.
If an immediate sale of the family home is not practicable or in the children's best interests, the court should consider awarding Maria the right to occupy the home during the children's minority, with a deferred sale and equitable division of proceeds thereafter. If the home is sold immediately, Maria should receive a credit in the overall property distribution reflecting the statutory preference for the primary custodial parent.
3. The Commercial Fishing Vessel
Tomas values the commercial fishing vessel at $45,000 and argues it should be awarded exclusively to him because it constitutes his primary income-generating asset. Maria acknowledges the vessel's functional importance to Tomas's livelihood but contends it must be included in the overall equitable distribution of the marital estate.
The vessel is a marital asset if it was acquired or substantially improved during the marriage, or if marital funds were used to reduce its acquisition debt or fund its operation. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(H) directs the court to consider "the time and manner of acquisition of the property in question," and AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(I) directs the court to consider "the income-producing capacity of the property and the value of the property at the time of division." These two factors must be weighed together: the vessel's value and income-producing capacity are precisely why it must be counted as part of the marital estate, not excluded from it.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Dragseth v. Dragseth, 210 P.3d 1206 (Alaska 2009), addressed a similar situation involving a sole proprietorship marine business and its income-producing assets used during the marriage. The court affirmed that business assets used during the marriage to generate income are properly treated as marital property subject to equitable division, even when one spouse operated the business and the other was the primary caregiver. In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the Alaska Supreme Court acknowledged that a commercial fishing vessel purchased, paid off, and overhauled prior to the marriage may constitute separate property, but the analysis turns on the specific timing and manner of acquisition. By contrast, where a vessel was acquired or substantially paid down during the marriage, it falls squarely within the marital estate.
Maria does not dispute that Tomas should be awarded the vessel in kind, given its role as his livelihood. She contends, however, that its $45,000 value must be counted as part of the total marital estate and that she must receive corresponding offsetting value from other assets, including the home equity and the joint savings account, to produce an equitable overall distribution. Awarding Tomas the $45,000 vessel without any corresponding offset to Maria would produce exactly the kind of unjustified disparity that the Alaska Supreme Court cautioned against in Hooper v. Hooper, 188 P.3d 681 (Alaska 2008).
The court should therefore award the fishing vessel to Tomas in kind, credit its $45,000 value to his share of the marital estate, and adjust the distribution of the remaining assets accordingly.
4. The Joint Savings Account
The joint savings account holds approximately $14,000 and is concededly marital property. In the absence of any demonstrated claim that either party made disproportionate contributions to the savings account or that any portion of the balance represents separate property, equal division of the $14,000 balance is the appropriate starting point, subject to adjustment to achieve an equitable overall distribution of the marital estate in light of the vessel and home equity allocations.
5. The Shared Credit Card Debt
The parties share approximately $22,000 in combined credit card debt. AS 25.24.160(a)(4) encompasses the allocation of marital obligations as well as assets. The court must consider each party's ability to service the debt, their respective earning capacities, and the circumstances and necessities of each party under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(G) in allocating the debt. Because Tomas has a demonstrated earning capacity from his commercial fishing employment, and Maria has been the primary caregiver for the children, an equal division of the debt may impose a disproportionate burden on Maria. The court should allocate the debt in a manner that accounts for each party's actual ability to pay, consistent with a just allocation of the economic effects of the dissolution.
6. Overall Distribution Summary
Taking the statutory factors as a whole and applying the framework endorsed in Hooper v. Hooper, 188 P.3d 681 (Alaska 2008), and Ogden v. Ogden, 39 P.3d 513 (Alaska 2001), the court should structure the overall distribution to ensure that neither party receives a substantially disparate share of the net marital estate without clear justification. The proposed framework that achieves that result is as follows: Tomas receives the fishing vessel ($45,000); Maria receives a substantially larger share of the home equity and the joint savings account, or retains the right to occupy the family home for a defined period; and the parties share the credit card debt in proportions reflecting their relative earning capacities. The court retains broad discretion in fashioning the specific numbers, so long as the resulting distribution fairly allocates the economic effect of the dissolution as required by AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
E. THE COURT SHOULD APPLY HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY IF ANY INDICIA OF AN INEQUITABLE AGREEMENT ARE PRESENT
AS 25.24.220(h) requires the court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to dissolution agreements where one party is represented by counsel and the other is not, where there is a minor child of the marriage, or where there is a patently inequitable division of the marital estate. At least two of those conditions are present here: the parties have two minor children, and any dissolution agreement that awards Tomas the $45,000 vessel without a corresponding equitable offset would constitute a patently inequitable division. Under AS 25.24.220(i), when heightened scrutiny applies, the court must examine the written agreements to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that the agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are in the best interests of the children.
Maria respectfully requests that the court apply this standard of review and decline to approve any dissolution agreement that does not provide her with equitable offsetting value for the fishing vessel awarded to Tomas.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Maria Sutter respectfully requests that the court enter a final dissolution decree that: (1) establishes joint legal custody with primary physical custody in Maria, alternating weekend parenting time for Tomas, and six weeks of summer parenting time for Tomas; (2) calculates Tomas's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) at 27% of his adjusted annual income, using multi-year income averaging to account for the fluctuating nature of his commercial fishing earnings; (3) orders Tomas to maintain the two minor children on his employer-sponsored group health insurance plan, with the cost allocated equally between the parties and uncovered health care expenses divided equally, all pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(d); (4) divides the marital estate equitably under AS 25.24.160(a)(4) by awarding the fishing vessel to Tomas at its $45,000 value, crediting that value against his share of the marital estate, and awarding Maria a corresponding equitable share of the home equity and joint savings account; (5) awards Maria the family residence or the right to occupy it for a reasonable period during the children's minority, consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F); and (6) allocates the $22,000 in shared credit card debt in proportions reflecting the parties' respective earning capacities and financial circumstances. The court should apply the heightened scrutiny mandated by AS 25.24.220(h) and (i) to ensure the overall dissolution agreement is just and fairly allocates the economic effects of this dissolution.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0038)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Petrova, the petitioner and primary caregiver of the parties' two minor children, respectfully submits this brief in support of her proposed custody arrangement, child support calculation, and equitable division of the marital estate. The parties were married in Fairbanks, Alaska in 2017 and have since experienced an irretrievable breakdown of their marriage due to persistent communication failures, incompatible approaches to parenting, and the geographical separation created by respondent Sarah Petrova's voluntary relocation to Anchorage. Ashley remains in Fairbanks, where the children have been raised, attend school, and maintain their established routines and social connections.
The central disputes before this Court involve: (1) the physical custody arrangement for the parties' two minor children, ages four and seven; (2) the proper calculation of child support under Alaska Civil Rule 90.3; (3) the equitable division of the marital home, shared vehicle, joint credit card debt, and two retirement accounts; and (4) whether spousal maintenance is warranted given the parties' respective financial circumstances.
Ashley respectfully urges this Court to award her primary physical custody, to calculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) using the primary custody formula, and to divide the marital estate in a manner that is just and equitable under AS 25.24.160, giving particular weight to her status as the children's primary physical caregiver and her role in maintaining the family home throughout the marriage.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Petrova and Sarah Petrova were married in Fairbanks, Alaska in 2017. The marriage produced two children: a seven-year-old and a four-year-old, both of whom currently reside with Ashley in Fairbanks. Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated significantly due to ongoing communication breakdowns and fundamentally incompatible parenting philosophies. The situation became practically unworkable when Sarah voluntarily relocated to Anchorage to pursue employment, placing approximately 360 miles between herself and the children's primary home.
Throughout the marriage, and particularly since Sarah's relocation, Ashley has served as the children's primary caregiver. Ashley has managed the children's daily schedules, medical appointments, schooling, and extracurricular activities. The seven-year-old is enrolled in school in the Fairbanks area, and the four-year-old attends preschool nearby. Both children are embedded in their Fairbanks community.
The parties jointly own a residence in Fairbanks carrying approximately $210,000 in equity. The parties also share one vehicle and carry approximately $34,000 in credit card debt accumulated during the marriage. Each party holds an individual retirement account that was funded, at least in part, during the marriage. Sarah earns a higher income through her Anchorage employment. Ashley's income is lower, reflecting in part the significant time she devotes to the children's daily care.
Ashley proposes that she retain primary physical custody of both children, with Sarah receiving visitation on alternating weekends and during school breaks, supplemented by a holiday schedule to be agreed upon by the parties. The parties would share joint legal custody. Sarah disputes this proposal and seeks a 60-40 physical custody split in her favor, citing her higher income and more stable housing. Sarah also proposes that child support be calculated using percentages corresponding to her preferred parenting time arrangement.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts exercise broad discretion in matters of child custody, child support, and property division in divorce proceedings. Under AS 25.24.160, the Court may provide for custody, child support, maintenance, and the division of marital property in any judgment of divorce. Property division must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce and must be based on consideration of the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the length of the marriage, the earning capacity of the parties, the financial condition of each party, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody of children, and the time and manner of acquisition of the property. Spousal maintenance, if sought, must be based on consideration of the factors listed in AS 25.24.160(a)(2).
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, child support is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: 20 percent for one child and 27 percent for two children. Where parents share physical custody, meaning the children reside with each parent for between 30 and 70 percent of the year as defined under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), the shared custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies. The definitions in Civil Rule 90.3(f) govern which formula controls.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the child support formula in Civil Rule 90.3 is designed to ensure that awards are adequate to meet the needs of children and to promote predictability and consistency in support obligations. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). The Alaska Supreme Court has further confirmed that the custody classification, specifically whether custody is primary or shared, determines which formula applies and controls the support calculation. See Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
With respect to property division, AS 25.24.160(a)(4) requires the Court to consider the totality of circumstances surrounding the marital estate. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts may, in appropriate circumstances, award a greater share of the marital estate to the spouse with lower earning capacity, particularly where that disparity is attributable to custodial responsibilities undertaken during the marriage. See Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002). Courts have also recognized that equal access of children to both parents is a guiding principle, balanced against the best interests of the children in light of all relevant circumstances. See AS 25.20.070.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THIS COURT SHOULD AWARD ASHLEY PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY BECAUSE SHE IS THE CHILDREN'S ESTABLISHED PRIMARY CAREGIVER AND THE PROPOSED ARRANGEMENT BEST SERVES THE CHILDREN'S INTERESTS
Ashley has served as the primary caregiver for both children throughout the marriage and, particularly, since Sarah's voluntary relocation to Anchorage. The children are settled in Fairbanks, where the seven-year-old attends school and the four-year-old attends preschool. Disrupting this stability by awarding Sarah a 60-40 majority of physical custody would require the children to spend the predominant portion of their time some 360 miles from their established home, school, and support network, contrary to their best interests.
Alaska law recognizes that children should, to the greatest degree practical, have equal access to both parents. AS 25.20.070. However, that principle operates in the context of what the Court finds to be practical given the circumstances, and it is expressly conditioned on a finding that such access is not detrimental to the welfare of the children. Id. Here, the geographic distance between Fairbanks and Anchorage renders a majority-Anchorage custody arrangement impractical for children of these ages. A four-year-old and a seven-year-old cannot be uprooted from their school, their preschool, and their Fairbanks community to spend the majority of their time in Anchorage simply because Sarah prefers it or because Sarah earns more money. Earning capacity and housing stability are not determinative of custody; the best interests of the children are paramount.
Ashley's proposed arrangement is reasonable and designed to preserve Sarah's meaningful relationship with the children. Alternating weekend visitation, school-break visitation, and a mutually agreed holiday schedule provide Sarah with regular, consistent, and substantial contact with both children. This proposal respects the children's need for continuity while honoring the practical realities of the parties' geographic separation.
Sarah's claimed basis for a 60-40 split in her favor, namely her higher income and more stable housing, reflects a misapplication of the relevant considerations. Income disparities and housing stability are factors relevant to child support and property division, not custody allocation. The applicable legal framework focuses on the children's welfare and their connections to their established environment. Ashley urges the Court to award her primary physical custody with joint legal custody shared between the parties, and to order a visitation schedule consistent with her proposal.
B. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) USING THE PRIMARY CUSTODY FORMULA
Because Ashley seeks, and this brief argues this Court should award, primary physical custody to Ashley, child support must be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), the primary physical custody formula. Under that provision, the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a percentage tied to the number of children. For two children, the applicable percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
The shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b) is triggered only when the children reside with each parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1). Primary physical custody, by contrast, exists where the children reside with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2). Under Ashley's proposed arrangement, the children would reside with Sarah only during alternating weekends and school breaks, which does not approach the 30-percent threshold required to trigger the shared custody formula. Accordingly, Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs.
The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), that the custody classification is the controlling factor in determining which formula applies. The Court further explained in Rowen v. Rowen, 963 P.2d 249 (Alaska 1998), that the formulas for shared and divided custody already account for the percentage of time each parent has physical custody and are not interchangeable with the primary custody formula. Sarah's proposal to calculate support using her preferred 60-40 parenting percentages would require application of the shared custody formula, which is only appropriate if the Court adopts her custody proposal. If this Court, as Ashley urges, awards primary physical custody to Ashley, Civil Rule 90.3(a) controls and Sarah's adjusted annual income must be multiplied by 27 percent to determine the annual support obligation, which is then divided into 12 equal monthly installments.
The Court should also take care in calculating each party's adjusted annual income consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), which defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus mandatory deductions, voluntary retirement contributions within the prescribed limits, and other enumerated items. The Court may further consider whether to impute potential income to either parent under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) if the evidence warrants such a finding, though no such finding is presently sought with respect to Ashley given her documented caregiving responsibilities.
C. THE MARITAL RESIDENCE SHOULD BE AWARDED TO ASHLEY, WHO HOLDS PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF THE CHILDREN
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), a court dividing marital property must consider the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children. This factor is directly applicable here. Ashley and the two minor children currently reside in the Fairbanks family home. Awarding the residence to Ashley, or alternatively awarding her the right to continue residing there, would ensure continuity and stability for the children and avoids the significant disruption that a forced sale would create for a four-year-old and a seven-year-old whose school and preschool are located in Fairbanks.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996), recognized the comprehensive nature of the property division factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including consideration of each party's earning capacity, financial condition, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division. The court in Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002), further demonstrated that unequal property division in favor of the lower-earning spouse is appropriate where the equities warrant it, particularly where that spouse faces educational or career limitations attributable in part to marital roles and responsibilities.
Here, several factors weigh in favor of awarding the family home to Ashley, or at minimum a greater share of the $210,000 in equity. Ashley has the lower earning capacity. She has devoted significant time to the children's care, which has necessarily limited her professional development during the marriage. She will continue to bear the primary burden of daily child-rearing after the divorce. Sarah, by contrast, voluntarily relocated to Anchorage for employment, demonstrating an ability to establish independent housing and financial stability outside the family home. Awarding the home to Ashley, with appropriate credit to Sarah for her share of the equity through either a buyout arrangement or an offset against other marital assets, is just under the circumstances.
D. THE MARITAL DEBT AND RETIREMENT ACCOUNTS SHOULD BE DIVIDED EQUITABLY WITH REFERENCE TO THE STATUTORY FACTORS
The parties carry approximately $34,000 in credit card debt accumulated during the marriage. Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the division of marital property, which encompasses both assets and obligations, must fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce. Each party's ability to service debt following the divorce must be considered. Given Sarah's higher income, and consistent with the principle of fair allocation under AS 25.24.160, it is equitable for Sarah to bear a proportionally greater share of the joint marital debt, or for the debt allocation to be offset against Sarah's share of marital assets.
With respect to the two retirement accounts, each held by one spouse, the Court must evaluate the marital portion of each account, meaning the contributions made and investment growth accrued during the period of the marriage from 2017 forward. AS 25.24.160(a)(4) authorizes the Court to divide retirement benefits acquired during the marriage in a just manner. The Alaska Supreme Court addressed retirement account division in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), recognizing that courts must consider each party's earning capacity and the financial disparities between them when allocating retirement assets. Where, as here, Sarah has enjoyed a higher income and presumably accumulated greater retirement contributions during the marriage, a straightforward equal division of the marital portions of both accounts may be appropriate, but the Court should consider whether any offset is warranted in light of the other allocations made in the property division as a whole.
Any division of retirement benefits must comply with the requirements of a qualified domestic relations order where applicable. AS 25.24.160(b). Ashley respectfully requests that the Court order the preparation of appropriate documentation to effectuate any division of retirement accounts as part of the final decree.
E. THE COURT SHOULD CONSIDER THE EQUITABLE FACTORS HOLISTICALLY TO ARRIVE AT A JUST OVERALL DIVISION
Under AS 25.24.160(a)(4), the Court is directed to consider all enumerated factors in arriving at a property division that fairly allocates the economic effect of divorce. The factors include the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, the earning capacity of the parties including their custodial responsibilities during the marriage, the financial condition of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the party with primary physical custody, and the circumstances and necessities of each party. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(A) through (I).
Viewing these factors as a whole, the equities favor Ashley. The marriage was relatively short, approximately seven years, but Ashley contributed substantially through her caregiving role, which constrained her professional advancement while benefiting the family unit. Sarah's voluntary relocation to a higher-paying position in Anchorage improved her own financial position without a corresponding benefit to Ashley or the children in terms of daily support. Ashley will be the parent primarily responsible for the children's day-to-day needs following the divorce, and the property division should reflect and support that ongoing responsibility.
Ashley does not seek an unreasonable or punitive award. She seeks a division that is genuinely fair: one that accounts for her caregiving contributions, recognizes her lower earning capacity going forward, ensures stability for the children in the family home, and treats the marital debt as a shared obligation to be allocated in proportion to ability to pay.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Ashley Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Award Ashley primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, with Sarah receiving visitation on alternating weekends and during school breaks plus a mutually agreed holiday schedule, and with both parties sharing joint legal custody.
2. Calculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on Sarah's adjusted annual income multiplied by 27 percent for two children, consistent with a primary physical custody arrangement.
3. Award Ashley the family residence in Fairbanks, or the right to reside in it for a reasonable period, with appropriate credit to Sarah for her equity share through an offset against other marital assets or a structured buyout.
4. Divide the approximately $34,000 in joint marital debt in proportion to the parties' respective abilities to pay, with Sarah bearing a proportionally greater share consistent with her higher income.
5. Divide the marital portions of both retirement accounts equitably, with any necessary qualified domestic relations orders to be prepared and entered as part of the final decree, consistent with AS 25.24.160(b).
6. Grant such other relief as this Court deems just and equitable under the circumstances.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0039)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Alaska Superior Court, Family Division, on the petition for dissolution of marriage filed by Petitioner Marcus Whitfield. Marcus and Michael Whitfield were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2016 and are the parents of two minor children, ages five and eight. The marriage has irretrievably broken down due to financial stress and persistent communication failures that have rendered the parties incompatible. Marcus now petitions this Court to dissolve the marriage, establish a primary physical custody arrangement that serves the best interests of the minor children, set child support in accordance with Alaska's guidelines, and divide the marital estate in a manner that is just and equitable under Alaska law.
Three principal issues require resolution. First, the Court must establish a custody and parenting time arrangement that promotes the children's well-being and continuity of care. Second, the Court must determine the appropriate child support award after resolving the dispute over Michael's income figures and any associated financial disclosures. Third, the Court must divide the marital estate, including the family home, two vehicles, and shared credit card debt, in a manner that fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution, with due consideration for Marcus's request to retain the family home in order to preserve stability for the children.
Marcus respectfully requests that this Court grant primary physical custody of the minor children to him, award child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3, and allocate the family home to Marcus, with the remaining marital assets and liabilities divided equitably between the parties.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Whitfield and Michael Whitfield were married in Anchorage, Alaska in 2016. The marriage produced two minor children: a child currently aged eight and a child currently aged five. Both children have resided in the family home throughout their lives and are enrolled in school in the Anchorage area. Over the past two years, the marriage deteriorated as a result of significant financial stress and persistent communication breakdowns between the parties. These circumstances have caused an irremediable breakdown of the marital relationship, rendering the parties incompatible.
Marcus filed a petition for dissolution of marriage in the Alaska Superior Court, Family Division. Marcus proposes that the two minor children reside with him during the school week as the primary physical custodian, with Michael exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and during school holidays. The parties would share joint legal custody and cooperate on all major decisions regarding education, healthcare, and the general well-being of the children. This arrangement would preserve the children's established school routines and provide continuity of care in the home they have known throughout their lives.
The parties are in partial agreement regarding child support. Marcus seeks an award calculated under Civil Rule 90.3 using income figures he has submitted to the Court. Michael disputes those income figures and requests that the Court order formal financial disclosures before a final child support award is entered.
The marital estate consists of the following assets and liabilities: a jointly owned home in Anchorage with approximately $60,000 in equity; two vehicles; and a shared credit card debt of approximately $18,000. Marcus seeks to retain the family home for the benefit of the minor children, recognizing that continued residence in the home promotes stability and continuity of care. Michael requests an immediate sale of the home and an equal division of the net proceeds. The parties have not reached agreement on the division of the vehicles or the allocation of the shared debt.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.200, a petition for dissolution of marriage may be filed when incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and the parties have reached, or the Court has resolved, agreements regarding custody, child support, visitation, property division, and allocation of debts. Where the parties have not fully agreed, the Court retains authority under AS 25.24.220 to examine the terms of any partial agreement and to consider whether those terms are just, in the best interests of the children, and constitute a fair allocation of the economic consequences of dissolution.
In any dissolution or divorce proceeding, the division of property must fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution by taking into consideration the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4). Spousal maintenance, if any, and property division must together achieve a fair economic allocation under AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4), as incorporated by reference in AS 25.24.200(e) and AS 25.24.220(d)(3).
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which requires that the award be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage for the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2) defines primary physical custody as an arrangement in which the children reside with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year.
In divorce and dissolution actions, Civil Rule 26.1(b) requires each party, without awaiting a discovery request, to provide the other party with detailed financial disclosures, including tax returns, pay stubs, account information, and documentation of all assets and liabilities.
Alaska courts have consistently held that custody determinations must serve the best interests of the children, and that agreements between parents on custody have no binding force on the court independent of a best-interests analysis. See Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that child support guidelines under Civil Rule 90.3 exist to ensure that support orders are adequate to meet children's needs and to promote predictability and consistency. See Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015). Courts applying these guidelines may impute potential income where a parent is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4).
Property division in Alaska begins with the marital estate, and Alaska courts have the authority to divide all property acquired during the marriage, as well as to invade separate property when the equities require. Brown v. Brown, 914 P.2d 206 (Alaska 1996). The standard for dissolution agreements requires that the property division fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution, and courts apply heightened scrutiny where a division appears patently inequitable. Richard v. Boggs, 162 P.3d 629 (Alaska 2007). In Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed the particular concerns that arise when one party proceeds without counsel and underscored the importance of ensuring that property settlements are genuinely just, not merely formally agreed upon.
IV. ARGUMENT
