A. THE PROPOSED PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT SERVES THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE MINOR CHILDREN AND SHOULD BE ADOPTED BY THIS COURT.
Alaska law requires that custody arrangements serve the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.220(d)(2) directs the Court to consider whether custody agreements are just as between the spouses and in the best interests of the children of the marriage. Marcus proposes that the minor children reside with him during the school week and that Michael exercise parenting time on alternating weekends and during school holidays, with both parents sharing joint legal custody and cooperating on all major decisions regarding education, healthcare, and general well-being.
This arrangement promotes continuity of care and stability for children who have lived in the Anchorage family home their entire lives and are actively enrolled in school. The children, ages five and eight, benefit from predictable weekday routines anchored by a consistent primary residence. Marcus's proposal allows Michael meaningful and regular parenting time while preserving the school-week structure the children depend upon. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the paramount importance of maintaining stability for children when evaluating custody arrangements. Schmitz v. Schmitz, 88 P.3d 1116 (Alaska 2004).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), a parent has primary physical custody when the children reside with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. Under the proposed schedule, Michael's alternating-weekend and holiday parenting time would fall below this threshold, placing Marcus in the role of primary physical custodian for child support calculation purposes. This definition is consistent with the practical reality of the proposed parenting plan and supports the application of the primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Joint legal custody is appropriate here because both Marcus and Michael have demonstrated a shared commitment to the children's education, healthcare, and well-being. Requiring the parties to cooperate on major decisions preserves each parent's meaningful involvement in the children's lives while vesting day-to-day responsibility with the primary residential parent. The Court should adopt the proposed custody and parenting time arrangement as serving the best interests of the minor children.
B. CHILD SUPPORT MUST BE CALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3 ON THE BASIS OF ACCURATE INCOME FIGURES, AND THE COURT SHOULD ORDER MICHAEL TO COMPLY WITH THE FINANCIAL DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS OF CIVIL RULE 26.1(b).
Civil Rule 90.3(a) mandates that child support for two children be calculated at 27 percent of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. The adjusted annual income is the non-custodial parent's total income from all sources, reduced by mandatory deductions such as federal, state, and local income tax, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and other enumerated deductions set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1). Because Marcus is proposed as the primary physical custodian, Michael is the non-custodial parent for purposes of this calculation, and the support obligation is to be determined from Michael's adjusted annual income.
Michael has disputed the income figures Marcus submitted and has requested that the Court order formal financial disclosures. Civil Rule 26.1(b) requires each party in a dissolution or divorce proceeding to provide, without awaiting a discovery request, comprehensive financial documentation, including federal tax returns for the past three years, pay stubs and proof of income for the past two months from all sources, bank account statements, documentation of all debts, and information regarding all assets. These disclosures exist precisely to ensure that child support calculations rest on a realistic and accurate income figure, consistent with the goal articulated by the Alaska Supreme Court in Ruppe v. Ruppe, 358 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2015), that the Rule 90.3 formula produce adequate and consistent support awards.
Marcus requests that the Court order Michael to provide full disclosures as required by Civil Rule 26.1(b) within the time permitted by that rule. Once accurate income figures have been established, the Court should calculate the child support obligation at 27 percent of Michael's adjusted annual income for two children, consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Additionally, if Michael's disclosed income reflects voluntary underemployment or unemployment, the Court has authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to impute potential income based on Michael's assets, work history, education, job skills, earning history, and other relevant factors. A determination of potential income may not be made if Michael is physically or mentally incapacitated or is caring for a child under two years of age to whom the parties owe joint legal responsibility. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E). Absent those circumstances, if the evidence supports a finding of voluntary underemployment, imputation would be appropriate to ensure that the children receive adequate support.
The Court should also consider the applicable low-income adjustment under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(5) only if Michael's total annual income is $30,000 or less, in which event Michael's adjusted annual income is the lesser of the amount calculated under the standard deduction formula or Michael's total income from all sources minus $7,500. No determination on this point can be made until Michael complies with the disclosure requirements of Civil Rule 26.1(b).
C. THE MARITAL ESTATE MUST BE DIVIDED IN A MANNER THAT FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION, AND THE COURT SHOULD AWARD THE FAMILY HOME TO MARCUS TO PRESERVE CONTINUITY AND STABILITY FOR THE MINOR CHILDREN.
Alaska law requires that the division of marital property "fairly allocate the economic effect of divorce by being based on consideration of" the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4). Among those factors are: the length of the marriage and station in life of the parties; the age and health of the parties; the earning capacity of the parties; the financial condition of the parties; the conduct of the parties, including whether there has been unreasonable depletion of marital assets; the desirability of awarding the family home to the party who has primary physical custody of the children; the circumstances and necessities of each party; the time and manner of acquisition of the property; and the income-producing capacity of the property and its value at the time of division.
One factor is particularly compelling in this case. AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) expressly identifies as a relevant consideration "the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it for a reasonable period of time, to the party who has primary physical custody of children." Marcus seeks primary physical custody of both minor children, ages five and eight, who have lived in the Anchorage home throughout their lives. Disrupting that residence by forcing an immediate sale would remove the children from their established home during an already difficult period of family transition. The statute directly contemplates this scenario and directs the Court to weigh the desirability of awarding the home to the primary custodial parent. This factor strongly favors awarding the family home to Marcus.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that property division agreements and court-ordered allocations must achieve genuine fairness, not merely formal symmetry. Richard v. Boggs, 162 P.3d 629 (Alaska 2007). In that case, the court approved a property division that departed from a precisely equal split because the parties demonstrated that their arrangement better served the interests of the children and the practical realities of the family. Similarly, here, awarding the home to Marcus does not produce an inequitable result; it reflects the legitimate priority of the children's stability and the explicit statutory directive of AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F).
To offset the equity that Marcus retains in the home, the parties should negotiate, or the Court should impose, an adjustment to the remaining marital assets, including the vehicles and the allocation of the shared credit card debt of approximately $18,000. A just resolution might include awarding Michael a greater share of any liquid assets or a credit against the debt allocation to account for Marcus retaining the approximately $60,000 in home equity. The Court has full authority under AS 25.24.160 to fashion a division of all marital property, including by requiring assignment or conveyance of real or personal property, that achieves a fair and equitable allocation overall.
Michael's demand for an immediate sale and equal division of the proceeds, while understandable from a purely financial perspective, fails to account for the statutory directive to consider the children's needs and the primary custodial parent's claim to the family home. It also ignores the disruption that a forced sale during an active custody arrangement would impose on two school-age children. The Court should decline to order an immediate sale and should instead award the family home to Marcus, with compensating adjustments to the division of remaining assets and liabilities as equity requires.
D. THE COURT MUST APPLY HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY TO ANY AGREEMENTS SUBMITTED BY THE PARTIES GIVEN THE PRESENCE OF MINOR CHILDREN AND ANY APPARENT INEQUITY IN THE PROPOSED DISTRIBUTION OF THE MARITAL ESTATE.
Under AS 25.24.220(h), the Court is required to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to agreements where there is a minor child of the marriage or where there is a patently inequitable division of the marital estate. Both of these triggers are present here. The parties have two minor children, ages five and eight. Additionally, Michael's proposal for an equal division of home sale proceeds without any offset for the children's stability interests, combined with potential disputes about the allocation of the credit card debt and vehicles, raises the possibility of a patently inequitable result if the estate is divided without careful judicial oversight.
When heightened scrutiny applies, the Court under AS 25.24.220(i) must examine the written agreements to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement between the parties, and that any agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are in the best interests of the children. This elevated standard is particularly important here because the income dispute means the child support figure has not yet been finally determined, and the custody and financial arrangements are interrelated.
The Alaska Supreme Court has addressed the particular concerns that arise when property is divided under conditions where the parties' understanding of value is limited or the negotiating process is unequal. Sandberg v. Sandberg, 322 P.3d 879 (Alaska 2014). In Sandberg, the court emphasized the need for careful judicial review of dissolution agreements to ensure they are substantively fair, especially where one party may lack full information. This Court should apply the same careful scrutiny to any agreement or proposed order that emerges from the pending disputes in this proceeding.
Marcus further notes that because the parties have not reached full agreement on child support pending resolution of the financial disclosure dispute, and because the property division remains contested, the comprehensive requirements of AS 25.24.210(e) have not yet been satisfied. That statute requires the petition to state in detail the terms of the agreement on custody, child support, visitation, and property division, and requires that agreements fairly allocate the economic effect of dissolution consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(2) and (4). The Court should not enter a final decree until these requirements are met and the disclosures required by Civil Rule 26.1(b) have been provided and reviewed.
E. THE FINANCIAL DISCLOSURE OBLIGATIONS UNDER CIVIL RULE 26.1(b) ARE MANDATORY AND NON-WAIVABLE IN THIS PROCEEDING, AND MICHAEL'S REFUSAL TO ACCEPT THE SUBMITTED INCOME FIGURES MAKES COMPLIANCE ESSENTIAL.
Civil Rule 26.1(b) requires that in all divorce and legal separation actions, each party shall, without awaiting a discovery request, provide to the other party a comprehensive array of financial documentation. This includes, among other items: the legal description and street address of all real property in which either party has an interest; signed releases authorizing the other party to obtain earnings, employee benefit, and retirement account information; a listing of all financial accounts with corresponding statements; a listing of all outstanding debts with documentation of balances and payment terms; a listing of all personal property with a current fair market value over $100; federal tax returns for the past three years; pay stubs and proof of income for the past two months from all sources; and a description of each party's current medical coverage.
Michael has placed the accuracy of the income figures in dispute. Until he provides the disclosures mandated by Civil Rule 26.1(b), the Court cannot calculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) on a reliable basis, cannot determine whether imputation of income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) is appropriate, and cannot fairly assess whether the proposed property division achieves the equitable allocation required by AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The disclosure requirements are not optional; they exist to facilitate accurate, fair, and consistent outcomes in exactly this type of contested dissolution proceeding.
Marcus requests that the Court enter an order directing Michael to provide full and complete disclosures under Civil Rule 26.1(b) within the applicable time period, and that no final child support order or property division decree be entered until the Court has had the opportunity to review those disclosures and to determine accurate income and asset figures for both parties.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Marcus Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Adopt the proposed primary physical custody arrangement, awarding Marcus primary physical custody of both minor children with Michael exercising parenting time on alternating weekends and during school holidays, and establishing joint legal custody with shared decision-making authority over education, healthcare, and the children's general well-being;
2. Order Michael to provide full financial disclosures as required by Civil Rule 26.1(b) within the applicable time period, and defer entry of a final child support order until those disclosures have been reviewed and accurate income figures established;
3. Calculate child support at 27 percent of Michael's adjusted annual income, consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), after resolving the income dispute, and consider imputation of potential income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) if the evidence supports a finding of voluntary underemployment;
4. Award the family home to Marcus in recognition of the statutory directive of AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F) favoring the primary custodial parent's retention of the family home, with compensating adjustments to the division of the remaining marital assets and liabilities, including the vehicles and the shared credit card debt of approximately $18,000, to achieve an overall fair and just allocation of the marital estate;
5. Apply the heightened scrutiny required by AS 25.24.220(h) to all agreements between the parties given the presence of minor children and the potential for inequity in the proposed property division; and
6. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper under Alaska law.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
DIVORCE/DISSOLUTION FILING INVOLVING MINOR CHILDREN
(doc-0040)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the Alaska Superior Court, First Judicial District, on the petition of Marcus Okafor for dissolution of his marriage to Sarah Okafor. The parties have reached a tentative agreement addressing child custody, child support, and division of the marital estate. They respectfully request that the Court review and approve the proposed agreement pursuant to AS 25.24.200 and AS 25.24.220, and enter a decree of dissolution consistent with the terms set forth herein.
Marcus and Sarah Okafor were married in 2014 and are the parents of two minor children, ages six and nine. The marriage has experienced an irremediable breakdown due to Marcus's extended seasonal absences as a commercial fisherman and irreconcilable differences concerning finances and parenting priorities. The parties have cooperated in reaching a comprehensive agreement that addresses primary physical custody in favor of Sarah during the school year, parenting time for Marcus during summers and school breaks, joint legal custody for major decisions, child support calculated using an income averaging methodology under Civil Rule 90.3, and an equitable division of the marital estate.
The proposed agreement is just, fair, and in the best interests of the children. The Court is respectfully asked to examine the agreement with the care required by Alaska law, confirm that all statutory conditions have been satisfied, and approve the dissolution.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Okafor is a commercial fisherman based in Juneau, Alaska. His annual fishing income fluctuates significantly depending on the salmon season, weather, and market conditions. Sarah Okafor is a registered nurse employed at Bartlett Regional Hospital in Juneau. The parties were married in 2014 and have two minor children: a nine-year-old and a six-year-old.
Over several years, the marriage deteriorated primarily as a result of Marcus's extended seasonal absences required by his commercial fishing operations and irreconcilable differences between the parties regarding financial priorities and parenting approaches. These circumstances have caused an irremediable breakdown of the marriage, satisfying the incompatibility condition required by AS 25.24.200(a)(1).
The parties have negotiated in good faith and have reached a tentative settlement agreement addressing all material issues arising from the dissolution. With respect to custody, the parties propose that Sarah receive primary physical custody of both children during the school year, and that Marcus exercise parenting time during summer months and school breaks consistent with his off-season availability. The parties further propose joint legal custody, with both parents sharing decision-making authority for major matters concerning the children's education, health care, and general well-being.
With respect to child support, the parties propose that Marcus pay monthly child support calculated under Civil Rule 90.3. Because Marcus's commercial fishing income varies substantially from year to year, the parties have stipulated to an income averaging approach to establish a fair and realistic adjusted annual income figure as the baseline for the support calculation.
The marital estate consists of the following assets and liabilities: the family home in Juneau, jointly titled and subject to an outstanding mortgage; a jointly held savings account; Marcus's commercial fishing vessel and associated gear, valued at approximately $180,000; and shared credit card debt of approximately $22,000. The parties seek equitable division of these assets and liabilities through the Court's review of their proposed property settlement agreement.
Neither party has been the subject of a domestic violence charge, protective order, or injunctive relief during the marriage. Both parties understand the nature and consequences of their action.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A petition for dissolution of marriage may be jointly filed under AS 25.24.200(a) when the spouses demonstrate that incompatibility of temperament has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, that they have agreed on custody, support, and visitation for any minor children, and that they have agreed as to the distribution of all real and personal property and the payment of all obligations. The agreement must be fair and just and must take into consideration the factors listed in AS 25.24.964(2) and (4) so that the economic effect of dissolution is fairly allocated.
Upon filing, the Court is required by AS 25.24.983 to examine the parties and consider whether each spouse fully understands the nature and consequences of the action, whether the written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the parties and in the best interests of the children, whether the agreements relating to property division are just, and whether the written agreements constitute the entire agreement between the parties.
Where heightened scrutiny is warranted under AS 25.24.220(h), the Court must examine the written agreements to determine that they are just and that child-related agreements are in the best interests of the children. In this case, because there are minor children of the marriage, AS 25.24.220(h)(3) requires the Court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the agreements, consistent with AS 25.24.991.
Child support must be calculated in conformity with Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: 27% for two children. Where an obligor's income is erratic or seasonal, the court may base the calculation on an income averaging approach. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Zimin v. Zimin, 837 P.2d 118 (Alaska 1992), that income averaging is appropriate in cases involving variable income, though the averaging period selected must produce a reliable indicator of the obligor's current earning capacity. The court further affirmed this principle in Keturi v. Keturi, 84 P.3d 408 (Alaska 2004), holding that the use of income averaging for an obligor with highly variable income is not an abuse of discretion.
Property division in a dissolution proceeding must fairly allocate the economic effect of the dissolution and take into consideration the factors set forth in AS 25.24.160(a)(4), including the length of the marriage, the age and health of the parties, earning capacity, financial condition, conduct of the parties, the desirability of awarding the family home to the primary custodial parent, the circumstances and necessities of each party, the time and manner of acquisition of the property, and the income-producing capacity and value of the property at the time of division.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE PETITION SATISFIES ALL CONDITIONS REQUIRED FOR DISSOLUTION UNDER AS 25.24.200(a).
The Okafors' joint petition satisfies each of the statutory prerequisites for dissolution. First, incompatibility of temperament, arising from Marcus's extended seasonal absences and irreconcilable differences over finances and parenting, has caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage within the meaning of AS 25.24.200(a)(1). Second, as required by AS 25.24.200(a)(2), the parties, who have two unmarried children under the age of nineteen, have reached a full agreement on custody, visitation, and child support. Third, as required by AS 25.24.200(a)(3), the parties have agreed to distribute all jointly held real and personal property, including retirement benefits if any, in a manner that fairly allocates the economic effect of the dissolution. Fourth, as required by AS 25.24.200(a)(4), the parties have agreed to the allocation of all shared debts and obligations, including the outstanding credit card debt of approximately $22,000.
The petition therefore presents a complete and facially valid basis for dissolution, and the Court should proceed to examine the proposed agreements under AS 25.24.220(d).
B. THE PROPOSED CUSTODY AND PARENTING TIME ARRANGEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
The parties propose that Sarah receive primary physical custody of the two minor children during the school year, with Marcus exercising parenting time during the summer months and school breaks. Both parents will share joint legal custody for major decisions regarding education, health care, and general well-being.
Under AS 25.24.220(d)(2), the Court must consider whether the written agreements concerning child custody, child support, and visitation are just as between the parties and in the best interests of the children. The proposed arrangement serves the children's best interests in several respects. The children will maintain stability and continuity during the school year in their primary residence with Sarah, who, as a registered nurse with a consistent employment schedule, is well-positioned to provide regular supervision and care. Marcus, whose commercial fishing schedule is inherently seasonal, will have meaningful and substantial parenting time during periods when he is not at sea, ensuring that the children maintain a close and ongoing relationship with both parents.
The joint legal custody component of the agreement reflects both parents' commitment to shared decision-making on matters of importance to the children's lives, furthering the children's well-being and ensuring that both parents remain engaged in their upbringing. The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in Mahan v. Mahan, 347 P.3d 91 (Alaska 2015), illustrates that dissolution agreements regarding custody are subject to careful scrutiny to ensure that the terms are genuinely in the children's best interests, and the arrangement proposed here reflects that standard.
Because minor children are involved, the Court must apply heightened scrutiny to the agreements under AS 25.24.220(h)(3) and AS 25.24.220(i). The Court should satisfy itself that the custody arrangement reflects the children's best interests and that neither party has been subject to any coercion in agreeing to these terms. The parties confirm that the agreement was reached freely and represents their genuine, mutual assessment of an arrangement suited to the children's needs and to the practical realities of Marcus's seasonal occupation.
C. CHILD SUPPORT MUST BE CALCULATED USING AN INCOME AVERAGING METHOD TO ARRIVE AT A FAIR AND REALISTIC ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME FOR MARCUS.
Because Sarah will have primary physical custody during the school year, child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a). For two children, the applicable percentage is 27% of Marcus's adjusted annual income as calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1). The critical issue is the determination of Marcus's adjusted annual income given the substantial year-to-year variation in his commercial fishing earnings.
The Alaska Supreme Court has addressed the income averaging issue in a line of cases consistent with the commentary to Civil Rule 90.3. In Zimin v. Zimin, 837 P.2d 118 (Alaska 1992), the court held that the goal of the Rule 90.3 guidelines is to obtain a realistic estimate of an obligor's adjusted annual income, and that income averaging over a reasonable period of years is appropriate where the obligor's income is erratic, while cautioning that an overly long averaging period may not accurately reflect current earning capacity. In Keturi v. Keturi, 84 P.3d 408 (Alaska 2004), the court affirmed that where an obligor's business income has been highly variable, income averaging over several years is a permissible and appropriate method, so long as the result reflects a reliable estimate of future earning potential. In Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), the court similarly approved determination of adjusted annual income based on a party's work history and employment patterns where annual earnings fluctuated.
The parties propose that the Court adopt an averaging period drawn from Marcus's documented fishing income over a representative number of recent years, adjusted for any deductions authorized under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including mandatory tax withholding, self-employment tax, Medicare tax, and any other enumerated deductions. The resulting adjusted annual income figure should then be multiplied by 27% pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to arrive at the annual child support obligation, which will be paid in equal monthly installments.
This approach is fair to both parties. It prevents Marcus from being assessed child support based on an unusually high single-year income that may not recur, while also preventing an artificially low calculation based on a poor season. Sarah and the children are assured a predictable and reasonable level of financial support, and Marcus is protected against an obligation he cannot realistically sustain across the full arc of his commercial fishing career.
The Court also has authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to consider whether either parent is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. There is no suggestion that either party is underemployed here. Marcus works in a demanding and inherently seasonal industry, and Sarah is fully employed as a registered nurse. Accordingly, no imputation of potential income is warranted, and the income averaging methodology is the appropriate tool for establishing Marcus's support obligation.
D. THE PROPOSED PROPERTY DIVISION FAIRLY ALLOCATES THE ECONOMIC EFFECT OF DISSOLUTION AND SATISFIES THE STATUTORY FACTORS UNDER AS 25.24.160(a)(4).
The Court must consider whether the property settlement agreement is just under AS 25.24.220(d)(3), and the agreement must reflect the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.160(a)(4). The parties propose to divide the following assets and liabilities: the jointly titled family home subject to an outstanding mortgage; the jointly held savings account; Marcus's commercial fishing vessel and gear, valued at approximately $180,000; and shared credit card debt of approximately $22,000.
Consideration of the AS 25.24.160(a)(4) factors supports the proposed division. The marriage lasted approximately ten years, providing a substantial marital period during which both parties contributed to the acquisition of marital assets. Sarah, as the primary custodial parent, has a compelling interest in the family home under AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(F), which specifically directs the court to consider the desirability of awarding the family home, or the right to live in it, to the party who has primary physical custody of the children. The parties' proposed agreement should address the home in a manner that gives appropriate weight to this factor and ensures that the children have a stable residential environment in Juneau.
The fishing vessel and associated gear, while substantial in value, represent the primary instrument of Marcus's livelihood. Awarding this property to Marcus is consistent with AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(I), which requires consideration of the income-producing capacity of the property, as well as AS 25.24.160(a)(4)(H), which directs attention to the time and manner of acquisition. The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in Sharon Thompson v. Everett Thompson, 454 P.3d 981 (Alaska 2019), confirms that assets integral to a party's ongoing business or livelihood are properly evaluated in light of each spouse's earning capacity and the income-producing function of the asset.
With respect to the shared credit card debt of approximately $22,000, the parties propose an equitable allocation of this obligation consistent with AS 25.24.200(a)(4), which requires agreement as to the payment of all unpaid obligations incurred by either or both spouses. The allocation should fairly reflect each party's ability to service debt in light of their respective incomes and post-dissolution financial circumstances.
The savings account, as a jointly held liquid asset, should be divided in a manner that reflects the equities between the parties, taking into account any imbalances in the overall property division, particularly the award of the high-value fishing vessel to Marcus.
As a whole, the proposed settlement should fairly allocate the economic effect of the dissolution in accordance with AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and AS 25.24.200(e). The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Fernau v. Rowdon, 42 P.3d 1047 (Alaska 2002), confirms that property division, rather than ongoing maintenance, is the preferred mechanism for addressing the parties' post-dissolution financial needs, and the parties' comprehensive property settlement is designed with that principle in mind.
E. THE WRITTEN AGREEMENTS CONSTITUTE THE ENTIRE AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE PARTIES AS REQUIRED BY AS 25.24.220(d)(4).
Under AS 25.24.220(d)(4), the Court must determine that the written agreements between the parties constitute the entire agreement. The parties confirm that no side agreements, oral understandings, or undisclosed arrangements exist between them. The petition and attached settlement documents represent the complete and integrated expression of the parties' mutual obligations and undertakings with respect to all issues arising from their dissolution, including custody, child support, parenting time, property division, and debt allocation. The forms required by AS 25.24.250 have been prepared and submitted in conformity with the requirements of the Alaska Rules of Civil Procedure and specify that the dissolution petition constitutes the entire agreement between the parties.
F. HEIGHTENED SCRUTINY IS SATISFIED AND THE COURT SHOULD APPROVE THE AGREEMENTS.
Because the parties have minor children, AS 25.24.220(h)(3) requires the Court to apply a heightened level of scrutiny to the written agreements. Under AS 25.24.220(i), the Court must examine the agreements to determine that they are just, that they constitute the entire agreement, and that the custody, child support, and visitation provisions are in the best interests of the children. The Court must require both parties to appear at the hearing unless appearance would constitute a significant hardship, which is not alleged here.
Both parties should appear at the hearing prepared to demonstrate to the Court's satisfaction that the agreements are just and were entered into freely, with full understanding of their nature and consequences. The Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012), decision reflects the Alaska Supreme Court's careful attention to the mechanics of child support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3, and the Faulkner v. Goldfuss, 46 P.3d 993 (Alaska 2002), decision confirms that the court independently evaluates the sufficiency of child-related agreements rather than deferring solely to the parties' stipulations. This brief and the supporting petition provide the factual and legal foundation necessary to satisfy the Court's heightened review.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Marcus Okafor respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that the conditions for dissolution under AS 25.24.200(a) have been satisfied, including the irremediable breakdown of the marriage due to incompatibility of temperament;
2. Approve the proposed parenting agreement providing for primary physical custody in Sarah Okafor during the school year, meaningful parenting time for Marcus Okafor during summer months and school breaks, and joint legal custody for major decisions, upon finding that the agreement is just and in the best interests of the children;
3. Calculate Marcus Okafor's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using an income averaging methodology applied to his documented commercial fishing earnings over a reasonable and representative period of years, with the annual obligation set at 27% of his adjusted annual income for two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B);
4. Review and approve the proposed property settlement agreement, including the allocation of the family home, the commercial fishing vessel and gear, the joint savings account, and the shared credit card debt, upon finding that the agreement fairly allocates the economic effect of dissolution in accordance with AS 25.24.160(a)(4) and AS 25.24.200(e);
5. Find that the written agreements constitute the entire agreement between the parties pursuant to AS 25.24.220(d)(4); and
6. Enter a decree of dissolution of the marriage of Marcus Okafor and Sarah Okafor consistent with the foregoing findings and the terms of the parties' agreement.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0041)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Whitfield respectfully petitions this Court to establish a formal custody and visitation order governing the care of the parties' minor daughter, Lily Whitfield, age two. Lily was born in Anchorage, Alaska, during the parties' relationship and has resided in Alaska her entire life. Since the parties' separation in early 2023, no court has entered any order addressing Lily's legal custody, physical custody, or visitation. The informal parenting arrangement that has developed in the absence of a court order has proven increasingly unstable and has left critical decisions regarding Lily's health, education, and welfare subject to ongoing disagreement between the parties. Renee brings this petition pursuant to AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150 to request that this Court establish a clear, binding custody arrangement that serves Lily's best interests, provides her with stability and continuity, and defines each parent's rights and responsibilities with the clarity that only a formal court order can provide.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Whitfield and Maria Whitfield were in a romantic relationship for approximately three years before separating in early 2023 following an extended period of conflict and incompatibility. The parties' daughter, Lily, was born during the relationship in Anchorage, Alaska, and is now approximately two years of age.
Following the separation, Lily has resided primarily with Maria in the former family home in Anchorage. Renee has maintained contact with Lily through an informal arrangement negotiated verbally between the parties. That arrangement has never been reduced to a written agreement or approved by any court, and no judicial body has ever entered any order governing Lily's custody or visitation.
The informal arrangement has deteriorated significantly over time. The parties have been unable to reach agreement on holiday schedules, resulting in repeated disputes during important family occasions. They have also been unable to agree on medical decisions for Lily, including decisions about routine pediatric care, which has caused delay and uncertainty in Lily's healthcare. Disagreements regarding childcare arrangements have further destabilized Lily's day-to-day environment.
Renee has consistently sought to maintain a meaningful and active parenting role in Lily's life, demonstrating love, affection, and commitment to Lily's physical, emotional, and developmental well-being. Renee is capable of and eager to meet Lily's needs and is prepared to support and encourage Lily's continued relationship with Maria.
The absence of a formal custody order has created an environment of instability and unpredictability that is contrary to Lily's best interests. A formal order establishing legal and physical custody, defining each parent's decision-making authority, and setting a clear parenting schedule is necessary to protect Lily's welfare and to provide both parents with enforceable rights and responsibilities.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060(a), either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of a child custody dispute, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. In determining the best interests of the child, the court must consider all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Neither parent is entitled to a preference in the award of custody. AS 25.20.060(b).
AS 25.24.150(c) sets forth the factors the court must consider in determining the best interests of the child, including: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference, if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form one; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the child's well-being; and any other factors the court considers pertinent.
Pursuant to AS 25.20.070, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child considering the factors under AS 25.24.150(c), or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) applies, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the period the court considers an award of custody.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that the paramount concern in any custody determination is the best interests of the child. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018); Limeres v. Limeres, 320 P.3d 291 (Alaska 2014). The court is not bound by the status quo where the existing informal arrangement is unstable or inadequate to serve the child's needs. Daves v. McKinley, 425 P.3d 92 (Alaska 2018). The court may award shared physical custody where such an arrangement is in the best interests of the child and will assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c).
Where a custody arrangement is at issue, the court may also address child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(b), which govern the calculation of support in cases involving primary and shared physical custody arrangements, respectively.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. This Court Has Jurisdiction and Authority to Enter a Custody Order for Lily.
This Court has full authority under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150 to establish a custody order for Lily. The statute expressly provides that either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of a child custody dispute. Lily was born in Anchorage, has resided in Alaska throughout her life, and Alaska is her home state. No other court has exercised jurisdiction over Lily's custody. Accordingly, this Court is the appropriate forum to adjudicate this matter and to enter an order establishing legal and physical custody.
B. A Formal Custody Order Is Necessary to Protect Lily's Best Interests.
The absence of any court order governing Lily's custody has created persistent instability in her life. At two years of age, Lily is in a critical developmental period during which consistency, predictability, and stability are essential to her physical, emotional, and social well-being. AS 25.24.150(c)(1) requires the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. A toddler's need for routine and security is well recognized, and the ongoing parental conflict over holiday schedules, medical decisions, and childcare arrangements directly undermines Lily's ability to experience the stable, nurturing environment she deserves.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. While Lily has resided primarily with Maria since the separation, continuity of environment must be weighed alongside the need for meaningful access to both parents and cannot be used as a mechanism to exclude a committed and capable parent from a child's life. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a child's need for stability is best served not merely by preserving the status quo, but by ensuring that the arrangement actually serving the child is grounded in a formal, enforceable order. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018).
C. Renee Is a Capable and Loving Parent Who Is Committed to Lily's Well-Being.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) directs the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. Renee has been an active and engaged parent throughout Lily's life, maintaining consistent contact and demonstrating genuine commitment to Lily's welfare despite the absence of a formal schedule. Renee is capable of providing Lily with a safe, nurturing, and developmentally appropriate home environment.
AS 25.24.150(c)(4) requires the court to consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. Lily shares a close and loving bond with Renee, and that bond has been maintained through Renee's consistent effort to remain present in Lily's life notwithstanding the challenges presented by the informal and unstable parenting arrangement.
There is no evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, child neglect, or substance abuse on Renee's part that would in any way limit her custodial rights. AS 25.24.150(c)(7) and (c)(8). The presumption set forth in AS 25.24.150(g) regarding a history of domestic violence is not applicable here. Accordingly, no statutory basis exists to restrict Renee's access to or custody of Lily.
D. Joint Legal Custody and a Defined Physical Custody Schedule Serve Lily's Best Interests.
Renee requests that this Court award joint legal custody to both parties, granting each parent an equal voice in major decisions affecting Lily's health, education, welfare, and religious upbringing. Joint legal custody is appropriate where, as here, both parents are committed to the child's well-being and are capable of participating meaningfully in decisions concerning her care. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that joint legal custody can serve a child's best interests where the parents demonstrate a capacity, with appropriate court-ordered structure, to communicate about their child. Jayda Roman v. Cleveland Karren, 461 P.3d 1252 (Alaska 2020).
With respect to physical custody, Renee requests that this Court award shared physical custody in a manner that maximizes Lily's contact with both parents. AS 25.20.060(c) provides that the court may award shared custody if it is determined to be in the best interests of the child, and that such an award shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.070 further provides that, absent a showing of detriment to the child or the applicability of the domestic violence presumption, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the period the court considers an award of custody.
A shared physical custody arrangement, structured around a clear and predictable parenting schedule, would resolve the recurring disputes over holidays and childcare that have plagued the parties' informal arrangement. It would ensure that Lily benefits from the active involvement of both of her parents during the formative early years of her life. A structured schedule, whether alternating weeks or another arrangement the Court finds appropriate given Lily's age and circumstances, would provide the consistency and routine that Lily needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) directs the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Renee has demonstrated willingness to foster Lily's relationship with Maria and is committed to cooperating with Maria in Lily's upbringing. Renee's petition itself reflects a desire not to exclude Maria from Lily's life, but to establish a clear framework within which both parents can participate meaningfully and cooperatively.
E. The Court Should Address Medical Decision-Making Authority.
One of the most pressing sources of conflict between the parties has been the inability to agree on medical decisions for Lily. An award of joint legal custody must be accompanied by clear provisions establishing how medical decisions will be made and, in the event of an impasse, which parent holds tie-breaking authority or how the dispute will be resolved. The Alaska Supreme Court has addressed the importance of clear legal custody provisions to avoid continued parental conflict that is harmful to children. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011). This Court should include in its order specific provisions addressing routine and emergency medical decision-making to prevent further delay or harm to Lily's healthcare.
F. Child Support Should Be Calculated in Accordance with Civil Rule 90.3.
Upon the entry of a custody order, this Court should also address child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. If the Court awards shared physical custody as Renee requests, child support shall be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for the percentage of time each parent will have physical custody of the child and the respective adjusted annual incomes of the parties as defined under Civil Rule 90.3(a). The resulting calculation will ensure that Lily's financial needs are met equitably and in proportion to each parent's means and custodial responsibility.
G. An Informal Trial Under Civil Rule 16.2(e) May Efficiently Resolve This Matter.
This case presents issues well suited to resolution through an informal trial under Civil Rule 16.2(e). The parties are not represented by counsel, and the core facts are not so complex as to require extensive formal evidentiary proceedings. Civil Rule 16.2(e) provides a structured process in which each party may speak to the court under oath, offer relevant documents and other evidence, and make a closing statement, with the court guiding the development of the factual record. Resolution through an informal trial would reduce cost, minimize adversarial tension, and focus the Court's attention efficiently on the best interests of Lily.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court enter an order:
1. Awarding joint legal custody of Lily Whitfield to both Renee Whitfield and Maria Whitfield, with clear provisions for medical and other major decision-making;
2. Awarding shared physical custody pursuant to AS 25.20.060(c) and AS 25.20.070, on a schedule that maximizes Lily's contact with both parents and provides her with the stability and continuity she needs;
3. Setting a parenting schedule that resolves recurring disputes over holidays, childcare, and routine parenting time;
4. Establishing child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(b) based on the shared physical custody arrangement and the parties' respective incomes; and
5. Granting such other and further relief as this Court deems just and necessary to serve the best interests of Lily Whitfield.
Renee Whitfield respectfully submits that a formal, binding custody order is not only warranted but essential to protect Lily's well-being, provide both parents with enforceable rights, and lay a stable foundation for Lily's growth and development.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0042)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Tomas Petrova respectfully petitions this Court for an initial determination of legal and physical custody of his daughter, Mia Petrova, born November 2021, who has resided in Anchorage, Alaska for the entirety of her life. No court has ever entered an order governing custody, visitation, or child support for Mia, leaving both parents without legally enforceable rights or obligations. The urgency of this petition is driven by Respondent Jennifer Petrova's stated intention to relocate Mia to Juneau, Alaska for a new employment opportunity, a move that would fundamentally alter Mia's living arrangements and significantly curtail Petitioner's ability to maintain a meaningful parental relationship with his daughter.
This Court has both the authority and the duty to enter an initial custody order that serves Mia's best interests. Alaska is unquestionably Mia's home state, and the superior court possesses subject matter jurisdiction to resolve this dispute. Petitioner seeks a formal order establishing joint legal custody, shared or primary physical custody structured to allow Mia frequent and continuing contact with both parents, and a child support determination calculated in accordance with the applicable guidelines. Without judicial intervention, Mia's relationship with her father may be severely and irreparably damaged by a unilateral parental relocation.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Petrova and Jennifer Petrova are the biological parents of Mia Petrova, born November 2021 in Anchorage, Alaska. The parties were never married but cohabited in Anchorage for approximately three years. Their relationship ended in early 2023 following an extended period of conflict centered on financial disagreements and incompatible approaches to parenting.
Since the separation, Mia has resided primarily with Jennifer in a two-bedroom apartment in Anchorage. Tomas has exercised parenting time on an informal, inconsistent basis, with the specific schedule varying from week to week depending solely on whatever the parties could negotiate between themselves at any given time. No court order of any kind has ever been entered with respect to Mia's custody, visitation schedule, or child support obligations.
Recently, Jennifer informed Tomas that she intends to relocate with Mia to Juneau, Alaska to accept a new job offer. Tomas has not consented to this relocation and is gravely concerned that such a move, absent a formal custody order, would deprive him of any enforceable right to parenting time and would disrupt Mia's established connections to Anchorage, including her relationships with extended family members and community resources.
Mia has lived in Alaska since birth. She is approximately three years old and has resided continuously in Anchorage. Alaska is and has always been her home state. No other state has ever exercised or claimed custody jurisdiction over Mia. No custody proceeding has ever been filed in any court in any jurisdiction. Tomas now petitions this Court for an initial custody determination to protect Mia's best interests and preserve his parental relationship with her.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Jurisdiction
This Court has jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination pursuant to AS 25.30.300. That statute provides that a court of this state has jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination if, among other grounds, "this state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding." AS 25.30.300(a)(1). The statute further provides that "the provisions of (a) of this section are the exclusive jurisdictional bases for making a child custody determination by a court of this state." AS 25.30.300(b). Mia has resided in Anchorage, Alaska since her birth in November 2021. Alaska is plainly her home state, and jurisdiction is therefore properly vested in this Court.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a superior court may make an initial custody determination only after establishing that it possesses subject matter jurisdiction under at least one of the grounds enumerated in AS 25.30.300. Dawn Maynor, f/k/a Dawn Golden v. Timothy B. Golden, 563 P.3d 1131 (Alaska 2025). Because Mia has lived in Alaska her entire life, the home-state basis is satisfied without question.
B. Standard for Initial Custody Determination
Under AS 25.20.060, when there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution, and the court "shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child." The court is directed to consider all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Neither parent is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b).
The best interests factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form one; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence of substance abuse affecting the child's well-being; and other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(c)(1)-(9).
The court may also award shared custody if it determines that shared custody is in the best interests of the child, and any such award "shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible." AS 25.20.060(c).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. This Court Has Subject Matter Jurisdiction to Enter an Initial Custody Order
Alaska is Mia's home state for purposes of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act as adopted in Alaska. AS 25.30.300(a)(1) confers jurisdiction on this Court when "this state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding." Mia has resided continuously in Anchorage, Alaska since her birth in November 2021. She has never resided in any other state. Accordingly, Alaska is unequivocally her home state, and this Court possesses subject matter jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that subject matter jurisdiction under the UCCJEA is a threshold requirement and that a court without such jurisdiction is without power to decide a custody case. Dawn Maynor, f/k/a Dawn Golden v. Timothy B. Golden, 563 P.3d 1131 (Alaska 2025). Here, that threshold is plainly satisfied. No court of any other state has ever exercised jurisdiction over Mia's custody, and no competing proceeding exists anywhere. Because AS 25.30.300(b) makes the grounds enumerated in subsection (a) the exclusive basis for jurisdiction, and because subsection (a)(1) is clearly met, this Court should proceed to the merits of Petitioner's custody petition without hesitation.
Moreover, because no prior custody order has ever been entered, there is no question of modification and no requirement that Petitioner demonstrate a change in circumstances. The Court's task is simply to conduct an initial best-interests analysis and enter an appropriate order. Once this Court enters a custody determination, it will retain exclusive, continuing jurisdiction pursuant to AS 25.30.310, unless and until the specific conditions for loss of that jurisdiction are met.
B. The Best Interests of Mia Require a Formal Custody Order Providing for Meaningful Parental Contact with Petitioner
1. The Statutory Best Interests Factors Support Petitioner's Request
The governing statute requires this Court to determine custody in accordance with the best interests of the child after considering all relevant factors listed in AS 25.24.150(c). The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently applied these factors in initial custody proceedings involving unmarried parents. Smith v. Weekley, 73 P.3d 1219 (Alaska 2003).
With respect to the first factor, Mia's physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs are best served by stability and continuity in Anchorage, where she has lived her entire life, and by the preservation of her relationship with both parents. AS 25.24.150(c)(1). Uprooting a child less than two years out of infancy, before any court order exists to regulate the transition, risks serious disruption to her developmental well-being.
With respect to the second factor, Tomas has demonstrated both the capability and desire to meet Mia's needs. AS 25.24.150(c)(2). Despite the absence of any court order, he has consistently sought informal parenting time and has now taken the affirmative step of petitioning this Court, demonstrating his commitment to responsible co-parenting. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of each parent's demonstrated desire and ability to care for a child in the initial custody calculus. Nancy M. v. John M., 308 P.3d 1130 (Alaska 2013).
With respect to the fifth factor, Mia has spent her entire life in a relatively stable environment in Anchorage. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). The desirability of maintaining that continuity weighs in favor of an order that keeps Mia connected to Anchorage and to both parents, rather than permitting a unilateral relocation that would sever her established ties.
With respect to the sixth factor, the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent is central to this case. AS 25.24.150(c)(6). Jennifer's unilateral announcement of an intended relocation, without seeking the Court's input or obtaining Petitioner's agreement, raises legitimate concerns about her disposition to support Mia's relationship with her father. The Alaska Supreme Court has treated one parent's willingness to foster the child's relationship with the other parent as a significant consideration in custody determinations. Nancy M. v. John M., 308 P.3d 1130 (Alaska 2013).
2. Shared or Meaningful Physical Custody Is in Mia's Best Interests
Petitioner requests that this Court consider an award of shared physical custody or, in the alternative, a primary physical custody arrangement that provides Petitioner with substantial, regularly scheduled parenting time. AS 25.20.060(c) provides that the court may award shared custody to both parents if such an arrangement is in the child's best interests, and that any such award "shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible."
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that frequent and continuing contact with both parents is a fundamental objective of Alaska custody law, and that courts must craft parenting schedules designed to achieve that objective in light of all relevant circumstances. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018). In that case, the court approved a week-on, week-off schedule as an initial arrangement consistent with equal parenting time, illustrating that the default orientation of Alaska law is toward maximizing each parent's involvement in the child's life.
Here, an arrangement that provides Tomas with structured, enforceable, and regularly scheduled parenting time is essential. The current informal, week-to-week negotiation has proven unreliable and leaves Tomas without any legal recourse when Jennifer declines to honor an agreed schedule. A formal order establishing specific custody and visitation rights will provide Mia with the consistency and predictability that serve her developmental best interests.
3. Joint Legal Custody Is Appropriate to Ensure Both Parents Participate in Major Decisions
Petitioner also requests joint legal custody, which would require both parents to participate in major decisions affecting Mia's education, healthcare, and general welfare. Joint legal custody reflects the principle that both parents have a right and a responsibility to be involved in the upbringing of their child, and it is consistent with the general policy of Alaska law favoring the involvement of both parents in a child's life. AS 25.20.060; AS 25.24.150(c)(2).
The Court should be mindful that in awarding custody, it "may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child." AS 25.24.150(d). Accordingly, the Court's focus should remain on Mia's needs and interests throughout its analysis, rather than on the grievances either parent may harbor against the other arising from the breakdown of their relationship.
C. Petitioner Is Entitled to an Order Establishing Child Support in Accordance with the Guidelines
In addition to a custody determination, Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court enter a child support order calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award in a primary physical custody case is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage specified in that rule. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), if the Court awards shared physical custody, a different calculation applies that accounts for the percentage of time each parent will have physical custody of the child and the income of each parent.
Because no child support order has ever been entered, Mia has been left without a legally enforceable financial safety net. Regardless of which custodial arrangement the Court determines to be in Mia's best interests, entry of a child support order consistent with the guidelines is necessary and appropriate. The Court should direct the parties to provide verified financial disclosure so that the applicable guideline amount may be calculated.
D. The Court Should Appoint a Guardian Ad Litem to Represent Mia's Best Interests
Given that Mia is a young child who cannot advocate for herself and given the complexity of the issues presented, including the proposed relocation, Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court consider appointing a guardian ad litem to represent Mia's best interests in these proceedings. Civil Rule 90.7(e) provides that "the guardian ad litem shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child" and that the guardian ad litem "shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes, except as otherwise provided in this rule."
A guardian ad litem would be well positioned to conduct an independent factual investigation, evaluate the proposed relocation, assess the parenting abilities of each party, and advocate for the outcome most beneficial to Mia. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the important role guardians ad litem play in contested custody proceedings involving young children. E.H. v. State, Department of Health and Social Services, Division of Family and Youth Services, 23 P.3d 1186 (Alaska 2001).
Alternatively or in addition, the Court may wish to appoint a neutral custody investigator or an independent expert witness pursuant to Alaska R. Evid. 706(a), which provides that "the court may on its own motion or on the motion of any party enter an order to show cause why expert witnesses should not be appointed." A custody investigator would be able to provide the Court with an expert opinion on the custody arrangement that is in Mia's best interests, particularly in light of the proposed relocation to Juneau.
E. Petitioner Has Standing to Seek an Initial Custody Determination Under Alaska Law
As Mia's biological father, Tomas Petrova has standing to petition this Court for a custody determination under AS 25.20.060(a), which provides that "if there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the matter." AS 25.20.060(b) further provides that "neither parent, regardless of the question of the child's legitimacy, is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody." Accordingly, Tomas stands on equal legal footing with Jennifer in this proceeding, and his petition should be heard and decided on the merits.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the absence of a prior custody order does not diminish either parent's standing to seek an initial determination. Layne v. Niles, 632 P.2d 234 (Alaska 1981). The lack of any existing order means that this Court starts from a blank slate and must conduct a full best-interests analysis without any presumption in favor of either parent based solely on who has been the de facto primary caregiver in the absence of a court order.
F. Jennifer's Proposed Relocation Cannot Occur Without Court Authorization in the Context of a Pending Custody Proceeding
Once this petition is filed, any attempt by Jennifer to relocate Mia to Juneau prior to the Court's resolution of this matter would be contrary to the purposes of Alaska's custody jurisdiction statutes and would risk undermining this Court's ability to enter an effective order. Under AS 25.30.310, once this Court makes a child custody determination, it retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over that determination. The filing of this petition initiates proceedings through which this Court will exercise that jurisdiction, and Jennifer should not be permitted to act unilaterally in a manner that would present the Court with a fait accompli before it has had an opportunity to rule.
To the extent Jennifer proceeds with her relocation before this Court enters an order, Petitioner reserves the right to seek enforcement of this Court's jurisdiction and any interim orders entered herein pursuant to AS 25.30.460, which sets forth the procedure for enforcement of custody determinations, including by ordering a respondent to appear with or without the child at a hearing.
Petitioner further notes that in Bruce H. v. Jennifer L., 407 P.3d 432 (Alaska 2017), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed a situation in which one parent announced an intention to relocate with the child while a custody modification motion was pending, and the court treated the relocation motion as requiring a joint evidentiary hearing alongside the pending custody motion. The same approach is warranted here: the Court should schedule a hearing at which both the initial custody determination and the proposed relocation are considered together, with both parents afforded a full opportunity to present evidence.
The Court should also be guided by Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011), which recognized the importance of stability and continuity in custody arrangements and the counterproductive effect of unnecessary litigation. A prompt initial order from this Court will serve those interests by giving both parents clear, enforceable rights and obligations, eliminating the uncertainty that has characterized the parties' co-parenting relationship since separation, and providing Mia with the stability she needs.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Tomas Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Accept jurisdiction over this initial custody proceeding pursuant to AS 25.30.300(a)(1), as Alaska is Mia's home state;
2. Schedule an evidentiary hearing at which both parties may present evidence on the best interests of the child and on Jennifer's proposed relocation to Juneau;
3. Enter an initial order awarding joint legal custody to both parents and either shared physical custody or a primary physical custody arrangement with substantial, regularly scheduled parenting time for Petitioner, as determined to be in Mia's best interests pursuant to AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150;
4. Enter a child support order calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) or Civil Rule 90.3(b), as applicable depending on the physical custody arrangement ordered;
5. Appoint a guardian ad litem to represent Mia's best interests pursuant to Civil Rule 90.7(e), and consider appointment of a neutral custody expert pursuant to Alaska R. Evid. 706(a); and
6. Enter any interim or temporary orders necessary to preserve the status quo and protect Mia's best interests pending the final hearing, including any appropriate restriction on relocation.
Petitioner submits that an initial custody order is both necessary and long overdue. Mia deserves the stability, predictability, and legal protection that only a formal court order can provide. Petitioner stands ready to cooperate fully with any investigation or process the Court deems appropriate and asks only that Mia's best interests remain the Court's paramount concern.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0043)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Petrova respectfully petitions this Court to establish a formal custody and parenting plan for his four-year-old son, Eli Petrova. Marcus and Colin Petrova were never married and ended their relationship in March 2023. Since that time, Eli has resided primarily with Marcus, while Colin has exercised informal, inconsistent parenting time without any governing court order. The informal arrangement has broken down entirely: Colin has begun taking Eli for extended, unannounced periods and refuses to communicate with Marcus regarding Eli's whereabouts, schooling, and day-to-day welfare.
Because no court order governing custody, visitation, or child support has ever been entered, Marcus now asks this Court to exercise its authority under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150 to establish a comprehensive custody and parenting plan that serves Eli's best interests, preserves continuity in his primary home environment, ensures meaningful access for both parents, and creates a clear legal framework for decisions about education, medical care, and general well-being. The absence of any formal order has left Eli vulnerable to the instability that results from Colin's unilateral, unannounced removal of the child and refusal to disclose his whereabouts. A formal parenting plan is not only appropriate under Alaska law, it is necessary to protect this child.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Petrova and Colin Petrova began a romantic relationship approximately five years ago and were never married. Their son, Eli Petrova, was born approximately four years ago. The couple separated in March 2023 following escalating disagreements regarding finances and differing parenting values. At no point before or after the separation have the parties obtained a court order addressing custody, visitation, or child support.
Since the separation, Eli has lived primarily with Marcus. Marcus has been the consistent, daily caregiver responsible for Eli's meals, medical appointments, early childhood education enrollment, and emotional stability. Colin works as a commercial fisherman, a profession characterized by irregular and often extended periods of absence from Anchorage. As a result of this schedule, Colin's parenting time has been informal and inconsistent, occurring when Colin's work permitted and arranged through ad hoc communication between the parties rather than through any structured plan.
The informal arrangement functioned, however inadequately, for a period following the separation. That arrangement has now broken down. In recent months, Colin has begun exercising what he characterizes as parenting time in a manner that is neither predictable nor communicated to Marcus. Specifically, Colin has taken Eli for extended, unannounced periods without providing Marcus any information regarding Eli's location, the identity of any adults caring for the child, or a timeline for the child's return. Colin has refused to communicate with Marcus regarding these absences, leaving Marcus without information about his son's basic safety and welfare.
Colin has also unilaterally interfered with Eli's educational enrollment by removing the child from his early childhood program for periods corresponding to Colin's unannounced possession. These disruptions have materially affected Eli's routine and developmental progress. Marcus has made repeated attempts to establish communication with Colin regarding a workable parenting schedule, but those efforts have been rebuffed.
Marcus now files this petition to establish formal legal custody, a structured parenting plan, and a child support order so that Eli's welfare, stability, and relationships with both parents are protected by enforceable court order.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060(a), when there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the matter, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. The statute requires the court to consider all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.933. Neither parent is entitled to a preference in custody solely on the basis of the parent's identity. AS 25.20.060(b).
The court shall determine custody in accordance with the best interests of the child, considering the nine factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c), which include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
Pending a final custody determination, AS 25.20.070 provides that, unless detrimental to the child's welfare or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) applies, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the period in which the court considers an award of custody.
Once custody is established, AS 25.20.130 provides that a parent who is not granted custody retains the same access to the child's medical, dental, school, and other records as the custodial parent.
In considering a custody petition, the Alaska Supreme Court has explained that the best-interests analysis is fact-intensive and child-centered, requiring the court to focus on the circumstances most directly bearing on the child's welfare. Geldermann v. Geldermann, 428 P.3d 477 (Alaska 2018). A parent's willingness and ability to facilitate the child's relationship with the other parent is among the most significant factors courts weigh. del Rosario v. Clare, 378 P.3d 380 (Alaska 2016). The courts have further recognized that a child's need for stability and continuity in his living environment is a weighty consideration in any custody determination. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT HAS AUTHORITY TO ESTABLISH CUSTODY AND A PARENTING PLAN UNDER AS 25.20.060 AND AS 25.24.150
AS 25.20.060(a) expressly authorizes a parent to petition the superior court for resolution of a custody dispute and directs the court to award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. This authority extends to the initial establishment of custody where no prior order exists. The statute requires the court to "consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), and the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g) under all circumstances." The court may also award shared custody under AS 25.20.968 if shared custody is determined to be in the best interests of the child, provided that any such award assures that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible.
Here, there is a genuine and material dispute over custody and parenting time. Colin's recent pattern of unannounced, extended removals of Eli from his primary home and refusal to communicate with Marcus demonstrates that the parties cannot manage Eli's upbringing cooperatively without judicial intervention. This Court has clear statutory authority and an affirmative obligation to resolve the matter.
