AS 25.24.150(c)(6) directs the Court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Jennifer's decision to inform Jacob of a planned relocation rather than to seek his input or consent in advance raises concerns about her willingness to support Olivia's relationship with her father going forward. The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a proposed move is not legitimate if it is primarily motivated by a desire to make visitation more difficult. Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011). While Jacob does not at this time allege that Jennifer's stated employment rationale is pretextual, he does note that Jennifer's failure to involve him in the decision, and her announced intention to proceed without his agreement, is relevant to this statutory factor.
By contrast, Jacob has consistently cooperated with the informal custody arrangement, has exercised his parenting time reliably, and has demonstrated a commitment to Olivia's relationship with both parents. This Court should weigh the parties' relative postures toward cooperation and parental facilitation when fashioning an initial custody order.
5. The Proposed Relocation Must Be Evaluated for Its Impact on Olivia's Best Interests Before It Is Permitted to Occur.
The proposed move from Anchorage to Fairbanks is not a trivial geographic change. It would place Olivia several hundred miles from her father, render alternating-weekend parenting time effectively impossible without substantial travel, and require a complete restructuring of any parenting plan the Court might otherwise enter. AS 25.24.150(c)(9) authorizes the Court to consider any other factors it deems pertinent to the best interests of the child, and the impact of a proposed relocation on the child's relationship with the non-relocating parent is precisely such a factor.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that in relocation cases, the trial court must evaluate whether the proposed move serves legitimate reasons and what effect it would have on the child's best interests, including the impact on the child's relationship with the parent who remains behind. Brett M. v. Amanda M., 445 P.3d 1005 (Alaska 2019); Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011). Because no custody order is currently in place, this Court has the opportunity and the obligation to conduct that analysis before, not after, a relocation takes place. Jacob respectfully requests that the Court issue an interim order preventing Jennifer from relocating Olivia outside the Anchorage area until a full evidentiary hearing on the initial custody determination has been completed.
C. OLIVIA IS ENTITLED TO EQUAL ACCESS TO BOTH PARENTS DURING THE PENDENCY OF THESE PROCEEDINGS.
While this custody determination is pending, Olivia's right to maintain contact with both parents is protected by AS 25.20.070, which provides that a child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents, absent a showing of detriment or a domestic violence presumption. There is no evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or substance abuse in this case. Both parents have cooperated informally since the separation, and no facts have been alleged that would support a finding that Jacob's continued involvement with Olivia poses any risk to her safety or well-being.
Jacob therefore requests that the Court enter an interim parenting order maintaining the existing alternating-weekend schedule at minimum, and prohibiting either parent from removing Olivia from the Anchorage area during the pendency of this proceeding, as authorized by AS 25.20.060 and consistent with AS 25.20.070.
D. THE COURT SHOULD CONSIDER APPOINTING A GUARDIAN AD LITEM TO REPRESENT OLIVIA'S BEST INTERESTS IF THE PROCEEDING PROVES UNUSUALLY COMPLEX.
Civil Rule 90.7(a) provides that in an action under AS 25.20 or AS 25.24 involving custody or visitation of a child, the Court may appoint a guardian ad litem when separate representation of the child's best interests is necessary, such as when the proceeding is unusually complex or when a guardian ad litem may be expected to present evidence not otherwise likely to be available or presented. If this proceeding develops into a contested relocation dispute with significant factual disputes regarding Olivia's needs and the impact of the proposed move, the appointment of a guardian ad litem may assist the Court in obtaining an independent perspective on what arrangement would truly serve Olivia's best interests.
Civil Rule 90.7(e) provides that the guardian ad litem "shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child" and shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes except as otherwise provided in the rule. Jacob does not insist upon such an appointment at this stage, but brings the option to the Court's attention and requests that the Court consider it if the contested nature of these proceedings warrants independent representation of Olivia's interests.
E. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE ADDRESSED CONCURRENTLY WITH THE CUSTODY DETERMINATION.
Once the Court enters a custody and parenting plan order, child support obligations should be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(b). If the Court awards shared physical custody, defined as an arrangement in which both parents have physical custody for a substantial period of time, the shared physical custody calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) applies. Jacob requests that the Court address child support concurrently with the custody order so that a comprehensive, integrated parenting plan is in place from the outset. Jacob is prepared to provide the Court with income information and any other documentation required for the child support calculation.
V. CONCLUSION
For the reasons set forth above, Jacob Larsen respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Exercise jurisdiction under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.30.310 to enter an initial legal and physical custody order governing minor child Olivia Larsen;
2. Enter an interim order during the pendency of these proceedings maintaining Olivia's current alternating-weekend parenting schedule with Jacob, consistent with AS 25.20.070, and prohibiting either parent from relocating Olivia outside the Anchorage area without prior court approval;
3. Conduct a full evidentiary hearing on the best interests of the child under AS 25.24.150(c) before any relocation of Olivia is permitted to occur;
4. Consider the appointment of a guardian ad litem under Civil Rule 90.7(a) and Civil Rule 90.7(e) if the complexity of this proceeding warrants independent representation of Olivia's best interests;
5. Enter a final custody order that establishes legal and physical custody rights for both parents, includes a detailed parenting plan that accounts for the proposed relocation and its impact on Olivia's relationship with Jacob, and serves the best interests of the child as required by AS 25.24.150; and
6. Address child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(b) concurrently with the custody determination.
Jacob Larsen respectfully submits that Olivia deserves a court-supervised process that protects her stability, preserves her relationship with both parents, and ensures that any major change to her living situation is carefully evaluated before it is permitted to occur. The Court's intervention at this stage is both appropriate and necessary.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0053)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Bergstrom respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for an initial custody determination regarding her six-year-old daughter, Maya Bergstrom. Maya has resided continuously in Eagle River, Alaska, with Priya throughout her life, and Alaska is unquestionably Maya's home state. No prior custody order has ever been entered for Maya. The parties, who were in a committed domestic partnership for approximately four years, initially hoped to resolve custody informally, but ongoing disputes over educational and medical decision-making authority, combined with Respondent Jennifer Bergstrom's announced intention to relocate to Fairbanks, have made a formal, legally binding parenting plan both necessary and urgent.
Priya seeks an initial custody order that preserves Maya's stability, clearly defines each parent's legal and physical custody rights, and establishes a workable parenting plan that accounts for a potential change in the geographic distance between the parents. This Court has subject matter jurisdiction under AS 25.30.300, and the best interests of the child standard under AS 25.24.150 and AS 25.20.060 compels the relief requested.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Bergstrom and Jennifer Bergstrom entered into a committed domestic partnership and lived together as a family in Eagle River, Alaska for approximately four years. During that relationship, their daughter Maya was born. Maya is currently six years old and has lived at the family home in Eagle River for her entire life.
In early 2023, the parties' relationship ended following irreconcilable differences. Jennifer relocated to a separate residence in Anchorage. Since the separation, Maya has continued to reside primarily with Priya at the Eagle River family home. Jennifer has exercised parenting time on an informal and inconsistent basis, but no court order has ever governed her contact with Maya or defined either parent's decision-making authority.
For a period following the separation, the parties believed they could reach a private co-parenting agreement and therefore did not seek court intervention. That effort has proved unsuccessful. The parties have experienced persistent and unresolved disputes regarding Maya's schooling, including which school Maya should attend and what educational services she requires, as well as disputes regarding consent for medical care. These disputes have occurred without any legal framework to resolve them, placing Maya in a position of uncertainty and exposing Priya to repeated challenges to her parenting decisions.
More recently, Jennifer has announced her intention to move to Fairbanks, Alaska for a new employment opportunity. This prospective relocation would place the parents at a significantly greater geographic distance from one another and would fundamentally alter any informal parenting arrangement the parties have attempted to maintain. Without a formal custody order in place, Jennifer's relocation would leave Maya's living situation, schedule, and welfare entirely undefined and unprotected by law.
Priya now petitions this Court for an initial custody determination establishing a formal parenting plan that reflects Maya's best interests, preserves her stability and continuity of care, and provides each parent with clearly defined rights and responsibilities.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Subject Matter Jurisdiction
Before making any custody determination, this Court must satisfy itself that it possesses subject matter jurisdiction. Under AS 25.30.300(a), a court of this state has jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination if, among other bases, this state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding. AS 25.30.300(b) provides that the provisions of AS 25.30.300(a) are the exclusive jurisdictional bases for making a child custody determination by a court of this state. As the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Jayda Roman v. Cleveland Karren, 461 P.3d 1252 (Alaska 2020), and reaffirmed in Dawn Maynor, f/k/a Dawn Golden v. Timothy B. Golden, 563 P.3d 1131 (Alaska 2025), the superior court may make an initial custody determination only if it possesses subject matter jurisdiction under at least one of the statutory provisions in AS 25.30.300.
B. Standard for Initial Custody Determinations
Under AS 25.20.060(a), if there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the matter. The court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. In determining the best interests of the child, the court shall consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), and the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g).
Alaska Statute 25.24.150(c) sets forth the specific factors the court must consider in any custody determination, including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
AS 25.24.150(d) further provides that in awarding custody the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child. Neither parent is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b).
The court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined by the court to be in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.060(c). An award of shared custody shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Id.
As the Alaska Supreme Court explained in Smith v. Weekley, 73 P.3d 1219 (Alaska 2003), both initial and final custody determinations require full consideration of the statutory best interests factors, and no single factor is presumptively controlling. The court in Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), further underscored that the trial court must weigh each statutory factor on the evidence before it and that stability and continuity of environment are meaningful considerations in that analysis.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. This Court Has Subject Matter Jurisdiction to Enter an Initial Custody Order for Maya.
Alaska is Maya's home state within the meaning of AS 25.30.300(a)(1). Maya is six years old and has lived continuously at the family home in Eagle River, Alaska for her entire life. No other state has any jurisdictional claim over Maya. Both parents reside in Alaska, Priya in Eagle River and Jennifer currently in Anchorage. No court of any other state has ever entered a custody order or commenced a custody proceeding with respect to Maya.
Because Alaska is Maya's home state on the date this proceeding commences, this Court has subject matter jurisdiction under AS 25.30.300(a)(1). AS 25.30.300(c) further clarifies that physical presence of or personal jurisdiction over a party or a child is not necessary or sufficient to make a child custody determination, but the facts here present no personal jurisdiction concerns: both parties are Alaska residents.
Because no prior custody determination has ever been made, there is no issue of exclusive continuing jurisdiction under AS 25.30.310. This is purely an initial custody determination, and jurisdiction is properly established in this Court.
B. The Best Interests of Maya Require a Formal Initial Custody Order.
1. Maya's Physical, Emotional, and Social Stability Weigh Heavily in Favor of Formalizing Priya's Primary Caregiving Role.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(1), the court must consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Under AS 25.24.150(c)(5), the court must consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity.
Maya is six years old and has lived at the Eagle River family home with Priya for her entire life. Priya has been Maya's primary caregiver since birth. Maya has established roots in her community, including her school, her neighborhood, and her social relationships, all of which are centered in Eagle River. Disrupting that environment without a formal legal framework to protect it would be contrary to Maya's best interests.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), illustrates that courts must take seriously the impact of parental relocation and geographic distance on a child's established routine. Here, Jennifer's announced move to Fairbanks would create a substantial geographic separation between the parents, making a clear, court-ordered parenting plan indispensable to Maya's continued stability.
2. The Parties' Ongoing Disputes Over Educational and Medical Decision-Making Demonstrate the Need for a Defined Legal Custody Framework.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(2), the court must consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet Maya's needs. Under AS 25.24.150(c)(9), the court may consider other factors that it deems pertinent.
The absence of any custody order has left Priya and Jennifer without any legal mechanism to resolve their recurring disagreements about Maya's schooling and medical care. These are not trivial disputes. Decisions about which school a child attends and what medical treatment a child receives are among the most significant decisions in a child's life. Without a clear allocation of legal custody authority, these conflicts will continue to recur, to Maya's detriment.
A formal custody order that clearly delineates legal decision-making authority is the appropriate remedy. Priya, as Maya's primary residential parent and day-to-day caregiver, is best positioned to make timely decisions on Maya's behalf. The court should consider awarding Priya primary physical custody and either sole or primary legal custody with defined consultation rights for Jennifer, depending on the evidence presented.
3. Both Parents' Willingness to Facilitate a Relationship with the Other Parent Must Be Assessed on the Record.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the court must consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. AS 25.20.060(c) further provides that any shared custody award shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible.
Priya does not seek to eliminate Jennifer's relationship with Maya. Jennifer is Maya's parent, and Maya's relationship with Jennifer is important to Maya's well-being. However, Jennifer's parenting time has been informal and inconsistent since the separation. A formal parenting plan, entered by this Court, will provide the structure necessary to ensure that Jennifer's contact with Maya is meaningful, regular, and predictable, even in the event of Jennifer's relocation to Fairbanks.
If Jennifer does relocate to Fairbanks, a parenting plan will need to account for the logistical realities of long-distance co-parenting, including defined holiday, school-break, and summer parenting periods for Jennifer, as well as regular telephonic and electronic contact. As recognized by the Alaska Supreme Court in Rosemarie P. v. Kelly B., 504 P.3d 260 (Alaska 2021), the court has broad authority to fashion a custody and visitation arrangement tailored to the specific circumstances of the parties and the needs of the child.
4. No Domestic Violence, Substance Abuse, or Child Safety Concerns Preclude a Standard Best Interests Analysis.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(7), the court must consider any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect in the proposed custodial household or a history of violence between the parents. Under AS 25.24.150(c)(8), the court must consider evidence that substance abuse by either parent or other members of the household directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child.
Priya is not aware of any basis to invoke the rebuttable presumption against custody under AS 25.24.150(g). There is no history of domestic violence between the parties, no allegations of child abuse or neglect, and no substance abuse issues affecting either household. The court's analysis therefore proceeds under a standard best interests framework, with no statutory presumption limiting the range of available custody arrangements.
C. The Court Should Enter a Parenting Plan That Provides Clarity and Protects Maya's Best Interests in Light of Jennifer's Anticipated Relocation.
The combination of unresolved legal custody disputes and Jennifer's announced intent to move to Fairbanks makes the entry of a formal parenting plan urgent. Under AS 25.20.060(a), this Court has full authority to resolve the custody dispute between these parties and to award custody on the basis of Maya's best interests. Under AS 25.24.150(a), the court may make an order for custody or visitation that may seem necessary or proper, including any order that provides for visitation by any person if that is in the best interests of the child.
Priya respectfully requests that the Court enter an initial custody order that provides:
First, that Priya shall have primary physical custody of Maya, reflecting the continuity and stability of Maya's existing home environment in Eagle River.
Second, that the parties shall share legal custody on a joint basis with a defined tie-breaking mechanism, or in the alternative, that Priya shall have primary legal custody with a requirement that she consult Jennifer on major decisions, given the parties' demonstrated inability to reach agreement on their own.
Third, that Jennifer shall have defined parenting time on a regular schedule, structured to account for any relocation to Fairbanks, including extended parenting periods during school breaks and summers, consistent with Maya's best interests and the requirements of AS 25.20.060(c).
Fourth, that the order shall include provisions for regular telephonic and electronic contact between Maya and Jennifer during periods when Jennifer does not have physical custody, in order to preserve and strengthen their relationship.
D. Child Support Should Be Calculated in Accordance with the Applicable Guidelines.
To the extent the Court enters a primary physical custody order in favor of Priya, child support should be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), using Jennifer's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage under that rule. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), a parent has primary physical custody for purposes of the support guidelines if the children reside with the other parent for a period specified in the custody order of less than 30 percent of the year.
If the parties are awarded a shared physical custody arrangement under which Maya resides with each parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year, child support should be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(b), which provides the formula applicable to shared custody situations.
V. CONCLUSION
Maya is six years old, has lived her entire life in Eagle River, Alaska, and depends on the stability and continuity that Priya has provided throughout her life. The absence of a formal custody order has left Maya's welfare subject to the parties' ongoing, unresolved disputes over education and medical care, and Jennifer's forthcoming relocation to Fairbanks will only deepen the need for a clear legal framework governing Maya's care.
This Court has subject matter jurisdiction under AS 25.30.300(a)(1) because Alaska is Maya's home state. The best interests factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.060(a) support the entry of an initial custody order that awards Priya primary physical custody, establishes a clear legal decision-making structure, and provides Jennifer with defined and meaningful parenting time consistent with Maya's best interests and the demands of geographic distance.
Priya respectfully requests that this Court enter an initial custody and parenting plan order as set forth herein, and for such other and further relief as the Court deems just and appropriate under the circumstances.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0054)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Colby brings this petition to establish custody, visitation, and child support for the parties' minor child, Rowan Colby, age three. The parties were never married and have never obtained a court order addressing parental rights or responsibilities with respect to Rowan. Since the parties separated in March 2024, Rowan has resided primarily with Danielle Colby in Anchorage, while Elena Colby has exercised informal parenting time without any enforceable structure. The urgency of this petition arises from Danielle Colby's stated intention to relocate with Rowan to Fairbanks within approximately 60 days to accept new employment, a unilateral move that would substantially diminish Elena Colby's parenting time and sever the child's existing community ties. No formal arrangement has been established, leaving both parents without enforceable rights and, more importantly, leaving Rowan without the legal protections and stability that a court order provides.
Elena Colby respectfully asks this Court to exercise its authority under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150 to establish legal and physical custody, a structured parenting plan, and appropriate child support calculated under Civil Rule 90.3. Elena further requests that this Court issue a temporary order restraining the proposed relocation until a full evidentiary hearing can be conducted, and that the Court appoint a guardian ad litem to represent Rowan's best interests given the child's young age and the significant consequences of a potential relocation.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Colby and Danielle Colby were in a romantic partnership for approximately two years. During that relationship, the parties jointly welcomed Rowan Colby, now three years old, into their family. The couple separated in March 2024 following a period of escalating conflict over finances and differing views on child-rearing. Since the separation, Rowan has lived primarily at Danielle Colby's Anchorage apartment.
Following the separation, the parties arranged parenting time informally and without court involvement. Elena Colby has exercised parenting time with Rowan approximately two to three times per week. This arrangement has been entirely voluntary and unenforceable, leaving Elena without any legal mechanism to protect her parenting relationship should Danielle refuse access at any time. No temporary or permanent court order has ever addressed custody, visitation, or child support for Rowan.
The immediate trigger for this petition is Danielle Colby's recent notice to Elena that she intends to relocate with Rowan to Fairbanks within 60 days to accept new employment. Fairbanks is located approximately 360 miles north of Anchorage. If Danielle relocates with Rowan before a court order is in place, Elena Colby will have no enforceable legal right to continued parenting time, no mechanism to object to the relocation, and no framework within which to seek modification. Rowan, who is only three years old, is at a critical developmental stage in which consistent, frequent contact with both parents is essential to the child's emotional and social well-being. Elena Colby files this petition to establish her parental rights, protect her relationship with Rowan, and ensure that any residential arrangement serves Rowan's best interests as determined by this Court.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Jurisdiction and Authority to Establish Custody
Under AS 25.20.060(a), either parent may petition the Superior Court for resolution of a custody dispute, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. The statute directs the court to consider all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), and to apply the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g). Neither parent is entitled to a preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b).
B. Best Interests of the Child Standard
The governing standard in all custody determinations is the best interests of the child. AS 25.24.150(c) sets forth the factors the court must consider, including: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence of substance abuse; and other pertinent factors. The court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child. AS 25.24.150(d).
The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that trial courts must conduct a thorough, individualized analysis of the statutory best-interests factors and must support their custody determinations with findings that address the relevant considerations. Blanton v. Yourkowski, 180 P.3d 948 (Alaska 2008). The court's overriding obligation is to the child's welfare, not to the preferences or convenience of either parent. Littleton v. Banks, 192 P.3d 154 (Alaska 2008).
C. Shared Custody Considerations
The court may award shared custody if it determines that shared custody is in the best interests of the child, and an award of shared custody shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c). In evaluating whether to award shared custody, the court shall consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, including the child's needs, the stability of the home environment each parent is likely to offer, the education of the child, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, including the actual time spent with each parent, the proximity of the parents to each other and to the child's school, the feasibility of travel, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. AS 25.20.090.
For purposes of child support calculation, shared physical custody exists when a child resides with a parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year as specified in the custody order. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1). Primary physical custody exists when the child resides with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2).
D. Relocation Jurisprudence
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that relocation cases require careful analysis because they pit one parent's freedom to move against the other parent's right to maintain a meaningful parenting relationship, and both must be evaluated through the lens of the child's best interests. Saffir v. Wheeler, 436 P.3d 1009 (Alaska 2019). A court may order alternative custody arrangements that are contingent on whether a proposed relocation occurs. Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011). The desirability of maintaining continuity in the child's current environment is a statutory best-interests factor that courts must weigh when a relocation is proposed. AS 25.24.150(c)(5).
E. Child Support
Child support shall be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), when one parent has primary physical custody, support is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: 20 percent for one child. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). Where the parents have shared physical custody, support is calculated under the shared custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 958(b). The court may vary the support award for good cause upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result if the award were not varied. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1). The minimum child support amount is $50 per month. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(3).
F. Guardian Ad Litem
Under AS 25.24.310(c), the court may appoint an attorney or other person as guardian ad litem to provide guardian ad litem services to a child in legal proceedings involving the child's welfare. The court shall require a guardian ad litem when representation of the child's best interests would serve the welfare of the child. Under Civil Rule 942(e), the guardian ad litem shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child and shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes except as otherwise provided by the rule.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THIS COURT HAS AUTHORITY AND AN OBLIGATION TO ESTABLISH A FORMAL CUSTODY ORDER FOR ROWAN COLBY
Because no prior court order has addressed custody, visitation, or child support for Rowan Colby, this matter comes before the Court as an initial custody determination. AS 25.20.060(a) expressly authorizes either parent to petition the Superior Court for resolution of a custody dispute, and the statute places the Court under an obligation to award custody based on the best interests of the child. AS 25.24.150(c) directs the court to consider all relevant statutory factors in reaching that determination.
The absence of any existing order means there is no threshold change-of-circumstances requirement to satisfy before the Court may act. The modification standard of AS 25.20.110 applies only when a prior custody order already exists. Here, there is no such order. The Court should therefore proceed directly to a best-interests analysis and establish a formal custody arrangement, parenting plan, and child support order. Establishing these rights promptly is particularly urgent given Danielle Colby's announced intention to relocate to Fairbanks within 60 days, a timeline that could render Elena Colby's parental access unenforceable before any order is in place.
B. THE STATUTORY BEST-INTERESTS FACTORS UNDER AS 25.24.150(c) SUPPORT A SHARED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT WITH SIGNIFICANT PARENTING TIME FOR ELENA COLBY
1. Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs of the Child
Rowan Colby is three years old, an age at which the child's attachment to both parents is foundational to healthy emotional and psychological development. The first statutory factor requires the Court to consider "the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child." AS 25.24.150(c)(1). Rowan's needs at this developmental stage are best served by consistent, predictable, and frequent access to both parents. Elena Colby has been actively engaged in Rowan's care, exercising parenting time two to three times per week since the separation, and her continued involvement serves the child's emotional and social needs.
2. Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Child's Needs
The second factor addresses "the capability and desire of each parent to meet these needs." AS 25.24.150(c)(2). Elena Colby has demonstrated both the capability and the strong desire to meet Rowan's needs by maintaining consistent informal parenting time throughout the post-separation period. Her consistent presence reflects the kind of parental commitment that the Alaska Supreme Court has recognized as relevant to custody determinations. Littleton v. Banks, 192 P.3d 154 (Alaska 2008).
3. Love and Affection Between the Child and Each Parent
The fourth statutory factor, "the love and affection existing between the child and each parent," AS 25.24.150(c)(4), supports a custody arrangement that preserves Rowan's bond with both parents. Rowan has an established, loving relationship with Elena Colby developed through regular contact since birth. Any arrangement that severely curtails Elena's access will damage that bond and harm the child's well-being.
4. Stability and Continuity in the Child's Current Environment
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(5), the Court must consider "the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity." Rowan has spent the entirety of the child's three years in the Anchorage community. The child's medical providers, social environment, and extended family connections are rooted in Anchorage. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized that continuity of environment is a weighty factor in the best-interests analysis. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018). The proposed relocation to Fairbanks would sever those community ties and disrupt Rowan's established, stable environment without any demonstrated benefit to the child.
5. Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Child
The sixth statutory factor requires the Court to consider "the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child." AS 25.24.150(c)(6). Elena Colby is committed to supporting Rowan's relationship with Danielle Colby. By contrast, Danielle Colby's unilateral announcement of a relocation on a compressed 60-day timeline, with no apparent effort to negotiate a revised parenting arrangement, raises concerns about her willingness to support Elena's parenting relationship with Rowan. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that the willingness of each parent to support the other's relationship with the child is a significant consideration in custody decisions. Dd v. Lah, 27 P.3d 757 (Alaska 2001).
6. The Additional Shared Custody Factors Under AS 25.20.090
Because Elena Colby seeks shared physical custody, the Court must also consider the factors set forth in AS 25.20.090. The most significant of those factors in this case are the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, AS 25.20.090(5); the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, AS 25.20.090(3); and the feasibility of travel between the parents, AS 25.20.090(6)(C). Rowan is currently rooted in Anchorage. The distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks (approximately 360 miles) makes frequent exchanges difficult and costly, which further counsels in favor of retaining Rowan in the Anchorage community and establishing a parenting schedule that permits Elena Colby to exercise meaningful parenting time without requiring young Rowan to endure frequent long-distance travel.
C. THIS COURT SHOULD ISSUE A TEMPORARY ORDER RESTRAINING RELOCATION PENDING A FULL EVIDENTIARY HEARING
The urgency of Danielle Colby's announced 60-day relocation timeline compels this Court to act on a temporary basis to preserve the status quo and protect Rowan's connections to Elena Colby and to the Anchorage community. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts have authority to issue alternative custody arrangements dependent on whether a proposed relocation occurs, and that the possibility that a court's decision may influence a parent's choice to move does not justify a refusal to act. Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011). Similarly, the Court in Saffir v. Wheeler, 436 P.3d 1009 (Alaska 2019), recognized the tension between parental mobility and a child's interest in continuity of relationships, a tension that must be resolved through a careful best-interests analysis.
Without a temporary order, Danielle Colby may relocate with Rowan before this Court can conduct a full hearing, leaving Elena Colby without any enforceable parenting time and forcing her to litigate modification from a position of fait accompli rather than from the current status quo. This result would undermine the integrity of the judicial process and harm Rowan by abruptly severing the child's established relationship with Elena Colby. Elena respectfully asks this Court to issue a temporary order: (1) directing that Rowan not be relocated outside the Anchorage area pending a full hearing; (2) formalizing Elena Colby's current parenting time on a structured basis in the interim; and (3) setting this matter for an expedited evidentiary hearing on permanent custody.
D. A FORMAL CHILD SUPPORT ORDER MUST BE ESTABLISHED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3
No child support order has ever been entered for Rowan Colby. This Court must establish a child support obligation in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. The applicable formula depends on the custody arrangement the Court ultimately orders.
If the Court awards primary physical custody to one parent, child support shall be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage. For one child, that percentage is 20 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). "Adjusted annual income" as used in Civil Rule 90.3 means the parent's total income from all sources minus the mandatory and permissible deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including mandatory taxes, union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, voluntary retirement contributions within the specified cap, prior child or spousal support obligations, work-related child care expenses, and qualifying health and life insurance premiums.
If the Court awards shared physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), meaning the child resides with each parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year, the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b) shall apply. That formula requires calculating what each parent would owe the other under the primary custody formula, multiplying each figure by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and then calculating the net obligation with the 1.5 multiplier as specified in Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(C).
In either case, the minimum support award is $50 per month. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(3). If the Court finds that the formula produces a result that would constitute manifest injustice, it may vary the award for good cause upon proof by clear and convincing evidence. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1). Elena Colby requests that both parties be required to submit verified income documentation so that the Court can calculate the appropriate support amount at the evidentiary hearing.
E. THE COURT SHOULD APPOINT A GUARDIAN AD LITEM TO REPRESENT ROWAN'S BEST INTERESTS
Rowan Colby is three years old and cannot articulate personal preferences or independently advocate for the parenting arrangement that best serves the child's needs. Under AS 25.24.310(c), this Court may appoint a guardian ad litem whenever, in the opinion of the court, representation of the child's best interests would serve the child's welfare. Civil Rule 90.7(e) provides that the guardian ad litem shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child and shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes except as otherwise specified.
The stakes of this proceeding are high: the Court is being asked to make an initial custody determination for a very young child in the context of a proposed cross-community relocation with significant consequences for Rowan's long-term stability and parental relationships. The complexity of the relocation issue, combined with Rowan's age and inability to express preferences, makes the appointment of a guardian ad litem particularly appropriate. The guardian ad litem can independently investigate Rowan's living conditions, attachment relationships, and the potential impact of relocation, and can present findings to the Court that are focused exclusively on the child's welfare rather than on either parent's litigation position.
Elena Colby respectfully urges the Court to appoint a guardian ad litem at the outset of these proceedings and to define the scope of the appointment to include investigation of both the custody and relocation questions, consistent with the authorization provided by AS 25.24.310(c) and Civil Rule 90.7(e).
F. THE COURT SHOULD CONDUCT AN INFORMAL TRIAL CONSISTENT WITH CIVIL RULE 16.2(e)
If the parties are unable to reach a negotiated resolution, this Court should set the matter for an informal trial consistent with Civil Rule 16.2(e). Under that rule, the court will request a summary of issues from each party, receive sworn testimony from each party, allow each party to offer relevant documents and other evidence, consider expert reports, and provide each party with an opportunity for closing argument. Civil Rule 16.2(e)(1)-(5). The informal trial process is particularly well-suited to an initial custody determination involving a single minor child, where the relevant facts can be efficiently presented through direct party testimony and documentary exhibits.
If the parties seek expert testimony regarding Rowan's developmental needs, parenting capacity, or the impact of relocation, either party may request, or the Court may on its own motion order, the appointment of an expert witness pursuant to Alaska R. Evid. 706(a). A court-appointed expert can advise the parties of the expert's findings, submit to deposition, and testify at the court's request or at the request of any party.
V. CONCLUSION
Elena Colby respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Accept jurisdiction and proceed to an initial best-interests determination under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150 to establish legal custody, physical custody, and a structured parenting plan for Rowan Colby;
2. Issue a temporary order restraining Danielle Colby from relocating Rowan outside the Anchorage area pending a full evidentiary hearing, and formalizing Elena Colby's current parenting time on an interim structured basis;
3. Set this matter for an expedited evidentiary hearing, utilizing the informal trial procedures of Civil Rule 16.2(e);
4. Award shared physical custody to both parties in a manner that ensures Rowan has frequent and continuing contact with Elena Colby consistent with AS 25.20.060(c) and the shared custody factors under AS 25.20.090, or, in the alternative, award primary physical custody to the parent whose home best serves Rowan's best interests with appropriate parenting time to the other parent;
5. Establish a child support order calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) or Civil Rule 90.3(b), as appropriate to the custody arrangement ordered, with a floor of no less than $50 per month as required by Civil Rule 90.3(c)(3);
6. Appoint a guardian ad litem pursuant to AS 25.24.310(c) and Civil Rule 90.7(e) to independently investigate and advocate for Rowan's best interests throughout these proceedings; and
7. Grant such other relief as this Court deems just and proper in Rowan's best interests.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0055)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Nakamura respectfully petitions this Court to establish legal and physical custody of his two-year-old daughter, Mia Nakamura. David and Colin Nakamura were never married but maintained a committed relationship for four years before separating in early 2023. Since the separation, Mia has resided primarily with David at his home in Anchorage, while Colin has exercised informal, inconsistent parenting time from his apartment in Fairbanks. No formal custody order has ever been entered.
The absence of a court order has now created a dangerous void. Colin has begun making unilateral decisions about Mia's medical care during visits and has threatened to retain Mia in Fairbanks indefinitely. David has no legal mechanism to compel her return. This Court should act promptly to establish a formal custody arrangement that protects Mia's safety, preserves her stability in the home where she has spent her entire life, and ensures that both parents exercise well-defined rights and responsibilities. The best interests of the child compel this result.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Nakamura and Colin Nakamura are the parents of Mia Nakamura, born approximately two years ago. The parties were never married. They maintained a committed relationship for approximately four years before separating in early 2023. The separation followed a prolonged period of conflict caused in significant part by Colin's decision to relocate to Fairbanks for employment, and by the parties' growing inability to co-parent cooperatively.
Since the separation, Mia has lived primarily with David at his residence in Anchorage. David has served as Mia's primary caregiver for essentially the entirety of her life. He manages her daily routines, attends her medical appointments, and provides a stable, consistent home environment. Colin rents an apartment in Fairbanks, approximately 360 miles from Anchorage. His contact with Mia has been informal and inconsistent, arranged through occasional text messages with no agreed schedule, no predictable visitation plan, and no enforceable parameters.
The parties initially believed they could manage the arrangement without court involvement. That belief has proven unfounded. During recent visits, Colin has made unilateral decisions regarding Mia's medical care without consulting David, despite David's role as her primary caregiver and his historical management of her health needs. More seriously, Colin has threatened to keep Mia in Fairbanks indefinitely. David has no existing court order that would allow him to demand Mia's return, leave him with a legal basis to involve law enforcement, or otherwise protect against an improper retention of the child.
David now petitions this Court for an order establishing sole legal custody in David, primary physical custody in David, and a structured parenting schedule for Colin that accounts for the geographic distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks. David seeks a formal order that will protect Mia's stability and welfare, define each parent's rights and responsibilities, and prevent future unilateral action by either party.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court with jurisdiction may make, modify, or vacate an order for the custody of or visitation with a minor child as may seem necessary or proper. AS 25.24.150(a). Where no prior order exists, the court proceeds to an initial custody determination guided entirely by the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.060(a).
In making that determination, the court considers all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Those statutory factors include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference, if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child; and other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(c).
Neither parent is entitled to a preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b). The court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.060(a).
The court may also award shared custody if that arrangement is determined to be in the best interests of the child, and any such award must assure frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c). However, where shared legal custody is contemplated, the ability of the parties to cooperate and communicate is a central consideration. Peterson v. Swarthout, 214 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2009).
Additionally, unless doing so would be detrimental to the child's welfare or the domestic violence presumption applies, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during any period in which the court considers an award of custody. AS 25.20.070.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH SOLE LEGAL CUSTODY IN DAVID NAKAMURA BECAUSE THE PARTIES ARE UNABLE TO COMMUNICATE AND COOPERATE IN MIA'S BEST INTERESTS.
Alaska law recognizes that legal custody governs the right and responsibility to make major decisions affecting a child's life, including decisions regarding medical care, education, and general welfare. While joint legal custody is generally preferred in Alaska, it is appropriate only when the parents are capable of cooperating and communicating in the child's best interest. Peterson v. Swarthout, 214 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2009); AS 25.20.060(a).
The record in this case demonstrates that the parties cannot meet that standard. Colin has already begun making unilateral medical decisions during Mia's visits, without David's knowledge or consent. This conduct directly undermines the cooperative framework that joint legal custody requires. In Peterson v. Swarthout, 214 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2009), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that sustained noncooperation by one parent may constitute grounds for modifying or withholding joint legal custody. Similarly, in Collier v. Harris, 377 P.3d 14 (Alaska 2016), the court acknowledged that a parent's inability to communicate effectively with the other parent weighs heavily against joint legal custody.
Here, the parties have never operated under a formal legal custody arrangement. The absence of any written or judicial agreement, the breakdown in communication to text-message-only contact, and Colin's recent unilateral conduct with respect to medical care all confirm that the parties lack the cooperative relationship necessary for joint legal custody to function. Awarding sole legal custody to David, who has served as Mia's primary caregiver throughout her life and who has historically managed her medical and developmental needs, is in Mia's best interests. AS 25.24.150(c)(1), (2).
B. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY TO DAVID NAKAMURA BECAUSE MIA HAS LIVED IN A STABLE, CONTINUOUS HOME ENVIRONMENT WITH DAVID SINCE BIRTH.
One of the central factors in an Alaska best-interests analysis is the length of time a child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity in that environment. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Mia is two years old. She has lived with David in Anchorage for essentially her entire life. David manages her daily care, her medical appointments, and her developmental routines. Disrupting that arrangement would undermine precisely the kind of stability and continuity the statute protects.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized the importance of avoiding unnecessary disruptions to a child's established environment. In Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), the court recognized that custody arrangements must account for geographic realities and the practical logistics of a child's life. Colin resides in Fairbanks, approximately 360 miles from Mia's established home. Requiring a two-year-old child to split time equally between two cities that far apart would impose significant disruption, travel burden, and instability on a child who is too young to navigate such transitions without harm.
The statutory factors further support primary custody in David. AS 25.24.150(c)(1) directs the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, and social needs of the child. A two-year-old child has a profound need for consistency in caregiving, routine, and environment. David has provided that consistency. AS 25.24.150(c)(2) asks the court to assess the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. David has demonstrated that capability through two years of primary caregiving. Colin's involvement, while not without value, has been informal, inconsistent, and geographically remote.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) directs the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. David has allowed Colin access to Mia throughout the separation, notwithstanding the lack of any formal arrangement. Colin, by contrast, has made unilateral medical decisions and threatened to retain Mia in Fairbanks, conduct that reflects a willingness to obstruct rather than facilitate David's relationship with the child.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), a parent has primary physical custody when the children reside with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. Given the geographic distance between the parties and the informal, inconsistent nature of Colin's parenting time to date, an arrangement recognizing David's primary physical custody and providing Colin with defined but structured parenting time is most consistent with Mia's best interests and with the factual realities of her life.
C. THE COURT SHOULD STRUCTURE COLIN'S PARENTING TIME TO PROVIDE MEANINGFUL CONTACT WHILE PROTECTING MIA FROM FURTHER INSTABILITY.
Even where primary physical custody is awarded to one parent, the child should have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents, unless such access would be detrimental to the child's welfare. AS 25.20.070. David does not seek to extinguish Colin's relationship with Mia. He seeks a formal, enforceable structure that defines Colin's parenting time in a way that is predictable for Mia, appropriate to her developmental stage, and protective of her stability.
The Alaska Supreme Court in In Re ACS, 171 P.3d 1148 (Alaska 2007), affirmed an arrangement in which one parent held sole legal custody while both parents shared physical custody on a structured basis, recognizing that such an arrangement can serve a child's best interests when the parents cannot effectively communicate on legal decisions but each maintains a meaningful relationship with the child. While David requests primary rather than shared physical custody here given the geographic distance, the principle applies: structured contact that preserves the parent-child bond without imposing an unworkable schedule serves the child's best interests.
Given the 360-mile distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks, a traditional week-on, week-off schedule would impose unreasonable travel burdens on a two-year-old child. The Court should consider a schedule that provides Colin with extended blocks of time during school breaks and holidays, as well as regular telephonic and electronic contact, which is more appropriate to Mia's age and the geographic realities of this case.
Any parenting schedule ordered by this Court should also include provisions requiring each parent to give timely notice of changes to address or contact information, and requiring that major decisions regarding Mia's medical care, education, and welfare be made exclusively by David as the sole legal custodian, without unilateral action by Colin during parenting time. Colin's recent conduct in making medical decisions unilaterally during visits makes such a provision essential. The court should make plain that Colin's parenting time does not confer decision-making authority.
D. THE COURT SHOULD CONSIDER APPOINTING A GUARDIAN AD LITEM TO REPRESENT MIA'S BEST INTERESTS IN THESE PROCEEDINGS.
Where custody is contested, the court has discretion to appoint a guardian ad litem to conduct a thorough factual investigation and advocate the course of action that is in the child's best interests. Civil Rule 90.7(e). A guardian ad litem is treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes and may participate in hearings, conduct discovery, introduce evidence, and examine witnesses, all for the purpose of ensuring that the child's interests are fully represented. Civil Rule 90.7(e).
Given Mia's young age, the geographic complexity of this case, and the pattern of unilateral and potentially harmful conduct by Colin, appointing a guardian ad litem would assist the Court in making a fully informed custody determination. Mia is two years old and cannot express a preference, but she has interests that are distinct from those of either parent. A guardian ad litem would be positioned to investigate the quality of care provided in each household, the practical logistics of any proposed parenting schedule, and any concerns regarding Colin's unilateral medical decisions.
David respectfully requests that the Court consider this appointment if the case proceeds to an evidentiary hearing.
E. THE COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH CHILD SUPPORT CONSISTENT WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3.
Once primary physical custody is established, child support should be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a). Under that rule, a child support award in a primary physical custody case equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage: 20 percent for one child. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). The adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources, reduced by mandatory deductions including federal, state, and local income tax, Social Security tax, and medicare tax, as well as certain voluntary retirement contributions and other qualifying deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Colin's income information is not yet before the Court. David requests that the Court require Colin to submit a complete financial disclosure, including documentation of all income sources and applicable deductions, so that a proper child support calculation can be made consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a). The Court should enter a child support order contemporaneously with the custody order so that Mia's financial needs are addressed without delay.
V. CONCLUSION
Mia Nakamura is a two-year-old child who deserves stability, consistency, and the protection of a formal court order that defines her parents' rights and responsibilities. She has lived with David Nakamura in Anchorage for her entire life. David has served as her primary caregiver in every meaningful sense. Colin Nakamura's involvement, while informal, has become a source of instability rather than support: he has made unilateral medical decisions without David's consent and has threatened to retain Mia in Fairbanks without legal authority to do so.
The statutory best-interests factors, applied to the facts of this case, support an award of sole legal custody and primary physical custody to David Nakamura, with structured parenting time for Colin Nakamura that is appropriate to Mia's developmental stage and the geographic distance between the parties. Child support should be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on Colin's adjusted annual income.
David Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court enter an order:
1. Awarding sole legal custody of Mia Nakamura to David Nakamura;
2. Awarding primary physical custody of Mia Nakamura to David Nakamura;
3. Establishing a structured parenting schedule for Colin Nakamura that includes extended holiday and school-break contact as well as regular telephonic and electronic contact;
4. Requiring Colin Nakamura to submit financial disclosure for the purpose of calculating child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a);
5. Entering a child support order consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a); and
6. Considering the appointment of a guardian ad litem pursuant to Civil Rule 90.7(e) to represent Mia's best interests throughout these proceedings.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0056)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Bergstrom ("Father") respectfully petitions this Court for an initial determination of legal custody, physical custody, and a formal parenting time schedule with respect to his daughter, Lily Bergstrom, born March 2021. Father and Danielle Bergstrom ("Mother") were never married but maintained a committed relationship of approximately four years, during which Lily was born. Since the parties separated in August 2023, Lily has resided primarily with Mother in Anchorage while Father exercised parenting time under an informal arrangement. That arrangement has broken down because Mother has begun restricting Father's access to Lily without explanation or justification. Father now seeks a formal court order to protect his parental rights and, most importantly, to safeguard Lily's long-term well-being by ensuring she maintains a meaningful, stable relationship with both of her parents.
Because no prior custody order exists, this matter requires an initial custody determination. Alaska law is clear that such determinations must be made according to the best interests of the child, without any presumption in favor of either parent. The record in this case, as set forth below, demonstrates that a shared or well-structured custody arrangement, with defined legal and physical custody terms, is firmly in Lily's best interests and is supported by the controlling statutory framework and Alaska case law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Bergstrom is Lily Bergstrom's biological father. Father and Mother were in a committed relationship for approximately four years before separating in August 2023. During the relationship, Father was an active and engaged parent, participating in Lily's daily care, attending to her physical and emotional needs, and forming a close and loving bond with her. Lily was born in March 2021 and is currently a young child at a critical stage of her emotional and developmental growth.
Following the parties' separation in August 2023, Lily remained primarily in Mother's care at her home in Anchorage. Father and Mother attempted to manage parenting time informally, relying on mutual agreement rather than a formal court order. For a period of time, this informal arrangement allowed Father to spend meaningful time with Lily. However, Mother has recently begun restricting Father's access to Lily without providing any explanation or legal justification for doing so. Father's parenting time has become unpredictable and increasingly curtailed at Mother's unilateral discretion.
Father has made good-faith efforts to communicate with Mother and resolve the access issue without court intervention. Those efforts have not succeeded. Father remains ready, willing, and able to provide a safe, nurturing, and stable home environment for Lily during any parenting time the Court may award. Father has a strong emotional bond with Lily, who has known him as her father since birth. No prior custody order governs the parties' respective parenting rights and responsibilities. Father accordingly brings this petition seeking the Court's initial determination of custody and a formal parenting time schedule to protect both his rights and Lily's well-being.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
This Court has jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination in this proceeding. Under AS 25.30.300, a court of this state has jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination if this state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding. Because Lily has resided in Anchorage, Alaska with Mother since the parties' separation, and Father also resides in Alaska, Alaska is unquestionably Lily's home state, and this Court has jurisdiction over the initial custody determination.
The substantive standard governing this proceeding is the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.060 provides that the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. In determining the best interests of the child, the court shall consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Critically, AS 25.20.060(b) provides that neither parent, regardless of the question of the child's legitimacy, is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody. The fact that the parties were never married does not diminish Father's right to seek custody or reduce the weight of his parental interests in this proceeding. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Rosenblum v. Perales, 303 P.3d 500 (Alaska 2013), that initial custody determinations between unmarried parents are of paramount importance and must allow parents to litigate on a fairly equal footing.
Under AS 25.20.060(c), the court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined by the court to be in the best interests of the child, and such an award shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible.
Further, AS 25.20.070 states that, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child considering the factors under AS 25.24.150(c), or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) is present, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody under AS 25.20.060 through AS 25.20.130. No such detriment has been alleged here, and the domestic violence presumption of AS 25.24.150(g) has no application to these facts. Accordingly, Lily is presumptively entitled to equal access to both parents while this proceeding is pending.
The factors the Court must consider in determining Lily's best interests are enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) and include, among others: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. An Initial Custody Determination Is Required Because No Prior Order Governs the Parties' Parental Rights
No prior custody order exists in this case. The parties, who were never married, relied on an informal parenting arrangement following their separation in August 2023. That arrangement has collapsed because Mother has unilaterally restricted Father's access to Lily without legal justification. The absence of a court order leaves both parents and, more importantly, Lily, without any enforceable framework governing her care, upbringing, and parental contact. This Court must make an initial determination of legal and physical custody to protect Lily's stability and well-being.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that custody disputes between unmarried parents are governed by the same statutory framework that applies in divorce proceedings, including AS 25.20.060 through AS 25.20.130. In Buness v. Gillen, 781 P.2d 985 (Alaska 1989), the court confirmed that either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of a custody dispute under AS 25.20.060, and that the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child without regard to the child's legitimacy or the parents' marital status. Father is Lily's biological father, has an established relationship with her, and has standing to bring this petition. This Court should proceed to make an initial custody determination consistent with the statutory framework.
B. The Best Interests of the Child Strongly Support a Meaningful Parenting Time Award for Father
The controlling inquiry in this proceeding is the best interests of Lily. Under AS 25.24.150(c), the court shall consider all relevant factors in reaching this determination. Each of the relevant statutory factors weighs in favor of awarding Father substantial and regularly scheduled parenting time.
1. Lily's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs
The first statutory factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(1) requires the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Lily is a young child at a formative stage of development. Research and common experience confirm that children at this age need consistent, loving contact with both parents for healthy emotional and social development. Father has been present in Lily's life since her birth and has actively participated in her care. Continued access to Father is not a preference; it is a developmental need.
2. Father's Capability and Desire to Meet Lily's Needs
The second statutory factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. Father is capable of providing Lily with a safe, nurturing, and stable home environment during any parenting time the Court awards. His demonstrated history of active parenting during and after the parties' relationship reflects both his desire and his ability to meet Lily's needs. Nothing in the record suggests any deficiency in Father's parenting capability.
3. Love and Affection Between Lily and Father
The fourth statutory factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(4) directs the court to consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. Father has maintained a close emotional bond with Lily since her birth. That bond is a direct product of years of parental involvement and daily caregiving. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Jaymot v. Skillings-Donat, 216 P.3d 534 (Alaska 2009), that the emotional and parental capacity of each parent is a relevant consideration in the best interests analysis, and that courts must look carefully at which custodial arrangement best serves the child's overall welfare. The love and affection existing between Father and Lily plainly supports a substantial parenting time award.
4. Stability and Continuity of Lily's Environment
The fifth statutory factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(5) requires the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. While Lily has lived primarily with Mother since the separation, Father's regular involvement in her life during the same period has itself been a source of stability. The breakdown of the informal arrangement has introduced instability and uncertainty into Lily's life. A formal court order establishing a predictable, consistent parenting schedule will restore and maintain the continuity and stability that Lily needs.
5. Mother's Restriction of Father's Access Weighs Against Her Under the Facilitation Factor
The sixth statutory factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(6) directs the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. This factor weighs significantly in Father's favor. Mother has begun restricting Father's parenting time without explanation, in direct contravention of Lily's best interests. Father, by contrast, has made good-faith efforts to maintain a cooperative co-parenting relationship.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), demonstrates that courts scrutinize conduct by one parent that undermines the other parent's relationship with the child. Mother's unilateral restriction of Father's access, if left unaddressed by a court order, risks causing lasting harm to Lily's relationship with her father. A formal order with enforceable parenting time provisions will prevent further erosion of this critical relationship. The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized in Harris v. Governale, 311 P.3d 1052 (Alaska 2013), that parenting time arrangements should be structured to ensure the child has meaningful access to both parents, not merely nominal contact.
6. Absence of Domestic Violence or Substance Abuse Concerns
The seventh and eighth statutory factors under AS 25.24.150(c)(7) and (c)(8) require the court to consider any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect, and any evidence that substance abuse directly affects the child's well-being. No such evidence exists here. The domestic violence presumption of AS 25.24.150(g) is not implicated by the facts of this case. There is no allegation of domestic violence, child abuse, or substance abuse on Father's part. The absence of these concerns removes any barrier to a substantial parenting time award and supports the Court's exercise of its authority to order shared or well-structured custody under AS 25.20.060(c).
C. Father Is Entitled to Joint Legal Custody and a Formal Physical Custody Schedule
Alaska law provides that the court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined by the court to be in the best interests of the child, and that such an award shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c). The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized the importance of frequent and continuing contact with both parents in the absence of countervailing concerns. See Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011) (recognizing the importance of stability and continuity in custody arrangements and cautioning against unnecessary interference with an established parental relationship).
Father requests that the Court award joint legal custody to both parents, granting each parent equal decision-making authority with respect to Lily's education, health care, religious upbringing, and other major life decisions. Joint legal custody will ensure that Father remains informed and involved in all significant decisions affecting Lily's life, as contemplated by AS 25.20.130, which provides that a parent who is not granted custody has the same access to the medical, dental, school, and other records of the child as the custodial parent.
With respect to physical custody, Father requests that the Court order a formal parenting schedule providing him with regular, predictable, and substantial parenting time. AS 25.20.070 mandates that Lily have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents while this proceeding is pending and as the Court considers a custody award. Father is prepared to work with the Court and with Mother to establish a schedule that meets Lily's developmental needs and reflects the geographic proximity of both parents within Anchorage.
D. The Court Should Enter an Interim Parenting Time Order Pending Final Resolution
Because Mother has already begun restricting Father's access to Lily, and because no enforceable order currently exists to protect Father's parental rights, Father respectfully requests that the Court enter an interim parenting time order on an expedited basis. AS 25.20.070 expressly provides that Lily shall have equal access to both parents to the greatest degree practical while the Court considers the custody award. An interim order consistent with this statutory mandate will protect Lily's relationship with Father during the pendency of this proceeding and prevent further unilateral restriction of parenting time by Mother.
E. Child Support Should Be Calculated Consistent with Civil Rule 90.3
To the extent the Court makes a physical custody determination in this proceeding, child support should be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. If the Court awards primary physical custody to Mother, child support from Father shall be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) by multiplying Father's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage for one child, which is 20 percent. If the Court awards shared physical custody, child support shall be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for the time each parent has physical custody and the relative incomes of the parties.
