David has provided for Eli's daily physical needs, maintained his routines, and ensured his social and developmental needs are being addressed. Under AS 25.24.150(c)(1), the court must consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. The record shows that Eli's needs are presently being met within the stable environment David provides.
2. David Has Demonstrated the Capability and Desire to Meet Eli's Needs.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(2), the court considers the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. David has been the parent primarily responsible for Eli's day-to-day care throughout the child's life, including throughout Wesley's extended North Slope work rotations both during and after the relationship. David's consistent presence in Eli's life demonstrates both the capacity and the commitment to serve as Eli's primary custodian. Wesley's employment, which regularly takes him away from Anchorage for extended consecutive periods, has necessarily limited his availability to serve as Eli's primary caregiver.
3. Continuity and Stability Favor Maintaining Eli's Current Anchorage Residence.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Eli has lived in Anchorage his entire life. He is four years old, an age at which consistency in environment, caregivers, and routine is particularly important to healthy development. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the child's need for stability and continuity in custody arrangements as a factor of considerable weight. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011). Allowing Wesley to relocate unilaterally with Eli to Fairbanks would rupture that continuity without any court determination that such a disruption serves Eli's interests.
4. Wesley's Threatened Unilateral Relocation Demonstrates Unwillingness to Facilitate David's Relationship with Eli.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Wesley's stated intention to take Eli to Fairbanks without David's consent reflects a willingness to sever Eli's daily relationship with his primary caregiver for the convenience of one parent. David, by contrast, has not sought to exclude Wesley from Eli's life. He has allowed Wesley to exercise informal parenting time during off-rotation weeks throughout the post-separation period. The contrast between the two parents on this factor weighs in David's favor.
The Alaska Supreme Court has examined relocation disputes and has consistently required that courts carefully weigh the impact of a proposed move on the child's relationship with the non-relocating parent. Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011); Bruce H. v. Jennifer L., 407 P.3d 432 (Alaska 2017). Where, as here, the relocating parent has not sought court approval and has given no notice to the other parent, the proposed relocation cannot be presumed to serve the child's best interests.
5. The Court May Also Award Shared Custody if Consistent with Eli's Best Interests.
David does not seek to exclude Wesley from Eli's life. David acknowledges that Wesley loves Eli and that Eli benefits from his relationship with both parents. AS 25.20.060(c) provides that the court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is in the best interests of the child, and that any such award shall assure the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible.
David requests that the Court consider a parenting plan that designates David as the primary physical custodian in Anchorage and provides Wesley with defined parenting time during his off-rotation weeks that is consistent with Wesley's North Slope work schedule. Such an arrangement would accommodate the reality of Wesley's employment pattern, preserve Eli's Anchorage stability, and ensure that Eli maintains a meaningful relationship with both parents. The Alaska Supreme Court has approved custody arrangements tailored to the practical realities of a parent's work schedule where those arrangements serve the child's best interests. Blanton v. Yourkowski, 180 P.3d 948 (Alaska 2008); Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001).
C. THE COURT SHOULD PROHIBIT ANY RELOCATION OF ELI PENDING RESOLUTION OF THIS PETITION.
The immediacy of Wesley's threat to relocate Eli to Fairbanks without David's consent requires the Court's prompt intervention. In the absence of a custody order, there is no legal instrument currently in place to prevent Wesley from acting on that threat at any time. Eli's best interests require that the Court issue, at minimum, a temporary order prohibiting either parent from removing Eli from Anchorage pending a full hearing on the custody petition.
Under Civil Rule 86(l), custody proceedings initiated by a parent to obtain custody of a child from another parent are to be commenced by order to show cause. This mechanism allows the Court to bring both parties before it expeditiously and to put protective conditions in place while the matter is resolved on the merits. David asks the Court to issue an order to show cause requiring Wesley to appear and to demonstrate why a temporary custody order should not issue, and to include in that order a prohibition on removing Eli from Anchorage pending hearing.
The Court is empowered to award custody on such terms as seem necessary or proper during the pendency of the action. AS 25.24.150(a). A temporary order maintaining the status quo, which is David as Eli's primary caregiver in Anchorage, is the appropriate interim measure while the Court conducts a full best-interest analysis. J. M. v. S. C., 552 P.3d 475 (Alaska 2024).
D. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE ESTABLISHED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3.
David also requests that the Court establish a child support order concurrent with the custody determination. Alaska courts are required to calculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. Where primary physical custody is awarded to one parent, the non-custodial parent's support obligation is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a). If the Court instead awards shared physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f), support is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b). David requests that the Court enter a child support order consistent with whichever custody arrangement the Court determines to be in Eli's best interests, and that the order reflect Wesley's actual income from his North Slope employment.
The court may vary the child support award for good cause upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result if the support award were not varied, and must specify in writing the reason for any such variation. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1). David does not anticipate that a variation will be necessary, but reserves the right to present evidence on this issue at hearing.
V. CONCLUSION
Eli Larsen is a four-year-old child who has no formal legal protection governing his custody, parenting time, or support. He has lived his entire life in Anchorage, primarily in the care of his father, David Larsen. Wesley Larsen's recent threats to relocate Eli to Fairbanks without David's consent expose Eli to the risk of sudden and harmful disruption to the only stable home environment he has known. Alaska law places Eli's best interests at the center of every custody determination, and those interests plainly favor maintaining Eli's stability in Anchorage under David's primary care while ensuring that Wesley remains a meaningful part of Eli's life consistent with his work schedule and the child's welfare.
David Larsen respectfully requests that the Court:
1. Issue an order to show cause pursuant to Civil Rule 86(l) requiring Wesley Larsen to appear and show cause why a custody order should not issue;
2. Enter a temporary order prohibiting either parent from removing Eli from Anchorage pending a full hearing on this petition;
3. Following hearing, enter a permanent custody order designating David Larsen as Eli's primary physical custodian in Anchorage, with defined parenting time for Wesley Larsen consistent with his North Slope rotation schedule and Eli's best interests under AS 25.24.150(c);
4. Award joint legal custody to both parents, or sole legal custody to David if the Court finds that Wesley's conduct warrants such a determination;
5. Establish a child support order in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3; and
6. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the best interests of Eli Larsen.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0062)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Larsen respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition to establish a formal custody and parenting plan order for the parties' minor child, Mia Larsen, date of birth approximately 2021, currently age four. Renee and Respondent Brandon Larsen are unmarried parents who shared a residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately three years before separating in early 2023. No court has ever entered a custody order, parenting plan, or any other judicial determination governing Mia's legal or physical custody. Mia has resided primarily with Renee in Anchorage since the separation, while Brandon has exercised parenting time on an informal, inconsistent basis under a loose verbal arrangement between the parties.
The absence of a formal court order now poses a concrete and immediate threat to Mia's stability and to Renee's ability to protect her custodial rights. Brandon has recently threatened to remove Mia from Anchorage and take her to his family's home in Fairbanks without Renee's knowledge or consent. Without an enforceable court order, Renee has no legal mechanism to prevent this removal or to compel Brandon's compliance with any agreed parenting arrangement. Renee therefore petitions this Court, pursuant to AS 25.20.943, to enter an initial custody determination awarding her primary physical custody of Mia, establishing a defined parenting time schedule for Brandon, and allocating legal decision-making authority over Mia's education, healthcare, and general welfare.
As set forth below, a careful consideration of all relevant best-interest factors under AS 25.24.929 compels the conclusion that primary physical custody with Renee serves Mia's best interests, and that a structured parenting plan with defined legal decision-making authority is both necessary and appropriate.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
A. The Parties and the Child
Renee Larsen and Brandon Larsen are the parents of Mia Larsen, a four-year-old girl currently residing in Anchorage, Alaska. The parties were never married. They lived together in Anchorage for approximately three years and separated in early 2023 following ongoing domestic conflict connected to Brandon's alcohol use and his extended, unexplained absences from the family home.
B. Mia's Living Arrangement Since Separation
Since the parties' separation in early 2023, Mia has lived primarily with Renee in Anchorage. Renee has been Mia's primary caregiver throughout her life, attending to her daily physical needs, medical appointments, developmental milestones, and educational programming. Brandon has seen Mia on an informal and inconsistent basis. The parties never reduced any parenting arrangement to writing, and no court has ever been asked to enter a custody or parenting plan order. The informal verbal arrangement has worked only to the extent that Brandon has been willing to follow it. That willingness can no longer be assumed.
C. Brandon's Alcohol Use and Absences
A significant contributing factor to the breakdown of the parties' relationship was Brandon's ongoing alcohol use. During the parties' time living together, Brandon's drinking led to periods of extended absence from the home, leaving Renee as the sole caregiver for Mia for days or weeks at a time. Renee has observed that Brandon's alcohol use continues to affect his availability and reliability as a parent during his current parenting time with Mia.
D. Brandon's Threat to Remove Mia to Fairbanks
Recently, Brandon threatened to take Mia from Anchorage to his family's home in Fairbanks without Renee's consent. This threat has created an urgent and immediate need for formal court intervention. Because no court order exists, Renee has no enforceable legal right to prevent Brandon from removing Mia from Anchorage on a temporary or indefinite basis, and Mia has no formal legal protection against disruption of the stable, continuous home environment she has known since birth.
E. Relief Sought
Renee petitions this Court to enter an initial custody determination designating her as the primary physical custodian of Mia, establishing a defined parenting time schedule for Brandon, and allocating legal decision-making authority over Mia's education, healthcare, and general well-being.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060(a), either parent of a child may petition the superior court for resolution of a child custody dispute, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. In determining the best interests of the child, the court shall consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) and the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g).
Neither parent is entitled to a preference in the award of custody by virtue of the parent's gender. AS 25.20.060(b). The court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is in the best interests of the child, and any award of shared custody shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.940.
AS 25.24.150(c) directs the court to consider: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect in the proposed custodial household or a history of violence between the parents; evidence that substance abuse by either parent or other members of the household directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child; and other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(d) further provides that in awarding custody the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child.
Where a parent has a history of perpetrating domestic violence, AS 25.24.150(g) establishes a rebuttable presumption that such parent may not be awarded sole legal custody, sole physical custody, joint legal custody, or joint physical custody of a child. Where domestic violence has occurred, AS 25.20.080(f) prohibits the court from ordering or referring the parties to mediation if a protective order is in effect, and restricts mediation if a party objects on the grounds that domestic violence has occurred between the parties.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that a child's need for stability and continuity in custody arrangements is a paramount consideration in best-interest determinations. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011). The court looks to the totality of circumstances affecting the child's welfare and does not apply a mechanical formula. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018). In resolving initial custody determinations, Alaska courts focus particularly on each parent's actual history of caregiving and the stability of the environment each can provide going forward. Rooney v. Rooney, 914 P.2d 212 (Alaska 1996).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. This Court Has Jurisdiction and Authority to Enter an Initial Custody Determination for Mia.
This Court has jurisdiction to enter an initial custody determination under AS 25.20.060. Mia has lived with Renee in Anchorage, Alaska since her birth and continuously since the parties' separation in early 2023. Alaska is unambiguously Mia's home state within the meaning of AS 25.30.909(7), which defines "home state" as the state in which a child lived with a parent or a person acting as a parent for at least six consecutive months immediately before the commencement of a child custody proceeding. Mia has resided in Alaska with Renee for the entirety of her four years of life. No competing custody determination exists in any other state. Alaska's jurisdiction to enter an initial determination is therefore secure.
Because no prior court has entered a custody or parenting plan order, this proceeding constitutes an initial determination as defined by AS 25.30.909(8), which defines "initial determination" as the first child custody determination concerning a particular child under all circumstances. The absence of any prior order underscores both the necessity and the appropriateness of this Court's intervention to protect Mia's best interests.
B. Primary Physical Custody with Renee Is in Mia's Best Interests Under the Statutory Factors.
1. Mia's Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs Are Best Met by Renee as Primary Custodian.
The first and foundational best-interest factor requires the Court to assess the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child and the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs. AS 25.24.150(c)(1) and (2). Here, Renee has been Mia's consistent, primary caregiver for all four years of Mia's life, including the more than two years since the parties separated. Renee has managed Mia's daily routine, medical care, nutrition, social development, and early educational programming. Brandon's parenting time has been inconsistent and informal. His documented pattern of extended absences during the parties' cohabitation, driven in significant part by his alcohol use, demonstrates a diminished capability to meet Mia's daily and developmental needs on a sustained basis.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the parent who has actually served as the child's day-to-day caregiver carries significant weight in this analysis. Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020). Renee's unbroken record of primary caregiving since Mia's birth provides the strongest available evidence of her capability and desire to meet Mia's needs.
2. The Desirability of Maintaining Stability and Continuity Strongly Favors Renee.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the Court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Mia has lived in Renee's Anchorage home for all four years of her life. That home is Mia's only known stable environment. Her friendships, routines, healthcare providers, and early educational setting are all rooted in Anchorage. Disrupting that environment, particularly by relocating Mia to Fairbanks without court approval and without her primary caregiver, would represent a serious and unnecessary shock to a young child's sense of security and continuity.
The Alaska Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized the importance of continuity for young children and cautioned against unnecessary disruption of stable custody arrangements. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011). The principle is especially pronounced for a child as young as Mia, for whom consistency of environment and primary attachment figures is critical to healthy development.
3. Brandon's Alcohol Use Directly Affects Mia's Emotional and Physical Well-Being.
AS 25.24.150(c)(8) requires the Court to consider evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child. Brandon's alcohol use was a central source of conflict throughout the parties' relationship and contributed directly to his pattern of extended absences from the family home. Renee has observed that his alcohol use continues to affect his reliability and availability as a parent during his current parenting time with Mia. A four-year-old child left in the care of a parent who is actively consuming alcohol, or who may be unavailable or impaired during his parenting time, is exposed to risks to both her physical safety and her emotional stability.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that substance abuse findings carry significant weight in custody determinations and that courts must examine the direct impact of a parent's substance use on the child, not just the fact of use in the abstract. Harris v. Governale, 311 P.3d 1052 (Alaska 2013). Here, the nexus between Brandon's alcohol use and his parenting deficits is direct and documented by the history of the parties' relationship.
4. Renee Has Demonstrated a Willingness to Facilitate Mia's Relationship with Brandon.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) asks the Court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Renee has demonstrated this willingness throughout the post-separation period. Despite the absence of any court order and despite Brandon's inconsistent engagement, Renee has allowed Brandon to exercise parenting time with Mia on a regular basis. She has not sought to cut off his contact with Mia and does not seek to do so now. Rather, Renee seeks a structured, defined parenting time schedule that will give Brandon consistent, reliable time with his daughter while protecting Mia's stability.
Brandon's recent threat to remove Mia to Fairbanks without Renee's consent raises serious questions about his willingness to support Mia's relationship with her primary caregiver. A parent who threatens unilateral relocation of a child in the absence of a court order demonstrates a disregard for the other parent's relationship with the child and for the child's own interest in maintaining her primary attachment relationships. The Alaska Supreme Court addressed similar conduct in Jaymot v. Skillings-Donat, 216 P.3d 534 (Alaska 2009), recognizing that a parent's unilateral action to disrupt existing custodial arrangements is a factor the court may properly weigh in the best-interest analysis.
5. Mia's Age and Attachment to Renee Support a Primary Custody Designation.
Mia is four years old. At this age, children are particularly dependent on consistent, nurturing caregiving from a stable primary attachment figure. Mia has known Renee as her primary parent for all four years of her life. While the Court may consider Mia's preference under AS 25.24.150(c)(3), at age four Mia does not yet possess the age and capacity to form a preference that a court can formally weigh. However, the totality of the remaining statutory factors strongly supports the conclusion that preserving Mia's primary relationship with Renee serves her best interests.
C. The Court Should Establish a Defined Parenting Time Schedule for Brandon.
Renee does not seek to eliminate Brandon's parenting time with Mia. She recognizes that Mia benefits from a relationship with her father, and AS 25.20.060(c) provides that the court shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible when shared custody is awarded, and the same principle of encouraging meaningful parental involvement underlies any parenting time order. A defined schedule will give Brandon predictable, enforceable time with Mia and will eliminate the uncertainty and conflict that the current informal arrangement has produced. The schedule should account for Brandon's current residence and any travel required for exchanges, and should include provisions addressing holidays, school breaks, and parental notification requirements for any proposed travel with Mia.
Given Brandon's documented issues with alcohol use and his inconsistent parenting history, Renee requests that any parenting time order include provisions requiring Brandon to refrain from consuming alcohol during his parenting time and for a defined period before exchanges, and permitting either party to return to court promptly if concerns about Mia's safety arise during Brandon's parenting time. James R. v. Kylie R., 320 P.3d 273 (Alaska 2014), illustrates that Alaska courts appropriately impose conditions on parenting time where a parent's conduct raises legitimate safety concerns, and that such conditions need not eliminate parenting time but rather structure it in a manner that protects the child's welfare.
D. The Court Should Allocate Legal Decision-Making Authority to Avoid Future Conflict.
Legal custody, encompassing the authority to make decisions about Mia's education, healthcare, and general well-being, must also be formally established. In the absence of a court order, each parent currently asserts an equal and unresolved right to make decisions for Mia. This creates a structural conflict that will only worsen as Mia approaches school age and as more significant medical and educational decisions arise.
Renee requests that this Court consider the parties' demonstrated ability to cooperate when allocating legal custody. Given the history of conflict between the parties and Brandon's threat to remove Mia without consent, a grant of sole legal custody to Renee may be warranted if the evidence demonstrates that the parties are unable to communicate and cooperate in Mia's best interests. Alternatively, if the Court determines that joint legal custody is appropriate, the order should include a clear dispute resolution mechanism and a designation of which parent holds tie-breaking authority in specific categories of decision-making. Rooney v. Rooney, 914 P.2d 212 (Alaska 1996), acknowledges the court's broad authority to craft custody orders that are tailored to the specific circumstances of the family and the needs of the child.
E. Child Support Should Be Calculated Under Civil Rule 90.3 Consistent with the Custody Designation Entered by the Court.
Once this Court enters a custody determination, child support must be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. If the Court designates Renee as primary physical custodian, child support will be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides that a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. For one child, that percentage is 20 percent of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A).
If the Court instead awards shared physical custody, as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1) as a custody arrangement in which the children reside with each parent for a period of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year, the shared custody calculation methodology of Civil Rule 90.3(b) would apply. Renee submits that the facts of this case support a primary custody designation in her favor rather than a shared custody arrangement, given Mia's age, the history of the parties' caregiving, and Brandon's documented inconsistency. Accordingly, Civil Rule 90.3(a) should govern the child support calculation.
Renee requests that the Court order the parties to submit current financial disclosures and that a Civil Rule 90.3 child support calculation be completed concurrent with the entry of the custody order.
F. The Threatened Removal of Mia to Fairbanks Must Be Addressed by a Formal Order with Appropriate Geographic Restrictions.
Brandon's recent threat to remove Mia to Fairbanks without Renee's consent is not merely a negotiating posture. It reflects a genuine risk that, without a court order, Brandon may unilaterally relocate Mia and leave Renee with no immediate legal recourse. AS 25.30.460 and AS 25.30.480 address the enforcement of custody determinations once entered, but these provisions can only be invoked once a custody order exists. The most effective protection against improper removal is the prompt entry of a formal custody order that designates Renee as primary physical custodian, requires both parents to provide advance written notice of any proposed travel with Mia outside the Anchorage area, and prohibits either parent from relocating Mia's primary residence outside of Anchorage without court approval or the other parent's written consent.
Civil Rule 86(l) further confirms that the appropriate mechanism when a parent seeks to obtain custody of a child from another parent is an order to show cause rather than a writ of habeas corpus, underscoring that this Court's formal custody order is the proper and necessary vehicle through which Renee's custodial rights can be protected and enforced.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Larsen respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Enter an initial custody determination under AS 25.20.060 designating Renee as the primary physical custodian of Mia Larsen.
2. Enter a defined parenting time schedule for Brandon Larsen that provides him with regular, consistent, and enforceable parenting time with Mia, subject to conditions addressing his alcohol use during parenting time.
3. Allocate legal decision-making authority over Mia's education, healthcare, and general welfare, with sole legal custody to Renee or, in the alternative, joint legal custody with a clear dispute resolution process and tie-breaking mechanism.
4. Prohibit either parent from relocating Mia's primary residence outside of Anchorage without prior court approval or the written consent of both parties, and require advance written notice of any travel with Mia outside the Anchorage area.
5. Order the parties to submit financial disclosures and calculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on a primary custody designation in favor of Renee.
6. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper in the best interests of Mia Larsen.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0063)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Petrova petitions this Court for a formal order establishing legal and physical custody of Lena Petrova, born in 2021, the minor child of David Petrova and Michael Petrova. The parties were never married and separated informally in March 2023 after approximately four years together. Since that time, Lena has resided primarily with David at his Anchorage home, while Michael has exercised parenting time on an informal, unscheduled basis. That arrangement has become increasingly unstable and contentious. Michael has now threatened to relocate Lena to Fairbanks during his informal parenting time without David's knowledge or consent. No court order currently governs custody, visitation, or parental decision-making authority for Lena.
David brings this petition to protect Lena's safety, stability, and well-being, and to prevent either parent from making unilateral decisions affecting the child in the absence of enforceable court-ordered terms. Without a formal custody determination, Lena remains vulnerable to disruption of the stable home environment David has maintained for her since the parties' separation. This Court has jurisdiction and authority to resolve the matter under AS 25.20.060, and David respectfully requests that the Court award him primary physical custody and sole or joint legal custody of Lena, with structured parenting time for Michael, all as the Court finds to be in Lena's best interests.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Petrova and Michael Petrova were involved in a romantic relationship for approximately four years. Their daughter, Lena, was born in 2021. The parties were never married. In March 2023, the parties separated informally. No court proceedings were initiated at that time and no court order has ever been entered addressing the custody, visitation, or decision-making authority for Lena.
Since the separation, Lena, who was approximately two years old at the time, has resided primarily with David at his residence in Anchorage, Alaska. David has served as Lena's primary caregiver, providing for her physical, emotional, educational, and social needs on a day-to-day basis. Lena has established a stable and consistent home environment with David in Anchorage.
Michael has exercised parenting time with Lena on an informal, unscheduled basis. That parenting time has become increasingly inconsistent. The informality of the arrangement has generated ongoing conflict between the parties regarding the timing, duration, and frequency of Michael's parenting time. There is no agreed-upon schedule and no mechanism to resolve disputes between the parties short of court intervention.
Most recently and critically, Michael has threatened to relocate Lena to Fairbanks during what would otherwise be informal parenting time, without David's knowledge or consent. Because no court order governs custody or parenting rights, David currently has no enforceable legal mechanism to prevent Michael from removing Lena from Anchorage and disrupting the stable environment she has known since birth. This threat of unilateral relocation, combined with the increasing instability of the informal arrangement, has made the entry of a formal custody order urgent and necessary to protect Lena's best interests.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska Statute 25.20.060 governs custody disputes between parents of children born outside of marriage. Under that statute, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of custody matters, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. The statute further provides that the court may award shared custody if that arrangement is determined to be in the child's best interests, and that any award of shared custody shall ensure frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Neither parent holds a preference by virtue of gender or the question of the child's legitimacy.
In determining best interests, the court shall consider all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Those factors include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference, if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse directly affects the child's well-being; and other pertinent factors.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that the best interests of the child is the paramount consideration in custody determinations. In Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011), the court recognized the counterproductive effect of unnecessary conflict on children and emphasized the importance of stability and continuity in custody arrangements. Similarly, in Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011), the court confirmed that the superior court has broad discretion to fashion custody awards tailored to the unique needs of the individuals involved, and that no single hard and fast rule governs all cases.
In Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court upheld a custody determination that weighed, among other factors, a parent's history of inconsistent conduct and the child's established routine and environment. In Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011), the court addressed parental relocation and emphasized the importance of notice, consent, and existing parenting plan provisions when one parent seeks to move a child. In Jayda Roman v. Cleveland Karren, 461 P.3d 1252 (Alaska 2020), the court reinforced the principle that the superior court must articulate the basis for its custody decisions and consider each relevant statutory best-interest factor.
The court may appoint a guardian ad litem for the child when it finds that separate representation of the child's best interests is necessary, such as when the proceeding is unusually complex or when evidence not otherwise likely to be presented is needed. Civil Rule 90.7(a). If appointed, the guardian ad litem shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child and shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes. Civil Rule 90.7(e). The court may also, at any time within 30 days after a custody petition is filed, order the parties to submit to mediation, subject to the limitations applicable when domestic violence concerns are present. AS 25.20.080.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. This Court Has Jurisdiction and Authority to Establish Custody of Lena
This Court has clear authority under AS 25.20.060 to resolve this custody dispute and enter a formal order governing legal custody, physical custody, and parenting time. The statute expressly authorizes either parent to petition the superior court for resolution of a custody matter. Lena was born in Alaska, has resided in Anchorage continuously since birth, and has no custody order governing her situation. Alaska is the child's home state, and this Court is the proper forum to enter the required determination. No competing order exists in any other jurisdiction that would limit this Court's authority.
B. The Absence of a Formal Custody Order Places Lena at Immediate Risk of Harm
The most pressing basis for this petition is Michael's recent threat to relocate Lena to Fairbanks without David's consent during an informal parenting period. Because no court order currently governs the parties' custody arrangement, David has no enforceable legal protection against such a unilateral act. The informal arrangement that has developed since March 2023 provides no mechanism to prevent removal, no defined parenting schedule, and no structure for resolving the parties' ongoing disputes.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that parental relocation and unilateral removal of a child from an established environment implicate serious best-interest considerations. In Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011), the court examined the importance of notice, consent, and structural parenting plan protections in relocation scenarios, highlighting how a child's stability can be fundamentally disrupted by an unannounced or contested move. Here, Michael's threatened relocation to Fairbanks without notice or consent is precisely the kind of unilateral action that a formal custody order is designed to prevent.
In the absence of a court order, there is no legal prohibition against either parent removing Lena from Anchorage, enrolling her in new schools, making unilateral medical decisions, or otherwise altering the conditions of her life without the other parent's knowledge or agreement. The entry of a formal custody order is therefore not only appropriate but urgent.
C. The Best Interests of Lena Support Awarding David Primary Physical Custody
Under AS 25.24.150(c), the Court must evaluate all relevant factors to determine the custody arrangement that best serves Lena's interests. An analysis of those factors supports awarding David primary physical custody.
1. Stability and Continuity of Environment
Since the parties separated in March 2023, Lena has lived primarily with David in Anchorage. AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the Court to consider the length of time a child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Lena has now been in David's primary care for a substantial period, during which David has provided her with consistent housing, routine, and care. Disrupting that arrangement, particularly by relocating Lena to Fairbanks, would undermine the stability and continuity that the statute recognizes as centrally important to a child's well-being.
The Alaska Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized this principle. In Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011), the court noted the importance of stability and continuity in custody arrangements and the counterproductive nature of conflict and unnecessary disruption for children. In Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011), the court affirmed the superior court's broad discretion to craft custody awards that address the unique circumstances of the child and family, recognizing that preserving an established, functional environment often serves the child's best interests.
2. Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet Lena's Needs
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the Court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs. David has been Lena's primary caregiver since birth. He has consistently met Lena's day-to-day needs, maintained her home environment, and ensured her physical and emotional well-being. Michael's parenting time, by contrast, has been increasingly inconsistent, unscheduled, and a source of ongoing conflict rather than a stable, enriching presence in Lena's life.
3. Love and Affection Between Lena and Each Parent
AS 25.24.150(c)(4) recognizes the love and affection between a child and each parent as a relevant factor. David does not dispute that Lena and Michael share a parental bond. This petition does not seek to sever that relationship. Rather, David seeks a structured parenting plan under which Lena's relationship with Michael can be maintained in a stable, predictable, and enforceable manner. A formal order that includes defined parenting time for Michael will serve this factor better than the current chaotic informal arrangement.
4. Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Child
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the Court considers each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. David has not sought to deny Michael parenting time. He has accommodated informal arrangements despite the conflicts they have generated. Michael's threatened unilateral relocation to Fairbanks, however, directly implicates this factor. A parent who threatens to remove a child from the child's established home without notice or the other parent's consent demonstrates a lack of willingness to cooperate in facilitating the child's relationship with her other parent. In Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed a custody decision that considered one parent's obstructive conduct toward the other parent's relationship with the child.
5. The Child's Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) directs the Court to assess the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Lena is very young, approximately three to four years old. Young children of her age have a particular need for routine, predictability, and a consistent primary caregiver. The current informal arrangement, marked by inconsistent contact and escalating conflict between the parents, does not serve those needs. A formal custody order with a defined parenting schedule will create the predictability and structure Lena requires for healthy development.
D. The Court Should Establish Defined Parenting Time for Michael
David does not seek to eliminate Michael's relationship with Lena. AS 25.20.060(c) provides that the Court may award shared custody if that is in the child's best interests and that any such award shall assure frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Even where primary physical custody is awarded to one parent, the Court may structure parenting time to ensure the other parent remains a meaningful presence in the child's life.
David requests that the Court enter a parenting plan that provides Michael with regular, defined parenting time, subject to appropriate notice requirements and geographic restrictions that prevent either parent from relocating Lena without advance notice and either the other parent's consent or a court order. Such provisions are consistent with the approach affirmed in Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011), where the court recognized the importance of structured notice and consent mechanisms in preventing unilateral relocation of a child.
E. Legal Custody Should Be Addressed to Prevent Unilateral Decision-Making
In addition to physical custody, this Court should address legal custody, which governs each parent's authority to make major decisions affecting Lena's education, health care, religious upbringing, and general welfare. AS 25.24.150(c) factors, considered as a whole, support entering a legal custody determination that prevents either parent from making unilateral major decisions without the other's input or court authorization.
In the absence of a legal custody order, Michael could make unilateral medical, educational, or other major decisions for Lena during his parenting time, including decisions incident to any attempted relocation to Fairbanks. A joint legal custody award with a defined dispute resolution mechanism, or sole legal custody to David as the primary caregiver, would protect Lena from the consequences of uncoordinated and potentially conflicting parental decisions.
In Jayda Roman v. Cleveland Karren, 461 P.3d 1252 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that the superior court must carefully analyze the relevant statutory best-interest factors in crafting its custody determination. Consideration of the parties' ability to cooperate and communicate regarding major decisions affecting the child is central to any legal custody award.
F. The Court Should Consider Appointment of a Custody Investigator
Given the disputed factual circumstances and the complexity of the parties' informal arrangements, David respectfully requests that the Court consider appointing a custody investigator to provide an independent expert analysis of the custody arrangement that best serves Lena's interests. Civil Rule 90.7(a) provides that in proceedings involving custody of a child, the court may appoint a guardian ad litem only when separate representation of the child's best interests is necessary. The Commentary to that rule notes that in most contested proceedings in which professional input is warranted, a child custody investigator should be appointed instead of a guardian ad litem, as the investigator can provide an independent analysis and may serve as a catalyst to settlement.
Appointment of a custody investigator under Alaska R. Evid. 706(a) would allow the Court to benefit from a neutral expert's assessment of the parenting capacities of each party, Lena's needs and current adjustment, and the custody arrangement most likely to serve her long-term interests. Such an appointment is particularly appropriate here, given that the parties have had no prior court involvement and there is no existing record from which the Court can assess the parenting history of either party.
G. Mediation Is Not Appropriate at This Time Given the Threatened Relocation
AS 25.20.080(a) provides that the court may order parties to submit to mediation within 30 days after a custody petition is filed. However, mediation is not appropriate under the present circumstances given Michael's recent threat to remove Lena to Fairbanks. The urgency of entering a protective custody order to prevent unilateral relocation outweighs the potential benefits of a mediation referral at this stage. David respectfully requests that the Court proceed to an expedited hearing on his request for temporary orders before any mediation referral is considered, so that Lena's safety and stability are protected in the interim.
V. CONCLUSION
David Petrova respectfully requests that this Court enter an order establishing formal legal and physical custody of Lena Petrova. Lena is a young child who has lived in a stable, primary home with David in Anchorage since the parties' informal separation in March 2023. Michael's threatened unilateral relocation to Fairbanks, combined with the increasingly inconsistent and conflict-ridden nature of the parties' informal parenting arrangement, makes the entry of a formal, enforceable custody order both necessary and urgent.
For the foregoing reasons, David respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Award David primary physical custody of Lena, with structured and defined parenting time for Michael;
2. Enter a legal custody determination that prevents unilateral major decision-making and protects Lena's stability;
3. Include in any parenting plan enforceable geographic and relocation restrictions requiring advance notice and either parental consent or a court order before either party may relocate Lena from the Anchorage area;
4. Consider appointment of a custody investigator to provide an independent expert analysis of the custody arrangement that best serves Lena's best interests; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court finds to be in Lena's best interests under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150.
All relief requested is grounded in and guided by the paramount standard of Lena's best interests, as required by Alaska law.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0064)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Okafor respectfully petitions this Court to establish legal and physical custody of Lily Okafor, a four-year-old child born to Petitioner and Respondent Wesley Okafor. The parties were never married and have no formal custody order governing their parental rights and responsibilities. Since the parties separated in early 2023, Lily has resided primarily with Petitioner in Anchorage. Respondent has recently begun taking Lily for extended, unannounced periods without Petitioner's knowledge or consent, creating instability and disruption that is harmful to the child's well-being. Petitioner seeks a binding court order establishing legal and physical custody, and a structured parenting plan, so that Lily may enjoy the stability, continuity, and security she deserves. This Court has authority under AS 25.20.060 to resolve this custody dispute and must do so in accordance with the best interests of the child.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Okafor and Wesley Okafor are the biological parents of Lily Okafor, born in 2019. The parties were never married. They cohabited in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately three years. In early 2023, ongoing conflicts made cohabitation untenable, and Wesley voluntarily moved out of the family home. Since that time, Lily has resided primarily with Renee at the Anchorage family home, and Renee has served as Lily's primary caregiver in all material respects, attending to Lily's daily physical, emotional, educational, and social needs.
Following separation, the parties operated under an informal, loosely agreed-upon parenting arrangement under which Wesley exercised parenting time on an irregular basis. No formal custody order has ever been entered by any court in this or any other jurisdiction. The informal arrangement functioned with varying degrees of cooperation until recently, when Wesley began taking Lily for extended periods without providing Renee advance notice and without Renee's consent. These unannounced removals have grown in frequency and duration, leaving Renee without knowledge of Lily's whereabouts and without the ability to ensure continuity in Lily's routine, medical care, or early childhood programming.
Lily is four years old and at a developmentally critical age during which stability, predictability, and consistent caregiving are essential to healthy development. The absence of a formal custody order has created an environment of legal uncertainty that benefits neither parent and, most importantly, harms Lily. Petitioner now seeks a formal determination of legal and physical custody and the entry of a structured parenting plan so that both parents understand their rights and obligations and so that Lily may thrive in a stable, well-defined environment.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts have authority to award custody of a child born to unmarried parents upon the petition of either parent. AS 25.20.060 provides the governing statutory framework for custody disputes between parents who were not married, directing that the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child and that in determining the best interests of the child, the court shall consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Under AS 25.20.923, neither parent is entitled to a preference in the awarding of custody regardless of the child's legitimacy, meaning the fact that the parties were unmarried confers no automatic advantage to either party.
The best interests factors the Court must consider under AS 25.24.150(c) include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference, if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the child's well-being; and other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(d) further specifies that in awarding custody the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child under all circumstances.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that the trial court must conduct a holistic analysis of all applicable best interests factors and that stability and continuity of environment are particularly significant considerations in custody determinations. Green v. Parks, 338 P.3d 312 (Alaska 2014). Where parents have operated under an informal arrangement and one parent has served consistently as the primary caregiver, courts consider the established caregiving pattern as relevant to the stability and continuity factor. Daves v. McKinley, 425 P.3d 92 (Alaska 2018). The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized that a parent's willingness to facilitate the child's relationship with the other parent is a meaningful factor in the best interests analysis. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THIS COURT HAS AUTHORITY TO ESTABLISH CUSTODY OF LILY OKAFOR UNDER AS 25.20.060
AS 25.20.060 expressly authorizes either parent to petition the superior court for resolution of a custody dispute, and directs the court to award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. Because no custody order has ever been entered for Lily, this petition is properly before the Court as an initial custody determination. The Court is not constrained by any prior order and should conduct a full best interests analysis to determine the custody arrangement that best serves Lily's needs. The absence of any existing order means there is no change-of-circumstances requirement, and the Court may proceed directly to an evaluation of the statutory best interests factors under AS 25.24.150(c). Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011).
B. THE BEST INTERESTS OF LILY OKAFOR FAVOR AN AWARD OF PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY TO PETITIONER WITH STRUCTURED PARENTING TIME FOR RESPONDENT
1. Lily's Need for Stability and Continuity Strongly Favors Primary Physical Custody with Petitioner.
Among the most significant best interests factors is the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Since the parties separated in early 2023, Lily has lived primarily with Renee in the Anchorage family home. Renee has been Lily's consistent caregiver throughout this period, attending to Lily's daily needs, health care, and early childhood development. This established, stable environment warrants protection. Disrupting Lily's primary living arrangement at age four, when consistency and routine are developmentally critical, would not serve her best interests. Green v. Parks, 338 P.3d 312 (Alaska 2014) (affirming primary physical custody where child had lived in stable environment with primary caregiver, and emphasizing desirability of maintaining that continuity).
Wesley's recent pattern of taking Lily for extended, unannounced periods without Renee's consent directly undermines the stability Lily requires. Far from providing a structured alternative caregiving environment, Wesley's conduct has introduced unpredictability and disruption into Lily's life. Courts consider the stability of the proposed custodial arrangement as a central best interests factor, and the record here demonstrates that Renee's home has provided and can continue to provide the stable, satisfactory environment Lily needs.
2. Renee Has Demonstrated Capability and Desire to Meet Lily's Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) and (c)(2) direct the Court to consider the child's physical, emotional, mental, and social needs and the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs. Renee has served as Lily's primary caregiver since the parties' separation, providing day-to-day care, medical attention, and emotional support. She has maintained Lily in a stable home environment and has been attentive to Lily's developmental needs as a young child. The record supports a finding that Renee has both the capability and desire to meet all of Lily's needs.
By contrast, Wesley's recent conduct, specifically taking Lily for extended periods without notice and without Renee's consent, reflects a disregard for the child's need for routine and for both parents' cooperation in managing Lily's care. At age four, Lily depends on predictable caregiving schedules. Wesley's unannounced removals interfere with Lily's routine and demonstrate a failure to consider how his conduct affects Lily's well-being. AS 25.24.150(d) limits the Court to considering only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child, and Wesley's pattern of conduct directly and adversely affects Lily's stability and security.
3. Petitioner Has Demonstrated Willingness to Facilitate Lily's Relationship with Her Father; Respondent Has Not Reciprocated.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the Court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Renee has permitted Wesley to exercise parenting time with Lily throughout the period since separation, operating under a loosely agreed-upon informal schedule. She has not sought to exclude Wesley from Lily's life, and she acknowledges the importance of Lily maintaining a meaningful relationship with her father.
Wesley, however, has not demonstrated a corresponding commitment to cooperation. His unannounced, extended takings of Lily without Renee's consent reflect a unilateral approach to parenting time that bypasses the cooperative communication necessary for shared parenting to function. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's willingness to facilitate the child's relationship with the other parent is an important indicator of that parent's fitness to serve in a primary custody role. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018). Where one parent consistently acts to undermine the other parent's ability to care for and communicate with the child, that conduct weighs against an award of primary custody to the undermining parent.
Petitioner is willing to support a formal parenting time schedule that provides Wesley with regular, meaningful time with Lily. A structured parenting plan that clearly delineates each parent's time and requires advance notice and mutual agreement for deviations will protect Lily's well-being while preserving her relationship with both parents.
4. The Love and Affection Between Lily and Each Parent Should Be Channeled Through a Structured Parenting Plan.
AS 25.24.150(c)(4) directs the Court to consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. Petitioner does not dispute that Lily has a loving relationship with both her mother and her father. However, the existence of love and affection between Lily and Wesley does not justify Wesley's unilateral, unannounced takings of the child. To the contrary, a formal parenting plan will best protect and nurture those loving relationships by giving each parent defined, reliable time with Lily without the disruption and conflict that the current informal arrangement has produced. Structured parenting time for Wesley, with clear provisions for regular contact, will allow Lily to enjoy a stable and loving relationship with her father within a framework that also protects her need for continuity in her primary home.
5. An Award of Shared Legal Custody with Primary Physical Custody to Petitioner Serves Lily's Best Interests.
AS 25.20.060(c) provides that the Court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined by the court to be in the best interests of the child, and directs that an award of shared custody shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Petitioner proposes that the Court award joint legal custody, so that both parents participate in major decisions affecting Lily's health, education, and welfare, while awarding primary physical custody to Renee. This arrangement reflects the caregiving reality that has existed since the parties separated and provides the continuity and stability the statutory framework directs courts to protect.
The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed custody arrangements that preserve the primary caregiver's role while affording meaningful parenting time to the non-primary parent, recognizing that frequent and continuing contact with both parents serves children's best interests. Jayda Roman v. Cleveland Karren, 461 P.3d 1252 (Alaska 2020); James R. v. Kylie R., 320 P.3d 273 (Alaska 2014). A formal parenting plan that awards Wesley regular, scheduled parenting time, including defined weeknight and weekend visits and notice requirements for any modifications, will protect Lily's relationship with her father while preserving the stability she has enjoyed in Renee's primary care.
C. THE COURT SHOULD ENTER A BINDING PARENTING PLAN THAT PROHIBITS UNANNOUNCED, EXTENDED TAKINGS OF THE CHILD
The Court has broad authority under AS 25.24.992 to make such orders for the custody and visitation of a minor child as may seem necessary or proper. Wesley's recent pattern of taking Lily for extended, unannounced periods without Renee's consent constitutes precisely the kind of conduct that necessitates a binding court order. Without a formal order, there is no enforceable mechanism to prevent Wesley from continuing to remove Lily without notice, and Renee has no legal recourse short of returning to court on an emergency basis each time it occurs.
A binding parenting plan should include, at minimum: a defined primary residence with Renee; a regular schedule of parenting time for Wesley with advance notice requirements; a prohibition on removing Lily from her primary residence for extended periods without written consent of both parents or court authorization; and provisions for communication and cooperation between the parents regarding Lily's health, education, and welfare. Such a plan is consistent with the Court's authority under AS 25.24.150 and with the Alaska Supreme Court's recognition that clarity and enforceability in parenting arrangements serves children's best interests. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018) (underscoring the importance of formal, enforceable custody arrangements to prevent unilateral manipulation of parenting time).
D. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3
Upon entry of a primary physical custody order, the Court should also address child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides that a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in the rule. For one child, that percentage is 20% of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). The adjusted annual income is calculated by subtracting from the non-custodial parent's total income from all sources the mandatory deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A) through (G). A formal child support order entered at the time of the custody determination will provide financial predictability for Lily's care and avoid future disputes over support obligations.
If the Court determines that a shared physical custody arrangement is more appropriate, child support would be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which applies the shared custody formula to ensure that both parents contribute to Lily's support proportionate to their incomes and the percentage of time each parent has physical custody.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Okafor respectfully requests that this Court enter an order: (1) awarding joint legal custody of Lily Okafor to both parents; (2) awarding primary physical custody of Lily Okafor to Petitioner Renee Okafor; (3) establishing a defined schedule of parenting time for Respondent Wesley Okafor, with clear notice requirements and prohibitions on unannounced, extended removals of the child; and (4) calculating and entering a child support obligation in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on Respondent's adjusted annual income. Such relief is warranted by the evidence, the governing statutory framework, and the overriding principle that all custody determinations must serve the best interests of Lily Okafor.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0065)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Bergstrom respectfully petitions this Court to establish a formal custody order, a parenting plan, and a child support determination for the parties' minor daughter, Mira Bergstrom, born in 2021. Ashley and Sarah Bergstrom are the unmarried parents of Mira, who has resided primarily with Sarah in Anchorage since the parties' separation in early 2023. No court has previously entered any order governing legal custody, physical custody, visitation, or child support for Mira. Ashley brings this petition because Sarah has indicated a plan to relocate with Mira to Fairbanks, a development that, absent a binding court order, would substantially impair Ashley's ability to maintain a meaningful and consistent parental relationship with her daughter. Ashley seeks an order establishing joint legal custody, a structured physical custody schedule that ensures Mira has frequent and continuing contact with both parents to the maximum extent consistent with Mira's best interests, and a child support award calculated in accordance with the applicable guidelines. This Court has authority to resolve this dispute and craft an appropriate order under AS 25.20.060, and it must do so with Mira's best interests as the paramount consideration.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Bergstrom and Sarah Bergstrom were in a committed romantic relationship for approximately three years before separating in early 2023. The parties were never married. From this relationship, their daughter Mira was born in 2021. Mira is presently approximately two years old.
Since the separation, Mira has resided primarily with Sarah at Sarah's residence in Anchorage. Ashley has exercised parenting time on an informal basis, pursuant to verbal arrangements between the parties rather than any court-sanctioned schedule. These arrangements have been inconsistent. Ashley has remained actively interested in Mira's upbringing and has maintained a loving bond with her daughter throughout the period following separation.
No court has ever entered an order establishing legal custody, physical custody, a parenting plan, or child support for Mira. The parties have operated entirely on informal agreements, which have proven inadequate to protect the stability of Mira's relationship with Ashley.
Sarah has recently communicated her intention to relocate with Mira from Anchorage to Fairbanks, citing new employment. Such a relocation, without a court order in place, would leave Ashley with no enforceable mechanism to preserve her parenting time or protect her rights as Mira's parent. Ashley now petitions this Court to establish a formal custody arrangement, a comprehensive parenting plan, and a child support order before any such relocation occurs.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060, either parent of a child whose custody is in dispute may petition the Superior Court for resolution of the matter. The Court is required to award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child, considering all relevant factors including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Neither parent is entitled to any preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b). The Court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined to be in the child's best interests, and any such award must assure that the child "has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible." AS 25.20.060(c).
The best interests factors that the Court must consider under AS 25.24.150(c) include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference, if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form one; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable and satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or neglect; evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the child's emotional or physical well-being; and any other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(c).
There is also a rebuttable presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) that a parent with a history of perpetrating domestic violence may not be awarded legal or physical custody, whether sole or joint.
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Where one parent has primary physical custody, support is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage based on the number of children. In shared physical custody cases, support is calculated under the methodology set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b). The Court may vary the guidelines calculation only upon a showing by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result from strict application of the guidelines. Civil Rule 90.3(c).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THIS COURT HAS JURISDICTION AND AUTHORITY TO ESTABLISH CUSTODY FOR MIRA
This Court has jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination for Mira under AS 25.20.060. No prior court order governing Mira's custody or parenting time exists in this state or any other state. Because Mira has resided in Anchorage, Alaska with Sarah since birth and throughout her life, Alaska is plainly the home state of the child and the appropriate forum for this initial determination. Because no prior custody determination has been made, the exclusive and continuing jurisdiction framework of AS 25.30.310 does not yet operate as a limitation. Rather, this Court has full authority to make an initial determination and, upon doing so, will acquire exclusive continuing jurisdiction over any future modifications. AS 25.30.310(a). The absence of any prior order underscores the urgency of prompt court action, particularly given Sarah's stated intent to relocate to Fairbanks.
B. THE BEST INTERESTS OF MIRA REQUIRE A FORMAL CUSTODY ORDER WITH MEANINGFUL PARENTING TIME FOR BOTH PARENTS
1. Mira's Best Interests Are the Governing Standard
Every custody determination in Alaska must be guided solely by the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.060(a); AS 25.24.150(c). The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently reinforced that the best interests analysis is multi-factored and requires the trial court to weigh all relevant circumstances with particularized attention to the individual child before the court. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018); Nancy M. v. John M., 308 P.3d 1130 (Alaska 2013). Mira is a two-year-old child who has known both of her parents throughout her life. Her best interests are served by an order that reflects the reality of her bond with Ashley and provides the structure necessary for that bond to continue and deepen.
2. Ashley Has a Meaningful and Loving Bond with Mira
Among the statutory factors the Court must consider is "the love and affection existing between the child and each parent." AS 25.24.150(c)(4). Ashley has maintained an active parental presence in Mira's life since birth, including throughout the period following the parties' separation. Although the parties' parenting time arrangements have been informal and inconsistent, this is attributable to the absence of a court order rather than any lack of commitment or involvement on Ashley's part. Ashley's consistent desire to be part of Mira's life and her decision to petition this Court rather than allow an unregulated relocation to proceed reflects her prioritization of Mira's stability and well-being.
3. Continuity, Stability, and the Desirability of a Formal Arrangement
The statutory factor addressing the length of time a child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity weighs in favor of a formal order. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of both geographic and relational stability in the lives of young children. Eniero v. Brekke, 192 P.3d 147 (Alaska 2008). Mira has spent her entire life in Anchorage, and both of her parents are currently located there. A formal custody order that secures Mira's relationship with Ashley provides precisely the relational continuity that this factor is intended to protect. Without such an order, Sarah's proposed relocation to Fairbanks would unilaterally disrupt the informal parenting arrangement that has existed since separation, leaving Ashley without any enforceable means to maintain her relationship with Mira.
4. Each Parent's Capability and Desire to Meet Mira's Needs
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(2), the Court must consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs. Ashley is a fit parent who is capable of meeting all of Mira's needs and who has consistently expressed a desire to do so. The informal nature of the current parenting arrangement has not resulted from any incapacity on Ashley's part; rather, it reflects the absence of a governing court order. Ashley requests this Court establish a parenting plan that gives both parents meaningful roles in Mira's upbringing so that Mira may benefit from the resources and love of both her parents.
5. Each Parent's Willingness to Facilitate the Other's Relationship with the Child
The Court must also consider "the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child." AS 25.24.150(c)(6). Sarah's indication that she intends to relocate Mira to Fairbanks without first securing a court order or reaching a parenting plan agreement raises a concern regarding this factor. Sarah's unilateral decision to relocate would sever the informal parenting time that Ashley has exercised and would force Ashley to pursue court intervention to protect her rights. By contrast, Ashley is committed to supporting Mira's relationship with Sarah and seeks only an equal opportunity to participate in Mira's life. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's willingness to facilitate the other parent's relationship with the child is a significant factor in the best interests analysis. Jaymot v. Skillings-Donat, 216 P.3d 534 (Alaska 2009).
6. Shared Custody Is in Mira's Best Interests
Ashley requests that this Court award joint legal custody and shared physical custody of Mira. Under AS 25.20.060(c), the Court may award shared custody if it determines that such an arrangement is in the best interests of the child, and any such award must assure "frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible." Both parents are fit, both reside currently in Anchorage, and Mira has bonds with both. Shared physical custody would allow Mira to maintain meaningful relationships with both parents, satisfying the legislative policy embodied in AS 25.20.060(c). The Alaska Supreme Court has upheld shared physical custody arrangements in circumstances where both parents are capable and involved, recognizing that frequent contact with both parents generally serves young children's developmental needs. Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020); Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005).
7. Neither Parent Is Entitled to a Preference
As expressly provided by AS 25.20.060(b), neither parent, regardless of the question of the child's legitimacy, is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody. The fact that Mira has resided primarily with Sarah since the separation does not entitle Sarah to a presumption of continued primary custody. The Court must evaluate all factors with a level analysis, giving no automatic advantage to either parent. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011).
C. THE COURT SHOULD ADDRESS THE PROPOSED RELOCATION IN FASHIONING THE PARENTING PLAN
Sarah's stated intent to relocate Mira from Anchorage to Fairbanks is a material circumstance that this Court must address in fashioning a parenting plan. While Alaska courts have the authority to structure parenting plans that account for geographic distance between parents, the relocation of a young child to a different city presents distinct challenges, particularly in the absence of any prior custody order.
