Colin has exercised only informal, inconsistent parenting time during periodic visits to Anchorage. No court order governing custody, visitation, or child support has ever been entered for Elliot.
Colin recently threatened to take Elliot to Fairbanks indefinitely. Because no legal custody order exists, Marcus has no enforceable mechanism to prevent the child's removal from his care. Without court intervention, Elliot faces disruption to the stable home environment he has known for his entire life. Marcus therefore seeks an order establishing primary physical custody in his favor, a structured parenting schedule for Colin, and a child support award consistent with Alaska's guidelines. This Court has authority and jurisdiction to act, and the best interests of Elliot plainly require the entry of a formal parenting plan without delay.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Petrova and Colin Petrova are the parents of Elliot Petrova, born approximately four years ago in Anchorage, Alaska. The parties were never married. Their romantic relationship continued for some period following Elliot's birth but became strained after Colin relocated to Fairbanks to accept new employment. The parties separated finally approximately two years ago, at which point Marcus assumed the role of Elliot's primary caregiver in the family's Anchorage home.
Since the separation, Elliot has lived with Marcus on a full-time basis. Colin has returned to Anchorage on an irregular schedule and has exercised parenting time with Elliot informally, without any court-sanctioned structure or consistency. No agreement between the parties has ever been reduced to writing. No court has ever entered any order addressing the custody, visitation, or financial support of Elliot.
Approximately at the time of the filing of this petition, Colin informed Marcus that he intended to take Elliot to Fairbanks indefinitely. This threat placed Marcus in the position of having no legal recourse to prevent removal of his son from the only stable home Elliot has ever known. Marcus filed the present petition to remedy that gap and to protect Elliot's well-being through a binding court order.
Elliot is a healthy four-year-old child who has spent his entire life in Anchorage. He has bonded with Marcus as his primary caregiver. Marcus has arranged and maintained Elliot's medical care, daily routine, social environment, and early childhood education. Colin, while Elliot's legal parent, has not maintained a consistent physical presence in Elliot's life since the parties' separation and currently resides in Fairbanks, approximately 360 miles from Anchorage.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060, either parent may petition the Superior Court for resolution of a custody dispute. The court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child, considering all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.905, and the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g). Neither parent is entitled to a preference in the custody determination regardless of gender or the circumstances of the child's birth.
In determining the best interests of the child, AS 25.24.150(c) directs the court to consider, among other factors: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child under all circumstances; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form one; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; and evidence that substance abuse directly affects the child's well-being.
AS 25.24.150(g) establishes a rebuttable presumption that a parent who has a history of perpetrating domestic violence against the other parent, a child, or a domestic living partner may not be awarded sole legal custody, sole physical custody, joint legal custody, or joint physical custody. That presumption is not implicated on the present facts as currently known, but Marcus reserves the right to raise relevant evidence should further facts emerge.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the best-interests analysis is the controlling framework in initial custody determinations between unwed parents. Elton H. v. Naomi R., 119 P.3d 969 (Alaska 2005). Continuity and stability of the child's existing environment are considerations of significant weight. C.R.B. v. C.C., 959 P.2d 375 (Alaska 1998). Courts have also recognized that a parent's failure to maintain consistent contact with a child, and a pattern of geographic distance, bear directly on several of the statutory best-interests factors. Koller v. Reft, 71 P.3d 800 (Alaska 2003).
Child support is governed by Civil Rule 928(a), which requires that a child support award be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage set forth in the rule. Civil Rule 90.3(c) permits the court to vary the guideline amount upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result, and requires the court to specify in writing the reason for any variation.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH A FORMAL CUSTODY ORDER AWARDING MARCUS PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF ELLIOT.
This case presents a straightforward application of Alaska's best-interests framework. No court order has ever governed Elliot's custody. Colin has threatened to remove Elliot from Anchorage to Fairbanks without Marcus's consent. The Court must now act to protect Elliot's welfare by establishing a binding parenting plan.
AS 25.20.060 provides that when a dispute over child custody exists, either parent may petition the Superior Court for resolution, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. The statute further provides that the court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is in the child's best interests, and that any such award "shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible." The statute also requires the court to consider all relevant factors, including those in AS 25.24.150(c), which the Court addresses below.
1. Elliot's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs Favor Continuity in Marcus's Home.
Elliot is four years old and has lived with Marcus in Anchorage for the entirety of his life. He has received consistent medical care, a daily routine, and social development under Marcus's supervision. AS 25.24.150(c)(1) directs the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. All of those needs are currently being met within the stable environment Marcus has maintained. Disrupting that environment by permitting an indefinite, unilateral relocation to Fairbanks would undermine Elliot's developmental stability without any corresponding benefit to the child.
2. Marcus Has Demonstrated the Capability and Desire to Meet Elliot's Needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. Marcus has been Elliot's de facto primary caregiver since the parties' separation two years ago. He has managed all aspects of Elliot's daily life, including medical appointments, childcare, and early education. Colin, by contrast, relocated to Fairbanks for employment purposes and has returned to Anchorage only on an irregular basis, exercising parenting time inconsistently. Colin's geographic distance and irregular involvement do not reflect the same level of demonstrated capability and sustained desire to meet Elliot's day-to-day needs as Marcus has shown.
3. The Stability and Continuity of Elliot's Current Environment Strongly Favor Marcus.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the Court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Elliot has spent his entire four years of life in Anchorage. His friendships, medical providers, childcare providers, and daily routines are all anchored in Anchorage. Relocating Elliot to Fairbanks at Colin's unilateral demand would eliminate that continuity entirely.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in C.R.B. v. C.C., 959 P.2d 375 (Alaska 1998), reinforces the importance courts place on the preservation of stable custodial environments, particularly for young children who have bonded with a consistent caregiver over a sustained period. The court's concern in that case about the disruption caused by removing a child from an established environment applies with equal force here. Similarly, in Elton H. v. Naomi R., 119 P.3d 969 (Alaska 2005), the Alaska Supreme Court examined circumstances involving an absent parent and a present, consistent caregiver, affirming that the depth of a parent's actual daily involvement in a child's life is a critical consideration under the best-interests standard.
4. Colin's Willingness and Ability to Facilitate Marcus's Relationship with Elliot Is in Question.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Colin's threat to take Elliot to Fairbanks indefinitely, without notice, without agreement, and without any legal authority to do so, directly calls into question his willingness to support Elliot's relationship with Marcus. A parent who threatens unilateral relocation of a child to a city 360 miles away does not demonstrate the cooperative parenting orientation that this statutory factor contemplates.
Marcus, by contrast, has never sought to prevent Colin from spending time with Elliot. Despite the absence of any court order, Marcus has allowed Colin to exercise informal parenting time during visits to Anchorage. Marcus's conduct reflects a genuine willingness to support Elliot's relationship with both of his parents, provided that parenting time is structured and consistent.
5. A Guardian Ad Litem Should Be Appointed to Represent Elliot's Best Interests.
Given Elliot's young age and the contested nature of this proceeding, Marcus respectfully requests that the Court consider whether appointment of a guardian ad litem is appropriate. Under AS 25.24.310(c), the court may, upon the motion of either party or upon its own motion, appoint an attorney or other person or the office of public advocacy to provide guardian ad litem services to a child in any legal proceedings involving the child's welfare. The court is required to appoint a guardian ad litem "when, in the opinion of the court, representation of the child's best interests, to be distinguished from preferences, would serve the welfare of the child."
Civil Rule 90.7(e) further provides that the guardian ad litem "shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child" and "shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes." At four years of age, Elliot cannot meaningfully articulate his own preferences, and the competing interests of his parents create a risk that his independent developmental needs may not be fully surfaced without independent advocacy. Marcus therefore encourages the Court to make a finding on the record regarding whether such appointment would serve Elliot's welfare, consistent with the mandate of AS 25.24.310(c).
B. THE COURT SHOULD ENTER A PARENTING PLAN THAT PROVIDES COLIN STRUCTURED, CONSISTENT PARENTING TIME WHILE PROTECTING ELLIOT'S STABILITY IN ANCHORAGE.
Marcus does not seek to eliminate Colin from Elliot's life. Elliot deserves a meaningful, ongoing relationship with both of his parents, and AS 25.20.060 recognizes that an award of shared custody shall assure that "the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible." However, that contact must be structured, predictable, and enforceable, not subject to Colin's unilateral decisions about when and how long to take the child to Fairbanks.
Marcus proposes that the Court establish a parenting plan in which Elliot's primary physical residence remains with Marcus in Anchorage, with Colin exercising parenting time on a structured schedule that accounts for the distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks. Such a plan might include extended parenting time for Colin during school breaks, summer vacation, and holidays, as well as regular video and telephonic contact during periods when in-person visits are not practicable, consistent with the principle that children benefit from maximum contact with both parents to the extent consistent with their best interests.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Blanton v. Yourkowski, 180 P.3d 948 (Alaska 2008), illustrates the care courts must take in crafting parenting arrangements when parents reside in different cities. That case involved a situation where one parent relocated and the court was required to design a schedule that preserved the child's relationship with both parents while maintaining stability. The same balancing is required here.
Platz v. Aramburo, 17 P.3d 65 (Alaska 2001), similarly demonstrates that when one parent has been geographically absent and has exercised only irregular contact, the court's primary obligation remains the protection of the child's best interests, not the accommodation of a parent's unilateral demands. In that case, the court recognized that the absence of consistent contact, combined with interference with the other parent's relationship with the child, bore heavily on the custody determination. Here, Colin's absence from Anchorage and his inconsistent parenting time over the past two years must inform the parenting plan the Court enters.
C. COLIN'S THREAT TO REMOVE ELLIOT FROM ANCHORAGE UNDERSCORES THE URGENCY OF A BINDING COURT ORDER AND MAY WARRANT INJUNCTIVE RELIEF.
Colin's recent threat to take Elliot to Fairbanks indefinitely is not a hypothetical concern. It is the precipitating reason Marcus has been compelled to seek judicial intervention. Because no custody order exists, Marcus currently lacks any legal tool to prevent Colin from physically removing Elliot from Anchorage and retaining him in Fairbanks. The Court should recognize the urgency of this situation and act promptly to establish enforceable rights.
AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Although that statute speaks to modification of existing orders, its framework reflects the broader principle that custody arrangements must remain responsive to changing circumstances. Here, Colin's threat represents a material change in the parties' informal arrangement that compels formal court action.
Civil Rule 86(l) provides that an order to show cause, and not a writ of habeas corpus, shall be issued initially if the action is brought by a parent to obtain custody of a child under the age of sixteen from another parent. Marcus has proceeded by petition in accordance with applicable procedural rules and respectfully requests that the Court treat this matter with appropriate urgency given the risk of imminent, irreversible harm to Elliot's stability.
Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011), reinforces the principle that unnecessary disruption of established custody arrangements is counterproductive to the welfare of children and all parties involved. Permitting Colin to unilaterally remove Elliot to Fairbanks without any court authorization would impose exactly the kind of destabilizing disruption that Alaska's custody framework is designed to prevent.
D. THE COURT SHOULD ENTER A CHILD SUPPORT ORDER CONSISTENT WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3.
No child support order has ever been entered for Elliot. Marcus has borne all of the financial costs of Elliot's upbringing since the parties' separation. Alaska law mandates the entry of a child support order consistent with the guidelines.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) requires that a child support award in a primary physical custody case be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage: for one child, that percentage is 20 percent. Adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources minus the mandatory and permissible deductions set forth in the rule.
Marcus requests that the Court order Colin to provide financial disclosure of his income and that the Court then calculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a). If the Court finds that Colin has voluntarily and unreasonably reduced his income or is underemployed, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes the Court to calculate child support based on a determination of Colin's potential income, taking into account his assets, employment history, job skills, educational attainment, and the local job market.
Civil Rule 90.3(c) permits the Court to vary the guideline amount upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result, and requires written findings specifying the reason for any variation, the amount that would otherwise have been required, and the estimated value of any property conveyed instead of guideline support. Marcus does not anticipate that a deviation from the guidelines will be appropriate on these facts, but notes the Court's authority to depart where the evidence warrants.
V. CONCLUSION
Elliot Petrova is a four-year-old child who deserves stability, predictability, and the legal protection that only a formal custody order can provide. For the past two years, Marcus Petrova has served as Elliot's primary caregiver in Anchorage, meeting all of his physical, emotional, and developmental needs without any court order and without any consistent financial contribution from Colin Petrova. Colin's recent threat to remove Elliot to Fairbanks indefinitely has made judicial intervention not merely appropriate but necessary.
For all of the foregoing reasons, Marcus Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Enter a custody order awarding Marcus Petrova primary physical custody of Elliot Petrova, with Colin Petrova exercising structured, consistent parenting time pursuant to a parenting plan established by this Court;
2. Retain Elliot's primary residence in Anchorage, Alaska, consistent with the child's best interests and the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c);
3. Consider whether appointment of a guardian ad litem under AS 25.24.310(c) and Civil Rule 90.7(e) would serve Elliot's welfare, and make a finding on the record accordingly;
4. Enter a child support order calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on Colin Petrova's adjusted annual income, with appropriate financial disclosure ordered from Colin; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just, necessary, and in the best interests of Elliot Petrova.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0071)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Whitfield respectfully petitions this Court to establish legal and physical custody of her daughter, Maeve Whitfield, born June 2022. No court has ever entered a custody or parenting plan order governing Maeve's care, and the child has been living primarily with Respondent Jennifer Whitfield under an informal, inconsistent arrangement since the parties separated in early 2023. Renee now brings this petition because Jennifer has recently indicated her intention to relocate with Maeve to Fairbanks and has begun actively restricting Renee's access to the child. A formal custody order is urgently necessary to define each parent's legal rights and responsibilities before any relocation disrupts the child's current circumstances and severs her meaningful relationship with Renee. This Court has jurisdiction and authority under AS 25.20.060 to resolve this dispute and enter an order that reflects the best interests of Maeve. Renee respectfully requests that the Court establish a parenting plan providing for shared physical custody, joint legal custody, and, at minimum, meaningful and enforceable parenting time, and that the Court address Jennifer's proposed relocation before it occurs.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Whitfield and Jennifer Whitfield were in a romantic relationship for approximately three years. The couple's daughter, Maeve Whitfield, was born in June 2022. The parties were never married. Their relationship deteriorated over a prolonged period of conflict and mutual disagreement about their future together, and they separated in early 2023.
Since separation, Maeve has lived primarily at Jennifer's apartment in Anchorage. Renee has maintained a parenting relationship with Maeve through informal, verbal arrangements with Jennifer. These arrangements have been inconsistent and entirely subject to Jennifer's unilateral control, as no court order has ever governed Renee's parenting time or defined either parent's legal rights with respect to Maeve.
Recently, Jennifer informed Renee of her intention to relocate with Maeve to Fairbanks, Alaska. Jennifer has also begun restricting Renee's access to Maeve, limiting and in some instances denying the informal parenting time Renee had previously exercised. Renee has not waived any parental rights. No custody proceeding has previously been initiated, and no order of any kind has been entered by any court regarding Maeve's custody, visitation, or parenting schedule.
Maeve is now approximately two years old. She has bonded with both parents during her young life. Renee has been consistently present and involved in Maeve's upbringing to the extent Jennifer has permitted. Renee is prepared and capable of meeting Maeve's physical, emotional, and developmental needs. Renee brings this petition to protect the parent-child relationship before Jennifer's proposed relocation to Fairbanks makes that relationship significantly more difficult to maintain.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of a custody dispute, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. In determining the best interests of the child, the court shall consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.922, and the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g). AS 25.20.060(a).
Alaska law provides that neither parent, regardless of the question of the child's legitimacy, is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b). The court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined by the court to be in the best interests of the child, and any such award shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c).
The factors a court must consider in determining the best interests of the child include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference, where the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the child's well-being; and other pertinent factors. AS 25.24.936.
While Jennifer and Renee were never married, the unmarried status of the parties does not diminish Renee's right to seek custody under Alaska law. AS 25.20.060 expressly applies to disputes between parents regardless of the parents' marital status or the legitimacy of the child.
In addition, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child, or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) is present, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody. AS 25.20.070.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that both parents in a same-sex domestic partnership may have cognizable parental interests in a child born or raised during the relationship. Rosemarie P. v. Kelly B., 504 P.3d 260 (Alaska 2021). The court has further recognized that a child's stability and continuity are central considerations in custody determinations, and that the willingness of each parent to foster an open relationship between the child and the other parent is a significant factor. Van Sickle v. McGraw, 134 P.3d 338 (Alaska 2006). Courts have also recognized that when parents cannot agree on custody, a formal order defining a parenting schedule promotes stability for the child. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH LEGAL AND PHYSICAL CUSTODY OF MAEVE BECAUSE NO ORDER CURRENTLY EXISTS AND THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILD REQUIRE JUDICIAL RESOLUTION.
Maeve's welfare depends on a court-ordered custody framework. The informal, verbal arrangement currently in place is entirely subject to Jennifer's unilateral decisions, as demonstrated by Jennifer's recent restriction of Renee's parenting time and her stated intention to relocate to Fairbanks without any court authorization or agreement from Renee. AS 25.20.060(a) provides that if there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the matter, and the court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. The dispute here is clear: the parties disagree about Renee's parenting time, and Jennifer has acted unilaterally to reduce it. Renee respectfully asks this Court to resolve this dispute by entering a formal custody and parenting plan order.
The Court should enter an order establishing joint legal custody so that both parents share in decisions regarding Maeve's education, healthcare, and general well-being. AS 25.20.130 provides that a parent who is not granted custody has the same access to the medical, dental, school, and other records of the child as the custodial parent. Ensuring that Renee's rights to information and participation in major decisions are formalized in a court order is a necessary step in protecting Maeve's best interests, because it ensures that both parents remain meaningfully informed and involved in her upbringing.
The Court should also establish a formal parenting time schedule. Under AS 25.20.060(c), the court may award shared physical custody if it is in the best interests of the child, and any such award shall assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Maeve is two years old and has bonded with both parents. Although the primary physical custody arrangement has informally favored Jennifer, Renee has been a consistent and loving presence in Maeve's life. Nothing in the record suggests that Renee is an unfit parent or that her parenting time poses any detriment to Maeve's welfare. Shared physical custody, or at minimum a clearly defined and enforceable parenting time schedule, would serve Maeve's best interests by preserving her bond with both parents.
B. THE RELEVANT BEST INTERESTS FACTORS UNDER AS 25.24.150(c) SUPPORT AN AWARD OF SHARED CUSTODY OR SUBSTANTIAL PARENTING TIME FOR RENEE.
The factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) guide this Court's best interests analysis. Applying those factors here supports an award in favor of shared custody or, at minimum, a significant and formal parenting time schedule for Renee.
First, Maeve's physical, emotional, mental, and social needs are best served by maintaining close relationships with both of her parents. AS 25.24.150(c)(1). Young children benefit from stability in their primary attachments. Maeve has formed bonds with both Renee and Jennifer throughout her life, and severing or severely curtailing Maeve's relationship with Renee would be contrary to Maeve's emotional and developmental interests.
Second, Renee is capable of and desires to meet Maeve's needs. AS 25.24.150(c)(2). Renee has been actively involved in Maeve's care throughout the child's life, to the extent that Jennifer has permitted. Renee's petition itself demonstrates her commitment to Maeve's welfare and her desire to be an engaged, responsible parent.
Third, the love and affection existing between Maeve and Renee supports an award of meaningful parenting time. AS 25.24.150(c)(4). Renee and Maeve have maintained a parent-child relationship throughout Maeve's life. The bond between them is real and worthy of protection.
Fourth, while maintaining continuity in Maeve's primary living arrangement may favor Jennifer in the short term, continuity of the parental relationship with Renee is equally important. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of preserving stability and continuity in custody arrangements. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011). Disrupting Renee's parenting relationship at this stage of Maeve's life, particularly through relocation, would undermine the continuity of a relationship that has existed since Maeve's birth.
Fifth, and critically, Jennifer's recent conduct raises significant concern about her willingness and ability to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between Maeve and Renee. AS 25.24.150(c)(6). Jennifer has begun limiting Renee's access to Maeve and has announced a plan to relocate to Fairbanks, a decision that, if implemented without a formal custody order in place, would unilaterally and substantially impair Renee's parenting relationship. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's willingness to foster an open relationship between the child and the other parent is a highly significant factor in custody determinations. Van Sickle v. McGraw, 134 P.3d 338 (Alaska 2006). Jennifer's conduct weighs against awarding her sole physical custody or permitting relocation without court oversight.
No evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, child neglect, or substance abuse exists in this record. AS 25.24.150(c)(7) and (c)(8). There is no basis to apply the rebuttable presumption against either parent under AS 25.24.150(g). Accordingly, the Court should apply the general best interests analysis and award custody consistent with Renee's right to a meaningful parenting relationship.
C. RENEE IS ENTITLED TO EQUAL ACCESS TO MAEVE DURING THE PENDENCY OF THESE PROCEEDINGS.
AS 25.20.070 provides that unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child, or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) is present, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody. Jennifer has not alleged, and cannot establish, that Renee's parenting time is detrimental to Maeve's welfare. No presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) applies. Accordingly, Renee respectfully requests that this Court enter an interim order providing for equal or substantial parenting time with Maeve during the pendency of this proceeding, to preserve the parent-child relationship and ensure that Maeve continues to have meaningful contact with both parents while the Court considers a final custody award.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the value of interim custody arrangements that maintain the status quo and protect the child's relationships during pending proceedings. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018) (describing the superior court's interim custody order providing equal parenting time while a custody investigation was conducted). Here, a similar interim order would serve Maeve's best interests by preventing Jennifer from further restricting Renee's access before a final custody determination is made.
D. THE COURT SHOULD REQUIRE NOTICE AND JUDICIAL APPROVAL BEFORE JENNIFER IS PERMITTED TO RELOCATE TO FAIRBANKS WITH MAEVE.
Jennifer's stated intention to relocate to Fairbanks with Maeve is a matter of urgent concern. A relocation from Anchorage to Fairbanks would materially alter Maeve's relationship with Renee and would make the informal parenting arrangement, already tenuous, functionally unworkable. Because no custody order is currently in place, Renee has no formal mechanism to prevent the relocation absent court intervention.
The Court should treat the pending relocation as a factor bearing directly on the custody determination. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parental relocation may constitute a material change in the child's circumstances and must be considered in the context of the child's best interests. Corbeau v. Dietrich, 580 P.3d 908 (Alaska 2008). Although that case arose in the context of a modification proceeding, the underlying principle applies with equal force here: a relocation that would significantly limit a child's contact with one parent is a matter for judicial resolution, not unilateral parental action.
Any final custody order should address the issue of relocation expressly, including notice requirements and a mechanism for court review before either parent may relocate with Maeve in a manner that would substantially affect the child's contact with the other parent. At minimum, this Court should enter an interim order requiring Jennifer to provide advance written notice to the Court and to Renee before implementing any relocation, so that the custody proceeding can be resolved on a complete record before Maeve is removed from Anchorage.
E. THE CHILD SUPPORT FRAMEWORK WILL NEED TO BE ADDRESSED ONCE PHYSICAL CUSTODY IS ESTABLISHED.
Once the Court determines the physical custody arrangement, any child support obligation will be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b) and Civil Rule 90.3(f). Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), a parent has shared physical custody if the children reside with that parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30, but no more than 70, percent of the year. If the Court awards shared physical custody as Renee requests, the child support calculation will be governed by the shared custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b). Renee respectfully requests that the Court enter a child support order consistent with the custody arrangement ultimately established.
V. CONCLUSION
Maeve Whitfield deserves the stability and security that a formal custody order provides. Jennifer's recent conduct, including her unilateral restriction of Renee's parenting time and her announced plan to relocate to Fairbanks, demonstrates that the informal arrangement between the parties is no longer workable and that judicial intervention is required to protect Maeve's best interests.
For the foregoing reasons, Renee Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Enter an interim order providing Renee with equal or substantial parenting time with Maeve during the pendency of this proceeding, consistent with AS 25.20.070;
2. Enter an interim order requiring Jennifer to provide advance written notice to the Court and to Renee before relocating with Maeve to Fairbanks or any other location that would substantially affect Renee's parenting time;
3. Following a full hearing, enter a final order establishing joint legal custody, with a parenting plan providing for shared physical custody or, at minimum, a substantial and enforceable parenting time schedule for Renee, consistent with AS 25.20.060, AS 25.20.060(c), and AS 25.24.150(c);
4. Confirm Renee's right to access Maeve's medical, dental, school, and other records under AS 25.20.130; and
5. Enter a child support order consistent with the custody arrangement established and calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(b) and Civil Rule 90.3(f).
Renee Whitfield respectfully submits that all of the foregoing relief is in the best interests of Maeve Whitfield and is supported by Alaska law.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0072)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Petrova respectfully requests that this Court exercise its authority under AS 25.20.060 to establish a formal legal and physical custody arrangement for the parties' minor daughter, Mila Petrova, born approximately two years ago. The parties, Priya Petrova and Jennifer Petrova, were never married and have no existing court order governing custody, visitation, or parental rights with respect to Mila. Since the parties ended their relationship in March 2024, Mila has resided primarily with Respondent Jennifer Petrova in Anchorage, while Petitioner has exercised informal parenting time on an inconsistent and unenforceable basis. Jennifer has recently communicated her intention to relocate with Mila to Juneau, Alaska, to accept new employment, a decision that would materially disrupt Mila's relationship with Priya and deprive Mila of the stability she has known in her Anchorage home. Without a binding court order, Priya has no enforceable mechanism to protect her parental rights or to ensure that Mila's best interests govern any future decisions about her care, residence, or upbringing. This brief sets forth the factual background, applicable legal standards, and arguments supporting entry of a custody order that serves Mila's best interests and preserves her meaningful relationship with both parents.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Petrova and Jennifer Petrova began a romantic relationship approximately five years ago and were together for approximately three years before separating in March 2024. During their relationship, the parties resided together in Anchorage, Alaska, and jointly welcomed Mila Petrova, who was born during the course of the relationship and is now approximately two years old. The parties were never married.
Their relationship deteriorated in the period preceding separation due to increasing conflict over financial matters and divergent philosophies regarding how best to raise Mila. Following the separation in March 2024, Mila remained in the Anchorage home with Jennifer, and the parties attempted to maintain an informal parenting schedule for Priya's time with Mila. That informal schedule has been inconsistent and difficult to follow, leaving both Mila's routine and Priya's parental relationship subject to ongoing uncertainty and disagreement.
No court has ever entered a formal order establishing legal custody, physical custody, or a parenting plan for Mila. There is no existing custody decree from any jurisdiction that addresses Mila's care and upbringing.
Jennifer has recently informed Priya of her intention to relocate with Mila from Anchorage to Juneau, Alaska, citing a new employment opportunity. If Jennifer relocates with Mila without a court order in place, Priya will have no legal mechanism to enforce her parenting time, prevent the move pending court review, or ensure that any transition serves Mila's best interests. Mila has spent the entirety of her young life in Anchorage, where she has developed relationships with Priya, extended family members, and her familiar caregiving environment.
Priya is a loving and capable parent who has been consistently involved in Mila's life and who is committed to meeting Mila's physical, emotional, mental, and social needs. Priya seeks a formal custody order not to limit Jennifer's role in Mila's life, but to ensure that both parents share in decisions about Mila's upbringing, that Priya has enforceable and consistent parenting time, and that any future changes to Mila's living situation are subject to judicial oversight guided by Mila's best interests.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
The Superior Court has authority to award custody of a minor child upon petition by either parent. AS 25.20.060 provides that if there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the matter. The court must award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child, considering all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) and the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g). AS 25.20.060(a). Neither parent is entitled to preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b).
In determining the best interests of the child, AS 25.24.150(c) directs the court to consider: (1) the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; (2) the capability and desire of each parent to meet these needs; (3) the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; (4) the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; (5) the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; (6) the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; (7) any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect in the proposed custodial household or a history of violence between the parents; (8) evidence that substance abuse by either parent or other members of the household directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child; and (9) other factors that the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(d) further provides that in awarding custody the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child.
The court may also award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined by the court to be in the best interests of the child, and any such award must assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c).
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently emphasized that the best interests of the child are the paramount consideration in all custody proceedings, and that courts must carefully weigh each statutory factor based on the specific facts before them. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018); Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020). The court also has discretion to appoint a guardian ad litem to advocate for the child's best interests in contested custody proceedings. Civil Rule 90.7(e) provides that the guardian ad litem shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child and shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes, except as otherwise provided in the rule.
Once custody is established, any future modification requires a showing of a change in circumstances and that modification serves the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THIS COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH FORMAL LEGAL AND PHYSICAL CUSTODY FOR MILA BECAUSE NO PRIOR ORDER EXISTS AND A CUSTODY DETERMINATION IS NECESSARY TO PROTECT HER BEST INTERESTS.
AS 25.20.060 expressly grants either parent the right to petition the superior court for resolution of a custody dispute, and directs the court to award custody based on the best interests of the child. Because no court has ever entered a formal custody order for Mila, this proceeding represents an initial custody determination in which this Court has full authority and responsibility to fashion an arrangement that serves Mila's best interests without any presumption in favor of the status quo.
The absence of any formal order has left Mila in a position of ongoing instability. The informal parenting arrangement the parties attempted to maintain since March 2024 has been inconsistently followed, depriving Mila of the predictable routine that is essential to the healthy development of a two-year-old child. A formal custody order will provide Mila with the stability and continuity she needs, will give both parents clear and enforceable rights and responsibilities, and will establish a framework to resolve any future disputes through proper legal channels rather than unilateral action.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that stability and continuity in a young child's life are central considerations in custody proceedings. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018). The desirability of maintaining continuity in a child's stable environment is expressly listed as one of the statutory best-interests factors under AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Mila has spent her entire life in Anchorage and has developed relationships and a routine in that community. A court order will ensure that any disruption to that environment, including a potential relocation, is subject to appropriate judicial review focused on Mila's needs.
B. THE BEST INTERESTS OF MILA SUPPORT AN AWARD OF JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY AND SUBSTANTIAL PHYSICAL CUSTODY TO PRIYA.
The court must evaluate each factor under AS 25.24.150(c) as applied to the specific facts of Mila's situation. Several factors weigh in favor of a custody arrangement that gives Priya meaningful legal authority and substantial parenting time.
1. Mila's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs Require Consistent Access to Both Parents.
A two-year-old child's development depends critically on stable, nurturing relationships with both parents. Priya has been consistently present in Mila's life from birth and has demonstrated a commitment to meeting Mila's physical, emotional, and social needs throughout the parties' relationship and after separation. An order ensuring Priya's continued involvement directly serves factor (1) of AS 25.24.150(c), which requires the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child.
2. Priya Has the Capability and Desire to Meet Mila's Needs.
Factor (2) of AS 25.24.150(c) directs the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. Priya seeks this custody order precisely because of her deep commitment to Mila's well-being. Priya has been an active and engaged parent throughout Mila's life and is prepared to provide a safe, stable, and nurturing home environment for Mila on a consistent basis.
3. The Love and Affection Between Mila and Priya Is a Substantial Factor.
Factor (4) of AS 25.24.150(c) calls on the court to consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. The bond between Priya and Mila, developed over Mila's entire lifetime and maintained through ongoing parenting time even after the parties' separation, is a compelling consideration in support of a custody arrangement that preserves and strengthens that bond. Severing or substantially diminishing Priya's parenting time, particularly through an unplanned relocation, would harm a relationship that is plainly in Mila's best interests to preserve.
4. The Desirability of Maintaining Continuity Weighs Against an Unilateral Relocation.
Factor (5) of AS 25.24.150(c) directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Mila has lived her entire life in Anchorage. Her home community, her relationship with Priya, and whatever additional community connections she has formed there represent the only stable environment she has ever known. A unilateral relocation to Juneau, without a court order governing custody and parenting time, would disrupt that continuity without any judicial weighing of whether the move serves Mila's best interests.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must carefully consider the disruptive effects of proposed changes on young children when evaluating custody arrangements. Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020). This Court should exercise its authority under AS 25.20.060 to ensure that any change to Mila's living situation is evaluated through a proper best-interests analysis rather than being imposed unilaterally by one parent.
5. Both Parents Should Be Required to Facilitate the Other's Relationship With Mila.
Factor (6) of AS 25.24.150(c) considers the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a parent's demonstrated willingness, or lack thereof, to foster the child's relationship with the other parent is a meaningful consideration in custody determinations. Van Sickle v. McGraw, 134 P.3d 338 (Alaska 2006). A formal custody order should require both Priya and Jennifer to actively support Mila's relationship with the other parent, and should specifically address the circumstances under which any potential relocation would be handled to ensure that Priya's parenting time is not unilaterally eliminated.
C. THE COURT SHOULD ENTER A JOINT LEGAL CUSTODY ORDER AND CONSIDER SHARED PHYSICAL CUSTODY AS A MEANS OF MAXIMIZING MILA'S CONTACT WITH BOTH PARENTS.
AS 25.20.060(c) authorizes the court to award shared custody if that arrangement is determined to be in the best interests of the child, and directs that any such award must assure that Mila has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Priya submits that joint legal custody, giving both parents equal authority over major decisions affecting Mila's health, education, and welfare, is plainly in Mila's best interests and appropriate given that both parents have been involved in her care.
With respect to physical custody, Priya seeks a substantial parenting schedule that allows Mila to maintain a strong, consistent bond with both parents. If the parties remain in Anchorage, a shared physical custody arrangement would be feasible and would serve Mila's interest in frequent contact with both parents. If Jennifer proceeds with her intended relocation to Juneau, this Court should determine, following a proper hearing and best-interests analysis, what physical custody arrangement best serves Mila under those changed circumstances, including whether the relocation itself is consistent with Mila's best interests.
Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1) defines shared physical custody as a period of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year with each parent. Should this Court award shared physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides the applicable framework for calculating child support under a shared custody arrangement. Priya requests that any custody order also address child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(b), using each parent's adjusted annual income and the applicable percentage guidelines.
D. THE COURT SHOULD APPOINT A GUARDIAN AD LITEM TO REPRESENT MILA'S BEST INTERESTS IN THESE PROCEEDINGS.
Given Mila's very young age, she is not capable of forming or expressing a preference regarding custody. Civil Rule 90.7(e) provides that the guardian ad litem shall represent and advocate the best interests of the child and shall be treated as a party to the proceeding for all purposes. Appointment of a guardian ad litem would provide the Court with an independent voice focused solely on Mila's best interests, untethered to either parent's litigation position. This is particularly important in a proceeding that involves a potential relocation and an initial custody determination for a child who has never had the benefit of court-established protections. Priya respectfully requests that the Court appoint a guardian ad litem for Mila pursuant to Civil Rule 90.7(e).
E. THE COURT SHOULD ENTER A FORMAL ORDER BEFORE ANY RELOCATION OCCURS SO THAT MILA'S BEST INTERESTS GOVERN THE DECISION.
Jennifer has communicated her intention to relocate with Mila to Juneau. Because there is currently no custody order in place, Jennifer is not technically prohibited from relocating with Mila. However, absent a court order, Priya has no legal mechanism to ensure that the relocation is evaluated through the best-interests framework that Alaska law requires to govern all custody determinations. Once Mila is relocated and a new routine is established in Juneau, the desirability-of-continuity factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(5) may weigh against restoring her Anchorage connections, creating a fait accompli that disadvantages Priya despite the absence of any judicial finding that the relocation serves Mila's best interests.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of ensuring that custody decisions are made through proper judicial processes rather than through unilateral parental action, and that courts should be attentive to arrangements that are imposed on the ground in advance of a ruling. Jayda Roman v. Cleveland Karren, 461 P.3d 1252 (Alaska 2020); Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011). Priya respectfully requests that the Court enter an interim order maintaining Mila's current residence in Anchorage and preserving Priya's parenting time pending a full hearing on custody, so that any decision about Mila's future residence is made by this Court on the basis of evidence and the statutory best-interests factors, not by one parent's unilateral choice.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Priya Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Exercise its authority under AS 25.20.060 and AS 25.24.150 to establish a formal legal and physical custody arrangement for Mila Petrova;
2. Award joint legal custody to both Priya Petrova and Jennifer Petrova, giving both parents equal authority over major decisions affecting Mila's health, education, and welfare;
3. Award Priya Petrova substantial physical custody of Mila, with a parenting schedule that ensures Mila has frequent and continuing contact with Priya to the maximum extent consistent with Mila's best interests;
4. Enter an interim order maintaining Mila's current residence in Anchorage and preserving Priya's parenting time pending a full evidentiary hearing on custody, to prevent any unilateral relocation from occurring before this Court has had the opportunity to evaluate the proposed move through the best-interests framework of AS 25.24.150(c);
5. Appoint a guardian ad litem for Mila pursuant to Civil Rule 90.7(e) to independently advocate for Mila's best interests throughout these proceedings;
6. Establish a child support obligation consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(b) based on the custody arrangement determined by the Court; and
7. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper in Mila's best interests.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0073)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Okafor respectfully petitions this Court to establish a formal custody order governing the care, custody, and parenting time of the parties' minor daughter, Maya Okafor, age two. Priya and Respondent Sarah Okafor separated in early 2023 following approximately three years together. Since the separation, Maya has resided primarily with Sarah in Anchorage, while Priya has exercised informal weekend parenting time under a loose verbal agreement that carries no legal force. No court has ever issued a custody order for Maya, and therefore this proceeding constitutes an initial custody determination.
The urgency of this petition is driven by Sarah's stated intention to relocate with Maya to Fairbanks for a new employment opportunity. Without a formal parenting plan in place, Priya has no legal mechanism to protect her relationship with her daughter, to object to the proposed relocation, or to enforce any parenting time whatsoever. The informal arrangement that has governed the parties' co-parenting since separation is wholly inadequate to address the significant change that a move from Anchorage to Fairbanks would impose on Priya and Maya's relationship.
Priya respectfully requests that this Court exercise jurisdiction over this initial custody determination, evaluate the best interests of the child under the applicable statutory factors, and enter a formal parenting plan that preserves Maya's meaningful relationship with both of her parents regardless of where either parent ultimately resides.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Okafor and Sarah Okafor were in a romantic relationship for approximately three years before separating in early 2023. During their relationship, the parties resided together in Anchorage, Alaska. Their daughter, Maya Okafor, was born during the relationship and is presently two years of age. Maya has lived her entire life in Anchorage, Alaska, and has therefore been a continuous resident of this state from birth through the date of this filing.
Upon the parties' separation, no custody proceeding was initiated and no court order was entered governing Maya's care. The parties reached a loose verbal agreement under which Maya would reside primarily with Sarah while Priya would spend time with Maya on weekends. This arrangement has been informal and unenforceable, resting entirely on the goodwill and cooperation of both parties. There is no written parenting plan, no specification of holiday or vacation parenting time, and no mechanism for resolving disputes.
The parties' separation stemmed in part from increasing conflict over finances and differing parenting philosophies. These areas of disagreement have not been resolved and continue to present challenges to co-parenting communication.
Priya has consistently exercised her weekend parenting time throughout the period since separation and has remained an active and engaged parent in Maya's life. Priya's bond with Maya is strong, and Maya has benefited from ongoing contact with both of her parents during this period.
Sarah has recently indicated her intention to relocate with Maya from Anchorage to Fairbanks in connection with a new job opportunity. Sarah has not sought Priya's consent to this move, nor has any court authorized such a relocation. Because no custody order exists, Priya currently has no legal recourse to prevent the move or to demand that her parenting time be preserved and formalized before any relocation occurs. The proposed move would significantly disrupt the parenting arrangement that has been in place since separation and would substantially diminish the frequency of Priya's in-person contact with Maya if no formal plan is established.
Both parties are residents of Alaska. Maya has lived her entire life in Alaska. All relevant evidence concerning Maya's care, protection, and personal relationships is located in this state. Alaska is the appropriate forum to adjudicate this initial custody determination.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Jurisdiction
Alaska courts have jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination when this state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding. AS 25.30.300(a)(1). Alaska is Maya's home state, as she has lived in Anchorage from birth through the present date, well in excess of the six consecutive months required to establish home state status. AS 25.30.300(a)(1). This Court therefore has proper jurisdiction to enter an initial custody determination for Maya.
B. Standard for Initial Custody Determination
Where a dispute over child custody exists between parents, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution under AS 25.20.060. The court is required to award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.060(a). In determining the best interests of the child, the court must consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). AS 25.20.060(a).
The factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c) include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable and satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence of substance abuse by either parent; and other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(c).
The court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined to be in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.060(c). An award of shared custody must assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c).
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that courts evaluating initial custody determinations must carefully and thoroughly analyze each applicable best interests factor on the record, and that failure to address the statutory factors is reversible error. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018). Courts must consider the totality of circumstances bearing on a child's welfare when fashioning a custody arrangement. Jaymot v. Skillings-Donat, 216 P.3d 534 (Alaska 2009).
C. Child Support
Once a custody arrangement is established, child support must be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 959(a), where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, child support is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). Where both parents are awarded shared physical custody, meaning the children reside with each parent for between thirty and seventy percent of the year, support is calculated under the shared custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 948(b). Civil Rule 919(f)(1) defines shared physical custody as a period specified in the custody order of at least 30, but no more than 70, percent of the year.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. This Court Has Jurisdiction to Enter an Initial Custody Order for Maya.
This Court has subject matter jurisdiction to adjudicate an initial custody determination for Maya because Alaska is Maya's home state within the meaning of AS 25.30.300. Maya was born in Anchorage and has resided in Anchorage continuously from birth through the present. AS 25.30.300(a)(1) grants jurisdiction to a court of this state to make an initial child custody determination when this state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding. Because Maya has lived in Alaska her entire life, this state is unquestionably her home state. No competing jurisdiction has issued a custody order for Maya, and no proceeding is pending in any other state. All relevant parties reside in Alaska, and all material evidence concerning Maya's care, protection, training, and personal relationships is available in this state. This Court therefore has full and proper jurisdiction to proceed.
Furthermore, because no prior custody determination exists for Maya in any jurisdiction, this is purely an initial custody proceeding and not a modification matter. There is no existing order to modify, no court that previously exercised jurisdiction, and no restriction on this Court's authority to enter whatever custody arrangement serves Maya's best interests. AS 25.30.310 governs the exclusive continuing jurisdiction of a court that has already made a custody determination; that statute has no application here, as no prior determination has been made. This Court proceeds on a clean slate and is authorized to fashion a parenting plan that serves Maya's welfare going forward.
B. Priya Has Standing to Petition for an Initial Custody Determination.
AS 25.20.060(a) provides that if there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the matter. Priya is Maya's parent and has exercised regular parenting time since the parties' separation. Priya has a direct, substantial, and legally cognizable interest in obtaining a formal custody order for her daughter. Sarah's stated intention to relocate Maya to Fairbanks without Priya's consent has created a concrete and immediate dispute over custody and parenting time. That dispute falls squarely within the subject matter covered by AS 25.20.060, and Priya has full standing to invoke this Court's authority to resolve it.
Neither parent is entitled to a preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b). Accordingly, the fact that Maya has been living primarily with Sarah since separation does not automatically favor Sarah in this proceeding. The Court must assess both parents evenhandedly in light of the statutory best interests factors.
C. The Best Interests of Maya Require the Entry of a Formal Custody Order.
1. The Statutory Best Interests Factors Support a Meaningful Role for Priya in Maya's Life.
The court must determine custody in accordance with the best interests of the child, considering the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). A thorough analysis of those factors supports entry of a formal parenting plan that preserves and protects Priya's relationship with Maya.
As to Maya's physical, emotional, mental, and social needs, AS 25.24.150(c)(1): Maya is two years old, a critical period of development during which attachment relationships with both caregiving parents are essential to healthy social and emotional growth. Formalizing the custody arrangement will provide stability, predictability, and security for Maya by ensuring that her relationships with both Priya and Sarah are protected and consistently maintained.
As to the capability and desire of each parent to meet Maya's needs, AS 25.24.150(c)(2): Priya has consistently shown up for Maya every weekend since the parties' separation, demonstrating both the capability and the strong desire to meet her daughter's needs. The fact that Priya is now bringing this petition reflects her commitment to ensuring that Maya's welfare is protected through a binding legal framework rather than a fragile verbal agreement.
As to the love and affection between the child and each parent, AS 25.24.150(c)(4): Maya has bonded with both of her parents throughout her young life. Priya's regular weekend contact has maintained and deepened that bond. Any custody arrangement that severs or severely curtails that bond would be contrary to Maya's best interests.
As to the length of time Maya has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity, AS 25.24.150(c)(5): Maya has lived her entire life in Anchorage. Her social connections, medical providers, and sense of place are rooted in Anchorage. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of maintaining continuity and stability in a young child's environment. Saffir v. Wheeler, 436 P.3d 1009 (Alaska 2019). A relocation to Fairbanks would disrupt that continuity and remove Maya from the community she has known since birth. A formal custody order can address this concern by establishing clear provisions governing any proposed relocation.
As to the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a continuing relationship between the child and the other parent, AS 25.24.150(c)(6): Sarah's unilateral statement of intent to relocate to Fairbanks without consulting Priya or seeking a court-approved modification raises legitimate concern about her willingness to prioritize Maya's relationship with Priya. There is no evidence before this Court that Priya has done anything to interfere with Sarah's relationship with Maya. This factor weighs in Priya's favor.
As to other pertinent factors, AS 25.24.150(c)(9): The absence of any formal custody order is itself a circumstance that has left Maya's legal security and Priya's parental rights entirely unprotected. The entry of a formal order will provide both parents with clear legal obligations and both the child and each parent with enforceable rights.
2. The Court Should Consider a Shared Custody Arrangement.
AS 25.20.060(c) expressly authorizes the court to award shared custody when that arrangement is in the best interests of the child, and directs that such an award must assure frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. Given that the parties have maintained an informal parenting arrangement since separation in which Priya exercises regular weekend parenting time, a formal shared or primary-with-substantial-visitation arrangement would reflect and build upon the status quo while providing the legal certainty and enforceability that the current situation lacks.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must carefully assess each best interests factor and may properly structure custody to reflect the realities of the parties' post-separation parenting practices. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018). In Pingree v. Cossette, the court noted that a week-on, week-off schedule can serve the best interests of a child when both parents are capable and engaged caregivers. Here, a similar shared arrangement may be achievable if both parties reside in the same city. If Sarah proceeds with relocation to Fairbanks, the Court should establish an alternative schedule that preserves extended blocks of parenting time for Priya, including extended summer parenting time and holidays, consistent with the framework the Alaska Supreme Court approved in Jaymot v. Skillings-Donat, 216 P.3d 534 (Alaska 2009), where the court awarded the non-primary parent substantial summer visitation to compensate for geographic distance during the school year.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized the authority of a trial court to enter alternative custody arrangements dependent on whether a proposed relocation actually occurs, so that the parenting plan reflects the actual circumstances of the parties at the time it takes effect. Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011); Saffir v. Wheeler, 436 P.3d 1009 (Alaska 2019). Priya requests that this Court enter exactly such a dual alternative parenting plan: one schedule applicable if both parties remain in the Anchorage area, and a second schedule applicable in the event that Sarah relocates to Fairbanks.
3. The Court Must Address Child Support Concurrent with the Custody Determination.
Once the Court determines the custody arrangement, it must calculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. If Sarah is awarded primary physical custody within the meaning of Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), meaning Maya resides with Priya for less than thirty percent of the year, child support would be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) as an amount equal to Priya's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage. If the Court awards shared physical custody within the meaning of Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), meaning Maya resides with each parent for between thirty and seventy percent of the year, support would be calculated under the shared custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b). Priya requests that the Court enter a child support order consistent with whichever custody structure is determined to serve Maya's best interests.
D. Sarah's Proposed Relocation Cannot Proceed Without Court Authorization Under a Formal Custody Order.
Because no custody order exists, Sarah's ability to relocate with Maya is currently unrestricted as a formal legal matter. However, the entry of a custody order by this Court will immediately change that status. Once a custody order is entered, any subsequent proposed relocation by the primary custodian that would materially affect the other parent's parenting time is subject to court review under AS 25.20.110. Any finding that a change in circumstances requires modification of the custody arrangement must be accompanied by a best interests analysis. AS 25.20.110(a). The entry of a formal order now will therefore create the legal framework necessary to protect Priya's rights going forward, including giving Priya the standing and legal mechanism to contest any future relocation that would be contrary to Maya's best interests.
The lack of a formal custody order has left Priya without any legal protection for her relationship with her daughter. That gap must be closed promptly. The entry of a formal parenting plan is not only appropriate, it is necessary.
E. Civil Rule 86(l) Governs the Procedural Mechanism for this Custody Petition.
Civil Rule 86(l) provides that an order to show cause, rather than a writ of habeas corpus, shall be issued initially if the action is brought by a parent to obtain custody of a child under the age of sixteen from another parent. Maya is two years old. Priya is her parent. This proceeding is therefore properly initiated by order to show cause, and Priya requests that the Court issue such an order directing Sarah to appear and show cause why a formal custody order should not be entered consistent with the relief requested in this petition.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Priya Okafor respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Exercise jurisdiction over this initial custody determination pursuant to AS 25.30.300(a)(1), as Alaska is Maya's home state;
2. Issue an order to show cause pursuant to Civil Rule 86(l) directing Sarah Okafor to appear and respond to this petition;
3. Conduct a hearing on the merits of the initial custody determination and evaluate the best interests of Maya under the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.060;
4. Enter a formal parenting plan that provides Priya with meaningful, enforceable parenting time, including alternative provisions addressing both the scenario in which the parties remain in Anchorage and the scenario in which Sarah relocates to Fairbanks;
5. Calculate and enter a child support order in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3, consistent with the custody arrangement the Court determines is in Maya's best interests; and
6. Grant such further relief as this Court deems just and proper in the best interests of Maya Okafor.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0074)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Bergstrom ("Father") petitions this Court to establish a formal order for legal and physical custody of his four-year-old daughter, Mia Bergstrom ("Mia"). No prior custody order has ever been entered for Mia. Since the parties separated in early 2023, Father has maintained an active and loving role in Mia's life through an informal, unscheduled parenting arrangement that has depended entirely on the mutual agreement of both parties. That arrangement is now threatened. Jennifer Bergstrom ("Mother") has announced her intention to relocate with Mia from Anchorage to Fairbanks, a decision that, without a binding court order in place, Father has no legal mechanism to contest or even to seek input upon.
Father does not seek to displace Mia from a loving home. He seeks only what Alaska law guarantees every child: a stable, court-ordered arrangement that reflects Mia's best interests, preserves her close bond with both parents, and ensures that no unilateral decision by either party can sever or substantially diminish her relationship with the other. The time for informal arrangements has passed. Father respectfully requests that this Court exercise its jurisdiction under AS 25.20.060 to enter an initial custody order that serves Mia's physical, emotional, and developmental needs, provides equal and meaningful access to both of her parents, and prevents any relocation from proceeding until this Court has had the opportunity to evaluate those needs fully.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Bergstrom and Jennifer Bergstrom are the unmarried parents of Mia Bergstrom, born in 2021 and currently four years old. The parties maintained an on-and-off romantic relationship for approximately three years before mutually deciding to separate in early 2023 when their relationship had become unworkable. Their separation was not the product of domestic violence, abuse, or any emergency circumstance; it was a mutual acknowledgment that their romantic partnership had run its course.
Since the separation, Mia has resided primarily with Mother in Anchorage, Alaska. Father has remained a consistent presence in Mia's life, exercising parenting time on an informal, unscheduled basis whenever both parties agreed to the arrangement. This ad hoc system has never been reduced to writing, has never been reviewed or approved by any court, and has never carried the force of a binding legal order. No court has ever entered any order governing legal custody, physical custody, or parenting time for Mia.
Father has at all relevant times resided in Anchorage, has been available and willing to care for Mia, and has sought to maintain frequent and meaningful contact with his daughter. The current arrangement, while workable in the short term, offers Father no legal protection and provides Mia no guarantee of stability or continuity of contact with her Father.
Mother recently informed Father that she intends to relocate with Mia to Fairbanks. This announcement has made clear that the informal arrangement cannot continue to serve Mia's interests. A move to Fairbanks would substantially alter the geographic and practical realities of Father's parenting time and would, if permitted to proceed without court oversight, effectively allow Mother to unilaterally restructure Mia's life and her access to her Father. Father now petitions this Court to establish a formal custody order that accounts for all relevant best-interest factors, protects his relationship with Mia, and ensures that any proposed relocation is subject to full judicial scrutiny before it is permitted to occur.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska Superior Courts have jurisdiction to adjudicate initial custody disputes between unmarried parents under AS 25.20.060. That statute provides that if there is a dispute over child custody, either parent may petition the superior court for resolution of the matter. The court is directed to award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child and to consider all relevant factors, including those enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Neither parent is entitled to any preference in the awarding of custody. AS 25.20.060(b). The court may award shared custody to both parents if shared custody is determined to be in the best interests of the child, and any such award must assure that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible. AS 25.20.060(c).
Under AS 25.20.070, during the pendency of a custody proceeding, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child considering the factors under AS 25.24.150(c), or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) is present, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents.
