Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), illustrates how a parent's relocation can constitute a substantial change in circumstances that warrants modification of a custody arrangement, even an interim one. Here, there is not even an interim order in place. If Maria relocates before an order is entered, Tomas will be left without any legal protection for his parenting rights while Lena is moved hundreds of miles away.
Furthermore, the Court's initial custody determination must include consideration of the proposed relocation as a pertinent factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(9). A relocation to Fairbanks would require Lena to leave her established Anchorage environment, sever her consistent contact with her father, and adjust to an entirely new community at an age when stability is paramount. These consequences directly affect Lena's well-being and must be weighed as part of the Court's best-interests analysis.
The Court should also be mindful that AS 25.30.310 provides that once this Court makes a custody determination consistent with AS 25.30.300, it retains exclusive continuing jurisdiction until neither the child, nor the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent have a significant connection with this state, or until neither the child nor any parent resides here. Allowing a relocation before this Court enters an order could create complications regarding the continuity of Alaska's jurisdiction and could force Tomas to litigate custody across state lines in the future.
D. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE DETERMINED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3
The Court should also establish child support as part of this proceeding. Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. If the Court awards shared physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f), the support calculation would proceed under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for the percentage of time each parent has physical custody and each parent's adjusted annual income.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), a parent has shared physical custody of a child for purposes of the rule if the child resides with that parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year, regardless of the status of legal custody. Tomas intends to present the Court with sufficient financial documentation to enable an accurate support calculation, and he respectfully requests that the Court enter a support order consistent with Civil Rule 90.3 concurrent with its custody determination.
In Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that custody and support issues should proceed together so that a comprehensive order protecting the child's interests can be entered. Consistent with that approach, Tomas requests that the Court address both custody and support in a single order.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Tomas Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Exercise jurisdiction under AS 25.30.300 and AS 25.20.060 to make an initial custody determination concerning Lena Bergstrom;
2. Award Tomas and Maria joint legal custody of Lena;
3. Enter a formal physical custody schedule providing Lena with frequent and continuing contact with both parents, consistent with her best interests under AS 25.24.150(c);
4. Address and rule upon Maria's proposed relocation to Fairbanks before any such relocation is permitted to occur, giving full consideration to the impact of any relocation on Lena's stability, her relationship with Tomas, and the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c);
5. Retain exclusive continuing jurisdiction over this matter under AS 25.30.310; and
6. Enter a child support order in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3.
The Court's intervention is necessary to protect Lena's well-being, to ensure the stability and continuity she needs at this critical stage of her development, and to preserve her close and continuing relationship with both of her parents. Tomas stands ready to present the Court with any additional evidence or documentation necessary to assist in the best-interests determination.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0079)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Larsen respectfully petitions the Alaska Superior Court to establish a formal custody and visitation order governing the parties' three-year-old daughter, Lily Larsen. Renee and Michael Larsen were never married. Their relationship ended in early 2023, and since that time Lily has resided primarily with Renee in Anchorage. No court order currently governs the parenting arrangement, leaving Lily vulnerable to unilateral decisions by either parent. Most urgently, Michael Larsen has recently indicated his intention to relocate Lily to Fairbanks to live with his parents while he works during the fishing season, a plan that would sever Lily's established routines, her primary caregiver relationship, and her connections to her community without any judicial oversight. Renee now seeks a formal order establishing legal and physical custody, defining a structured parenting schedule consistent with Lily's best interests, and preventing Michael from removing Lily from Anchorage without court approval. The Alaska Superior Court has authority to resolve this dispute and must exercise that authority to protect Lily's stability and well-being.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Larsen and Michael Larsen were in a romantic relationship for approximately two years. The relationship ended in early 2023 due to ongoing conflicts over finances and Michael's repeated, extended absences for seasonal fishing work on the Kenai Peninsula. The parties were never married.
The parties' daughter, Lily Larsen, is approximately three years old. Since the separation, Lily has resided primarily with Renee in Anchorage. Renee has served as Lily's day-to-day caregiver, providing for her physical, emotional, and social needs. Lily has developed consistent routines in Anchorage, including her childcare environment and her social relationships.
Michael exercises parenting time with Lily on an informal, loosely scheduled basis when he returns from his seasonal work on the Kenai Peninsula. The parenting arrangement between the parties has never been reduced to a court order, and no formal custody or visitation agreement is in place.
Michael has recently expressed his intention to take Lily to Fairbanks to reside with his parents during the fishing season. Renee has not consented to this arrangement. The proposed relocation would remove Lily from her primary caregiver, her established home, and her community in Anchorage for an indefinite period, and would place her in the care of paternal grandparents without any judicial determination that such an arrangement serves Lily's best interests.
Renee now petitions the court to establish legal custody, physical custody, and a defined parenting schedule, and to prohibit Michael from relocating Lily without a court order authorizing such a change.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.060, either parent of a child may petition the superior court to resolve a custody dispute. The court shall award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child. In determining the best interests of the child, the court shall consider all relevant factors, including those factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), and the presumption established in AS 25.24.150(g). AS 25.20.060 also authorizes shared custody where that arrangement is in the best interests of the child and assures that the child has frequent and continuing contact with each parent to the maximum extent possible.
The factors the court must consider under AS 25.24.150(c) include the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence of substance abuse; and other factors the court considers pertinent.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the best interests of the child is the paramount and controlling standard in all custody determinations. Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011); Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011). Courts must assess the totality of circumstances bearing on the child's welfare and must weigh each statutory factor with care. Harris v. Governale, 311 P.3d 1052 (Alaska 2013).
Stability and continuity of environment are significant factors under the best interests analysis. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a child's need for stability and continuity in custody arrangements is a weighty consideration, and courts should avoid disruptions that undermine an established caregiving relationship. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011); Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005).
Additionally, each parent's willingness to facilitate a continuing relationship between the other parent and the child is expressly enumerated as a factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(6). The Alaska Supreme Court has treated a parent's interference with the other parent's relationship with the child as a serious negative factor in custody determinations. Blanton v. Yourkowski, 180 P.3d 948 (Alaska 2008).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. THE COURT HAS AUTHORITY AND JURISDICTION TO ESTABLISH CUSTODY AND VISITATION FOR LILY.
The Alaska Superior Court has jurisdiction to establish custody and visitation for Lily. Under AS 25.20.060, either parent may petition the superior court to resolve a custody dispute. Because Lily resides in Anchorage, Alaska, this court is the appropriate forum to make an initial custody determination. Under AS 25.30.310, once this court makes a child custody determination, it retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over that determination until a court finds that neither the child, the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent have a significant connection with this state, or until neither the child nor a parent presently resides in this state. Establishing a custody order now will therefore secure this court's continuing authority to protect Lily and will prevent Michael from attempting to have a different jurisdiction resolve future disputes.
There is no existing order in place. This proceeding is not a modification action but an initial custody determination. The absence of any prior order makes the need for judicial intervention more urgent, not less. Without a formal order, neither parent has defined rights or responsibilities, Lily has no legal protection against unilateral decisions, and Michael is free to remove her from Anchorage without any judicial check. The court should act promptly to fill this gap.
B. THE BEST INTERESTS OF LILY REQUIRE THAT RENEE BE AWARDED PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY AND THAT BOTH PARENTS SHARE LEGAL CUSTODY.
1. Lily's Established Stability and Continuity of Environment Favor Primary Physical Custody with Renee.
Among the most important factors under AS 25.24.150(c) is the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Lily has lived with Renee in Anchorage since the parties' separation in early 2023. Since Lily was an infant she has been cared for primarily by Renee. Lily's routines, her childcare arrangements, and her social environment are all anchored in Anchorage.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized that disrupting an established primary caregiver relationship and a stable home environment is harmful to young children and must be weighed heavily against any proposed change. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011); Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005). Lily is only three years old. At this stage of her development, consistency in her primary attachment relationship, her home, and her daily routines is essential to her emotional and psychological well-being.
Michael's work pattern, which requires him to spend extended periods on the Kenai Peninsula during the fishing season, has prevented him from serving as Lily's primary caregiver. He exercises parenting time informally and only when his work schedule permits. While this court does not question Michael's affection for Lily, his inconsistent availability is relevant to the court's assessment of his current capability to meet Lily's day-to-day needs. AS 25.24.150(c)(2).
Awarding Renee primary physical custody preserves the stability Lily has known since birth. It avoids a disruptive transfer of Lily's primary residence to a household, whether in Fairbanks with paternal grandparents or elsewhere, that Lily has not inhabited and that would require her to adjust to new caregivers, a new community, and a new daily structure without adequate preparation or court oversight.
2. The Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs of Lily Are Best Met by Renee Serving as Primary Custodian.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(1), the court must consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Lily is a toddler whose developmental needs require consistent, responsive caregiving. Renee has been the parent meeting those needs every day since the separation. Michael's extended seasonal absences mean that Lily would face prolonged periods without contact with her primary parent if Michael were awarded primary physical custody.
The court must also consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet Lily's needs. AS 25.24.150(c)(2). Renee has demonstrated, through her consistent day-to-day caregiving, that she is both willing and capable of meeting Lily's needs. Michael, through no fault reflected on his character, has a work schedule that structurally limits his availability during the fishing season.
3. Joint Legal Custody Is Appropriate Provided Michael Demonstrates a Willingness to Cooperate.
Renee does not seek to exclude Michael from meaningful participation in Lily's life. Rather, Renee seeks a formal framework that protects Lily's stability while preserving Michael's role as her father. Under AS 25.20.060, the court may award shared custody where it is in the best interests of the child. Shared legal custody, meaning joint decision-making authority over major decisions affecting Lily's education, health care, and welfare, is appropriate here so long as Michael demonstrates a willingness to cooperate and to prioritize Lily's interests over his own convenience.
However, the court should take careful note that Michael's stated intention to relocate Lily to Fairbanks without Renee's consent and without a court order is itself a factor bearing on his willingness to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between Lily and Renee. AS 25.24.150(c)(6). The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a parent's interference with the other parent's access to the child, including efforts to disrupt established caregiving arrangements, is a serious negative factor in custody determinations. Blanton v. Yourkowski, 180 P.3d 948 (Alaska 2008). The court should weigh Michael's proposed unilateral relocation accordingly.
C. MICHAEL SHOULD NOT BE PERMITTED TO RELOCATE LILY TO FAIRBANKS WITHOUT A COURT ORDER.
Michael's stated intention to remove Lily from Anchorage and place her with his parents in Fairbanks during the fishing season would, if carried out, cause immediate and significant harm to Lily's stability and to Renee's custodial relationship with her daughter. Such a unilateral relocation, in the absence of any court order and without Renee's consent, would be inconsistent with Lily's best interests under AS 25.24.150 and AS 25.20.060.
No court has authorized such a relocation. No custody order permits Michael to place Lily with third parties, including his parents, as a substitute for his own parenting time. The absence of any formal order does not give Michael authority to make this decision unilaterally. To the contrary, the absence of an order is precisely the reason Renee now seeks judicial intervention, so that no parent may take unilateral action affecting Lily's welfare without court oversight.
The court should enter an order expressly prohibiting either party from removing Lily from Anchorage, or from placing Lily in the care of any third party as a substitute for primary residence with either parent, without prior court approval or written consent of the other parent. This geographic restriction is necessary to protect Lily's stability while these proceedings are resolved.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that parenting plans in custody agreements commonly include provisions requiring notice and court approval before relocation, and that courts may impose such restrictions in the best interests of the child. Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011); Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011). Although those cases arose in the context of dissolution proceedings, the underlying principle, that a child's interests are protected by requiring judicial oversight before a significant geographic change is made, applies with equal force in an initial custody determination under AS 25.20.060.
D. THE COURT SHOULD ESTABLISH A STRUCTURED PARENTING SCHEDULE THAT PROVIDES MICHAEL WITH MEANINGFUL PARENTING TIME WHILE PROTECTING LILY'S STABILITY.
Renee recognizes that Lily benefits from a meaningful relationship with Michael and does not seek to limit his involvement in Lily's life. The goal of this proceeding is to establish a formal, predictable parenting schedule that gives Lily the stability she needs and gives Michael defined, reliable parenting time consistent with his work schedule.
The court has broad authority under AS 25.24.150 and AS 25.20.060 to craft a parenting schedule tailored to the specific circumstances of this family. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently upheld custody arrangements that account for the realities of a parent's work schedule while ensuring that the child has frequent and continuing contact with both parents. Harris v. Governale, 311 P.3d 1052 (Alaska 2013); Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005).
A workable parenting schedule for this family might include regular parenting time for Michael during periods when he is present in Anchorage, extended parenting time during his off-season, and defined holiday and vacation periods. Any parenting schedule should require that Michael provide Renee with advance notice of his availability so that Lily's childcare arrangements can be planned accordingly. The schedule should also specify that during any period in which Michael exercises parenting time, he is the responsible caregiver, and that he may not delegate that responsibility to his parents or other third parties without Renee's written consent or court approval.
E. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3.
Once the court establishes a custody arrangement, it should also address child support. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, child support is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which for one child is 20% (.20). Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). Adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources, reduced by mandatory deductions and other qualifying expenses as specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Because Michael's income may be seasonal in nature, reflecting the patterns of commercial fishing work, the court may order that child support payments be structured to account for periods of higher and lower income during the year, as authorized by Civil Rule 90.3(c)(5). In the event Michael claims that application of the standard guidelines would result in manifest injustice, he bears the burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1), and the court must specify in writing the reason for any variation and the amount that would otherwise have been required.

V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Renee Larsen respectfully requests that the Alaska Superior Court enter an order:

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION BETWEEN UNMARRIED PARENTS
(doc-0080)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Okafor ("David") petitions this Court for an initial child custody determination concerning Mara Okafor ("Mara"), age two, who has resided primarily with David in Anchorage, Alaska since her parents' separation in early 2023. David and Wesley Okafor ("Wesley") are unmarried former partners who have never obtained a court order governing custody, visitation, or parental rights with respect to Mara. Wesley has recently threatened to relocate Mara to Fairbanks indefinitely without David's knowledge or consent. Because no enforceable parenting plan exists, David has no legal mechanism to prevent such a unilateral removal and no means to compel Wesley's compliance with any agreed arrangement. This Court has jurisdiction to enter an initial custody determination under AS 25.30.300 because Alaska is Mara's home state. The best interests of the child require a formal, legally enforceable parenting plan that protects Mara's stability, preserves her primary relationship with David, and establishes clear boundaries on Wesley's parenting time. David respectfully requests that this Court enter an order awarding him primary physical custody of Mara, with structured visitation for Wesley, and prohibiting either party from removing Mara from the State of Alaska without court authorization.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Okafor and Wesley Okafor were unmarried partners for approximately three years. Their relationship produced one child, Mara Okafor, who is currently two years of age. The parties ended their relationship in early 2023, separating under difficult circumstances following a period of escalating conflict in the household.
Since the separation, Mara has resided primarily with David in Anchorage, Alaska. David has served as Mara's consistent, primary caregiver throughout her entire life. Wesley has provided only informal and inconsistent care, participating in Mara's life on a roughly every-other-weekend basis, and no formal schedule has been memorialized in any court order or written agreement.
No court has ever entered an order governing custody, visitation, parental rights, or any other aspect of Mara's care. As a result, neither parent has any legally enforceable rights or obligations with respect to the other concerning Mara's custody or residence.
Wesley has recently threatened to take Mara to Fairbanks, Alaska, indefinitely, without David's consent, without advance notice, and without any court authorization. This threat is credible given the acrimonious nature of the parties' separation and Wesley's pattern of exercising parenting time on an inconsistent and unilateral basis. Without a court order, David has no legal means to prevent Wesley from removing Mara from Anchorage or even from the State of Alaska.
Mara has spent her entire two years of life primarily in David's care in Anchorage. She has established bonds, routines, and a stable environment in David's home. Disrupting this environment through an unplanned relocation to Fairbanks would cause Mara significant harm by depriving her of stability, continuity of care, and her primary attachment relationship. David brings this petition to protect Mara's well-being and to obtain a legally enforceable order that will govern the parties' parental rights going forward.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Jurisdiction
Before addressing the merits of a custody petition, this Court must confirm that it has jurisdiction to enter a custody determination. Under AS 25.30.300(a), an Alaska court has jurisdiction to make an initial child custody determination if, among other grounds, Alaska is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding. The term "home state" is defined in AS 25.30.909(7) as "the state in which a child lived with a parent or a person acting as a parent for at least six consecutive months, including any temporary absences of the child or parent or person acting as a parent, immediately before the commencement of a child custody proceeding," and, in the case of a child less than six months of age, the state in which the child lived from birth with any of the persons mentioned.
Under AS 25.30.300(b), the jurisdictional grounds set forth in subsection (a) are the exclusive bases for an Alaska court to enter a child custody determination.
Because Mara has lived with David in Anchorage for the entirety of her life, Alaska is unambiguously her home state, and this Court has jurisdiction to enter the requested order.
B. Best Interests Standard
Once jurisdiction is established, Alaska courts determine child custody in accordance with the best interests of the child. AS 25.24.150(c) sets forth the factors a court must consider in making that determination. Those factors include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect, or a history of violence between the parents; and evidence that substance abuse by either parent or other members of the household directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child. See AS 25.24.150(c)(1)-(9).
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that the best interests analysis under AS 25.24.150(c) is the controlling framework for initial and ongoing custody determinations. Smith v. Weekley, 73 P.3d 1219 (Alaska 2003). All relevant factors are weighed in light of the specific facts presented, and no single factor is automatically dispositive.
C. Exclusive, Continuing Jurisdiction
Once an Alaska court enters an initial custody determination, that court acquires exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over the determination unless and until a court finds that neither the child, the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent have a significant connection with Alaska and that substantial evidence is no longer available here, or that neither the child nor any parent or person acting as a parent continues to reside in Alaska. AS 25.30.310(a). This framework ensures stability and prevents unilateral forum shopping after a custody order is entered. Fox v. Grace, 435 P.3d 883 (Alaska 2018).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. This Court Has Jurisdiction to Enter an Initial Custody Determination Because Alaska Is Mara's Home State.
Alaska is the only state with jurisdiction to enter an initial custody determination regarding Mara. Mara, age two, has lived with David in Anchorage for the entirety of her life. She has never resided in any other state. Under AS 25.30.300(a)(1), this Court has jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination because Alaska is Mara's home state on the date this proceeding commences. The definition of "home state" under AS 25.30.909(7) is satisfied: Mara has lived with David, her parent, in Alaska for well more than six consecutive months. No other state has any basis to claim home state jurisdiction. This Court is therefore the proper and exclusive forum to enter the requested custody determination.
Under AS 25.30.300(b), the grounds set forth in AS 25.30.300(a) are the exclusive bases for Alaska to exercise jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination. That basis is plainly satisfied here. Once this Court enters an order, it will acquire exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over the determination pursuant to AS 25.30.310(a), ensuring that Wesley cannot avoid the order by voluntarily relocating to another jurisdiction and seeking a competing order elsewhere. Fox v. Grace, 435 P.3d 883 (Alaska 2018) (explaining that for another state to modify an Alaska custody order, certain conditions must be met concerning the child's and parents' residency and another court's relinquishment of jurisdiction).
B. The Best Interests of Mara Require That David Be Awarded Primary Physical Custody.
1. Mara's Need for Stability and Continuity Favors David.
Among the most significant factors under AS 25.24.150(c) in a case involving a very young child is the desirability of maintaining continuity in a stable, satisfactory environment. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Mara is two years old. She has spent her entire life primarily in David's care in Anchorage. The bond between Mara and David, the routines David has established, and the stability of her current home environment are precisely the kinds of interests that Alaska law directs courts to protect. Disrupting a young child's primary attachment relationship and relocating her without notice or consent can cause lasting harm to the child's emotional and social development.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of stability and continuity in custody determinations, particularly for young children who depend on consistent caregiving relationships. Mendel-Gleason v. Harris, 261 P.3d 397 (Alaska 2011). Awarding primary physical custody to David preserves the only stable environment Mara has ever known.
2. David Has Demonstrated the Capability and Desire to Meet Mara's Needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs. David has been Mara's consistent, primary caregiver since her birth. He has met her day-to-day needs, provided a stable home, and ensured her well-being throughout a period of significant family disruption. Wesley, by contrast, has engaged in only informal and inconsistent parenting, participating on a roughly every-other-weekend basis with no structured plan or demonstrated commitment to a consistent parenting role.
While Wesley's interest in parenting Mara is not disputed, Wesley's pattern of inconsistent involvement and the recent threat to relocate Mara without David's consent raise serious questions about Wesley's ability to prioritize Mara's stability and well-being over Wesley's own preferences. The capability and desire factor thus weighs in favor of awarding primary physical custody to David.
3. The Love and Affection Between Mara and David Supports the Requested Award.
AS 25.24.150(c)(4) directs the court to consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. Mara's primary attachment is with David, her consistent caregiver. This attachment is not merely a product of time but of the sustained, daily caregiving relationship that David has provided. Protecting this bond by awarding primary physical custody to David serves Mara's emotional and developmental needs.
4. Wesley's Threat to Remove Mara Without Consent Is a Factor Bearing on the Parenting Plan.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) provides that the court shall consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Wesley's stated intent to remove Mara to Fairbanks indefinitely, without David's consent and without a court order authorizing the relocation, reflects a disregard for David's parental rights and for Mara's need for consistent contact with her primary caregiver. Courts have looked unfavorably upon a parent who takes unilateral action to disrupt a child's established custody arrangement or who threatens to do so. Jacob G. v. Savanah F., 545 P.3d 885 (Alaska 2024) (describing a court's issuance of a writ of assistance after a parent removed a child without the other parent's knowledge or consent).
Wesley's threatened relocation, if carried out, would sever Mara's daily relationship with David, uproot her from her established environment, and subject her to the instability of an unplanned move to another city. This conduct is inconsistent with the obligations of a parent who genuinely prioritizes the child's best interests and who is willing to foster Mara's relationship with her other parent.
5. Wesley Should Receive Structured Visitation Consistent with Mara's Best Interests.
David does not seek to terminate or minimize Wesley's relationship with Mara. A court-ordered parenting plan that provides Wesley with regular, structured visitation will serve Mara's interest in maintaining a meaningful relationship with both parents, while also providing David with the legal certainty he currently lacks. Civil Rule 65(e) recognizes the importance of preventing the unauthorized removal of a child who is the subject of a domestic relations action from the State of Alaska without the written consent of the other party. A formal parenting plan incorporating a prohibition on unauthorized removal will protect Mara from the very threat Wesley has made.
Structured visitation for Wesley, clearly defined in a court order, will also reduce the opportunity for future conflict between the parties by establishing predictable, enforceable expectations. Geldermann v. Geldermann, 428 P.3d 477 (Alaska 2018) (illustrating the difficulties that arise when custody and visitation arrangements lack clear court-ordered boundaries and the parties fail to comply with agreed terms).
C. An Order Prohibiting Removal of Mara from Alaska Is Necessary to Protect the Child.
Wesley has explicitly threatened to take Mara to Fairbanks indefinitely. While Fairbanks remains within Alaska, Wesley's willingness to threaten unilateral relocation without David's consent reflects a broader disregard for David's parental rights that, left unchecked, could escalate to an out-of-state removal. Civil Rule 65(e) permits a court in a domestic relations action to restrain the parties from removing a child who is the subject of the action from the State of Alaska without the written consent of the other party. This Court should incorporate such a prohibition into any custody order it enters.
Furthermore, AS 25.24.150(c)(5) and (c)(6) together support restricting either parent from relocating Mara outside Anchorage, or outside Alaska, without prior court approval or the written consent of the other parent. Rosemarie P. v. Kelly B., 504 P.3d 260 (Alaska 2021) (recognizing the court's broad authority to fashion a custody arrangement that serves the child's best interests in cases involving unmarried former partners). The threat of relocation is not speculative; Wesley has stated an intent to act. This Court should not wait for the harm to materialize before providing relief.
D. Proceeding Under Civil Rule 86(l) Is the Appropriate Procedural Mechanism.
Civil Rule 86(l) provides that an order to show cause, and not a writ of habeas corpus, shall be issued initially when a parent brings an action to obtain custody of a child under the age of sixteen from another parent or person. Mara is two years old. David, as her parent, is the proper petitioner in this proceeding. Proceeding by way of the custody petition and order to show cause framework established by Civil Rule 86(l) is the correct procedural vehicle for this action, and David has proceeded accordingly.
E. Once Entered, This Court's Order Will Carry Exclusive, Continuing Jurisdiction.
As noted above, upon entry of an initial custody determination, this Court will acquire exclusive, continuing jurisdiction under AS 25.30.310(a). This means that any future modification proceeding must be brought before this Court unless and until both the child and all parents cease to reside in Alaska, or unless this Court determines that significant connections and substantial evidence no longer exist in Alaska. AS 25.30.310(a)(1)-(2). This jurisdictional continuity is essential to protecting Mara's stability going forward. Wesley will not be permitted to circumvent this Court's order by relocating and seeking a competing order in another jurisdiction without satisfying the conditions set forth in AS 25.30.310 and AS 25.30.300. Fox v. Grace, 435 P.3d 883 (Alaska 2018).
V. CONCLUSION
This Court has jurisdiction under AS 25.30.300(a)(1) to enter an initial child custody determination concerning Mara Okafor. Alaska is Mara's home state, and no other state has any basis to exercise jurisdiction. The best interests of Mara, analyzed under AS 25.24.150(c), strongly favor awarding primary physical custody to David Okafor. David has been Mara's consistent, primary caregiver since her birth. He has provided stability, love, and continuity of care throughout Mara's entire life. Wesley's participation has been informal and inconsistent, and Wesley's recent threat to remove Mara to Fairbanks without David's consent underscores the urgent need for a legally enforceable order.
David respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Enter an initial custody determination awarding David Okafor primary physical custody of Mara Okafor;
2. Award Wesley Okafor regular, structured visitation according to a schedule determined by this Court to be consistent with Mara's best interests;
3. Order that neither party may remove Mara from the State of Alaska without the written consent of the other party or prior court authorization;
4. Order that any future modification of this custody determination must be brought before this Court consistent with AS 25.30.310; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper in the best interests of Mara Okafor.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0081)
I. INTRODUCTION
Jacob Okafor respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order entered in 2021 to reflect a long-distance parenting plan appropriate to the current geographic circumstances. Since the entry of the original order, Brandon Okafor has permanently relocated with the parties' two minor children from Fairbanks to Juneau, a distance of approximately 600 miles. This relocation has rendered the existing every-other-weekend and weekly evening parenting schedule physically and financially impractical. Jacob Okafor seeks an order establishing extended summer parenting time of eight consecutive weeks, alternating school-year holidays, and one annual spring break visit. The requested modification is supported by a substantial change in circumstances and is consistent with the best interests of the children under Alaska law, which recognizes that children benefit from meaningful and continuing contact with both parents to the greatest degree practicable.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties, Jacob Okafor and Brandon Okafor, were divorced in 2021. Pursuant to the Superior Court order entered at that time, Brandon Okafor was awarded primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, currently ages seven and nine. Jacob Okafor was awarded parenting time consisting of every other weekend and one evening per week. This schedule was workable when both parties resided in Fairbanks, Alaska.
Following entry of the custody order, Brandon Okafor accepted a permanent job transfer and relocated with the children to Juneau, Alaska, approximately 600 miles from Fairbanks. Jacob Okafor continues to reside in Fairbanks. The geographic distance between the two cities renders the existing parenting schedule logistically impossible to maintain. Travel between Fairbanks and Juneau is costly and time-consuming, making biweekly weekend visits and weekly evening contact impractical without imposing significant financial burdens on Jacob Okafor and subjecting the children to repeated disruptions to their schooling and routines.
Jacob Okafor has maintained a loving and involved relationship with his children throughout the period since the divorce. He seeks a modified parenting plan that accounts for the new geographic reality while preserving his meaningful participation in the children's lives. The proposed plan includes eight consecutive weeks of summer parenting time, alternating school-year holidays, and one annual spring break visit. This structure is consistent with long-distance parenting plans commonly adopted by Alaska courts in analogous circumstances and serves the children's need for consistent contact with both parents.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A custody order may be modified when the moving party demonstrates two distinct elements. First, there must be a change in circumstances that has occurred since the entry of the prior order. Second, the proposed modification must be in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child.
In assessing the best interests of the child, the court must consider the statutory factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
Additionally, AS 25.20.070 establishes that, unless detrimental to the child's welfare or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) applies, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the period the court considers a custody award. Alaska courts have also recognized, as illustrated in Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), that when a military transfer or permanent parental relocation makes a prior shared or frequent-contact schedule impossible to continue, the court must fashion a modified arrangement that preserves meaningful parental access while providing the child with stability. Similarly, Hayes v. Hayes, 922 P.2d 896 (Alaska 1996) confirms that continuity of the parental relationship may, in appropriate circumstances, outweigh the disruption caused by a change in geographic location or schooling arrangements.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Brandon Okafor's Permanent Relocation to Juneau Constitutes a Material Change in Circumstances.
The threshold requirement for modification under AS 25.20.110(a) is a change in circumstances since entry of the prior order. Brandon Okafor's acceptance of a permanent job transfer and relocation with the minor children from Fairbanks to Juneau, a distance of approximately 600 miles, plainly satisfies this requirement. The original custody order was premised on both parents residing in the same city. The every-other-weekend and weekly evening parenting schedule is structured around geographic proximity that no longer exists. The distance between Fairbanks and Juneau is not a minor inconvenience; it is a fundamental alteration of the factual landscape underlying the original order.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), is instructive here. In that case, a parent's transfer to a distant location made continuation of the existing shared custody arrangement impossible, and the court was required to craft a new parenting structure. The court there acknowledged that a parental relocation of significant distance, particularly one that is permanent in nature, constitutes a materially changed circumstance warranting judicial reconsideration of the custody arrangement. The same principle applies with full force here. Brandon Okafor's transfer is permanent, not temporary. The children's residence has shifted to a city accessible only by air or ferry from Fairbanks, at substantial cost and travel time. Jacob Okafor respectfully submits that this relocation is a textbook change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a).
Furthermore, the practical impossibility of the current schedule is itself a changed circumstance. The existing order contemplates contact every two weeks and once during each week. Neither form of contact is feasible across a 600-mile distance without extraordinary expense and repeated disruption to the children's education. A court order that cannot be practically implemented no longer serves the interests of any party, and modification is therefore required.
B. Modification to a Long-Distance Parenting Plan Is in the Best Interests of the Children.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court's inquiry turns to whether the proposed modification serves the best interests of the children. Under AS 25.24.150(c), the court must consider multiple statutory factors. Each of those factors, applied to the facts of this case, supports adoption of the proposed long-distance parenting plan.
1. The Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs of the Children Support Continued Contact with Jacob Okafor.
The parties' two children, ages seven and nine, are at formative stages of development during which a consistent and nurturing relationship with both parents is particularly important to their emotional well-being. AS 25.24.150(c)(1) directs the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. A child's need for a relationship with both parents does not diminish because one parent lives at a geographic distance. An eight-week summer block, alternating holidays, and an annual spring break visit provide a structured, predictable framework through which the children can maintain a deep and meaningful bond with Jacob Okafor. Without such a plan, Jacob Okafor's contact would be effectively reduced to infrequent and logistically burdensome visits that fail to sustain a genuine parent-child relationship.
2. Jacob Okafor Has the Capability and Desire to Meet the Children's Needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the children's needs. Jacob Okafor has consistently demonstrated his commitment to his children throughout the period since the divorce. He has maintained his parenting time to the extent the schedule has permitted and now brings this motion precisely because he desires to continue playing an active and meaningful role in his children's lives. The requested plan reflects a realistic and thoughtful effort to adapt to changed circumstances rather than to diminish his parental role.
3. The Love and Affection Between Jacob Okafor and the Children Supports the Proposed Plan.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(4), the court shall consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. Jacob Okafor has been an involved parent since the entry of the original order. The children have a meaningful relationship with him, and it is in their interest that this relationship be actively preserved. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Hayes v. Hayes, 922 P.2d 896 (Alaska 1996), that the continuity and stability of a parental relationship is a weighty factor that courts must take seriously when evaluating competing considerations in a custody modification. The continuity of Jacob Okafor's relationship with his children is best protected through the structured long-distance plan he proposes.
4. The Desirability of Maintaining Continuity of the Parental Relationship Supports the Modification.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. This factor operates in two directions in this case. Brandon Okafor has already relocated the children to Juneau, and some degree of adjustment to that new environment is inevitable. At the same time, continuity of the children's relationship with Jacob Okafor must also be preserved. The long-distance parenting plan accomplishes this by providing extended, uninterrupted periods of parenting time during summer and school breaks that allow the children to spend meaningful blocks of time with Jacob Okafor without disrupting their school-year schedule in Juneau.
5. Each Parent's Willingness to Facilitate Contact Is a Relevant Consideration.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Jacob Okafor brings this motion in good faith with the express goal of fostering and preserving the children's relationship with their primary custodial parent as well as with himself. He asks only for a schedule that is realistic given the geographic reality. The court should similarly expect that Brandon Okafor, having accepted a permanent relocation that fundamentally altered the parenting landscape, will cooperate fully with whatever plan the court establishes to protect the children's relationship with Jacob Okafor.
C. The Policy of Equal Access Under AS 25.20.070 Supports the Proposed Plan.
AS 25.20.070 provides that, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child considering the factors under AS 25.24.150(c), or unless the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) is present, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody. There is no claim of domestic violence or other factor that would trigger the presumption under AS 25.24.150(g). There is no suggestion that contact with Jacob Okafor is detrimental to the children. The proposed long-distance parenting plan, consisting of eight consecutive summer weeks, alternating holidays, and an annual spring break visit, represents the greatest degree of practical access that the geographic distance permits. It is squarely consistent with the legislative policy embedded in AS 25.20.070.
D. The Proposed Long-Distance Schedule Appropriately Accounts for Shared Custody Considerations and Child Support Implications.
To the extent the proposed modification results in extended periods during which Jacob Okafor has physical custody of the children during the summer, the court should consider the child support implications under Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(b). Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated based on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. Civil Rule 90.3(b) governs shared physical custody arrangements and provides a different calculation methodology. The court may also consider the extended visitation credit available under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3), which permits a reduction of child support payments of up to 75 percent for any period during which the obligor parent has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days. Because the proposed plan includes eight consecutive weeks of summer parenting time, Jacob Okafor respectfully requests that the court address the appropriate child support adjustment in connection with the modification, ensuring that the financial arrangement reflects the actual parenting time each parent will exercise.
E. Alaska Case Law Supports Crafting a Workable Long-Distance Parenting Plan When Relocation Makes Prior Arrangements Impractical.
The Alaska Supreme Court's decisions confirm that courts must fashion custody arrangements that reflect the practical realities facing the parties. In Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), the court acknowledged that when a permanent change in a parent's location makes a prior parenting schedule impossible to continue, the appropriate judicial response is to construct a new plan that serves the children's best interests within the new factual constraints. The parties in that case agreed on a school-year-with-one-parent and summer-with-the-other-parent framework precisely because it preserved meaningful contact with the non-primary parent despite a significant relocation.
In Havel v. Hogan, 216 P.3d 1142 (Alaska 2009), the Alaska Supreme Court emphasized that when a court establishes or modifies a parenting schedule, it must do so in a manner that accurately reflects the realistic division of time each parent will have with the child and must not reduce a parent's time below the level supported by the evidence without adequate justification. This principle supports Jacob Okafor's position: the current order, which on its face grants him every-other-weekend and weekly evening contact, is illusory in the post-relocation context because it cannot be meaningfully exercised at a distance of 600 miles. The court must replace that theoretical parenting time with a plan that actually delivers meaningful contact.
Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011), further underscores the court's authority to respond to changed geographic circumstances by modifying parenting arrangements. In that case, the court addressed a situation in which one parent relocated from the area where both parties had previously resided, triggering a re-examination of the parenting plan. The case affirms that relocation-driven modifications are within the proper scope of AS 25.20.110(a) review and that the court should fashion a plan suited to the new geographic realities rather than leaving in place a schedule that no longer functions.
V. CONCLUSION
Jacob Okafor has satisfied both elements required for modification under AS 25.20.110(a). Brandon Okafor's permanent relocation with the minor children from Fairbanks to Juneau constitutes a material change in circumstances. The modification Jacob Okafor proposes, consisting of eight consecutive weeks of summer parenting time, alternating school-year holidays, and one annual spring break visit, is in the best interests of the children under the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c) and is consistent with the policy of maximum practical parental access codified in AS 25.20.070.
Jacob Okafor respectfully requests that this Court enter an order modifying the 2021 custody order to establish the proposed long-distance parenting plan, to address any appropriate child support adjustment under Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(b) consistent with the new parenting time division, and to grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and equitable in the best interests of the children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0082)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Bergstrom ("Father") respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child custody order entered in 2021 to award him primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, or in the alternative, to substantially expand his parenting time during summer months and school vacation periods. This petition arises from Danielle Bergstrom's ("Mother") unilateral relocation from Anchorage to Fairbanks, a distance of approximately 360 miles, and her enrollment of the children in new schools in Fairbanks without providing the 30-day advance written notice required by the existing custody order. Mother's conduct constitutes a significant change in circumstances justifying modification under AS 25.20.110 and applicable Alaska case law. The best interests of the children, as measured by the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), support either a transfer of primary physical custody to Father or, at minimum, a substantial expansion of Father's parenting time to compensate for the near-total elimination of his regular weekly and biweekly contact with the children.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus and Danielle Bergstrom were divorced in 2021. The divorce decree incorporated a custody order granting Danielle primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children. Under that order, Marcus was awarded parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. The order further required that either party provide at least 30 days advance written notice before relocating with the children.
Following entry of the custody order, Danielle accepted a job transfer requiring her to move from Anchorage to Fairbanks, Alaska, a distance of approximately 360 miles. Rather than comply with the notice provision of the custody order and afford Marcus a meaningful opportunity to respond or seek relief from the Court, Danielle unilaterally enrolled the children in new schools in Fairbanks without providing Marcus the contractually and court-ordered 30-day advance written notice. Marcus learned of the relocation and school enrollment only after the fact.
The practical consequence of the relocation is devastating to Marcus's parenting relationship with the children. The 360-mile distance makes it logistically and financially impossible for Marcus to exercise his every-other-weekend and weekly evening parenting time on any regular basis. His court-ordered contact has been effectively nullified by Danielle's unilateral decision. The children, who have been established in an Anchorage community, now find themselves in a new city, new schools, and a new environment, separated from their father's consistent and regular presence in their lives.
Marcus brings this petition seeking a modification that either awards him primary physical custody or, in the alternative, significantly expands his parenting time during summer months and all school vacation periods so that the children can maintain the close and meaningful relationship with their father that the original order was designed to preserve.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), a custody award may be modified when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Both prongs must be satisfied. The party seeking modification bears the initial burden of demonstrating a significant change in circumstances affecting the children's best interests.
In determining the best interests of the child following a finding of changed circumstances, the court considers the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), including: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Additional factors include any evidence of domestic violence or substance abuse.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that one parent's relocation from a prior residence constitutes a significant change in circumstances as a matter of law, triggering a hearing on the children's best interests. See Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001). Furthermore, where the change in circumstances was not contemplated or planned for in the original custody order, the policy concern against repeated relitigation of custody does not counsel against modification. See Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. MOTHER'S RELOCATION TO FAIRBANKS CONSTITUTES A SIGNIFICANT CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES WARRANTING A CUSTODY MODIFICATION HEARING.
The threshold requirement for custody modification under AS 25.20.110(a) is that a change in circumstances has occurred. Alaska courts have squarely held that a parent's relocation constitutes a material change of circumstances sufficient to trigger a best-interests hearing. In Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that a parent's move to another location is a material change of circumstances warranting a hearing on the children's best interests, and further held that a parent who uproots children from a stable environment may face an adverse custody determination as a result. The Court in that case found particularly significant the fact that the relocating parent had disrupted what had been a stable environment serving the children's social, cultural, and emotional needs.
Here, the change in circumstances is even more pronounced than in Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001). Mother did not merely relocate across town. She moved the children 360 miles away from Anchorage to Fairbanks, a relocation that effectively destroys Marcus's ability to exercise any meaningful regular parenting time. The every-other-weekend and weekly evening schedule that the 2021 order established assumed both parents resided in the same metropolitan area. That foundational assumption has been obliterated by Mother's transfer.
Moreover, this relocation was not anticipated in the existing custody order. The Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011) court made clear that a change in circumstances must be demonstrated relative to the facts and circumstances that existed at the time of the prior custody order, and further that courts should avoid disturbing children with repeated custody changes when a move was already contemplated by the parties. Here, the 2021 order contained a 30-day notice provision precisely because the parties recognized a future relocation was possible, but nothing in the order anticipated or planned for the specific custody arrangement that would govern if such a relocation occurred. The existing order made no provision for how parenting time would be restructured in the event of a long-distance move. That silence, combined with Mother's failure to honor even the procedural requirement of providing advance written notice, establishes that the existing order is wholly inadequate to govern the new reality. This is not a situation like that in Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011), where the parties had actually agreed upon what the custody arrangement would look like post-relocation. No such agreement exists here.
The Sheffield v. Sheffield, 265 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2011) decision further illustrates that when a custody order contains a relocation provision and one parent fails to comply with that provision, the court's attention is properly drawn to the circumstances of the move and its impact on the children. Here, Danielle's failure to provide the required 30-day written notice denied Marcus any opportunity to seek a court order before the children were enrolled in Fairbanks schools and before the status quo was unilaterally altered. This procedural violation underscores that the change in circumstances was neither anticipated nor consented to by Father.
Accordingly, Mother's relocation to Fairbanks, combined with her unilateral enrollment of the children in new schools and her failure to comply with the mandatory notice provision, constitutes a significant and material change of circumstances within the meaning of AS 25.20.110(a).
B. THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN SUPPORT MODIFYING CUSTODY TO AWARD FATHER PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY, OR IN THE ALTERNATIVE, SUBSTANTIALLY EXPANDED PARENTING TIME.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must evaluate whether modification serves the children's best interests under AS 25.24.150(c). Each factor weighs in favor of modification here.
1. The Children's Physical, Emotional, Mental, Religious, and Social Needs.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(1), the court considers the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the children. Prior to Mother's relocation, the children were established in Anchorage schools, had formed friendships and community connections in Anchorage, and maintained consistent, frequent contact with their father. The relocation has severed those community ties. Remaining in Anchorage with Father, or at minimum, spending the bulk of the school vacation months with Father, would restore some measure of stability. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), that uprooting children from a stable environment that served their social, cultural, and emotional needs weighs against the relocating parent in a best-interests analysis.
2. The Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Children's Needs.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(2), the court examines each parent's capability and desire to meet the children's needs. Marcus has consistently exercised his parenting time under the existing order and has demonstrated both the capability and the desire to be an active and engaged parent. Mother's willingness to relocate 360 miles away without providing the required notice, and without making any arrangement to preserve Father's parenting relationship with the children, casts doubt on her commitment to facilitating a healthy co-parenting arrangement.
3. Stability and Continuity.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(5), the court considers the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. In Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that when a military transfer made a prior shared custody schedule impossible, the court must craft a new arrangement that accounts for the new realities while preserving the children's connections to familiar surroundings, friends, and community. The same principle applies here. The children's connections to Anchorage, their friends, their schools, and their father are elements of stability that the Court should preserve to the greatest extent possible through modification of the custody arrangement.
4. The Willingness and Ability of Each Parent to Facilitate and Encourage a Close and Continuing Relationship with the Other Parent.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the court shall consider "the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child." This factor weighs heavily against Mother. She relocated 360 miles away without providing the required 30-day written notice, denied Father any opportunity to seek relief before the move, and enrolled the children in new schools without his knowledge or consent. These actions are inconsistent with a parent who is willing and able to facilitate the other parent's relationship with the children.
By contrast, Marcus has fully complied with all terms of the existing custody order and now seeks a modification through proper judicial channels rather than by self-help. Father's conduct demonstrates his commitment both to his children and to the integrity of the court's orders.
5. Child Support Considerations.
Any modification of physical custody will necessarily require the Court to recalculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(f). If the Court awards Father primary physical custody, child support would be calculated based on Mother's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). Under Civil Rule 90.3(f), a parent has primary physical custody when the children reside with the other parent for less than 30 percent of the year. If the Court instead awards shared physical custody, under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), a parent has shared physical custody when the children reside with that parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. Father respectfully requests that the Court order updated financial disclosure from both parties so that child support may be correctly recalculated consistent with whatever custody arrangement the Court determines to be in the children's best interests.
C. FATHER'S PETITION IS TIMELY AND PROPER, AND THE COURT HAS AUTHORITY TO ORDER MOTHER'S APPEARANCE WITH THE CHILDREN.
The 2021 custody order was entered by this Court. This Court retains jurisdiction over modification proceedings because the existing order originates here and the jurisdictional framework of AS 25.30.310(a) provides that a court that has made a child custody determination retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction until it determines that neither the child, the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent have a significant connection with this state, or until neither the child nor either parent presently resides in this state. Marcus Bergstrom resides in Anchorage, Alaska. The children, although now enrolled in Fairbanks schools, remain Alaska residents. This Court therefore retains full jurisdiction to modify the existing order.
Furthermore, under AS 25.30.390(a), this Court has authority to order Danielle Bergstrom, as a party currently residing within Alaska, to appear before the Court personally, with or without the children, to respond to this petition. Father respectfully requests that the Court exercise that authority and schedule a hearing at the earliest practicable time.
Father also requests that the Court take judicial notice of the distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks, Alaska, which is a matter of geographic fact susceptible to ready determination, upon request and with adequate notice to all parties, pursuant to Alaska R. Evid. 201(d).
D. AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO A CHANGE IN PRIMARY CUSTODY, THE COURT SHOULD SUBSTANTIALLY EXPAND FATHER'S PARENTING TIME DURING SUMMER AND SCHOOL VACATION PERIODS.
Should this Court decline to award Marcus primary physical custody, Father respectfully requests in the alternative that the Court substantially expand his parenting time to compensate for the effective elimination of his regular weekly and biweekly contact. Specifically, Father requests that the Court award him the children for the full summer vacation period, all school breaks lasting five or more days, and at minimum, alternating school breaks during the academic year.
This alternative is consistent with the approach endorsed in Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), where the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that when military transfer rendered a shared custody schedule impossible, the appropriate response was to award the children to one parent during the school year and to the other parent during summers and holidays. The same equitable logic applies where, as here, a long-distance relocation renders the original schedule unworkable. An expanded vacation and summer schedule would ensure that the children continue to enjoy meaningful, sustained contact with their father rather than seeing him only on isolated, logistically complicated visits.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3), the Court also has discretion to allow the obligor parent to reduce child support payments by up to 75 percent for any period in which that parent has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days. To the extent the Court grants Marcus an extended summer parenting period, the Court should specify in any new order the amount of reduction allowable if the extended visitation is exercised, consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3).
V. CONCLUSION
Marcus Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that Mother's unilateral relocation to Fairbanks, combined with her failure to provide the required 30-day written notice and her enrollment of the children in new schools without Father's knowledge, constitutes a significant change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a) and applicable Alaska case law;
2. Schedule an evidentiary hearing on the children's best interests pursuant to AS 25.20.110(a);
3. Order Mother to appear before this Court personally, pursuant to AS 25.30.390(a), to respond to this petition;
4. Upon hearing, modify the existing custody order to award Father primary physical custody of the two minor children, consistent with the best-interests factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c); or in the alternative,
5. Substantially expand Father's parenting time to include the full summer vacation period, all school breaks of five or more days, and alternating breaks during the academic year, with corresponding child support recalculation pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(f); and
6. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and equitable.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0083)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Petrova ("Petitioner") respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order entered in 2021, which currently awards primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, ages 7 and 9, to Colin Petrova ("Respondent"). Since that order was entered, material changes in circumstances have occurred on both sides of the custodial equation. Petitioner has secured stable, well-compensated employment as a civil engineer in Anchorage, substantially improving his capacity to provide for the children's daily needs. Respondent, by contrast, has been placed on a 90-day administrative leave from his employment due to documented workplace misconduct, generating financial instability and forcing the children into full-time after-school care on every weekday. Taken together, these developments constitute a substantial change of circumstances that requires this Court to conduct a fresh best-interests analysis under AS 25.20.110. Petitioner requests that the Court award him primary physical custody of both children, with Respondent receiving alternating weekend visitation consistent with what Petitioner currently receives.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties were divorced in 2021. The divorce decree and accompanying custody order granted Respondent Colin Petrova primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, a 7-year-old and a 9-year-old. Under that order, Petitioner David Petrova received alternating weekend visitation and two weeks of uninterrupted parenting time each summer. The order represented the Court's assessment of the children's best interests as those interests existed at the time of entry.
Following entry of the order, Petitioner accepted a position as a civil engineer in Anchorage. This relocation was motivated by the professional and financial opportunities the position affords. The Anchorage position is stable, higher-paying than Petitioner's prior employment, and provides Petitioner with the economic resources and scheduling capacity to serve as the children's primary custodial parent. Petitioner has established a residence in Anchorage capable of accommodating both children on a full-time basis.
Respondent, in the period since the order was entered, has been placed on a 90-day administrative leave from his job due to documented workplace misconduct. This administrative leave has created financial instability in Respondent's household. As a direct consequence of Respondent's reduced availability and financial uncertainty, both children are now placed in after-school care five days per week. The children are no longer benefiting from the consistent parental presence in the after-school hours that presumably informed the original custody arrangement. The circumstances that existed at the time of the 2021 order no longer reflect the present reality for either parent or for the children.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a child custody or visitation award upon a determination that a change in circumstances requires the modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110. The parent seeking modification bears the burden of demonstrating, as a threshold matter, that a substantial change of circumstances has occurred since entry of the prior custody order. Long v. Long, 816 P.2d 145 (Alaska 1991); McLane v. Paul, 189 P.3d 1039 (Alaska 2008). Only after the moving party satisfies that threshold showing does the Court proceed to evaluate whether modification is warranted under a best-interests analysis. Long v. Long, 816 P.2d 145 (Alaska 1991).
The change-of-circumstances requirement is intended to discourage continual relitigation of custody matters and to promote finality and certainty, which are critical to a child's emotional welfare. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). The circumstances presented must be assessed relative to the facts existing at the time of the prior custody order. Geldermann v. Geldermann, 428 P.3d 477 (Alaska 2018). A change is sufficiently substantial when it affects the children's welfare and reflects more than the mere passage of time. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022).
Once a change of circumstances is established, the Court conducts a best-interests analysis guided by the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Those factors include, among others, the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close relationship between the child and the other parent; and any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect in the proposed custodial household. AS 25.24.150(c). The Court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child. AS 25.24.150(d).
Additionally, Alaska law provides that, unless doing so would be detrimental to the child's welfare or the domestic violence presumption of AS 25.24.150(g) is present, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents while custody is under consideration. AS 25.20.962.
Child support consequences following any modification of primary physical custody are governed by Civil Rule 934(a), which calculates a support obligation based on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage for the number of children at issue. Civil Rule 921(h) permits modification of a final support award upon a showing of a material change of circumstances, with a rebuttable presumption of materiality arising when the recalculated support differs from the existing order by more than 15 percent.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PETITIONER HAS DEMONSTRATED A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES SINCE ENTRY OF THE 2021 CUSTODY ORDER.
The threshold inquiry in any custody modification proceeding is whether a substantial change of circumstances has occurred since the entry of the prior order. AS 25.20.110; Long v. Long, 816 P.2d 145 (Alaska 1991). The change must be measured against the baseline facts and circumstances that existed at the time the prior order was entered. Geldermann v.
