Geldermann, 428 P.3d 477 (Alaska 2018). Here, two independent developments, each significant on its own and together overwhelming, satisfy that standard.
1. Respondent's Administrative Leave and the Resulting Financial Instability Constitute a Substantial Change.
At the time the 2021 order was entered, Respondent was employed and presumably financially capable of supporting the children in a primary custodial arrangement. That foundational assumption has been undermined by Respondent's placement on a 90-day administrative leave due to documented workplace misconduct. This development affects the children's welfare in at least two concrete ways.
First, the administrative leave has introduced financial instability into Respondent's household. A custodial parent's financial condition directly implicates his capacity to provide for the physical, emotional, mental, and social needs of the children in his care. AS 25.24.150(c)(1). Where employment circumstances have changed materially since the prior order, courts appropriately treat that change as a relevant shifted circumstance. Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001) (recognizing that a significant change in a parent's circumstances, including employment and stability, supports a finding of changed circumstances warranting a hearing on modification).
Second, and more immediately visible to the children on a daily basis, the administrative leave has caused both children to be placed in after-school care five days per week. At the time the 2021 order was entered, a custody arrangement favoring Respondent presumably reflected, at least in part, his availability and capacity to be present for the children in their daily routine. Whatever parental presence justified the original primary custody award is no longer being provided by Respondent during the after-school hours. The children are now in third-party care every weekday, a circumstance that did not exist at the time of the prior order and that directly affects their well-being and their experience of stability in their current custodial placement. This is precisely the type of change that reflects more than the mere passage of time, and that affects the children's welfare in a concrete and demonstrable way. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022).
2. Petitioner's Relocation and Improved Circumstances Reinforce the Case for a Change of Circumstances.
Courts evaluating whether changed circumstances exist properly consider changes in either parent's situation, not only the custodial parent's. Geldermann v. Geldermann, 428 P.3d 477 (Alaska 2018). Since 2021, Petitioner has relocated from Juneau to Anchorage and secured stable, higher-paying employment as a civil engineer. These changes substantially improve Petitioner's ability to provide for the children's physical, emotional, and social needs should the Court award him primary custody.
Petitioner's improved financial circumstances are directly relevant to the best-interests factors the Court must ultimately weigh. His stable position provides the economic foundation necessary to support two children on a full-time basis, including housing, healthcare, educational expenses, and extracurricular activities. His professional stability also signals that his current circumstances are not temporary or speculative. The combination of Petitioner's improved capacity and Respondent's diminished stability, compared to the 2021 baseline, presents a materially different factual landscape and satisfies the threshold showing required under AS 25.20.110.
B. MODIFICATION OF PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY TO PETITIONER IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
Once the threshold showing of changed circumstances is established, the Court must determine whether modification is in the best interests of the children by evaluating the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c). Long v. Long, 816 P.2d 145 (Alaska 1991). The burden of demonstrating that modification serves the children's best interests remains with the moving party. Id. Petitioner submits that the relevant statutory factors weigh in favor of awarding him primary physical custody.
1. Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs of the Children.
The first best-interests factor directs the Court to consider "the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child." AS 25.24.150(c)(1). Children ages 7 and 9 require consistent parental involvement in their daily routines, homework, meals, and social development. An arrangement in which the primary custodial parent is on administrative leave of uncertain duration, and in which the children are placed in after-school care every weekday, does not serve these needs as well as a primary placement with a parent who has stable employment, established housing, and the financial capacity to be engaged in the children's daily lives. Petitioner's position as a civil engineer in Anchorage provides him with that capacity. His income allows him to provide for the children's needs without the financial uncertainty that currently characterizes Respondent's household.
2. Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Children's Needs.
The second factor requires assessment of "the capability and desire of each parent to meet these needs." AS 25.24.150(c)(2). Petitioner has demonstrated his desire and capability to serve as the children's primary custodial parent by pursuing this modification and by establishing the stable home and employment circumstances necessary to support it. Respondent's current circumstances, marked by workplace misconduct resulting in administrative leave and the consequent financial uncertainty, raise legitimate questions about his present capability to meet the children's needs at the level contemplated by the 2021 order.
3. Stability and Continuity of Environment.
The fifth statutory factor directs attention to "the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity." AS 25.24.150(c)(5). This factor is sometimes read to favor maintaining the existing custodial arrangement. However, continuity serves the children's interests only when the existing environment remains stable and satisfactory. Where, as here, the current primary custodial environment has become materially less stable since the entry of the original order due to the custodial parent's administrative leave, financial instability, and the children's daily placement in after-school care, the stability rationale does not counsel strongly against modification. Courts have recognized that a change that disrupts the stability of a child's existing environment can itself justify modification. Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001).
4. Willingness to Facilitate the Relationship Between the Children and the Other Parent.
The sixth factor considers each parent's "willingness and ability to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child." AS 25.24.150(c)(6). Petitioner is committed to ensuring that the children maintain a meaningful and regular relationship with Respondent. The proposed arrangement, awarding Respondent alternating weekend visitation, mirrors the access that Petitioner currently receives and has been found adequate to maintain a parent-child relationship under the existing order. Petitioner will cooperate fully with a visitation schedule that serves the children's interests and fosters their bond with both parents. Kelly v. Joseph, 46 P.3d 1014 (Alaska 2002) (a superior court must engage in a full best-interests analysis considering, among other factors, each parent's cooperation with custody and visitation arrangements).
5. The Children's Interest in Equal Access to Both Parents.
Alaska law provides that, absent detriment to the child's welfare or the applicability of the domestic violence presumption, the children "shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents" while custody is under consideration. AS 25.20.070. Petitioner does not seek to limit Respondent's role in the children's lives. He seeks only a reallocation of primary physical custody that reflects the present-day realities of each parent's circumstances. The proposed order preserving alternating weekend visitation for Respondent ensures that both children retain a meaningful relationship with each parent and honors the policy reflected in AS 25.20.070.
C. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE RECALCULATED CONSISTENT WITH ANY MODIFICATION OF PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY.
If the Court awards Petitioner primary physical custody, a corresponding modification of the child support obligation is warranted. Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of child support where one parent holds primary physical custody. Under that rule, the support obligation is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage: 27 percent for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Upon modification of custody, Respondent would become the non-custodial parent, and his child support obligation would be calculated based on his adjusted annual income as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Civil Rule 90.3(h) permits modification of a final child support award upon a showing of a material change of circumstances, and provides that "a material change of circumstances will be presumed if support as calculated under this rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order under all circumstances." Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1). Given the shift in custodial status contemplated by this motion and the disparity between the parties' current incomes, a recalculated support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) will almost certainly differ from any existing support amount by more than 15 percent, triggering the presumption of materiality under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1). Petitioner requests that the Court, upon granting the custody modification, enter a concurrent order addressing child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and the formula applicable to the number of children and the parties' respective adjusted annual incomes. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025) (courts must apply the Rule 90.3 income-based framework carefully, including through evidentiary hearings where necessary, when calculating or modifying child support obligations).
V. CONCLUSION
Petitioner David Petrova respectfully requests that this Court find that a substantial change of circumstances has occurred since entry of the 2021 custody order, conduct a best-interests analysis as required by AS 25.20.110 and AS 25.24.150, and enter an order modifying primary physical custody of both minor children to Petitioner, with Respondent receiving alternating weekend visitation. Petitioner further requests that the Court enter a concurrent order recalculating child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), based on Respondent's adjusted annual income as the newly designated non-custodial parent. Such relief is necessary, appropriate, and in the best interests of the children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0084)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Larsen respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order to grant her primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, ages seven and nine, during Michael Larsen's anticipated twelve-month military deployment. The circumstances giving rise to this petition are substantial and compelling. Michael Larsen has accepted a deployment assignment requiring him to leave Alaska for approximately twelve months, and he has proposed placing the children in the primary care of his girlfriend of four months, a person who is largely unknown to the children. Meanwhile, Elena Larsen has undergone a documented transformation since the entry of the original custody order in 2021. She has successfully completed a court-ordered substance abuse treatment program, secured stable full-time employment as a registered nurse, and established a three-bedroom residence within two miles of the children's school in Anchorage. These combined developments constitute a material change in circumstances that warrants judicial review and modification of the existing order. Most critically, placing the children in the care of an unfamiliar caregiver for twelve months, rather than with their own mother who has demonstrated sustained rehabilitation and stability, is contrary to the children's best interests. Elena respectfully requests that this Court enter a modified custody order granting her primary physical custody for the duration of Michael's deployment, with a structured transition plan governing the restoration of the existing order upon his return.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties, Elena Larsen and Michael Larsen, were divorced in 2021. The existing custody order grants Michael Larsen primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, now ages seven and nine. Elena Larsen receives visitation on alternating weekends and every Wednesday evening under the current arrangement.
Since entry of the 2021 order, several significant developments have occurred. Elena Larsen has successfully completed a court-ordered substance abuse treatment program. She has obtained stable full-time employment as a registered nurse. She has secured a three-bedroom apartment located within two miles of the children's school in Anchorage, placing her in close geographic proximity to the children's established educational community and social environment.
Michael Larsen has recently accepted a military deployment assignment that will require him to leave Alaska for approximately twelve months. He has proposed that his girlfriend of four months serve as the primary temporary caregiver for the children during his absence. The girlfriend is largely unknown to the children and does not meet the statutory definition of a family member eligible to receive a delegation of a deployed parent's visitation or custodial rights under Alaska law.
The children's mother, Elena Larsen, is available, willing, and fully capable of providing the children with a stable, nurturing, and familiar home environment throughout the entire period of Michael's deployment. Elena now petitions this Court for a modification of the custody order to reflect the changed circumstances and to protect the best interests of the children.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A custody order may be modified upon a determination that a change in circumstances requires modification and that the modification serves the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a). When a parent opposes the modification and modification is granted, the court must enter on the record its reason for granting the modification. AS 25.20.110(a).
Alaska law provides a specific rule governing custody and visitation when a parent is subject to military deployment. A parent's temporary duty, mobilization, or deployment and the resulting temporary disruption to the child's schedule may not, standing alone, be a basis for a permanent modification of custody. AS 25.20.110(d). However, the court is expressly authorized to enter a temporary modification of a custody order during the period of a parent's deployment to make reasonable accommodation for that deployment. AS 25.20.110(e). Any such temporary order must specify that deployment is the basis of the order and include provisions for custody or reasonable visitation during any leave granted to the deployed parent if such contact is in the child's best interest, as well as provisions for termination of the temporary order and resumption of the permanent order within ten days after the deployed parent notifies the court and the other parent of the ability to resume custody or visitation. AS 25.20.110(e).
In all custody proceedings, including modification proceedings, the court determines custody in accordance with the best interests of the child. AS 25.24.150(c). The relevant best interests factors include the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the love and affection between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of substance abuse by either parent that directly affects the child's well-being; and other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(c).
In considering whether to award shared or modified custody, the court also weighs the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the education of the child, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child currently resides, and the optimal time each parent can spend with the child considering actual time spent, the proximity of each parent to the school the child attends, and the feasibility of travel between the parents. AS 25.20.090.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's relocation constitutes a material change of circumstances warranting a custody hearing. Barrett v. Alguire, 696 P.3d 244 (Alaska 2001). The court has further held that in considering the best interests of children when a parent has a history of deployments, deployment circumstances are properly weighed by the superior court in its best interests analysis. Rosenblum v. Perales, 303 P.3d 500 (Alaska 2013). The court has also recognized the importance of stability and continuity of environment in custody determinations, and has approved school-year and summer custody arrangements tailored to a military parent's availability. Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998); Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005).
Additionally, during the pendency of any custody modification proceedings, Elena is entitled to seek telephonic, video, or internet participation at hearings as needed, and the court shall allow video or internet testimony where the hearing involves the custody of a child of a deployed parent. Civil Rule 99(a).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. MICHAEL LARSEN'S IMPENDING DEPLOYMENT CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES JUSTIFYING MODIFICATION.
Alaska law expressly recognizes that a court may provide for a temporary modification of a custody or visitation order during the period of a parent's deployment to military service to make reasonable accommodation for the deployment. AS 25.20.110(e). The deployment of the primary custodial parent for an anticipated twelve-month period is plainly among the most significant changes in a child's custodial circumstances that the law contemplates. The children's daily caregiver is leaving Alaska for an extended period and will be physically unable to provide primary care. The question before this Court is not whether any modification is warranted, but rather what arrangement best serves the children's interests during the deployment period.
Michael's proposed solution, placing the children in the primary care of his girlfriend of four months, does not satisfy that inquiry. Alaska law permits a deployed parent to petition to delegate visitation rights to a family member who has an existing close relationship to the child, where such delegation is in the child's best interest. AS 25.20.095(b), (c). The girlfriend does not qualify as a family member under the statutory definition, which is limited to adult siblings, aunts, uncles, first cousins, grandparents related by blood, adoption, or marriage, and stepparents. AS 25.20.095(h)(2). Furthermore, even if the girlfriend were eligible as a delegate, the statute requires that the family member receiving delegation have an existing close relationship with the child. AS 25.20.095(c)(1). A girlfriend of four months who is largely unknown to the children cannot satisfy that requirement.
By contrast, Elena Larsen is the children's mother. She has an existing and established relationship with both children. She is immediately available to provide primary care in Anchorage, where the children currently reside and attend school. A modification granting Elena primary physical custody during the deployment is both legally appropriate under AS 25.20.110(e) and supported by every relevant consideration of the children's welfare.
B. ELENA LARSEN'S DEMONSTRATED REHABILITATION AND STABILITY CONSTITUTE AN INDEPENDENT BASIS FOR MODIFICATION.
Beyond the deployment itself, the substantial changes in Elena Larsen's circumstances since 2021 independently support modification of the existing order. At the time the original order was entered, the court had concerns sufficient to limit Elena to alternating weekend and Wednesday evening visitation and to require her to complete a substance abuse treatment program. Those concerns have been addressed in full. Elena has completed the court-ordered treatment program. She is now employed full time as a registered nurse, demonstrating sustained responsibility and professional capacity. She has established a stable three-bedroom residence within two miles of the children's school.
These are precisely the kinds of changes in circumstances that the Alaska Supreme Court has recognized as warranting modification review. In Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), the court held that a parent's relocation and the resulting change in the children's environment constituted a material change of circumstances. Here, it is not only Elena's relocation closer to the children's school that matters, but the entirety of her demonstrated rehabilitation, which collectively establishes that the factual predicate for the 2021 custody arrangement no longer reflects the parties' current circumstances.
The best interests factors under AS 25.24.150(c) now weigh in Elena's favor. First, Elena has the physical, emotional, and professional capacity to meet the children's needs. Her work as a registered nurse reflects both the discipline and the caregiving orientation that the children's upbringing requires. Second, Elena's residence within two miles of the children's school preserves continuity of education and the social environment the children have established in Anchorage. The desirability of maintaining such continuity is an expressly enumerated best interests factor. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Third, the prior concern about substance abuse, which was reflected in the original custody arrangement, has been directly addressed. AS 25.24.150(c)(8) directs the court to consider evidence of substance abuse that directly affects the well-being of the child. Elena's completion of the court-ordered treatment program removes that negative consideration from the court's analysis and replaces it with affirmative evidence of rehabilitation. Fourth, AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the court to evaluate the capability and desire of each parent to meet the children's needs. Elena is present, available, employed, and rehabilitated. Michael will be absent from Alaska for twelve months and is unable to personally provide primary care.
C. PLACING THE CHILDREN WITH AN UNFAMILIAR CAREGIVER IS CONTRARY TO THEIR BEST INTERESTS AND THE COURT SHOULD AWARD ELENA PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY DURING THE DEPLOYMENT.
The central question in any custody determination is what arrangement best serves the interests of the children. AS 25.24.150(c). Placing the children, ages seven and nine, with a woman who has been their father's girlfriend for only four months and who is largely unknown to them does not serve their interests. These are school-age children at formative stages of their development. The disruption of removing them from familiar parental care and placing them with an unfamiliar adult for twelve months poses real risks to their emotional stability and well-being.
AS 25.20.943 provides that, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child, or unless the domestic violence presumption applies, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody. Elena is a parent. The girlfriend is not. Maximizing the children's access to a parent, rather than placing them with a non-parent caregiver, is the outcome most consistent with this statutory directive.
In Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the importance of stability, familiar surroundings, and the child's existing social bonds in resolving custody disputes arising from a military parent's transfer. That case illustrates that when a military parent's assignment renders the existing arrangement impractical, the court properly looks to the totality of circumstances to craft an order that gives the children stability, community continuity, and parental access. Here, those considerations all point to Elena. She lives near the children's school, she is their mother, and she has demonstrated the sustained stability required to serve as their primary caregiver.
The Alaska Supreme Court's recognition in Rosenblum v. Perales, 303 P.3d 500 (Alaska 2013), that deployment circumstances may properly be considered in a best interests analysis further supports this Court's authority to craft a temporary modification that accounts for the full reality of Michael's absence. And in Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005), the court recognized that custody arrangements must be revisited when a military parent's circumstances change materially, including when a change in military assignment affects the availability of the custodial parent. The same principle applies here with equal force.
D. THE TEMPORARY MODIFICATION SHOULD INCLUDE PROVISIONS FOR MICHAEL'S CONTACT DURING LEAVE AND FOR RESTORATION OF THE PRIOR ORDER UPON HIS RETURN.
Elena does not seek to deprive Michael Larsen of his parental relationship with the children. She recognizes that Alaska law protects the rights of deployed parents and that a deployed parent must be given reasonable visitation during any period of leave if such contact is in the children's best interest. AS 25.20.110(e)(1). Elena supports the court's entry of a temporary order that expressly preserves Michael's right to contact with the children during any leave period and that specifies the conditions for restoration of the existing custody arrangement upon his return from deployment.
Alaska law provides that a temporary modification entered on the basis of deployment must include provisions for termination of the temporary order and resumption of the permanent order within ten days after notification of the deployed parent's ability to resume custody or visitation, unless the court finds that resumption of the prior order is no longer in the children's best interest. AS 25.20.110(e)(2). Under that provision, the burden of proving that resumption is no longer in the children's best interest rests with the nondeployed parent. AS 25.20.110(e)(2). Elena does not oppose an appropriate restoration provision and invites the court to include such terms in any modified order, consistent with the framework established by AS 25.20.110(e).
Additionally, AS 25.20.095(f) requires that each parent facilitate contact between the other parent and the children, including telephonic and electronic contact, if such contact is in the children's best interest, with video contact required whenever feasible. Elena commits to facilitating meaningful and regular contact between the children and Michael throughout the deployment period, consistent with these statutory requirements and with the children's best interests.
E. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE RECALCULATED TO REFLECT THE MODIFIED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT.
If this Court grants Elena primary physical custody during the deployment, child support should be recalculated accordingly. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award in a case in which one parent has primary physical custody is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage, which is 27% for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Because Michael will be the non-custodial parent during the deployment period, his adjusted annual income, accounting for mandatory deductions as provided in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), should serve as the basis for the recalculated support obligation. Elena respectfully requests that the court enter a modified child support order consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) for the duration of the temporary custody modification, and that any such order be made effective as of the date of service of this motion on Michael, consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(h)(2), which provides that a modification effective on or after the date a motion for modification is served on the opposing party is not considered a retroactive modification.
V. CONCLUSION
The existing custody order no longer reflects the reality of the parties' circumstances. Michael Larsen is preparing to leave Alaska for twelve months of military deployment. His proposed caregiver for the children is a girlfriend of four months who is a virtual stranger to them. Meanwhile, Elena Larsen has completed every court-ordered condition placed upon her, secured stable professional employment, and established a home within walking distance of the children's school. The children's best interests are plainly served by residing with their mother, a known and loving parent who has demonstrated sustained rehabilitation and stability, rather than with an unfamiliar adult.
Alaska law both authorizes and contemplates exactly the kind of temporary modification Elena seeks. AS 25.20.110(e) provides a clear statutory vehicle for a temporary custody order during the period of a parent's deployment. The best interests factors of AS 25.24.150(c) weigh in Elena's favor. The deployment framework of AS 25.20.095 protects Michael's right to contact and provides a clear path for restoration of the prior order upon his return.
For all the foregoing reasons, Elena Larsen respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that Michael Larsen's military deployment and Elena Larsen's demonstrated rehabilitation and changed circumstances constitute a material change of circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a);
2. Enter a temporary modification granting Elena Larsen primary physical custody of the children for the duration of Michael Larsen's deployment;
3. Include in the temporary order provisions for Michael Larsen's visitation during any leave period, for regular telephonic and electronic contact, and for restoration of the prior custody arrangement within ten days of Michael Larsen's notification of his ability to resume custody, consistent with AS 25.20.110(e);
4. Recalculate child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) to reflect the modified custody arrangement; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the best interests of the children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0085)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court modify the existing child custody order entered in 2021, which currently awards Danielle Bergstrom primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, with Priya receiving parenting time every other weekend and two evenings per week. Since the entry of that order, two substantial changes in circumstances have occurred that, taken together, compel a modification in the best interests of the children. First, Priya has relocated from Juneau to Anchorage to accept a significant career advancement, altering the geographic and logistical landscape of the existing parenting arrangement. Second, and most critically, Danielle has been diagnosed with a serious chronic illness that has required multiple hospitalizations over the past eight months, substantially limiting her capacity to meet the children's daily physical, emotional, and developmental needs.
Under AS 25.20.110 and AS 25.24.150, the Court has both the authority and the obligation to modify a custody order when changed circumstances require it and when modification serves the best interests of the children. The evidence presented in this matter satisfies both prongs of that standard. Priya respectfully asks the Court to award her primary physical custody of the children and to establish a parenting time schedule for Danielle that is reasonable, flexible, and calibrated to her current medical condition and the children's school schedule.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Bergstrom and Danielle Bergstrom were divorced in 2021. At that time, the Superior Court entered a custody order granting Danielle primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, with Priya receiving parenting time every other weekend and two evenings per week. This arrangement reflected the circumstances of the parties as they existed at the time of the 2021 order.
Since the entry of that order, the circumstances of both parties and the children have changed substantially. Priya has relocated from Juneau to Anchorage to accept a significant career advancement. This relocation was undertaken in good faith for professional reasons and has altered the geographic relationship between the parties. Priya's new position provides her with increased financial stability and resources that directly benefit the children.
More significantly, Danielle has been diagnosed with a serious chronic illness that has required multiple hospitalizations over the past eight months. These hospitalizations have been frequent and have substantially limited Danielle's physical capacity to meet the children's daily needs, including supervision, transportation to school and extracurricular activities, preparation of meals, assistance with schoolwork, and attendance at medical and other appointments. The children have, as a result of Danielle's repeated hospitalizations, experienced instability and disruption in their daily lives and routines.
Priya is ready, willing, and able to provide the children with a stable, nurturing home environment in Anchorage. She seeks an arrangement that awards her primary physical custody while preserving Danielle's parenting relationship through a schedule that accounts for Danielle's medical condition and accommodates the children's school calendar.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska law provides a two-part framework governing modifications of child custody orders. Under AS 25.20.110(a), a custody order may be modified only if the Court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. Both elements must be satisfied. If a parent opposes the modification and the modification is granted, the Court must enter on the record its reason for the modification.
The Alaska Supreme Court has interpreted this framework to require a meaningful showing of changed circumstances before a court proceeds to the best interests analysis. In Siekawitch v. Siekawitch, 956 P.2d 447 (Alaska 1998), the court recognized that changed circumstances warranting modification can arise from the inability of the existing order to function as intended or from material shifts in the situation of either parent or the children. Similarly, in Alisa Burns v. John Everett Burns, 466 P.3d 352 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that a court properly focuses its best interests analysis on the factors most directly relevant to the children's welfare in light of the specific circumstances that triggered the modification proceeding.
In determining the best interests of the children, the Court must consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child, among other factors.
In evaluating whether to award shared custody, the Court may also consider the factors set forth in AS 25.20.090, including the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the needs of the child, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent considering the actual time spent with each parent, the proximity of each parent to the school in which the child is enrolled, and the feasibility of travel between the parents.
Additionally, AS 25.20.070 reflects the legislative policy that, absent detriment to the child's welfare, a child should have equal access to both parents to the greatest degree practical during any custody proceeding.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES EXISTS WARRANTING MODIFICATION OF THE 2021 CUSTODY ORDER
The threshold requirement under AS 25.20.110(a) is satisfied by two independent and significant changes in circumstances that have occurred since the entry of the 2021 custody order.
First, Danielle's diagnosis with a serious chronic illness and her resulting multiple hospitalizations over the past eight months constitute a change in circumstances of the highest order. The existing custody order was premised on Danielle's ability to serve as the children's primary caregiver on a day-to-day basis. That premise has been materially undermined. Danielle's medical condition has substantially limited her physical ability to supervise the children, transport them to school and activities, assist with their homework, and attend to their daily needs. This is not a temporary inconvenience but a chronic condition that has already caused repeated hospitalizations and ongoing disruption to the children's lives.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Siekawitch v. Siekawitch, 956 P.2d 447 (Alaska 1998), recognized that a material change from the fundamental premise upon which an original custody agreement was based warrants re-examination of the custody arrangement. Here, the fundamental premise of the 2021 order, namely that Danielle was capable of serving as the children's primary daily caregiver, has been undermined by her serious illness.
Second, Priya's relocation from Juneau to Anchorage for a significant career advancement constitutes an additional change in circumstances. This relocation has altered the geographic relationship between the parties and the logistical framework underlying the 2021 visitation schedule. The every-other-weekend and two-evenings-per-week schedule was designed for parents living in the same city. That schedule is no longer workable in its current form given the distance between Juneau and Anchorage, and a modification of the overall custody arrangement is necessary to establish an order that reflects the parties' current circumstances.
Together, these two changes are more than sufficient to satisfy the changed circumstances prong under AS 25.20.110(a) and to require the Court to proceed to the best interests analysis.
B. MODIFICATION TO AWARD PRIYA PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN
Having established changed circumstances, the Court must determine whether modification is in the children's best interests. AS 25.24.150(c) sets forth the factors the Court must consider. An analysis of those factors demonstrates that awarding Priya primary physical custody, with reasonable parenting time for Danielle, best serves the children's welfare.
1. The Children's Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) requires the Court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. The children's needs are most immediately and consistently met by a parent who is physically present and able to provide daily care, supervision, and attention. Due to Danielle's serious chronic illness and repeated hospitalizations, she has been unable, through no fault of her own, to meet these needs on a consistent basis during the past eight months. Children require stability and reliable caregiving. The pattern of hospitalizations that has characterized Danielle's recent medical history demonstrates that the current arrangement does not adequately address the children's needs for consistent, daily parental care.
Priya, by contrast, is available to provide the children with stable, attentive, and consistent parenting on a daily basis. Her career advancement in Anchorage has increased her financial resources and professional stability, enabling her to provide the children with a secure and nurturing environment.
2. The Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Children's Needs
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the Court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the children's needs. Both parents no doubt love their children and desire to meet their needs. However, capability is a separate inquiry from desire. Danielle's chronic illness and the hospitalizations she has suffered over the past eight months have materially limited her present capability to serve as a full-time primary caregiver. This is not a reflection of her character or commitment as a parent. It is a medical reality that the Court must account for in crafting an order that genuinely serves the children.
Priya is fully capable of meeting the children's daily needs. She has maintained a consistent relationship with her children throughout the pendency of the existing order, she has demonstrated her commitment to their well-being, and she is prepared to assume the role of primary caregiver in a stable Anchorage home.
3. The Desirability of Maintaining a Stable Environment
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the Court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. The Alaska Supreme Court in Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018), emphasized that the stability of the children's environment is a key factor in custody determinations and that courts must give it meaningful weight. Continuity in a stable and satisfactory environment is the goal, but when the environment in which children currently reside has been disrupted repeatedly by the custodial parent's hospitalizations, continuity of that disruption does not serve the children's interests.
The Court should consider whether the current arrangement, which has involved the children experiencing repeated disruptions to their daily routines due to Danielle's hospitalizations, actually provides the stable, satisfactory environment that AS 25.24.150(c)(5) seeks to preserve. Where the existing arrangement has become a source of instability rather than continuity, a modification to place the children in a more stable home environment is warranted.
4. Each Parent's Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Children
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the Court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Priya expressly seeks a modification that includes reasonable and flexible parenting time for Danielle, calibrated to Danielle's medical condition and the children's school schedule. This demonstrates Priya's commitment to preserving the children's relationship with Danielle notwithstanding the modification. Priya does not seek to eliminate or substantially curtail Danielle's role as a parent. She seeks only to ensure that the children have a stable primary home while maintaining a meaningful and flexible bond with Danielle.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Alisa Burns v. John Everett Burns, 466 P.3d 352 (Alaska 2020), underscored the importance of each parent's willingness to support the children's relationship with the other parent, noting that interference with that relationship is a serious concern in any custody analysis. Priya's proposed arrangement demonstrates her good faith commitment to fostering the children's bond with Danielle.
5. Consideration of Shared Custody Factors and Access to Both Parents
Under AS 25.20.090, when the Court considers the allocation of physical custody, it must examine the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the needs of the children, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, including the proximity of each parent to the children's school and the feasibility of travel between the parents. Given the distance between Juneau and Anchorage, a traditional shared physical custody arrangement of roughly equal division is logistically impractical on a week-to-week basis. A primary custody arrangement in Anchorage, with Danielle exercising parenting time during school vacations, holidays, and other extended periods consistent with her health, best accommodates these practical realities.
AS 25.20.070 reflects the public policy preference that children have equal access to both parents to the greatest degree practical. Priya's proposed arrangement honors this principle by providing for meaningful, flexible parenting time for Danielle rather than a punitive or restrictive schedule. The proposed order would give Danielle the maximum contact with the children that her medical condition and the geographic distance will allow, consistent with the children's best interests.
6. Child Support Obligations Must Be Recalculated Following Any Modification
Any modification of physical custody will require recalculation of child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a). Under Civil Rule 90.3(f), the classification of each parent's physical custody status, whether primary, shared, or otherwise, determines the formula applicable to the child support calculation. If the Court awards Priya primary physical custody as defined by Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), Danielle's child support obligation will be calculated based on her adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage for two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). The Court should order the parties to submit updated financial documentation sufficient to allow accurate calculation of the new support obligation contemporaneously with any modification of the custody arrangement.
V. CONCLUSION
The circumstances of these parties and their children have changed substantially since the entry of the 2021 custody order. Danielle's serious chronic illness, evidenced by multiple hospitalizations over the past eight months, has materially limited her capacity to serve as the children's primary daily caregiver. Priya's relocation to Anchorage for a significant career advancement has further altered the factual landscape underlying the existing order. Taken together, these changes constitute the kind of changed circumstances that AS 25.20.110(a) recognizes as sufficient to warrant modification.
The best interests factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) weigh in favor of awarding Priya primary physical custody. The children require a stable, consistent primary home with a caregiver who is physically able to meet their daily needs. Priya is that caregiver. At the same time, a generous, flexible parenting time schedule for Danielle will preserve the children's bond with their mother and honor the legislative preference expressed in AS 25.20.070 for maximum access to both parents to the greatest degree practical.
For the foregoing reasons, Priya Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court enter an order: (1) finding that a substantial change in circumstances exists warranting modification of the 2021 custody order; (2) awarding Priya primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children; (3) granting Danielle reasonable and flexible parenting time consistent with her medical condition and the children's school schedule; and (4) ordering recalculation of child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(f) based on the modified custody arrangement.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0086)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Petrova ("Father") respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child custody order entered in 2021, which currently grants Brandon Petrova ("Mother") primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, ages 8 and 11. Brandon Petrova has accepted a new employment position requiring relocation from Anchorage to Juneau, a distance that would severely curtail David Petrova's ability to exercise regular visitation and would sever the children's established ties to their schools, medical providers, and extracurricular communities in Anchorage. Because Brandon's proposed relocation constitutes a substantial change in circumstances as a matter of Alaska law, and because the children's best interests are better served by remaining in Anchorage with their Father, this Court should grant the requested modification and award David primary physical custody, with Brandon receiving generous visitation during school breaks and summer periods.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Petrova and Brandon Petrova were divorced in 2021 pursuant to an Alaska Superior Court order. That order awarded Brandon primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, currently ages 8 and 11. David was awarded visitation on alternating weekends and for a period of two consecutive weeks each summer.
Since entry of the original custody order, David has remained continuously employed and stably housed in Anchorage. He has exercised all of his court-ordered visitation consistently and has maintained a close, loving relationship with both children. The children are enrolled in Anchorage schools where they have established friendships, participate in extracurricular activities, and receive ongoing medical and therapeutic care from providers familiar with their individual needs.
Brandon has recently accepted a new employment position located in Juneau, Alaska. Brandon intends to relocate permanently with the children to Juneau. This relocation would effectively eliminate David's ability to exercise regular every-other-weekend visitation, as the geographic distance between Anchorage and Juneau makes frequent travel both logistically impractical and financially burdensome. In addition, the move would require the children to change schools mid-enrollment, abandon their established extracurricular commitments, and transition to new medical providers, disrupting the continuity of care and stability they currently enjoy.
David brings this motion to modify custody so that the children may remain in Anchorage with him, preserving their existing routines, relationships, and support networks, while Brandon receives scheduled visitation during school breaks and summer vacations.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.931, a custody award may be modified when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Alaska courts have established a two-part inquiry: the moving party must first demonstrate a substantial change in circumstances, and then show that modification serves the child's best interests. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017); Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011).
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a custodial parent's decision to relocate out of a child's established community constitutes a substantial change in circumstances as a matter of law, triggering a full best-interests analysis. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must evaluate whether modification is in the best interests of the child by reference to the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001).
AS 25.20.915 further provides that, unless detrimental to the child's welfare or unless the domestic violence presumption under AS 25.24.150(g) applies, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during custody proceedings.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. BRANDON'S PROPOSED RELOCATION CONSTITUTES A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER AS 25.20.921.
The first requirement for custody modification is satisfied here. Alaska law is clear that a custodial parent's decision to relocate constitutes a change in circumstances that triggers a hearing on the children's best interests. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). The Alaska Supreme Court has stated that a custodial parent's planned move out of a child's established location amounts to a substantial change in circumstances as a matter of law. Id. The same principle applies to a relocation within Alaska that would similarly disrupt the child's life and the other parent's access.
Brandon's announced intent to relocate permanently from Anchorage to Juneau is precisely this kind of triggering event. The relocation is not temporary, not contemplated by the existing order, and not anticipated by either party at the time the 2021 custody arrangement was established. In Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that a change in circumstances must be evaluated relative to the facts and circumstances that existed at the time of the prior custody order. Here, the 2021 order was entered when both parties resided in Anchorage, and no relocation was planned or provided for. Brandon's decision to move to Juneau therefore represents a meaningful departure from the circumstances underlying the existing order and satisfies the threshold showing required by AS 25.20.110(a).
AS 25.20.110(a) states that an award of custody "may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification of the award and the modification is in the best interests of the child." Both elements are addressed in the sections that follow.
B. BRANDON'S PROPOSED RELOCATION MUST SERVE A LEGITIMATE PURPOSE, AND THE COURT MUST CONDUCT A FULL BEST-INTERESTS ANALYSIS.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must determine whether there are legitimate reasons for the proposed move. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). If legitimate reasons exist, no presumption favors either parent, and the relocating parent bears the burden of demonstrating that living with that parent in the new location better serves the children's interests than living with the non-relocating parent in the current location. Id.
David does not dispute that Brandon may have professional reasons for the move. However, the existence of a career opportunity does not automatically justify uprooting two children from their established schools, medical providers, and extracurricular activities. In Ronny M. v. Nanette H., 303 P.3d 392 (Alaska 2013), the Alaska Supreme Court examined whether a parent's relocation served the children's interests and scrutinized the totality of impact on the children's lives. A job change, standing alone, is insufficient to override the children's demonstrated need for stability and continuity in Anchorage.
C. THE BEST-INTERESTS FACTORS UNDER AS 25.24.150(c) FAVOR AWARDING PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY TO DAVID.
The court is required to determine custody in accordance with the best interests of the children, considering the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Several of those factors weigh strongly in David's favor.
1. The Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs of the Children.
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) requires the court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the children. The children, ages 8 and 11, are at developmental stages where established routines, peer relationships, and consistent educational environments are critically important. Both children are enrolled in Anchorage schools, participate in extracurricular activities, and receive ongoing medical care from providers who know them. Disrupting all of these connections simultaneously, as Brandon's relocation would require, is contrary to the children's physical and emotional well-being.
2. Continuity of Environment.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. The children have lived in Anchorage throughout their lives and have developed meaningful ties to their community. In Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed a custody modification where the relocating parent had uprooted children from a stable environment that served their social, cultural, and emotional needs. The same logic applies here: Brandon's relocation would sever the children from the stable Anchorage environment they have known, while David's continued residence in Anchorage would allow the children to maintain that continuity.
3. Willingness and Ability to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship With the Children.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) requires the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. David has consistently exercised all of his court-ordered visitation. Brandon's decision to relocate to Juneau, without apparent consideration for David's ability to maintain regular contact with the children, raises serious questions about Brandon's willingness to support that relationship. By contrast, if David is awarded primary custody, Brandon will remain able to exercise visitation during school breaks and summer periods, preserving a meaningful parent-child relationship with both parents.
4. Equal Access to Both Parents Under AS 25.20.070.
AS 25.20.070 mandates that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during custody proceedings. If Brandon relocates to Juneau with the children, David's current every-other-weekend visitation would become logistically and financially impossible to maintain on a regular basis. Awarding primary custody to David, who remains in Anchorage, allows both parents to maintain regular contact with the children because Brandon can exercise visitation during school breaks and extended summer periods without the geographic barrier affecting day-to-day access.
5. The Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Children's Needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) directs the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the children's needs. David is continuously and stably employed in Anchorage, maintains stable housing, and has demonstrated consistent and committed involvement in the children's lives. He is capable of providing the children with the care, attention, and support they require on a day-to-day basis. The record demonstrates no deficiency in David's parenting, and his petition for primary custody reflects his commitment to the children's continued stability and well-being.
6. The Love and Affection Between the Children and Each Parent.
AS 25.24.150(c)(4) requires the court to consider the love and affection existing between the child and each parent. David shares a close and loving bond with both children, maintained through consistent visitation and active involvement in their daily lives. In McQuade v. McQuade, 901 P.2d 421 (Alaska 1995), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that it is a parent's present ability to provide for the needs of the child that is at issue. David's present circumstances, his stable employment, established home, and demonstrated commitment to the children, make him well-suited to serve as the primary custodial parent.
D. MODIFYING CUSTODY SERVES THE LEGISLATIVE POLICY OF ENSURING CHILDREN HAVE MAXIMUM PRACTICAL ACCESS TO BOTH PARENTS.
Alaska's statutory framework reflects a legislative commitment to ensuring children maintain meaningful relationships with both parents. AS 25.20.070 provides that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents. Relocating the children to Juneau would functionally eliminate David's ability to exercise regular visitation, reducing him to a parent the children see only during school breaks and one extended summer period. This outcome is inconsistent with the policy underlying AS 25.20.070.
Awarding primary physical custody to David, with Brandon receiving visitation during school breaks and summer vacations, preserves the children's established ties to their Anchorage community while ensuring that Brandon retains a meaningful and structured role in the children's lives. This arrangement best reflects the statutory directive that children enjoy the greatest degree of practical access to both parents.
E. ANY CHILD SUPPORT MODIFICATION SHOULD FOLLOW FROM THE CUSTODY CHANGE UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3.
Should the Court grant David primary physical custody, a corresponding modification of child support will be necessary. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage, which is 27% for two children. Under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1), a material change of circumstances, including a change in custody, supports modification of a final child support award, and a material change of circumstances is presumed when support as calculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. David respectfully requests that the Court also address child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) following any modification of custody.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, David Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that Brandon Petrova's proposed relocation from Anchorage to Juneau constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a);
2. Conduct a full best-interests analysis pursuant to AS 25.24.150(c);
3. Modify the existing custody order to award David Petrova primary physical custody of the two minor children, with the children remaining enrolled in their Anchorage schools and continuing to receive their existing medical and extracurricular care;
4. Award Brandon Petrova scheduled visitation during school breaks and extended summer periods consistent with the children's best interests and the policy of AS 25.20.070; and
5. Modify child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) to reflect the change in custody.
The children's stability, continuity, and access to both parents are best protected by granting this petition. David Petrova stands ready to provide the children with the consistent, nurturing, and stable home environment they deserve.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0087)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Okafor respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing visitation schedule set forth in the 2021 custody order. The parties share joint legal custody of their two minor children, with primary physical custody vested in Petitioner. Petitioner has accepted a permanent employment position in Fairbanks, Alaska, requiring her to relocate with the children approximately 360 miles from the parties' current residence in Anchorage. Because the geographic distance renders the current weekly and biweekly visitation schedule impractical, Petitioner seeks a restructured parenting time arrangement that preserves and protects Respondent Maria Okafor's meaningful relationship with the children through extended holiday parenting time and a continuous six-week summer block. The proposed modification serves the best interests of the children, satisfies Alaska's change-of-circumstances standard, and ensures that both parents remain actively involved in the children's lives to the greatest degree practicable.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
1. On or about 2021, the Alaska Superior Court entered a custody order granting the parties joint legal custody of their two minor children. Primary physical custody was awarded to Petitioner Priya Okafor, and Respondent Maria Okafor was awarded parenting time consisting of every other weekend and one weeknight per week.
2. Since the entry of the 2021 order, Petitioner has accepted a permanent, full-time employment position located in Fairbanks, Alaska. The new position offers significantly improved income and long-term stability for the family. Petitioner intends to relocate to Fairbanks by the start of the upcoming school year.
3. Fairbanks is approximately 360 miles from the parties' current residence in Anchorage. The geographic separation makes the existing parenting time schedule, which was designed for parties residing in the same metropolitan area, logistically unworkable for the children and both parties.
4. Neither the 2021 custody order nor the parties' prior agreement contemplated or made provision for one party relocating to a distant city within Alaska.
5. Petitioner proposes that Respondent's parenting time be restructured to consist of extended blocks during Thanksgiving, winter, and spring school holidays, as well as a continuous six-week period during the summer. This arrangement would preserve substantial parenting time for Respondent while accounting for the geographic realities of the relocation.
6. The children are currently enrolled in school in Anchorage. Upon relocation, they will be enrolled in school in Fairbanks. The proposed schedule is structured around the school calendar so as to minimize disruption to the children's educational continuity.
7. Petitioner remains committed to facilitating a close and continuing relationship between the children and Respondent, and she is willing to cooperate on reasonable travel arrangements.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A custody or visitation order may be modified when the court finds both that a substantial change in circumstances has occurred and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody or visitation "may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification of the award and the modification is in the best interests of the child." Under this two-step framework, the party seeking modification must first demonstrate a material change in circumstances relative to the facts and conditions existing at the time of the prior order. Nelson v. Nelson, 685 P.3d 849 (Alaska 2011); McLane v. Paul, 189 P.3d 1039 (Alaska 2008). Once a change in circumstances is established, the court proceeds to a best-interests analysis guided by the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.972. Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001).
Throughout this analysis, Alaska law requires that the children have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents. AS 25.20.070 provides that, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child considering the factors under AS 25.24.150(c), "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody." The court's overriding obligation is to craft an arrangement that serves the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.150(c).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PETITIONER'S RELOCATION TO FAIRBANKS CONSTITUTES A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES.
The threshold requirement for modification under AS 25.20.110(a) is satisfied here because Petitioner's acceptance of permanent employment in Fairbanks and her consequent relocation approximately 360 miles from Anchorage represent a substantial change in circumstances affecting the children's best interests. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011), that a change in circumstances must be measured relative to the facts existing at the time the prior order was entered. Here, the 2021 order was entered while both parties resided in the Anchorage area. The order's parenting time structure, specifically every other weekend and one weeknight per week, was plainly designed for parties living in close geographic proximity. Nothing in the 2021 order or the parties' prior arrangement contemplated or provided for a relocation of this magnitude.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that one parent's relocation out of a shared geographic area constitutes a significant change in circumstances as a matter of law. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011). Although Nelson addressed relocation outside of Alaska, the principle it articulates applies with full force to a 360-mile intrastate move that renders the existing parenting schedule functionally impossible to perform. A move of this distance is not a minor adjustment; it converts weekly overnight exchanges and mid-week visits into logistically and financially burdensome undertakings that cannot reasonably be maintained on the current schedule. The substantial disruption to the existing parenting time structure that results from Petitioner's permanent relocation satisfies the change-of-circumstances requirement under AS 25.20.110(a).
Additionally, the Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that courts should consider whether a change in circumstances was anticipated or planned for at the time of the original order. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011). The 2021 order contains no relocation provision and does not address the possibility that Petitioner would move to another city. Because the relocation was not anticipated by the existing order, it qualifies as a new and substantial change in circumstances warranting a hearing on modification.
B. MODIFICATION OF THE VISITATION SCHEDULE IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must determine whether the proposed modification serves the children's best interests by reference to the statutory factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c). Those factors include, among others: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. AS 25.24.150(c)(1), (2), (5), (6).
The proposed restructured schedule serves the children's best interests for the following reasons.
1. The Proposed Schedule Maintains Stability and Educational Continuity.
The children's primary residence with Petitioner has been the stable, consistent arrangement since the 2021 order. Petitioner's relocation to Fairbanks for permanent employment preserves that stability by keeping the children with their primary custodial parent in a settled home environment. Maintaining continuity of the primary custodial relationship is a significant factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(5). The proposed schedule, which aligns Respondent's extended parenting time with school holiday breaks and the summer recess, allows the children to attend school in Fairbanks without frequent, disruptive cross-state travel during the academic year. Courts have recognized the importance of avoiding repeated disruptions to children's living arrangements. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011).
2. The Proposed Schedule Preserves and Protects Respondent's Meaningful Parenting Time.
Petitioner's proposed schedule is not designed to diminish Respondent's role in the children's lives. To the contrary, it replaces a schedule that would become functionally unenforceable with one that provides Respondent substantial, meaningful, and predictable parenting time. Extended holiday blocks and a continuous six-week summer period offer Respondent uninterrupted time with the children that allows for genuine relationship-building rather than brief, logistically strained visits.
Alaska law strongly favors ensuring that children have maximum access to both parents. AS 25.20.070 requires that children have equal access to both parents to the greatest degree practical. The operative word is "practical." A schedule requiring a 360-mile commute for weeknight visits and biweekly weekend exchanges is not practical by any reasonable measure. The proposed modification recalibrates the schedule to what is genuinely achievable and meaningful given the new geographic reality, consistent with AS 25.20.070.
3. Petitioner's Willingness to Facilitate the Relationship Weighs in Favor of Modification.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the court considers the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Petitioner is committed to supporting Respondent's ongoing involvement in the children's lives. Petitioner is willing to cooperate on reasonable travel logistics and to ensure that Respondent has reliable communication access to the children during periods between in-person parenting time. This cooperative posture supports the proposed modification and reflects the spirit of joint legal custody that both parties share under the 2021 order.
4. The Children's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs Favor the Proposed Schedule.
The children's physical, emotional, mental, and social needs are best served by a stable primary residence in Fairbanks with their primary custodial parent, combined with extended, predictable time with Respondent during breaks from school. AS 25.24.150(c)(1) and (2). Frequent long-distance travel during the school year imposes stress, fatigue, and educational disruption on children. Concentrated parenting time during holidays and summer reduces travel frequency while providing Respondent extended, quality time with the children. This arrangement is consistent with the approach Alaska courts have approved in cases involving parents who no longer share the same geographic area. Hope P. v. Flynn G., 503 P.3d 765 (Alaska 2015); Havel v. Hogan, 216 P.3d 1142 (Alaska 2009).
C. THE COURT SHOULD ADDRESS TRAVEL EXPENSE ALLOCATION AS PART OF THE MODIFICATION ORDER.
Civil Rule 90.3(g) provides that, after determining a child support award, "the court shall allocate reasonable travel expenses which are necessary to exercise visitation between the parties as may be just and proper for them to contribute." The geographic distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks will necessarily generate travel costs for the exercise of Respondent's restructured parenting time. Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court allocate reasonable travel expenses in a manner that is just and equitable given the parties' respective financial circumstances. A fair allocation will ensure that the parenting time awarded to Respondent is exercisable in practice and not rendered illusory by unaddressed financial burden.
D. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE RECALCULATED TO REFLECT THE NEW PARENTING TIME STRUCTURE.
Because the proposed modification restructures the parenting time arrangement from a schedule that includes a weekly weeknight visit and biweekly weekend exchanges to one based on extended holiday and summer blocks, the existing child support calculation will require adjustment. Child support in primary custody cases is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent. The shift to extended-block parenting time may also implicate the extended visitation credit provisions of Civil Rule 90.3(a)(3), which permit a reduction of up to 75 percent of child support payments for any period in which the obligor parent has extended visitation of over 27 consecutive days. The Court should order recalculation of child support consistent with the new parenting time schedule at the time it enters the modification order.
V. CONCLUSION
Petitioner Priya Okafor has established a substantial change in circumstances, namely her permanent relocation to Fairbanks for employment, that warrants modification of the 2021 visitation schedule. The proposed restructured schedule, providing Respondent with extended holiday parenting time and a continuous six-week summer block, is in the best interests of the children. It preserves the children's educational continuity and residential stability, ensures Respondent meaningful and practical parenting time, and reflects Petitioner's sincere commitment to fostering the children's relationship with both parents, consistent with AS 25.20.070, AS 25.24.150(c), and AS 25.20.110(a).
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a substantial change in circumstances has occurred warranting modification of the 2021 custody and visitation order;
2. Enter a modified visitation schedule providing Respondent extended parenting time during Thanksgiving, winter, and spring school breaks, and a continuous six-week summer parenting period;
3. Allocate reasonable travel expenses between the parties pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(g); and
4. Recalculate child support consistent with the modified parenting time schedule pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a).

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0088)
I. INTRODUCTION
Jacob Sutter respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order entered in Anchorage Superior Court two years ago. That order awarded Sarah Sutter primary physical custody of the parties' nine-year-old daughter, with Jacob receiving visitation every other weekend and two weeks each summer. Since entry of that order, material circumstances have changed dramatically. Jacob has secured stable, higher-paying employment with the State of Alaska in Juneau, establishing a more financially secure environment for the child. More critically, Sarah has been arrested twice for driving under the influence, including one incident in which the child was a passenger in the vehicle. These events constitute a substantial change in circumstances warranting modification of custody under Alaska law. The child's safety and best interests require that Jacob be awarded primary physical custody, with Sarah receiving supervised visitation on alternating weekends, conditioned on her completion of a court-approved substance abuse treatment program and demonstration of at least six consecutive months of sobriety.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jacob Sutter and Sarah Sutter are the parents of one daughter, now nine years of age. Approximately two years ago, the Anchorage Superior Court entered a custody order granting Sarah primary physical custody of the child and awarding Jacob visitation every other weekend and two weeks during each summer.
Following entry of that order, Jacob accepted a stable, higher-paying position with the State of Alaska and relocated to Juneau. His employment with the State provides financial security and a consistent schedule that would support the child's day-to-day needs. Jacob has maintained regular contact with his daughter and has fulfilled all obligations under the existing order.
Since the order was entered, Sarah's conduct has given rise to serious concerns about the child's safety in her care.
