Sarah has been arrested on two separate occasions for driving under the influence of alcohol. Of particular concern, one of those arrests occurred while the child was present in Sarah's vehicle. That incident placed the child in direct physical danger and demonstrates that Sarah's substance abuse is not merely a personal failing but an ongoing threat to the child's well-being.
There is no indication that Sarah has successfully completed a substance abuse treatment program or that she has attained any period of sustained sobriety. Jacob now moves the Court to modify the existing custody order to reflect the changed circumstances and to protect the child's safety and best interests.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.948(a), a custody award may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. If a parent opposes the modification and the modification is granted, the court must enter on the record its reason for the modification. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized, consistent with the holding in Havel v. Hogan, 216 P.3d 1142 (Alaska 2009), that a moving parent must demonstrate a substantial change in circumstances to justify modification of a custody award.
Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the court evaluates the child's best interests under the factors set out in AS 25.24.150(c). Those factors include the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child under all circumstances; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; and evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child.
Where a history of perpetrating domestic violence is found, AS 25.24.150(g) establishes a rebuttable presumption that such a parent may not be awarded sole or joint legal or physical custody. Under AS 25.24.994, if a court finds that a parent has a history of perpetrating domestic violence, the court shall allow only supervised visitation by that parent, conditioned on participation in and successful completion of a batterers intervention program. Even absent that specific finding, Alaska courts have recognized, consistent with the holding in Kristina B. v. Edward B., 512 P.3d 294 (Alaska 2014), that a parent's substance abuse history directly informs custodial fitness and may justify limitations on unsupervised custody.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES HAS OCCURRED
The threshold requirement for modification under AS 25.20.110(a) is met here. Two independent and significant changes have occurred since the existing order was entered two years ago.
First, Jacob has relocated to Juneau and accepted stable, higher-paying employment with the State of Alaska. This change substantially alters his financial capacity to provide for the child and his ability to offer a structured, secure home environment.
Second, and far more critically, Sarah has been arrested twice for driving under the influence of alcohol since entry of the existing order. One of those arrests occurred while the child was in the vehicle. This is not a marginal or technical change in circumstances. It is a recurring pattern of conduct that directly endangered the child's physical safety and demonstrates that Sarah's ability to exercise safe parental judgment has materially deteriorated since the court last evaluated custody. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Havel v. Hogan, 216 P.3d 1142 (Alaska 2009), that both courts and parties must demonstrate that the change in circumstances is substantial; there can be little question that a parent's repeated criminal conduct for impaired driving, including one incident endangering the child, satisfies that standard.
Additionally, AS 25.20.110(c) provides that a finding that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred since the last custody determination constitutes a finding of change in circumstances under subsection (a). While the DUI arrests as described do not constitute domestic violence as that term is typically defined, the broader principle embedded in AS 25.20.110 is that post-order criminal conduct bearing on child safety qualifies as a changed circumstance. The DUI arrest while the child was in the vehicle reflects at minimum reckless disregard for the child's physical safety, a factor the court should weigh heavily.
Taken together, Jacob's improved financial and employment stability and Sarah's documented, recurring pattern of substance-related criminal conduct constitute a substantial change in circumstances warranting a full best-interests analysis.
B. MODIFICATION TO AWARD JACOB PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY IS IN THE CHILD'S BEST INTERESTS
Under AS 25.24.150(c), the court must determine custody in accordance with the child's best interests, considering the enumerated statutory factors. As set forth below, the relevant factors favor awarding primary physical custody to Jacob.
1. The Child's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs, and Each Parent's Capability to Meet Them
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) and (c)(2) require the court to examine the child's needs and each parent's capability and desire to meet those needs. A nine-year-old child requires, above all, safety and consistency. Sarah's two DUI arrests, including one with the child present in the vehicle, demonstrate a serious impairment in her capacity to ensure the child's physical safety. By contrast, Jacob's stable state employment in Juneau, his consistent compliance with the visitation schedule throughout the pendency of the existing order, and his demonstrated commitment to the child establish his capability to meet her needs. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Littleton v. Banks, 192 P.3d 154 (Alaska 2008), that a parent's substance abuse history is a significant factor in evaluating custodial fitness, particularly when that history is ongoing rather than resolved.
2. Stability of Environment and Desirability of Maintaining Continuity
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. While the child has resided with Sarah since the original order, that environment has become demonstrably unstable due to Sarah's repeated criminal conduct related to alcohol. Stability means more than physical continuity of residence; it encompasses freedom from danger, consistent parental supervision, and a home environment that promotes the child's development. Jacob's employment with the State of Alaska provides financial predictability and a structured home setting in Juneau. The court in Rooney v. Rooney, 914 P.2d 212 (Alaska 1996), recognized that courts must weigh the stability of each parent's proposed environment in determining which placement better serves the child's interests, particularly where one parent has demonstrated a pattern of problematic conduct.
3. Substance Abuse Directly Affecting the Child's Well-Being
AS 25.24.150(c)(8) expressly requires the court to consider evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child. Sarah's substance abuse is not an abstract or historical concern. One of her DUI arrests occurred while the child was physically present in her vehicle. This is direct, concrete evidence that Sarah's substance abuse has endangered the child. The court in Kristina B. v. Edward B., 329 P.3d 202 (Alaska 2014), recognized that a parent's pattern of substance abuse may render that parent incapable of meeting the child's needs at the time custody is being determined, and that this incapacity justifies a custody arrangement that protects the child while creating a pathway for the affected parent to demonstrate sustained recovery. The same principle applies here. Sarah's conduct places the AS 25.24.150(c)(8) factor squarely against continuing primary custody in her home.
4. The Child's Preference
AS 25.24.150(c)(3) authorizes the court to consider the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference. At nine years of age, the child may be capable of articulating meaningful views regarding her living situation, particularly in light of her experience during Sarah's DUI arrest while she was in the vehicle. The court may wish to speak with the child in camera or appoint a guardian ad litem to assess and represent her interests. Alaska R. Evid. 601 confirms that a person is competent to be a witness unless the court finds the proposed witness incapable of communicating concerning the matter so as to be understood, or incapable of understanding the duty to tell the truth. The child's direct observations of Sarah's conduct are relevant and potentially admissible through appropriate procedures.
5. Facilitation of the Other Parent's Relationship with the Child
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) calls on the court to consider each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Jacob's proposed custody arrangement does not seek to eliminate Sarah from the child's life. Jacob proposes that Sarah receive supervised visitation on alternating weekends, with a pathway to expanded contact tied to demonstrated sobriety and treatment completion. This approach reflects Jacob's recognition that the child benefits from a relationship with both parents, consistent with the principle expressed in AS 25.20.070, which provides that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time the court considers a custody award, unless such access is shown to be detrimental to the child's welfare. Given Sarah's documented substance abuse and the direct endangerment of the child, equal unsupervised access is currently detrimental, and the proposed visitation structure appropriately balances those concerns.
C. THE COURT SHOULD ORDER SUPERVISED VISITATION FOR SARAH UNTIL SHE COMPLETES A SUBSTANCE ABUSE TREATMENT PROGRAM AND DEMONSTRATES SIX CONSECUTIVE MONTHS OF SOBRIETY
Jacob requests that this Court order supervised visitation for Sarah on alternating weekends, conditioned on her completion of a court-approved substance abuse treatment program and demonstration of at least six consecutive months of sobriety. This relief is consistent with Alaska law and the protective purpose of the custody statutes.
AS 25.24.150(j) provides that where a court finds a parent has a history of perpetrating domestic violence, supervised visitation shall be required, conditioned on participation in and completion of an intervention program. While Jacob does not assert that Sarah has perpetrated domestic violence as formally defined, the same protective framework reflects the legislature's recognition that a parent whose conduct endangers the child must demonstrate rehabilitation before enjoying unsupervised access. Sarah's two DUI arrests, including one with the child present, establish precisely that kind of endangering pattern.
The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Jaymot v. Skillings-Donat, 216 P.3d 534 (Alaska 2009), that the statutory best-interests factors require the court to account for evidence of substance abuse that directly affects the child's physical well-being. The court in Wee v. Eggener, 225 P.3d 1120 (Alaska 2010), further confirmed that supervised visitation conditioned on completion of a substance abuse treatment program is an appropriate remedy when a parent's conduct poses a danger to the child, and that unsupervised visitation requires affirmative showings of sobriety and the absence of risk of mental or physical harm to the child.
Imposing supervised visitation now, with a defined and achievable pathway to expanded contact, protects the child while preserving Sarah's opportunity to demonstrate that she can safely parent. This measured approach reflects the structure contemplated by AS 25.24.150(c) and (j), and is consistent with the holdings in both Wee v. Eggener and Kristina B. v. Edward B., 329 P.3d 202 (Alaska 2014).
D. THE COURT RETAINS JURISDICTION TO MODIFY THE EXISTING ORDER
The existing custody order was entered by the Anchorage Superior Court, a court of this state. Under AS 25.30.310(a), a court of this state that has made a child custody determination has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over the determination until a court of this state determines that neither the child, the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent have a significant connection with this state, or until a court of this state or another state determines that none of the relevant parties presently reside in this state. Jacob has relocated within Alaska to Juneau, and the child continues to reside in Alaska with Sarah in Anchorage. Both parents and the child remain in Alaska. Accordingly, this Court retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction to modify the existing custody order. No inconvenient forum issue arises under AS 25.30.360, as all parties and relevant evidence are located within Alaska.
E. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE RECALCULATED UPON MODIFICATION OF CUSTODY
Should the Court grant Jacob primary physical custody, the existing child support arrangement will require modification. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary custody case is calculated by multiplying the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent by the applicable percentage: 20 percent for one child. Should the Court determine that a shared physical custody arrangement is more appropriate, Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides the framework for calculating support under a shared custody model. Jacob requests that the Court recalculate child support in accordance with whichever applicable provision of Civil Rule 90.3 governs the custody structure the Court ultimately orders, using current verified income information from both parties.
V. CONCLUSION
Jacob Sutter respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the existing custody order, based on Jacob's relocation to Juneau for stable state employment and Sarah's two DUI arrests, including one in which the child was a passenger in the vehicle;

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0089)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Colby respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order entered in March 2022 and establish a week-on, week-off shared physical custody arrangement for the parties' nine-year-old daughter, Lily. Since the prior order was entered, significant and substantial changes in circumstances have occurred on both sides of this case. Elena has achieved sobriety through the successful completion of a two-year alcohol treatment program, secured stable and well-compensated employment as a licensed electrician, and relocated from Fairbanks to Anchorage, placing her within five miles of Lily's school and Maria's residence. Maria, meanwhile, has been diagnosed with a serious chronic illness that has materially limited her ability to transport Lily to school and extracurricular activities, and Lily's teacher has reported declining attendance and academic performance during the weeks when Elena is not involved in her care. These changes, taken together, compel modification of the existing order. Equal parenting time in a week-on, week-off schedule is in Lily's best interests and should be ordered by this Court.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Colby and Maria Colby are parties to a Superior Court custody order entered in Anchorage in March 2022. That order awarded Maria Colby primary physical custody of the parties' daughter, Lily, who is now nine years old. Under the existing order, Elena receives parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. The order was entered at a time when Elena resided in Fairbanks, approximately 360 miles from Lily's school and Maria's home in Anchorage, and when Elena was actively struggling with alcohol dependency.
Since the entry of the March 2022 order, Elena has undertaken significant and demonstrable steps to improve her life and her capacity to parent Lily. Elena completed a full two-year alcohol treatment program and has maintained her sobriety. She obtained her license as an electrician and secured stable employment in Anchorage. She relocated from Fairbanks to Anchorage and now resides within five miles of Lily's school and within five miles of Maria's residence. These changes eliminate the geographic barrier that was a significant factor in the original custody determination and fundamentally alter the practical landscape of shared custody.
Maria Colby's circumstances have also changed materially since March 2022. Maria has been recently diagnosed with a serious chronic illness. That illness has significantly limited her physical capacity to transport Lily to school and to extracurricular activities on a consistent basis. As a result, Lily's attendance and academic performance have declined. Lily's teacher has specifically reported that attendance and performance are diminished during the weeks when Elena is not involved in Lily's care. These reports reflect a direct and negative impact on Lily's educational needs and day-to-day welfare.
Elena now petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order. Elena seeks a week-on, week-off shared physical custody arrangement that would allow Lily to benefit from consistent, stable involvement of both parents in her daily life.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A custody order may be modified when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a). The threshold inquiry is whether a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since the prior custody determination. Moore v. McGillis, 408 P.3d 1196 (Alaska 2018). That change must be substantial, must affect the child's welfare, and must be evaluated relative to the facts and circumstances that existed at the time of the prior order. Moore v. McGillis, 408 P.3d 1196 (Alaska 2018). Only after the court finds a qualifying change in circumstances does the analysis proceed to the question of whether the proposed modification serves the child's best interests. McLane v. Paul, 189 P.3d 1039 (Alaska 2008).
In determining the best interests of the child, the court considers all relevant factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c). Those factors include the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if she is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence that substance abuse directly affects the child's well-being; and other pertinent factors. AS 25.24.150(c).
When evaluating whether to award shared custody, the court additionally considers the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, including the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the child's school, the feasibility of travel between the parents, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. AS 25.20.090(6)(B), (6)(C).
During the pendency of a custody modification proceeding, Alaska law provides that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents, unless detrimental to the child's welfare or unless the domestic violence presumption applies. AS 25.20.070.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. SUBSTANTIAL CHANGES IN CIRCUMSTANCES HAVE OCCURRED SINCE THE MARCH 2022 ORDER AND WARRANT MODIFICATION.
The first inquiry in any custody modification proceeding is whether a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since the prior order. AS 25.20.110(a). A substantial change is one that affects the child's welfare and that is demonstrated relative to the facts and circumstances existing at the time of the prior custody order. Moore v. McGillis, 408 P.3d 1196 (Alaska 2018). Here, multiple independent substantial changes have occurred on both sides of this case, each of which independently affects Lily's welfare, and which together overwhelmingly satisfy the threshold showing.
1. Elena's Sobriety, Employment, and Relocation to Anchorage Constitute Substantial Changes in Circumstances.
When the March 2022 order was entered, Elena resided in Fairbanks and was engaged in treatment for alcohol dependency. The geographic distance between Elena and Lily's school, combined with Elena's then-existing substance use, were material factors informing the limited parenting schedule established in that order. Both of those conditions have now changed entirely.
Elena has completed a two-year alcohol treatment program and maintained her sobriety. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Yvonne S. v. Wesley H., 245 P.3d 430 (Alaska 2011), that a parent's changed circumstances, including relocation, can constitute a substantial change warranting a modification in custody. Elena's completion of alcohol treatment and her sustained sobriety represent a profound and lasting change from the circumstances that existed in March 2022. Evidence that substance abuse by a parent directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of a child is a statutory best-interests factor under AS 25.24.150(c)(8). Correspondingly, Elena's documented rehabilitation from alcohol dependency directly removes a previously existing barrier to expanded parenting time and affirmatively demonstrates that she can now safely and consistently meet Lily's needs.
Elena has also obtained stable employment as a licensed electrician in Anchorage and relocated from Fairbanks to within five miles of Lily's school and Maria's residence. This relocation is itself a substantial change. In Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that a parent's relocation constitutes a significant change in circumstances warranting reconsideration of a custody arrangement. The proximity factors under AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (6)(C), specifically the proximity of each parent to the other and to the child's school, and the feasibility of travel between the parents, are now dramatically more favorable to shared custody than they were when the 2022 order was entered. The geographic barrier that once made week-on, week-off sharing impractical no longer exists.
2. Maria's Serious Chronic Illness and Its Effect on Lily's Attendance and Academic Performance Constitute Additional Substantial Changes.
Maria's diagnosis with a serious chronic illness since the entry of the March 2022 order constitutes an independent substantial change in circumstances. AS 25.20.110(a). The illness has materially limited Maria's ability to transport Lily to school and extracurricular activities. The direct consequence of this limitation is documented: Lily's teacher has reported declining attendance and academic performance during the weeks when Elena is not involved in Lily's care. A child's academic performance and attendance are directly related to her educational needs, which are among the enumerated best-interests factors under AS 25.24.150(c)(1) (physical, emotional, mental, and social needs of the child). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a marked drop in a child's academic performance constitutes a matter of serious concern in custody modification analysis. Yvonne S. v. Wesley H., 245 P.3d 430 (Alaska 2011).
The reported decline in Lily's attendance and performance during periods of reduced Elena involvement reflects a direct nexus between the existing custody arrangement and a negative impact on the child's welfare. This satisfies the requirement articulated in Moore v. McGillis, 408 P.3d 1196 (Alaska 2018), that a substantial change in circumstances must be one that affects the child's welfare.
3. The Aggregate of These Changes Satisfies the Threshold Showing.
Even where individual changes might not independently satisfy the substantial change threshold, courts consider allegations of changed circumstances in the aggregate. Yvonne S. v. Wesley H., 245 P.3d 430 (Alaska 2011). Here, each of the material changes identified above, namely Elena's sobriety, her stable employment, her relocation to within five miles of Lily's school, and Maria's serious chronic illness and its documented effect on Lily's attendance and performance, is substantial standing alone. Taken together, these changes present an overwhelming basis for this Court to find that modification of the existing order is warranted.
B. MODIFICATION TO A WEEK-ON, WEEK-OFF SHARED PHYSICAL CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT IS IN LILY'S BEST INTERESTS.
Having established the requisite change in circumstances, the analysis proceeds to whether the proposed modification serves Lily's best interests. AS 25.20.110(a). The court is to assess the best interests of the child in light of all relevant statutory factors under AS 25.24.150(c) and, for shared custody specifically, the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090. Each of these factors supports an equal parenting time arrangement in the present case.
1. Lily's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs Are Best Served by Equal Access to Both Parents.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(1), the court considers the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Lily is nine years old and, according to her teacher, her attendance and academic performance are declining in correlation with reduced involvement by Elena. This direct evidence demonstrates that Lily's educational and developmental needs are not being fully met under the current arrangement. Equal parenting time, with Elena available five days out of every fourteen to transport Lily to school and extracurricular activities, would directly address the deficiency that Maria's illness has created.
Furthermore, Alaska public policy, as expressed in AS 25.20.070, provides that a child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, "equal access to both parents" during custody proceedings, absent a showing of detriment or the domestic violence presumption. No such detriment or presumption is present here. Elena's completed alcohol treatment and documented sobriety affirmatively negate any concern about substance-related harm to Lily under AS 25.24.150(c)(8). The policy of equal access therefore weighs in favor of the week-on, week-off schedule Elena proposes.
2. Elena Is Fully Capable of Meeting Lily's Needs.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(2), the court considers the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's needs. Elena has demonstrated remarkable rehabilitation since the 2022 order. She completed a full two-year alcohol treatment program, maintained her sobriety, obtained a licensed electrician credential, and secured stable employment in Anchorage. She has also voluntarily relocated from Fairbanks to Anchorage, demonstrating a genuine commitment to being present in Lily's daily life. These facts directly establish Elena's capability and desire to meet Lily's needs on a day-to-day basis in a shared custody arrangement.
3. The Proximity of Elena's Residence to Lily's School Makes Shared Custody Feasible and Optimal.
Under AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (6)(C), the court considers the proximity of each parent to the other and to the child's school, and the feasibility of travel between the parents. Elena now resides within five miles of both Lily's school and Maria's residence. This proximity makes week-on, week-off transitions not merely feasible but straightforward. Concerns about travel disruption, missed school days during transitions, or logistical complications are eliminated by the parties' present proximity. The Anchorage Supreme Court emphasized proximity as a meaningful shared custody factor in Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018), where the court analyzed shared custody arrangements in light of each statutory factor.
4. Stability and Continuity Support a Shared Arrangement With Elena More Actively Involved.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(5), the court considers the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. While continuity in a satisfactory environment is an important value, it must be weighed against the documented evidence that the current arrangement is no longer satisfactory for Lily. Declining attendance and academic performance during weeks when Elena is not involved suggests that the current arrangement has become an obstacle to Lily's stability rather than a source of it. A transition to week-on, week-off shared custody would provide Lily with continuous and reliable access to the parent who has demonstrated the greater current capacity to meet her day-to-day logistical and educational needs, while preserving her relationship with Maria.
5. Elena's Willingness to Facilitate Lily's Relationship With Maria Supports Shared Custody.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6) and AS 25.20.090(6)(E), the court considers each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. Elena's petition for equal parenting time, rather than for primary custody, itself reflects her recognition that Lily benefits from a close relationship with Maria. Elena does not seek to diminish Maria's role; she seeks to participate equally. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's demonstrated willingness to support the child's relationship with the other parent is a positive factor in shared custody analysis. Sweeney v. Organ, 371 P.3d 609 (Alaska 2016).
6. The Optimal Time Lily Should Spend With Each Parent, Considering All Circumstances, Favors Equal Parenting Time.
Under AS 25.20.090(6), the court considers the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, taking into account the actual time spent with each parent, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the child's school, the feasibility of travel, and any special needs of the child. Each of these sub-factors now favors equal parenting time. Elena is geographically proximate. Travel between the parties is simple. Lily has no reported special needs that would be better served by one parent exclusively. And the actual parenting time Elena has been exercising, every other weekend and one evening per week, falls far short of what is now feasible and beneficial given the changed circumstances.
C. SHARED PHYSICAL CUSTODY TRIGGERS THE CHILD SUPPORT CALCULATION UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(b).
If this Court grants the requested modification to a week-on, week-off schedule, the child support calculation will be governed by Civil Rule 90.3(b), which addresses shared physical custody arrangements. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), shared physical custody exists when "the children reside with that parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30, but no more than 70, percent of the year." A week-on, week-off arrangement results in each parent having physical custody of approximately 50 percent of the year, which falls squarely within the shared physical custody definition. Civil Rule 90.3(b) would therefore apply to any recalculation of child support, and Elena requests that the Court address child support consistent with that rule upon entry of a modified custody order.
D. THE COURT SHOULD EXERCISE ITS AUTHORITY UNDER AS 25.20.070 TO MAXIMIZE LILY'S ACCESS TO ELENA DURING THE PENDENCY OF THESE PROCEEDINGS.
During the pendency of any custody modification proceeding, AS 25.20.070 directs that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents, absent a finding of detriment to the child's welfare or the presence of the domestic violence presumption under AS 25.24.150(g). Neither detriment nor the domestic violence presumption is present in this case. Elena's documented sobriety and stable circumstances support, rather than undermine, expanded access. Accordingly, Elena respectfully requests that this Court enter interim orders during the pendency of this matter substantially increasing Elena's parenting time consistent with the equal access principle embodied in AS 25.20.070.
V. CONCLUSION
The record in this matter presents precisely the kind of substantial and documented change in circumstances that Alaska law recognizes as warranting modification of an existing custody order. Elena has completed alcohol treatment, achieved and maintained sobriety, secured stable employment as a licensed electrician, and relocated from Fairbanks to within five miles of Lily's school and Maria's residence. Maria has been diagnosed with a serious chronic illness that has materially impaired her ability to meet Lily's day-to-day transportation and attendance needs, and Lily's teacher has reported a direct correlation between Elena's absence and declining school performance. Every relevant statutory factor under AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.090 supports modification to a week-on, week-off shared physical custody arrangement. Elena respectfully requests that this Court find a substantial change in circumstances, determine that a week-on, week-off shared custody arrangement is in Lily's best interests, enter a modified custody order accordingly, recalculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(b), and enter interim orders maximizing Elena's parenting time during the pendency of these proceedings consistent with AS 25.20.070.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0090)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Colby respectfully asks this Court to modify the existing child custody order and award her primary physical custody of Maya Colby, age nine. The basis for this petition is Respondent Danielle Colby's announced intention to relocate with Maya from Anchorage to Juneau, a distance of approximately 600 miles, within sixty days. That planned relocation constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under Alaska law and, when evaluated against the statutory best-interests factors, warrants a transfer of primary physical custody to Renee. Renee has remarried, maintains a stable and consistent home environment in Anchorage, and works a predictable Monday through Friday schedule. Maya attends school and participates in established extracurricular activities in Anchorage. Requiring Maya to uproot from that community so that Danielle may pursue a career opportunity, while simultaneously eliminating any practical opportunity for Renee to exercise her court-ordered visitation, would not serve Maya's best interests. This Court should modify the current order to place primary physical custody with Renee in Anchorage and award Danielle generous block parenting time during school breaks, holiday periods, and the summer months.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Colby and Danielle Colby are the parents of Maya Colby, born nine years ago. Approximately two years ago, the Alaska Superior Court entered a custody order awarding Danielle primary physical custody of Maya. That order granted Renee alternating weekend visitation from Friday evening through Sunday evening, as well as two consecutive weeks of uninterrupted summer parenting time. The order was premised on the circumstances that existed at the time of entry, including the understanding that both parties resided in the Anchorage area and that the alternating weekend schedule was therefore feasible.
Since the entry of the order, material circumstances have changed on both sides of this dispute. On Renee's side, the changes have been stabilizing and beneficial to Maya. Renee has remarried and now has a stable two-parent household with an established support network in Anchorage. She is employed on a consistent Monday through Friday schedule, meaning that she is reliably available to care for Maya on weekday evenings and throughout the weekend. Her home environment is settled, predictable, and capable of meeting Maya's physical, emotional, and educational needs on a primary basis.
On Danielle's side, the changes are disruptive to the existing order and to Maya's established community ties. Danielle has accepted a permanent position with a Juneau-based employer and intends to relocate with Maya from Anchorage within the next sixty days. Juneau is approximately 600 miles from Anchorage. There is no road connection between the two cities; travel between them requires either a commercial flight or an extended ferry journey. The cost and logistical complexity of such travel would render the current alternating weekend visitation schedule financially impractical and effectively impossible to exercise on any regular basis. If the relocation proceeds with Maya, Renee would lose meaningful, consistent access to her daughter, and Maya would be severed from her school, her extracurricular activities, and her established community in Anchorage.
Renee now petitions this Court for a modification of the custody order, seeking primary physical custody of Maya in Anchorage, with Danielle receiving substantial parenting time during school breaks, holiday periods, and the summer vacation.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska law permits modification of a child custody order when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110. The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that a custodial parent's decision to move out of state, or to relocate a significant distance from the other parent, amounts to a substantial change in circumstances as a matter of law for purposes of physical custody modifications. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). The same principle applies where the relocation effectively destroys the other parent's ability to exercise the visitation rights established by the existing order.
When a proposed relocation is found to be legitimate, there is no presumption favoring either parent when the court considers the child's best interests in the context of a custody modification. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). The court must consider the full range of best-interests factors set forth in AS 25.24.933, including the physical, emotional, mental, and social needs of the child; the capability of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form one; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. AS 25.24.150(c).
Throughout the custody evaluation period, the child is entitled to the greatest degree of practical access to both parents. AS 25.20.070 provides that, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the child's welfare, "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody." The court may also consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090 when evaluating whether to award shared or primary custody, including the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, and the optimal time each parent can realistically spend with the child given geographic proximity and travel feasibility.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Danielle's Planned Relocation to Juneau Constitutes a Substantial Change in Circumstances.
As a threshold matter, modification of the existing custody order requires a showing of changed circumstances. AS 25.20.110. That threshold is plainly met here. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a custodial parent's decision to relocate a significant distance constitutes a substantial change in circumstances as a matter of law. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). Danielle's planned move from Anchorage to Juneau, approximately 600 miles away and accessible only by air or sea, falls squarely within that recognized category of changed circumstance. The existing custody order was entered when both parties lived in the Anchorage area, and it was structured around the assumption that alternating weekend exchanges were feasible. That assumption no longer holds. Once Danielle relocates to Juneau, the weekend visitation schedule Renee currently enjoys will become geographically and financially untenable. The existing order will be rendered a practical nullity with respect to Renee's visitation rights.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized that modification analysis must account for the practical effect of a relocation on the non-relocating parent's ability to maintain a meaningful relationship with the child. West v. Lawson, 951 P.2d 1200 (Alaska 1998). In that case, the court emphasized that divided physical custody arrangements premised on proximity assumptions lose their validity when those assumptions change, and that evidence demonstrating harm to the child from a disrupted schedule weighs heavily in the modification analysis. The facts here present precisely that situation. The relocation does not merely alter the schedule at the margins; it eliminates Renee's ability to exercise regular parenting time entirely.
Additionally, Renee's own changed circumstances independently support the finding of a material change. At the time of the original order, the factual predicate for awarding Danielle primary custody included whatever circumstances existed at that time. Since then, Renee has remarried, established a stable two-parent household, and secured consistent weekday employment. These changes, when combined with Danielle's relocation, present a materially different picture than the one before the court two years ago. Taken together, the changed circumstances on both sides satisfy the threshold requirement of AS 25.20.110.
B. Modification of Primary Physical Custody to Renee Is in Maya's Best Interests.
Once changed circumstances are established, the court must determine whether modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110. The court's analysis is governed by the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c). When evaluated against those factors, the record supports awarding Renee primary physical custody of Maya in Anchorage.
1. Maya's Established Community in Anchorage Favors Continuity of Placement.
Among the most important best-interests factors is the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Maya is nine years old and has lived her entire life in Anchorage. She attends school there and participates in extracurricular activities in that community. Her friendships, her school relationships, and her activities are all anchored in Anchorage. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that courts should be cautious about disrupting a child's established community, and that continuity of environment is a significant factor in the best-interests analysis. Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011).
If Maya relocates to Juneau with Danielle, she will be separated from her school, her activities, her extended support network, and her daily access to Renee. She will face the challenge of beginning again in a new community at an age when peer relationships and academic stability are particularly important. By contrast, if primary custody is transferred to Renee and Maya remains in Anchorage, she maintains the continuity of her established environment while Danielle, as the relocating parent, takes on the burden of travel to exercise her parenting time. This is the more child-centered outcome. AS 25.20.090(5) likewise identifies the advantages of keeping the child in the community where she presently resides as a relevant consideration in the custody determination.
2. Renee's Home Environment Is Stable and Capable of Meeting Maya's Needs.
The best-interests analysis requires the court to consider the capability and desire of each parent to meet the child's physical, emotional, mental, and social needs, as well as the stability of the home environment each parent can offer. AS 25.24.150(c)(1), (c)(2); AS 25.20.090(3). Renee has remarried and now has a consistent, two-parent household in Anchorage. She works a predictable Monday through Friday schedule, meaning she is available to provide after-school care, attend school events, supervise extracurricular activities, and maintain the kind of routine that supports a child's healthy development. She has an established support network in Anchorage that can assist with Maya's care when needed.
Danielle, by contrast, is in the process of starting a new position with a new employer in a new city. While accepting employment is a legitimate life decision, the transition period that accompanies a relocation to a new job in a new city does not represent the most stable environment for a nine-year-old child. The court is entitled to weigh the relative stability of each parent's household as it currently exists, and on that measure, Renee's long-established Anchorage home and employment situation compares favorably. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018).
3. Maya's Access to Both Parents Is Best Preserved by Awarding Renee Primary Physical Custody.
A core principle of Alaska custody law is that children should have, to the greatest degree practical, access to both parents. AS 25.20.070 provides that "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody." If Maya relocates to Juneau with Danielle, Renee's practical access to Maya is destroyed. Travel between Anchorage and Juneau requires air or sea travel, imposes significant cost, and is inherently irregular. The alternating weekend schedule that the existing order provides becomes impossible to maintain, and Maya's relationship with Renee would be reduced to infrequent, long-distance visits.
If, however, primary custody is awarded to Renee and Maya remains in Anchorage, Danielle retains the ability to travel to Anchorage and exercise parenting time, and Maya is available to spend substantial blocks of time with Danielle during school breaks, holidays, and summer vacation. This arrangement preserves meaningful contact between Maya and both of her parents, which AS 25.20.070 identifies as the paramount access goal. The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in D.D. v. L.A.H., 27 P.3d 757 (Alaska 2001), confirms that courts must carefully evaluate which custody arrangement will best preserve the child's relationships with both parents when relocation creates a geographic barrier.
The willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child is also a statutory best-interests factor. AS 25.24.150(c)(6); AS 25.20.090(6)(E). Renee has consistently exercised her court-ordered visitation. By petitioning for modification rather than simply seeking to prevent the relocation, Renee demonstrates a commitment to maintaining a legal framework that affords Danielle generous and structured parenting time, including block periods during school breaks, holidays, and summer. A proposed custody structure that gives Danielle extended, uninterrupted time periods is more conducive to meaningful parenting across geographic distance than the current weekly alternating schedule, and it reflects Renee's genuine desire for Maya to maintain a strong relationship with both of her parents.
4. The Feasibility of Travel and the Proposed Custody Structure Support the Requested Modification.
In evaluating a shared or modified custody arrangement, AS 25.20.090(6) directs the court to consider the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, including the proximity of each parent to the other, the feasibility of travel between the parents, and any special needs unique to the child. All three sub-factors weigh in favor of the proposed modification. The proximity factor strongly favors awarding primary custody to the Anchorage-based parent. The feasibility of travel for a nine-year-old child across 600 miles of roadless terrain, on a biweekly basis, is nil. The proposed parenting plan offered by Renee, in which Danielle receives substantial block parenting time during school breaks, holiday periods, and summer vacation, is the standard structure that Alaska courts have recognized as appropriate when geographic distance makes frequent exchanges impractical. West v. Lawson, 951 P.2d 1200 (Alaska 1998).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support would be calculated based on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income and the resulting percentage obligation, and the court should set support accordingly if primary custody is transferred to Renee. The court should also establish appropriate provisions for summer and holiday block parenting time for Danielle, ensuring that the child support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) or, if block time meets the threshold for shared custody, Civil Rule 959(b), accurately reflects the actual parenting time each parent will exercise.
5. Modification Should Be Granted to Protect the Integrity of the Existing Order and Maya's Stability.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that an existing custody arrangement loses its validity when the assumptions underlying it are no longer true. West v. Lawson, 951 P.2d 1200 (Alaska 1998). The original order in this case was built on the premise that both parents would reside in the Anchorage area and that alternating weekend exchanges would be feasible. Danielle's relocation dissolves that premise entirely. Allowing Danielle to relocate with Maya while the current order remains in place would reduce Renee's court-ordered visitation rights to a theoretical entitlement with no practical means of exercise. It would also deprive Maya of consistent, frequent contact with Renee, contrary to the policy expressed in AS 25.20.070. Iverson v. Griffith, 180 P.3d 943 (Alaska 2008), confirms that where changed circumstances render the existing custody arrangement unworkable, modification in the child's best interests is appropriate and the court should not hesitate to act.
Modifying the order to award primary physical custody to Renee, with Danielle receiving generous block parenting time, preserves the best of both relationships. It keeps Maya in her established community, school, and extracurricular environment. It gives Renee, the parent remaining in Anchorage, the ability to exercise day-to-day primary custody. And it gives Danielle extended, meaningful parenting time concentrated during school breaks, holidays, and the summer, which is the most realistic structure for a long-distance parenting relationship. That outcome serves Maya's best interests under every relevant statutory factor.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Colby respectfully requests that this Court find a substantial change in circumstances based on Respondent Danielle Colby's planned relocation to Juneau, conduct a best-interests analysis under AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.110, and enter an order modifying the existing custody decree to award Renee primary physical custody of Maya Colby in Anchorage. Renee further requests that the modified order grant Danielle generous block parenting time during school breaks, holiday periods, and summer vacation, establish a child support obligation calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), and include such other provisions as the Court deems necessary to serve Maya's best interests and to facilitate a meaningful, ongoing relationship between Maya and both of her parents.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0091)
I. INTRODUCTION
Jacob Petrova ("Petitioner") respectfully requests that this Court modify the existing custody order entered in 2021 to establish a shared physical custody arrangement for the parties' two minor children, ages seven and nine. The current order grants Brandon Petrova ("Respondent") primary physical custody and limits Jacob's parenting time to every other weekend and alternating holidays. Since that order was entered, a substantial change in circumstances has occurred on both sides of this custody arrangement. Jacob has completed a two-year substance abuse treatment program, obtained stable full-time employment as a licensed electrician, and relocated to a home within three miles of the children's school in Anchorage. Brandon, by contrast, has accepted a position that requires him to travel out of state for three to four weeks at a time, regularly leaving the children in the care of various relatives during his extended absences.
These changed circumstances, considered individually and collectively, satisfy Alaska's legal threshold for custody modification under AS 25.20.110. More importantly, the modification Jacob seeks, a shared physical custody schedule providing each parent with roughly equal parenting time, serves the best interests of the children under AS 25.24.150 and the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.934. Jacob files this brief in support of his petition and asks the Court to grant a shared physical custody arrangement.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jacob and Brandon Petrova were divorced in 2021. The Superior Court entered a custody order at that time granting Brandon primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children. Under that order, Jacob receives parenting time every other weekend and on alternating holidays. The order was entered during a period when Jacob was struggling with substance abuse issues, which, along with his then-unstable employment and living situation, weighed against a larger share of parenting time.
Since the entry of the 2021 order, Jacob has taken substantial and demonstrable steps to transform his circumstances. He successfully completed a full two-year substance abuse treatment program. He has secured stable, full-time employment as a licensed electrician, giving him a reliable income and a consistent daily schedule. He has relocated to a residence within three miles of the children's school in Anchorage, placing him in close geographic proximity to their educational environment and making transitions between households both practical and minimally disruptive.
Brandon's circumstances have also materially changed, but in a direction that raises concerns about the children's day-to-day care. Brandon has accepted a new position that requires him to travel out of state for periods of three to four weeks at a time. During these extended absences, the children are not in the care of either parent but are left with various relatives. The identity, stability, and qualifications of these rotating caregivers vary. The children are therefore regularly spending significant stretches of time without access to either of their parents.
Jacob seeks a modified custody arrangement in which each parent has roughly equal parenting time. This shared schedule would give the children meaningful, consistent access to both parents, provide stability through Jacob's nearby residence and flexible work schedule, and ensure that Brandon's work-related absences do not continue to deprive the children of parental contact for weeks at a time.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska law permits modification of a custody order when two conditions are met. First, the court must determine that a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the prior order. Second, the court must find that the proposed modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody "may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification of the award and the modification is in the best interests of the child."
The Alaska Supreme Court has explained that the change-of-circumstances requirement is intended to discourage continual relitigation of custody decisions, recognizing that finality and certainty in custody matters are critical to a child's emotional welfare. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). Courts evaluate whether circumstances have changed by comparing present conditions to the facts that existed at the time the prior order was entered. Id. A change is not substantial if it reflects only the mere passage of time, but it may be substantial when it meaningfully affects the welfare of the children. Id.
Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the court conducts a full best-interests analysis. AS 25.24.150(c) sets out the factors the court must consider, including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; any evidence of substance abuse; and other factors the court considers pertinent.
Additionally, AS 25.20.090 sets out factors specific to shared custody determinations, including the child's preference, the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment each parent is likely to offer, the educational environment, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, and the optimal time the child should spend with each parent considering the actual time spent, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the school, and the feasibility of travel between households.
AS 25.20.070 further provides that, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child, "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents" during a custody proceeding.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), a parent has shared physical custody for child support calculation purposes if the children reside with that parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. A modification of the underlying custody schedule may trigger a corresponding recalculation of child support, which would proceed under Civil Rule 90.3(b).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Substantial Change in Circumstances Has Occurred Since Entry of the 2021 Custody Order.
The threshold requirement for modification is met here. Since the 2021 order was entered, Jacob's circumstances have changed dramatically for the better, and Brandon's circumstances have changed in ways that significantly affect the children's daily care. Courts compare current conditions against the baseline that existed when the prior order was entered. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). The relevant baseline here is 2021, when Jacob was in the midst of substance abuse struggles and had not yet secured stable employment or a suitable residence. That baseline looks nothing like Jacob's current situation.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's recovery from substance abuse, combined with improved employment and housing stability, can constitute a substantial change in circumstances. Siekawitch v. Siekawitch, 956 P.2d 447 (Alaska 1998). Jacob has completed a full two-year substance abuse treatment program. He is now employed full-time as a licensed electrician. He lives within three miles of the children's school. Each of these changes is meaningful on its own; taken together, they reflect a comprehensive and lasting transformation in Jacob's ability to parent effectively and consistently.
Brandon's changed circumstances are equally significant to the analysis. At the time the 2021 order was entered, Brandon was available on a full-time basis to provide primary care for the children. He has since accepted a position requiring him to leave the state for three to four weeks at a time. During these absences, neither parent is present in the home. The children are rotated among various relatives. This is not a minor scheduling adjustment. It is a fundamental alteration in who is actually parenting the children on a day-to-day basis. Courts have held that actions by a custodial parent that substantially affect the children's welfare and stability constitute changed circumstances. Kelly v. Joseph, 46 P.3d 1014 (Alaska 2002). Brandon's regular, extended work-related absences fall squarely within this principle.
In sum, the combined effect of Jacob's recovery, stability, and proximity, alongside Brandon's new pattern of extended out-of-state absences, constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a). The Court should proceed to the best-interests analysis.
B. Modification to Shared Physical Custody Is in the Best Interests of the Children.
Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the Court must determine whether modification serves the children's best interests under AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.090. A thorough evaluation of those factors supports the shared custody arrangement Jacob proposes.
1. The Children's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs Are Best Served by a Shared Custody Arrangement.
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) directs the Court to consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Children benefit from consistent, meaningful contact with both parents. The current every-other-weekend schedule provides Jacob with approximately fifteen percent of the parenting time on an annualized basis, far below the minimum threshold for shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1). Meanwhile, the children are already spending weeks at a time without either parent during Brandon's work trips. A shared custody arrangement would replace weeks of rotating relative care with consistent parenting by Jacob, serving the children's emotional and developmental needs in a direct and concrete way.
2. Jacob Is Now Fully Capable of and Committed to Meeting the Children's Needs.
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) calls for the Court to assess the capability and desire of each parent to meet the children's needs. Jacob's completion of a two-year substance abuse treatment program is direct evidence that he has addressed the very issue that most constrained his parenting role in 2021. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's completion of substance abuse treatment is highly relevant to a best-interests determination. Siekawitch v. Siekawitch, 956 P.2d 447 (Alaska 1998). Jacob is now employed full-time with a stable income and a consistent schedule. He resides within three miles of the children's school. He is positioned to be a fully capable, present, and engaged parent for substantial periods of time, not merely alternating weekends.
3. Jacob's Home Offers Stability; Brandon's Frequent Absences Undermine Stability in His Home.
AS 25.24.150(c)(5) and AS 25.20.902 both direct the Court to consider the stability of the home environment each parent is likely to offer and the desirability of maintaining continuity. Jacob's new residence is close to the children's school, providing geographic and logistical stability. His employment as a licensed electrician provides financial stability. By contrast, Brandon's recurring out-of-state assignments, lasting three to four weeks at a time, mean the children do not have a consistently stable home environment in their primary residence. Rotating care among various relatives, however well-intentioned, does not provide the consistent, stable environment that serves children's best interests. Courts have recognized that the stability of the proposed custodial household is a central consideration in custody modification proceedings. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018).
4. Jacob's Proximity to the Children's School Supports the Proposed Modification.
AS 25.20.090(6)(B) directs the Court to consider the proximity of each parent to the school in which the child is enrolled. Jacob now lives within three miles of the children's school in Anchorage. This proximity would minimize transportation time and disruption to the children's educational routines. It would also allow Jacob to participate in school activities, pick-ups, and events on a far more meaningful basis than his current schedule permits. Brandon, while also residing in Anchorage when he is not traveling, is frequently absent from the state for weeks at a time, making his proximity to the school effectively irrelevant during those periods.
5. A Shared Custody Arrangement Promotes Each Child's Access to Both Parents.
AS 25.20.070 provides that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents. The current order does not approach this standard. Jacob receives parenting time for approximately two days every two weeks, while the children spend weeks with rotating relatives when Brandon is traveling. A roughly equal time-sharing arrangement would meaningfully expand the children's access to Jacob while preserving their relationship with Brandon during his periods at home.
The Alaska Supreme Court has approved graduated implementation of shared custody to ease transitions. Restol v. Manshen, 391 P.3d 385 (Alaska 2020). If the Court has any concerns about a sudden shift from the current schedule, it retains discretion to phase in a shared arrangement over a reasonable period while still moving toward equal parenting time.
6. Each Parent's Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Children Is a Relevant Factor.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) and AS 25.20.090(6)(E) require the Court to consider each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Jacob has demonstrated his commitment to a cooperative co-parenting relationship by pursuing this modification through proper legal channels rather than taking unilateral action. He does not seek to eliminate or minimize Brandon's role. He seeks equal time, which by definition requires both parents to remain actively involved in the children's lives.
7. There Is No Evidence of Domestic Violence or Substance Abuse Concerns That Would Bar Modification.
AS 25.24.150(c)(7) and (c)(8) require the Court to consider any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or neglect, as well as substance abuse that directly affects the children's well-being. AS 25.24.150(g) establishes a rebuttable presumption against custody for a parent with a history of perpetrating domestic violence. There is no evidence of domestic violence by either party. As to substance abuse, Jacob has successfully completed a two-year treatment program. His recovery is an affirmative factor in his favor, not a basis for continued restriction of his parenting time. AS 25.24.150(h) recognizes that successful completion of treatment is among the factors a court considers in evaluating whether a prior substance abuse history should continue to limit a parent's custodial role.
8. Child Support Should Be Recalculated Upon Entry of a Shared Custody Order.
Should the Court grant the modification and establish a shared physical custody arrangement, the existing child support order must be recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which governs child support in shared custody cases. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), if the children reside with Jacob for at least 30 percent of the year under the new order, the shared custody calculation formula applies. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) provides that a material change of circumstances will be presumed if support as calculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. A shift from an every-other-weekend schedule to a roughly equal time-sharing arrangement would almost certainly trigger this presumption, and Jacob respectfully requests that the Court order updated financial disclosures and recalculate child support upon entry of the modified custody order.
V. CONCLUSION
The evidence before this Court establishes both elements required for custody modification under Alaska law. First, Jacob's successful completion of substance abuse treatment, his stable full-time employment, and his relocation to a home within three miles of the children's school, combined with Brandon's new pattern of extended out-of-state work absences that leave the children in the care of rotating relatives, constitute a substantial change in circumstances since the 2021 order was entered. Second, a shared physical custody arrangement providing each parent with roughly equal parenting time is in the best interests of the parties' two children. Such an arrangement would give the children consistent parental care during periods when Brandon is traveling, provide them with meaningful access to a now-stable and geographically proximate Jacob, and honor the statutory directive that children have equal access to both parents to the greatest degree practical.
For all these reasons, Jacob Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the 2021 custody order;
2. Modify the existing order to establish a shared physical custody arrangement providing each parent with approximately equal parenting time;
3. Order updated financial disclosures from both parties; and
4. Recalculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(b) to reflect the new shared physical custody arrangement.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0092)
I. INTRODUCTION
Sarah Whitfield respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing custody order entered in 2021, which awarded primary physical custody of the parties' minor daughter, Lily Whitfield, to Renee Whitfield, with Sarah exercising parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. Since the entry of that order, Renee has unilaterally relocated Lily approximately 570 miles from Anchorage to Juneau, enrolled Lily in a new school without court approval or notice to Sarah, and effectively severed Lily from her established community, extended family, and educational environment. These actions constitute a substantial change in circumstances sufficient to warrant modification of the existing custody order under AS 25.20.110. A thorough analysis of the statutory best-interest factors under AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.090 demonstrates that transferring primary physical custody to Sarah, with Renee receiving parenting time during school breaks and summer vacation, is in Lily's best interests. Sarah therefore requests that this Court grant her motion to modify.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The Alaska Superior Court entered a custody order in 2021 establishing shared legal custody of Lily Whitfield, born in 2016, with Renee Whitfield designated as primary physical custodian. Under that order, Sarah Whitfield exercised parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. The order was predicated on the family's residence in Anchorage and contemplated the continuation of Lily's life in that community.
Following entry of the order, Renee accepted a permanent employment transfer to Juneau, Alaska, a city located approximately 570 miles from Anchorage. Renee thereafter enrolled Lily in a new school in Juneau without seeking court approval, without petitioning to modify the existing custody order, and without obtaining Sarah's consent. Sarah did not agree to this relocation and has not waived any rights arising from it. As a result of Renee's unilateral action, Lily has been removed from the school she attended in Anchorage, separated from her extended family members who reside in Anchorage, and distanced from the friends, teachers, and community connections she developed over the first years of her life.
Sarah Whitfield resides in Anchorage and is capable of providing Lily with a stable home, continuity in her existing educational environment, and regular contact with her extended family and established social network. Sarah proposes that Renee receive parenting time during Lily's school breaks and summer vacation, a schedule that would afford Renee meaningful access to Lily while preserving Lily's stability in Anchorage.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), a court may modify a custody or visitation award upon a determination that a change in circumstances requires modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. If a parent opposes the modification and the court grants it, the court must enter its reasons on the record. AS 25.20.110(a).
In evaluating the best interests of the child, the court must consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c), including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if she is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity under all circumstances; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; evidence of substance abuse that directly affects the child's well-being; and other pertinent factors. AS 25.24.150(c).
When the court considers whether to award shared custody, it must additionally evaluate the factors set forth in AS 25.20.090, including the stability of the home environment each parent is likely to offer, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where she presently resides, the proximity of each parent to the child's school, the feasibility of travel between the parents, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. AS 25.20.090.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a parent's unilateral relocation of a child may constitute a substantial change in circumstances justifying custody modification. Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 575 P.3d 332 (Alaska 2005). A significant change in the child's living situation, educational placement, and community connections can independently satisfy the change-in-circumstances threshold under AS 25.20.110(a). Yvonne S. v. Wesley H., 245 P.3d 430 (Alaska 2011). The court must then evaluate whether modification serves the child's best interests, with particular attention to continuity and stability. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018). Courts further recognize that preserving a child's established educational and community ties weighs heavily in the best-interest analysis. Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. RENEE'S UNILATERAL RELOCATION OF LILY TO JUNEAU CONSTITUTES A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER AS 25.20.110
The threshold inquiry under AS 25.20.110(a) requires the moving party to demonstrate a change in circumstances that warrants modification of the existing order. Renee's decision to permanently relocate Lily from Anchorage to Juneau, approximately 570 miles away, without court approval or Sarah's consent, plainly satisfies this standard.
The 2021 custody order was entered with the understanding that Lily would remain in Anchorage, where both parents resided and where Lily's educational, familial, and social life was centered. Renee's unilateral and permanent relocation fundamentally altered the circumstances on which the original order was premised. As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005), a military transfer and the resulting geographic separation between parents can constitute a substantial change in circumstances warranting custody modification. The principle established in that case applies with equal force here: when a primary custodian permanently relocates a child hundreds of miles away without consent or judicial authorization, the foundational assumptions of the prior order no longer hold.
The relocation has also produced concrete, material changes in Lily's circumstances. She has been removed from her school in Anchorage. She has been separated from her extended family members who live in the Anchorage area. She has lost daily proximity to the friends and community she built during the first years of her life. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a significant deterioration in a child's stability, educational environment, and community connections can satisfy the change-in-circumstances requirement. Yvonne S. v. Wesley H., 245 P.3d 430 (Alaska 2011).
Moreover, Renee's failure to seek court approval before enrolling Lily in a new school in Juneau is itself a circumstance the Court should weigh. The existing shared legal custody arrangement required joint decision-making, including decisions about education. Renee acted unilaterally, bypassing both the Court and Sarah. Under AS 25.20.110(a), such conduct reflects directly on Renee's willingness to abide by the terms of the existing order and to respect Sarah's legal rights as a joint legal custodian. A substantial change in circumstances exists, and this Court should proceed to the best-interest analysis.
B. THE BEST INTERESTS OF LILY REQUIRE THAT PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY BE TRANSFERRED TO SARAH
Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the court must determine whether modification is in the child's best interests. AS 25.20.110(a). The factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.090 collectively support transferring primary physical custody to Sarah so that Lily may remain in Anchorage.
1. The Desirability of Maintaining Continuity and Stability Favors Sarah
Among the most important factors in the best-interest analysis is the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. AS 25.24.150(c)(5). Lily spent the first years of her life in Anchorage. Her schooling, her extended family relationships, and her social bonds are all rooted in that community.
