Continuity of schooling, friendships, extracurricular activities, and community ties is a core component of stability for school-age children. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that preserving a child's established environment is a significant consideration in custody determinations. Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005); Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998).
In Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the relevance of the children's ties to familiar surroundings, friends, and community in determining which custody arrangement best serves their interests. The Tompkins case arose from a military transfer that made a prior shared custody arrangement unworkable, a situation directly analogous to the one presented here. Similarly, in Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005), the court affirmed a modification of custody to the non-relocating parent so that the children could remain in their established community during the school year when the other parent's military transfer made the prior shared schedule impossible to maintain.
Allowing the children to remain in Fairbanks during the school year with Renee preserves their enrollment in their current schools, maintains their existing friendships and peer relationships, and keeps them close to extended family and community connections they have built over their lifetimes. Disrupting this stability by requiring them to relocate to Juneau with Danielle, or by subjecting them to costly and time-consuming air travel on a biweekly basis to maintain the current schedule, would serve neither the children's educational interests nor their broader well-being.
2. The Proximity of Each Parent to the School and the Feasibility of Travel Support the Proposed Modification.
AS 25.20.090 sets forth specific factors the court must consider when evaluating a proposed custody arrangement. Among the most directly applicable here are "the proximity of each parent to the other and to the school in which the child is enrolled" and "the feasibility of travel between the parents." AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (C). Renee resides in Fairbanks, within the same community where the children attend school. Danielle now resides in Juneau, approximately 600 miles away, with no road connection. Travel between Fairbanks and Juneau requires air travel or extended ferry service, imposing significant financial cost and logistical burden on any parenting schedule that requires frequent exchanges.
The current every-other-weekend schedule is simply not feasible across a 600-mile, no-road-access distance. Implementing the existing schedule would require the children to miss school or travel on school days, accumulate substantial air travel expenses, and endure repeated disruption of their academic routines. The proposed modification, by contrast, concentrates Danielle's parenting time in extended blocks during school breaks, when travel is more manageable and does not interrupt the children's schooling. This structure is consistent with how Alaska courts have approached custody arrangements when a military transfer or other relocation has made a prior shared schedule unworkable. Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005); Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998).
3. The Children's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs Favor Placement with Renee During the School Year.
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) requires the court to consider "the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child." School-age children benefit from routine, consistency, and proximity to their primary social networks. The children's established school, peer friendships, and extracurricular activities are all located in Fairbanks. Renee has remained in the family's home community throughout this period and is positioned to provide daily, consistent parenting that supports the children's academic performance and social development during the school year.
The court in D.D. v. L.A.H., 27 P.3d 757 (Alaska 2001), recognized that a child's entry into school and the resulting inability of the parties to maintain a prior custody arrangement constitutes a substantial change in circumstances warranting modification. The court acknowledged that school-year custody arrangements must account for the practical realities of where the children are enrolled and which parent is best positioned to support their educational needs on a daily basis. Here, Renee is geographically situated to provide that daily support, while Danielle, residing 600 miles away in Juneau, is not.
4. The Proposed Arrangement Preserves Meaningful Contact with Both Parents and Reflects the Goal of Equal Access.
AS 25.20.070 reflects the legislative policy that children should, to the greatest degree practical, have equal access to both parents. The proposed modification is not designed to diminish the children's relationship with Danielle. To the contrary, it proposes to concentrate Danielle's parenting time in extended, meaningful blocks during summer, winter, and spring breaks, providing Danielle with substantial parenting time in a manner that is consistent with the children's school calendar and the geographic realities of the situation. Extended summer parenting time, in particular, can provide Danielle with weeks of uninterrupted parenting time each year, which may be more meaningful and less disruptive than a series of brief weekend visits requiring repeated long-distance travel.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) instructs the court to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Renee is committed to facilitating the children's relationship with Danielle and is prepared to support regular communication, video contact, and generous parenting time during school breaks. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that a custody arrangement should maximize both parents' involvement in the children's lives to the extent practical given the geographic circumstances. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018). The proposed arrangement achieves that goal in a manner that is workable given the 600-mile separation between the parties.
5. The Stability of the Home Environment Renee Offers Supports the Requested Modification.
AS 25.20.090(3) and AS 25.24.150(c)(5) both direct the court to consider the stability of the home environment each parent is likely to offer and the desirability of maintaining the children's established continuity of environment. Renee has remained in the family's established community in Fairbanks throughout the post-divorce period. She has continuously exercised her parenting time, maintained close involvement in the children's schooling and activities, and provided a stable home environment. Danielle, by contrast, has uprooted her household with a permanent employment-driven relocation to a geographically isolated city 600 miles away. While Danielle's decision to relocate is understandable and not condemned, its effect is to make her home the less stable option for the children during the school year, particularly given the disruption a mid-school-year transfer to Juneau would cause.
The court's analysis under the best interests standard must consider "other factors that the court considers pertinent." AS 25.24.150(c)(9). Among those pertinent factors here is the fact that requiring the children to relocate to Juneau with Danielle during the school year would remove them from every established anchor of their daily lives: their school, their teachers, their classmates, their extended family, and their community. The disruption this would cause is substantial and weighs heavily in favor of the proposed modification.
C. THE PROPOSED CHILD SUPPORT ADJUSTMENT SHOULD REFLECT THE MODIFIED PHYSICAL CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT.
Because the proposed modification would change the physical custody arrangement from one in which Danielle holds primary physical custody to one in which Renee holds primary physical custody during the school year, the child support obligation should be recalculated consistent with Civil Rule 90.3. If the court adopts a schedule in which each parent has the children for a substantial portion of the year, the court should calculate support under the shared physical custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for the percentage of time each parent exercises physical custody and the adjusted annual income of each parent. If the court determines that Renee holds primary physical custody for the school year and Danielle holds extended parenting time during school breaks, the appropriate calculation may fall under Civil Rule 90.3(a) depending on how the annual allocation of parenting time is structured. In either event, the court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(c) to vary the calculated support award upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would otherwise result, and to consider any unusual circumstances that make a strict application of the guidelines unjust given the parties' respective financial situations and the costs each parent will bear in facilitating long-distance parenting time.
Renee requests that the court order updated financial disclosures from both parties and recalculate support in accordance with the applicable provisions of Civil Rule 90.3 once the modified custody arrangement is established.
D. THIS COURT HAS JURISDICTION TO MODIFY THE EXISTING CUSTODY ORDER.
The existing custody order was entered by this Court in 2021, and the children continue to reside in Alaska. AS 25.30.320 governs the authority of an Alaska court to modify a child custody determination. Because the existing order was entered by this Court and the children remain residents of Alaska with Renee in Fairbanks, this Court retains jurisdiction to modify the custody arrangement. No jurisdictional barrier prevents this Court from proceeding to the merits of Renee's petition.
The Court may also take judicial notice of publicly available information, including the geographic distance between Fairbanks and Juneau and the absence of road access between the two cities, upon request by a party. Alaska R. Evid. 201(d).
V. CONCLUSION
Danielle's permanent relocation from Fairbanks to Juneau, approximately 600 miles away with no road connection, constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a) that renders the existing custody order unworkable. The 2021 order was premised on both parents residing in or near Fairbanks. That premise no longer holds. A modification of the order is both legally required and necessary to protect the children's best interests.
The proposed modification, awarding Renee primary physical custody during the school year with Danielle receiving extended parenting time during summer, winter, and spring breaks, best serves the children's educational stability, preserves their community ties in Fairbanks, maximizes meaningful contact with both parents, and reflects the practical geographic realities of the parties' current circumstances. Every applicable best interests factor under AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.090 supports this arrangement.
For the foregoing reasons, Renee Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court: (1) find that Danielle's permanent relocation to Juneau constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a); (2) modify the existing custody order to award Renee primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children during the school year; (3) award Danielle extended parenting time during summer, winter, and spring breaks; (4) require updated financial disclosures from both parties and recalculate child support consistent with Civil Rule 90.3; and (5) grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the best interests of the children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0098)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Sutter respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody and visitation order entered in 2021. Since that order was entered, a substantial change in circumstances has occurred: Ashley has accepted a permanent employment transfer to Juneau, approximately 600 miles from Anchorage, where the parties' two minor children, ages 8 and 11, have resided with their father, Wesley Sutter, on an informal basis for the past four months. The current order no longer reflects the realities of the family's geographic situation, and its terms cannot practicably be followed given the distance between the parents' respective residences. Ashley does not seek to diminish Wesley's role in the children's lives. Rather, she seeks a formal modification that acknowledges the children's current living arrangements, preserves meaningful and substantial parenting time for both parents, and serves the best interests of the children as required by Alaska law. Specifically, Ashley requests that the Court enter a modified order granting Wesley primary physical custody during the school year, while granting Ashley extended parenting time during all school breaks and the entirety of summer vacation. Such a modification is warranted under AS 25.20.110, is supported by the factors the Court must consider under AS 25.24.150 and AS 25.20.090, and is in the best interests of the children.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Sutter and Wesley Sutter were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the Superior Court entered a custody order awarding the parties joint legal custody of their two minor children, currently ages 8 and 11. That order granted primary physical custody to Ashley and provided Wesley with a standard visitation schedule consisting of parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. The order was entered when both parents resided in Anchorage, and it was designed around a geographic reality that no longer exists.
Following entry of the original order, Ashley was offered and accepted a permanent employment transfer to Juneau, Alaska. Juneau is located approximately 600 miles from Anchorage and is not accessible by road, making routine travel between the two cities difficult and costly. Ashley's relocation was not a short-term or speculative move; it reflects a permanent change in her employment and residential situation. In anticipation of and during her relocation, Ashley and Wesley reached an informal agreement under which the children would remain with Wesley in Anchorage on a temporary basis while Ashley secured stable housing in Juneau. That informal arrangement has now been in place for approximately four months.
During this four-month period, the children have been residing primarily with Wesley in Anchorage, attending their established schools, maintaining friendships, and continuing their extracurricular activities. Wesley has demonstrated the capability and willingness to serve as the primary residential parent during the school year. Ashley has secured stable housing in Juneau and is now in a position to exercise extended parenting time during the children's school breaks and summer vacation.
The existing custody order, which contemplates both parents residing in Anchorage and provides for weekly mid-week visits and alternating weekends, cannot function as written given the 600-mile separation between the parents. A formal modification is necessary to provide the children with a stable, predictable custody arrangement that reflects their current lives and that both parents can lawfully and practically follow.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), an award of custody or visitation may be modified if the Court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Where a parent opposes modification and it is granted, the Court must enter on the record its reason for the modification.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a custodial parent's relocation out of the family's established community constitutes a substantial change in circumstances sufficient to trigger a custody modification analysis under AS 25.20.110(a). Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001). Additionally, in Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that when a parent moves out of state or out of the shared community, the change in the parties' geographic circumstances provides the basis for the court to revisit and restructure a custody arrangement that is no longer workable. The threshold for establishing changed circumstances is met when the changed facts, taken together, are significant or substantial. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011).
Once a change in circumstances is established, the Court must determine whether the proposed modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.24.150(c) sets forth the factors the Court shall consider in making that determination, including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference; the length of time the child has lived in a stable and satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
In determining whether to award shared or modified custody arrangements, the Court shall also consider the factors set forth in AS 25.20.090, including the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment offered by each parent, the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the child's school, and the feasibility of travel between the parents.
As a baseline principle, AS 25.20.070 provides that, unless it would be detrimental to the child's welfare, "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents" during the period when the Court is considering a custody award. The proposed modification honors this principle by maximizing each parent's meaningful time with the children within the constraints imposed by the parties' geographic separation.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES HAS OCCURRED SUFFICIENT TO INVOKE THE COURT'S AUTHORITY TO MODIFY THE EXISTING CUSTODY ORDER.
Under AS 25.20.110(a), the Court may modify a custody award upon a determination that a change in circumstances requires the modification. Ashley's permanent relocation to Juneau, a city approximately 600 miles from Anchorage that is inaccessible by road, plainly constitutes such a change. The original 2021 custody order was constructed around a geographic reality in which both parents lived in the same city. The order's provisions, including weekly mid-week evening visits and alternating weekend exchanges, presuppose that both parents are within close proximity to one another and to the children's schools. That presupposition no longer holds.
The Alaska Supreme Court held in Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), that a parent's relocation to a different city or state following a custody order constitutes a material change in circumstances warranting a hearing and, if the best interests analysis supports it, a modification of the custody arrangement. Here, Ashley's relocation is not temporary or speculative. It is a permanent employment transfer that has already taken effect. The children have already adjusted their primary residence accordingly, having lived with Wesley in Anchorage for the past four months. The existing custody order is, as a practical matter, inoperative in its current form. The standard weekend and mid-week visitation schedule it prescribes cannot be exercised when one parent resides 600 miles away with no road connection between the two cities.
Furthermore, in Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that changed geographic circumstances, including a move by the custodial parent, can constitute a change in circumstances as a matter of law when they materially alter the structure of the custody arrangement. Ashley's relocation, combined with the four months during which the children have been living informally with Wesley, satisfies the threshold requirement of AS 25.20.110(a). The Court should find that a substantial change in circumstances exists and proceed to the best interests analysis.
B. THE PROPOSED MODIFICATION SERVES THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN AS REQUIRED BY AS 25.24.150(c).
Once changed circumstances are established, the Court must determine whether the proposed modification is in the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.150(c). The modification Ashley proposes, namely, primary physical custody with Wesley during the school year and extended parenting time with Ashley during all school breaks and summer vacation, satisfies each relevant best interests factor.
1. Physical, Emotional, Mental, and Social Needs of the Children.
The children are ages 8 and 11. They are established in Anchorage schools, have friendships in the Anchorage community, and have been residing continuously with Wesley for the past four months. Formalizing Wesley's role as the primary residential parent during the school year will avoid disruption to the children's academic progress and social connections during the school year. At the same time, extended parenting time with Ashley during school breaks and the full summer will ensure that the children maintain a close and continuous bond with their mother. This arrangement directly addresses the children's physical, emotional, and social needs as contemplated by AS 25.24.150(c)(1).
2. Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Children's Needs.
Nothing in the record suggests any deficiency in either parent's ability to meet the children's needs. AS 25.24.150(c)(2). Wesley has demonstrated his capability during the past four months by serving as the children's primary caregiver while Ashley completed her relocation. Ashley, for her part, has taken concrete steps to secure stable housing in Juneau and has remained engaged in the children's lives throughout this transition period. Both parents are capable and loving, and the proposed modification allocates responsibility in a manner consistent with the current geographic realities while ensuring that both parents remain meaningfully involved in the children's upbringing.
3. Stability, Continuity, and the Existing Living Arrangement.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(5), the Court shall consider the length of time the children have lived in a stable and satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. For the past four months, the children have been living with Wesley in Anchorage in a stable and satisfactory environment. They are attending their established schools and living in familiar surroundings. Granting Wesley primary physical custody during the school year formalizes and provides legal certainty to an arrangement that is already working well for the children. Disrupting this continuity at this stage, particularly during the school year, would not serve the children's interests.
In Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that stability and continuity in a child's living environment and community are significant factors in the best interests analysis, particularly when the existing arrangement is functioning well for all members of the family. Here, the informal arrangement with Wesley has been operating satisfactorily, and formalizing it serves the children's interest in continuity.
4. Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Children.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the Court shall consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the children and the other parent. Ashley's petition itself demonstrates her commitment to Wesley's ongoing parental relationship. She is not seeking to minimize Wesley's role or to relocate the children to Juneau, away from their established community. On the contrary, she proposes that Wesley serve as the primary residential parent during the school year, precisely because she recognizes that this arrangement is best for the children given the geographic realities. In return, she seeks extended parenting time during school breaks and summer, ensuring that her own bond with the children remains close and continuous.
The Court should also consider, under AS 25.20.090(6)(E), the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the children. Ashley's proposed arrangement is expressly designed to maximize each parent's meaningful time with the children within the constraints imposed by the 600-mile distance between Anchorage and Juneau.
5. The Geographic Realities and Feasibility of Travel.
Under AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (C), the Court shall consider the proximity of each parent to the other and to the children's school, and the feasibility of travel between the parents. These factors weigh heavily in favor of the proposed modification. Anchorage and Juneau are separated by approximately 600 miles, and there is no road connection between the two cities. Travel requires either a flight or a ferry, both of which are costly and logistically challenging for routine exchanges. The standard alternating-weekend and mid-week visitation schedule in the existing order is simply not feasible across this distance. The proposed modification restructures parenting time around longer, more substantial blocks, which are both logistically achievable and, critically, provide the children with extended periods of uninterrupted time with each parent, rather than fragmentary visits that can never realistically occur given the geographic separation.
C. THE PROPOSED MODIFICATION APPROPRIATELY MAXIMIZES EACH PARENT'S ACCESS TO THE CHILDREN CONSISTENT WITH AS 25.20.070.
Alaska law recognizes a strong policy in favor of ensuring that children have the maximum practicable access to both parents. AS 25.20.070 provides that "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents" during the period the Court is considering a custody award, unless detrimental to the child's welfare. Nothing in this record suggests that contact with either parent is detrimental to the children's welfare. The proposed modification, granting Wesley primary physical custody during the school year and Ashley extended parenting time during all school breaks and the full summer vacation, is the arrangement that most closely approximates equal and meaningful access to both parents given the geographic constraints of this case. A modification that attempts to preserve the letter of the old order, while ignoring the 600-mile geographic reality, would in practice deprive the children of meaningful time with at least one parent. The proposed arrangement avoids that outcome.
D. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE RECALCULATED TO REFLECT THE MODIFIED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT.
Any modification to the physical custody arrangement necessarily requires recalculation of child support obligations. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage, which is 27% for two children. Under the proposed modification, Wesley will serve as the primary residential parent during the school year, and the respective support obligations of the parties should be recalculated accordingly. Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides an alternative calculation framework for shared physical custody arrangements. Given that the proposed modification creates a structure in which each parent has the children for substantial, defined periods, the Court should carefully analyze which framework applies and should recalculate support consistent with the applicable rule. To the extent that unusual circumstances exist that would produce a manifestly unjust result under the standard calculation, Civil Rule 90.3(c) authorizes the Court to vary the award upon proof by clear and convincing evidence. The parties' respective financial circumstances, travel costs associated with the long-distance arrangement, and the children's needs should all be considered in setting a fair and workable support obligation.
E. THIS COURT HAS JURISDICTION TO MODIFY THE EXISTING ORDER.
This Court has jurisdiction to modify the existing Alaska custody order. The original order was entered by this Court in 2021. Both children have been residing in Anchorage, Alaska, with Wesley since the informal arrangement began approximately four months ago. Under AS 25.30.320, a court of this state may modify a child custody determination made by a court of another state under specified conditions, but where, as here, the original order was entered by this same court and the children remain in Alaska, that statute does not present a jurisdictional barrier. This Court retains jurisdiction to modify its own order pursuant to AS 25.20.110.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Ashley Sutter respectfully requests that this Court find that a substantial change in circumstances has occurred warranting modification of the existing custody order, and that the modification she proposes serves the best interests of the children. Specifically, Ashley requests that the Court enter a modified order: (1) granting Wesley Sutter primary physical custody of the two minor children during the school year; (2) granting Ashley Sutter extended parenting time during all school breaks, including winter, spring, and fall breaks, as well as the entirety of summer vacation; (3) maintaining joint legal custody as between the parties; and (4) directing that child support be recalculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3 to reflect the modified custody arrangement. This proposed modification reflects the geographic realities now facing this family, preserves the children's stability and continuity during the school year, maximizes each parent's meaningful access to the children, and serves the best interests of the children as required by AS 25.20.110(a) and AS 25.24.150.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0099)
I. INTRODUCTION
This brief is submitted on behalf of Maria Colby, Respondent and Cross-Petitioner, in opposition to Priya Colby's petition to modify the existing custody order and to relocate the parties' minor child, Declan Colby, age eight, from Fairbanks to Juneau, Alaska. Maria respectfully requests that this Court deny Priya's petition for relocation and grant Maria's cross-petition to modify the existing order by designating Maria as Declan's primary physical custodian, thereby allowing Declan to remain in Fairbanks, where he is enrolled in school, participates in extracurricular activities, and maintains a stable and nurturing support network.
The existing order, entered by the Alaska Superior Court two years ago, grants the parties joint legal custody, designates Priya as the primary physical custodian, and awards Maria visitation every other weekend and for six weeks each summer. Priya's proposed relocation to Juneau, a city approximately 600 miles from Fairbanks, would fundamentally sever Declan's connections to his school, his established friendships, his extracurricular community, and his day-to-day relationship with his mother. The financial justification Priya advances does not, standing alone, satisfy the legal standard for modifying a custody order, and Priya's proposed arrangement would cause substantial harm to Declan's stability and well-being. Under Alaska law, the best interests of the child are paramount, and those interests are best served by allowing Declan to remain in Fairbanks in Maria's primary physical custody.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties, Priya Colby and Maria Colby, are the parents of Declan Colby, born eight years ago. The Alaska Superior Court entered a custody and visitation order two years ago awarding the parties joint legal custody of Declan, designating Priya as the primary physical custodian, and granting Maria parenting time every other weekend and for six weeks during the summer.
Since the entry of that order, Declan has been enrolled in school in Fairbanks and has participated in established extracurricular activities in that community. Maria continues to reside in Fairbanks and exercises her visitation rights consistently. Declan has lived in Fairbanks his entire life and has formed meaningful friendships, educational relationships, and a support network rooted in that community.
Priya has accepted a permanent job transfer to Juneau, Alaska. Juneau is located approximately 600 miles from Fairbanks. Priya now asks the Court to permit her to relocate Declan to Juneau, arguing that the transfer will improve the family's financial stability and Declan's overall well-being. Priya seeks a modification of the existing order to designate her as the sole primary physical custodian with authority to relocate Declan.
Maria opposes the relocation. Maria cross-petitions for modification of the existing order to designate her as Declan's primary physical custodian so that Declan may remain in Fairbanks, preserving continuity in his schooling, friendships, extracurricular activities, and his close and ongoing relationship with Maria. A relocation to Juneau would reduce Maria's contact with Declan to infrequent visits, functionally eliminating the meaningful parenting relationship she has built with him over the course of his life.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Modification of Custody Requires a Showing of Changed Circumstances and Best Interests
Under AS 25.20.110(a), a custody award may be modified only if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. Where a parent opposes a proposed modification and the court grants it, the court must enter on the record its reason for the modification. This two-part threshold, change in circumstances and best interests, applies to both Priya's relocation petition and Maria's cross-petition for modification.
B. Best Interests of the Child
In determining the best interests of the child, the court must consider the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c). Those factors include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child under all circumstances; and any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect. Under AS 25.24.905, "the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child."
C. Shared and Primary Physical Custody Considerations
Where the court evaluates whether to award shared or primary physical custody, AS 25.20.090 requires consideration of factors including the child's preference, the needs of the child, the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the education of the child, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, and the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent. The willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate a close relationship between the child and the other parent is also a statutory consideration. AS 25.20.090(6)(E).
D. Equal Access to Both Parents
AS 25.20.996 provides that, unless it is shown to be detrimental to the welfare of the child or unless the domestic violence presumption under AS 25.24.941 is present, "the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the time that the court considers an award of custody."
E. Jurisdiction
The Alaska Superior Court retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over this custody determination under AS 25.30.310(a), as Declan and at least one parent continue to reside in Alaska and substantial evidence concerning Declan's care, protection, training, and personal relationships remains available in this state.
F. Child Support
Should the Court modify the custody arrangement, any resulting child support award will be calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award in a case of primary physical custody is based on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), if the Court awards shared physical custody, the award is calculated through an offset formula that accounts for each parent's income and the percentage of time each parent has physical custody. The Court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(c) to vary the award upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would otherwise result.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PRIYA'S PROPOSED RELOCATION CONSTITUTES A CHANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES, BUT MODIFICATION IN FAVOR OF RELOCATION IS NOT IN DECLAN'S BEST INTERESTS.
1. A Change of Circumstances Exists, But It Does Not Favor Relocation.
Priya's acceptance of a permanent job transfer to Juneau and her stated intention to remove Declan from Fairbanks constitute a material change of circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a). The parties do not dispute that a change has occurred. The critical question is not whether circumstances have changed, but whether modification of the custody order in the manner Priya proposes serves Declan's best interests. As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Rego v. Rego, 259 P.3d 447 (Alaska 2011), the change of circumstances inquiry and the best interests inquiry are distinct, and satisfying the first does not guarantee the outcome of the second.
Maria's cross-petition likewise satisfies the change of circumstances threshold. Priya's relocation and the resulting fundamental disruption to the existing custody arrangement constitute changed circumstances that justify the Court's consideration of a modification in Maria's favor. The Court should therefore address the best interests question comprehensively as to both petitions.
2. The Best Interests of Declan Favor Remaining in Fairbanks with Maria as Primary Physical Custodian.
a. Stability, Continuity, and Community Connection
Among the most significant factors under AS 25.24.150(c) is "the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity." Declan, age eight, has lived his entire life in Fairbanks. He is enrolled in school there, participates in extracurricular activities there, and has developed a network of friendships and community relationships rooted in that city. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized, in Hayes v. Hayes, 922 P.2d 896 (Alaska 1996), that continuity of environment and stability of relationships are important factors in custody determinations, even when competing considerations may have independent merit.
Relocating Declan to Juneau, 600 miles away, would disrupt each of these connections simultaneously. He would be required to change schools mid-childhood, leave behind established friendships, and abandon extracurricular activities in which he has invested time and effort. These disruptions are not abstract; they directly affect the emotional, social, and educational well-being of an eight-year-old child. The plain text of AS 25.24.150(c)(5) instructs the Court to weigh "the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity." That desirability strongly favors Fairbanks.
AS 25.20.090(5) separately directs the court, in evaluating shared or primary custody, to weigh "the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides." Fairbanks is Declan's community. His school, his activities, and his social identity are embedded there. This statutory factor independently supports denying the relocation petition and granting Maria's cross-petition.
b. Maria's Ability to Facilitate Declan's Relationship with Priya
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the court must consider "the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child." Maria has consistently exercised her visitation rights under the existing order and has demonstrated through her conduct that she supports Declan's relationship with both of his parents. Maria's cross-petition does not seek to eliminate Priya's parental role; it seeks to preserve Declan's stability while ensuring that both parents remain meaningfully involved in his life.
If Declan were relocated to Juneau with Priya, Maria's current every-other-weekend visitation schedule would become logistically untenable. A 600-mile separation between Fairbanks and Juneau, compounded by the absence of direct road access between the two cities, would effectively transform Maria's parenting time into rare, expensive, and logistically difficult visits. The Alaska Supreme Court's reasoning in Ronny M. v. Nanette H., 303 P.3d 392 (Alaska 2013), underscores that the willingness of each parent to facilitate the other's relationship with the child is a central consideration in primary custody determinations. Maria, remaining in Fairbanks and prepared to serve as primary physical custodian, is the parent best positioned to ensure that Declan maintains a meaningful relationship with Priya through scheduled visits, extended summer parenting time, and other contact.
c. Each Parent's Capability and Desire to Meet Declan's Needs
AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires the court to assess "the capability and desire of each parent to meet these needs." Maria has lived in Fairbanks throughout Declan's life, has been actively involved in his schooling and extracurricular activities, and has exercised her parenting time diligently. She is prepared to serve as Declan's primary physical custodian, to maintain his enrollment at his current school, and to support his ongoing activities and friendships.
Priya's desire to improve the family's financial circumstances is understandable, and the Court need not discount the sincerity of that motivation. However, financial improvement is not the legal standard for custody modification. Under AS 25.24.150(d), "the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child." An improvement in Priya's income, standing alone, does not directly establish that Declan's well-being will be served by uprooting him from every established connection in his life. Priya's financial argument must be weighed against the concrete, immediate, and well-documented harms that relocation would impose on Declan.
d. Equal Access to Both Parents
AS 25.20.070 provides that the child shall have, "to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents." A relocation to Juneau would effectively deny Declan that access. The 600-mile distance, combined with the lack of direct road connectivity between Fairbanks and Juneau, would make frequent, routine contact between Declan and Maria impractical on an every-other-weekend schedule. By contrast, if Maria is designated primary physical custodian and Declan remains in Fairbanks, Priya retains the ability to travel to Fairbanks for visits, to exercise extended summer parenting time, and to maintain regular contact through electronic means. The burden of travel is more equitably and more appropriately placed on the relocating parent than on the child and the remaining parent.
B. MARIA'S CROSS-PETITION FOR MODIFICATION OF PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY SHOULD BE GRANTED.
1. The Changed Circumstances Threshold Is Met.
As set forth above, Priya's permanent job transfer and stated intention to remove Declan from Fairbanks satisfy the changed circumstances requirement of AS 25.20.110(a). The existing custody arrangement, which was premised on both parties residing in Fairbanks, is no longer viable in its current form. The Court must determine the arrangement that best serves Declan's interests given the new circumstances, and Maria respectfully submits that the evidence supports designating Maria as primary physical custodian.
2. The Best Interests Factors, Considered Together, Favor Awarding Primary Physical Custody to Maria.
The AS 25.24.150(c) factors, considered as a whole, support Maria's cross-petition. Declan has lived his entire life in a stable environment in Fairbanks. His school placement, extracurricular activities, and friendships are all established in that community. Maria has been a consistent and engaged parent throughout Declan's life and has exercised her visitation time reliably. She is willing and able to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between Declan and Priya. She resides in the community where Declan presently lives, attends school, and has formed lasting relationships.
The factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, applicable to the shared and primary custody determination, further support Maria's cross-petition. Specifically: the needs of the child for educational and social continuity favor Fairbanks; the stability of the home environment Maria can offer in Fairbanks is well-established; the advantages of keeping Declan in his current community are substantial; and the proximity of Maria to Declan's school weighs in her favor. AS 25.20.090(2), (3), (4), (5), (6)(B).
As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Hayes v. Hayes, 922 P.2d 896 (Alaska 1996), courts may appropriately conclude that geographic and relational stability outweigh other competing considerations in custody determinations. That principle applies with full force here. The disruption that Priya's relocation would impose on Declan, taken together with the strength of the factors supporting Maria's cross-petition, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that modifying the order to designate Maria as primary physical custodian is in Declan's best interests.
3. If the Court Grants Maria's Cross-Petition, a Robust Parenting Plan for Priya Must Be Established.
Maria does not seek to diminish Priya's role in Declan's life. Consistent with AS 25.20.070 and the policy favoring both parents' involvement reflected throughout AS 25.24.150(c), Maria proposes that the Court enter a modified order providing Priya with extended parenting time during school vacations, including winter break, spring break, and a substantial portion of the summer, as well as regular electronic contact. Such an arrangement would allow Priya to maintain a meaningful parenting relationship with Declan while preserving his stability in Fairbanks.
C. CHILD SUPPORT SHOULD BE CALCULATED IN ACCORDANCE WITH CIVIL RULE 90.3 UPON MODIFICATION OF THE ORDER.
If the Court grants Maria's cross-petition and designates Maria as primary physical custodian, child support should be established in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), based on Priya's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage for one child. If the Court instead fashions a shared physical custody arrangement, Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides the applicable calculation methodology. In either case, the Court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(c) to vary the award upon clear and convincing proof of manifest injustice, and it may consider Priya's increased income from her Juneau employment in setting the appropriate support level. Maria requests that the Court order prompt exchange of income documentation and enter a child support order consistent with Rule 90.3 concurrent with any custody modification.
D. THE COURT RETAINS JURISDICTION TO RESOLVE THIS MATTER.
The Alaska Superior Court retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over this custody determination under AS 25.30.310(a). Declan currently resides in Alaska, Maria resides in Alaska, and substantial evidence concerning Declan's care, education, personal relationships, and well-being remains available in this state. Jurisdiction is proper and this Court is the appropriate forum to resolve the competing petitions.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Maria Colby respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Deny Priya Colby's petition to modify the existing custody order to permit relocation of Declan Colby to Juneau, Alaska;
2. Grant Maria Colby's cross-petition for modification of the existing custody order and designate Maria Colby as Declan's primary physical custodian, with Declan to remain enrolled in school and residing in Fairbanks, Alaska;
3. Enter a modified parenting plan providing Priya Colby with extended parenting time during school vacations and the summer, as well as regular electronic contact, consistent with Declan's best interests and the mandate of AS 25.20.070;
4. Establish a child support award calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3, based on Priya's adjusted annual income, with modification as justice requires; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the best interests of Declan Colby.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0100)
I. INTRODUCTION
Wesley Petrova respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order entered in 2021 by the Anchorage Superior Court. The current order grants Tomas Petrova primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, ages eight and ten, with Wesley receiving only alternating weekend visitation and two weeks of summer parenting time. Since the entry of that order, the circumstances of both parties have changed substantially and materially. Wesley has achieved two years of sobriety, obtained stable professional employment, and purchased a home in the children's school district. Tomas, meanwhile, has accepted a position requiring him to be absent from Alaska for approximately fifteen days each month, leaving the children in the care of a rotating series of babysitters rather than a consistent parental figure.
These changed circumstances, viewed together, satisfy the threshold legal standard under AS 25.20.110 and warrant a full best-interests analysis. Wesley seeks modification to a week-on, week-off, equal 50-50 physical custody schedule. Such an arrangement would provide the children with stability, consistent parental involvement, and equal access to both parents. The existing order no longer reflects the realities of the parties' lives or the best interests of the children. For the reasons set forth below, this Court should grant Wesley's motion to modify custody.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The Anchorage Superior Court entered the operative custody order in 2021, following the divorce of Wesley Petrova and Tomas Petrova. That order awarded Tomas primary physical custody of the two minor children, currently ages eight and ten. Under the order, Wesley was granted alternating weekend visitation from Friday evening through Sunday evening, along with two weeks of uninterrupted summer parenting time.
At the time the original order was entered, Wesley was addressing sobriety challenges that informed the court's decision to award primary custody to Tomas. Wesley has since successfully completed a two-year sobriety program and has maintained his sobriety consistently. He is now a licensed electrician with stable, ongoing employment. He has purchased a three-bedroom home located within the same school district where the children are currently enrolled. These developments represent a meaningful, sustained transformation in Wesley's circumstances since the 2021 order.
Tomas's circumstances have changed as well, though in a direction that raises significant concerns for the children's stability and welfare. Tomas has accepted a new employment position that requires him to travel outside Alaska for approximately fifteen days each month. During these frequent absences, the children are not cared for by a consistent parental figure or a known, stable adult; rather, they are left in the care of a rotating series of babysitters. This arrangement deprives the children of consistent supervision, emotional continuity, and the kind of stable home environment that courts consistently recognize as central to children's well-being.
The children are currently ages eight and ten, and both are enrolled in school in the district where Wesley now resides. Given the proximity of Wesley's home, his stable schedule as a licensed electrician, and his sobriety, he is able to offer the children a predictable, nurturing environment. Wesley seeks modification to a week-on, week-off schedule that would afford each parent equal parenting time and provide the children with the consistent presence of both parents in their daily lives.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), a custody award may be modified when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. The Alaska Supreme Court has held that the change-in-circumstances requirement is intended to discourage continual relitigation of custody decisions and to protect the child's emotional welfare through finality and certainty. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). Courts evaluate changed circumstances by comparing current conditions to the baseline facts that existed at the time the prior custody order was entered. Id.
Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the court proceeds to a best-interests analysis. McLane v. Paul, 189 P.3d 1039 (Alaska 2008). In conducting that analysis for purposes of a shared custody determination, the court considers the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, including the child's needs, the stability of the home environment each parent can offer, the proximity of each parent to the child's school, the feasibility of travel between parents, the willingness of each parent to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent, and any evidence of substance abuse that directly affects the child's well-being.
Additionally, AS 25.20.990 establishes that, absent a showing that equal access would be detrimental to the child's welfare, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents while a custody award is under consideration. Civil Rule 938(f)(1) defines shared physical custody as a arrangement in which the children reside with each parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year, as specified in writing in the custody order. Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides the framework for calculating child support in shared custody arrangements, and Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) provides that a final child support award may be modified upon a showing of a material change of circumstances, with a presumption of such a change when the recalculated support amount differs from the outstanding order by more than 15 percent.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Substantial Change in Circumstances Has Occurred Since Entry of the 2021 Custody Order.
The threshold requirement for modification under AS 25.20.110(a) is that a change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the prior order. Courts compare present circumstances to those existing at the time of the order being challenged. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). The change must be substantial enough to affect the children's welfare and must reflect more than the mere passage of time. Id. Here, the combined changes in both parties' circumstances easily satisfy this standard.
At the time of the 2021 order, Wesley was working through sobriety challenges. The court, in awarding Tomas primary custody, necessarily relied on the then-existing conditions, including Wesley's sobriety status. Wesley has since completed a two-year sobriety program and maintained his recovery. He has secured licensed, stable employment as an electrician. He has purchased a three-bedroom home in the same school district where the children are enrolled. These are not superficial or transient changes; they represent a sustained, verified transformation that goes to the very foundations upon which the 2021 order was premised. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's changed circumstances, including changes in employment and housing stability, can constitute a substantial change in circumstances warranting modification review. Hope P. v. Flynn G., 355 P.3d 559 (Alaska 2015).
Equally significant are the changes in Tomas's circumstances. Tomas now works in a position that requires him to be absent from Alaska for approximately fifteen days each month. During those absences, the children are placed in the care of a rotating series of babysitters, with no consistent parental or adult presence in the home. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that changes in a custodial parent's work schedule and the resulting impact on the children's day-to-day care can constitute a substantial change in circumstances. Hope P. v. Flynn G., 355 P.3d 559 (Alaska 2015). The situation here is even more pronounced: Tomas is absent from the state for roughly half of each month, and no stable substitute caregiver has been identified.
The combination of Wesley's dramatically improved circumstances and Tomas's substantially changed and destabilizing work schedule, viewed together against the 2021 baseline, constitutes a substantial change in circumstances that requires this Court to proceed to a best-interests analysis. AS 25.20.110(a); Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022); McLane v. Paul, 189 P.3d 1039 (Alaska 2008).
B. Modification to an Equal Week-On, Week-Off Schedule Is in the Best Interests of the Children.
Having established a substantial change in circumstances, the Court must consider whether the proposed modification serves the children's best interests. AS 25.20.110(a). For shared custody determinations, the relevant factors are set out in AS 25.20.090. Those factors, applied to the facts of this case, strongly support a modification to an equal 50-50 week-on, week-off parenting schedule.
1. The Children's Needs and the Stability of Each Home Environment.
The children, ages eight and ten, are at developmental stages where consistency, predictability, and the presence of engaged parents are particularly important. Wesley's home offers all of these qualities. He has a three-bedroom home within the children's school district, a stable employment schedule as a licensed electrician, and two years of maintained sobriety. His home environment is organized, proximate to the children's school, and free from the instability that characterized the circumstances at the time of the original order.
By contrast, the current custodial arrangement under Tomas no longer provides the stability it was designed to protect. When Tomas is absent from Alaska for approximately fifteen days each month, the children are cared for by a revolving set of babysitters. This arrangement lacks the continuity and emotional consistency that children of these ages need. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized the importance of stability in the custodial environment and has held that courts must give meaningful weight to factors that directly affect children's day-to-day well-being. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018); Siekawitch v. Siekawitch, 956 P.2d 447 (Alaska 1998). Rotating, unvetted babysitters do not provide the kind of stable home environment contemplated by AS 25.20.090(3).
2. The Children's Equal Access to Both Parents.
Alaska law reflects a strong policy preference for children having meaningful access to both parents. AS 25.20.070 provides that, absent a showing of detriment, the child shall have, "to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents" while custody is under consideration. Under the current order, Wesley receives only alternating weekends and two summer weeks per year. This arrangement was appropriate in 2021 given the then-existing circumstances, but it is no longer adequate given the transformation in Wesley's life and the reduction in Tomas's effective availability to the children.
The week-on, week-off schedule Wesley proposes falls squarely within the definition of shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), which provides that shared physical custody means the children reside with each parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year as specified in the custody order. A 50-50 schedule satisfies this definition and ensures neither parent is relegated to a peripheral role in the children's lives. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a 50-50 custody schedule is often the appropriate starting point and that courts must conduct a careful best-interests analysis rather than mechanically favor one parent's existing advantage. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018).
3. Proximity to School and Feasibility of the Proposed Schedule.
AS 25.20.944(B) directs the court to consider the proximity of each parent to the other and to the school in which the child is enrolled. Wesley has purchased a three-bedroom home within the same school district where the children are enrolled. This means a week-on, week-off schedule would not require the children to change schools, alter their established routines, or travel significant distances between parental homes. The transition between households would be logistically straightforward, minimizing disruption to the children's academic and social lives. This factor weighs clearly in favor of the proposed schedule.
4. Each Parent's Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Children.
AS 25.20.090(6)(E) requires consideration of each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. Wesley has demonstrated, through his actions since the 2021 order, that he is committed to the children's overall well-being. His completion of a two-year sobriety program, his investment in a home suitable for the children, and his pursuit of modification through proper legal channels rather than by undermining the existing order all reflect a good-faith commitment to the children's relationship with both parents. Nothing in the record suggests that Wesley has interfered with the children's relationship with Tomas or that he would do so under a modified order.
5. Prior Substance Abuse History and Its Current Relevance.
AS 25.20.090(9) directs the court to consider evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child. This factor was plainly relevant to the 2021 order. It is no longer a barrier to Wesley's request. Wesley has completed a formal two-year sobriety program. His recovery is not merely alleged; it has been demonstrated through a structured, extended program of treatment and sustained abstinence. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must evaluate parents' current circumstances rather than rely solely on historical conduct, particularly when the parent has demonstrated genuine and lasting change. Blanton v. Yourkowski, 180 P.3d 948 (Alaska 2008). Wesley's sobriety history weighs in favor of the modification rather than against it, as it demonstrates his capacity for sustained personal responsibility and commitment to his children's welfare.
6. The Proposed Schedule Serves the Children's Best Interests and Should Govern Child Support Recalculation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), child support in shared physical custody cases is calculated using a specific formula that accounts for each parent's income and the percentage of time the children reside with each parent. Because the proposed modification would convert the arrangement from one of primary custody with limited visitation to true shared physical custody, a recalculation of child support under Civil Rule 90.3(b) would be required. Additionally, under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1), a material change of circumstances is presumed when the recalculated support amount is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. Given the substantial increase in Wesley's parenting time under the proposed schedule, it is highly likely that the recalculated support obligation will reflect a difference exceeding 15 percent, triggering the presumption and warranting a formal modification of any existing support order as well.
The overall weight of the AS 25.20.090 factors supports granting Wesley's motion. The children will benefit from equal time with a sober, employed, and stably housed father, while also maintaining a meaningful relationship with Tomas during his periods of availability. The week-on, week-off schedule avoids long stretches away from either parent, provides logistical simplicity given the shared school district, and honors the legislative preference for equal parental access expressed in AS 25.20.070. As the Alaska Supreme Court noted in Martin v. Martin, 303 P.3d 421 (Alaska 2013), courts have authority to fashion custody schedules that are in the best interests of the children, and that authority includes modifying existing arrangements when the underlying circumstances have shifted in ways that make the current order inadequate.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Wesley Petrova respectfully requests that this Court find that a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the 2021 custody order, proceed to a best-interests analysis under AS 25.20.110(a) and AS 25.20.090, and enter an order modifying physical custody to a week-on, week-off, equal 50-50 shared custody schedule consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1). Wesley further requests that the Court order recalculation of child support under Civil Rule 90.3(b) to reflect the modified custody arrangement, and that the Court enter any additional orders necessary to protect and promote the children's best interests.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0101)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Nakamura respectfully petitions this Court to modify the 2021 custody order governing her nine-year-old daughter. The existing order established an equal week-on, week-off shared physical custody schedule between Elena and Maria Nakamura, with both parents residing in Anchorage. Elena's acceptance of a permanent position with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game and her resulting relocation to Juneau in January 2024 have rendered the current schedule physically impossible to maintain. The roughly 600-mile distance between Anchorage and Juneau, combined with the absence of direct road access between the two cities, makes weekly transitions wholly impractical during the school year. Elena therefore petitions this Court to modify the existing order to establish primary physical custody with Maria during the school year, with the child residing with Elena during extended summer, winter, and spring breaks, and with both parents retaining joint legal custody. This modification is supported by a material and substantial change in circumstances and is firmly in the best interests of the child.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Nakamura and Maria Nakamura are subject to a custody order entered by the Superior Court in 2021. That order awarded the parties equal shared physical custody of their daughter, now nine years old, on a week-on, week-off alternating schedule, with both parents sharing joint legal custody over major decisions. At the time the order was entered, both parents lived in Anchorage, making the alternating schedule practical and beneficial to the child.
In or around late 2023, Elena accepted a permanent, full-time position with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game that required her relocation to Juneau. This was not a temporary assignment or a short-term duty; it is a permanent career position with the State of Alaska. Elena completed her relocation to Juneau in January 2024. Juneau is not accessible by road from Anchorage. Travel between the two cities requires air travel or a combination of ferry and surface transportation, each of which involves significant time and expense. The cost and duration of travel between Anchorage and Juneau make weekly transitions between the parents' homes entirely unfeasible during the academic school year.
The child currently attends school in Anchorage, where she has been enrolled throughout her academic life, has established friendships, and benefits from the stability and continuity of her existing community. Maria Nakamura continues to reside in Anchorage. Elena does not seek to uproot the child from her school or her Anchorage community during the school year. Rather, Elena proposes that the child reside primarily with Maria during the school year, while spending extended time with Elena during summer break, winter break, and spring break. Joint legal custody would continue, preserving both parents' equal roles in major decisions affecting the child's education, health, and welfare.
Since the 2021 order was entered, no finding of domestic violence has been made against either party, and no other circumstances affecting the fundamental suitability of either parent to provide care have been presented. Both parents remain capable and loving. The sole driver of the requested modification is the logistical impossibility created by Elena's permanent relocation, a change in circumstances that the current order did not and could not have anticipated.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110, a court may modify a prior custody award when the moving party demonstrates two elements: first, that a change in circumstances has occurred since the prior order; and second, that the requested modification is in the best interests of the child. Both elements must be established before the court may revise an existing custody arrangement.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a parent's permanent relocation to another city can constitute a substantial change in circumstances sufficient to satisfy the threshold requirement for modification. In Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005), the court affirmed a custody modification arising directly from a parent's military transfer to another state, recognizing that a geographic change that renders an existing shared schedule unworkable qualifies as a material change. Similarly, in Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), the court addressed the need to restructure a shared custody arrangement following a parent's transfer overseas, affirming that logistical impossibility resulting from relocation justifies a new custody framework. In Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020), the court analyzed a modification motion in which one parent relocated to Washington State and affirmed that the child's best interests, considered in light of the relocation, supported a school-year, summer-break custody division between the parents.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must evaluate whether the proposed modification serves the child's best interests, taking into account the factors set forth under the statutory framework governing shared and primary custody arrangements, including AS 25.20.090 and AS 25.20.070.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. ELENA'S PERMANENT RELOCATION TO JUNEAU CONSTITUTES A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER AS 25.20.110
AS 25.20.110(a) provides that a custody award "may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification of the award and the modification is in the best interests of the child." Elena's permanent relocation to Juneau, completed in January 2024, plainly satisfies the change-in-circumstances threshold.
When the 2021 order was entered, both parents lived in Anchorage. The week-on, week-off schedule operated smoothly precisely because the parents lived in the same city. That foundational geographic premise no longer exists. Elena now resides in a city that cannot be reached by road from Anchorage, requiring air travel or extended ferry connections to complete each transition. The financial cost and travel time associated with weekly transitions between Anchorage and Juneau would impose an unreasonable burden on the child and on both parents. No child of nine years old can realistically change homes every seven days across a 600-mile geographic gap during an active school year without suffering significant disruption to her education, sleep, social relationships, and emotional stability.
The Alaska Supreme Court recognized precisely this kind of situation in Chesser-Witmer v. Chesser, 117 P.3d 711 (Alaska 2005), where a military parent's transfer to a distant duty station rendered an existing shared custody schedule unworkable and justified a court-ordered modification. The court affirmed that the geographic disruption caused by a parent's reassignment satisfied the change-in-circumstances requirement and supported a restructured arrangement dividing the school year from the summer months. Similarly, in Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), the court sanctioned a restructured arrangement giving one parent primary custody during the school year and the other parent custody during summers and holidays when a military transfer to Germany made shared custody across that distance impossible.
Elena's relocation is permanent, not temporary. It is connected to a stable, professional government position, not a discretionary personal choice to abandon proximity to the child without cause. The relocation does not reflect any intent to distance the child from Maria; Elena expressly proposes a plan that keeps the child in Anchorage during the school year, maintains joint legal custody, and ensures substantial time with Elena during school vacation periods. The change in circumstances is clear, material, and supported by the record.
B. THE PROPOSED MODIFICATION IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILD
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must determine whether the proposed modification serves the child's best interests. Under AS 25.20.090, when evaluating whether to award shared or primary custody, the court must consider factors including: the child's needs; the stability of the home environment offered by each parent; the child's education; the advantages of keeping the child in the community where she presently resides; the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent considering the proximity of each parent, the feasibility of travel, and each parent's willingness to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent; and other pertinent factors.
Each of these factors supports the modification Elena proposes.
1. The Child's Educational Stability and Community Continuity Favor Primary Placement with Maria During the School Year
The child is nine years old, currently enrolled in school in Anchorage, and has spent her entire academic life in that community. She has established friendships and familiarity with her Anchorage environment. AS 25.20.090(4) and (5) direct the court to consider the child's education and the advantages of keeping the child in the community where she currently resides. Both of these factors weigh in favor of the child remaining in Anchorage during the school year under Maria's primary physical custody, which is precisely what Elena proposes.
Maintaining the child's school placement and community ties during the academic year avoids the disruption and instability that would result from requiring weekly travel between two cities separated by a geographic barrier. Consistent school attendance, uninterrupted peer relationships, and stability in daily routine are well-recognized components of a child's healthy development. The Alaska Supreme Court acknowledged the importance of community stability and familiar surroundings in Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998), where the custody investigator specifically recommended keeping the children with the Anchorage-based parent during the school year to preserve continuity of environment, friendships, and family relationships.
2. Extended Time with Elena During School Vacations Preserves a Meaningful Relationship with Both Parents
AS 25.20.070 provides that the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents. The word "practical" is key. A week-on, week-off schedule between Anchorage and Juneau is not practical. The proposed modification replaces the impossible with the achievable: Elena will have the child for extended summer break, winter break, and spring break. These are substantial blocks of uninterrupted time that allow the child to reside fully in Elena's Juneau home, form a routine there, and maintain a close bond with her parent.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020), approved just such a structure when one parent relocated out of state, awarding the relocating parent primary custody during the school year and the other parent custody during the summer. That court recognized that a school-year, vacation-break division can serve the child's best interests when geography makes a more even split impossible. In Harris v. Governale, 311 P.3d 1052 (Alaska 2013), the court similarly affirmed a custody schedule that allocated summer time to the out-of-state parent and school-year time to the local parent, recognizing that recreational and extended time with a geographically distant parent remains consistent with a child's best interests. In Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018), the court recognized that reducing the frequency of transitions between parents can itself serve a child's best interests when transitions are logistically burdensome.
Elena's proposal ensures that the child spends meaningful, extended time with Elena in Juneau, where she can develop familiarity with Elena's home, neighborhood, and life, rather than brief, exhausting weekly visits requiring air travel. The school vacation model provides the child with the stability of a settled school-year home and the enrichment of extended time with both of her parents.
3. Both Parents Remain Suitable Custodians and Joint Legal Custody Should Continue
No allegation of unfitness, domestic violence, substance abuse, or child neglect has been raised against either parent. Under AS 25.20.090(8) and (9), the court must consider any evidence of domestic violence or substance abuse in the proposed custodial household. The absence of any such evidence here supports the court's confidence in both parents as suitable custodians.
Elena does not seek to diminish Maria's parental role.
