She proposes to maintain joint legal custody in its current form, preserving Maria's co-equal voice in all major decisions affecting the child's education, medical care, and general welfare. This reflects Elena's genuine commitment to cooperative co-parenting despite the geographic separation. The court in Hope P. v. Flynn G., 355 P.3d 559 (Alaska 2015), recognized that a parent's willingness to accommodate the logistical realities of the other parent's schedule and to cooperate in the child's care is a relevant consideration in the best-interests analysis. Elena's proposal demonstrates exactly that cooperative spirit.
The child's preference, while not dispositive at age nine, may also be considered under AS 25.20.090(1) if the court finds she is of sufficient age and capacity to form a preference. The court is invited to conduct an in camera interview or appoint a guardian ad litem to assess the child's views, consistent with Alaska R. Evid. 706(a), which permits the court to appoint expert witnesses on its own motion when the interests of justice so require.
4. Elena's Feasibility-of-Travel Analysis Under AS 25.20.090 Confirms the Proposed Structure
AS 25.20.090(6) instructs the court to consider the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, including the proximity of each parent to the other, the feasibility of travel between the parents, and special needs unique to the child. The distance between Anchorage and Juneau, the absence of road access, and the cost and duration of air or ferry travel make weekly transitions infeasible. This factor alone compels restructuring the existing order. The current week-on, week-off arrangement, if enforced as written, would require the child to travel by air or ferry every seven days at significant expense and time cost, disrupting school attendance and imposing a level of logistical stress inappropriate for a nine-year-old.
The proposed modification responds directly to this factor by concentrating the child's time with each parent in consecutive blocks rather than alternating weekly segments. Blocks of extended time are feasible; weekly air travel is not. The structure Elena proposes is therefore the arrangement most likely to allow the child to benefit meaningfully from both parental relationships given the geographic reality.
5. Child Support Should Be Recalculated to Reflect the Modified Custody Arrangement
Any modification to physical custody requires a corresponding review of child support obligations. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated based on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage for the number of children. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), shared physical custody calculations apply when parents share custody above a defined threshold. Because the proposed modification shifts the arrangement from shared physical custody to primary physical custody with Maria during the school year, with extended vacation time for Elena, the court should calculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) unless the total vacation time Elena exercises qualifies as shared physical custody under the definitions in Civil Rule 90.3(b). The court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(c) to vary an award upon a showing of good cause by clear and convincing evidence if manifest injustice would otherwise result.
Elena requests that the court set child support in accordance with the applicable Civil Rule 90.3 provision consistent with the modified custody arrangement, taking into account both parties' adjusted annual incomes, relevant deductions, and the actual time the child will spend with each parent.
V. CONCLUSION
Elena Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court enter an order modifying the 2021 custody order as follows: (1) granting Maria Nakamura primary physical custody of the parties' daughter during the school year, with the child residing at Maria's Anchorage home; (2) granting Elena Nakamura primary physical custody of the child during extended summer break, winter break, and spring break, with the child residing at Elena's Juneau home during those periods; (3) continuing joint legal custody in its current form, with both parents retaining equal decision-making authority over major issues affecting the child's education, health, and welfare; and (4) recalculating child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3 to reflect the modified physical custody arrangement.
The threshold change-in-circumstances requirement under AS 25.20.110 is met by Elena's permanent relocation to Juneau, which rendered the existing week-on, week-off schedule physically impossible. The proposed modification serves the child's best interests under AS 25.20.090 and AS 25.20.070 by preserving her educational stability and community ties in Anchorage during the school year, while ensuring extended and meaningful time with Elena during school vacation periods. Both parents remain suitable custodians and committed co-parents. The modification Elena proposes is the arrangement most consistent with the child's needs, the feasibility of travel, and the goal of preserving a close relationship with both parents to the greatest degree practical under the circumstances.
For the foregoing reasons, Elena Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court grant the petition to modify custody as set forth above.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0102)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Colby brings this motion to modify the existing custody order entered in 2021, which grants Colin Colby primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children and limits David to parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. Since that order was entered, David's circumstances have changed substantially and materially. He has completed a two-year substance abuse treatment program, secured stable full-time employment as a licensed electrician, and relocated to a residence within five miles of the children's school in Anchorage. These developments, taken together, represent the kind of substantial change in circumstances that Alaska law requires before a court may revisit a custody arrangement. More importantly, a modification to a 50/50 parenting schedule is in the best interests of the children. David respectfully requests that this Court modify the existing order to establish an equal parenting time arrangement that reflects his current stability, his proximity to the children's school, and the children's right to a meaningful relationship with both of their parents.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Colby and Colin Colby dissolved their marriage by decree entered in 2021. The resulting superior court order awarded Colin primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children and granted David parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. Under the custody definitions applicable in Alaska, this arrangement confers primary physical custody on Colin and limits David's parenting time well below the 30 percent threshold that would qualify as shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f).
At the time of the 2021 order, David was managing a substance abuse problem that reasonably influenced the court's custody determination. Since that time, David has taken concrete and sustained steps to address those concerns. He successfully completed a two-year substance abuse treatment program. He secured and has maintained stable full-time employment as a licensed electrician. He relocated his residence to within five miles of the children's school in Anchorage, placing him in close geographical proximity to the children's daily educational environment and to Colin's household. None of these facts existed at the time the original order was entered. These changes are not superficial or temporary. They reflect a fundamental improvement in David's stability, fitness, and capacity to serve as an active, engaged parent.
The children, who have continued to reside primarily with Colin, are enrolled in school in Anchorage. Both parents are now in close proximity to that school. There is no evidence that David poses any danger to the children. He has maintained his sobriety through the completion of a formal treatment program, remains gainfully employed, and has arranged his living situation specifically to facilitate more involvement in the children's lives. The current every-other-weekend schedule deprives the children of the meaningful relationship with David that Alaska law recognizes as important to their well-being.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A custody order may be modified when the moving party demonstrates both a substantial change in circumstances since the prior order was entered and that the requested modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a). Alaska courts apply the substantial-change requirement consistently to discourage relitigation of settled custody arrangements and to protect children from unnecessary disruption. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). Courts compare current circumstances against a baseline established at the time of the most recent order. Id. A change is not likely to be substantial enough to justify modification if it reflects only the passage of time without affecting the children's welfare. Id.
Once a substantial change is found, the court conducts a full best-interests analysis under AS 25.24.150(c). The relevant factors include the physical, emotional, mental, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; each parent's willingness to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment; evidence of substance abuse by either parent; and other pertinent factors. AS 25.24.150(c).
Alaska law also establishes a general policy favoring the child's access to both parents. AS 25.20.070 directs that, unless detrimental to the child's welfare, the child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the pendency of custody proceedings. The factors specifically governing shared custody awards are set forth at AS 25.20.090, and include the stability of each parent's home environment, each parent's proximity to the child's school, the feasibility of travel between the parents' residences, the optimal time for the child to spend with each parent, and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate the child's relationship with the other parent.
In conducting any best-interests analysis, the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child. AS 25.24.150(d).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. DAVID HAS DEMONSTRATED A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES SUFFICIENT TO INVOKE THE COURT'S AUTHORITY TO MODIFY THE EXISTING ORDER.
The threshold inquiry in any modification proceeding is whether the circumstances have changed substantially since the entry of the prior order. AS 25.20.110(a). This requirement is intended to protect children from being shuffled between parents as a consequence of routine fluctuations in adult circumstances. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). The change must affect the children's welfare and must be more than the mere passage of time. Id. Here, the changes in David's circumstances are neither routine nor superficial. They are objective, documented, and directly relevant to his parenting capacity.
At the time of the 2021 order, David's substance abuse was a live concern that appropriately informed the court's decision to limit his parenting time. That concern no longer exists in the same form. David has completed a two-year substance abuse treatment program, providing the court with a formal, sustained record of recovery rather than a bare assertion of sobriety. Alaska courts recognize that the circumstances existing at the time of the original order serve as the baseline against which changed circumstances are measured. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). The prior order was entered against the backdrop of active substance abuse; the present motion is brought against the backdrop of completed treatment, stable employment, and residential proximity to the children's school. These are categorically different circumstances.
Beyond his sobriety, David has established stable full-time employment as a licensed electrician, demonstrating the financial and personal stability that courts consider when evaluating a parent's fitness for expanded custody. He has also relocated to within five miles of the children's school, a concrete step that eliminates logistical barriers to more frequent parenting time and demonstrates a deliberate commitment to remaining present in the children's daily lives.
McLane v. Paul, 189 P.3d 1039 (Alaska 2008), illustrates that a superior court does not err in finding a substantial change in circumstances when the evidence supports that the relevant facts at the time of the motion differ meaningfully from those at the time of the prior order. Here, the combination of completed substance abuse treatment, stable employment, and residential proximity constitutes precisely the kind of substantial, welfare-affecting change that clears the threshold and requires the court to proceed to a best-interests analysis.
B. MODIFICATION TO A 50/50 PARENTING SCHEDULE IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the court must determine whether the requested modification serves the children's best interests under AS 25.24.150(c). A thorough analysis of the statutory factors supports modification to a 50/50 schedule.
1. David's Completed Substance Abuse Treatment Eliminates the Concern That Most Significantly Limited His Prior Parenting Time.
Among the factors the court must consider is evidence that substance abuse by either parent directly affects the emotional or physical well-being of the child. AS 25.24.150(c)(8). At the time of the original order, David's substance use was the primary justification for limiting his parenting time to an every-other-weekend schedule. David has now completed a full two-year treatment program. This is not a temporary or unverified claim of sobriety; it is a documented, sustained period of recovery that directly addresses the concern that animated the original custody restriction. The reason for the limitation no longer exists in the way it did when the order was entered. A custody schedule that continues to reflect a concern that has been formally addressed and resolved does not serve the children's best interests; it simply perpetuates a penalty for circumstances that David has worked diligently to correct.
2. David's Stable Employment and Housing Establish a Satisfactory Home Environment.
The court must consider the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent. AS 25.20.090(3). David's full-time employment as a licensed electrician provides him with consistent income and the ability to provide for the children's physical needs during his parenting time. His residence, established within five miles of the children's school, offers a settled and convenient home environment. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's ability to maintain emotional and physical stability for the children is a central component of the best-interests analysis. Brett M. v. Amanda M., 445 P.3d 1005 (Alaska 2019). David can now offer the children both the physical stability of a consistent home and the financial stability of steady employment.
3. David's Proximity to the Children's School Supports an Equal Parenting Schedule.
The shared custody factors set forth in AS 25.20.090 expressly require the court to consider the proximity of each parent to the other and to the school in which the child is enrolled, and the feasibility of travel between the parents. AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (C). David now lives within five miles of the children's school in Anchorage. This proximity eliminates the logistical concerns that sometimes make shared custody impractical when parents live in different communities or far from a child's school. The children can move between households without significant disruption to their school attendance, extracurricular activities, or daily routine. The feasibility of travel between the parents' residences is high. This geographic reality strongly supports the practicability of a 50/50 schedule.
4. An Equal Parenting Schedule Is Consistent with Alaska's Policy Favoring Each Parent's Access to the Child.
Alaska law directs that a child shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents, unless such access is shown to be detrimental to the child's welfare. AS 25.20.070. The existing schedule, which limits David to every other weekend and one evening per week, falls far short of equal access. With David's substance abuse treatment completed, his employment stable, and his residence close to the children's school, there is no longer a basis grounded in the children's welfare to maintain so restricted a schedule. AS 25.20.070's mandate carries real weight in this analysis. The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a court may not simply arrive at an intermediate custody division without engaging in a proper best-interests analysis anchored in the statutory factors. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018). Here, the statutory factors, considered carefully and in light of David's current circumstances, support moving toward the equal access that AS 25.20.070 directs.
5. An Equal Schedule Serves the Children's Need for Continuity and a Close Relationship with Both Parents.
The court must consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity, as well as each parent's willingness to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. AS 25.24.150(c)(5) and (6). Continuity matters, but it should not be confused with rigidity. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that where circumstances have changed and a more balanced schedule is appropriate, courts must conduct a fresh analysis rather than simply preserving the status quo. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018). David seeks not to destabilize the children's lives but to become a more consistent presence within them. A 50/50 schedule allows the children to form and deepen a meaningful relationship with David at a stage of their development when that relationship matters greatly to their long-term emotional well-being.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized the importance of parents facilitating a close relationship between the child and the other parent. Siekawitch v. Siekawitch, 956 P.2d 447 (Alaska 1998). An equal parenting schedule, supported by both parents' physical proximity to the children's school, gives the children the best opportunity for a stable and continuous relationship with both of their parents.
6. The Shared Custody Factors Under AS 25.20.090 Weigh in Favor of the Requested Modification.
The factors specifically applicable to shared custody awards under AS 25.20.090 align with the modification David requests. The children's needs, AS 25.20.090(2), are best served by access to both parents in a stable, predictable schedule. The stability of David's home environment, AS 25.20.090(3), is established by his employment and housing. The proximity of each parent to the school and the feasibility of travel, AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (C), favor equal parenting time given David's location within five miles of the school. The actual time currently spent with each parent, AS 25.20.090(6)(A), is severely lopsided and does not reflect David's current capabilities or the children's interest in a balanced parental relationship.
Courts have recognized that a trial judge has substantial discretion in crafting parenting schedules but that discretion must be exercised through a proper analysis of the relevant statutory factors, not by defaulting to an intermediate arrangement without a principled basis. Co v. Matson, 313 P.3d 521 (Alaska 2013). Here, a proper analysis of all applicable factors supports an equal schedule.
C. THE MODIFICATION SHOULD BE STRUCTURED AS SHARED PHYSICAL CUSTODY WITHIN THE MEANING OF CIVIL RULE 90.3(f).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(f), a parent has shared physical custody for purposes of child support calculation when the children reside with that parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. A 50/50 parenting schedule places David squarely within the shared physical custody category, which affects how child support obligations are calculated going forward. If the court grants the modification, the child support order should be reviewed under Civil Rule 90.3(h) to determine whether the change in the parenting schedule constitutes a material change of circumstances justifying a corresponding modification of the support award. A material change of circumstances is presumed when support as calculated under the rule would be more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1). The court should address this issue concurrently with the custody modification to ensure that the financial arrangements accurately reflect the new parenting reality.
V. CONCLUSION
David Colby has met both requirements for modification of the existing custody order. He has demonstrated a substantial change in circumstances since the 2021 order was entered, including the completion of a two-year substance abuse treatment program, the establishment of stable full-time employment, and his relocation to within five miles of the children's school. A full analysis of the best-interests factors under AS 25.24.150(c) and the shared custody factors under AS 25.20.090 supports modification to a 50/50 parenting schedule. Such a schedule is consistent with Alaska's policy under AS 25.20.070 that children should have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents. The existing every-other-weekend restriction no longer reflects the realities of David's circumstances or the best interests of the children. David respectfully requests that this Court grant his petition, modify the existing custody order to establish an equal 50/50 parenting schedule, and review the current child support order for conformance with Civil Rule 90.3(h).

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0103)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Petrova ("Mother") respectfully petitions this Court for modification of the existing custody and visitation order entered in 2021. The current order awards primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children to Colin Petrova ("Father") and grants Mother visitation every other weekend and for six weeks during the summer. Since the entry of that order, Father unilaterally relocated from Anchorage to Fairbanks without providing Mother the court-required 90-day advance notice, fundamentally disrupting Mother's ability to exercise her court-ordered parenting time and materially altering the circumstances upon which the existing order was premised.
Father's unannounced relocation constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under Alaska law. Mother now seeks either primary physical custody of the children, or in the alternative, a substantial expansion of her parenting time and a court order requiring Father to bear the transportation costs associated with visitation exchanges. The existing schedule is logistically and financially untenable given the distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks. The best interests of the children require a revised arrangement that preserves and protects their meaningful relationship with both parents.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Petrova and Colin Petrova were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, both parties resided in Anchorage, Alaska. The Superior Court entered a custody order granting Father primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children. Under that order, Mother was awarded visitation every other weekend and for six weeks during the summer. The order further required that either party provide at least 90 days advance written notice before relocating outside the Anchorage area.
At some point after entry of the 2021 order, Father accepted a job transfer and relocated from Anchorage to Fairbanks, Alaska. Father did not provide Mother with the court-required 90-day advance notice of his intent to relocate, nor did he seek prior court approval for the move. Mother learned of the relocation after it had already occurred.
The distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks is approximately 360 miles by road and requires either a lengthy drive or commercial air travel. The every-other-weekend visitation schedule ordered by the Court in 2021 was designed around the parties residing in the same city. Father's relocation has rendered that schedule functionally impossible for Mother to maintain on a regular basis without incurring substantial transportation expense. Mother's financial resources do not allow her to absorb the cost of round-trip airfare or equivalent travel expenses every two weeks. As a result, Mother has been unable to exercise her court-ordered parenting time as frequently as the order contemplates, directly harming her relationship with the children and the children's access to their Mother.
The children's daily routine, school contacts, extracurricular activities, and support network have all shifted to Fairbanks as a consequence of Father's relocation, a relocation that Mother had no opportunity to anticipate, prepare for, or challenge before it occurred.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a custody or visitation order upon finding that a change in circumstances has occurred and that modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.948 provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child.
Alaska courts require that the moving party first establish a substantial change of circumstances as a threshold matter before the court proceeds to a best-interests analysis. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022); Corbeau v. Dietrich, 412 P.3d 844 (Alaska 2016). The change-in-circumstances requirement is intended to promote finality and protect children from repeated custody litigation, but it also ensures that custody arrangements remain responsive to material shifts in the parties' lives. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022).
A relocating parent's decision to move out of the area where the existing custody order was fashioned constitutes a substantial change in circumstances as a matter of law. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017); Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020). Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the court proceeds to evaluate whether modification serves the best interests of the child, taking into account all relevant statutory factors. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011).
Additionally, Civil Rule 90.3(g) authorizes the court, after determining a child support award, to allocate reasonable travel expenses necessary to exercise visitation between the parties as may be just and proper.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. FATHER'S UNILATERAL RELOCATION FROM ANCHORAGE TO FAIRBANKS CONSTITUTES A SUBSTANTIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER AS 25.20.110(a).
Father's decision to accept a job transfer and relocate from Anchorage to Fairbanks without providing the court-required 90-day advance notice to Mother is precisely the type of material change in circumstances that Alaska law recognizes as sufficient to trigger a custody modification inquiry. AS 25.20.110(a) expressly authorizes modification of a custody award when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires it and the modification is in the best interests of the child.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a custodial parent's relocation out of the area where the existing custody order was fashioned amounts to a substantial change in circumstances as a matter of law. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). This principle applies with full force here. The 2021 custody order was entered when both parties lived in Anchorage. The every-other-weekend and summer visitation schedule was crafted around that shared geographic reality. Father's move to Fairbanks, a city roughly 360 miles from Anchorage, fundamentally altered the conditions under which that order was designed to operate.
The Alaska Supreme Court has further confirmed that a parent's anticipated or completed relocation is a substantial change in circumstances sufficient to justify considering a physical custody modification. Brian Ott v. Haley Runa, 463 P.3d 180 (Alaska 2020). Courts are required to evaluate the legitimacy of the move and then assess the best interests of the child in light of the new circumstances. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). Father's relocation cannot be said to have been contemplated or planned for in the 2021 order, which instead required advance notice precisely to allow for judicial oversight of any such move. Where the parties' agreement and prior order did not anticipate or account for relocation, a subsequent move qualifies as a change in circumstances warranting further inquiry. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011).
Compounding the significance of the relocation itself, Father violated the court's 90-day advance notice requirement. This unilateral disregard for the existing order prevented Mother from seeking a preemptive modification, arranging her finances, or taking any steps to protect her parenting rights before Father removed the children to Fairbanks. Alaska courts have recognized that actions by a custodial parent that substantially interfere with the noncustodial parent's visitation rights can independently constitute a change in circumstances. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). Father's conduct here both interfered with Mother's visitation rights and violated a direct court order, reinforcing the conclusion that a substantial change has occurred.
Accordingly, Mother respectfully urges this Court to find that Father's unilateral relocation from Anchorage to Fairbanks, in violation of the 90-day notice requirement, constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a), thereby opening the door to a full best-interests analysis.
B. MODIFICATION OF CUSTODY OR EXPANSION OF MOTHER'S PARENTING TIME IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
Once a substantial change in circumstances is established, the court must determine whether modification of the existing order is in the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.110(a). When a custodial parent relocates, the court weighs whether the move is legitimate and then assesses whether the children's interests are better served by modifying custody or parenting-time arrangements. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017).
Mother does not dispute that Father may have had legitimate professional reasons for accepting the Fairbanks job transfer. However, a legitimate reason for a move does not insulate the relocating parent from a custody modification if the resulting arrangement no longer serves the children's best interests. Judd v. Burns, 397 P.3d 331 (Alaska 2017). Where the relocating parent who holds primary custody bears primary responsibility for the disruption caused to the children's relationship with the other parent, courts have found that a custody modification may be appropriate. Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001). In Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed a transfer of primary custody where the relocating parent had uprooted the children from a stable environment and thereby disrupted the children's relationship with the other parent.
The present circumstances are analogous. Father's unilateral relocation has not only disrupted the children's established environment in Anchorage but has also made it effectively impossible for Mother to maintain the every-other-weekend contact that the existing order was designed to provide. The children's ability to sustain a meaningful, ongoing relationship with Mother is central to their well-being. An arrangement that nominally preserves Mother's visitation rights but renders those rights logistically and financially inaccessible does not serve the children's best interests.
Mother requests the following relief in the alternative:
First, Mother requests that this Court modify the existing custody order to award her primary physical custody of the children, with Father receiving comparable visitation. Father's violation of the notice requirement and the resulting harm to Mother's parenting relationship weigh in favor of this remedy. Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001); Ronny M. v. Nanette H., 598 P.3d 878 (Alaska 2013).
Second, if the Court declines to transfer primary physical custody, Mother requests a substantial expansion of her parenting time, including extended blocks of time during school breaks, holidays, and the summer, designed to compensate for the practical inability to exercise every-other-weekend visitation given the Anchorage-Fairbanks distance.
C. THE COURT SHOULD ALLOCATE TRANSPORTATION COSTS TO FATHER GIVEN THAT HIS UNILATERAL RELOCATION CREATED THE FINANCIAL BURDEN ON MOTHER.
Civil Rule 90.3(g) provides that the court, after determining a child support award, shall allocate reasonable travel expenses which are necessary to exercise visitation between the parties as may be just and proper for them to contribute. This provision expressly contemplates that the court will consider the equities of the parties' situations in assigning transportation costs.
Here, the financial burden of transportation falls entirely and exclusively on Mother as a direct consequence of Father's unilateral decision to relocate. Mother derived no benefit from the move and had no meaningful opportunity to object before the children were removed to Fairbanks. Father, by contrast, accepted the job transfer voluntarily and in violation of the court's notice requirement. It is neither just nor equitable to require Mother to absorb the cost of round-trip airfare or comparable travel expenses every other weekend simply to exercise the parenting time she was already awarded by this Court.
Consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(g), Mother requests that the Court allocate all or the substantial majority of reasonable travel expenses associated with visitation exchanges to Father, given that his unilateral relocation created those expenses. At a minimum, the Court should require the parties to share such costs in proportion to their respective incomes, as justice and equity demand. If Father elects to remain in Fairbanks with primary custody, the financial consequences of that choice should not be externalized onto Mother.
D. THE COURT IS REQUESTED TO TAKE JUDICIAL NOTICE OF THE GEOGRAPHIC DISTANCE BETWEEN ANCHORAGE AND FAIRBANKS AND THE ASSOCIATED TRAVEL LOGISTICS.
Alaska R. Evid. 201(d) provides that upon request of a party, the court shall take judicial notice of each matter specified in subdivision (b) if the requesting party furnishes sufficient information and has given each party notice adequate to enable the party to meet the request. Mother respectfully requests that this Court take judicial notice of the geographic distance between Anchorage and Fairbanks, Alaska, the absence of a direct road route that can be traveled in a short period, and the general cost and logistical burden associated with commercial air travel between the two cities. These facts are not subject to reasonable dispute and are capable of accurate and ready determination from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned. This judicially-noticed context is relevant to understanding why the existing every-other-weekend schedule is no longer workable and why a modification is necessary to protect Mother's relationship with the children.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Mother Ashley Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that Father Colin Petrova's unilateral relocation from Anchorage to Fairbanks, in violation of the court-required 90-day advance notice provision, constitutes a substantial change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a);
2. Conduct a best-interests hearing and thereafter modify the existing custody order to award Mother primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, with Father receiving substantial visitation;
3. In the alternative, substantially expand Mother's parenting time to include meaningful blocks of contact during school breaks, holidays, and the summer, structured to account for the geographic distance between the parties;
4. Pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(g), allocate all or the majority of reasonable travel expenses necessary to exercise visitation to Father, given that his unilateral decision to relocate created those costs; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the best interests of the children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0104)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Petrova respectfully requests that this Court modify the existing custody order entered in 2021 to designate her as the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children. Since the 2021 order was entered, the circumstances of both parties have changed substantially and materially. Renee has relocated to Anchorage to accept stable, long-term employment, completed a 90-day parenting skills program, and established a consistent, suitable home environment for the children. Respondent Maria Petrova, by contrast, has moved four times in the past year, including a period in which the children resided with her in a friend's one-bedroom apartment, demonstrating a pattern of housing instability that directly and adversely affects the children's welfare. These changes satisfy the threshold requirement of a substantial change in circumstances under AS 25.20.110, and the balance of the best-interests factors under AS 25.24.150 and AS 25.20.913 weighs clearly in favor of awarding primary physical custody to Renee. This Court should therefore enter a modified order designating Renee as the primary physical custodian, with appropriate parenting time for Maria.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
In 2021, the Superior Court entered a custody order granting the parties joint legal custody of their two minor children. Under that order, Maria Petrova holds primary physical custody of the children, and Renee Petrova exercises parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week.
Following entry of the 2021 order, Renee secured stable, long-term employment in Anchorage and relocated there accordingly. Her relocation was motivated by a genuine professional opportunity that has provided her with financial stability and the capacity to maintain a suitable, permanent residence for the children. In addition, Renee voluntarily completed a 90-day parenting skills program, reflecting her ongoing commitment to improving her ability to meet the children's needs. Renee has established a consistent and appropriate home environment in Anchorage that is capable of serving the children's physical, emotional, and educational needs.
In sharp contrast, Maria's circumstances have deteriorated significantly since the 2021 order. Over the past year alone, Maria has moved four times. At one point, she and the children lived together in a friend's one-bedroom apartment, an arrangement that was cramped, temporary, and plainly inadequate for two children who require stability, space, and predictability in their home lives. This pattern of repeated, short-term relocations has disrupted the children's routines and deprived them of the stable environment that is central to their well-being.
The cumulative effect of these changes: Renee's improved stability and parenting readiness, and Maria's ongoing housing instability, constitutes a substantial and material change in circumstances since the 2021 order and warrants a modification of primary physical custody in favor of Renee.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a custody order when it determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a). The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that the change-in-circumstances requirement is designed to discourage continual relitigation of custody decisions and to preserve finality in custody arrangements, recognizing that stability is critical to a child's emotional welfare. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). Courts compare current circumstances to the baseline that existed at the time of the most recent custody order. Id.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court conducts a best-interests analysis under AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.961. The factors the court must consider include: the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence, child abuse, or child neglect; and any other factors the court considers pertinent. AS 25.24.150(c).
The court may award primary physical custody to either parent on the basis of this analysis, and neither parent is entitled to preference by reason of gender or any other consideration unrelated to the child's welfare. AS 25.20.060(b). The court's overarching obligation is to award custody on the basis of the best interests of the child, considering all relevant factors. AS 25.20.060(a).
Where child support is at issue following any modification of physical custody, the award shall be calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) for primary physical custody arrangements and Civil Rule 90.3(b) for shared physical custody arrangements. A modification of a final child support award requires a showing of a material change in circumstances, with a presumption of materiality arising when the recalculated support amount differs from the outstanding order by more than 15 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Substantial Change in Circumstances Has Occurred Since the 2021 Order.
The threshold question in any custody modification proceeding is whether a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the prior order. AS 25.20.110(a). The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that courts must compare current circumstances to the factual baseline existing at the time of the most recent order to determine whether the change is substantial enough to warrant reconsideration of the custody arrangement. Laramie Rainer v. Ryan Poole, 510 P.3d 476 (Alaska 2022). Here, the changes since the 2021 order are numerous, significant, and directly relevant to the children's welfare.
At the time the 2021 order was entered, both parties resided in Juneau, and the custody arrangement was structured with that shared geographic proximity in mind. Since that time, Renee has relocated to Anchorage to accept stable, long-term employment, while Maria has moved four times in the past year, including a period of residing with the children in a friend's one-bedroom apartment. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's relocation constitutes a material change in circumstances when it alters the structure and functioning of the existing custody arrangement. Barrett v. Alguire, 611 P.3d 404 (Alaska 2001). In Barrett, the court found that a parent's move to another state warranted a hearing on custody modification because it disrupted the children's previously stable environment. The parallel is apt here: the geographic separation of the parties, combined with Maria's documented housing instability, represents a fundamental departure from the conditions that existed when the 2021 order was crafted.
Maria's pattern of repeated moves, four relocations within a single year, and her temporary placement of the children in a single-bedroom apartment shared with a friend, constitutes a direct and concrete change affecting the children's day-to-day welfare. The stability of the custodial home is among the most critical considerations in any custody determination, and a dramatic deterioration in housing stability since the last order plainly satisfies the change-in-circumstances standard. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018) (noting that the stability of the children's environment encompasses a multitude of factors, including the home provided by the custodial parent).
Simultaneously, Renee's circumstances have improved materially. She has obtained long-term, stable employment, completed a 90-day parenting skills program, and established a consistent home environment. These positive developments, viewed alongside Maria's declining housing stability, together establish that the conditions underpinning the 2021 order have changed substantially and that the court must now revisit the custody arrangement to protect the children's interests.
B. Modification of Primary Physical Custody to Renee Is in the Best Interests of the Children.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must determine whether modification is in the children's best interests. AS 25.20.110(a). The factors enumerated in AS 25.24.150(c) guide this inquiry. Analyzed here, those factors weigh substantially in favor of designating Renee as primary physical custodian.
1. The Children's Physical, Emotional, and Social Needs.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(1), the court must consider the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child. Children require a stable, safe, and predictable living environment as a foundation for their physical health, emotional development, and social adjustment. Maria's four moves in one year, and her temporary housing of the children in a one-bedroom apartment with a third party, do not reflect an environment capable of consistently meeting these needs. A child who is repeatedly uprooted from one residence to another experiences disruption to schooling, friendships, routines, and the sense of security that is essential to healthy development.
Renee's established residence in Anchorage, by contrast, provides the children with a permanent and stable home. Renee's completion of a 90-day parenting skills program further demonstrates her active commitment to developing the tools necessary to meet the children's emotional and developmental needs.
2. The Capability and Desire of Each Parent to Meet the Children's Needs.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(2), the court must evaluate the capability and desire of each parent to meet the children's needs. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that it is a parent's present ability to provide for the needs of the child that is at issue. McQuade v. McQuade, 901 P.2d 421 (Alaska 1995). Renee has demonstrated her present capability through her acquisition of stable employment, her completion of a formal parenting skills program, and her establishment of a suitable household. These are affirmative, concrete steps that reflect both the desire and the capacity to serve as a primary caregiver.
Maria's recent history, characterized by repeated relocations and inadequate housing, raises legitimate questions about her present ability to provide the children with the stable environment they require. The court is entitled to consider a parent's track record in the period since the last order as probative of current parenting capacity. Pingree v. Cossette, 424 P.3d 371 (Alaska 2018).
3. Stability and Continuity of the Children's Environment.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(5), the court must consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. This factor, often cited as among the most weighty in custody determinations, cuts strongly in Renee's favor under the present circumstances. Blanton v. Yourkowski, 180 P.3d 948 (Alaska 2008). While continuity is ordinarily a factor favoring the existing custodial arrangement, it cannot serve to perpetuate an unstable environment that no longer provides the children with the consistency they need. Where the current custodial home is itself the source of instability, continuity in that arrangement does not serve the children's interests.
Maria's four moves in the past year, including the one-bedroom apartment episode, have already disrupted whatever continuity existed under the 2021 order. Renee's Anchorage residence offers the prospective continuity and stability that the children need going forward. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must consider the home provided by the custodial parent as part of the stability analysis, and that a custodial parent's inability to maintain adequate housing is relevant to this inquiry. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018).
4. Each Parent's Willingness to Facilitate the Other Parent's Relationship with the Children.
Under AS 25.24.150(c)(6), the court must consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Renee does not seek to eliminate Maria's relationship with the children. She requests only that the primary custodial designation be modified to reflect the current realities of each parent's circumstances. Renee is prepared to support an appropriate parenting time schedule for Maria that preserves the children's bond with both parents. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's demonstrated willingness to facilitate the other parent's relationship with the children is an important positive factor in a custody determination. Ronny M. v. Nanette H., 303 P.3d 392 (Alaska 2013).
5. The Best-Interests Standard Requires Modification.
Taken together, the AS 25.24.150(c) factors demonstrate that modifying primary physical custody to Renee is in the children's best interests. The court's paramount duty is to award custody on the basis of what best serves the children's welfare. AS 25.20.060(a). As the Alaska Supreme Court held in Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018), a custody arrangement must be the product of a genuine best-interests analysis that appropriately weighs all relevant factors and does not assign disproportionate weight to any single consideration to the exclusion of others. Here, the weight of the relevant factors favors Renee. She offers the children stability, a permanent home, employment-backed financial security, and demonstrated commitment to her role as a parent. Maria's recent history of housing instability undermines the foundational premise of the current arrangement, namely that the children's primary home provides them with a safe and stable environment.
C. Any Resulting Child Support Obligation Should Be Recalculated Under Civil Rule 90.3.
Should the court grant the requested modification and designate Renee as primary physical custodian, the parties' child support obligations must be recalculated accordingly. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage: 20 percent for one child, and 27 percent for two children. Upon modification, Maria would become the non-custodial parent, and her support obligation should be calculated using the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula.
A modification of child support is appropriate upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1). A material change of circumstances is presumed when the recalculated support amount differs from the outstanding order by more than 15 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1). A modification of the custody designation will almost certainly produce a recalculated support figure that exceeds this threshold, thereby establishing the material change required to modify any existing child support order.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Renee Petrova respectfully requests that this Court find a substantial change in circumstances has occurred since the 2021 custody order, conduct a best-interests analysis under AS 25.24.150(c) and AS 25.20.060, and enter a modified custody order designating Renee as the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children, with appropriate parenting time for Maria Petrova. Renee further requests that the Court recalculate the parties' child support obligations in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) to reflect the modified custody arrangement.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0105)
I. INTRODUCTION
This brief is submitted in support of Petitioner Ashley Bergstrom's motion to modify the existing child custody and parenting time order entered in 2021. The parties, Ashley Bergstrom and Colin Bergstrom, share joint legal custody of their two minor children, with primary physical custody currently residing in Ashley and scheduled parenting time to Colin every other weekend and one weeknight per week. Ashley has accepted a permanent employment transfer to Juneau, Alaska, approximately 600 miles from the family's established home in Fairbanks, where Colin continues to reside and where the children currently attend school. Rather than uproot the children mid-year from their schools, community ties, and relationship with their father, Ashley petitions this court to temporarily award Colin primary physical custody during the school year while preserving her meaningful and substantial parenting time during summer break, winter recess, and spring break. This proposed arrangement prioritizes the children's educational continuity and stability while simultaneously protecting the children's close and continuing relationship with both parents. The modification Ashley seeks is narrowly tailored, grounded in the children's best interests, and fully supported by Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Bergstrom and Colin Bergstrom were divorced in 2021 by order of the Superior Court. The existing order awards the parties joint legal custody of their two minor children and grants Ashley primary physical custody. Colin exercises parenting time every other weekend and one weeknight per week under the existing schedule.
Following entry of the 2021 order, Ashley was offered and accepted a permanent job transfer to Juneau, Alaska. Juneau is located approximately 600 miles from Fairbanks, making regular weekday exchanges between the two cities logistically infeasible due to the geographic distance and lack of road access between the two communities. Colin continues to reside in Fairbanks, where the children are currently enrolled in school and have established friendships, community connections, and a stable daily routine.
Ashley does not seek to permanently divest herself of her parenting role or to restrict Colin's access to the children. Rather, she proposes a modified arrangement in which the children remain in Fairbanks with Colin as the primary physical custodian during the school year, ensuring no disruption to their education, while Ashley exercises extended parenting time during summer break, winter recess, and spring break. This proposal reflects Ashley's good-faith effort to balance her professional obligations against the children's demonstrated need for educational stability and their established relationship with both parents.
The existing order no longer reflects the practical realities of the parties' circumstances. Ashley's permanent relocation constitutes a substantial change in circumstances that requires judicial attention and a modification of the current parenting plan to serve the children's best interests going forward.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under Alaska law, a court may modify a custody or visitation award when it determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a). A relocating parent's move out of the area can constitute a change of circumstances warranting reconsideration of the existing custody arrangement. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011). Once a qualifying change of circumstances is established, the court conducts a comprehensive best interests analysis guided by the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c), including the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; each parent's willingness and ability to facilitate a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child; any evidence of domestic violence or substance abuse; and other pertinent factors. AS 25.24.150(c).
Additionally, AS 25.20.070 provides that, unless doing so would be detrimental to the welfare of the child or unless the domestic violence presumption of AS 25.24.150(g) applies, the children shall have, to the greatest degree practical, equal access to both parents during the pendency of custody proceedings. In awarding shared or modified physical custody arrangements, the court may also consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, including the stability of each parent's home environment, the optimal time for the children to spend with each parent given their proximity and the feasibility of travel, and each parent's willingness to facilitate the children's relationship with the other parent.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that custody modification decisions must reflect a thorough, individualized best interests analysis and must not place disproportionate weight on any single factor at the expense of a balanced overall assessment. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018). The court must consider the totality of circumstances affecting the children's well-being. AS 25.24.150(d) provides that in awarding custody the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Ashley's Permanent Relocation to Juneau Constitutes a Substantial Change of Circumstances Under AS 25.20.110(a).
A modification of custody is warranted when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires it and that the modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a). A custodial parent's permanent relocation to a community hundreds of miles away from the children's school and the other parent is precisely the type of change of circumstances that triggers modification review under Alaska law. Nelson v. Nelson, 263 P.3d 49 (Alaska 2011) (a move out of state by a custodial parent constitutes a change of circumstances as a matter of law under the framework of AS 25.20.110(a)). While the present relocation is within Alaska rather than out of state, the practical effect of a 600-mile move to a community with no road access to Fairbanks is, for purposes of the children's daily lives and the existing parenting schedule, equally transformative. The existing parenting plan, which contemplates weeknight parenting time and every-other-weekend exchanges, is a physical impossibility under the new geographic circumstances. The current order is therefore unworkable as written, and the threshold requirement for modification is satisfied.
Furthermore, Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001) makes clear that a relocating parent's move, particularly one that displaces children from a stable environment and disrupts their established routines, supports a finding of material change of circumstances justifying modification. Here, Ashley does not seek to relocate the children. To the contrary, she affirmatively proposes that the children remain in Fairbanks with Colin during the school year precisely to avoid that disruption. This forward-looking, child-centered proposal underscores that a genuine and substantial change of circumstances exists, and that a modified order is necessary to address it.
B. Modification to Award Colin Primary Physical Custody During the School Year Serves the Children's Best Interests Under AS 25.24.150(c).
Once a change of circumstances is established, the court must determine what custody arrangement serves the children's best interests by examining the factors listed in AS 25.24.150(c). A careful application of those factors to the present circumstances supports the modification Ashley proposes.
1. Educational Stability and Environmental Continuity Favor the Proposed Modification.
Among the most significant best interests factors is "the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity." AS 25.24.150(c)(5). The children are currently enrolled in Fairbanks schools, have established friendships in that community, and have lived in that environment for the duration of their young lives. Requiring the children to relocate mid-year to Juneau, a community with a different school system, different peer networks, and no established support structure for them, would be directly contrary to their interest in continuity and stability.
Ashley's proposal solves this problem entirely. By voluntarily proposing that the children remain with Colin in Fairbanks during the school year, Ashley ensures that the children's educational placement, friendships, and daily routines are maintained without interruption. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that educational stability and the preservation of familiar surroundings weigh heavily in custody determinations. Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998) (noting that a custody investigator's preference for the arrangement that minimized disruption to the children's established community ties was a legitimate and important consideration). The proposed modification is therefore consistent with this principle.
2. Ashley's Willingness to Propose This Modification Demonstrates Her Commitment to Facilitating the Children's Relationship with Colin.
AS 25.24.150(c)(6) directs the court to consider "the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child." Ashley's voluntary proposal to place the children in Colin's primary physical custody during the school year is perhaps the clearest possible demonstration of her willingness to foster the children's relationship with their father. Rather than insisting on retaining physical custody at the expense of the children's connection to Colin and their established community, Ashley is placing the children's relationship with both parents above her own residential preference.
AS 25.20.090(6)(E) similarly instructs the court, in evaluating shared or modified custody arrangements, to consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child. Ashley's proposal is the practical embodiment of that willingness. The court should recognize this posture as a factor weighing in favor of approving the modification as proposed.
3. The Proposed Schedule Allows for Meaningful and Substantial Contact Between Ashley and the Children.
AS 25.20.070 establishes that, to the greatest degree practical, children shall have equal access to both parents. While geographic distance necessarily limits the frequency of contact between Ashley and the children during the school year, the proposed modification compensates for this reduction in frequency by providing for extended, uninterrupted parenting time during summer break, winter recess, and spring break. These extended periods allow Ashley to maintain a deep and meaningful parenting relationship with the children, even across geographic distance.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the structure of a custody arrangement must be evaluated in light of actual geographic and logistical realities rather than abstract ideals. Tompkins v. Tompkins, 961 P.2d 419 (Alaska 1998). The logistical constraints posed by the distance between Fairbanks and Juneau make a school-year/vacation-period division the arrangement most consistent with both the children's educational continuity and their continued access to both parents.
4. The Needs of the Children and the Capability of Each Parent to Meet Those Needs Support the Proposed Arrangement.
AS 25.24.150(c)(1) directs the court to consider "the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child," and AS 25.24.150(c)(2) requires consideration of "the capability and desire of each parent to meet these needs." Both parents in this matter are capable and loving parents. The 2021 order itself reflects the court's prior determination that joint legal custody was appropriate and that Ashley was a fit primary custodian. Nothing has changed with respect to either parent's capability or desire to meet the children's needs.
What has changed is the logistical reality of the family's geography. The proposed modification is designed precisely to ensure that both parents continue to meet the children's needs: Colin by providing a stable home base in Fairbanks during the school year, and Ashley by providing extended, enriching parenting time during school vacations. The arrangement also preserves the joint legal custody structure, ensuring that both parents continue to participate in decisions regarding the children's education, health, and welfare.
5. The Proximity and Feasibility of Travel Between the Parents Supports the School-Year/Vacation-Period Division.
AS 25.20.090(6)(B) and (C) require the court to consider the proximity of each parent to the other and to the children's school, as well as the feasibility of travel between the parents. Fairbanks and Juneau are separated by approximately 600 miles, and there is no road connecting the two cities. Travel between them requires either air transportation or a combination of ferry and road travel, each of which is costly and time-consuming. The feasibility of the existing weeknight parenting arrangement is therefore eliminated entirely.
The school-year/vacation-period division accounts for these travel realities directly. During the school year, the children remain in Fairbanks where their school is located and where Colin lives. During extended vacation periods, the children travel to Juneau to be with Ashley. This division matches the natural rhythm of the school calendar to the geographic realities of the family's new circumstances and minimizes the burden that travel places on the children themselves. Brett M. v. Amanda M., 445 P.3d 1005 (Alaska 2019) (affirming that a custody arrangement that accounts for geographic distance and the children's established ties to a community is consistent with a proper best interests analysis).
6. A Thorough and Balanced Best Interests Analysis Supports Approval of the Proposed Modification.
The Alaska Supreme Court has cautioned that courts must conduct a thorough and balanced best interests analysis, and must not elevate any single factor disproportionately at the expense of the overall picture. Weathers v. Weathers, 425 P.3d 131 (Alaska 2018). Here, the totality of the relevant factors converges on the same result. The children's educational stability is preserved. Their relationship with Colin is protected and enhanced. Ashley's relationship with the children is maintained through meaningful extended parenting time. The geographic and logistical realities of the family's new circumstances are fully accounted for. No factor identified in AS 25.24.150(c) or AS 25.20.090 weighs against the proposed modification.
AS 25.24.150(d) directs that in awarding custody the court may consider only those facts that directly affect the well-being of the child. Every element of the proposed modification is directly tied to the children's well-being: their continuity of education, their relationships with both parents, and their physical and emotional stability. The court should approve the modification as proposed.
C. Child Support Should Be Recalculated to Reflect the Modified Physical Custody Arrangement.
A modification of the physical custody arrangement will necessarily require recalculation of the child support obligation. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage: 20% for one child and 27% for two children. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b), if the parties are awarded shared physical custody, a different calculation applies that accounts for the percentage of time each parent exercises physical custody.
The school-year/vacation-period arrangement proposed by Ashley may qualify as shared physical custody depending on the precise allocation of parenting days. The court should make findings regarding the percentage of time each parent will exercise physical custody and apply the appropriate formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) or Civil Rule 90.3(b) accordingly. Ashley requests that the court conduct this analysis at the modification hearing and enter an updated child support order consistent with the modified physical custody arrangement.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Ashley Bergstrom respectfully requests that this court find that her permanent relocation to Juneau constitutes a substantial change of circumstances under AS 25.20.110(a), conduct a best interests analysis under AS 25.24.150(c), and enter an order modifying the existing custody arrangement as follows: awarding Colin Bergstrom primary physical custody of the two minor children during the school year, with Ashley Bergstrom exercising primary physical custody during summer break, winter recess, and spring break, and with the parties retaining joint legal custody. Ashley further requests that the court recalculate child support consistent with the modified custody arrangement under Civil Rule 90.3(a) or Civil Rule 90.3(b) as applicable. This modification is in the best interests of the children, accounts for the logistical realities of the family's changed circumstances, and preserves the children's meaningful relationships with both of their parents.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO MODIFY AN EXISTING CUSTODY OR VISITATION ORDER
(doc-0106)
I. INTRODUCTION
Maria Sutter respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing custody order entered in 2021 and transfer primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children to her. Since the entry of the original order, Elena Sutter has accepted a permanent position with a fisheries management agency in Juneau, requiring her to relocate approximately 600 miles from Anchorage, where the children currently reside, attend school, and are embedded in their community. This relocation constitutes a substantial change in circumstances warranting modification of the custody arrangement. Transferring primary physical custody to Maria will serve the children's best interests by preserving the stability of their school enrollment, extended family relationships, extracurricular activities, and community ties. Elena may be awarded extended summer visitation and regular video contact during the school year, ensuring that both parents remain meaningfully present in the children's lives.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Sutter and Maria Sutter were divorced in 2021 pursuant to a Superior Court order. That order granted Elena primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children. Maria was awarded visitation every other weekend and on alternating holidays. Both children currently reside in Anchorage, attend school there, and are actively engaged in extracurricular activities. Maria also continues to reside in Anchorage and has maintained consistent involvement in the children's lives throughout the post-divorce period.
Following entry of the 2021 custody order, Elena accepted a permanent employment position with a fisheries management agency located in Juneau, Alaska. This position requires Elena to permanently relocate from Anchorage to Juneau, a distance of approximately 600 miles. Elena's relocation is not temporary in nature; it is a permanent change of her residence and employment. The children's extended family on Maria's side, the children's school, and their established social and extracurricular networks are all located in Anchorage.
Elena's move to Juneau would, under the existing custody order, require the children to be uprooted from their current school, separated from Maria on a day-to-day basis, and removed from the community and extended family that have provided a stable foundation for their development. Maria now petitions this Court to modify the custody arrangement by granting her primary physical custody so that the children may remain in Anchorage, with Elena receiving extended summer visitation and regular electronic contact during the school year.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), a custody award may be modified when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires modification and that modification is in the best interests of the child. When a parent opposes the modification and modification is granted, the court must enter its reasons for the modification on the record.
The best interests of the child are evaluated under the factors set forth in AS 25.24.150(c), which directs the court to consider, among other things, the physical, emotional, mental, religious, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; the child's preference if the child is of sufficient age and capacity; the love and affection existing between the child and each parent; the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity; and the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate and encourage a close and continuing relationship between the other parent and the child.
Where shared physical custody is at issue, the court may also consider the factors enumerated in AS 25.20.090, including the stability of the home environment likely to be offered by each parent, the advantages of keeping the child in the community where the child presently resides, the proximity of each parent to the other and to the school in which the child is enrolled, and the feasibility of travel between the parents.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a parent's relocation can constitute a material change in circumstances sufficient to support modification of a custody order. In Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), the court held that a custodial parent's move to another state was a material change in circumstances warranting a hearing on custody modification, with the best interests factors under AS 25.24.150(c) guiding the ultimate determination.
Similarly, in Hayes v. Hayes, 922 P.2d 896 (Alaska 1996), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that while geographic continuity is an important consideration, it must be weighed against other competing factors, including the stability of the child's relationship with each parent and the strength of community ties. The court applies a best interests standard without placing a heightened burden on either party to demonstrate the appropriateness of a proposed relocation or its resulting custody consequences.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Elena's Permanent Relocation to Juneau Constitutes a Material Change in Circumstances.
A threshold showing of changed circumstances is required before a court may consider modifying a custody award. AS 25.20.110(a) provides that modification is appropriate when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification. Elena's permanent relocation from Anchorage to Juneau satisfies this threshold. The relocation is not a temporary disruption; it is a fundamental and enduring change to the factual foundation upon which the original 2021 custody order was premised. At the time the order was entered, both parents resided in Anchorage, and the children's day-to-day needs could be met in proximity to both parents. That premise no longer holds.
As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Barrett v. Alguire, 35 P.3d 1 (Alaska 2001), the relocation of a custodial parent is precisely the kind of material change in circumstances that warrants judicial reconsideration of a custody arrangement. Elena's acceptance of a permanent position 600 miles from the children's current home, school, and community is not a mere change in routine. It fundamentally alters the terms under which custody was originally awarded and demands that the Court reassess what arrangement will serve the children's best interests going forward.
B. Modification of Primary Physical Custody to Maria Is in the Best Interests of the Children.
Once a change in circumstances is established, the court must determine what modification, if any, is in the best interests of the children. AS 25.24.150(c) sets forth the factors the court must consider. When evaluated in light of the present circumstances, these factors weigh in favor of transferring primary physical custody to Maria.
1. Stability and Continuity of Environment
The most immediate consideration is the desirability of maintaining the stable environment the children currently enjoy. AS 25.24.150(c)(5) directs the court to consider the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment and the desirability of maintaining continuity. The children have lived in Anchorage throughout their lives. They attend school there, participate in extracurricular activities there, and maintain relationships with extended family there. Requiring the children to relocate 600 miles to Juneau would sever each of these connections simultaneously.
The Alaska Supreme Court examined this precise tension in Hayes v. Hayes, 922 P.2d 896 (Alaska 1996), where it acknowledged that continuity of geographic location and schooling is a legitimate concern, but held that other factors, including the strength of relationships and stability of parenting arrangements, can outweigh geographic continuity.
