IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0131)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Sutter, Petitioner, respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for a domestic violence protective order against Respondent Maria Sutter. The parties are married and have cohabited in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately four years. On October 3, 2024, Maria Sutter physically assaulted Elena Sutter by grabbing her by the throat and shoving her against a kitchen wall, leaving visible bruising on her neck. On October 17, 2024, Maria Sutter sent threatening text messages warning that she would "make Elena regret leaving" and that Elena should "watch her back." Since that date, Maria has appeared uninvited outside Elena's workplace on two separate occasions. Elena Sutter now resides at an undisclosed location with a friend and fears for her physical safety. She respectfully requests that this Court issue a protective order prohibiting all contact by Maria Sutter, establishing a 500-foot exclusion zone around her person and workplace, and requiring Maria Sutter to vacate the marital home.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena and Maria Sutter were married and have resided together at a shared residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately four years. Their relationship is governed by Alaska's domestic violence statutes as both parties are household members and spouses within the meaning of applicable Alaska law.
On October 3, 2024, during an argument about finances, Maria Sutter grabbed Elena Sutter by the throat and shoved her against a kitchen wall. The assault left visible bruising on Elena's neck. This physical assault constitutes a crime involving domestic violence as defined under Alaska law.
On October 17, 2024, Maria Sutter sent Elena Sutter a series of text messages stating that she would "make Elena regret leaving" and that Elena should "watch her back." These communications constitute threats of further harm and harassment.
Following the October 17, 2024 threats, Elena Sutter relocated from the marital home and is now residing temporarily with a friend at an undisclosed address for her personal safety. Despite Elena's efforts to distance herself from Maria, Maria has appeared uninvited outside Elena's workplace on two separate occasions since October 17, 2024. These appearances demonstrate a pattern of conduct that places Elena in reasonable fear for her physical safety.
Elena Sutter now petitions this Court for a protective order under AS 18.66.100 that: (1) prohibits Maria Sutter from contacting Elena by any means, directly or indirectly; (2) prohibits Maria Sutter from approaching within 500 feet of Elena's person or workplace; and (3) requires Maria Sutter to vacate the marital home so that Elena may safely return to her own residence.
Because Elena is appearing pro se in this proceeding, she has filed her mailing address and telephone number on a separate confidential form pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1, rather than including that information in this petition.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petition for a protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide at least 10 days' notice to the respondent. The statute provides that if the court finds by a preponderance of evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c).
Where immediate action is necessary, AS 18.66.110(a) authorizes the court to issue an ex parte protective order without notice to the respondent upon a finding of probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that it is necessary to protect the petitioner from domestic violence. An ex parte protective order issued under that provision expires 20 days after issuance unless dissolved earlier by the court.
A protective order may grant broad relief, including prohibiting the respondent from communicating with the petitioner directly or indirectly, removing and excluding the respondent from the petitioner's residence, directing the respondent to stay away from the petitioner's workplace, and ordering other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner. AS 18.66.100(c).
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts possess broad discretion in fashioning appropriate relief in domestic violence proceedings. Wee v. Eggener, 225 P.3d 1120 (Alaska 2010). Additionally, the court has confirmed that the protective provisions of AS 18.66.100(c)(1), prohibiting the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, remain effective until further order of the court, while other relief under AS 18.66.100(c)(2) through (16) is effective for one year unless earlier dissolved. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018).
Critically, AS 18.66.130(a) makes clear that any subsequent invitation by a petitioner to have contact with the respondent does not waive or nullify any provision in a protective order. Furthermore, under AS 18.66.130(e), a protective order issued under Alaska's domestic violence chapter is in addition to and not in place of any other civil or criminal remedy, and a petitioner is not barred from seeking relief because of the existence of another civil action between the parties.
A court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.100(e)(1).
Under Civil Rule 3(h), a petition for a protective order on domestic violence under AS 18.66 may be filed in the judicial district or the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. All three of those locations are in Anchorage, Alaska, making this Court the proper venue.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Elena Sutter Has Established Probable Cause and a Preponderance of Evidence That Maria Sutter Committed a Crime Involving Domestic Violence.
The physical assault of October 3, 2024, in which Maria Sutter grabbed Elena Sutter by the throat and shoved her against a kitchen wall, leaving visible bruising, constitutes a crime involving domestic violence as recognized under AS 18.66.100. The parties are spouses who share a household, satisfying the household member requirement for petitioning under AS 18.66.100(a). The visible bruising on Elena's neck corroborates the severity and reality of the physical assault.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that direct physical violence by one spouse against another, including grabbing and choking, constitutes domestic violence justifying the issuance of a protective order. Veronica Louise Hudson v. Daniel Lee Hudson, 532 P.3d 272 (Alaska 2023). In that case, the court affirmed that testimony regarding grabbing and being seized by the throat, combined with threats of physical violence, supported a finding of domestic violence. The facts presented here parallel those circumstances and support the issuance of the requested protective order.
The subsequent threatening text messages sent by Maria Sutter on October 17, 2024, stating that she would "make Elena regret leaving" and that Elena should "watch her back," constitute harassment and threatening conduct that compounds and continues the pattern of domestic violence. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that patterns of threatening behavior and harassment following physical assault are directly relevant to a court's protective order determination. Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010).
A court may not deny Elena's petition solely because of the lapse of time between the initial October 3, 2024 assault and the filing of this petition. AS 18.66.100(e)(1). Moreover, the threats made on October 17, 2024, and Maria's subsequent uninvited appearances outside Elena's workplace are ongoing acts that independently support the requested relief and demonstrate the continuing nature of the danger Elena faces.
B. The Requested Protective Relief Is Authorized and Appropriate Under AS 18.66.100(c).
Elena Sutter requests three principal forms of relief, each of which is expressly authorized by AS 18.66.100(c).
First, Elena requests that this Court prohibit Maria Sutter from contacting her by any means, directly or indirectly. This relief is authorized under AS 18.66.100(c)(2), which provides that a protective order may "prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner." The threatening text messages of October 17, 2024, demonstrate that Maria Sutter has used electronic communication to threaten and harass Elena, making this prohibition both necessary and appropriate.
Second, Elena requests that this Court prohibit Maria Sutter from approaching within 500 feet of her person or her workplace. This relief is authorized under AS 18.66.100(c)(4), which provides that a protective order may "direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member." Maria Sutter's two uninvited appearances outside Elena's workplace since the October 17, 2024 threats demonstrate that this restriction is essential to Elena's safety. The Alaska Supreme Court has noted that courts must consider the full course of a respondent's behavior in assessing the need for protective relief. Yelena R. v. George R., 326 P.3d 989 (Alaska 2014). Maria's deliberate appearances at Elena's workplace following her explicit threats establish that a stay-away restriction is not only justified but necessary.
Third, Elena requests that this Court order Maria Sutter to vacate the marital residence so that Elena may safely return. This relief is authorized under AS 18.66.100(c)(3), which provides that a protective order may "remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence." The marital home is Elena's residence as well as Maria's. Elena has been forced to flee her own home and seek refuge with a friend at an undisclosed location due solely to Maria's violent and threatening conduct. Requiring Maria to vacate is the appropriate remedy to restore Elena to her home.
Importantly, even if Maria attempts to invite Elena to make contact or to return to the shared residence, that invitation does not invalidate any provision of the protective order. AS 18.66.130(a). This Court should therefore issue the order without concern that any subsequent conduct by Elena could nullify its terms.
The court should further note that AS 18.66.130(b) expressly prohibits a court from granting protective orders against both the petitioner and the respondent in the same action under that chapter. Accordingly, any attempt by Maria Sutter to seek a cross-order in this proceeding would be improper.
C. Elena Sutter Is Entitled to Confidentiality of Her Address Information Pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1.
Because Elena Sutter is appearing pro se and is a victim of domestic violence seeking a protective order under AS 18.66.100, she is entitled to submit her mailing address and telephone number on a separate confidential form and to omit that information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. Civil Rule 65.1. Access to the form containing that information is limited to the court, authorized court system personnel, and Elena herself. This protection is critical given that Maria Sutter has already appeared uninvited at Elena's workplace and Elena fears that disclosure of her current temporary address could allow Maria to locate and harm her.
D. The Spousal Relationship Does Not Bar This Action or Impede the Court's Consideration of the Evidence.
Because this is a civil proceeding brought by one spouse against the other, the spousal immunity privilege does not preclude Elena's testimony regarding Maria's conduct. Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(A) provides that there is no spousal immunity privilege in "a civil proceeding brought by or on behalf of one spouse against the other spouse." Furthermore, Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(D)(v) provides that there is no privilege in a proceeding in which one spouse is charged with a crime involving domestic violence as defined in AS 18.66.990.
Similarly, no privilege bars the consideration of communications between the spouses regarding the conduct at issue. Alaska R. Evid. 505(b)(2)(B) provides that there is no privilege for confidential marital communications if "the communication was made, in whole or in part, to enable or aid anyone to commit or plan to commit a crime or a fraud." To the extent Maria Sutter's threatening text messages constitute communications made in furtherance of threatened criminal conduct, no marital communications privilege protects them from consideration by this Court.
E. The Standing Injunction Under Civil Rule 65(e) Provides Additional Support for Restraining Maria Sutter's Conduct.
In domestic relations actions, the presiding judge of each judicial district may issue a standing injunction restraining the parties from threatening, harassing, or harming the other party. Civil Rule 65(e)(3). The physical assault, threatening text messages, and uninvited appearances at Elena's workplace by Maria Sutter constitute exactly the type of threatening, harassing, and harmful conduct that such a standing injunction is designed to prevent. The requested protective order is consistent with and reinforced by the policy underlying Civil Rule 65(e).
F. The Court Should Issue Necessary Relief to Protect Elena's Safety.
AS 18.66.100(c)(16) authorizes the court to "order other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member." To the extent that any additional measures beyond those specifically requested are warranted by the evidence presented, this Court possesses full authority to impose them. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized the broad discretion available to courts in fashioning protective order relief in domestic violence cases. Wee v. Eggener, 225 P.3d 1120 (Alaska 2010); Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015).
The totality of the circumstances, including the physical assault, the subsequent explicit threats, and the deliberate appearances at Elena's workplace, establishes that immediate and comprehensive protective relief is warranted.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Elena Sutter respectfully requests that this Court issue a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 providing the following relief:
1. Prohibiting Maria Sutter from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence against Elena Sutter, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(1), effective until further order of this Court;
2. Prohibiting Maria Sutter from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with Elena Sutter, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(2);
3. Removing and excluding Maria Sutter from the marital residence, regardless of ownership, so that Elena Sutter may safely return, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3);
4. Directing Maria Sutter to stay away from Elena Sutter's person and her place of employment, and prohibiting Maria from approaching within 500 feet of either, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4); and
5. Ordering any other relief this Court determines necessary to protect Elena Sutter, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).
Elena Sutter further requests that the Court maintain the confidentiality of her address information pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1 and AS 18.66.110, and that it grant any ex parte emergency relief available under AS 18.66.110(a) pending the full hearing on this matter.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0132)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Tomas Okafor respectfully requests that this Court issue a long-term domestic violence protective order against Respondent Colin Okafor pursuant to AS 18.66.915. The record establishes that Colin Okafor committed multiple acts of domestic violence against Tomas Okafor, including a physical assault causing documented injury and a pattern of threatening and intimidating conduct at Tomas Okafor's place of employment. The requested order would prohibit Colin Okafor from contacting Tomas Okafor in any manner, require Colin Okafor to vacate the shared marital residence, and prohibit Colin Okafor from coming within 500 feet of Tomas Okafor's home, workplace, and vehicle. The evidence satisfies the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard required for issuance of a long-term protective order, and the relief requested is necessary to protect Tomas Okafor's physical safety and well-being.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Okafor and Colin Okafor are married and reside together at a shared residence in Anchorage, Alaska. The parties have been subject to escalating incidents of physical violence and threatening conduct, the most recent of which are described below.
On March 4, 2024, during an argument over finances, Colin Okafor grabbed Tomas Okafor by the throat, shoved him forcefully into the kitchen counter, and then threatened to "make him regret it" if Tomas disclosed what had happened. As a direct result of this assault, Tomas Okafor sustained visible bruising to his neck and back. These injuries were documented the following day, March 5, 2024, when a friend photographed the bruising. Those photographs constitute physical evidence corroborating Tomas Okafor's account of the assault.
On March 11, 2024, Colin Okafor appeared uninvited at Tomas Okafor's workplace and remained standing outside the entrance for approximately two hours. During this time, Colin Okafor sent Tomas Okafor a series of text messages stating that he was "watching" and that Tomas "would not be safe" if he attempted to leave the marriage. This conduct was calculated to intimidate Tomas Okafor, to surveil him at his place of employment, and to threaten him with further harm should he seek to exercise his legal right to end the marriage.
Taken together, these incidents reflect a pattern of domestic violence and threatening conduct that places Tomas Okafor in reasonable fear for his physical safety. The March 4 assault and the March 11 threatening conduct are separate and distinct events occurring within a single week, establishing a pattern of abuse rather than an isolated incident.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), after a properly noticed hearing, a court may issue a long-term protective order if it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner. This standard applies regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must consider the totality of the circumstances when evaluating domestic violence claims, including both physical acts of violence and threatening or intimidating conduct. Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007); Parks v. Parks, 214 P.3d 295 (Alaska 2009). A petition for a protective order may not be denied solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.100(e)(1). Furthermore, violations of a prior protective order may themselves constitute additional acts of domestic violence. Parks v. Parks, 214 P.3d 295 (Alaska 2009).
Where multiple incidents of threatening and physically harmful conduct occur in close temporal proximity, the Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that such a pattern is relevant to the court's assessment of the petitioner's need for protection. Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010); Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018). Importantly, under AS 18.66.130(a), an invitation by the petitioner to have contact does not waive or nullify any provision of a protective order once issued, ensuring that the order's protections are not undermined by subsequent communications.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also held that a court may not deny a protective order petition solely because a prior petition was filed or a prior order was in effect if the petitioner alleges changed circumstances. AS 18.66.100(e)(3). The evidence in this matter establishes independent, recent acts of domestic violence sufficient to satisfy the preponderance standard under AS 18.66.100(b).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Colin Okafor Has Committed Acts of Domestic Violence Against Tomas Okafor Within the Meaning of AS 18.66.100, and the Preponderance of the Evidence Supports Issuance of a Long-Term Protective Order.
The evidence before the Court establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that Colin Okafor has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Tomas Okafor. AS 18.66.100(b) authorizes the Court to issue a long-term protective order upon such a finding. The March 4, 2024 incident, in which Colin Okafor grabbed Tomas Okafor by the throat, shoved him into the kitchen counter, and issued a direct threat of retaliation, constitutes physical domestic violence. The bruising documented photographically the following day provides objective corroboration of that assault. Threats made in the immediate aftermath of physical violence, particularly threats designed to deter the victim from seeking help, are part of the same act of domestic violence and heighten the danger to the petitioner.
The March 11, 2024 incident at Tomas Okafor's workplace constitutes a separate and additional act of threatening conduct. Colin Okafor's presence at the workplace entrance for approximately two hours, combined with text messages stating that he was "watching" and that Tomas "would not be safe" if he attempted to leave the marriage, constitute both harassment and criminal threatening. Conduct of this nature goes beyond mere argument and rises to the level of conduct that the protective order statute is designed to prevent. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that stalking and threatening behavior are properly considered in evaluating the totality of domestic violence conduct. Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010).
These two incidents, occurring within seven days of each other, establish not merely an isolated dispute but a pattern of conduct designed to control, intimidate, and harm Tomas Okafor. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized the importance of evaluating domestic violence in context, taking into account both physical assaults and surrounding threatening behavior. Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007); Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020).
B. The Court Has Authority to Grant Each Element of the Requested Relief Under AS 18.66.100(c).
Tomas Okafor requests three specific forms of relief, each of which is expressly authorized by AS 18.66.100(c).
First, Tomas Okafor requests that the Court prohibit Colin Okafor from contacting him in any manner, whether directly or indirectly. This relief is authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(1), which permits the Court to prohibit the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment, and by AS 18.66.100(c)(2), which permits the Court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner. The March 11 text messages, in which Colin Okafor threatened Tomas Okafor's safety, demonstrate that Colin Okafor will use communications as a vehicle for continued intimidation and harassment. Prohibiting all contact is necessary to prevent further harm.
Second, Tomas Okafor requests that the Court require Colin Okafor to vacate the shared marital residence. This relief is authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(3), which permits the Court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. The fact that both parties currently share the residence does not limit the Court's authority to issue such an order. Because the March 4 assault occurred within the home, and because Colin Okafor has demonstrated a willingness to use physical violence during domestic arguments, continued cohabitation poses an ongoing and serious risk to Tomas Okafor's physical safety.
Third, Tomas Okafor requests that the Court prohibit Colin Okafor from coming within 500 feet of Tomas Okafor's home, workplace, and vehicle. This relief is authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(4), which permits the Court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member, and by AS 18.66.100(c)(5), which permits the Court to prohibit the respondent from entering a propelled vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the petitioner. The March 11 incident, in which Colin Okafor stationed himself outside Tomas Okafor's workplace for two hours, demonstrates precisely the kind of conduct this provision is designed to prevent. A 500-foot exclusion zone provides a meaningful buffer and enables law enforcement to respond effectively to any violation.
C. The Court Should Award Additional Relief Necessary to Protect Tomas Okafor, Including Possession of the Shared Vehicle and Any Other Relief the Court Deems Appropriate.
AS 18.66.100(c)(10) authorizes the Court to give the petitioner possession and use of a vehicle and other essential personal items, regardless of ownership. Given that the parties share a residence and marital property, and given Colin Okafor's pattern of controlling behavior, the Court should consider awarding Tomas Okafor temporary possession of any shared vehicle necessary for his transportation to and from work. Additionally, AS 18.66.100(c)(16) authorizes the Court to order other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member. Tomas Okafor respectfully requests that the Court exercise this broad authority to craft any additional relief necessary to secure his safety.
D. Mediation Is Not Appropriate in This Matter and May Not Be Ordered by the Court.
Should the question of mediation arise, the Court is prohibited from ordering or referring the parties to mediation while a protective order is in effect in this matter. AS 25.24.060(f) expressly provides that a court may not order or refer parties to mediation in a divorce proceeding if a protective order issued or filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180 is in effect. Similarly, AS 18.66.130(c) states that a court may not order parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of the issues arising from a petition for a protective order under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. Mediation is structurally inappropriate in cases involving domestic violence because it places the victim and perpetrator in a setting requiring negotiation and compromise, which can expose the victim to further intimidation and harm. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the danger of exposing domestic violence victims to further contact with their abusers through dispute resolution processes. Fidler v. Fidler, 296 P.3d 11 (Alaska 2013).
E. Tomas Okafor's Address and Contact Information Are Protected Under Civil Rule 65.1.
Because Tomas Okafor is appearing pro se in this protective order proceeding, he is entitled to submit his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and to omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court, pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1. Access to this information is limited to the court, authorized court system personnel, and the petitioner. This protection is critical in the present matter, given Colin Okafor's demonstrated willingness to appear at Tomas Okafor's place of employment unannounced and to send threatening messages. Disclosure of Tomas Okafor's contact information through publicly accessible court filings could enable further threatening conduct and undermine the purpose of the requested protective order.
F. The Pendency of a Divorce or Separation Proceeding Does Not Limit the Court's Authority to Issue a Protective Order, and Tomas Okafor's Rights as a Spouse Are Preserved.
During the pendency of any related divorce proceeding, Tomas Okafor is entitled to apply for protective orders as a matter of statutory right. AS 25.24.140(b) provides that, during the pendency of a divorce action, a spouse is entitled to necessary protective orders, including orders providing for the freedom of each spouse from the control of the other spouse, orders for protection under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180, orders directing one spouse to vacate the marital residence or the home of the other spouse, and orders restraining a spouse from communicating directly or indirectly with the other spouse. These statutory protections apply independently of and in addition to the protections available under AS 18.66.100.
Furthermore, AS 18.66.130(e) confirms that a protective order issued under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180 is in addition to and not in place of any other civil or criminal remedy, and that a petitioner is not barred from seeking a protective order because of the existence of another civil action between the petitioner and respondent. Accordingly, the pendency of any divorce proceedings between the parties does not in any way limit Tomas Okafor's entitlement to the relief requested herein.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized the importance of providing full protection to spouses who are victims of domestic violence during the dissolution process, noting that domestic violence can intensify when a victim attempts to leave a marriage. Corbeau v. Dietrich, 505 P.3d 611 (Alaska 2023). The March 11 text messages, in which Colin Okafor explicitly threatened that Tomas "would not be safe" if he attempted to leave the marriage, are precisely the type of conduct identified in Hudson as a basis for heightened concern and protective intervention.
G. The Standing Preliminary Injunction Under Civil Rule 903(e) Independently Prohibits Colin Okafor From Threatening, Harassing, or Harming Tomas Okafor.
Civil Rule 65(e) authorizes the presiding judge of each judicial district to issue a standing injunction in all domestic relations actions restraining the parties from, among other things, threatening, harassing, or harming the other party. This standing injunction operates independently of and in addition to the relief available under AS 18.66.100. The conduct described in this brief, specifically the March 4 physical assault and the March 11 threatening messages and workplace surveillance, constitutes exactly the type of threatening and harassing conduct that the standing injunction is designed to prevent. Colin Okafor's conduct has already violated the spirit of these protections, and formal issuance of the requested long-term protective order will provide enforceable legal mechanisms to address any future violations.
V. CONCLUSION
The evidence in this matter establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that Colin Okafor has committed multiple acts of domestic violence against Tomas Okafor, including a physical assault causing documented injury and a pattern of threatening and intimidating conduct. Each form of relief requested, namely a no-contact order, an order requiring Colin Okafor to vacate the shared marital residence, and a 500-foot exclusion zone around Tomas Okafor's home, workplace, and vehicle, is expressly authorized by AS 18.66.100(c) and is necessary to protect Tomas Okafor's physical safety and well-being.
Tomas Okafor therefore respectfully requests that the Court:
1. Issue a long-term domestic violence protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.100 prohibiting Colin Okafor from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment against Tomas Okafor;
2. Prohibit Colin Okafor from contacting Tomas Okafor directly or indirectly by any means, including telephone, text message, electronic communication, or communication through third parties;
3. Order Colin Okafor to vacate the shared marital residence immediately and exclude him from returning to that residence;
4. Prohibit Colin Okafor from coming within 500 feet of Tomas Okafor's residence, place of employment, and any vehicle in Tomas Okafor's possession or occupied by him;
5. Award Tomas Okafor possession of any shared vehicle and essential personal items necessary for his safety and independence; and
6. Grant such other and further relief as the Court determines is necessary to protect Tomas Okafor pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).

Alaska law authorizes a victim of a crime involving domestic violence to petition the district or superior court for a protective order against a household member. AS 18.66.100(a). IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0134)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Petrova ("Petitioner") respectfully petitions this Court for a domestic violence protective order against his wife, Sarah Petrova ("Respondent"). The Respondent physically assaulted the Petitioner on March 3, 2025, and subsequently threatened him on March 17, 2025, both in writing and in person at his place of employment. These acts constitute crimes involving domestic violence as defined under Alaska law, and the Petitioner requires immediate court protection to ensure his safety. The Petitioner seeks a protective order requiring the Respondent to vacate their shared Anchorage residence, prohibiting all forms of contact, and barring the Respondent from coming within 500 feet of the Petitioner's home, workplace, and vehicle.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus and Sarah Petrova are married and have lived together at a shared residence in Anchorage, Alaska, for approximately six years. They are household members within the meaning of applicable Alaska law.
On March 3, 2025, following a dispute about finances, the Respondent grabbed the Petitioner by the collar, shoved him forcefully into a kitchen cabinet, and struck him twice in the face with an open hand. The assault left visible bruising near the Petitioner's left eye. This physical attack occurred within the shared marital residence.
Approximately two weeks later, on March 17, 2025, the Respondent sent the Petitioner a series of text messages warning that if he attempted to leave the marriage or contact an attorney, she would "make sure he regretted it." Later that same day, the Respondent appeared unannounced outside the Petitioner's workplace and screamed threats in the parking lot in front of his coworkers. This conduct constitutes both threatening communications and a threatening public confrontation at the Petitioner's place of employment.
The Petitioner now seeks a protective order excluding the Respondent from the shared residence, prohibiting all direct and indirect contact, and requiring the Respondent to stay at least 500 feet away from his home, workplace, and vehicle. The Petitioner is a pro se litigant and has submitted his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form in accordance with applicable court rules, omitting that information from this pleading.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petition for a protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide at least 10 days' notice to the respondent. If the court finds by a preponderance of evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.977, regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
The term "domestic violence" and "crime involving domestic violence" are defined under AS 18.66.964 to include offenses under AS 11.41, which encompasses crimes against the person, committed by a household member against another household member. The term "household member" is defined under AS 18.66.990(5) to include, among others, adults who are current or former spouses and adults who live together or who have lived together.
Under AS 18.66.926, a petitioner who is a victim of a crime involving domestic violence may request an ex parte protective order. If the court finds that the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that it is necessary to protect the petitioner, the court shall issue a protective order ex parte and without notice to the respondent. An ex parte order may grant the protections provided by AS 18.66.100(c)(1) through (5), (8) through (12), and (16).
Additionally, AS 18.66.130(e) provides that a protective order issued under this chapter is in addition to and not in place of any other civil or criminal remedy, and a petitioner is not barred from seeking an order because of the existence of another civil action between the petitioner and the respondent.
Regarding venue, Civil Rule 3(h) permits a petition for a protective order based on domestic violence under AS 18.66 to be filed in either the judicial district or the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. Because both parties reside in Anchorage and the acts of domestic violence occurred in Anchorage, venue is proper in this Court.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. The Respondent Is a Household Member Whose Conduct Constitutes Domestic Violence Under Alaska Law.
The threshold requirement for a protective order under AS 18.66.100 is that the respondent must be a household member who has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner. Both elements are plainly satisfied here.
First, the Respondent qualifies as a household member. AS 18.66.990(5) defines "household member" to include "adults or minors who are current or former spouses" and "adults or minors who live together or who have lived together." Sarah Petrova is the Petitioner's current spouse, and the parties have lived together in Anchorage for approximately six years. There is no question that the Respondent is a household member under this definition.
Second, the Respondent's conduct constitutes a crime involving domestic violence. AS 18.66.990(3) defines "domestic violence" to mean, in relevant part, a crime against the person under AS 11.41, committed by a household member against another household member. On March 3, 2025, the Respondent grabbed the Petitioner by the collar, shoved him into a kitchen cabinet, and struck him twice in the face, causing visible bruising. This conduct constitutes assault, a crime against the person under AS 11.41, committed by a household member. The visible bruising near the Petitioner's left eye provides physical evidence corroborating that this assault resulted in bodily injury.
Furthermore, the Respondent's March 17, 2025 conduct, including threatening text messages and a threatening confrontation at the Petitioner's workplace, also falls within the scope of AS 18.66.990(3), which includes terrorist threatening and harassment offenses under AS 11.56 and AS 11.61 within the definition of domestic violence when committed by a household member. Statements that the Petitioner would "regret" seeking to leave the marriage or contact an attorney, combined with an unannounced appearance at his workplace to scream threats in front of coworkers, constitute threatening conduct designed to intimidate and coerce.
The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), confirms that courts will examine a pattern of conduct over time when evaluating domestic violence, including both physical acts and threatening communications. Similarly, in Veronica Louise Hudson v. Daniel Lee Hudson, 532 P.3d 272 (Alaska 2023), the Alaska Supreme Court acknowledged that a party's fear of domestic violence retaliation, based on prior threats and incidents, is a legitimate consideration in the context of proceedings involving household members. The pattern of conduct here, physical assault followed by threatening communications and a workplace confrontation, establishes the type of ongoing danger that the domestic violence protective order statutes are designed to address.
B. The Court Has Authority to Grant All of the Protective Relief the Petitioner Seeks.
The Petitioner seeks three categories of relief: (1) exclusion of the Respondent from the shared residence, (2) prohibition on all forms of contact, and (3) a 500-foot stay-away requirement covering his home, workplace, and vehicle. Each form of requested relief is expressly authorized under AS 18.66.100(c).
With respect to exclusion from the residence, AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to "remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence." This provision permits the court to order the Respondent to vacate the shared Anchorage home even though both parties have resided there. The Petitioner should not be required to leave his own home as a result of the Respondent's violent and threatening behavior.
With respect to the prohibition on contact, AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the court to "prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner." The Respondent's threatening text messages of March 17, 2025, demonstrate that electronic and written contact poses a real and ongoing risk to the Petitioner. A no-contact provision is both appropriate and necessary.
With respect to the stay-away requirement, AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to "direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member." The Respondent's unannounced appearance at the Petitioner's workplace on March 17, 2025, to scream threats in front of coworkers makes clear that such a provision is essential. Additionally, AS 18.66.100(c)(5) authorizes the court to "prohibit the respondent from entering a propelled vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the petitioner," providing a further basis for the vehicle-related protection sought.
Under AS 18.66.100(c)(16), the court may also "order other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member," providing a broad catchall authority to fashion any additional protective terms warranted by the specific circumstances presented here.
The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), addressed the duration and scope of protective orders under AS 18.66.100(c), confirming that the provisions available under subsections (c)(2) through (16) are effective for one year unless earlier dissolved by court order. While the Petitioner has requested a 90-day protective order, the Court is authorized to issue relief for up to one year under the statute, and the Court should tailor the duration as necessary to protect the Petitioner in light of the severity and recency of the Respondent's conduct.
C. A Lapse of Time Between Acts of Domestic Violence and Filing of This Petition Does Not Bar Relief.
The Petitioner is aware that some time has passed between the March 3, 2025 assault and the filing of this petition. Under AS 18.66.100(e), "a court may not deny a petition for a protective order under this section solely because there is a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition." The Petitioner's delay in filing does not undermine the validity or urgency of his request. The Respondent's conduct on March 17, 2025, including both written threats and a workplace confrontation, demonstrates that the danger to the Petitioner is ongoing and not merely historical.
D. The Respondent's Invitation or Contact Cannot Nullify the Protective Order Once Issued.
The Petitioner wishes to ensure that this Court and all parties understand that any future contact initiated by the Respondent will not operate to waive or nullify the terms of the protective order. AS 18.66.130(a) provides that if a respondent is prohibited from communicating with the petitioner or ordered to stay away from the petitioner, "an invitation by the petitioner to communicate, enter the residence or vehicle, or have other prohibited contact with the petitioner does not waive or nullify any provision in a protective order." This provision ensures that the Respondent remains bound by the terms of any order issued, regardless of any subsequent interactions between the parties.
E. The Petitioner as a Pro Se Litigant Is Entitled to Address Confidentiality Protections.
Civil Rule 65.1 provides that a petitioner who is appearing pro se in a proceeding to obtain a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 or 18.66.110 may submit the petitioner's mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. The Petitioner has availed himself of this protection. Given the Respondent's pattern of appearing unannounced at locations associated with the Petitioner, this address confidentiality measure is not merely procedural but a meaningful safeguard for the Petitioner's safety during the pendency of this action.
F. Spousal Privilege Does Not Bar Consideration of the Respondent's Threatening Communications.
The Petitioner acknowledges that the parties are currently married and anticipates that questions regarding spousal privilege may arise in connection with the threatening text messages sent by the Respondent on March 17, 2025. However, the evidentiary privileges associated with spousal communications do not shield the Respondent's conduct from consideration here.
Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(D)(v) provides that there is no spousal immunity privilege in a proceeding involving "a crime involving domestic violence as defined in AS 18.66.990 under all circumstances." Because this proceeding arises directly from crimes involving domestic violence, the Respondent may not invoke spousal immunity to prevent the Petitioner from testifying about her conduct.
Similarly, Alaska R. Evid. 505(b)(2)(A) provides that the confidential marital communications privilege does not apply if any of the exceptions under subdivision (a)(2) of that rule apply. Because the exception for domestic violence proceedings under Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(D)(v) applies here, the confidential communications privilege likewise does not shield the Respondent's threatening text messages from evidence. These messages were not private marital communications made in confidence; they were explicit threats transmitted for the purpose of intimidating the Petitioner and preventing him from exercising his legal rights.
V. CONCLUSION
The record before this Court establishes, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Sarah Petrova has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Marcus Petrova, a household member, through a physical assault on March 3, 2025, and through threatening communications and a threatening public confrontation on March 17, 2025. The Petitioner is entitled to the full range of protective relief he seeks under AS 18.66.100(c).
The Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Issue a protective order under AS 18.66.100 requiring the Respondent to vacate and remain excluded from the shared Anchorage residence, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3);
2. Prohibit the Respondent from contacting the Petitioner directly or indirectly, by telephone, text, electronic means, or in person, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(2);
3. Direct the Respondent to remain at least 500 feet away from the Petitioner's residence, place of employment, and vehicle, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4) and (c)(5); and
4. Order any additional relief the Court deems necessary to protect the Petitioner's safety and well-being, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).
The Petitioner further requests that if this Court determines that the foregoing showing establishes probable cause, an ex parte protective order be issued immediately under AS 18.66.110(a) pending the noticed hearing, to protect the Petitioner from further acts of domestic violence during the intervening period.
