IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0145)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Colby respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for a domestic violence protective order against Respondent Maria Colby. Priya and Maria are married spouses who have shared a residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately four years. On October 3, 2024, Maria physically assaulted Priya by grabbing her by the throat, shoving her into a kitchen counter, and threatening to prevent her from leaving the home. Less than one week later, on October 9, 2024, Maria appeared uninvited at Priya's place of employment, screamed threats in the parking lot, and warned Priya that she would "regret it" if she contacted police. These acts constitute crimes involving domestic violence within the meaning of Alaska law, and Priya is entitled to immediate protective relief. She seeks a protective order requiring Maria to vacate the shared Anchorage residence, prohibiting Maria from contacting Priya at home or at her workplace, and granting Priya temporary use of the marital vehicle necessary for her continued employment.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Colby and Maria Colby are married and have resided together at a shared residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately four years. As spouses who reside together, Maria is a household member of Priya within the meaning of AS 18.66.990(5)(A) and (5)(B).
On October 3, 2024, during an argument over finances, Maria grabbed Priya by the throat and shoved her into the kitchen counter. Maria then threatened to "make sure she never left the house again." This conduct constitutes a crime against the person under AS 11.41, which is expressly enumerated as a crime involving domestic violence under AS 18.66.990(3)(A). The threatening statement also constitutes threatening conduct directed at a household member.
On October 9, 2024, Maria escalated her course of threatening behavior by appearing uninvited at Priya's place of employment. Maria screamed threats at Priya in the workplace parking lot and warned Priya that she would "regret it" if she contacted police. This conduct constitutes additional threatening and harassing acts directed at Priya, and Maria's specific warning against involving law enforcement further demonstrates her intent to prevent Priya from seeking protection.
As a result of Maria's conduct, Priya fears for her physical safety at the shared residence and at her workplace. Priya requires the use of the marital vehicle to travel to and from work. Priya now seeks the protection of this Court through a domestic violence protective order.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(a), a person who is or has been a victim of a crime involving domestic violence may file a petition in the district or superior court for a protective order against a household member. The court must schedule a hearing and provide at least 10 days' notice to the respondent. Under AS 18.66.100(b), if the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.964, regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
AS 18.66.990(3)(A) defines "domestic violence" and "crime involving domestic violence" to include crimes against the person under AS 11.41 committed by a household member against another household member. AS 18.66.990(5)(A) and (5)(B) define "household member" to include current spouses and persons who live together or who have lived together.
In addition to the protective order provisions of AS 18.66.100, AS 25.24.140(b) independently authorizes the court, during the pendency of a divorce or related domestic relations action, to issue necessary protective orders including orders directing one spouse to vacate the marital residence and restraining a spouse from communicating directly or indirectly with the other spouse.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a protective order should be issued when the petitioner demonstrates by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent committed a qualifying act of domestic violence. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018). The court in Whalen confirmed that criminal trespass against a former spouse qualifies as a crime involving domestic violence and that AS 18.66.100 provides the statutory mechanism for obtaining relief in such circumstances. Courts have broad discretion in fashioning protective relief appropriate to the circumstances presented. Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015).
Under Civil Rule 933, a pro se petitioner in a proceeding to obtain a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 or AS 18.66.110 may submit her mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit that information from other pleadings filed with the court. Petitioner invokes this rule to protect her safety during the pendency of this matter.
Under Civil Rule 3(h), a petition for a protective order on domestic violence under AS 18.66 may be filed in the judicial district or the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. Because all three locations are in Anchorage, venue is proper before this Court.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Maria Colby Is a Household Member Who Has Committed Multiple Crimes Involving Domestic Violence Against Priya Colby.
Maria Colby is a household member of Priya Colby under AS 18.66.990(5)(A) because they are current spouses, and under AS 18.66.990(5)(B) because they reside together. Priya therefore has standing to petition for a protective order under AS 18.66.100(a).
The October 3, 2024 incident, during which Maria grabbed Priya by the throat and shoved her into a kitchen counter, constitutes a crime against the person under AS 11.41 committed by a household member. Physical assault by grabbing a person by the throat is an act of physical force directed at the body of another, squarely within the category of crimes against the person enumerated in AS 18.66.990(3)(A). Maria's accompanying threat, that she would "make sure she never left the house again," constitutes threatening conduct that independently supports a finding of domestic violence. As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), the preponderance standard governing protective order proceedings is satisfied when competent evidence establishes that a qualifying crime occurred.
The October 9, 2024 incident at Priya's workplace constitutes a second and independent act of domestic violence. Maria arrived uninvited at the location, screamed threats at Priya in a public parking lot, and specifically warned Priya against contacting police. This threatening conduct constitutes an additional crime involving domestic violence under AS 18.66.990(3)(A). Maria's attempt to discourage Priya from seeking law enforcement assistance further demonstrates her intent to maintain power and control over Priya through intimidation.
Taken together, these two incidents within six days establish a pattern of threatening and physically violent conduct that satisfies the preponderance standard. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts consider the overall course of a respondent's behavior when evaluating petitions for domestic violence protective orders. Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015). Furthermore, AS 18.66.100(e) expressly provides that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because there is a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition, reinforcing the legislature's intent that courts assess the full circumstances presented to them.
B. The Court Should Order Maria to Vacate the Shared Residence.
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. Maria's physical assault of Priya occurred within the shared Anchorage home, and Maria's continuing threat that Priya would never "leave the house" demonstrates that the home itself is a site of danger for Priya. Allowing Maria to remain in the shared residence would force Priya to choose between her safety and her home.
AS 25.24.140(b)(3) independently provides that during the pendency of a domestic relations action, upon application, a spouse is entitled to a protective order directing one spouse to vacate the marital residence or the home of the other spouse. This provision reinforces Priya's entitlement to exclusive occupancy of the shared residence during the pendency of these proceedings.
The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed that courts have broad discretion to fashion interim relief designed to protect a petitioner's safety and well-being. Thomas E. Jordan v. Cheryl A. Jordan, 480 P.3d 626 (Alaska 2021). Ordering Maria to vacate the residence is the appropriate measure here, as it addresses both the immediate danger Maria poses to Priya within the home and the longer-term need to provide Priya with a safe and stable environment.
C. The Court Should Prohibit Maria From Contacting Priya at Her Home or Workplace.
AS 18.66.100(c)(1) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner. AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member.
Maria's appearance at Priya's workplace on October 9, 2024, screaming threats and warning Priya against contacting police, demonstrates that Maria's threatening conduct is not confined to the shared home. Without a no-contact order that encompasses both the home and the workplace, Priya has no meaningful protection from further harassment, intimidation, or violence.
AS 18.66.130(a) provides that if a respondent is prohibited from communicating with the petitioner or ordered to stay away from the petitioner, any invitation by the petitioner to have otherwise prohibited contact does not waive or nullify any provision of the protective order. This provision ensures that a no-contact order will remain effective and enforceable regardless of any future interactions the parties might have.
Additionally, AS 25.24.140(b)(4) provides that during the pendency of a domestic relations action, upon application, a spouse is entitled to a protective order restraining a spouse from communicating directly or indirectly with the other spouse. This ground independently supports the relief requested.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that protective orders must be comprehensive enough to address the specific patterns of threatening conduct at issue. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018). Because Maria has already demonstrated her willingness to follow Priya to her workplace and threaten her there, a no-contact and stay-away order covering both locations is necessary and appropriate.
D. The Court Should Grant Priya Temporary Use of the Marital Vehicle.
AS 18.66.100(c)(10) authorizes the court to give the petitioner possession and use of a vehicle and other essential personal items, regardless of ownership of those items. Priya requires the use of the marital vehicle for her employment. Without access to this vehicle, Priya's ability to remain employed and financially independent would be jeopardized, further compounding the harm caused by Maria's violent and threatening conduct.
AS 25.24.140(b) reinforces the court's authority to issue protective orders necessary to safeguard a spouse's safety, autonomy, and basic needs during the pendency of a domestic relations action. Providing Priya with temporary use of the marital vehicle falls squarely within this authority, as it enables Priya to maintain her employment and thereby her independence from Maria.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts fashioning domestic violence protective relief should consider the practical needs of the petitioner, including access to resources necessary for self-sufficiency. Thomas E. Jordan v. Cheryl A. Jordan, 480 P.3d 626 (Alaska 2021). Granting Priya temporary use of the marital vehicle is a measured and proportionate remedy that addresses a concrete and immediate need.
E. The Protective Order May Not Be Issued Against Priya as a Mutual Order.
Under AS 18.66.130(b), a court may not grant protective orders against the petitioner and the respondent in the same action under the domestic violence chapter. The Alaska Supreme Court in Cooper v. Cooper, 144 P.3d 451 (Alaska 2006) held that mutual restraining orders are disfavored in domestic violence cases when only one partner has committed acts of domestic violence, and that this principle extends to divorce litigation. See also Wee v. Eggener, 225 P.3d 1120 (Alaska 2010) (affirming that a domestic violence protective order may not be entered against the petitioner and confirming the independent-basis requirement for any restraining order against the non-offending party). The evidence here establishes that Maria is the perpetrator of domestic violence against Priya. The Court may not issue a mutual protective order in this proceeding.
F. Petitioner's Filing of This Petition Is Proper, and Her Location Information Is Protected.
As noted in Section III, Civil Rule 3(h) permits Priya to file her petition in the court location closest to her current residence, the respondent's residence, or the location where the domestic violence occurred. All three locations are in Anchorage, making this Court the proper venue.
Pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1, because Priya is appearing pro se, she may submit her mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. Access to that form is limited to the court, authorized court system personnel, and the petitioner. Given Maria's history of appearing uninvited at Priya's locations and threatening her against contacting police, protection of Priya's location information is critical to her safety.
V. CONCLUSION
For the reasons set forth above, Priya Colby respectfully requests that this Court enter a domestic violence protective order:
1. Finding by a preponderance of the evidence that Maria Colby has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Priya Colby, as defined under AS 18.66.990(3) and AS 18.66.100;
2. Ordering Maria Colby to vacate and remain excluded from the shared Anchorage residence pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3);
3. Prohibiting Maria Colby from threatening, contacting, or communicating with Priya Colby directly or indirectly, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(1) and AS 18.66.100(c)(2);
4. Directing Maria Colby to stay away from Priya Colby's residence and place of employment pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4);
5. Granting Priya Colby temporary possession and use of the marital vehicle necessary for her employment pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(10); and
6. Granting such other and further relief as the Court deems necessary to protect Priya Colby's safety and well-being pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).

Petitioner Priya Bergstrom respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for a long-term domestic violence protective order against Respondent Michael Bergstrom pursuant to AS 18.66.944. The Court should issue a protective order prohibiting Michael Bergstrom from contacting Priya Bergstrom in any form, excluding him from the shared residence, and requiring him to remain at least 500 feet from her home, workplace, and vehicle.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Bergstrom and Michael Bergstrom are married and have resided together at a shared residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately seven years. On March 4, 2025, during an argument over household finances, Michael Bergstrom grabbed Priya Bergstrom by the throat, shoved her forcibly against the kitchen wall, and stated that he would "make sure she never left him alive." This physical attack caused visible bruising to Priya Bergstrom's neck and arms. The incident occurred within the shared marital home.

He blocked her vehicle in the parking lot, preventing her from leaving, and screamed at her that she would regret contacting her sister for assistance. This conduct left Priya Bergstrom in reasonable and well-founded fear for her physical safety.
Priya Bergstrom now petitions this Court for a protective order prohibiting Michael Bergstrom from contacting her in person, by telephone, or electronically; excluding him from the shared marital residence; and requiring him to maintain a distance of at least 500 feet from her home, workplace, and vehicle at all times.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.942, when a petition for a protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide at least ten days' notice to the respondent. If the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.920, regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
Alaska courts have interpreted the preponderance standard in this context to require that it be more likely than not that the domestic violence occurred. In Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the issuance of a long-term protective order based on a physical assault within the home, recognizing that the trial court had broad discretion in fashioning appropriate relief to protect the petitioner's safety.
Additionally, AS 18.66.100(e) provides that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because there is a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. This provision ensures that petitioners who require time to find safety before seeking court intervention are not penalized for that delay.
Under AS 18.66.110(a), where a petitioner demonstrates probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and certifies her efforts to provide notice to the respondent, the court may issue an ex parte protective order prior to the full hearing. Such an ex parte order may include the protections authorized under AS 18.66.100(c)(1) through (5), (8) through (12), and (16), and expires within 20 days unless dissolved earlier by the court.
Civil Rule 65(b) further provides that a temporary restraining order may be granted without notice to the adverse party when it clearly appears from specific facts shown by affidavit or by verified complaint that immediate and irreparable injury will result before the adverse party can be heard in opposition.
Pursuant to AS 18.66.130(a), any invitation by a petitioner to a respondent who is subject to a no-contact or stay-away provision does not waive or nullify any provision of a protective order. This rule protects petitioners from manipulation or coercion by respondents who might seek to characterize a petitioner's communication as a voluntary waiver of the order's protections.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PRIYA BERGSTROM HAS ESTABLISHED BY A PREPONDERANCE OF THE EVIDENCE THAT MICHAEL BERGSTROM COMMITTED CRIMES INVOLVING DOMESTIC VIOLENCE
The conduct Michael Bergstrom engaged in on March 4, 2025 and March 9, 2025 satisfies the preponderance standard under AS 18.66.100(b). Physical strangulation, forcible shoving, and a death threat constitute serious crimes involving domestic violence. The visible bruising to Priya Bergstrom's neck and arms is direct physical evidence of the assault. The subsequent workplace confrontation, during which Michael Bergstrom blocked Priya Bergstrom's vehicle and screamed threatening statements at her, constitutes additional criminal conduct demonstrating a continuing pattern of violence and intimidation.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), is instructive. In that case, the court affirmed a protective order based on an assault in which the respondent pushed and struck the petitioner. Here, Priya Bergstrom suffered an assault involving strangulation, which is an especially serious form of physical violence, combined with an explicit verbal death threat and a subsequent workplace confrontation that reinforced the threat and demonstrated Michael Bergstrom's willingness to pursue Priya Bergstrom outside the home. The totality of this conduct more than satisfies the preponderance standard.
The parties are married and lived together in the same residence, making Michael Bergstrom a household member within the meaning of the domestic violence statutes. The conduct therefore falls squarely within the scope of AS 18.66.100.
B. THE COURT SHOULD PROHIBIT ALL CONTACT BETWEEN MICHAEL BERGSTROM AND PRIYA BERGSTROM
AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner. The March 9, 2025 workplace incident demonstrates that Michael Bergstrom will seek out Priya Bergstrom in person when he believes she has sought outside help. His conduct in blocking her vehicle and making threatening statements shows that any contact, direct or indirect, poses a continuing danger to Priya Bergstrom's safety. A comprehensive no-contact provision covering in-person contact, telephone calls, and electronic communication is necessary and appropriate.
Furthermore, AS 18.66.130(a) clarifies that even if Priya Bergstrom were to initiate communication with Michael Bergstrom for any reason, such contact would not waive or nullify the protective order's provisions. This protection is especially important in cases involving spouses, where a respondent may attempt to exploit a petitioner's communication as a pretext for claiming the order is no longer operative.
In State v. Strane, 61 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2003), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that protective order provisions prohibiting contact with the petitioner are legally cognizable and enforceable under Alaska law, and that knowing violations of such provisions constitute criminal conduct. The issuance of a comprehensive no-contact order here is therefore both legally authorized and practically necessary.
C. THE COURT SHOULD EXCLUDE MICHAEL BERGSTROM FROM THE SHARED RESIDENCE
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. Priya Bergstrom has resided at the shared Anchorage home for seven years. The violent assault on March 4, 2025 occurred within that residence. She cannot be expected to return to or remain in safety at a residence she shares with a person who has physically attacked her and threatened her life there.
The fact that Michael Bergstrom may share ownership or tenancy of the residence does not bar exclusion under this provision. The statute expressly states that exclusion is available regardless of ownership, recognizing that a victim's safety must take precedence over a respondent's property interest when domestic violence has occurred.
D. THE COURT SHOULD REQUIRE MICHAEL BERGSTROM TO MAINTAIN A DISTANCE OF AT LEAST 500 FEET FROM PRIYA BERGSTROM'S HOME, WORKPLACE, AND VEHICLE
AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member. AS 18.66.100(c)(5) further authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from entering a propelled vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the petitioner under all circumstances.
The March 9, 2025 incident at Priya Bergstrom's workplace demonstrates that Michael Bergstrom is willing and able to appear at her place of employment to confront and intimidate her. By blocking her vehicle in the parking lot, he also prevented her escape and exercised physical control over her movements. A 500-foot distance requirement from her home, workplace, and vehicle is a reasonable and necessary measure to prevent future confrontations of this kind.
The Alaska Supreme Court's holding in Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), confirms that courts retain broad authority to fashion the terms of protective orders to address the particular circumstances of each case, including the scope and geographic reach of stay-away provisions. The conduct here, involving two separate incidents at two separate locations within five days, supports a broad stay-away provision covering all locations where Priya Bergstrom is known to spend time.
E. THE COURT MAY NOT ORDER MEDIATION IN THIS PROCEEDING
AS 18.66.130(c) provides that a court may not order the parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition for a protective order under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. Civil Rule 100(a) similarly states that mediation may not be ordered between the parties to, or in, a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. These provisions reflect the legislature's and court system's recognition that mediation is inappropriate in domestic violence protective order proceedings, where power imbalances and ongoing danger to the petitioner make a negotiated resolution unsafe and unjust.
F. PRIYA BERGSTROM'S ADDRESS AND CONTACT INFORMATION ARE ENTITLED TO PROTECTION
Civil Rule 65.1 provides that a petitioner who is appearing pro se in a proceeding to obtain a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 or 18.66.110 may submit her mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. Access to the form containing the petitioner's mailing address and telephone number is limited to the court, authorized court system personnel, and the petitioner.
Priya Bergstrom invokes this protection and respectfully requests that the Court maintain her contact and location information as confidential in accordance with Civil Rule 65.1. Given that Michael Bergstrom has already appeared uninvited at her workplace, the risk that he would use publicly filed court documents to locate and confront her is substantial and immediate.
G. PRIYA BERGSTROM MAY FILE THIS PETITION IN THE JUDICIAL DISTRICT WHERE THE VIOLENCE OCCURRED
Civil Rule 3(h) provides that a petition for a protective order on domestic violence under AS 18.66 may be filed in either the judicial district or the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. The March 4, 2025 assault occurred at the shared marital residence in Anchorage. The March 9, 2025 confrontation occurred at Priya Bergstrom's workplace in Anchorage. This Court, sitting in Anchorage, is the proper venue for this petition under all three prongs of Civil Rule 3(h).
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Priya Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court issue a long-term domestic violence protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.100 that:

2. Prohibits Michael Bergstrom from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with Priya Bergstrom, including in person, by telephone, and by any electronic means, as authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(2);
3. Removes and excludes Michael Bergstrom from the shared marital residence in Anchorage, regardless of ownership, as authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(3);
4. Directs Michael Bergstrom to stay at least 500 feet away from Priya Bergstrom's residence, place of employment, and any vehicle in her possession or occupied by her, as authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(4) and AS 18.66.100(c)(5); and
5. Orders any other relief this Court determines necessary to protect Priya Bergstrom from further domestic violence, as authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(16).

Because Elena and Wesley continue to reside at the same address, Elena faces ongoing danger every day that Wesley remains in the home. AS 18.66.110(a) provides that the court shall issue an ex parte protective order without notice to the respondent if the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that it is necessary to protect the petitioner. The facts stated above, supported by photographic evidence and preserved electronic communications, plainly establish probable cause.
The relief available under an ex parte order under AS 18.66.110(a) includes the protections provided by AS 18.66.100(c)(1) through (c)(5) and (c)(8) through (c)(12) and (c)(16). Specifically, Elena seeks: prohibition of any further threatening or violent conduct under AS 18.66.100(c)(1); prohibition of all direct or indirect contact under AS 18.66.100(c)(2); removal and exclusion of Wesley from the marital residence under AS 18.66.100(c)(3); and direction to Wesley to stay away from Elena's residence, workplace, and the children's school under AS 18.66.100(c)(4). Each of these forms of relief is expressly authorized and is directly responsive to the documented conduct.
Civil Rule 65(b) also supports ex parte emergency relief. The specific facts here, a recent physical strangulation, a death threat, and a threatening workplace confrontation within a five-day period, demonstrate that immediate and irreparable injury will result to Elena if Wesley is not restrained before a hearing can be held. Continued cohabitation with an abuser who has threatened to kill his spouse if she contacts police presents exactly the circumstances that emergency relief is designed to address.
C. ELENA IS ENTITLED TO A LONG-TERM PROTECTIVE ORDER FOLLOWING THE NOTICED HEARING.
Following the issuance of any ex parte order, Elena requests that the court issue a long-term protective order upon the noticed hearing prescribed by AS 18.66.100(b). At that hearing, Elena will present photographic evidence of her injuries, the preserved threatening text message, and the testimony of coworkers who witnessed Wesley's March 9 confrontation at her workplace.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), confirms that courts must examine the full course of a respondent's conduct, including multiple incidents, when determining whether a long-term protective order is warranted. Here, the record reflects two separate incidents of threatening and violent conduct within five days, a pattern that compels the conclusion that Elena requires sustained court protection.
Under AS 18.66.100(c)(3), the court may remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. Wesley has no right to remain in the marital home as a shield against protective relief. Under AS 18.66.100(c)(4), the court may direct the respondent to stay away from Elena's residence, her workplace on Benson Boulevard, and any school frequented by the children. The 500-foot buffer Elena requests is a reasonable and well-recognized minimum distance necessary to prevent further confrontation.
Elena also notes that AS 25.24.140(b) independently authorizes protective orders during the pendency of a dissolution or divorce action, including orders providing for freedom from the other spouse's control, orders for protection under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180, and orders directing a spouse to vacate the marital residence. Should Elena file for dissolution of the marriage, these statutory protections would operate in parallel with and reinforce the domestic violence protective order sought here.
D. THE COURT SHOULD ENSURE ELENA'S CONTACT INFORMATION REMAINS PROTECTED THROUGHOUT THESE PROCEEDINGS.

V. CONCLUSION

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0148)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Okafor ("Petitioner") respectfully submits this brief in support of his petition for a domestic violence protective order against his spouse, Wesley Okafor ("Respondent"). The Petitioner and Respondent are married and have resided together in Anchorage, Alaska for six years. On October 3, 2024, Respondent physically assaulted Petitioner by grabbing him by the throat, shoving him into a kitchen cabinet, and threatening future harm. On October 5, 2024, Respondent appeared uninvited at Petitioner's place of employment, screamed obscenities at him in front of his coworkers, and subsequently sent threatening text messages stating that Petitioner would not be safe anywhere. These acts of domestic violence, both physical and threatening in nature, entitle Petitioner to immediate and comprehensive relief under Alaska law. Petitioner seeks a protective order requiring Respondent to vacate the marital residence, remain at least 500 feet from Petitioner's home, workplace, and vehicle, and surrender any firearms in his possession. The record establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that Respondent has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Petitioner, and that a protective order is necessary to protect Petitioner's safety and well-being.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Petitioner Marcus Okafor and Respondent Wesley Okafor are spouses who have lived together in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately six years. The following events precipitated this petition.
On October 3, 2024, the parties became involved in an argument regarding their household finances. During this argument, Respondent grabbed Petitioner by the throat, shoved him forcefully into a kitchen cabinet, and threatened that he would "make sure he would regret leaving." This physical assault caused Petitioner immediate fear for his safety and constitutes a crime involving domestic violence under Alaska law.
Two days later, on October 5, 2024, Respondent appeared uninvited at Petitioner's workplace in Anchorage. Without provocation, Respondent screamed obscenities at Petitioner in front of his coworkers, creating a scene that endangered Petitioner's sense of safety and security in his professional environment. That same evening, Respondent sent Petitioner a series of text messages containing the statement, "You won't be safe anywhere you go." This message constitutes an explicit threat of future harm and, taken together with the workplace confrontation and the October 3 physical assault, reflects a pattern of escalating threatening behavior.
Petitioner has reason to believe that Respondent possesses firearms. The escalating nature of Respondent's conduct, including physical strangulation, property-related assault, workplace confrontation, and explicit threats of future harm, creates a substantial and credible risk of serious physical injury to Petitioner. Petitioner has vacated the marital residence out of fear for his personal safety and now seeks the court's protection.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A protective order may be issued under AS 18.66.100 when a petitioner who is or has been a victim of a crime involving domestic violence files a petition against a household member. The statute provides that if the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c), regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
Under AS 18.66.110, a court may also issue an ex parte protective order prior to a full hearing upon a finding of probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that a protective order is necessary to protect the petitioner.
Venue for a petition filed under AS 18.66 is proper in either the judicial district or the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. Civil Rule 3(h). Here, venue in Anchorage is proper because both parties reside in Anchorage and the acts of domestic violence occurred there.
A pro se petitioner seeking a domestic violence protective order may submit his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other court filings. Civil Rule 65.1. This protection is available to Petitioner in this action.
Alaska courts have consistently upheld the authority of trial courts to issue broad protective relief upon a preponderance finding of domestic violence. In Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that domestic violence protective order statutes are to be construed to protect victims and that a court may issue broad relief when the statutory threshold is met. In Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020), the court upheld a protective order based on findings of assault and criminal trespass constituting domestic violence, confirming that physical contact combined with threatening behavior is sufficient to support full protective relief. In Andrea C. v. Marcus K., 355 P.3d 521 (Alaska 2015), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that protective order findings can have significant downstream consequences, including in custody proceedings, underscoring that courts must take such proceedings seriously and apply the law fully.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. RESPONDENT HAS COMMITTED CRIMES INVOLVING DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AGAINST PETITIONER, SATISFYING THE THRESHOLD REQUIREMENT FOR A PROTECTIVE ORDER UNDER AS 18.66.100.
AS 18.66.100(b) provides that if the court finds by a preponderance of evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c). The preponderance standard requires only that it be more likely than not that the domestic violence occurred.
Respondent's conduct on October 3, 2024, satisfies this standard independently. Grabbing a person by the throat and shoving that person into a hard surface constitutes assault under Alaska law, and such conduct against a household member qualifies as a crime involving domestic violence. The additional statement that Respondent would "make sure he would regret leaving" constitutes a direct threat of future violence, which itself may independently support protective relief under AS 18.66.100(c)(1).
Respondent's conduct on October 5, 2024, further corroborates the pattern of threatening and harassing behavior. Appearing uninvited at Petitioner's workplace and screaming obscenities at him in front of coworkers constitutes harassment. The subsequent text messages threatening that Petitioner "won't be safe anywhere you go" constitute threatening behavior directed at a household member, providing a second and independent basis for the issuance of a protective order.
Taken together, the physical assault, workplace confrontation, and explicit written threats present a clear and credible pattern of domestic violence. These facts, accepted as true and viewed in their totality, more than satisfy the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard under AS 18.66.100(b).
B. THE COURT SHOULD ORDER RESPONDENT TO VACATE THE MARITAL RESIDENCE AND MAINTAIN A DISTANCE OF AT LEAST 500 FEET FROM PETITIONER'S HOME, WORKPLACE, AND VEHICLE.
AS 18.66.100(c) enumerates the forms of relief a court may grant in a domestic violence protective order. Specifically, AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to "remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence." AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to "direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member." AS 18.66.100(c)(5) authorizes the court to "prohibit the respondent from entering a propelled vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the petitioner."
Respondent's demonstrated willingness to appear at Petitioner's workplace on October 5, 2024, just two days after the physical assault in the marital home, demonstrates that Respondent does not recognize boundaries and poses an ongoing threat to Petitioner wherever Petitioner may be found. The explicit text message threat sent that evening confirms that Respondent intends to continue his threatening conduct across multiple locations. Accordingly, relief under AS 18.66.100(c)(3), (c)(4), and (c)(5) is fully warranted.
Furthermore, AS 25.24.140(b) independently authorizes a court, during the pendency of a marital action, to issue necessary protective orders including orders directing one spouse to vacate the marital residence, restraining a spouse from communicating directly or indirectly with the other spouse, and restraining a spouse from entering a vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the other spouse. This provision provides an additional, concurrent basis for the residential and proximity relief requested by Petitioner.
In Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020), the Alaska Supreme Court upheld a protective order that limited the respondent's physical access to the petitioner and imposed restrictions on contact and communication, based on findings of assault and criminal trespass. The conduct in this case is at least as serious as that in Stephan P., and the same relief is warranted here.
C. THE COURT SHOULD ORDER RESPONDENT TO SURRENDER ANY FIREARMS IN HIS POSSESSION.
AS 18.66.100(c)(7) authorizes the court to "direct the respondent to surrender any firearm owned or possessed by the respondent if the court finds that the respondent was in the actual possession of or used a firearm during the commission of the domestic violence." Even where a firearm was not directly used during the specific acts of domestic violence at issue, AS 18.66.100(c)(6) also allows the court to prohibit the respondent from using or possessing a deadly weapon if the court finds the respondent was in actual possession of or used a weapon during the commission of domestic violence.
More broadly, AS 18.66.100(c)(16) authorizes the court to "order other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member." The explicit threat that Petitioner "won't be safe anywhere you go," combined with the physical violence already inflicted, gives the court a sufficient basis to conclude that Respondent's possession of any firearm poses a specific and elevated danger to Petitioner's safety. Firearms surrender is among the most important safeguards available when a respondent has demonstrated a capacity for physical violence and has issued explicit threats of future harm.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), acknowledged the broad remedial scope of AS 18.66.100(c) and the legislature's intent to give courts the tools necessary to protect domestic violence victims comprehensively. Petitioner respectfully urges the court to exercise that authority here and order immediate firearms surrender.
D. RESPONDENT'S INVITATION BY PETITIONER, IF ANY, CANNOT NULLIFY THE PROTECTIVE ORDER'S PROVISIONS.
AS 18.66.130(a) makes clear that if a respondent in a protective order issued under AS 18.66.100 is prohibited from communicating with the petitioner, excluded from the residence of the petitioner, or ordered to stay away from the petitioner, any invitation by the petitioner to communicate, enter the residence or vehicle, or have other prohibited contact with the petitioner does not waive or nullify any provision in the protective order. This provision is critical in domestic violence cases because perpetrators often pressure victims to re-initiate contact, and any such contact should not be construed as a waiver of the protections the court has ordered. The court should include the mandatory notice language required by AS 18.66.130(d) in any protective order it issues.
Additionally, AS 18.66.130(e) confirms that a protective order issued under this chapter is in addition to and not in place of any other civil or criminal remedy, and that a petitioner is not barred from seeking a protective order because of the existence of another civil action between the parties. The parties' marital relationship and any pending or future divorce proceedings do not preclude or diminish the protective relief sought here.
E. THE COURT MAY NOT ORDER MEDIATION IN THIS MATTER.
Because Petitioner is seeking a protective order under AS 18.66.100, and because the facts establish that domestic violence has occurred between the parties, the court is expressly prohibited from ordering or referring the parties to mediation. AS 18.66.130(c) provides that "a court may not order parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of the issues arising from a petition for a protective order under AS 18.66.100, 18.66.180." Civil Rule 100(a) similarly provides that "mediation may not be ordered between the parties to, or in, a case filed under AS 18.66.100, 18.66.180." Additionally, AS 25.24.140(d) provides that the court may not order or refer parties to mediation or family counseling if a protective order issued or filed under AS 18.66.100 is in effect, and AS 25.24.060(f) contains a parallel prohibition in divorce proceedings. These provisions collectively ensure that Petitioner cannot be compelled into a mediation process with a person who has physically assaulted him and threatened his safety.
F. THE STANDING PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION PROVIDES ADDITIONAL PROTECTION FOR PETITIONER DURING THIS PROCEEDING.
Civil Rule 65(e) provides that in domestic relations actions, a standing injunction may restrain the parties from threatening, harassing, or harming the other party, as well as from disposing of, encumbering, or transferring marital property without the written consent of the other party. To the extent such a standing injunction has been issued in this judicial district, it independently restrains Respondent from threatening, harassing, or harming Petitioner during the pendency of these proceedings. Petitioner respectfully brings this provision to the court's attention as an additional, immediate source of protection.
G. RESPONDENT'S PRIOR STATEMENTS TO PETITIONER DURING THE MARRIAGE ARE NOT SHIELDED BY THE MARITAL COMMUNICATIONS PRIVILEGE IN THIS PROCEEDING.
Respondent may seek to invoke the confidential marital communications privilege to prevent Petitioner from testifying about communications that occurred during the marriage. However, Alaska R. Evid. 505(b)(2)(A) provides that there is no privilege under the confidential marital communications rule if any of the exceptions under subdivision (a)(2) of that rule apply. Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(D)(v) provides that there is no spousal immunity privilege in a proceeding involving a crime involving domestic violence as defined in AS 18.66.990. Because this is precisely such a proceeding, neither the spousal immunity privilege under Alaska R. Evid. 505(a) nor the confidential marital communications privilege under Alaska R. Evid. 505(b) bars Petitioner's testimony about Respondent's threatening statements and conduct. Petitioner may testify fully and completely about all relevant communications and acts, including the October 3, 2024 threat and the October 5, 2024 text messages.
V. CONCLUSION
The evidence presented in this brief establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that Respondent Wesley Okafor has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Petitioner Marcus Okafor. Respondent physically assaulted Petitioner by grabbing him by the throat and shoving him into a kitchen cabinet. Respondent threatened Petitioner with future harm on multiple occasions, both in person and by text message. Respondent appeared uninvited at Petitioner's workplace just two days after the physical assault, demonstrating both the ongoing nature of the threat and Respondent's willingness to pursue Petitioner in multiple settings. These acts, individually and collectively, satisfy the statutory requirements for issuance of a protective order under AS 18.66.100.
Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court issue a protective order providing the following relief:
1. Prohibiting Respondent from threatening to commit or committing further acts of domestic violence, stalking, or harassment against Petitioner, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(1);
2. Prohibiting Respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with Petitioner, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(2);
3. Removing and excluding Respondent from the marital residence in Anchorage, Alaska, regardless of ownership, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3);
4. Directing Respondent to stay at least 500 feet away from Petitioner's residence, workplace, and any other place frequented by Petitioner, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4);
5. Prohibiting Respondent from entering any propelled vehicle in the possession of or occupied by Petitioner, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(5); and
6. Directing Respondent to surrender any and all firearms in his possession to the appropriate law enforcement agency, and ordering such other weapons-related relief as the court deems necessary to protect Petitioner, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(7) and AS 18.66.100(c)(16).
Petitioner further requests that the court include all mandatory notice language required by AS 18.66.130(d) in the protective order, and that the court enter such other relief as it deems necessary and just to protect Petitioner from further harm.

THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER

I. INTRODUCTION
David Nakamura respectfully petitions this Court for a domestic violence protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.908 and AS 18.66.965, prohibiting respondent Colin Nakamura from contacting petitioner in any form and requiring respondent to vacate the marital residence at 412 Spruce Glen Drive, Juneau, Alaska 99801. II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Petitioner David Nakamura and respondent Colin Nakamura are married spouses who have resided together at 412 Spruce Glen Drive, Juneau, Alaska 99801 for approximately four years. As household members and current spouses, respondent qualifies as a person against whom a domestic violence protective order may issue under AS 18.66.100.
On October 3, 2024, during an argument about household finances, respondent Colin Nakamura grabbed petitioner David Nakamura by the throat and shoved him into a wall. The attack left visible bruising on petitioner's neck and shoulder. This physical assault constitutes a crime involving domestic violence, specifically an assault causing physical injury, committed by a household member against another household member.
On October 17, 2024, approximately two weeks after the physical assault, respondent appeared unannounced at petitioner's place of employment. In front of petitioner's coworkers, respondent told petitioner that if David ever tried to leave him, he would "make sure David regretted it." This statement, made in a public setting and in front of witnesses, constitutes a credible threat of future harm and demonstrates a continuing pattern of intimidation and control.
Petitioner has not provoked, consented to, or invited respondent's threatening conduct. Petitioner reasonably fears for his safety and well-being both at the marital residence and at his workplace. Petitioner files this petition in the judicial district where both parties reside and where the acts of domestic violence occurred.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), if the court finds by a preponderance of evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c), regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing. The statute establishes a preponderance-of-evidence standard, which requires that the evidence show it is more likely than not that the domestic violence occurred.
For an ex parte protective order under AS 18.66.110(a), the court must find that the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that it is necessary to protect the petitioner from domestic violence. An ex parte protective order may be issued without notice to the respondent upon a written certification by the petitioner of the efforts made to provide notice. Such an order may grant the protection provided by AS 18.66.100(c)(1) through (5), (8) through (12), and (16).
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must give careful consideration to evidence of physical violence and threatening conduct in evaluating domestic violence petitions. In Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010), the court underscored the importance of allowing petitioners full opportunity to present evidence of domestic violence and held that trial courts must make adequate findings when domestic violence evidence is properly presented. In Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), the court confirmed that the plain language of AS 18.66.100 provides a clear statutory method for victims of domestic violence to obtain protective relief against household members, including former and current spouses.
Additionally, Civil Rule 65(b) permits a court to issue a temporary restraining order without notice to the adverse party where specific facts shown by affidavit or verified complaint establish that immediate and irreparable injury will result before the adverse party can be heard in opposition.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Petitioner Has Established Probable Cause, and the Evidence by a Preponderance Supports Issuance of a Protective Order.
The two incidents described in the Statement of Facts establish both probable cause for an ex parte protective order under AS 18.66.110(a) and a preponderance of evidence sufficient to support a long-term protective order under AS 18.66.100(b).
First, the October 3, 2024 assault in which respondent grabbed petitioner by the throat and shoved him into a wall, causing visible bruising to his neck and shoulder, constitutes a crime involving domestic violence. The physical injury is documented and occurred between household members who are married spouses living together. This single incident alone provides sufficient grounds for the issuance of protective relief.
Second, the October 17, 2024 threatening statement made at petitioner's workplace compounds the severity of the situation. Respondent's statement, delivered in front of witnesses, that David would "regret" leaving him constitutes a credible threat of future harm. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), that courts may properly rely on a pattern of conduct, including multiple incidents occurring in sequence, in evaluating petitions for domestic violence protective orders. The progression from physical assault to workplace intimidation demonstrates an escalating course of conduct that heightens the risk to petitioner.
Importantly, AS 18.66.100(e) provides that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. Similarly, AS 18.66.110(d) provides that a court may not deny a petition for an ex parte protective order solely because of a lapse of time between the act and the filing. The two-week interval between the assault and the workplace threat, and the short period between those events and the filing of this petition, therefore do not diminish petitioner's entitlement to relief.
B. The Court Should Prohibit All Contact Between Respondent and Petitioner.
AS 18.66.100(c)(2) expressly authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from "telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner." Given respondent's demonstrated willingness to appear unannounced at petitioner's workplace and to deliver threatening statements in front of third parties, a comprehensive no-contact order is essential to protect petitioner's safety.
Petitioner requests that this prohibition extend to in-person contact, telephone contact, and electronic contact of all kinds, including text messages, email, and contact through third parties acting on respondent's behalf. The broad scope of this requested relief is justified by respondent's conduct, which shows both a capacity for physical violence and a willingness to use public spaces and the presence of others as settings for intimidation.
The court should further note that under AS 18.66.130(a), if respondent is prohibited from communicating with petitioner, any invitation by petitioner to communicate does not waive or nullify the provision in the protective order. Petitioner is advised and understands this principle, and requests that the order reflect its terms clearly.
C. The Court Should Order Respondent to Vacate the Marital Residence.
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to "remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence." AS 18.66.100(c)(4) further authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner.
Petitioner and respondent currently share the marital residence at 412 Spruce Glen Drive, Juneau, Alaska 99801. Petitioner cannot safely remain in the same residence as respondent given the severity of the October 3 assault and the October 17 threat. Requiring respondent to vacate the marital home is necessary to provide petitioner with a safe place to live during the pendency of these proceedings and for the duration of the protective order.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), illustrates the court's recognition that exclusion from the marital residence is an appropriate and important component of protective relief when a pattern of threatening and violent conduct has been demonstrated. The facts of this case, involving both physical injury and a subsequent threatening confrontation, plainly support the exclusion of respondent from the marital home.
D. The Court Should Order Respondent to Stay Away from Petitioner's Workplace.
In addition to vacating the marital residence, respondent should be directed to stay away from petitioner's workplace pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4), which authorizes the court to direct a respondent to stay away from "the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner." Respondent has already demonstrated a willingness to appear at petitioner's workplace for the purpose of delivering threatening statements. Without a specific order prohibiting respondent from appearing at or near petitioner's employer, petitioner cannot safely perform his job duties or maintain his employment.
E. The Lapse of Time Between Incidents Does Not Bar Relief.
AS 18.66.100(e)(1) provides that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because there is a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.110(d) contains identical language with respect to ex parte protective orders. These provisions reflect the Alaska Legislature's recognition that victims of domestic violence frequently face barriers to immediate reporting and that a brief delay does not diminish the reality or severity of the violence they have experienced.
In this case, the period between the October 3 assault and the filing of this petition is short, and the October 17 threatening statement is itself a recent act of domestic violence. The recency and sequence of both incidents demonstrate the ongoing nature of the threat petitioner faces.
F. Petitioner's Address May Be Protected Under Civil Rule 65.1.
Petitioner, appearing pro se in this proceeding, is entitled under Civil Rule 65.1 to submit his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. Access to the form containing petitioner's mailing address and telephone number is limited to the court, authorized court system personnel, and the petitioner. Petitioner requests the benefit of this protection to prevent respondent from using information in the court file to locate or contact him.
G. Mediation Is Not Appropriate in This Proceeding.
AS 18.66.130(c) expressly provides that "a court may order parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of the issues arising from a petition for a protective order under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180." Civil Rule 100(a) reinforces this prohibition, providing that mediation may not be ordered between the parties to, or in, a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. The court should therefore not refer the parties to mediation in connection with this petition.
H. The Standing Injunction Under Civil Rule 65(e) Also Applies.
During the pendency of any domestic relations action arising from these circumstances, Civil Rule 65(e) provides that a standing injunction may restrain the parties from threatening, harassing, or harming the other party, and from disposing of or encumbering marital property without written consent of the other party. While the domestic violence protective order sought herein provides more specific relief, the standing injunction provisions reinforce the legal framework that prohibits respondent from threatening or harming petitioner during the pendency of these proceedings.

PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
