I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Tomas Sutter brings this action pursuant to AS 18.66.100 and AS 18.66.110, seeking a protective order against his spouse, Respondent Danielle Sutter, following acts of domestic violence committed on March 4, 2025, and threatening communications made on March 7, 2025. Tomas has been physically assaulted in the marital home, has received explicit threats against his physical safety, and has been forced to relocate temporarily to avoid further harm. He now seeks an order from this Court prohibiting Danielle from contacting him in any form, requiring that she remain at least 500 feet from his person and his temporary residence, and directing her to vacate the marital home so that Tomas may safely retrieve his essential belongings. The relief sought is expressly authorized under Alaska law and is necessary to protect Tomas from further domestic violence.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Sutter and Danielle Sutter are a married couple who have resided together at a shared residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately six years. The parties remain legally married. On March 4, 2025, inside the marital residence, Danielle grabbed Tomas by the collar, shoved him forcefully into a kitchen cabinet, and struck him across the face with an open hand. This assault left visible bruising on Tomas's cheek, constituting physical injury caused by a household member and therefore a crime involving domestic violence under Alaska law.
Three days later, on March 7, 2025, Danielle sent Tomas a series of text messages in which she stated that she would "make sure he regretted leaving" and that he "would not walk away from this marriage in one piece." These messages constitute explicit threats of bodily harm and harassment communicated directly to Tomas following a recent physical assault.
As a result of these events, Tomas relocated from the marital residence to a friend's home to protect himself from further harm. He retains a reasonable and well-founded fear that Danielle is capable of carrying out her stated threats, based on both the March 4 physical assault and what he describes as her history of escalating anger. Tomas seeks to return to the marital residence to retrieve essential personal belongings, but fears for his safety in doing so without court-ordered protection. Tomas filed this petition for a protective order at the court location serving the judicial district where both the marital residence and his current temporary residence are located, consistent with Civil Rule 3(h).
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petition for a protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and, if it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c). The court may issue this relief regardless of whether the respondent appears at the scheduled hearing.
Where immediate danger exists, AS 18.66.110(a) authorizes the court to issue an ex parte protective order without notice to the respondent, provided that the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred, that the order is necessary to protect the petitioner, and that the petitioner has certified in writing the efforts, if any, made to provide notice to the respondent.
Civil Rule 65(b) further provides that a temporary restraining order may be granted without notice to the adverse party where it clearly appears from specific facts shown by affidavit or verified complaint that immediate and irreparable injury, loss, or damage will result to the applicant before the adverse party can be heard in opposition.
In addition, Civil Rule 65(e) establishes a standing injunction applicable in domestic relations actions restraining parties from, among other things, threatening, harassing, or harming the other party, and from disposing of marital property without consent or court order.
Under AS 25.24.140(b), during the pendency of a domestic relations action, a spouse is entitled to necessary protective orders including orders for protection under AS 18.66.100 through AS 18.66.180, orders directing one spouse to vacate the marital residence, and orders restraining a spouse from communicating directly or indirectly with the other spouse.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. The Record Establishes Probable Cause and, at a Full Hearing, a Preponderance of Evidence That Danielle Sutter Committed a Crime Involving Domestic Violence Against Tomas Sutter.
The physical assault on March 4, 2025, in which Danielle grabbed Tomas by the collar, shoved him into a kitchen cabinet, and struck him across the face hard enough to leave visible bruising, constitutes a crime involving domestic violence. Danielle is a household member, as the parties are married and have shared the same residence for six years. The use of physical force resulting in visible injury satisfies the statutory predicate for domestic violence.
Alaska courts have recognized that findings of domestic violence must be grounded in the totality of the record and that courts are not to minimize credible evidence of physical harm inflicted by one spouse upon the other. In Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that acts of physical aggression in a shared household constitute domestic violence regardless of property ownership or other contextual factors, and that courts must carefully evaluate such evidence and make appropriate findings. In Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010), the Alaska Supreme Court reiterated that once domestic violence is credibly raised, the court must directly address the issue and make findings accordingly.
The text messages sent on March 7, 2025 stating that Danielle would "make sure he regretted leaving" and that he "would not walk away from this marriage in one piece" constitute threats of further violence and harassment against Tomas. Taken together with the prior physical assault, this course of conduct demonstrates an ongoing and escalating threat to Tomas's physical safety. AS 18.66.100(c)(1) expressly authorizes the court to prohibit a respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. AS 18.66.100(e) further provides that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition, confirming that the court must consider the full context of events including continuing threats.
B. The Court Should Issue an Ex Parte Protective Order Because Tomas Faces Immediate Risk of Harm.
AS 18.66.110(a) authorizes the court to issue an ex parte protective order where the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that the order is necessary to protect the petitioner. The physical assault of March 4, 2025, is documented by visible bruising, and the threatening text messages of March 7, 2025, are preserved communications that directly threaten bodily harm. These facts, taken together, establish the requisite probable cause. Tomas has been forced to leave his own home and currently lives with a friend precisely because he fears Danielle's capacity for violence. These circumstances satisfy the requirements of AS 18.66.110(a) for immediate ex parte relief.
Civil Rule 65(b) independently supports issuance of a temporary restraining order without prior notice, as the verified facts presented show that immediate and irreparable injury will result to Tomas if Danielle is permitted to continue contacting him or maintaining exclusive possession of the marital residence before a full hearing can be held. A physical assault followed within three days by explicit death-adjacent threats presents precisely the circumstance that warrants emergency judicial action.
In Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized the intersection of criminal domestic violence proceedings and civil divorce and protective order proceedings, underscoring that courts must be attentive to the ongoing risks faced by victims of domestic violence and take all necessary steps to protect them throughout the pendency of proceedings.
C. The Court Should Issue the Full Range of Protective Relief Requested by Tomas, Including a No-Contact Order, a Stay-Away Requirement, and an Order Directing Danielle to Vacate the Marital Residence.
AS 18.66.100(c) enumerates the specific relief a protective order may provide. Tomas requests three categories of relief, each of which is expressly authorized.
First, AS 18.66.100(c)(1) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. The threatening text messages of March 7, 2025, confirm that Danielle has already engaged in this conduct after the physical assault, and a prohibition on all future contact is necessary and appropriate.
Second, AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner. Given that Danielle used text messaging to communicate threats just three days after the assault, a complete no-contact order encompassing all forms of communication is warranted.
Third, AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member. A requirement that Danielle remain at least 500 feet from Tomas and his temporary residence is within the scope of this provision and is necessary given the explicit nature of her threats.
Fourth, AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. Tomas has been effectively displaced from the marital residence by Danielle's conduct. Ordering Danielle to vacate the residence so that Tomas may safely return and retrieve his belongings is expressly authorized under this subsection. The Alaska Supreme Court in Thomas E. Jordan v. Cheryl A. Jordan, 480 P.3d 626 (Alaska 2021), recognized the authority of courts to award interim possession of a marital residence as part of domestic relations protective relief, confirming that possession and use of shared property during the pendency of proceedings is a proper subject of judicial order.
Fifth, AS 18.66.100(c)(8) authorizes the court to request that a peace officer accompany the petitioner to the petitioner's residence to ensure that the petitioner safely obtains possession of the residence, vehicle, or personal items, and is able to safely remove personal items from the residence. Should the court direct Danielle to vacate, Tomas further requests that a peace officer be authorized to accompany him to the marital residence so that he may safely retrieve his essential belongings.
Tomas also notes that under AS 25.24.140(b), during the pendency of a domestic relations action he is entitled to protective orders including those for protection under AS 18.66.100 through AS 18.66.180, orders requiring Danielle to vacate the marital residence, and orders restraining Danielle from communicating directly or indirectly with him. This independent statutory basis reinforces that the relief requested is appropriate in the context of a marital relationship.
D. AS 18.66.110 Establishes the Proper Vehicle for Emergency Relief and Permits the Requested Protection Pending a Full Hearing.
AS 18.66.110(a) provides that an ex parte protective order expires 20 days after it is issued unless dissolved earlier by the court. Upon service of the ex parte order, the court shall schedule a hearing under AS 18.66.100(b) giving Danielle at least 10 days' notice and the opportunity to appear and be heard. At that hearing, Tomas will present the full evidentiary record, including photographic documentation of his injuries, the preserved text messages, and any additional corroborating evidence, to meet the preponderance of the evidence standard required for issuance of a long-term protective order.
Tomas acknowledges that the protective orders available under AS 18.66.100(c)(2) through (c)(16) are, by the terms of AS 18.66.100(b)(2), effective for one year unless earlier dissolved by court order. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), confirms that this one-year limitation governs most categories of protective relief, while the prohibition against threatening to commit domestic violence under AS 18.66.100(c)(1) remains effective until further order of the court. Tomas requests that the no-contact and stay-away provisions entered at the full hearing remain in effect for the statutory one-year period, and that the prohibition against threats of domestic violence under AS 18.66.100(c)(1) remain in effect until further order of the court.
E. The Marital Relationship Does Not Shield Danielle's Communications from Evidence, and Tomas's Account Is Properly Before the Court.
Because this is a civil proceeding brought by one spouse against the other, Alaska R. Evid. 505(a) provides that the spousal immunity rule does not apply. Specifically, Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(A) provides that there is no spousal immunity privilege in a civil proceeding brought by or on behalf of one spouse against the other spouse. Accordingly, Tomas may testify freely regarding all communications and conduct by Danielle.
Similarly, under Alaska R. Evid. 505(b)(2)(A), the confidential marital communications privilege does not apply where any of the exceptions under subdivision (a)(2) apply. Because this is a civil proceeding between spouses, the threatening text messages and any other communications from Danielle to Tomas are fully admissible and are not shielded by any evidentiary privilege. The Court may therefore consider the full content of Danielle's March 7, 2025, text messages in evaluating the need for protective relief.
Additionally, under Civil Rule 65.1, Tomas, as a pro se petitioner in a domestic violence protective order proceeding under AS 18.66.100 or AS 18.66.110, may submit his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court, thereby protecting his current location from disclosure to Danielle. Tomas requests that the court maintain the confidentiality of his temporary address pursuant to this rule.
F. Peace Officers Were Required to Inform Tomas of His Rights and Available Relief Following the March 4, 2025, Incident.
AS 18.65.520(a) requires that a peace officer investigating a crime involving domestic violence shall orally and in writing inform the victim of the rights of victims of domestic violence and the services available to them, including specifically the right to request assistance in obtaining an emergency protective order and the right to file a petition in court requesting a protective order. To the extent law enforcement responded to or investigated the March 4, 2025, assault, Tomas was entitled to receive this notice. The detailed statutory notice set forth in AS 18.65.520(a) makes clear that a victim of domestic violence has the right to petition the court for relief including orders prohibiting the abuser from contacting the victim, removing the abuser from the residence, and awarding temporary custody of belongings and essential items, all of which Tomas now requests in this petition.
G. Veronica Louise Hudson v. Daniel Lee Hudson Confirms That Courts Must Carefully Examine Domestic Violence Allegations in the Context of an Ongoing Marriage.
In Veronica Louise Hudson v. Daniel Lee Hudson, 532 P.3d 272 (Alaska 2023), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed a divorce proceeding in which one spouse alleged a history of domestic violence and feared the other spouse's reaction to the dissolution of the marriage. The court's analysis confirms that domestic violence allegations must be taken seriously in the context of ongoing marital relationships, that a victim's subjective fear of a spouse based on prior conduct is relevant and cognizable, and that courts should not minimize the significance of prior incidents when evaluating requests for protective relief. Tomas's fear of Danielle, grounded in the concrete events of March 4 and March 7, 2025, is precisely the type of well-founded, evidence-based concern that Alaska courts are directed to consider carefully.
V. CONCLUSION
For all of the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Tomas Sutter respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Issue an ex parte protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.110(a), immediately prohibiting Respondent Danielle Sutter from contacting Tomas in any form, approaching within 500 feet of his person or temporary residence, and directing her to vacate the marital residence;
2. Schedule a full hearing pursuant to AS 18.66.100(b) at which the Court may consider the full evidentiary record and issue a long-term protective order;
3. At the full hearing, issue a protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(1) prohibiting Danielle from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence against Tomas, effective until further order of the court;
4. Issue a no-contact order pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(2) prohibiting Danielle from communicating with Tomas in any form, effective for one year;
5. Issue a stay-away order pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4) requiring Danielle to remain at least 500 feet from Tomas's person and temporary residence, effective for one year;
6. Issue an order pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3) removing and excluding Danielle from the marital residence so that Tomas may safely return and recover his belongings;
7. Authorize a peace officer to accompany Tomas to the marital residence pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(8) to ensure his safety while he retrieves his essential personal items;
8. Maintain the confidentiality of Tomas's current mailing address pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1; and
9. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems necessary and appropriate to protect Tomas's safety.

I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Sutter petitions this Court for a domestic violence protective order against his spouse, Michael Sutter, pursuant to AS 18.66.100. Over the course of six days in early March 2025, Michael subjected Marcus to physical violence, credible death threats, and a pattern of threatening conduct that continued into Marcus's workplace. Marcus seeks an order prohibiting all contact, requiring Michael to vacate the shared Fairbanks residence, and establishing a 500-foot exclusion zone around his home, workplace, and vehicle. The facts presented establish by a preponderance of the evidence that Michael has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Marcus, and that immediate, comprehensive protective relief is necessary to secure Marcus's safety.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Sutter and Michael Sutter are married and have lived together in Fairbanks, Alaska for approximately six years. Their shared residence has been the center of their domestic life throughout the marriage.
On March 3, 2025, the parties became involved in an argument concerning household finances. During that argument, Michael grabbed Marcus by the throat, shoved him forcefully against the kitchen wall, and threatened to "make him regret it" if he ever attempted to leave the relationship. This single incident involved both physical assault and a direct verbal threat tied explicitly to Marcus's ability to exercise his freedom to leave the marriage.
On March 9, 2025, six days after the physical assault, Michael appeared uninvited at Marcus's place of employment. In the presence of Marcus's coworkers, Michael screamed threats at Marcus, causing a scene that subjected Marcus to public humiliation and terror in a setting where he had no ready means of retreat. Later that same day, Michael sent Marcus a series of text messages in which he stated that he would "not let him walk away alive." This explicit death threat, delivered in writing, leaves no room for ambiguity regarding the danger Michael poses to Marcus.
The conduct described above represents a rapid escalation of violence and intimidation directed at Marcus in both his domestic and professional spheres. Marcus has no adequate remedy at law to address this ongoing danger other than a protective order from this Court.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), a court may issue a long-term protective order if it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner. The statute does not require that the respondent appear at the hearing; a court may grant relief regardless of the respondent's presence. AS 18.66.100(b). The court may not deny a petition solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.100(e)(1).
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized that courts must take seriously credible, documented threats of violence within the domestic setting, particularly where a pattern of escalating conduct is present. In Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020), the court affirmed the issuance of a protective order where the respondent had committed assault and had appeared at the petitioner's home without invitation. Onslow v. Brackeen, 348 P.3d 770 (Alaska 2018), the court upheld protective relief following physical violence accompanied by threatening and controlling behavior. In Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010), the court emphasized that physical acts of violence, such as choking, weigh heavily against a respondent in domestic violence proceedings and that courts must fully consider all credible evidence of domestic violence.
A petition for a protective order may be filed in the court location closest to where the petitioner resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. Civil Rule 3(h). All three of those locations are within the Fairbanks judicial district, making venue in this Court appropriate.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Michael Sutter Has Committed Crimes Involving Domestic Violence Against Marcus Sutter, Satisfying the Preponderance Standard Under AS 18.66.100.
The statutory framework governing domestic violence protective orders requires the Court to find, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the respondent committed a crime involving domestic violence. AS 18.66.100(b). Spouses are expressly included within the class of household members against whom such acts may be committed, and the conduct described in Section II plainly constitutes criminal assault and criminal threatening under Alaska law.
Michael's act of grabbing Marcus by the throat and shoving him against a wall on March 3, 2025, constitutes physical assault. The accompanying verbal threat, warning Marcus that he would "make him regret it" if he tried to leave, adds a coercive dimension that demonstrates Michael's intent to control Marcus through fear. The March 9, 2025 workplace confrontation, combined with text messages explicitly threatening to prevent Marcus from "walking away alive," constitutes criminal threatening and a sustained pattern of intimidation. The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020), is instructive: the court there affirmed a protective order where the respondent committed assault and made uninvited, threatening contact with the petitioner. The facts before this Court are at least as compelling.
The court in Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010), specifically noted that choking or grabbing a victim by the throat is a serious act of violence that weighs heavily against a respondent in domestic violence proceedings. That factor is directly present here and strongly supports issuance of the requested order.
Under AS 18.66.904, a protective order may prohibit the respondent from communicating with the petitioner, remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner regardless of ownership, direct the respondent to stay away from the petitioner's residence, workplace, or other specified places frequented by the petitioner, and prohibit the respondent from entering a vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the petitioner. Each of those provisions is warranted by the facts presented.
B. Marcus Sutter Is Entitled to Comprehensive Protective Relief, Including a No-Contact Order, Exclusion from the Residence, and a Distance Restriction.
AS 18.66.999(2) authorizes the Court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner. Michael's use of text messages to deliver explicit death threats demonstrates that electronic communication represents a continued and documented vector of danger. A total no-contact order encompassing in-person, telephone, and electronic communication is therefore appropriate and necessary.
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the Court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner regardless of ownership. Although Marcus and Michael share the marital home, Michael's violent conduct within that home, including the March 3, 2025 assault, makes it unsafe for Marcus to remain there alongside Michael. The shared nature of ownership or tenancy does not bar exclusionary relief; the statute expressly removes ownership as an obstacle to this remedy.
AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the Court to direct the respondent to stay away from the petitioner's residence, workplace, or any other place frequented by the petitioner. Michael's uninvited appearance at Marcus's workplace on March 9, 2025, and his screaming of threats before coworkers, demonstrates that he is willing to pursue Marcus into professional settings. A 500-foot exclusion zone around Marcus's residence, workplace, and vehicle is a proportionate and necessary measure to protect Marcus from further contact in these locations.
AS 18.66.100(c)(5) authorizes the Court to prohibit the respondent from entering a propelled vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the petitioner. This provision should be included in the order to address any scenario in which Michael attempts to intercept or confront Marcus in or near his vehicle, which represents a particularly vulnerable point of contact.
AS 18.66.100(c)(16) further authorizes the Court to order any other relief it determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member. This catchall provision supports a broadly protective order tailored to the specific circumstances Marcus faces.
C. Michael's Invitation-Based Waiver Argument, If Raised, Is Foreclosed by Statute.
To the extent Michael attempts to argue that any prior reconciliatory communication from Marcus could waive the protections of this order or nullify its terms, that argument is explicitly foreclosed by AS 18.66.130(a). Under that statute, an invitation by the petitioner to communicate, enter the residence, or have other prohibited contact does not waive or nullify any provision of a protective order. The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Andrea C. v. Marcus K., 355 P.3d 521 (Alaska 2015), reflects the broader principle that the integrity of protective orders must be maintained regardless of subsequent contact, and that courts must evaluate the full context of a domestic violence proceeding rather than isolating individual acts. Marcus's safety cannot be held hostage to any argument that past conciliatory conduct on his part diminishes the severity of Michael's violence.
D. Mediation Is Prohibited Under These Circumstances.
AS 18.66.130(c) expressly states that a court may not order parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition for a protective order under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. Civil Rule 100(a) similarly provides that mediation may not be ordered between the parties to a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. To the extent any future motion seeks to divert this proceeding to mediation, such a motion would be contrary to both statute and rule. Additionally, AS 25.24.140(d) confirms that the court may not order or refer parties to mediation or family counseling if a protective order issued or filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180 is in effect.
E. As a Pro Se Petitioner, Marcus Is Entitled to Address Confidentiality Protections.
Civil Rule 65.1 permits a petitioner appearing pro se in a domestic violence protective order proceeding to submit his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and to omit that information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. Access to the form containing the petitioner's mailing address and telephone number is limited to the court, authorized court system personnel, and the petitioner. Marcus requests that the Court apply this protection to all filings in this proceeding to prevent Michael from using court records as a means of locating or monitoring Marcus.
F. Any Attempt by Michael to Use Marital Communications Privilege Is Unavailing in This Proceeding.
Should Michael seek to invoke spousal privilege to exclude relevant evidence in this proceeding, that effort is foreclosed by Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(D)(v) and Alaska R. Evid. 505(b)(2)(A). Alaska R. Evid. 505(a) provides that the general spousal immunity rule carries no privilege in a proceeding in which one spouse is charged with a crime involving domestic violence as defined in AS 18.66.990. Alaska R. Evid. 505(b) provides that the confidential marital communications privilege likewise carries no privilege if any of the exceptions under subdivision (a)(2) of that rule apply. Because this proceeding concerns crimes involving domestic violence, both forms of privilege are unavailable to Michael, and all relevant communications, including the threatening text messages, may be considered by this Court.
G. The Conduct Described Satisfies the Statutory Definition and Supports the Relief Requested Under AS 25.24.140 as Well.
Because the parties are married and divorce proceedings may follow, the Court should also note that AS 25.24.140(b) independently entitles a spouse, during the pendency of a domestic relations action, to necessary protective orders, including orders providing for freedom from the control of the other spouse and orders for protection under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. The conduct described here, including Michael's explicit threat that he would not allow Marcus to leave the relationship and his subsequent death threat, demonstrates precisely the kind of controlling behavior this provision is designed to address. The statutory framework, taken as a whole, supports the full scope of relief Marcus requests.
V. CONCLUSION
The evidence presented establishes by a preponderance that Michael Sutter has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Marcus Sutter, including physical assault by strangulation, repeated death threats, and threatening workplace confrontation. The rapid escalation of Michael's conduct over a six-day period demonstrates both the seriousness of the danger Marcus faces and the inadequacy of any remedy short of a comprehensive protective order.
Marcus Sutter respectfully requests that this Court issue a protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.100 that:
1. Prohibits Michael Sutter from contacting Marcus Sutter in person, by telephone, or by any electronic means, directly or indirectly, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(2);
2. Removes and excludes Michael Sutter from the shared Fairbanks residence regardless of ownership, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3);
3. Directs Michael Sutter to remain at least 500 feet from Marcus Sutter's residence, workplace, and vehicle, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4) and AS 18.66.100(c)(5);
4. Orders any other relief this Court determines necessary to protect Marcus Sutter, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16); and
5. Applies address confidentiality protections consistent with Civil Rule 65.1.

In addition, under AS 18.66.110(a), a petitioner who demonstrates probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and who certifies efforts to provide notice to the respondent may obtain an ex parte protective order without prior notice to the respondent, where immediate danger requires it.
Under Civil Rule 65(b), a temporary restraining order may be granted without notice to the adverse party where specific facts shown by affidavit or verified complaint establish that immediate and irreparable injury will result before the adverse party can be heard, provided the applicant certifies in writing the efforts made to give notice.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must carefully evaluate the totality of a respondent's conduct when assessing petitions for protective relief, and that a pattern of threatening behavior, even when individual acts vary in severity, may justify the issuance and extension of a protective order. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018). The court has also emphasized that protective order proceedings require a fair and complete record to ensure that the rights of all parties, including minor children, are fully protected. Andrea C. v. Marcus K., 355 P.3d 521 (Alaska 2015).
Under AS 25.24.910, during the pendency of a divorce or family law action, a spouse is entitled to necessary protective orders, including orders providing for the freedom of each spouse from the control of the other, orders for protection under AS 18.66.100 through AS 18.66.180, orders directing a spouse to vacate the marital residence, and orders restraining a spouse from communicating directly or indirectly with the other spouse.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. PETITIONER HAS ESTABLISHED BY A PREPONDERANCE OF THE EVIDENCE THAT SARAH BERGSTROM HAS COMMITTED CRIMES INVOLVING DOMESTIC VIOLENCE
Alaska Statute AS 18.66.100(b) authorizes the court to issue a protective order where it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner. The three documented incidents set forth in the Statement of Facts satisfy this standard independently and collectively.
The October 3, 2024 physical assault, in which Sarah Bergstrom grabbed Marcus Bergstrom by the throat and shoved him into a wall with sufficient force to leave visible bruising, constitutes assault under Alaska law and falls squarely within the definition of domestic violence between household members. The October 14, 2024 text message threatening to "make him regret everything" constitutes a threat of harm communicated directly to Petitioner. The October 17, 2024 incident, in which Respondent blocked Petitioner's vehicle, screamed threats against both Petitioner and the minor children, and specifically threatened harm if Petitioner sought legal counsel, constitutes additional threatening conduct directed against Petitioner and the children.
The Alaska Supreme Court held in Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), that courts evaluating domestic violence protective order petitions must consider the full context of the respondent's conduct. The pattern here, spanning fourteen days and escalating from physical assault to written threats to physical obstruction accompanied by verbal threats against children, demonstrates the need for court intervention. The court in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), affirmed that a magistrate's finding of multiple acts of domestic violence supported the issuance of a long-term protective order with communication restrictions. Petitioner's situation is analogous: he has documented three distinct incidents of threatening and violent conduct within a brief window of time, establishing a clear pattern of domestic violence.
The Alaska Supreme Court further held in State v. Strane, 61 P.3d 1284 (Alaska 2003), that the provisions of AS 18.66.956(1) through (7) set out distinct and enforceable categories of protective relief, and that knowing violation of any such provision constitutes a criminal offense. This underscores the importance of obtaining a comprehensive protective order that clearly delineates all prohibited conduct.
B. PETITIONER IS ENTITLED TO AN ORDER REQUIRING SARAH BERGSTROM TO VACATE THE MARITAL RESIDENCE
Under AS 18.66.100(c)(3), a protective order may "remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence." This provision applies even where the respondent has a property interest in the home. Because Sarah Bergstrom has committed physical violence within the shared residence and has made ongoing threats that make continued cohabitation dangerous, removal of Respondent from the residence is both authorized and necessary.
Additionally, AS 25.24.140(b)(3) expressly authorizes the court, during the pendency of a family law action, to direct one spouse to vacate the marital residence or the home of the other spouse. Petitioner and the minor children should not be displaced from their home as a result of Respondent's violent and threatening conduct. Requiring Respondent to vacate will allow Petitioner and the children to remain in familiar, stable surroundings during a period of significant upheaval.
C. PETITIONER IS ENTITLED TO AN ORDER PROHIBITING SARAH BERGSTROM FROM CONTACTING HIM OR THE MINOR CHILDREN
Under AS 18.66.100(c)(1), a protective order may prohibit the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. Under AS 18.66.100(c)(2), a protective order may prohibit the respondent from "telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner." Respondent has already used text messaging to threaten Petitioner, and she has made verbal threats in person. A no-contact provision encompassing all forms of direct and indirect communication is essential to prevent further threatening conduct.
With respect to the minor children, AS 18.66.100(c)(9) authorizes the court to award temporary custody of minor children to the petitioner and to arrange for visitation only where the safety of the child and the petitioner can be protected. Respondent directly threatened to harm the children during the October 17, 2024 incident. That threat, directed at the children in the context of coercing Petitioner, raises serious concerns about the children's immediate safety in Respondent's presence. Petitioner requests that the court award him temporary custody of the minor children and permit contact between Respondent and the children only under conditions that fully protect the children's safety.
Under AS 25.24.140(b)(4), during the pendency of a domestic relations action, the court may restrain a spouse from communicating directly or indirectly with the other spouse. This independent statutory basis further supports the issuance of a comprehensive no-contact order.
Importantly, AS 18.66.130(a) provides that an invitation by the petitioner to have otherwise prohibited contact does not waive or nullify any provision of a protective order. Petitioner is aware that any future invitation to communicate would not eliminate the legal protections of the order, and he does not intend to issue such an invitation.
D. PETITIONER IS ENTITLED TO AN ORDER REQUIRING SARAH BERGSTROM TO REMAIN AT LEAST 500 FEET FROM HIS WORKPLACE AND THE CHILDREN'S SCHOOL
Under AS 18.66.100(c)(4), a protective order may "direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member under all circumstances." E. AN EX PARTE PROTECTIVE ORDER SHOULD ISSUE IMMEDIATELY GIVEN THE ONGOING DANGER
Under AS 18.66.110(a), the court shall issue an ex parte protective order without notice to the respondent where the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred, that it is necessary to protect the petitioner, and that the petitioner has certified in writing the efforts made to provide notice. Petitioner has certified those efforts with this filing. The three incidents, including a physical assault with documented injury, written threats, and threats against the children made while Petitioner was physically prevented from leaving the property, establish probable cause well beyond any doubt. The escalating nature of the conduct over fourteen days demonstrates that further harm is likely if an order is not issued on an emergency basis before a hearing can be scheduled.
Civil Rule 65(b) similarly authorizes a temporary restraining order without notice where specific facts establish that immediate and irreparable injury will result before the adverse party can be heard. Petitioner's documented injuries and the ongoing verbal and written threats satisfy this standard. Petitioner respectfully requests that the court issue an ex parte temporary protective order immediately, to be followed by a hearing on a long-term order as provided by AS 18.66.100(b).
F. MEDIATION IS PROHIBITED IN THIS PROCEEDING
AS 18.66.130(c) expressly states that a court may not order parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition for a protective order. Civil Rule 100(a) similarly provides that mediation may not be ordered between the parties to, or in, a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through AS 18.66.180. No referral to mediation is appropriate in this proceeding.
G. PETITIONER'S ADDRESS AND CONTACT INFORMATION SHOULD BE PROTECTED
Civil Rule 942 provides that a pro se petitioner in a domestic violence protective order proceeding under AS 18.66.100 or AS 18.66.110 may submit mailing address and telephone number on a separate form, omitting such information from other filed pleadings, with access limited to the court and authorized personnel. Given that Respondent has expressly threatened Petitioner to prevent him from seeking legal counsel, and given the risk that disclosure of Petitioner's location could expose him to further threats or violence, Petitioner respectfully requests that the court allow him to file his address and contact information on a separate protected form consistent with Civil Rule 65.1.
H. THE STANDING PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION UNDER CIVIL RULE 65(e) APPLIES TO THIS ACTION
Civil Rule 65(e) provides that a standing injunction may be issued in domestic relations actions restraining the parties from, among other things, "threatening, harassing, or harming the other party." This rule operates in conjunction with the protective order statutes to establish a floor of minimum conduct protections for both parties from the outset of any domestic relations action. Respondent's ongoing threatening conduct is in direct violation of the conduct standards applicable to domestic relations proceedings under this rule.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Marcus Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court:

2. Order that Sarah Bergstrom immediately vacate the shared marital residence at Anchorage, Alaska, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3) and AS 25.24.140(b)(3);
3. Prohibit Sarah Bergstrom from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with Petitioner or the minor children, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(1) and (c)(2);
4. Direct Sarah Bergstrom to stay at least 500 feet away from Petitioner's place of employment and the children's school, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4);
5. Award Petitioner temporary custody of the minor children during the pendency of these proceedings, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(9);
6. Authorize Petitioner to file his address and contact information on a separate protected form pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1; and

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0153)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Colby respectfully requests that this Court issue a domestic violence protective order against Respondent Jennifer Colby pursuant to AS 18.66.100. Renee and Jennifer Colby are married spouses who have shared a residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately four years. On March 2, 2025, Jennifer physically attacked Renee by grabbing her hair and slamming her head into a kitchen wall, causing a laceration that required emergency medical treatment. On March 16, 2025, Jennifer sent threatening text messages to Renee and appeared uninvited at Renee's workplace, where she screamed threats in front of Renee's coworkers. These acts constitute crimes involving domestic violence and demonstrate an ongoing pattern of intimidation and physical harm. Renee seeks an order prohibiting Jennifer from contacting her, requiring Jennifer to vacate the shared residence, and directing Jennifer to remain at least 500 feet from Renee's home, workplace, and vehicle. As set forth below, the evidence more than satisfies the preponderance standard required under Alaska law, and the relief Renee requests is expressly authorized by statute.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Colby and Jennifer Colby are legally married and have lived together at the same Anchorage address for approximately four years, making them household members within the meaning of Alaska domestic violence law.
On March 2, 2025, Jennifer grabbed Renee by the hair and forcefully slammed Renee's head against the kitchen wall of their shared residence. The blow caused a laceration serious enough to require stitches at Providence Alaska Medical Center. Medical records from that visit document the injury and the circumstances as reported by Renee at the time of treatment. This physical assault constitutes a crime involving domestic violence committed by Jennifer against Renee in the home they share.
On March 16, 2025, two weeks after the physical assault, Jennifer escalated her threatening conduct. Jennifer sent Renee a series of text messages stating, in substance, "If you try to leave me, I will make sure you regret it." That same day, Jennifer appeared at Renee's workplace without invitation and screamed threats at Renee in front of her coworkers. This conduct caused Renee fear for her physical safety and created a hostile and dangerous situation at her place of employment.
Renee has made no invitation to Jennifer to engage in threatening or harassing behavior. Renee continues to fear for her safety because she and Jennifer currently share the same residence and Jennifer has demonstrated both the willingness to commit violence and the intent to intimidate Renee should Renee attempt to leave the relationship.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petition for a domestic violence protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide at least 10 days' notice to the respondent. If the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order relief under AS 18.66.925, regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that courts are granted broad discretion in fashioning protective relief in domestic violence cases. In Wee v. Eggener, 225 P.3d 1120 (Alaska 2010), the court recognized the wide scope of remedial authority available to trial courts in domestic violence proceedings. In Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), the court confirmed that protective relief under AS 18.66.100(c)(1), prohibiting the respondent from threatening or committing further domestic violence, remains effective until further order of the court, while relief under AS 18.66.100(c)(2) through (16) is effective for one year unless earlier dissolved.
Venue for this petition is proper in Anchorage under Civil Rule 3(h), which provides that a petition for a domestic violence protective order may be filed in the judicial district or court location closest to where the petitioner currently resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. All three locations are in Anchorage, Alaska.
Because Renee is appearing pro se, she is entitled under Civil Rule 65.1 to submit her mailing address and telephone number on a separate form, omitting that information from other pleadings, with access to that form limited to the court and authorized court system personnel.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Jennifer Colby Has Committed Crimes Involving Domestic Violence Against Renee Colby, Satisfying the Preponderance Standard.
The preponderance standard under AS 18.66.100(b) requires Renee to show that it is more likely than not that Jennifer committed a crime involving domestic violence. The evidence here easily satisfies that standard.
The March 2, 2025 incident involved Jennifer grabbing Renee by the hair and slamming her head against the kitchen wall hard enough to require stitches. This constitutes physical assault between household members and is unambiguously a crime of domestic violence. The injury was documented at Providence Alaska Medical Center and occurred inside the home the parties share.
The March 16, 2025 conduct constitutes criminal threatening and harassment. Jennifer's text messages, explicitly warning Renee that she would "regret" any attempt to leave, and Jennifer's uninvited appearance at Renee's workplace where she screamed threats in front of colleagues, demonstrate an intent to intimidate and control Renee through the threat of harm.
The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020), that conduct such as going to a protected party's location without invitation, after having been instructed to stay away, can independently support a finding of domestic violence sufficient to sustain a protective order. Here, Jennifer appeared at Renee's workplace without invitation following a prior act of physical violence, in a manner plainly calculated to intimidate and threaten Renee.
The court in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), addressed the interplay between ongoing conduct and protective order proceedings, recognizing that a course of threatening and physically violent behavior supports the entry of broad protective relief. Renee's situation reflects precisely that kind of escalating danger.
Finally, under AS 18.66.961, the court may not deny a petition solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. This provision ensures that Renee's petition cannot be dismissed on timing grounds alone. Both incidents are recent, and both are directly relevant to Renee's current safety.
B. The Specific Relief Renee Requests Is Expressly Authorized by Statute.
Renee requests three categories of protective relief, each of which is expressly authorized under AS 18.66.100(c).
First, Renee requests that Jennifer be prohibited from threatening, contacting, or otherwise communicating with Renee directly or indirectly. This relief is authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(1) and (c)(2). Jennifer's threatening text messages on March 16, 2025, demonstrate that electronic and written contact poses a direct threat to Renee's safety and peace of mind.
Second, Renee requests that Jennifer be required to vacate the shared residence. This relief is expressly authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(3), which permits the court to "remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence." The shared home is the site of the March 2, 2025 physical assault, and it is not safe for Renee to continue residing there with Jennifer.
Third, Renee requests that Jennifer be ordered to stay at least 500 feet away from Renee's home, workplace, and vehicle. This relief is authorized by AS 18.66.100(c)(4) and (c)(5). Jennifer has already demonstrated that she will appear uninvited at Renee's workplace to scream threats, and the workplace no-contact provision is essential to protecting Renee's ability to remain employed and safe. The stay-away provision as to the vehicle is authorized because Jennifer's threatening conduct encompasses control over Renee's freedom of movement.
Under AS 18.66.130(a), any invitation by Renee to Jennifer to communicate or enter the residence or vehicle would not waive or nullify any provision of the protective order. This provision is particularly important given the history of abusive relationships in which a victim may feel pressured to make contact with an abuser; the Legislature has expressly provided that such contact cannot be weaponized against the petitioner.
The court also has authority under AS 18.66.100(c)(16) to "order other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member under all circumstances," which provides an independent basis for any additional protective measures the court deems appropriate to address Jennifer's escalating pattern of violence and intimidation.
C. Renee's Request Reflects Sound Policy and Is Consistent With the Purpose of Alaska's Domestic Violence Statutes.
The Legislature enacted Alaska's domestic violence protective order framework to provide swift and effective protection to victims of domestic violence. In Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that courts handling domestic violence matters must be attentive to the safety of the victim throughout the proceedings. Criminal no-contact conditions may coexist with civil protective order proceedings, and courts are directed to fashion relief that actually protects the petitioner.
AS 18.66.130(e) provides that a protective order issued under the chapter is "in addition to and not in place of any other civil or criminal remedy," and that a petitioner is not barred from seeking an order because of the existence of another civil action between the parties. The parties' marital status is therefore no barrier to this petition; it is, if anything, a reason the court should take particular care to ensure Renee's safety.
AS 18.66.130(c) further provides that the court may not order the parties into mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition for a domestic violence protective order. This reflects the Legislature's recognition that mediation is inappropriate where, as here, a power imbalance created by violence and threats makes voluntary negotiation unsafe and ineffective.
The evidentiary record in this matter, including medical records from Providence Alaska Medical Center documenting the March 2, 2025 injury and text message records from March 16, 2025, supports each element of the relief requested. Renee's testimony as a spouse in a civil proceeding is permissible; Alaska R. Evid. 907(a) expressly provides an exception to spousal immunity in civil proceedings brought by one spouse against the other spouse. Accordingly, Renee's own testimony is fully available to support this petition.
V. CONCLUSION
The evidence before this Court demonstrates, by a preponderance, that Jennifer Colby has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Renee Colby, including a physical assault on March 2, 2025, that caused injuries requiring emergency medical treatment, and threatening conduct on March 16, 2025, directed at Renee at her workplace and via text message. These acts, committed by a household member within the meaning of Alaska's domestic violence statutes, entitle Renee to the full protection of AS 18.66.100.
Renee Colby respectfully requests that this Court enter a domestic violence protective order:
(1) prohibiting Jennifer Colby from threatening, harassing, or otherwise committing domestic violence against Renee Colby, effective until further order of the Court pursuant to AS 18.66.100(b)(1);
(2) prohibiting Jennifer Colby from contacting or communicating with Renee Colby in any manner, directly or indirectly;
(3) removing and excluding Jennifer Colby from the shared Anchorage residence, regardless of ownership;
(4) directing Jennifer Colby to remain at least 500 feet away from Renee Colby's residence, workplace, and vehicle; and
(5) ordering any other relief the Court deems necessary to protect Renee Colby's safety and well-being pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).
Renee Colby is appearing pro se and respectfully requests that the Court permit her to submit her contact information on a separate confidential form pursuant to Civil Rule 65.1.

Elena Petrova, Petitioner, respectfully moves this Court to issue a domestic violence protective order against her husband, Brandon Petrova, Respondent, pursuant to AS 18.66.932. II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Petrova, age 34, and Brandon Petrova, age 37, are married and have resided together at a shared residence in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately six years. Their relationship qualifies them as household members under Alaska law.
On the evening of October 3, 2024, Brandon grabbed Elena by the throat, slammed her against the kitchen wall, and explicitly threatened to kill her if she attempted to leave the marriage. This assault caused visible bruising to Elena's neck and shoulder. Brandon's conduct on that date constitutes assault, a crime against the person under AS 11.41, committed by a household member against another household member.
On October 17, 2024, approximately two weeks after the physical assault, Brandon appeared uninvited at Elena's place of employment in Anchorage. He screamed profanities at Elena in front of her coworkers and stated, "You will regret this," before security personnel escorted him from the building. This conduct constitutes harassment and threatening behavior that confirms a continuing pattern of domestic violence.
Elena now petitions this Court for a protective order that: (1) prohibits Brandon from contacting her in person, by telephone, or through third parties; (2) requires Brandon to vacate the shared Anchorage residence; and (3) directs Brandon to remain at least 500 feet from her home, workplace, and vehicle.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petition for a protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide at least 10 days' notice to the respondent. If the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.962, regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
Alaska law defines "domestic violence" and "crime involving domestic violence" to include crimes against the person under AS 11.41 committed by a household member against another household member. AS 18.66.990(3)(A). The term "household member" expressly includes adults who are current or former spouses. AS 18.66.990(5)(A).
A court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.100(e)(1). Once the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that domestic violence has occurred, it holds broad discretion to fashion appropriate relief to protect the petitioner. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018).
Venue for this petition is proper under Civil Rule 3(h), which permits filing in the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Brandon Petrova Has Committed Crimes Involving Domestic Violence Against Elena Petrova
The preponderance of evidence standard requires that Elena demonstrate it is more likely than not that Brandon committed crimes involving domestic violence against her. She readily meets this burden.
Brandon's actions on October 3, 2024, including grabbing Elena by the throat, slamming her against a wall, and threatening to kill her, constitute assault and threatening conduct directed at a household member. These acts are crimes against the person under AS 11.41. Because Brandon is Elena's current spouse and they have lived together for six years, he is unquestionably a household member as that term is defined under AS 18.66.990(5)(A). The resulting bruising to Elena's neck and shoulder is direct physical evidence corroborating that the assault occurred.
Brandon's conduct on October 17, 2024, at Elena's workplace further demonstrates a continuing pattern of threatening and harassing behavior. His statement, "You will regret this," combined with screaming profanities at Elena in front of coworkers, constitutes harassment and threatening conduct committed by a household member. This incident satisfies the definition of domestic violence under AS 18.66.990(3)(A) and (H).
Together, these two incidents establish by a preponderance of the evidence that Brandon has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Elena. This Court therefore has full authority under AS 18.66.100(b) to issue a protective order granting the relief requested.

AS 18.66.100(c)(1) authorizes this Court to prohibit Brandon from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the Court to prohibit Brandon from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with Elena. Both provisions are squarely applicable here.

He traveled to Elena's workplace and publicly confronted her, evidencing a willingness to seek out Elena in contexts beyond the home. Accordingly, a prohibition on all contact, whether in person, by telephone, or through third parties, is necessary and appropriate to protect Elena from further harm.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must broadly construe the no-contact provisions of protective orders in order to give full effect to their protective purpose. Cooper v. Cooper, 144 P.3d 451 (Alaska 2006). The no-contact provisions of a protective order issued under AS 18.66.100(c)(2) encompass direct and indirect communications alike. It should also be noted that under AS 18.66.994, any invitation by Elena to communicate or have contact with Brandon would not waive or nullify any provision of the protective order. This protection is important given the dynamics of domestic violence relationships, where a victim may feel pressured or manipulated into permitting contact.
C. The Court Should Order Brandon to Vacate the Shared Residence and Maintain a 500-Foot Distance from Elena's Home, Workplace, and Vehicle
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the Court to remove and exclude Brandon from the shared Anchorage residence, regardless of ownership. AS 18.66.100(c)(5) authorizes the Court to prohibit Brandon from entering a vehicle in the possession of or occupied by Elena.

The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts possess broad authority under the protective order statute to fashion relief that is tailored to the specific circumstances of the case and necessary to protect the petitioner. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018). The specific distances and locations requested by Elena are directly responsive to the pattern of conduct Brandon has exhibited, and this Court should grant them.
D. Additional Statutory Protections Support the Requested Relief
AS 18.66.100(c)(16) authorizes this Court to order any other relief it determines is necessary to protect Elena or any household member. This catch-all provision reinforces the Legislature's intent that courts act decisively and comprehensively to protect victims of domestic violence. To the extent the specific relief requested by Elena is not fully encompassed by AS 18.66.100(c)(2) through (5), this Court may and should grant it under the authority of AS 18.66.100(c)(16).

Any argument by Brandon that Elena delayed in seeking relief is therefore legally insufficient as a basis to deny the petition.
Under AS 18.66.130(e), the protective order sought here would operate in addition to, and not in place of, any civil or criminal remedies available to Elena. The existence of this petition does not preclude Elena from pursuing other legal remedies, and the Court should not treat the availability of other remedies as a reason to limit or deny the relief requested.
E. The Court Should Consider an Ex Parte Emergency Protective Order Pending the Full Hearing
If Elena presents evidence demonstrating probable cause that domestic violence has occurred and that it is necessary to protect her from further domestic violence before the full hearing can be held, this Court has authority under AS 18.66.110(a) to issue an ex parte protective order without notice to Brandon. This protection is particularly important given Brandon's demonstrated willingness to seek out Elena at known locations.
Elena respectfully requests that the Court apply this confidentiality protection and ensure that her address and contact information are not disclosed to Brandon or made part of the public record.
V. CONCLUSION
The evidence presented in this petition establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that Brandon Petrova has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Elena Petrova, his spouse and household member.
