IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0155)
I. INTRODUCTION
Elena Larsen respectfully petitions this Court for a long-term domestic violence protective order against Danielle Larsen pursuant to AS 18.66.100. The facts of this case are grave. Within a span of five days, Danielle Larsen committed two separate and escalating acts of violence against Elena Larsen: a physical assault that required emergency medical treatment, followed by a direct, credible death threat made at gunpoint. Elena Larsen seeks an order prohibiting Danielle Larsen from contacting her in any form, requiring Danielle Larsen to vacate their shared residence, and prohibiting Danielle Larsen from possessing or using firearms for the duration of the protective order. The evidence presented satisfies every element required under Alaska law, and the relief requested is necessary to protect Elena Larsen from further, potentially lethal, harm.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Elena Larsen and Danielle Larsen are married and reside together in Anchorage, Alaska. As defined under AS 18.66.990(5)(A), current spouses qualify as household members for purposes of the domestic violence statutes.
On March 4, 2025, Danielle Larsen grabbed Elena Larsen by the hair and forcibly slammed her head against the kitchen wall of their shared residence. This assault caused a laceration that required emergency medical treatment at Providence Alaska Medical Center. The medical records from this visit document the injury and the circumstances under which it was sustained.
Five days later, on March 9, 2025, Elena Larsen informed Danielle Larsen of her intention to leave the marriage. In direct response to that statement, Danielle Larsen cornered Elena Larsen in their bedroom, raised a hunting rifle, pointed it directly at Elena Larsen, and stated: "If you try to leave, I will kill you and then myself." This statement constituted a direct, specific, and credible threat to take Elena Larsen's life, made while Danielle Larsen was in actual physical possession of a deadly weapon, specifically a hunting rifle.
Elena Larsen is a victim of crimes involving domestic violence as defined by AS 18.66.990(3). The physical assault of March 4, 2025, constitutes a crime against the person under AS 11.41, specifically assault causing physical injury. The armed threat of March 9, 2025, constitutes, at minimum, assault by threat of imminent physical injury, also a crime against the person under AS 11.41, committed while Danielle Larsen was in actual possession of a firearm. Both offenses were committed by a household member against another household member.
Elena Larsen now seeks this Court's protection before Danielle Larsen can carry out her stated threat.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petition for a protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide at least ten days' notice to the respondent. If, upon hearing, the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c), regardless of whether the respondent appears at the hearing.
AS 18.66.990(3) defines "domestic violence" and "crime involving domestic violence" to mean offenses including crimes against the person under AS 11.41, committed by a household member against another household member, or an attempt to commit such an offense.
AS 18.66.990(5)(A) defines "household member" to include adults who are current or former spouses. Because Elena Larsen and Danielle Larsen are married and residing together, Danielle Larsen qualifies as a household member whose conduct is subject to this chapter.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that placing a person in fear of imminent physical injury through words or conduct constitutes assault and qualifies as domestic violence. Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015). The court in that case also confirmed that brandishing a weapon and making a threat while in possession of that weapon is conduct that must be factored into the protective order and custody analysis. Id. Additionally, in Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), the court recognized that a history of physical assault, supported by contemporaneous reporting, provides a sufficient basis for granting protective relief.
Under AS 18.66.100(a), a person who is or has been a victim of a crime involving domestic violence may file a petition in the district or superior court for a protective order against a household member. Elena Larsen meets this standard.
Regarding venue, Civil Rule 3(h) provides that a petition or request for a protective order on domestic violence under AS 18.66 may be filed in the judicial district or court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. Because both parties reside in Anchorage and both incidents occurred in Anchorage, filing in this Court is proper.
Because Elena Larsen is appearing pro se, Civil Rule 65.1 permits her to submit her mailing address and telephone number on a separate confidential form and to omit that information from other pleadings, protecting her location from disclosure to the respondent.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. The Preponderance of the Evidence Establishes That Danielle Larsen Has Committed Crimes Involving Domestic Violence Against Elena Larsen.
The legal threshold for issuance of a long-term protective order under AS 18.66.100(b) is proof by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner. This is a more-likely-than-not standard, and the evidence here far exceeds it.
First, the assault of March 4, 2025, is documented by emergency medical records from Providence Alaska Medical Center. Danielle Larsen grabbed Elena Larsen by the hair and slammed her head against a wall, causing a laceration requiring emergency treatment. Physical assault causing injury is a crime against the person under AS 11.41 and therefore constitutes domestic violence as defined by AS 18.66.990(3)(A).
Second, the threat of March 9, 2025, was direct, specific, and accompanied by the display of a loaded hunting rifle pointed at Elena Larsen. Pointing a firearm at a person while declaring an intent to kill them constitutes, at minimum, assault by threat of imminent serious physical injury. As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), placing another person in fear of imminent physical injury by words or other conduct is assault, and brandishing a weapon while making a threat is conduct that qualifies as domestic violence. The court in John E. v. Andrea E., 445 P.3d 649 (Alaska 2019), similarly confirmed that the serious nature of the injury threatened, including conduct that could produce serious physical injury or death, is a critical factor in evaluating domestic violence claims.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also held that a history of escalating violence between household members is relevant to the court's assessment of danger, and that prior incidents need not each independently satisfy a heightened threshold where the totality of the conduct establishes domestic violence. Yelena R. v. George R., 326 P.3d 989 (Alaska 2014). Here, the two incidents over five days reflect a clear escalation, from physical assault to a credible death threat made at gunpoint.
Accordingly, Elena Larsen has established by a preponderance of the evidence that Danielle Larsen has committed crimes involving domestic violence against her, and the Court is authorized to grant the full range of relief under AS 18.66.100(c).
B. The Court Should Prohibit Danielle Larsen From Contacting Elena Larsen in Any Form.
AS 18.66.100(c)(1) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner.
Given Danielle Larsen's explicit statement that she would kill Elena Larsen if she attempted to leave, any further contact between the parties carries a substantial risk of further violence or intimidation. The no-contact provisions of AS 18.66.100(c)(1) and (c)(2) are precisely designed to sever this avenue of continued threat and coercion. The Court should order that Danielle Larsen be prohibited from contacting Elena Larsen in any form, including but not limited to telephone calls, text messages, electronic messages, social media contact, third-party contact, and any other direct or indirect communication.
The Alaska Supreme Court emphasized in Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), that a protective order exists not merely to acknowledge past misconduct but, primarily, to protect the petitioner from future harm. The credible death threat made at gunpoint on March 9, 2025, makes clear that Elena Larsen requires ongoing protection from all forms of contact by Danielle Larsen.
C. The Court Should Order Danielle Larsen to Vacate the Shared Residence.
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. AS 18.66.100(c)(4) further authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence of the petitioner.
Both incidents of domestic violence occurred inside the home that Elena Larsen and Danielle Larsen share. Allowing Danielle Larsen to remain in the residence would place Elena Larsen in immediate and ongoing danger. The right to exclude a respondent from a shared residence, regardless of who holds title, is expressly recognized under AS 18.66.100(c)(3). As the Alaska Supreme Court noted in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), ownership of a shared residence does not determine whether a respondent may be excluded when domestic violence has been established. The shared home is both the scene of the assaults and the ongoing location of danger. Exclusion of Danielle Larsen from that residence is necessary to protect Elena Larsen's safety and is squarely authorized by statute.
D. The Court Should Prohibit Danielle Larsen From Possessing or Using Firearms for the Duration of the Order.
AS 18.66.100(c)(6) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from using or possessing a deadly weapon if the court finds the respondent was in actual possession of or used a weapon during the commission of domestic violence. AS 18.66.100(c)(7) authorizes the court to direct the respondent to surrender any firearm owned or possessed by the respondent if the court finds that the respondent was in actual possession of or used a firearm during the commission of domestic violence.
On March 9, 2025, Danielle Larsen was in actual possession of a hunting rifle, which she pointed directly at Elena Larsen while making an explicit threat to kill her. This unambiguous conduct satisfies the statutory predicate for both the weapons prohibition and the firearm surrender order under AS 18.66.100(c)(6) and (c)(7). There is no question that Danielle Larsen both possessed and actively used a firearm as an instrument of intimidation and threatened lethal violence during the commission of an act of domestic violence.
The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), that the firearms provisions of AS 18.66.100(c)(6) and (c)(7) are available to the court under the appropriate factual circumstances. Those circumstances are unambiguously present here. Permitting Danielle Larsen to retain possession of the hunting rifle or any other firearm while a protective order is in effect would expose Elena Larsen to an ongoing risk of lethal harm. The Court should order the immediate surrender of all firearms in Danielle Larsen's possession and prohibit her from acquiring or possessing any deadly weapon for the duration of the protective order.
E. No Additional Procedural Barriers Exist to the Relief Requested.
AS 18.66.100(e) provides that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because there is a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. Although Elena Larsen is filing promptly after the incidents of March 4 and March 9, 2025, this provision confirms that even if some time were to elapse before filing, delay alone is not grounds for denial.
Moreover, AS 25.24.060(f) provides that the court may not order or refer parties to mediation in a divorce proceeding if a protective order issued or filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180 is in effect. Civil Rule 100(a) confirms that mediation may not be ordered in a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. These provisions collectively ensure that Danielle Larsen cannot seek to divert this matter into a mediation process in order to approach or pressure Elena Larsen. The parties' marital status does not diminish Elena Larsen's right to full protective relief, nor does it subject her to any mandatory mediation requirement. To the contrary, the existence of documented domestic violence forecloses any such referral.
With respect to evidence, the Court should be aware that Alaska R. Evid. 505(a)(2)(D)(v) provides that there is no spousal privilege in a proceeding involving a crime involving domestic violence as defined in AS 18.66.990. This means that any communications between Elena Larsen and Danielle Larsen that are relevant to the domestic violence at issue are admissible, and Danielle Larsen cannot invoke the marital communications privilege to shield her threatening statements or other relevant conduct from the Court's consideration.
V. CONCLUSION
Elena Larsen has established by more than a preponderance of the evidence that Danielle Larsen committed two serious crimes involving domestic violence against her within a five-day period: a physical assault causing a laceration requiring emergency medical treatment, and an armed death threat made at gunpoint. Both incidents were committed by a household member against another household member and are cognizable offenses under AS 18.66.990(3)(A).
The relief requested is expressly authorized by AS 18.66.100(c) and is necessary to protect Elena Larsen from further and potentially fatal harm. Specifically, Elena Larsen respectfully requests that the Court:
1. Issue a long-term protective order prohibiting Danielle Larsen from threatening, contacting, or communicating with Elena Larsen in any form, directly or indirectly, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(1) and (c)(2);
2. Order Danielle Larsen to vacate and remain away from the shared residence, regardless of ownership, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3) and (c)(4); and
3. Prohibit Danielle Larsen from possessing or using any deadly weapon and order her to surrender all firearms currently in her possession, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(6) and (c)(7).
Elena Larsen respectfully urges the Court to grant this petition in full. The facts are documented, the legal standard is satisfied, and the need for protection is urgent.

AS 18.66.100(b) authorizes this Court to issue a protective order upon a finding by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner. He grabbed Petitioner by the throat, slammed her against a kitchen wall, and threatened to kill her, resulting in visible bruising to her neck and shoulder. The facts presented here satisfy the preponderance standard and warrant the issuance of a protective order.

AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the Court to remove and exclude a respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership. AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the Court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner, or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member. AS 18.66.100(c)(5) authorizes the Court to prohibit the respondent from entering a propelled vehicle in the possession of or occupied by the petitioner.

AS 25.24.140(b)(3) likewise confirms that during the pendency of a domestic relations action, a spouse is entitled to orders directing the other spouse to vacate the marital residence or the home of the other spouse. Granting Petitioner exclusive use and possession of the marital home is precisely the kind of relief contemplated by AS 18.66.100(c)(3) and AS 25.24.140(b)(3).
The Alaska Supreme Court in Jmr v. Str, 15 P.3d 253 (Alaska 2001), confirmed the breadth of the ex parte protective order process under AS 18.66.110 and the seriousness with which courts should approach requests to remove a respondent from a shared residence. The protective order statute is designed to empower victims to reclaim safety and stability in their daily lives, and granting Petitioner exclusive use of the marital home serves that purpose directly.
E. AN EX PARTE PROTECTIVE ORDER IS WARRANTED PENDING THE FULL HEARING
Under AS 18.66.110(a), a court shall issue an ex parte protective order without notice to the respondent if the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred, it is necessary to protect the petitioner from domestic violence, and the petitioner has certified in writing the efforts made to provide notice to the respondent. The combination of physical injury already inflicted and ongoing threatening behavior satisfies this standard.
An ex parte protective order under AS 18.66.110(a) may grant the protections provided by AS 18.66.100(c)(1) through (5), (8) through (12), and (16), which includes all of the relief Petitioner seeks in this matter. Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court enter such an order immediately and schedule a full hearing within the 20-day period provided by the statute.
F. MEDIATION IS NOT APPROPRIATE IN THIS PROCEEDING
AS 18.66.130(c) expressly prohibits the Court from ordering or referring the parties to mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition for a protective order. Civil Rule 100(a) likewise confirms that mediation may not be ordered between the parties to a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. Similarly, AS 25.24.140(d) provides that the Court may not order or refer parties to mediation or family counseling when a protective order issued or filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180 is in effect.
Accordingly, Petitioner specifically requests that this Court not refer the parties to mediation or any form of alternative dispute resolution in connection with this petition. The Legislature has made clear that the safety concerns underlying domestic violence proceedings make mediation inappropriate, and the facts of this case, involving a death threat and physical assault, confirm the wisdom of that policy.
V. CONCLUSION
Petitioner Ashley Bergstrom has presented clear and specific facts establishing that Respondent Brandon Bergstrom committed crimes involving domestic violence against her, including a physical assault causing visible injury and multiple explicit threats to her life and safety. The evidence more than satisfies the preponderance of the evidence standard required under AS 18.66.100(b) for issuance of a domestic violence protective order.
Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Issue an immediate ex parte protective order under AS 18.66.110(a) prohibiting Respondent from contacting Petitioner in person, by telephone, or electronically, pending a full hearing;
2. Upon full hearing, issue a protective order under AS 18.66.100 prohibiting Respondent from threatening, contacting, or communicating with Petitioner in any manner;

4. Grant Petitioner exclusive use and possession of the marital home, excluding Respondent from that residence, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3) and AS 25.24.140(b)(3); and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems necessary to protect Petitioner from further domestic violence, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).

The court is similarly instructed that it may not deny a petition solely because of a lapse of time between the act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.100(e)(1).
The relief available upon a finding of domestic violence is broad. Under AS 18.66.100(c), the court may prohibit the respondent from contacting the petitioner by any means, remove and exclude the respondent from the petitioner's residence, direct the respondent to stay away from the petitioner's place of employment, and grant the petitioner possession and use of a shared vehicle. All of these forms of relief are expressly authorized and applicable to the facts of this case.
Under AS 18.66.901, a petitioner who fears imminent danger may also seek an ex parte protective order prior to the full hearing. An ex parte order may be issued without notice to the respondent if the court finds probable cause that a crime of domestic violence has occurred and that the order is necessary to protect the petitioner. An ex parte protective order expires twenty days after it is issued unless dissolved earlier by the court.
Additionally, AS 18.66.130(a) makes clear that even if the respondent is invited by the petitioner to make contact after an order is issued, that invitation does not waive or nullify any provision of the protective order. This provision is important in the domestic violence context because it protects petitioners from arguments that any subsequent contact was consensual.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. TOMAS HAS ESTABLISHED BY A PREPONDERANCE OF THE EVIDENCE THAT COLIN COMMITTED CRIMES INVOLVING DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AGAINST HIM
The two incidents described above, the physical assault and death threat on March 4, 2024, and the workplace confrontation on March 18, 2024, each independently constitute crimes involving domestic violence as defined under Alaska law. Together, they establish a pattern of escalating violence and intimidation that fully satisfies the preponderance standard of AS 18.66.100(b).
The March 4 incident involved Colin grabbing Tomas by the throat and shoving him into a kitchen cabinet. These acts constitute physical assault: intentional, unlawful physical contact made without Tomas's consent and causing pain and physical impact. Colin's accompanying statement that he would kill Tomas if he ever tried to leave constitutes criminal threatening, a separate crime involving domestic violence. Colin made this threat immediately after committing a physical assault, lending it credibility and causing Tomas to fear for his life. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts must evaluate threatening statements in context, and here the context is unambiguous: Colin used physical force and then delivered a death threat to prevent Tomas from exercising his legal right to separate from the marriage. Williams v. Barbee, 243 P.3d 995 (Alaska 2010).
The March 18 incident further demonstrates that Colin's threatening conduct is deliberate, premeditated, and continuing. Colin traveled to Tomas's workplace, located his car, and physically blocked it so that Tomas could not leave. This act alone constitutes unlawful restraint. Colin then screamed threats in front of Tomas's coworkers, causing public humiliation and fear. This conduct reinforces that Colin's behavior is not an isolated outburst but rather a calculated effort to control, intimidate, and harm Tomas.
Together, these incidents satisfy the preponderance standard. The evidence demonstrates that Colin has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Tomas on at least two occasions within a two-week period, and the escalating nature of the conduct places Tomas at ongoing and serious risk of harm.
B. THE COURT SHOULD PROHIBIT COLIN FROM CONTACTING TOMAS BY ANY MEANS
AS 18.66.100(c)(2) expressly authorizes the court to prohibit a respondent from "telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner." Given Colin's history of physically assaulting Tomas and threatening to kill him, and given that Colin has already demonstrated his willingness to track Tomas to his workplace and confront him publicly, a complete no-contact order is necessary and appropriate.
Permitting any form of contact, whether in person, by telephone, or electronically, would expose Tomas to further intimidation, harassment, and potential violence. The pattern of escalation from the March 4 home assault to the March 18 workplace confrontation demonstrates that Colin does not recognize boundaries and will use whatever means of access he has to continue threatening Tomas. Only a comprehensive no-contact prohibition will provide Tomas with the protection he needs.
Additionally, AS 18.66.100(c)(4) permits the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the petitioner's place of employment. Given that Colin appeared uninvited at Tomas's workplace and screamed threats in front of his coworkers, an order requiring Colin to stay away from Tomas's place of employment is independently warranted. Tomas should not be forced to fear for his safety at work or to worry that further confrontations will jeopardize his employment.
The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized the importance of comprehensive protective relief in domestic violence cases where the respondent has demonstrated a willingness to pursue the petitioner across locations. Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007). The facts here compel the same conclusion.
C. THE COURT SHOULD REQUIRE COLIN TO VACATE THE MARITAL HOME
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to "remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence." This provision applies here even though the home is the shared marital residence. The plain language of the statute makes clear that ownership is not a bar to exclusion: Colin may be ordered to leave even if he holds an ownership interest in the property.
Requiring Colin to vacate the marital home is essential to Tomas's safety. Colin has already committed physical violence against Tomas in that home and has threatened to kill him in that same space. If Colin is permitted to remain in the home alongside Tomas, Tomas will continue to face the daily risk of physical assault and further threats. The home, which should be a place of safety, has instead become a site of violence and fear.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that removal of a respondent from the shared residence is a core protective remedy in domestic violence proceedings, and that courts should not hesitate to order such relief when the petitioner's safety requires it. Thomas E. Jordan v. Cheryl A. Jordan, 867 P.3d 536 (Alaska 2021). Here, that safety imperative is clear. Tomas has nowhere else to go if he is forced to leave the marital home, and it would be unjust to require a victim of domestic violence to abandon his own residence while his abuser remains inside.
Additionally, AS 25.24.140(b)(3) independently authorizes the court, during the pendency of a related divorce or separation action, to direct one spouse to vacate the marital residence or the home of the other spouse. Even setting aside the protective order statute, this provision confirms that the legislature has specifically contemplated and authorized this relief in the context of married parties experiencing domestic violence.
D. THE COURT SHOULD GRANT TOMAS TEMPORARY EXCLUSIVE USE OF THE SHARED VEHICLE
AS 18.66.100(c)(10) authorizes the court to give the petitioner "possession and use of a vehicle and other essential personal items, including a pet, regardless of ownership of the items under all circumstances." Tomas requests that the court award him temporary exclusive use of the vehicle shared by the parties.
Tomas's ability to use the shared vehicle is essential to his safety and independence. Without access to reliable transportation, Tomas cannot get to and from work, cannot seek medical care or legal assistance, and cannot take other steps to protect himself from further violence. Colin has already demonstrated, on March 18, 2024, that he is willing to use the vehicle as a tool of control by physically blocking Tomas's car to prevent him from driving away. Allowing Colin to retain access to the shared vehicle would give him an ongoing means of exercising coercive control over Tomas's movements.
The relief requested under AS 18.66.100(c)(10) does not require Tomas to demonstrate that he is the sole or primary owner of the vehicle. The statute expressly applies "regardless of ownership," meaning that any ownership interest Colin may hold is not a basis for denying this relief. The court need only find that awarding Tomas possession and use of the vehicle is appropriate given the circumstances, and the facts presented here plainly support that finding.
E. THE COURT MAY NOT ORDER MEDIATION IN THIS MATTER
The Court should note that mediation is not an appropriate or permissible resolution mechanism in this case. Under AS 18.66.130(c), a court may not order parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition for a protective order filed under AS 18.66.100. Civil Rule 100(a) further specifies that mediation may not be ordered between the parties to a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. Likewise, AS 25.24.060(f) provides that the court may not order or refer parties to mediation in a divorce proceeding if a protective order issued or filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180 is in effect.
These provisions reflect the legislature's recognition that mediation in a domestic violence context is inherently coercive and potentially dangerous, as it may expose victims to further intimidation. If the parties' marriage leads to a related divorce proceeding, these statutory protections remain in force.
F. ADDITIONAL PROTECTIVE MEASURES ARE WARRANTED UNDER THE CIRCUMSTANCES
AS 18.66.100(c)(16) authorizes the court to "order other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member." Given the severity and escalating nature of Colin's conduct, Tomas respectfully requests that the court consider any additional measures it deems necessary to ensure his safety.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that protective orders must be fashioned to address the specific dangers a respondent poses to the petitioner, and that courts have broad discretion under the statute to craft relief that meets those needs. Reed v. Parrish, 868 P.3d 896 (Alaska 2012). Colin has demonstrated that he will pursue Tomas to multiple locations and use both physical force and verbal threats to intimidate him. The court is empowered to respond comprehensively to that threat.
Furthermore, if Tomas proceeds as a self-represented petitioner, Civil Rule 65.1 permits him to submit his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form, omitting this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court, with access to that information limited to the court and authorized personnel. This protection is particularly important here, as Colin has already demonstrated his willingness to track Tomas to his workplace, and disclosure of Tomas's address through court records could further endanger him.
V. CONCLUSION
The evidence presented in this brief establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that Respondent Colin Petrova has committed crimes involving domestic violence against Petitioner Tomas Petrova on at least two separate occasions within a two-week period. The acts involved physical assault, a credible death threat made during ongoing violence, and a subsequent confrontation at Tomas's workplace in which Colin blocked his vehicle and screamed threats in public. The pattern of conduct is serious, escalating, and ongoing.
Tomas Petrova respectfully requests that this Court issue a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 that:
1. Prohibits Colin Petrova from contacting Tomas Petrova in person, by telephone, electronically, or by any other direct or indirect means, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(2);
2. Requires Colin Petrova to stay away from Tomas Petrova's place of employment and all other places Tomas frequents, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(4);
3. Removes and excludes Colin Petrova from the marital residence, regardless of ownership, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3);
4. Awards Tomas Petrova temporary exclusive possession and use of the shared vehicle, regardless of ownership, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(10); and
5. Orders any other relief the Court determines necessary to protect Tomas Petrova from further domestic violence, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).
The statutory authority is clear, the facts are compelling, and the relief requested is narrowly tailored to address the specific and ongoing danger that Colin Petrova poses to Tomas Petrova. This Court should grant the petition in full.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0158)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Larsen respectfully petitions this Court for a domestic violence protective order against his brother, Wesley Larsen, pursuant to AS 18.66.100. The two men share a residence at 412 Birch Creek Road in Fairbanks, Alaska, and therefore qualify as household members under Alaska's domestic violence statutes. Over the course of one week in March 2025, Wesley Larsen twice subjected David Larsen to acts of domestic violence: first by physically shoving him into a kitchen counter, and second by appearing in his bedroom doorway while holding a hunting knife and delivering an explicit verbal threat. These acts, taken together, establish by a preponderance of the evidence that David Larsen has been a victim of domestic violence committed by a household member and that immediate, sustained court protection is necessary to preserve his safety.
David Larsen requests that this Court issue a protective order prohibiting Wesley Larsen from communicating with him in any manner, requiring Wesley Larsen to vacate the shared residence at 412 Birch Creek Road, and prohibiting Wesley Larsen from possessing firearms or other deadly weapons for the duration of the order. Each form of relief is expressly authorized by AS 18.66.100(c) and is warranted by the facts presented.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Larsen and his brother Wesley Larsen are adult household members who have resided together at 412 Birch Creek Road in Fairbanks, Alaska, at all times relevant to this petition. Their cohabitation makes each a "household member" of the other within the meaning of Alaska's domestic violence statutes.
On March 3, 2025, Wesley Larsen and David Larsen became involved in an argument concerning unpaid rent obligations. During that argument, Wesley Larsen shoved David Larsen forcefully into the kitchen counter. The impact caused visible bruising to David Larsen's lower back. This physical contact was not accidental: it was an intentional act of force directed at David Larsen during an interpersonal confrontation in their shared home.
On March 9, 2025, just six days after the physical assault, Wesley Larsen escalated his threatening conduct. He appeared in the doorway of David Larsen's bedroom holding a hunting knife. Standing there, Wesley stated to David: "Next time you run your mouth, I will make sure you regret it." Wesley's possession of the knife during this encounter, combined with the explicit threat, constituted both a threatening display of a deadly weapon and a direct verbal threat of future physical harm.
David Larsen now fears for his safety within the shared residence. Because Wesley Larsen continues to reside at 412 Birch Creek Road, David Larsen remains in ongoing proximity to his abuser. David Larsen files this petition seeking court intervention to protect his physical safety and well-being. This petition is filed in the judicial district where the domestic violence occurred and where both parties currently reside, as authorized by Civil Rule 3(h).
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petitioner files for a domestic violence protective order, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide the respondent with notice and an opportunity to be heard. If the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c). The preponderance standard requires only that the petitioner demonstrate that it is more likely than not that the acts of domestic violence occurred.
In emergency circumstances, AS 18.66.110(a) authorizes the court to issue an ex parte protective order, without prior notice to the respondent, upon a finding of probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that the protective order is necessary to protect the petitioner. An ex parte order remains in effect for 20 days unless dissolved earlier.
Alaska courts have recognized that the primary purpose of a protective order is to protect the petitioner from future harm, not merely to acknowledge a past wrong. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018). The Alaska Supreme Court has further confirmed that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because time has elapsed between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.100(e). This principle ensures that victims who face ongoing threats are not penalized for any delay in seeking court protection.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also emphasized that the issuance of a protective order is a forward-looking remedy, designed to protect petitioners from continuing danger. Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018). The facts presented in this petition demonstrate both a history of physical violence and an escalating pattern of threatening behavior, fully satisfying the legal standard for the relief requested.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. David Larsen Is a Victim of Domestic Violence Committed by a Household Member, Satisfying the Threshold Requirement for a Protective Order.
AS 18.66.100(a) provides that a person who is or has been a victim of a crime involving domestic violence may file a petition for a protective order against a household member. David Larsen and Wesley Larsen are brothers who share a residence, making them household members as defined under Alaska law. The acts committed by Wesley Larsen on March 3 and March 9, 2025, each independently constitute crimes involving domestic violence: the March 3 shove into the kitchen counter constitutes assault by intentional physical contact causing injury, and the March 9 threat delivered while Wesley held a hunting knife constitutes threatening and menacing conduct with a deadly weapon.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts evaluating domestic violence petitions must carefully consider patterns of escalating behavior, not merely isolated incidents. Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007). Here, the conduct escalated from physical violence to a weapon-accompanied threat within six days, a trajectory that strongly supports the conclusion that David Larsen faces a genuine and ongoing risk of serious harm.
The preponderance of the evidence standard is readily satisfied. David Larsen experienced the shove firsthand, sustained visible bruising to his lower back, and personally heard Wesley's explicit threat while Wesley held a knife. These facts, taken together, establish that it is more likely than not that Wesley Larsen committed crimes of domestic violence against David Larsen. The Court should therefore proceed to address each form of relief requested.
B. The Court Should Prohibit Wesley Larsen from Contacting David Larsen in Any Manner.
AS 18.66.100(c)(1) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. AS 18.66.100(c)(2) further authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner.
Both forms of relief are warranted here. Wesley Larsen has already escalated from physical assault to armed verbal threats. Given this progression, any continued contact between Wesley and David Larsen poses a threat to David's safety. The no-contact provisions of AS 18.66.100(c)(1) and (c)(2) are designed precisely for situations such as this, where the respondent has demonstrated a willingness to use physical force and threatening language against the petitioner in their shared home.
Importantly, AS 18.66.130(a) makes clear that even if David Larsen were to invite contact after such an order is issued, that invitation would not waive or nullify any provision of the protective order. This statutory protection prevents the abusive dynamic present in many domestic violence relationships from undermining the force of the court's order.
Additionally, AS 18.66.130(c) expressly provides that a court may not order the parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition under AS 18.66.100 to 18.66.180. Civil Rule 100(a) reinforces this prohibition, confirming that mediation may not be ordered between the parties in a case filed under AS 18.66.100 to 18.66.180. Any suggestion that the parties should resolve this dispute through mediation or informal agreement would be contrary to both the statute and the applicable court rule.
C. The Court Should Order Wesley Larsen to Vacate the Shared Residence.
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) expressly authorizes the court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. AS 18.66.100(c)(4) further authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member.
These provisions directly address David Larsen's circumstances. The shared residence at 412 Birch Creek Road is the location where both acts of domestic violence occurred. The kitchen where Wesley shoved David and the bedroom doorway where Wesley appeared wielding a knife are both within the four walls of their shared home. So long as Wesley Larsen remains in the residence, David Larsen cannot feel safe in his own home, cannot sleep without fear of further assault, and cannot avoid the proximity to his abuser that enabled both incidents.
The legislature's inclusion of the phrase "regardless of ownership of the residence" in AS 18.66.100(c)(3) reflects a deliberate policy choice: a respondent's property interest in a shared home does not supersede the petitioner's right to physical safety within that home. This Court should therefore order Wesley Larsen to vacate 412 Birch Creek Road and to stay away from that address for the duration of the protective order.
D. The Court Should Prohibit Wesley Larsen from Possessing Firearms or Other Deadly Weapons.
AS 18.66.100(c)(6) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from using or possessing a deadly weapon if the court finds the respondent was in the actual possession of or used a weapon during the commission of domestic violence. AS 18.66.100(c)(7) further authorizes the court to direct the respondent to surrender any firearm owned or possessed by the respondent if the court finds that the respondent was in the actual possession of or used a firearm during the commission of the domestic violence.
On March 9, 2025, Wesley Larsen was in the actual possession of a hunting knife, a deadly weapon, at the time he made an explicit threat against David Larsen. This factual predicate satisfies the statutory threshold for both provisions. The court in Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), acknowledged the propriety of weapon-related restrictions in domestic violence protective orders where the record supports a finding that the respondent possessed or used a weapon during the commission of the domestic violence. The March 9 incident is precisely such a situation.
A hunting knife is a deadly weapon by any ordinary definition. Wesley Larsen chose to hold that weapon while standing in David Larsen's bedroom doorway and while delivering a direct, specific threat of future harm. The decision to arm himself for that confrontation, rather than appearing unarmed, signals both that Wesley has access to deadly weapons and that he is willing to deploy them as instruments of intimidation and threat in the context of his conflict with David. Prohibiting Wesley from possessing firearms or other deadly weapons, and requiring surrender of any firearms he currently possesses, is a proportionate and necessary response to this demonstrated conduct.
E. The Court May Issue the Requested Order on an Ex Parte Basis Pending a Full Hearing.
Given the immediacy of the threat Wesley Larsen poses, David Larsen respectfully requests that the Court consider issuing an ex parte protective order under AS 18.66.110(a) pending a full hearing on this petition. AS 18.66.110(a) provides that if the court finds that the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that it is necessary to protect the petitioner from domestic violence, and if the petitioner has certified in writing the efforts made to provide notice to the respondent, the court shall issue a protective order ex parte and without notice to the respondent.
The facts set forth in this petition establish probable cause that Wesley Larsen committed crimes of domestic violence against David Larsen on both March 3 and March 9, 2025. The escalating nature of that conduct, concluding with an armed threat just days before the filing of this petition, demonstrates the necessity of immediate court intervention. An ex parte order under AS 18.66.110(a) may grant the protection provided by AS 18.66.100(c)(1) to (5), (8) to (12), and (16), encompassing each category of relief David Larsen has requested.
Moreover, Civil Rule 65(b) provides that a temporary restraining order may be granted without notice to the adverse party if it clearly appears from specific facts shown by affidavit or verified complaint that immediate and irreparable injury, loss, or damage will result to the applicant before the adverse party can be heard in opposition. David Larsen continues to reside in close quarters with a person who has physically assaulted him and subsequently threatened him with a knife. The risk of irreparable injury is not speculative; it is ongoing and immediate.
F. This Court Is a Proper Venue for This Petition.
Civil Rule 3(h) provides that a petition for a protective order on domestic violence under AS 18.66 may be filed in either the judicial district or the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred. All three bases for venue are satisfied in this case. Both David and Wesley Larsen reside at 412 Birch Creek Road in Fairbanks, Alaska, and both acts of domestic violence occurred at that same address. This Court, sitting in Fairbanks, is therefore a proper forum for this petition.
G. David Larsen's Address Information Is Entitled to Confidentiality Protection Under Civil Rule 65.1.
Civil Rule 65.1 provides that a petitioner appearing pro se in a proceeding to obtain a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 or AS 18.66.110 may submit the petitioner's mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. Access to the form containing the petitioner's mailing address and telephone number is limited to the court, authorized court system personnel, and the petitioner. David Larsen invokes this protection and requests that his contact and address information be maintained on a separate confidential form, consistent with Civil Rule 65.1.
V. CONCLUSION
David Larsen has suffered two serious acts of domestic violence at the hands of his household member and brother, Wesley Larsen, within the span of six days. The first act involved intentional physical force causing injury; the second involved an armed, explicit threat of future harm. These acts satisfy the statutory standard for the issuance of a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100, and each specific form of relief requested is expressly authorized by that statute.
David Larsen respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Issue a protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.100 prohibiting Wesley Larsen from threatening, committing domestic violence against, or contacting David Larsen in any manner, directly or indirectly, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(1) and (c)(2);
2. Order Wesley Larsen to vacate and stay away from the residence at 412 Birch Creek Road, Fairbanks, Alaska, regardless of any ownership interest Wesley may hold in that property, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(3) and (c)(4);
3. Prohibit Wesley Larsen from using or possessing any deadly weapon, including but not limited to firearms and knives, and require Wesley Larsen to surrender any firearms he currently owns or possesses, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(6) and (c)(7);
4. Consider issuing an ex parte protective order under AS 18.66.110(a) providing immediate interim protection pending a full hearing; and
5. Grant such other relief as the Court determines necessary to protect David Larsen's safety, pursuant to AS 18.66.100(c)(16).
The evidence presented in this petition demonstrates by a preponderance of the evidence, and at minimum by probable cause, that Wesley Larsen committed crimes involving domestic violence against David Larsen and that continued, immediate protection is necessary to safeguard David Larsen's physical safety and well-being.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0159)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Whitfield, Petitioner, respectfully submits this brief in support of his petition for a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100. On March 4, 2025, Respondent Wesley Whitfield grabbed Marcus by the throat, shoved him into a kitchen cabinet, and threatened his life. This incident followed an earlier act of violence on February 18, 2025, in which Wesley destroyed Marcus's phone and threatened him with retaliation for contacting family. The pattern of violence, physical injury, property destruction, and threats of harm compels immediate court intervention. Marcus seeks an order prohibiting all contact by Wesley, requiring Wesley to vacate the marital residence at 4712 Birchwood Lane, Anchorage, and prohibiting Wesley from approaching within 500 feet of Marcus's workplace and any shelter or temporary residence Marcus may occupy.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Whitfield and Wesley Whitfield are a married couple who have shared a residence at 4712 Birchwood Lane, Anchorage, Alaska for approximately six years. They are household members as contemplated by Alaska's domestic violence statutes.
On February 18, 2025, during an argument in which Marcus attempted to call his sister, Wesley forcibly seized and smashed Marcus's mobile phone. Wesley then warned Marcus that if he attempted to contact family members again, he would "regret it." This act of property destruction combined with an express threat constituted an act of coercive control and intimidation designed to isolate Marcus from his support network.
On March 4, 2025, the situation escalated significantly. During an argument over household finances, Wesley grabbed Marcus by the throat with sufficient force to cause visible bruising. Wesley then shoved Marcus into a kitchen cabinet, causing further bruising to Marcus's shoulder. Wesley concluded this attack by threatening to "make sure he would never leave," a statement Marcus reasonably understood as a threat against his safety and freedom. Marcus sustained visible physical injuries, including bruising to his neck and shoulder, as a direct result of Wesley's actions.
The two incidents, separated by approximately two weeks, reflect a continuing pattern of physical violence, threats, property destruction, and efforts to isolate Marcus from family support. Marcus filed this petition seeking a protective order to protect his safety and well-being.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), a court may issue a long-term protective order after a hearing if it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner. The preponderance standard requires that the evidence show it is more likely than not that the alleged conduct occurred.
Under AS 18.66.110(a), a court may issue an ex parte protective order without notice to the respondent if the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and it is necessary to protect the petitioner from domestic violence. An ex parte order issued under this provision expires 20 days after issuance unless dissolved earlier, at which point a full hearing is held under AS 18.66.100.
Civil Rule 65(b) governs the issuance of temporary restraining orders without notice, requiring a showing by specific facts, through affidavit or verified complaint, that immediate and irreparable injury will result before the adverse party can be heard. Civil Rule 3(h) permits the filing of a petition for a domestic violence protective order in the judicial district or at the court location closest to where the petitioner currently or temporarily resides, where the respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred.
The Alaska Supreme Court has addressed the standards for evaluating evidence in domestic violence protective order proceedings. In Andrea C. v. Marcus K., 355 P.3d 521 (Alaska 2015), the court recognized that prior findings of domestic violence and violations of related orders are significant factors in assessing the need for ongoing protection. In Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), the court affirmed the issuance of protective orders where a petitioner demonstrated a documented pattern of physical violence by the respondent. In Whalen v. Whalen, 425 P.3d 150 (Alaska 2018), the court clarified the duration provisions of protective orders issued under AS 18.66.100(b), confirming that certain forms of protective relief remain effective until further court order, while other provisions operate for one year unless dissolved earlier.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. MARCUS WHITFIELD IS A VICTIM OF CRIMES INVOLVING DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AND IS ENTITLED TO A PROTECTIVE ORDER UNDER AS 18.66.100.
AS 18.66.100(a) authorizes a person who is or has been a victim of a crime involving domestic violence to file a petition for a protective order against a household member. Marcus satisfies each element of this provision.
First, Wesley Whitfield is Marcus's spouse and a member of his household. The parties have cohabitated at 4712 Birchwood Lane, Anchorage for six years. Wesley therefore qualifies as a household member against whom a protective order may be sought.
Second, the conduct Wesley committed on both February 18, 2025, and March 4, 2025, constitutes crimes involving domestic violence. The act of grabbing Marcus by the throat with sufficient force to cause visible bruising constitutes assault. Shoving Marcus into a kitchen cabinet causing additional bruising constitutes a further act of physical violence. Threatening that Marcus would "never leave" constitutes a criminal threat. These acts are crimes committed by a household member against another household member and fall squarely within the scope of Alaska's domestic violence statutes.
Third, the preponderance of the evidence standard is readily satisfied here. Marcus sustained visible physical injuries documented by bruising to his neck and shoulder from the March 4, 2025, incident alone. The pattern of conduct, including the earlier phone destruction and isolation threat on February 18, 2025, corroborates a continuing course of coercive and violent behavior. AS 18.66.100(e) further provides that a court may not deny a petition for a protective order solely because of a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. Accordingly, both incidents are properly before this Court.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed, in Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007), that courts are authorized to issue protective orders where petitioners demonstrate a documented pattern of physical violence. Marcus's two documented incidents, occurring within fourteen days of each other, establish precisely such a pattern.
B. THIS COURT SHOULD PROHIBIT ALL CONTACT BY WESLEY WHITFIELD WITH MARCUS WHITFIELD.
AS 18.66.100(c)(1) authorizes a protective order to prohibit the respondent from threatening to commit or committing domestic violence, stalking, or harassment. AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the court to prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner.
Wesley's conduct demonstrates that direct and indirect contact poses a continuing danger to Marcus. Wesley has already demonstrated a willingness to destroy Marcus's means of communication in order to isolate him and prevent him from seeking help. Wesley has issued explicit threats, both in the February 18, 2025, warning against contacting family and in the March 4, 2025, threat that Marcus would never leave. These threats, combined with the physical violence, establish that any ongoing contact by Wesley is inherently threatening to Marcus's safety and well-being.
Accordingly, this Court should order Wesley to refrain from any and all direct or indirect contact with Marcus, including by telephone, text message, electronic communication, written correspondence, third-party intermediaries, or any other means.
AS 18.66.130(a) expressly provides that an invitation by the petitioner to have otherwise prohibited contact does not waive or nullify any provision of a protective order. This Court should include the required notice language in any protective order issued, consistent with AS 18.66.130(d).
C. THIS COURT SHOULD REQUIRE WESLEY WHITFIELD TO VACATE THE MARITAL RESIDENCE.
AS 18.66.100(c)(3) authorizes the court to remove and exclude the respondent from the residence of the petitioner, regardless of ownership of the residence. AS 18.66.100(c)(4) further authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the residence of the petitioner.
The shared marital residence at 4712 Birchwood Lane is the site of both documented acts of violence. The March 4, 2025, assault occurred there. Wesley's control of that physical space, including Wesley's demonstrated ability and willingness to engage in violence within it, renders that location unsafe for Marcus so long as Wesley is present. Requiring Wesley to vacate is the only means of restoring Marcus's access to his own home.
Importantly, AS 18.66.100(c)(3) makes clear that removal may be ordered regardless of ownership. Wesley cannot rely on any property interest claim to resist removal from the residence when such presence poses an ongoing threat to Marcus's physical safety.
AS 18.66.100(c)(10) also authorizes the court to give the petitioner possession and use of a vehicle and other essential personal items, regardless of ownership. To the extent Marcus requires access to shared vehicles or personal property located at the residence, this Court is authorized to award such access as part of the protective order.
Under AS 25.24.140(b)(3), during the pendency of a domestic relations action, a spouse is entitled to necessary protective orders directing one spouse to vacate the marital residence. While Marcus brings this petition under AS 18.66.100, this provision further underscores the legislative recognition that vacating an abusive spouse is appropriate and necessary in circumstances such as these.
D. THIS COURT SHOULD PROHIBIT WESLEY WHITFIELD FROM APPROACHING WITHIN 500 FEET OF MARCUS'S WORKPLACE AND ANY SHELTER OR TEMPORARY RESIDENCE.
AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from the school or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member. This provision directly supports Marcus's request that Wesley be prohibited from approaching within 500 feet of his workplace.
Wesley has demonstrated a capacity for escalating violence and has threatened that Marcus would never leave, a threat suggesting Wesley may attempt to track, monitor, or confront Marcus at locations outside the home. Marcus's workplace is a foreseeable location where such confrontation could occur. Prohibiting Wesley from approaching Marcus's place of employment is necessary to ensure that Marcus can maintain employment, financial independence, and freedom of movement without fear of encountering Wesley.
Additionally, because Marcus may be required to seek temporary shelter or housing during the duration of the protective order, this Court should order Wesley to stay away from any shelter or temporary residence Marcus may occupy. AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes orders covering any specified place frequented by the petitioner. The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015), is instructive: courts have upheld stay-away provisions covering residential locations beyond the primary marital home in order to ensure the continuing safety of a domestic violence victim.
AS 18.65.520 establishes the policy of Alaska law that victims of domestic violence have the right to request that officers assist in ensuring their physical safety and in locating a place of safety. This policy reflects the legislature's recognition that the protective sphere of a domestic violence victim must extend beyond a single address. This Court's order should reflect that legislative intent by specifying a 500-foot stay-away zone covering Marcus's workplace and any shelter or temporary residence he may occupy.
E. THE COURT SHOULD AWARD ADDITIONAL APPROPRIATE RELIEF, INCLUDING REIMBURSEMENT OF COSTS AND PARTICIPATION IN A BATTERER INTERVENTION PROGRAM.
AS 18.66.100(c)(13) authorizes the court to require the respondent to reimburse the petitioner for expenses associated with the domestic violence, including medical expenses and costs incurred in bringing the action. Marcus sustained physical injuries requiring attention and was forced to replace his destroyed phone as a result of Wesley's conduct. This Court may order Wesley to reimburse Marcus for those expenses.
AS 18.66.100(c)(14) authorizes the court to require the respondent to pay costs and fees incurred by the petitioner in bringing the action. AS 18.66.100(c)(15) authorizes the court to order the respondent to participate, at the respondent's expense, in a program for the rehabilitation of perpetrators of domestic violence that meets the standards set by and is approved by the Department of Corrections, or in treatment for the abuse of alcohol or controlled substances or both. Wesley's pattern of controlling and violent behavior suggests that mandatory participation in such a program would serve both the goals of rehabilitation and the prevention of future harm to Marcus and others.
F. MEDIATION IS PROHIBITED AND INAPPROPRIATE IN THIS MATTER.
AS 18.66.130(c) expressly states that a court may not order parties into mediation or refer them to mediation for resolution of issues arising from a petition for a protective order under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. Civil Rule 100(a) independently confirms that mediation may not be ordered between parties to a case filed under AS 18.66.100 through 18.66.180. Accordingly, this Court may not order or suggest mediation in this proceeding, and Marcus respectfully requests that no such referral be made.
G. THE PETITIONER'S CONFIDENTIALITY INTERESTS ARE PROTECTED UNDER CIVIL RULE 65.1.
As a pro se petitioner, Marcus is entitled under Civil Rule 65.1 to submit his mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit this information from other pleadings and papers filed with the court. Given that Wesley has already demonstrated a pattern of isolating Marcus and controlling his ability to communicate and move freely, the confidentiality protections of Civil Rule 65.1 are particularly important in this matter. Marcus respectfully requests that the court honor these protections and limit access to his contact information accordingly.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Marcus Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court issue a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 granting the following relief:
1. Prohibiting Wesley Whitfield from threatening to commit or committing any further acts of domestic violence, stalking, or harassment against Marcus Whitfield;
2. Prohibiting Wesley Whitfield from contacting Marcus Whitfield directly or indirectly by any means, including by telephone, electronic communication, written correspondence, or through third parties;
3. Requiring Wesley Whitfield to vacate the marital residence at 4712 Birchwood Lane, Anchorage, Alaska, and prohibiting Wesley from returning to or approaching that residence;
4. Prohibiting Wesley Whitfield from coming within 500 feet of Marcus Whitfield's place of employment and any shelter or temporary residence Marcus may occupy during the duration of the order;
5. Awarding Marcus possession of the marital residence and any shared vehicle necessary for his transportation during the pendency of this matter;
6. Ordering Wesley Whitfield to reimburse Marcus Whitfield for medical expenses, the cost of replacing his destroyed phone, and costs incurred in bringing this action;
7. Ordering Wesley Whitfield to participate, at Wesley's expense, in a Department of Corrections-approved batterer intervention program; and
8. Granting such other and further relief as this Court deems necessary to protect Marcus Whitfield's safety and well-being.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
REQUEST FOR A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PROTECTIVE ORDER
(doc-0160)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Colby respectfully submits this brief in support of her petition for a domestic violence protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.946. Michael Colby, Respondent and Petitioner's husband, has engaged in a pattern of physical violence and threatening conduct directed at Petitioner and her two minor children. On October 14, 2024, Respondent shoved Petitioner into a kitchen cabinet, breaking her wrist. On October 22, 2024, Respondent appeared uninvited at Petitioner's mother's home and screamed threats through the front door, causing Petitioner and the children to flee in fear. Petitioner seeks a long-term protective order prohibiting all contact between Respondent and Petitioner, the minor children, and Petitioner's mother, and requiring Respondent to maintain a distance of at least 500 feet from Petitioner's mother's home, Petitioner's workplace, and the children's school. The evidence establishes by a preponderance that Respondent has committed crimes involving domestic violence and that the requested relief is necessary to protect Petitioner and her children from further harm.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Colby and Michael Colby have been married and residing together in Anchorage, Alaska for approximately six years. The parties share two minor children who reside with Petitioner. On October 14, 2024, during an argument about household finances, Respondent shoved Petitioner into a kitchen cabinet with sufficient force to break Petitioner's wrist. As a direct result of this physical assault, Petitioner vacated the marital residence that same day and sought refuge at her mother's home.
Eight days later, on October 22, 2024, Respondent appeared at Petitioner's mother's home without invitation or warning. Respondent screamed through the front door that he would "make her regret leaving," a statement Petitioner reasonably understood as a direct threat of further physical violence. Petitioner and the two minor children fled to a back bedroom out of fear for their safety. A neighbor who witnessed the incident called police. Respondent's conduct on October 22, 2024, constituted criminal threatening and harassment directed at a location where Respondent knew minor children were present.
Petitioner filed the instant petition for a domestic violence protective order seeking to prohibit Respondent from contacting Petitioner, the children, or Petitioner's mother, and seeking a 500-foot stay-away order with respect to Petitioner's mother's home, Petitioner's workplace at Midtown Dental Associates, and the children's school.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 18.66.100(b), when a petition for a protective order is filed, the court shall schedule a hearing and provide at least 10 days' notice to the respondent. If the court finds by a preponderance of evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence against the petitioner, the court may order any relief available under AS 18.66.100(c). The preponderance standard requires only that the existence of the relevant facts be more likely than not.
Where a petitioner requires immediate protection before a full hearing can be conducted, AS 18.66.110 authorizes the court to issue an ex parte protective order upon a finding of probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that a protective order is necessary to protect the petitioner. An ex parte protective order issued under AS 18.66.110 remains effective for 20 days after issuance unless dissolved earlier.
Civil Rule 65(b) independently authorizes the court to issue a temporary restraining order without notice to the adverse party where specific facts shown by affidavit or verified complaint establish that immediate and irreparable injury will result before the adverse party can be heard. Civil Rule 923 further provides that a pro se petitioner seeking a domestic violence protective order under AS 18.66.100 or AS 18.66.110 may submit her mailing address and telephone number on a separate form and omit that information from other filed pleadings, protecting Petitioner's location from disclosure to Respondent during these proceedings.
This petition may be filed in the judicial district or court location closest to where Petitioner currently resides, where Respondent resides, or where the domestic violence occurred, pursuant to Civil Rule 3(h). Venue is proper in Anchorage, as the acts of domestic violence occurred in Anchorage and Petitioner currently resides in Anchorage.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts have broad discretion to fashion protective relief that addresses the specific circumstances of domestic violence within the household. Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007). The court may issue a protective order even where there has been a lapse of time between an act of domestic violence and the filing of the petition. AS 18.66.100(e)(1).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. RESPONDENT HAS COMMITTED CRIMES INVOLVING DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AGAINST PETITIONER, SATISFYING THE STANDARD FOR ISSUANCE OF A PROTECTIVE ORDER.
AS 18.66.100(b) requires the court to find by a preponderance of evidence that the respondent has committed a crime involving domestic violence in order to issue a protective order. The facts presented here easily satisfy that standard with respect to two separate incidents.
First, Respondent's act of shoving Petitioner into a kitchen cabinet with sufficient force to fracture her wrist constitutes physical assault. This single incident, standing alone, establishes a crime involving domestic violence under Alaska law, as the parties are married household members and the conduct resulted in physical injury to Petitioner. The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that a physical assault by one spouse against the other within the context of their shared household falls squarely within the scope of conduct that domestic violence protective order statutes are designed to address. Thomas v. Thomas, 171 P.3d 98 (Alaska 2007).
Second, Respondent's conduct on October 22, 2024, constitutes a separate and independent basis for relief. Respondent appeared uninvited at the residence where Petitioner was staying and screamed a direct verbal threat, stating that he would "make her regret leaving." This threatening statement, combined with Respondent's physical presence at a location where he knew Petitioner and the children were residing, constitutes harassment and threatening conduct under Alaska law. The Alaska Supreme Court has affirmed that threatening statements made in conjunction with unwanted physical presence at a victim's location support the issuance of protective relief. Sarah D. v. John D., 352 P.3d 419 (Alaska 2015). That incident caused Petitioner and two minor children to hide in fear, a reaction that reflects the objectively reasonable apprehension the conduct was calculated to produce.
Together, these two incidents demonstrate not an isolated lapse in judgment but a continuing pattern of escalating violent and threatening conduct by Respondent directed at Petitioner and, by extension, the minor children. Courts have recognized that such patterns support broad protective relief. Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020). The preponderance standard is satisfied by a wide margin on these facts.
B. THE SPECIFIC PROTECTIVE RELIEF PETITIONER REQUESTS IS AUTHORIZED BY STATUTE AND APPROPRIATE UNDER THE CIRCUMSTANCES.
AS 18.66.100(c) enumerates the specific forms of relief a court may grant in a domestic violence protective order. Petitioner's requested relief falls within several expressly authorized categories.
1. No-Contact Orders as to Petitioner, the Children, and Petitioner's Mother
AS 18.66.100(c)(2) authorizes the court to "prohibit the respondent from telephoning, contacting, or otherwise communicating directly or indirectly with the petitioner." Respondent's demonstrated willingness to appear at Petitioner's location and make verbal threats establishes that direct and indirect contact prohibitions are necessary. Further, AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from any specified place frequented by "any designated household member." Petitioner's children are household members within the meaning of the statute, and a no-contact provision as to them is independently warranted.
With respect to Petitioner's mother, her home serves as Petitioner's current place of residence. Respondent has already appeared there uninvited and made threats. A no-contact provision that protects Petitioner's mother is supported by AS 18.66.100(c)(16), which authorizes "other relief the court determines necessary to protect the petitioner or any household member under all circumstances." The presence of minor children at Petitioner's mother's home, combined with Respondent's recent threatening appearance at that location, makes protective relief as to the mother's household appropriate and necessary.
Importantly, AS 18.66.130(a) provides that even if Petitioner were to invite contact, such an invitation would not waive or nullify any provision of the protective order. This protection is critical in cases such as this, where Respondent may attempt to characterize any subsequent communication as voluntary.
2. Stay-Away Orders as to Petitioner's Mother's Home, Workplace, and Children's School
AS 18.66.100(c)(4) authorizes the court to direct the respondent to stay away from "the residence, school, or place of employment of the petitioner or any specified place frequented by the petitioner or any designated household member." Petitioner requests that Respondent be required to maintain a distance of at least 500 feet from her mother's home, her place of employment at Midtown Dental Associates, and the children's school.
Respondent has shown that he knows the location of Petitioner's current residence at her mother's home, and has already used that knowledge to appear and make threats. Petitioner's workplace and the children's school are locations she and the children must attend regularly, making them predictable targets for further threatening or harassing conduct. A 500-foot stay-away provision tied to each of these locations is a well-established and proportionate form of relief in Alaska domestic violence proceedings. Ruerup v. Ruerup, 641 P.3d 783 (Alaska 2018) (discussing court's authority to impose geographic stay-away conditions in a domestic violence protective order and its discretion to modify such conditions to address the specific circumstances of the parties).
3. Temporary Custody of the Minor Children
AS 18.66.100(c)(9) permits the court to award temporary custody of a minor child to the petitioner and to arrange for visitation with the minor child "if the safety of the child and the petitioner can be protected." Given Respondent's conduct, which has already forced the minor children to hide in a back bedroom out of fear, an award of temporary custody to Petitioner is appropriate and supported by the record. Courts have recognized that the best interests of children are best served by placing them with the parent who can provide a safe environment free from the threat of domestic violence. Stephan P. v. Cecilia A., 464 P.3d 266 (Alaska 2020).
AS 25.24.140(b) separately authorizes the court to issue necessary protective orders during the pendency of a domestic relations action, including orders "for protection under AS 18.66.100 -- 18.66.180." To the extent any separate domestic relations proceeding is or may be pending, AS 25.24.140(b)(2) independently supports the protective relief sought here.
C. AN EX PARTE TEMPORARY PROTECTIVE ORDER SHOULD BE ISSUED IMMEDIATELY PENDING THE FULL HEARING.
Petitioner respectfully requests that the court issue an ex parte temporary protective order pursuant to AS 18.66.110(a) prior to the full hearing. AS 18.66.110(a) provides that if the court finds that the petition establishes probable cause that a crime involving domestic violence has occurred and that a protective order is necessary to protect the petitioner, the court shall issue a protective order ex parte and without notice to the respondent. The facts set forth in this petition, including the documented physical assault resulting in a fractured wrist and the threatening confrontation at Petitioner's current residence eight days later, establish probable cause well beyond the threshold required for emergency ex parte relief.
Respondent has already demonstrated that he knows where Petitioner is staying and is willing to appear there to make threats. The gap between the October 22, 2024, incident and the scheduling of a full hearing represents a period during which Petitioner and the children remain at risk of further contact and potential violence. Immediate ex parte relief is therefore necessary to protect Petitioner during the interval before Respondent can be served and a hearing conducted.
Civil Rule 65(b) similarly supports issuance of emergency relief, as specific facts shown in this petition establish that immediate and irreparable injury will result to Petitioner before Respondent can be heard in opposition.
