I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Colby respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021, which currently requires Brandon Colby to pay $850 per month. Since that order was entered, multiple material changes in circumstances have occurred that together compel an upward modification. Brandon's annual income has increased from $52,000 to approximately $94,000, the parties' informal custody arrangement has shifted so that the children now reside with Ashley approximately 70 percent of the time, and the younger child has been diagnosed with a developmental disability requiring ongoing therapeutic care that generates substantial additional expenses. Under AS 25.24.170, AS 25.20.110, and Civil Rule 90.3(h), each of these developments independently qualifies as a material change of circumstances, and the combination of all three strongly supports the requested modification to approximately $1,650 per month. The children's current needs are no longer adequately addressed by the 2021 order, and continued enforcement of that order without modification would be contrary to the children's best interests.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Colby and Brandon Colby were divorced in 2021 pursuant to a decree entered by this Court. At the time of the divorce, the Court entered a child support order requiring Brandon to pay $850 per month. That amount was calculated based on Brandon's gross annual income of $52,000, derived from his employment as a warehouse supervisor, and Ashley's part-time gross annual income of $18,000. The order was premised on a shared physical custody arrangement under which the parties exercised roughly equal parenting time, approximately 50 percent each.
Following entry of that order, circumstances have changed substantially. Brandon accepted a new position as a regional logistics manager. His current gross annual income is approximately $94,000 per year, representing an increase of approximately $42,000 annually, or approximately 81 percent above his income at the time the 2021 order was entered. This new role involves extensive travel, which has made it practically difficult for Brandon to maintain the previously ordered equal custody schedule.
As a direct result of Brandon's travel obligations, the children have been residing primarily with Ashley. The children now spend approximately 70 percent of their time in Ashley's home, a substantial departure from the equal-time arrangement that formed the basis of the 2021 order.
Additionally, the parties' younger child has been diagnosed with a developmental disability requiring ongoing therapy appointments and specialized care. Ashley has reduced her work hours in order to transport the child to therapy, attend appointments, and provide the level of supervision and support the child's condition demands. These therapeutic and care expenses are recurring, ongoing, and were entirely unforeseeable at the time the 2021 order was entered.
Ashley now petitions this Court for an upward modification of child support to approximately $1,650 per month, an amount that more accurately reflects the parties' current incomes, the children's primary residence with Ashley, and the additional costs associated with the younger child's therapeutic needs.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170(a), this Court retains authority, at any time after judgment and upon the motion of either party, to alter or modify so much of the judgment as provides for the maintenance of minor children. A motion to modify child support requires a showing of a material change of circumstances. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) provides that a material change of circumstances is presumed when child support as recalculated under the Rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that trial courts retain broad discretion in deciding whether to modify child support orders, and that the primary purpose of Rule 90.3 is to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
A change in a parent's income constitutes a classic basis for modification. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). A change in custodial or visitation patterns may also constitute a material change in circumstances. Id. In evaluating whether a support obligation should be increased, the Court must consider not only the needs of the children, but also the financial abilities of both parents. Headlough v. Headlough, 639 P.2d 1010 (Alaska 1982).
Where exceptional circumstances exist, the Court may vary the support award under Civil Rule 90.3(c) upon clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result from strict application of the guidelines. Good cause for such a variance may include unusual circumstances that require variation in order to achieve an award that is just and proper, taking into account the custodial parent's income.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. BRANDON'S SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED INCOME CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES THAT PRESUMPTIVELY TRIGGERS MODIFICATION
The most immediate basis for modification is the dramatic increase in Brandon's earning capacity since the 2021 order was entered. Brandon's annual gross income has risen from $52,000 to approximately $94,000, an increase of roughly $42,000 per year. When child support is recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3 using Brandon's current income as the non-primary residential parent and Ashley's reduced income as the primary residential parent, the resulting support obligation will exceed the current $850 per month by well more than 15 percent. Under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1), a material change of circumstances "will be presumed if support as calculated under this rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order." That threshold is plainly met here.
The Alaska Supreme Court addressed a factually analogous situation in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), in which a significant discrepancy between the income used to set the original order and the obligor's actual current income supported a finding of material change and a motion to modify child support. The Court's analysis in that case reinforces that an obligor's substantially increased earnings constitute a proper and compelling basis for seeking upward modification.
Furthermore, the Alaska Supreme Court in Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), confirmed that Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) creates a presumption of material change when the recalculated support differs from the standing order by more than 15 percent. Here, a recalculation based on Brandon's current income of $94,000 and Ashley's reduced income would plainly generate an obligation materially exceeding $850 per month, triggering that presumption directly.
Because the presumption of a material change of circumstances arises from the income differential alone, this Court is entitled to reopen the child support question in its entirety, including consideration of the changed custody schedule and the children's special needs costs. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
B. THE SUBSTANTIAL SHIFT IN PHYSICAL CUSTODY CONSTITUTES AN INDEPENDENT MATERIAL CHANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES
The 2021 child support order was premised on an approximately equal division of parenting time. That premise no longer reflects reality. The children now reside with Ashley approximately 70 percent of the time, a shift directly attributable to the demands of Brandon's travel-intensive employment. This departure from the prior custody arrangement is substantial, well-documented, and constitutes an independent material change of circumstances under controlling authority.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), explicitly recognized that a change in custodial or visitation patterns may constitute a material change in circumstances sufficient to support modification of a child support order. The practical shift here, from a 50/50 arrangement to a 70/30 arrangement, is precisely the kind of change the Court identified as modification-worthy in Bunn.
Under AS 25.20.110(a), a modification of a custody or visitation award is appropriate where a change in circumstances warrants modification and the modification serves the best interests of the children. Although Ashley is not formally requesting a modification of the legal custody order at this time, the de facto shift in physical custody is directly relevant to the child support analysis. The children's increased time with Ashley means Ashley bears a substantially greater share of the children's daily living costs, including food, clothing, transportation, and household expenses. The current support order was not designed to account for this imbalance. Continued enforcement of an order premised on equal time sharing when the reality is a 70/30 split would be inequitable and contrary to the children's needs.
Under AS 25.27.060(a), the court shall carefully consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet their support obligations, the extent to which each parent has supported the child, and the economic ability of the parents after separation. Each of these factors weighs in favor of upward modification when the primary residential parent bears the greater daily burden of the children's care.
C. THE YOUNGER CHILD'S DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITY AND ASSOCIATED THERAPEUTIC COSTS WARRANT A VARIANCE OR UPWARD ADJUSTMENT UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(c)
The younger child's recent diagnosis of a developmental disability introduces an additional and wholly new category of expense that was not contemplated in the 2021 order. The child requires ongoing therapy appointments and specialized care. Ashley has been required to reduce her employment hours to meet the demands of the child's therapeutic schedule, further reducing her income. These are precisely the kind of unusual and unforeseen circumstances that warrant departure from a strictly mechanical application of the guidelines.
Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) provides that the Court may vary the child support award for good cause upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result if the award were not varied, and that good cause "may include a finding that unusual circumstances exist which require variation of the award in order to award an amount of support which is just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children." The Rule further directs the Court to consider the custodial parent's income in this determination. Here, Ashley's reduced income and the children's extraordinary therapeutic expenses together satisfy this standard.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Headlough v. Headlough, 639 P.2d 1010 (Alaska 1982), recognized that in determining whether a support obligation should be increased, the court must consider not only the needs of the children but also the financial abilities of both parents. Brandon's substantially increased earning capacity, combined with Ashley's reduced income and the children's increased care costs, makes a compelling case for an upward variance consistent with the Rule 90.3(c)(1) good-cause standard.
The best-interests framework of AS 25.24.150(c) is also instructive in this context. That statute directs courts to consider, among other factors, the physical, emotional, and mental needs of the child, the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs, and the length of time the child has lived in a stable, satisfactory environment. A child with a developmental disability has heightened physical and therapeutic needs. An adequate support award must reflect those needs, not merely the general costs of child-rearing as they existed at the time of the original order.
D. THE COMBINATION OF CHANGED CIRCUMSTANCES SUPPORTS AN AWARD OF APPROXIMATELY $1,650 PER MONTH
Ashley requests that child support be modified to approximately $1,650 per month. This amount reflects a recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3 based on Brandon's current gross annual income of approximately $94,000 as the non-primary residential parent and Ashley's reduced income, adjusted to account for the children's primary residence with Ashley at approximately 70 percent of the time. The requested amount also incorporates a reasonable upward adjustment under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) to address the younger child's ongoing therapeutic expenses.
Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) creates a presumption of a material change of circumstances when recalculated support exceeds the outstanding order by more than 15 percent. As noted above, that presumption is clearly triggered here, as a recalculation under the current income figures and custody percentages will yield a support obligation materially exceeding $850 per month. THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0167)
I. INTRODUCTION
This matter comes before the court on cross-petitions to modify the child support order entered in 2021. David Colby (hereinafter "Father") seeks a court determination of a revised support obligation consistent with current income figures under Civil Rule 90.3. Jennifer Colby (hereinafter "Mother") cross-petitions for an upward modification to approximately $1,350 per month, reflecting the substantial shift in the parties' respective financial circumstances since the original order was entered. Neither party seeks to alter the existing custody arrangement, and the minor child continues to reside primarily with Mother under the previously established 70/30 schedule. Because both parties' incomes have materially changed since the 2021 order, a modification of child support is warranted and necessary to serve the child's best interests and to comply with applicable Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties divorced in 2021. At the time of divorce, the superior court entered a child support order requiring Father to pay $850 per month. That obligation was calculated based on Father's annual income of $52,000 as a warehouse supervisor and Mother's part-time income of $18,000 per year. The court established a primary physical custody schedule in Mother's favor on a 70/30 basis, meaning the minor child resides with Mother approximately seventy percent of the time and with Father approximately thirty percent of the time. The child, now seven years old, has remained in Mother's primary care throughout the period since the original order.
Since entry of the 2021 order, Father accepted a new position as a regional logistics coordinator. Father's current annual gross income in that role is $84,000, representing an increase of $32,000 per year over the income figure used to calculate the existing support obligation. This increase is not temporary or speculative; Father occupies a permanent salaried position in his new role.
Mother's financial circumstances have moved in the opposite direction. Following the 2021 order, Mother received a documented medical diagnosis that limits her capacity to work. As a result, she has reduced her hours and now earns approximately $14,000 per year, a decrease of $4,000 from the $18,000 annual income attributed to her in the original order. Mother's reduced income is not a voluntary choice but is instead the product of a medically documented condition.
Neither party disputes the accuracy of the other's current income figures. Neither party seeks to modify the existing custody arrangement. The sole issue before the court is the proper amount of child support under the Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines as applied to the parties' current financial circumstances.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Modification of Child Support Requires a Material Change of Circumstances
Under AS 25.24.170, a court may, upon the motion of either party at any time after judgment, set aside, alter, or modify so much of a judgment as provides for child support. Modification is permitted upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) provides that a material change of circumstances is presumed when support as calculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized that a significant shift in the income of either parent constitutes a material change in circumstances justifying modification. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). The court examines the totality of the change in circumstances, including increases or decreases in either parent's earnings, in determining whether a modification is appropriate. Id.
B. Child Support Is Calculated Under Civil Rule 90.3
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of child support in cases where one parent holds primary physical custody. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), the support obligation is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage, which for one child is 20 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus enumerated mandatory and permissible deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A) provides the multiplier of 20 percent for one child.
The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed the proper application of this formula in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), where the court outlined the step-by-step process of calculating adjusted annual income and applying the Rule 90.3 multiplier. See also Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025) (addressing modification of child support based on material change in parent's income and the court's authority to impute income where a parent voluntarily reduces earnings). Similarly, Koller v. Reft, 71 P.3d 800 (Alaska 2003), confirms that a trial court must ground its income determination in the evidentiary record before it when setting or modifying a child support obligation.
C. Income Imputation Standards
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits the court to calculate child support based on a determination of a parent's potential income when that parent voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed. However, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E) expressly provides that a determination of potential income may not be made for a parent who is physically or mentally incapacitated. Where a parent's reduced income results from a documented medical condition rather than voluntary choice, imputation of higher income is not appropriate. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change of Circumstances Exists Justifying Modification of the Existing Support Order
The original support order was entered in 2021 based on Father's income of $52,000 per year and Mother's income of $18,000 per year. Father's income has since increased to $84,000 annually, and Mother's income has decreased to approximately $14,000 annually. Both of these changes are documented and uncontested. These shifts in income constitute a material change in circumstances under both AS 25.24.170 and Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1).
Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) establishes a presumption of a material change of circumstances when support as recalculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. Applying even a preliminary estimate of the Rule 90.3(a) formula to Father's current adjusted annual income of $84,000, the resulting monthly support figure substantially exceeds the existing obligation of $850 per month by a margin well in excess of 15 percent. That threshold is clearly met here. See Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017) (describing the operation of the 15 percent presumption under Rule 90.3(h)(1)). See also Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008) (holding that where the percentage difference between prior and current income calculations significantly exceeds the 15 percent threshold, the presumption of material change is established).
The Alaska Supreme Court has long recognized that changes in parental income are among the most common and well-established bases for child support modification. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). Father's $32,000 annual income increase, taken together with Mother's $4,000 decrease in annual earnings due to a medical condition, creates a combined shift in the financial circumstances of the parties that is substantial and well-documented. Modification is not merely permitted; it is required to ensure that the child support obligation accurately reflects the parties' current financial realities. See Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989) (recognizing that the purpose of the modification framework is to ensure child support remains calibrated to current circumstances).
B. The Court Should Calculate Father's Support Obligation Based on His Actual Current Income of $84,000 Per Year
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), Father's adjusted annual income is calculated by subtracting from his gross annual income of $84,000 the mandatory deductions enumerated in the rule, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, and any other applicable deductions listed in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A) through (G). After those deductions are applied, the resulting adjusted annual income is then multiplied by 20 percent, the applicable percentage for one child under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A).
Father's position as a regional logistics coordinator is a permanent, salaried role. There is no basis in the record to treat his income as temporary or uncertain. The court should use his actual gross annual income of $84,000 as the starting point for the Rule 90.3(a) calculation. See Koller v. Reft, 71 P.3d 800 (Alaska 2003) (emphasizing that income calculations must be grounded in the evidentiary record and that a court must have adequate evidentiary support for its income determination).
Applying the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula to Father's current income, and accounting for standard mandatory deductions, produces a monthly obligation that substantially exceeds the existing $850 order. Mother's requested modification to approximately $1,350 per month is consistent with a proper application of Civil Rule 90.3 to Father's current income and is supported by the record.
C. Mother's Reduced Income Should Not Be Imputed Upward
Father may argue that Mother's reduced income results from a voluntary decision to work fewer hours and that the court should impute her prior earning level of $18,000 or a higher figure. That argument is without merit. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E) expressly prohibits the court from imputing potential income to a parent who is physically or mentally incapacitated. Mother's reduced work schedule is the direct consequence of a documented medical diagnosis. Her current income of approximately $14,000 per year reflects the limits imposed by her medical condition, not a voluntary and unreasonable choice to reduce earnings.
Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), underscores that the imputation analysis turns on whether the reduction in income reflects a voluntary personal choice rather than a genuine constraint on the parent's ability to earn. Where the record contains documentation of a medical condition that limits a parent's capacity to work, the court should accept the parent's actual income as the appropriate figure for child support calculation purposes. Mother's medical documentation establishes that her reduced income is not a strategic or voluntary choice, and the court should therefore use her actual income of approximately $14,000 per year in performing the Rule 90.3(a) calculation on her side of the ledger.
D. The Modification Should Be Effective as of the Date the Petition Was Served
Civil Rule 90.3(h)(2) provides that a modification effective on or after the date a motion for modification is served on the opposing party is not considered a retroactive modification. Accordingly, the court should make the revised support obligation effective as of the date Father was served with Mother's cross-petition, or the date Mother was served with Father's petition, whichever is earlier. No portion of the increased obligation should be applied to periods before service of the petition. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(2).
E. The Revised Support Order Should Include an Income Withholding Provision
Under AS 25.27.062(a), any court order providing for child support must contain an income withholding order unless a specific exception applies. Because this matter involves a modification of an ongoing support obligation and no exception under AS 25.27.062(m) has been established, the revised order must include an income withholding provision directing Father's employer to withhold the support amount from his earnings and remit it to the agency as required by AS 25.27.062(b). This requirement is mandatory and ensures consistent and timely payment of the revised obligation.
V. CONCLUSION
The record demonstrates a clear and substantial material change of circumstances since entry of the 2021 child support order. Father's annual income has increased by $32,000 to a total of $84,000, and Mother's income has decreased by $4,000 to approximately $14,000 per year due to a documented medical condition. These changes are uncontested, well-documented, and more than sufficient to meet the material change of circumstances standard under AS 25.24.170 and Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1).
The court should grant Mother's cross-petition for an upward modification of child support. Applying the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula to Father's current adjusted annual income produces a monthly obligation consistent with Mother's requested amount of approximately $1,350 per month. Mother's actual income of $14,000 per year should be used without upward imputation, as her reduced earnings are attributable to a documented medical condition that falls within the protection of Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E). The modified order should be made effective as of the date of service of the first petition and must include a mandatory income withholding provision under AS 25.27.062.
For all of these reasons, the court should enter a revised child support order in an amount consistent with Civil Rule 90.3 as applied to the parties' current incomes, with an effective date tied to service of the modification petition, and with all required statutory provisions included in the order.

Elena Okafor and Maria Okafor are the parents of two minor children. III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170(a), a court may modify a child support judgment upon motion of either party. For a motion to modify child support, the moving party must demonstrate a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.170(b) provides that a material change in circumstances exists when recalculation under the applicable guidelines yields a support amount that differs from the existing order by the threshold amount prescribed by the guidelines.
Civil Rule 90.3 governs the calculation of child support in Alaska. The rule establishes a formula based on each parent's adjusted annual income and the custody arrangement in place. Where parents share physical custody, the support obligation is determined by reference to both parents' incomes and the percentage of time each parent has physical custody of the children. A material change in circumstances triggering modification is presumed when the support amount as calculated under the rule is more than fifteen percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that a significant change in a parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances supporting modification of child support. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018); Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). The Court has also recognized that the adoption or significant amendment of child support guidelines constitutes a material change in circumstances, underscoring the importance of ensuring that support orders remain tethered to current guidelines and actual incomes. Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989); AS 25.24.170(b).
Additionally, AS 25.20.110(a) provides that a child support or custody award may be modified upon a finding that a change in circumstances requires modification and that modification is in the best interests of the child. Courts have held that modification is improper in the absence of a material change in circumstances. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). Here, such a change plainly exists.

The threshold requirement for modification of a child support order is a material change in circumstances. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). That presumption is readily satisfied here.
At the time of the existing order, Maria earned approximately $38,000 per year. She now earns $67,000 per year, an increase of approximately seventy-six percent. The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a significant income change, particularly one of this magnitude, supports modification. In Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the Court considered a modification motion premised on a change in employment and resulting change in a party's pay, reinforcing the principle that income fluctuations bearing on the Rule 90.3 calculation are central to the modification analysis. Similarly, in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), the Court addressed the proper determination of a parent's income for Rule 90.3 purposes, affirming that support obligations must reflect a parent's actual earnings and that significant discrepancies between income used in a prior order and current income support modification.
Maria's income increase was not temporary or speculative. She has accepted a permanent salaried position paying $67,000 per year. This is precisely the kind of lasting, substantial change in a parent's financial circumstances that courts have recognized as grounds for upward modification. Allowing the current order to remain in place would leave the children without the support to which they are entitled under the guidelines.
B. RECALCULATION UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3 REFLECTS A SUBSTANTIALLY HIGHER SUPPORT OBLIGATION CONSISTENT WITH THE SHARED CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides the formula for calculating child support when one parent has primary physical custody, defined as custody for more than seventy percent of the year. Here, the custody arrangement places the children with Elena for approximately 210 overnights per year, which represents approximately 57.5 percent of the year, and with Maria for approximately 155 overnights per year, or approximately 42.5 percent of the year. Because each party has the children between thirty and seventy percent of the year, this arrangement constitutes shared physical custody under the rule.
The Court must therefore apply the shared physical custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3, which accounts for both parents' incomes and the respective percentages of time each parent has physical custody. Under that formula, the support calculation begins with each parent's adjusted annual income as defined in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), which is total income from all sources reduced by mandatory deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, among other enumerated items. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A).
Applying the guideline percentages applicable to two children, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) provides that the relevant percentage is twenty-seven percent (.27). The Court calculates each parent's theoretical support obligation as if the other parent were the sole custodian, then accounts for the actual time-share to arrive at the net obligation. Because Maria's current adjusted annual income substantially exceeds the income figure on which the existing $650 monthly order is based, a proper recalculation will yield a meaningfully higher monthly obligation, one that accurately reflects her current earning capacity and the custody arrangement.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013), emphasized that child support determinations must conform to the analysis specified in Rule 90.3(a). Deviation from the guideline formula is not appropriate absent specific findings of fact justifying departure. Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008). Elena does not seek any deviation from the guidelines. She seeks only that the Court apply the formula as written to the parties' actual current incomes and the existing custody arrangement, which will result in a higher monthly support obligation for Maria.
C. MODIFICATION IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
Modification of a child support order must serve the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.110(a). AS 25.27.060(d) provides that an order for prospective child support may be modified or revoked under AS 25.24.170. V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Elena Okafor respectfully requests that this Court find a material change in circumstances, recalculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3 using the parties' current incomes and the existing custody arrangement, and enter an upward modification of the child support order consistent with that recalculation. Elena further requests that the Court include an income withholding order in the modified support order, that the modification be made effective as of the date of this petition, and that the Court grant such other relief as is just and proper.

III. LEGAL STANDARD
A child support order may be modified upon a showing that there has been a material change in circumstances and that modification is in the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.110(a). Additionally, AS 25.24.170(a) provides the court with broad authority to set aside, alter, or modify so much of a judgment as may provide for the maintenance of a party or for the care and education of minor children. For purposes of a motion to modify child support, AS 25.24.170(b) confirms that a significant amendment to guidelines for determining support constitutes a material change in circumstances when the guidelines are relevant to the motion.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs child support calculations in cases where one parent holds primary physical custody. Under that rule, the support award is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage tied to the number of children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) provides that the applicable percentage for two children is 27 percent (.27) of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income.

Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 787 P.2d 329 (Alaska 1996). Modification is appropriate and necessary when the formula, applied to current incomes, yields a result materially different from the existing order. Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989); Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997).

Applying this formula to Tomas's current gross annual income of $94,000, and accounting for applicable deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), yields a monthly support obligation substantially in excess of the current $850 order, easily clearing the 15 percent threshold presumed to constitute a material change in circumstances under the rule. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), that this 15 percent differential gives rise to a presumption of material change, shifting the burden to the opposing party to overcome that presumption.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), held that an obligor parent who experiences an increase in income cannot avoid paying additional support merely by showing that the children's needs are being met by an existing support award. Tomas may argue that the children are adequately supported under the current order. That argument fails under Alaska law. The Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines presume that the appropriate measure of a non-custodial parent's contribution is the amount produced by the formula when applied to his or her current income. Any departure from that formula requires an extraordinary showing that Tomas cannot make on these facts.
Sarah's reduction in income is equally significant. Her documented medical condition, which forced a reduction in working hours, is not a voluntary choice that would justify imputing higher income to her under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E) explicitly provides that a determination of potential income may not be made for a parent who is physically or mentally incapacitated under all circumstances. Sarah's medical diagnosis falls squarely within this protection. Accordingly, her current income of approximately $16,000 per year must be used as the baseline for any calculation relevant to the parties' respective financial circumstances. The reduction in Sarah's income increases the children's dependence on Tomas's contribution and further demonstrates that the existing order no longer reflects the financial realities of the family.
The court in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), recognized that a significant discrepancy between a parent's income at the time of the original order and current income, as revealed through tax returns and other financial documentation, supports recalculation of child support under Rule 90.3 and may justify imputation of income where a parent has voluntarily reduced earnings. Here, however, the situation is the reverse: Tomas has increased his earnings voluntarily and substantially, while Sarah's reduction is involuntary and medically necessitated. The equities strongly favor upward modification.
B. THE REDUCTION IN TOMAS'S PARENTING TIME PROVIDES AN INDEPENDENT BASIS FOR MODIFICATION.
In addition to the changes in income, the actual parenting schedule has changed materially since the 2021 order. Tomas now exercises approximately 80 overnights per year with the children, compared to the 110 overnights previously ordered. This reduction is attributable to Tomas's decision to remarry and relocate approximately 45 miles from the children's school.
As noted in Section II, 80 overnights per year represents approximately 22 percent of the year. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(2), primary physical custody is defined as the children residing with a parent for a period specified in the custody order of less than 30 percent of the year. This means Tomas is unambiguously a non-custodial parent under the Civil Rule 90.3(a) framework. The prior order may have been calculated, at least in part, with reference to a higher number of overnights. To the extent any credit or adjustment was built into the prior order based on Tomas having 110 overnights per year, that adjustment is no longer appropriate. The children now spend substantially more of their time in Sarah's care, which increases her costs for food, clothing, transportation, school-related expenses, and other necessities.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a change in custodial or visitation patterns may constitute a material change in circumstances sufficient to warrant modification of child support. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). The reduction from 110 to 80 overnights is not a trivial scheduling adjustment. It represents a 27 percent reduction in the time the children spend in Tomas's home, with a corresponding increase in Sarah's day-to-day financial obligations. This shift in the parenting schedule, considered alongside the changes in both parties' incomes, strongly supports an upward modification of the support order.
Furthermore, AS 25.20.110(b) directs the court to consider the past history of the parents with respect to compliance with child support obligations when making any custody-related determination. While Sarah does not allege willful nonpayment, the statutory framework confirms that the court's analysis must be holistic, considering how all relevant financial and parenting factors interact to serve the best interests of the children.
C. MODIFICATION IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILDREN.
AS 25.20.110(a) requires not only a finding of changed circumstances but also a determination that modification is in the best interests of the children. This requirement is satisfied here. The children are living primarily with Sarah, whose income has decreased due to a medical condition outside her control. Tomas's income has increased substantially. The existing support order of $850 per month was calculated based on incomes and a parenting schedule that no longer reflect the parties' current situation. Allowing the outdated order to remain in effect deprives the children of financial support commensurate with their non-custodial parent's current ability to pay.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that the Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines are designed to approximate what a non-custodial parent would have contributed to the children's expenses had the family remained intact. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996). Tomas now earns $94,000 per year. The children should benefit from that income in a manner proportionate to what the Rule 90.3 formula provides. An upward modification to approximately $2,115 per month, which is 27 percent of Tomas's gross annual income of $94,000 divided by 12, before applicable deductions are applied, would reflect the current financial realities and serve the children's best interests. The precise calculation should be made by the court following submission of current financial documentation from both parties, including verification of all deductions permitted under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
To facilitate accurate and efficient presentation of the financial information underlying this petition, Sarah intends to submit a summary chart of income documentation pursuant to Alaska R. Evid. 1006, given the volume of financial records involved. All underlying originals and duplicates will be made available to Tomas for examination or copying at a reasonable time and place.
D. INCOME WITHHOLDING SHOULD BE ORDERED TO ENSURE COMPLIANCE WITH THE MODIFIED SUPPORT OBLIGATION.
Upon entry of a modified support order, this Court should also enter an income withholding order pursuant to AS 25.27.062. AS 25.27.062(a) provides that a court order providing for support must contain an income withholding order, and AS 25.27.062(a)(2) directs that the income withholding order provide for immediate income withholding for support orders issued or modified on or after July 8, 1994. Because any modified order entered in this proceeding will be issued after that date, immediate income withholding is mandatory absent a specific exception that does not apply here.
Income withholding will ensure consistent delivery of the modified support amount to Sarah for the benefit of the children, reduce the risk of arrearages, and eliminate the need for future enforcement proceedings. The definition of "arrearage" under AS 25.27.900(2) includes any debt that is past due and equal to at least one monthly obligation under the support order. Immediate withholding prevents the accumulation of such arrearages and protects the financial stability of the children's household.
Additionally, the court should reexamine and, if appropriate, modify the medical support provisions of the order consistent with AS 25.27.060(c), which requires the court to issue a medical support order requiring health care insurance coverage for the children if such coverage is available to either parent at a reasonable cost.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Sarah Okafor respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a material change in circumstances has occurred based on the substantial increase in Tomas Okafor's annual income, the medically necessitated decrease in Sarah Okafor's annual income, and the reduction in Tomas's parenting time from 110 to approximately 80 overnights per year;
2. Recalculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using the parties' current incomes and the current parenting schedule, resulting in an upward modification of the monthly support obligation;
3. Enter an income withholding order pursuant to AS 25.27.062 requiring immediate withholding of the modified support amount from Tomas's wages;
4. Confirm or modify the medical support provisions of the existing order in accordance with AS 25.27.060(c); and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the best interests of the parties' minor children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0170)
I. INTRODUCTION
Sarah Whitfield respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Since that order was entered, substantial changes in circumstances have occurred warranting upward modification: Marcus Whitfield's annual income has increased from $52,000 to $78,000; Sarah Whitfield's annual income has decreased from $24,000 to approximately $18,000 due to caregiving demands imposed by their younger child's chronic medical diagnosis; and the parties' actual custody arrangement has shifted from a shared physical custody schedule to one in which the two minor children reside primarily with Sarah, with Marcus exercising parenting time only every other weekend and one weeknight per week. No formal order has been entered reflecting this de facto change in custody. The existing support order of $850 per month no longer reflects the children's actual living arrangements, the parties' current financial circumstances, or the increased medical expenses generated by the younger child's ongoing treatment. Modification is both required and appropriate under Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Whitfield and Sarah Whitfield divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce decree, the court entered a child support order requiring Marcus to pay $850 per month. That figure was calculated based on Marcus's annual income of $52,000 as a warehouse supervisor, Sarah's part-time annual income of $24,000, and a shared physical custody arrangement in which the two minor children resided with each parent on a roughly equal basis.
Since entry of that order, Marcus has accepted a new position as a logistics manager. He now earns $78,000 per year, representing an increase of $26,000 annually from the income figure used to calculate the existing order. Sarah, by contrast, has reduced her working hours in order to care for the parties' younger child, who was recently diagnosed with a chronic medical condition requiring ongoing treatment. As a result, Sarah's current annual income is approximately $18,000, a reduction of approximately $6,000 from the income figure used in the original support calculation.
Additionally, the parties informally restructured their parenting arrangement last year. The children now reside primarily with Sarah. Marcus exercises parenting time on alternating weekends and one weeknight per week. Under Alaska Rule of Civil Procedure 90.3, this parenting schedule does not constitute shared physical custody because Marcus's parenting time falls well below thirty percent of the year. Despite this material change in the residential arrangement, no formal modification of the custody order has been entered by this Court. The children's primary residence with Sarah, combined with the younger child's medical needs, has substantially increased the costs Sarah bears on a day-to-day basis for the children's care, protection, and well-being.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a child support order upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.170(a) provides that, after judgment, the court may, upon the motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify so much of a judgment as provides for the maintenance of either party or the care, nurture, and education of minor children of the marriage. AS 25.24.170(b) further provides that a modification of child support may be made where there is a material change in circumstances.
Likewise, AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified where the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Where a parent opposes such a modification and it is nonetheless granted, the court must enter on the record its reasons for the modification.
The child support formula applicable where one parent has primary physical custody is found in Civil Rule 979(a), which provides that a child support award shall be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage, which for two children is twenty-seven percent.
Under Rule 90.3, the court may also calculate child support based on a determination of the potential income of a parent who voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed. Civil Rule 917(a)(4). However, that provision explicitly excepts from its reach a parent who is caring for a child under two years of age to whom the parents owe a joint legal responsibility. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E).
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a material change of circumstances is presumed when the support amount as recalculated under Rule 90.3 differs from the existing order by more than fifteen percent. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). A court may not retroactively modify a child support obligation, and any modification takes effect prospectively from the date of the motion. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification of the Child Support Order.
Sarah Whitfield's motion to modify is firmly grounded in multiple, independent, and concurrent changes in circumstances, any one of which would suffice to justify modification, and all of which together compel it.
First, Marcus Whitfield's income has increased by $26,000 per year since the existing order was entered. His current annual salary of $78,000 as a logistics manager is substantially higher than the $52,000 figure on which the original $850 monthly support obligation was calculated. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a significant increase in the obligor parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances justifying modification of child support. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025). Under the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula for primary physical custody with two children, Marcus's adjusted annual income of $78,000, subject to applicable deductions, multiplied by twenty-seven percent yields a monthly support figure substantially greater than the existing $850 order. Because the recalculated support under Rule 90.3 would differ from the existing order by well in excess of fifteen percent, a material change of circumstances is presumed as a matter of law. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017).
Second, Sarah's income has decreased from $24,000 to approximately $18,000 per year. This reduction is not a voluntary or unreasonable choice. It is a direct and necessary response to the medical needs of the parties' younger child, who requires additional care and supervision as a result of a recently diagnosed chronic condition. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that changed financial circumstances of the custodial parent are relevant to the child support calculation under Rule 90.3. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). Moreover, the court may not impute income to a parent who has reduced earnings in order to care for a child with special needs. Attributing potential income to Sarah under these circumstances would be inconsistent with the child-welfare purposes underlying Rule 90.3 and with the equitable considerations the Alaska Supreme Court has directed courts to examine. See Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E) (no imputation of potential income to a parent caring for a child under two; by analogy, imputation is similarly inappropriate where a parent's reduced employment is driven by the documented medical needs of a dependent minor child, and the totality of circumstances weighs against imputation under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(B)).
Third, and critically, the physical custody arrangement that formed the basis of the original child support order no longer exists. The 2021 order was calculated under a shared physical custody framework. The children now reside primarily with Sarah. Marcus exercises parenting time every other weekend and one weeknight per week, a schedule that plainly falls below thirty percent of the year and therefore constitutes primary, not shared, physical custody under Rule 90.3. This shift in residential arrangement fundamentally changes the support calculation methodology. Under a primary custody framework, the obligation is calculated solely on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, rather than on the shared custody formula. Compare Civil Rule 90.3(a) with Civil Rule 90.3(b). The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a change in the actual custody arrangement, including one that occurs informally before a formal order is entered, constitutes a material change in circumstances. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016).
B. The Revised Child Support Obligation Should Be Calculated Under the Primary Physical Custody Formula of Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Because the children now reside primarily with Sarah and Marcus's parenting time falls well below thirty percent of the year, the applicable support formula is that set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a), which governs cases in which one parent has primary physical custody. Under that provision, child support is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2) under all circumstances. For two children, that percentage is twenty-seven percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Marcus's adjusted annual income must be calculated by subtracting from his gross income of $78,000 the mandatory deductions specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including federal and state income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, and any other mandatory deductions applicable to his employment. The resulting adjusted annual income, multiplied by twenty-seven percent, will yield the annual child support obligation, which when divided by twelve will establish the monthly payment amount.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently required courts to follow the Rule 90.3 formula faithfully and to avoid formulas that deviate from the prescribed calculation without proper justification. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). A court that departs from the Rule 90.3 formula must articulate specific findings justifying the deviation. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997); Halvers v. Pruitt, 355 P.3d 629 (Alaska 2009). No basis for downward deviation exists here. To the contrary, the facts compel strict application of the formula at Marcus's actual income level.
C. The Younger Child's Medical Expenses Must Be Addressed in the Modified Support Order.
The younger child's chronic medical condition generates ongoing treatment expenses that were not contemplated at the time of the original order. AS 25.27.060(c) requires the court, in any proceeding where child support is at issue, to ensure that the support structure addresses health care coverage for the children. That provision specifically authorizes the court to allocate the cost of reasonable health care expenses not covered by private insurance equally between the parents unless there is good cause to allocate costs unequally. Where, as here, Marcus's income has substantially increased and Sarah has reduced her income specifically to care for the child with the medical condition, good cause exists to allocate a greater share of uncovered medical expenses to Marcus.
Sarah requests that the modified order expressly provide for allocation of uncovered medical expenses consistent with AS 25.27.060(c), and that the order require Marcus to bear his proportionate share of health care costs not covered by insurance, with reimbursement due within thirty days of receipt of documentation of each expense.
D. The Existing Income Withholding Framework Should Be Updated to Reflect the Modified Order.
Once the Court enters a modified child support order, an income withholding order must accompany it. AS 25.27.062(a) requires that any court order providing for support contain an income withholding order providing for immediate income withholding. Marcus's new employment provides a stable wage base from which withholding can be administered efficiently. Sarah requests that the Court include an income withholding order directed to Marcus's current employer as part of the modified judgment, consistent with AS 25.27.062(a) and (b).
E. This Court Retains Jurisdiction to Enter the Modified Order.
This Court entered the original divorce decree and child support order in 2021. The children currently reside in Alaska with Sarah. Marcus resides in Alaska. Because both parents and the children continue to reside in this state, this Court retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over all child custody and support determinations under AS 25.30.310(a). No basis exists for any challenge to jurisdiction. The Court may proceed to modify the existing order without any preliminary jurisdictional determination.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Sarah Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a material change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the 2021 child support order, based on Marcus Whitfield's increased income, Sarah Whitfield's decreased income, and the de facto shift to primary physical custody with Sarah;
2. Modify the child support order to reflect Marcus's current adjusted annual income of $78,000, calculated under the primary physical custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) at twenty-seven percent for two children, and enter a revised monthly support obligation consistent with that calculation;
3. Order that uncovered medical expenses for the younger child be allocated between the parties under AS 25.27.060(c), with Marcus bearing a proportionate share commensurate with his substantially higher income;
4. Enter an income withholding order directed to Marcus's current employer pursuant to AS 25.27.062(a); and
5. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper in the best interests of the children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0171)
I. INTRODUCTION
Jennifer Okafor moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Since the original order was entered, the financial circumstances of both parties have changed substantially. Renee Okafor, the non-custodial parent for a majority of the time, has seen her annual income increase from $52,000 to $94,000. Jennifer Okafor, the primary physical custodian, was laid off and now earns only $22,000 annually through part-time employment while she continues to search for full-time work. Additionally, the parties entered into a stipulated custody modification that shifted the parenting schedule so that Jennifer has the children approximately sixty percent of the year and Renee has them approximately forty percent of the year. These developments, taken together, constitute a material change in circumstances warranting upward modification of child support under AS 25.20.110, AS 25.24.170, and Civil Rule 90.3. Jennifer respectfully requests that the Court recalculate support under the applicable guidelines formula and enter a new order reflecting the parties' current incomes and the current custody arrangement.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties, Renee Okafor and Jennifer Okafor, divorced in 2021 following dissolution of their marriage. At the time of the original divorce decree, the Court entered a child support order requiring Renee to pay $850 per month. That amount was based on Renee's gross annual income of $52,000 as a dental hygienist. Jennifer earned approximately $38,000 per year as a retail supervisor at that time and held primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children.
Three material changes have occurred since the 2021 order was entered. First, Renee accepted a position as a regional sales manager and now earns $94,000 annually, representing an increase of approximately $42,000 per year, or roughly eighty-one percent above her income at the time of the original order. Second, Jennifer was laid off from her retail supervisor position approximately six months ago and currently earns $22,000 per year through part-time employment. Jennifer is actively seeking full-time work and her current reduced income reflects economic circumstances rather than a voluntary choice to remain underemployed. Third, the parties entered into a written stipulation last year modifying their custody arrangement. Under that stipulation, Jennifer has the children for approximately sixty percent of the year and Renee has the children for approximately forty percent of the year.
Because Renee holds the children for forty percent of the year, the custody arrangement falls within the shared physical custody definition under Civil Rule 90.3(f), which provides that shared custody exists when a parent has the children for at least thirty but no more than seventy percent of the year. Accordingly, the shared physical custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies to any new support calculation. The 2021 order of $850 per month was calculated under the primary physical custody formula and does not reflect the current parenting schedule, Renee's substantially higher income, or Jennifer's substantially reduced income. Jennifer now seeks modification of the support order to conform to current circumstances.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), an award of child support may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. If a parent opposes the modification and it is granted, the court must enter on the record its reasons for the modification.
Alaska courts have consistently held that substantially changed income for either party is a recognized basis for modifying a child support order. Civil Rule 90.3 governs the calculation of child support in Alaska. Under Civil Rule 952(a)(1), a parent's adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources minus certain mandatory and permissible deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, among others. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) then multiplies the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent by a specified percentage, which for two children is twenty-seven percent.
Where the parties share physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) governs. That provision requires the court to calculate what each parent would owe the other assuming the other parent had primary custody, multiply each figure by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and then award the difference between the two resulting figures, multiplied by 1.5, to the parent with the larger obligation, subject to the ceiling that the award may not exceed what would be owed under a primary custody calculation.
AS 25.24.170 independently authorizes the court, on motion of either party, to set aside, alter, or modify so much of a judgment as provides for the maintenance of minor children, subject to AS 25.20.110.
A modification of child support is presumed to reflect a material change in circumstances if the recalculated support amount under Civil Rule 90.3 is more than fifteen percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017); Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). The modification may not be made retroactive to a date earlier than the date the motion for modification was filed. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013).
Courts may also consider imputing income to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). However, a determination of potential income is not appropriate where the parent's reduced income results from economic factors rather than purely personal choices, and where the parent is actively seeking work consistent with prior employment. Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification of the Existing Support Order.
The existing child support order of $850 per month is no longer accurate or appropriate. Three independent developments, each of which independently satisfies the statutory standard for modification, have occurred since the 2021 order was entered.
First, Renee's income has increased by approximately $42,000 per year, from $52,000 to $94,000. This increase of approximately eighty-one percent is far beyond any de minimis fluctuation. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a substantial change in a parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances supporting modification. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). When the existing $850 monthly obligation is compared to the amount that would be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3 using Renee's current income of $94,000, the difference will plainly exceed fifteen percent, triggering the presumption of a material change in circumstances recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), and Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997).
Second, Jennifer's income has dropped from $38,000 to $22,000 per year, a decrease of approximately forty-two percent. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), both parents' incomes factor into the shared custody child support calculation. Jennifer's significantly reduced income affects the shared custody formula and thus the net support obligation. This change in Jennifer's financial circumstances is a further basis for modification of the existing order.
Third, the parties' stipulated modification of the custody arrangement constitutes an independent change in circumstances that directly affects the applicable child support formula. The original order was entered under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which governs primary physical custody situations. Under the new parenting schedule, Renee has physical custody of the children approximately forty percent of the year. Because forty percent falls within the range of at least thirty but no more than seventy percent, the arrangement now qualifies as shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f). The shared custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) must now apply. Kelly v. Joseph, 46 P.3d 1014 (Alaska 2002) (discussing the application of the correct Civil Rule 90.3 formula to the parties' actual custody arrangement). Application of the shared custody formula, rather than the primary custody formula that underpinned the 2021 order, is itself a basis for recalculation.
AS 25.20.110(a) requires only that a change in circumstances exist and that the modification be in the best interests of the children. Both elements are satisfied. The children benefit from an accurate support order that reflects the current economic realities of both households and the current parenting schedule.
B. The Child Support Recalculation Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) Supports a Higher Monthly Award.
Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) requires a specific, multi-step calculation for shared physical custody cases. The Court must first calculate the annual amount each parent would owe the other if the other parent had primary custody, applying the Civil Rule 90.3(a) primary custody formula. For two children, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) specifies a multiplier of twenty-seven percent of the paying parent's adjusted annual income. The Court then multiplies each parent's hypothetical primary-custody obligation by the percentage of time the other parent actually has physical custody. The parent with the larger resulting figure is the obligor, and the annual award equals the difference between the two figures, multiplied by 1.5, subject to the cap set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(C).
Applying the framework to the present facts: Renee's gross annual income is $94,000. After applicable mandatory deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including estimated federal and state income taxes, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax, Renee's adjusted annual income will be substantially above what it was in 2021. Jennifer's adjusted annual income, calculated from her current gross of $22,000 and applicable deductions, will be considerably lower. The difference in the parties' financial positions, when run through the shared custody formula, will produce a net obligation substantially higher than $850 per month. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025) (affirming that the court must accurately account for the obligor parent's actual income, including all sources, when calculating child support under Rule 90.3). Jennifer respectfully requests that the Court require both parties to submit updated Civil Rule 90.3 financial affidavits so that precise figures can be computed and a new order entered reflecting the correct support amount.
C. Income Should Not Be Imputed to Jennifer Based on Her Current Underemployment.
Renee may argue that Jennifer's current income of $22,000 per year understates her earning capacity and that the Court should impute a higher income to her for purposes of the Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) calculation. That argument should be rejected.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits a court to calculate child support based on a determination of potential income when a parent voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed. However, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(A) makes clear that underemployment exists when the parent's current situation and earnings reflect the parent's decision to not work or to earn less than the parent is capable of earning. Here, Jennifer was laid off from her retail supervisor position as a result of forces beyond her control. She is actively seeking full-time employment. Her reduced earnings stem from economic factors, not from a personal choice to remain underemployed.
The Alaska Supreme Court addressed a similar situation in Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013), in which a parent's reduced income was characterized as temporary and linked to circumstances outside the parent's full control. The Court there required a closer examination of whether the reduction was voluntary before permitting imputation. Jennifer's situation is analogous: her reduced income is temporary, she is diligently pursuing full-time work, and the reduction reflects economic displacement rather than voluntary choice. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(B) further requires the court to consider whether the parent's reduced income is temporary and whether it results from economic factors or purely personal choices. Both considerations favor Jennifer here. Imputation is therefore not appropriate at this time.
D. The Modification Should Be Effective as of the Filing Date of This Motion.
Any modification of child support may not be made retroactive to a date earlier than the filing of the motion to modify. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). Jennifer filed this motion promptly upon recognizing that the circumstances had materially changed. The Court should order that the new child support obligation take effect as of the date this motion was filed so that the children receive the benefit of the corrected support obligation without undue delay.
E. Income Withholding Should Be Ordered to Secure the New Support Obligation.
AS 25.27.927 requires that any court order providing for support contain an income withholding order. Because any modified support order entered by this Court will be subject to that statutory requirement, Jennifer requests that the Court include an income withholding order directed to Renee's employer consistent with AS 25.27.062(b), which directs the obligor's employer to withhold money due or to be due the obligor and pay it to the agency in the amount determined under AS 25.27.062(i). Immediate income withholding is appropriate here given that the modification will result in an increased obligation. AS 25.27.062(a)(2).
V. CONCLUSION
The record establishes that a material change in circumstances has occurred since the 2021 child support order was entered. Renee Okafor's annual income has increased by approximately eighty-one percent, from $52,000 to $94,000. Jennifer Okafor's annual income has decreased by approximately forty-two percent, from $38,000 to $22,000, due to an involuntary layoff. The parties have stipulated to a parenting schedule that now qualifies as shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f), requiring application of the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) rather than the primary custody formula that underpinned the existing order. Each of these changes, independently and collectively, satisfies the statutory standard for modification under AS 25.20.110 and AS 25.24.170.
