IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0172)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Renee Larsen respectfully submits this brief in support of her motion to modify the existing child support order entered by this Court in 2021. Two significant changes in circumstances have occurred since the original order was entered. First, Respondent Jennifer Larsen has experienced a substantial increase in her annual income, rising from $48,000 to $87,000 per year following her acceptance of a new position as a project manager. Second, the residential custody arrangement between the parties has shifted materially, with the parties' two minor children now residing primarily with Petitioner approximately 70 percent of the time. These changes, considered together and separately, warrant upward modification of the existing child support order in accordance with Alaska law and the guidelines set forth in Civil Rule 936. The current award of $650 per month no longer reflects the financial realities of the parties or the actual residential schedule of the children. Modification is both legally required and necessary to serve the best interests of the children.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Renee Larsen and Jennifer Larsen were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the Court entered a child support order requiring Jennifer to pay $650 per month to Renee. That award was based on Jennifer's then-current adjusted annual income of $48,000 and a shared physical custody arrangement under which each parent exercised approximately equal parenting time with the parties' two minor children.
Since entry of the 2021 order, two material changes have occurred. Jennifer has accepted a new position as a project manager and now earns $87,000 annually, an increase of $39,000 per year over the income figure used to calculate the original child support award. Renee remains employed as a dental hygienist and earns $62,000 annually. Her income has not changed significantly from the time of the original order.
In addition to the change in Jennifer's income, the parties' residential custody schedule has shifted substantially. Following Jennifer's relocation to a different part of Anchorage and a corresponding adjustment to the parenting schedule, the children now reside with Renee approximately 70 percent of the time. Under the current arrangement, Jennifer has the children approximately 30 percent of the time. This transition from a shared custody arrangement to one in which Renee is the primary residential parent is a fundamental change in the conditions underlying the original child support calculation.
Renee now petitions this Court to modify the child support order upward to reflect these changed circumstances and to enter an award consistent with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170, a court may, upon motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify a judgment providing for the maintenance of minor children. Modification of a child support order requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a significant change in either parent's income, or a change in the custody arrangement, constitutes a material change in circumstances sufficient to support modification. See Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997); Holmes v. Holmes, 573 P.3d 147 (Alaska 2018).
Once a material change in circumstances is established, the court recalculates child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. That rule prescribes formulas for calculating child support based on the custody arrangement and the income of the parties. Civil Rule 90.3(b) governs awards in shared physical custody cases, while the formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) applies when one parent has primary physical custody. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that a court presumptively does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3. See Restol v. Manshen, 408 P.3d 791 (Alaska 2014).
Civil Rule 90.3(c) permits the court to vary the calculated award upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result, but departure from the Rule 90.3 formula is the exception and not the rule. See State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification of the Child Support Order.
Modification of child support is appropriate when a material change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the prior order. AS 25.24.170 expressly authorizes the court to modify a child support judgment at any time upon motion of either party. Two independent grounds for modification exist here, each of which, standing alone, would be sufficient to support upward modification of the existing award.
1. Jennifer's Substantial Increase in Income Constitutes a Material Change in Circumstances.
Jennifer's annual income has increased from $48,000 to $87,000 since the 2021 order was entered. This represents an increase of $39,000 per year, or more than 81 percent over the baseline income used in the original calculation. The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that an increase in an obligor parent's income provides a basis for modification of child support. In State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999), the court emphasized that an obligor parent who experiences an increase in income cannot avoid paying additional support by showing that the children's needs are currently being met. The court explained that Civil Rule 90.3 operates on the principle that as income available to both parents increases, the amount available to support the children should also increase. The children are entitled to benefit from Jennifer's improved financial position, and the current award of $650 per month does not reflect that improved position.
2. The Shift from Shared to Primary Residential Custody Constitutes an Independent Material Change in Circumstances.
The residential custody arrangement has shifted significantly since the 2021 order. At the time of the original award, the parties exercised approximately equal parenting time, placing the case squarely within the shared physical custody framework under Civil Rule 90.3(b). The children now reside with Renee approximately 70 percent of the time. Under Alaska law, a parent has primary physical custody when the children reside with that parent for more than 70 percent of the year. See Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). The current arrangement places the children at or near that threshold, fundamentally altering the custody classification that underpinned the original child support calculation.
This shift has direct and significant consequences for child support. The shared physical custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b) takes into account the incomes of both parents and the time each parent has physical custody of the children, and produces a lower net obligation because both parents are assumed to be directly bearing comparable shares of the children's daily expenses. When one parent becomes the primary residential parent, that parent absorbs a disproportionate share of the children's day-to-day costs, and the guideline formula changes accordingly. The original award was calculated under the shared custody formula. Now that Renee has primary residential custody, the applicable formula is that set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a), which calculates child support based on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the percentage prescribed for two children.
The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), that the classification of custody, whether shared or primary, drives which formula applies under Civil Rule 90.3, and that the two formulas produce materially different results. Applying the shared custody formula to a situation where one parent now has the children 70 percent of the time would produce a result inconsistent with the rule and inconsistent with the equitable allocation of child-rearing costs between the parents.
B. The Child Support Award Should Be Recalculated Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Based on Jennifer's Current Income.
Because Renee now has primary physical custody of the children, the court should calculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a). That provision requires calculation of child support as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, the applicable percentage is 27 percent. See Marine v. Marine, 957 P.2d 314 (Alaska 1998); Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016).
Based on Jennifer's current gross annual income of $87,000, and before accounting for permissible deductions to arrive at adjusted annual income, a preliminary calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) at 27 percent produces an annual support obligation of approximately $23,490, or approximately $1,957.50 per month, before adjustment for any permissible deductions. The precise figure will depend on Jennifer's adjusted annual income as reported on her Child Support Guidelines Affidavit, DR-305, accounting for allowable deductions. Renee requests that the court require Jennifer to submit an updated affidavit so that the precise Rule 90.3 calculation may be made.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a trial court presumptively does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3. See Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016). Conversely, departure from the formula requires proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result if the formula amount were applied. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) provides that the court may vary the child support award for good cause upon such proof, and requires the court to specify in writing the reason for any variation.
There is no basis here for departure from the guideline amount. Jennifer's income is below the $138,000 threshold at which the standard formula ceases to apply under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(2). No unusual circumstances are present that would suggest manifest injustice from application of the formula. The Alaska Supreme Court in State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999), cautioned against downward departures from Rule 90.3 that are not grounded in appropriate legal justification, and the same principle militates against any informal reduction of the support amount here. The full guideline amount, calculated on Jennifer's current adjusted annual income, should be awarded.
C. The Modification Should Be Made Effective as of the Date of Renee's Motion.
Under AS 25.24.170, the court has authority to modify a child support judgment upon motion of either party. Under Alaska law, prospective modification of child support is the standard remedy, and the court should make the modified award effective as of the filing date of this motion. See Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013) (noting that retroactive modification of child support is prohibited). Renee does not seek modification retroactive to a date before filing. She requests only that the new award take effect as of the date this motion was filed, consistent with Alaska law.
D. The Court Should Also Address Medical Support in Its Modified Order.
AS 25.27.060(c) provides that in any proceeding where the support of a minor child is at issue, the court or agency shall issue a medical support order. That provision specifies that a medical support order shall require health care insurance coverage for the child if coverage is available to either parent at a reasonable cost. The court shall allocate equally the cost of health care insurance for the child between the parents unless there is good cause to allocate the costs unequally. AS 25.27.060(c) further provides that the cost of reasonable health care expenses not covered by private insurance shall be allocated equally between the parents unless there is good cause to allocate those costs unequally.
To the extent the existing order does not address health insurance or allocates those costs based on the parties' prior income levels and custody arrangement, Renee respectfully requests that the court revisit the medical support component of the order at the same time it modifies the base child support award, to ensure that the allocation of health care costs accurately reflects the parties' current circumstances.
V. CONCLUSION
For the reasons set forth above, Renee Larsen respectfully requests that this Court find that a material change in circumstances has occurred, specifically Jennifer Larsen's increased income and the shift to primary residential custody in favor of Renee, and enter an order modifying child support upward consistent with Alaska Civil Rule 90.3(a). The modified award should be calculated based on 27 percent of Jennifer's current adjusted annual income, should take effect as of the date of this motion, and should include an updated allocation of medical support costs as required by AS 25.27.060(c).

I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Colby respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Two significant changes in circumstances have occurred since that order was entered: Wesley Colby's annual income has increased substantially, rising from $52,000 to $94,000, and the custody arrangement has shifted from a shared physical custody schedule to one in which the children reside primarily with Marcus, with Wesley exercising parenting time only on alternating weekends and one weeknight per week. These changes are material and warrant recalculation of child support under Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 to reflect current circumstances and the genuine financial needs of the two minor children.
The existing order of $850 per month was calculated under a shared custody framework. That framework no longer reflects reality. Wesley now earns nearly twice his former income, and Marcus bears the overwhelming daily financial burden of raising the children. A revised support award consistent with the guidelines and the applicable legal standards is both appropriate and necessary.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Colby and Wesley Colby were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce decree, the court established a child support order requiring Wesley to pay $850 per month. That order was based on Wesley's annual income of approximately $52,000 and a shared physical custody arrangement under which each parent had roughly equal parenting time with the parties' two minor children.
Since entry of that order, circumstances have changed materially in two respects. First, Wesley accepted a new position as a project manager. He now earns approximately $94,000 per year, representing an increase of approximately $42,000 annually, or more than 80 percent above the income figure used to calculate the existing support obligation. Second, the custody arrangement has changed substantially. The children no longer reside with each parent on an approximately equal basis. Instead, the children now live primarily with Marcus. Wesley's parenting time is limited to alternating weekends and one weeknight per week, which represents a significant reduction from the shared arrangement that existed when the current support order was entered.
Marcus remains employed part-time as a dental hygienist, earning approximately $31,000 per year. He bears the primary daily costs of housing, feeding, clothing, and caring for the two minor children. The current support order of $850 per month was designed for a shared custody structure and was based on income figures that are now substantially outdated. Neither the custody schedule nor the income figures underlying the existing order reflect the current situation of either party or the actual needs of the children.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a child support order upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.170 provides that, subject to AS 25.20.110, the court upon motion of either party may set aside, alter, or modify so much of the judgment as may provide for the maintenance of either party or for the care, custody, and nurture of minor children. AS 25.27.060 further directs that the court shall carefully consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet their support obligations, and the economic ability of the parents to pay after separation and divorce.
Under Civil Rule 903(a), when one parent is awarded primary physical custody, child support is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a specified percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies to shared physical custody arrangements, in which both parents' incomes and the percentage of time each parent has physical custody are factored into the calculation.
A material change of circumstances is presumed when support as calculated under Civil Rule 90.3 is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005); Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). A shift in income or a change in the custodial arrangement may each independently constitute a material change of circumstances justifying modification. Bunn v. House, 526 P.2d 416 (Alaska 1997). The court must apply the Rule 90.3 formula to calculate the appropriate support obligation once a material change has been demonstrated. Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change of Circumstances Exists Justifying Modification.
Two independent and concurrent changes in circumstances have occurred since the 2021 support order was entered. Either one standing alone would be sufficient to trigger modification. Together, they compel it.
First, Wesley's income has increased dramatically. At the time the 2021 order was entered, Wesley earned approximately $52,000 per year. He now earns approximately $94,000 per year in his role as a project manager. This represents an increase of approximately $42,000, or more than 80 percent. A support order calculated on Wesley's current income under Civil Rule 90.3 would produce a result that differs from the existing order by well in excess of 15 percent. Under the standard applied in Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005), and affirmed in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), a material change of circumstances is presumed when the recalculated support amount diverges from the existing order by more than 15 percent. That threshold is plainly met here. In Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that a parent's significantly increased income, as reflected in tax and employment records, provides a basis for finding a material change in circumstances warranting modification of a support order. The same principle applies with equal force here.
Second, the custody arrangement has changed fundamentally. When the 2021 order was entered, both parties shared physical custody on an approximately equal basis, which triggered application of the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b). That arrangement no longer exists. The children now reside primarily with Marcus, and Wesley has parenting time only on alternating weekends and one weeknight per week. This schedule plainly does not satisfy the threshold for shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3. As recognized in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), a parent has shared physical custody only when the children reside with that parent for at least 30 percent of the year as specified in the custody order. Wesley's current parenting time falls well below that threshold. The change in the custodial arrangement is itself a separate and independently sufficient material change of circumstances. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997).
B. The Correct Formula Is Now Civil Rule 90.3(a), Not Civil Rule 90.3(b).
Because the children now reside primarily with Marcus and Wesley exercises only limited parenting time, the applicable formula for calculating child support is Civil Rule 90.3(a), which governs cases in which one parent has primary physical custody. Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that child support is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) specifies a percentage of 27 percent.
The existing order was calculated under the shared custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for both parents' incomes and each parent's percentage of custodial time. Continued application of that formula is no longer appropriate because the factual predicate for shared custody, namely that each parent has the children for at least 30 percent of the year, is no longer present. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). Applying the shared custody formula to a situation in which one parent bears virtually all daily custodial responsibility would result in a support award that undercompensates the custodial parent and does not reflect the actual allocation of child-rearing expenses. This Court should therefore apply Civil Rule 90.3(a) to calculate the revised support obligation.
C. Wesley's Adjusted Annual Income Supports a Substantially Higher Support Award.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), adjusted annual income means Wesley's total income from all sources minus certain mandatory deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax, as well as any other permissible deductions enumerated in the rule. Wesley's gross annual income is now approximately $94,000. After application of standard mandatory deductions, his adjusted annual income will be substantially higher than the $52,000 figure on which the existing order was based.
Applying the 27 percent multiplier for two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to Wesley's adjusted annual income will yield a support obligation that is significantly greater than the current $850 per month. The precise calculation will depend on the deductions to which Wesley is entitled under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), but even a conservative estimate demonstrates that the resulting support figure will exceed the existing order by well more than 15 percent, confirming that modification is warranted.
Marcus's income as a part-time dental hygienist, approximately $31,000 per year, is relevant context but does not diminish Wesley's obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) in a primary custody arrangement. The Rule 90.3(a) framework focuses on the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent. The disparity between Wesley's income of $94,000 and Marcus's income of $31,000 further underscores the equitable necessity of recalculating support to reflect current circumstances.
D. The Modified Order Should Include an Income Withholding Provision.
To ensure reliable payment of the revised support obligation, this Court should include an income withholding order in any modified support order it enters. AS 25.27.947 provides that a judgment or court order providing for support must contain an income withholding order, and AS 25.27.062(a)(2) specifies that the income withholding order must provide for immediate income withholding when the support order is not being enforced by the agency and was issued on or after July 8, 1994. An income withholding order will protect Marcus and the children from the risk of delayed or missed payments and will ensure that the support obligation is met consistently going forward.
E. The Best Interests of the Children Support Modification.
AS 25.20.110(a) provides that modification of a custody or related order is appropriate when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. The two minor children at the center of this proceeding reside with Marcus on a full-time primary basis. Their daily needs for food, housing, clothing, education, and medical care are borne primarily by Marcus. The current support order of $850 per month was calibrated to a shared custody arrangement in which both parents bore roughly equal day-to-day costs. That arrangement no longer exists. Adjusting the support order to reflect the children's current living situation and Wesley's substantially increased ability to pay is directly in the children's best interests and is consistent with the legal standard set forth in AS 25.20.110(a).
Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), and Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008), both reflect the principle that courts applying Civil Rule 90.3 must faithfully calculate support based on current income and current custody arrangements. Failure to update the support order in this case would leave the children underserved and would impose a financial burden on Marcus that is disproportionate to his income relative to Wesley's significantly greater earning capacity.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Marcus Colby respectfully requests that this Court enter an order modifying the 2021 child support order as follows: (1) finding that a material change of circumstances exists based on Wesley Colby's substantially increased annual income and the fundamental change in the custody arrangement; (2) applying the primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) to calculate a revised monthly support obligation using Wesley's adjusted annual income of approximately $94,000 and the 27 percent multiplier applicable to two children; (3) entering the revised support order with an income withholding provision pursuant to AS 25.27.062; and (4) making the modification effective as of the date of Marcus Colby's motion, consistent with Alaska law and the equities of this case.
The children are entitled to support that reflects their father's actual income and their actual living situation. The existing order does neither. This Court should modify it accordingly.

Ashley Sutter and Maria Sutter divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the superior court entered a child support order requiring Maria to pay $850 per month, calculated based on her annual salary of $52,000. The custody arrangement entered at that time granted Ashley primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, then ages seven and nine, with Maria exercising parenting time on an every-other-weekend schedule. That arrangement remains in effect today, with Ashley continuing to serve as the children's primary custodian.
Since the entry of the 2021 order, Maria has accepted a new position as a project manager with an annual salary of $94,000. Maria's current income has not been reflected in any modification of the child support order.
Ashley remains employed part-time as a dental assistant and earns approximately $28,000 per year. The disparity in earning capacity between the parties has grown substantially since the original order was entered.
In addition, the parties' younger child has recently been diagnosed with a chronic medical condition that requires ongoing therapeutic treatment. Ashley has assumed the primary responsibility for coordinating and attending to this child's care, which has placed additional time and financial burdens on Ashley's household. The cost of therapy and related medical services constitutes an ongoing and recurring expense that was not accounted for in the original 2021 child support order.
These changed circumstances, taken together, form the basis for Ashley's petition seeking upward modification of the existing child support order.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A child support order may be modified upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. Under AS 25.24.170(a), the court retains authority after judgment to modify provisions relating to child support. AS 25.24.170(b) further provides that "a periodic modification of child support may be made without a showing of a material change in circumstances if the child support order being modified on the periodic basis has not been modified or adjusted during the three years preceding the periodic modification." Because the 2021 order has not been modified since entry, this provision independently supports modification here.
Additionally, AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody or visitation "may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification of the award and the modification is in the best interests of the child." The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a significant change in income constitutes a material change in circumstances supporting modification of child support. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025); Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016).
The amount of any modified support award is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which establishes guidelines for calculating child support when one parent holds primary physical custody. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), the award is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage based on the number of children. For two children, the applicable percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
A court may depart from the guideline amount under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) only upon clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result from applying the formula. That exception does not apply here. Rather, Ashley seeks application of the standard formula to Maria's current income, yielding a support obligation that more accurately reflects the parties' present financial circumstances and the children's needs.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Maria's Substantially Increased Income Constitutes a Material Change in Circumstances.
The threshold inquiry on a motion to modify child support is whether a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the prior order. Courts applying AS 25.24.170 and Civil Rule 90.3 have recognized that a significant increase in the non-custodial parent's income qualifies as such a change. In Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed a motion to modify child support where the obligor parent's income as reflected in tax records differed substantially from the income underpinning the existing order, confirming that such a discrepancy may establish the factual predicate for modification. Similarly, in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), the court recognized that changed financial circumstances following a parent's change in employment status provided grounds for revisiting the child support obligation.
In this case, Maria's annual income has increased from $52,000 to $94,000, an increase of $42,000, or approximately 81 percent. This increase is not marginal or temporary. Maria has accepted a new, higher-paying position as a project manager, and there is no indication that this income level is anything other than ongoing. The 15 percent threshold recognized in Alaska practice as a benchmark for a material change in income is far exceeded here. This alone establishes the material change in circumstances required to support modification.
Furthermore, AS 25.24.170(b) provides an independent basis for modification. Because the original 2021 order has not been modified or adjusted in the intervening years, Ashley is entitled to seek a periodic modification without any additional showing of changed circumstances. The passage of time since the original order, combined with the parties' substantially altered financial positions, makes modification not only legally permissible but equitable and appropriate.
B. The Existing Child Support Amount No Longer Comports with Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Must Be Recalculated.
Once a material change in circumstances is established, the court must recalculate the child support obligation in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a). That rule provides that a child support award "in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody as defined by paragraph (f) will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." The applicable percentage for two children is 27 percent under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Maria's gross annual income is $94,000. After accounting for applicable mandatory deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including federal and state income tax, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax, Maria's adjusted annual income will be reduced to some extent. Even applying conservative estimates for those deductions, Maria's adjusted annual income is expected to significantly exceed the income base used to calculate the 2021 order of $850 per month. A recalculation under the current guideline will produce a substantially higher monthly obligation.
The Alaska Supreme Court's holding in State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999) is directly instructive. In that case, the court made clear that an obligor parent who experiences an increase in income cannot avoid paying additional support simply because the children's current needs are nominally being met. The court emphasized that Rule 90.3 operates on the principle that as parental income rises, so does the level of support available for the children. Ashley does not seek a windfall. Ashley seeks only the application of the formula to which Maria is subject under Alaska law.
In Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), the Alaska Supreme Court similarly addressed the calculation of support in cases involving higher-income obligors, reinforcing that the standard formula applies within the income range it covers, and that a departure from the guideline amount requires a specific showing of manifest injustice. Maria's $94,000 annual income does not place her in the elevated income category addressed by Civil Rule 90.3(c)(2), which applies only when a parent's adjusted annual income exceeds $138,000. Accordingly, the standard formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) controls without any discretionary overlay, and the court must apply it as written.
C. The Children's Heightened Medical and Financial Needs Further Support an Upward Modification.
In addition to the guideline-based calculation, the younger child's recent diagnosis of a chronic medical condition requiring ongoing therapy represents an independent, concrete change in circumstances that warrants careful consideration. Under AS 25.27.060(a), the court "shall carefully consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet such support obligations, the extent to which the parents supported the child before divorce, and the economic ability of the parents to pay after separation and divorce." The ongoing cost of therapeutic treatment for a child with a chronic medical condition falls squarely within the category of needs the court must weigh.
AS 25.27.060(c) further provides that the court or agency may order either parent or both parents to pay "the amount necessary for support, maintenance, nurture, and education of the child." Medical expenses associated with a chronic condition and its required ongoing treatment are encompassed within that standard. The court also has authority to consider whether health care insurance coverage is available through either parent and to allocate uncovered medical costs between the parties.
Ashley bears the primary caregiving burden for both children, including the management of the younger child's medical appointments, therapy, and associated coordination. This caregiving responsibility compounds the financial demands on Ashley's household and underscores why the current support level, calibrated to a different financial reality in 2021, is insufficient to meet the children's present needs. Maria, by contrast, has seen her income nearly double and is far better positioned than Ashley to contribute at a higher level to the children's support.
D. The Court Has Jurisdiction to Modify the Existing Order.
Jurisdiction to modify the existing child support order rests with this Court. Because the divorce and original child support order were entered by an Alaska superior court, and because at least one parent and the children continue to reside in Alaska, Alaska retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over custody and support matters under AS 25.30.310(a). No facts suggest that any other state has acquired jurisdiction, or that a court of another state has made a conflicting determination. Modification by this Court under AS 25.30.320 is therefore appropriate without any additional jurisdictional analysis.
E. The Court Should Decline to Vary from the Guideline Amount.
There is no basis for the Court to depart from the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) permits variation only upon clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result from applying the guideline amount. No such evidence exists here. Maria's income is within the range governed by the standard formula. The custody arrangement is unchanged. The children's needs have increased, not decreased. Applying the formula as written will produce a result that is just, proper, and consistent with the purposes of the child support guidelines. As Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018) confirms, the guidelines framework is designed to apply predictably based on income and custody percentages, and courts should adhere to the formula absent a compelling reason to deviate.
Should the Court determine that any portion of the modified support amount is in question, Ashley requests that the Court consider the totality of the parties' financial circumstances, including Ashley's modest part-time income of $28,000 annually, the children's ongoing medical expenses, and the disparity in earning capacity between the parties, all of which support an upward adjustment that reflects the current realities of this family's financial life.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Ashley Sutter respectfully requests that this Court grant the motion to modify child support and enter an order:
1. Finding that a material change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the 2021 child support order, based on Maria Sutter's substantially increased annual income of $94,000, the children's ongoing medical needs, and the passage of more than three years without modification;
2. Recalculating child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) using Maria's current adjusted annual income and the applicable 27 percent multiplier for two children;
3. Directing Maria to provide current income documentation, including recent pay stubs and tax returns, to facilitate an accurate guideline calculation;
4. Allocating uncovered medical expenses for the younger child's ongoing therapeutic treatment between the parties as authorized by AS 25.27.060(c); and
5. Entering a modified child support order consistent with the foregoing, effective as of the date of this motion or such earlier date as the Court deems appropriate.
Ashley Sutter respectfully submits that the evidence supports modification and that the children's best interests require an updated support obligation that reflects the parties' current financial circumstances.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0175)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Whitfield ("Petitioner") respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Since that order was entered, the financial circumstances of both parties have changed substantially, and the parties have informally restructured their custody arrangement to reflect a near-equal division of parenting time. The existing order no longer accurately reflects the parties' current incomes, the actual custody schedule being exercised, or the children's increased needs. Modification is warranted under AS 25.24.170, AS 25.20.110, and Civil Rule 90.3, and the Court should enter a new order that accurately captures the present circumstances of both parties and serves the best interests of the two minor children.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties, Marcus Whitfield and Jennifer Whitfield, divorced in 2021. At the time of divorce, the Court entered a child support order based on a custody schedule in which the parties' two minor children, currently ages eight and eleven, resided primarily with Jennifer on a 70/30 basis, with Marcus exercising parenting time approximately 30 percent of the year. The original support obligation was calculated under Civil Rule 960(a), which applies when one parent holds primary physical custody.
Since 2021, the circumstances of both parties have changed materially. Marcus, a licensed electrician employed in Anchorage, has received a substantial raise and now earns approximately $72,000 per year. Jennifer, a medical billing specialist, has obtained a second part-time position and now earns approximately $38,000 per year in combined income. Neither party's income was reflected in the original order at these levels.
Of equal significance, the parties have informally shifted from the 70/30 custody schedule incorporated into the original order to a near-equal schedule under which each parent exercises parenting time for approximately half of the year. This informal arrangement has not been reduced to a formal modification order. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f)(1), shared physical custody exists when children reside with a parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year as specified in a written custody order. Because the current schedule approaches an equal division, Petitioner requests that the Court formally recognize the revised arrangement and apply the shared custody calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(b).
Additionally, the children's expenses have grown since 2021. Both children now participate in extracurricular activities involving registration fees, equipment, and travel costs. Medical expenses not covered by insurance have also increased. These increased costs affect the overall support needs of the children and warrant consideration in any recalculation.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts retain continuing jurisdiction to modify child support orders following divorce. Under AS 25.24.170(a), the Court may, upon the motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify any portion of a judgment that provides for the maintenance of either party or the care, nurture, and education of minor children. The statute expressly incorporates the framework of AS 25.20.110, which requires the moving party to demonstrate a change in circumstances and that modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a).
With respect to child support specifically, AS 25.24.170(b) provides that a material change in circumstances is presumed where the applicable guidelines have been amended in a significant way. More directly, Civil Rule 90.3 itself creates a presumption of a material change in circumstances when support as calculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. This standard was applied by the Alaska Supreme Court in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), where the Court confirmed that a recalculation resulting in a more than 15 percent variance from the existing order triggers the presumption of a material change.
The calculation method depends upon the custody arrangement. Civil Rule 90.3(a) applies where one parent holds primary physical custody and establishes the child support award as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage. Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies where the parents share physical custody, and it employs a formula based on both parents' incomes and each parent's respective custody percentage. As confirmed in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the distinction between primary and shared physical custody determines which calculation method the court applies.
Courts have broad discretion to impute potential income to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). As the Alaska Supreme Court addressed in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), when a parent possesses income-producing capacity beyond wages actually reported, the Court must examine whether imputation is appropriate to ensure an accurate and fair support determination.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Justifying Modification of the Existing Order.
The threshold requirement for modifying a child support order is a demonstration of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.20.110(a). Three independent grounds satisfy this threshold here, each of which independently warrants modification and which together present a compelling case for recalculation.
First, both parties' incomes have changed substantially since the 2021 order. Marcus now earns approximately $72,000 per year, a figure meaningfully higher than his income at the time the original order was entered. Jennifer now earns approximately $38,000 per year from combined employment. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), both parents' adjusted annual incomes are relevant inputs when calculating shared custody support, and the change in both parents' earnings alters the calculation significantly. The Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), that when recalculation under the rule produces a result more than 15 percent different from the outstanding order, a material change is presumed. Given the magnitude of the income changes on both sides, that threshold is almost certainly met.
Second, the parties' custody arrangement has materially changed. The original order was premised on a 70/30 schedule under which Jennifer held primary physical custody, and support was calculated accordingly under Civil Rule 90.3(a). The parties have since informally shifted to a near-equal custody schedule. As noted in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the applicable calculation method shifts depending on whether the arrangement constitutes primary or shared custody. A custody schedule approaching equal time triggers the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for both parents' incomes and time shares. This shift in custody percentage, standing alone, constitutes a material change in circumstances warranting recalculation.
Third, the children's needs have increased. Both children now participate in extracurricular activities generating recurring costs, and uninsured medical expenses have grown. Under AS 25.27.975, courts must consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet support obligations, and the economic ability of the parents to pay. Increased costs for the children's activities and medical care represent a change in the very needs the support order is designed to address.
B. The Court Should Apply the Shared Custody Formula Under Civil Rule 90.3(b).
The existing order was calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), reflecting Jennifer's status as primary physical custodian under the original 70/30 schedule. That calculation method is no longer appropriate given the parties' current parenting arrangement.
Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) governs child support calculations when parents share physical custody. Under that provision, the Court first calculates the annual amount each parent would owe the other under Civil Rule 90.3(a) assuming the other parent had primary custody. Each amount is then multiplied by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody, and the parent with the larger figure is designated the obligor, with the annual award equal to the difference between the two figures multiplied by 1.5. Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(A)-(C).
The near-equal schedule the parties are currently exercising places this arrangement squarely within the shared custody definition. Because the children now reside with each parent for approximately half the year, the Court should formally modify the custody order to reflect the shared arrangement and apply the Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) formula to calculate a new support amount. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), that applying the correct formula is essential to ensuring the award accurately reflects the parties' actual arrangement.
C. The Adjusted Annual Incomes of Both Parties Must Be Calculated Accurately Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Regardless of which custody formula ultimately applies, the Court must first determine each parent's adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as total income from all sources reduced by specific mandatory and permitted deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory retirement contributions, and health insurance premiums paid solely for the parent, subject to applicable caps.
For Marcus, his gross income of approximately $72,000 will be reduced by applicable mandatory deductions to arrive at his adjusted annual income. For Jennifer, her combined earnings of approximately $38,000 from her primary employment and part-time position must both be included as total income before deductions are applied. The Alaska Supreme Court made clear in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), that courts must examine the totality of a parent's income from all sources when determining the support obligation and that income-producing capacity should be accurately captured.
Additionally, if the Court finds that either party is voluntarily and unreasonably underemployed or earning less than capable, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes imputation of potential income. The factors to be considered include the parent's employment history, job skills, educational attainment, the local job market, and any other relevant factors. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(C). The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), illustrates that courts must scrutinize income figures carefully to ensure the calculation reflects actual earning capacity.
D. The Court Must Include a Medical Support Order and Equitably Allocate Uncovered Health Care Costs.
Any modified child support order must include a medical support order consistent with AS 25.27.060(c). That statute requires the Court or agency to issue a medical support order directing that health care insurance be provided for the children if coverage is available to either parent at a reasonable cost. The statute further requires that the cost of health care insurance for the children be allocated equally between the parents unless there is good cause to do otherwise, and that uncovered health care expenses be similarly divided equally absent good cause. AS 25.27.060(c).
Given the children's increased medical expenses, the Court should carefully examine what health insurance coverage is available through each parent's employer and allocate premiums and uncovered costs in accordance with the statute. Any amount Marcus pays for the children's portion of health insurance premiums should be credited against the support calculation consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(F) and the formula set forth in AS 25.27.060(c).
E. The Modified Order Must Include an Income Withholding Provision.
Any order modifying child support must contain an income withholding order as required by AS 25.27.905(a). That provision mandates that a support order include an income withholding component directing the obligor's employer to withhold the specified support amount from earnings and remit it to the Child Support Services Division. The withholding order takes priority over other attachments or executions against the same income. AS 25.27.062(g). Including this provision in the modified order ensures compliance with state and federal law and provides a reliable mechanism for consistent payment.
F. The Modification Should Be Effective Prospectively.
Alaska law prohibits retroactive modification of child support. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed this principle in Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013), where it vacated a modification that improperly reached back to alter amounts already due under an existing order. Accordingly, Marcus requests that any modification be effective as of the date of filing of this motion, or such other prospective date as the Court deems appropriate, and not retroactively altered to reduce obligations that accrued before the filing of this petition.
V. CONCLUSION
Marcus Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court enter an order modifying the existing child support obligation to reflect:
(1) the current adjusted annual incomes of both Marcus and Jennifer Whitfield;
(2) a formal recognition of the parties' near-equal custody schedule, with child support recalculated under the shared custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b);
(3) an equitable allocation of health insurance premiums and uncovered medical expenses pursuant to AS 25.27.060(c);
(4) consideration of the children's increased extracurricular and medical expenses in determining the appropriate support level; and
(5) the inclusion of a mandatory income withholding order consistent with AS 25.27.062.
Modification of the 2021 order is necessary and proper under AS 25.24.170, AS 25.20.110, and Civil Rule 90.3. The existing order no longer reflects the parties' circumstances, the children's needs, or the custody arrangement the parties have actually been exercising. A recalculated order consistent with current Alaska law will serve the best interests of the two minor children and ensure that both parents contribute equitably to their support.

PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0176)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Nakamura respectfully submits this brief in support of her motion to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. The original order required Respondent Brandon Nakamura to pay $850 per month in child support, a figure calculated on the basis of Brandon's then-annual salary of $52,000 as a warehouse supervisor and Priya's part-time income of $24,000. Since that order was entered, Brandon has accepted a new position as a logistics manager earning $78,000 per year, representing an increase of $26,000 in annual gross income. When Brandon's increased earnings are applied to the formula prescribed by Civil Rule 972(a), the resulting support obligation exceeds the current order of $850 per month by more than fifteen percent, triggering a presumption of a material change in circumstances. Modification is also warranted by the child's increased financial needs, including recently incurred medical and educational expenses that the current order does not address. Under AS 25.24.170 and AS 25.20.110, this Court has full authority to alter the existing support judgment to serve the best interests of the parties' nine-year-old daughter. For the reasons set forth below, Priya respectfully requests that the Court modify the child support order upward to an amount consistent with Civil Rule 926(a) and the current financial realities of both parents.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Nakamura and Brandon Nakamura were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the Superior Court entered a child support order requiring Brandon to pay $850 per month. That figure was calculated based on Brandon's gross annual income of $52,000 as a warehouse supervisor and Priya's part-time gross annual income of $24,000. The parties operate under a primary physical custody arrangement whereby the parties' daughter, now nine years old, resides primarily with Priya. Brandon exercises parenting time on alternating weekends and one evening per week.
Following entry of the 2021 order, Brandon accepted a new position as a logistics manager. He now earns $78,000 per year, an increase of $26,000 over the income on which the current support obligation was based. Priya remains employed part-time and earns approximately $26,000 per year, a modest increase of $2,000 from her income at the time of the original order.
The parties' daughter has incurred medical and educational expenses since the original order was entered that were not anticipated at the time of the 2021 proceeding. These expenses reflect the child's growing needs and contribute to the financial burden currently carried by Priya as the primary custodial parent. The existing support order of $850 per month is no longer adequate to meet the child's needs in light of Brandon's substantially increased earning capacity.
Applying the percentage formula under Civil Rule 927(a) to Brandon's current adjusted annual income of $78,000 produces a monthly support obligation that is more than fifteen percent greater than the standing order of $850 per month. Under Alaska case law, that arithmetic difference alone creates a presumption of a material change in circumstances sufficient to support modification. Brandon has not previously sought or obtained any modification of the 2021 order, and the order has not been adjusted or modified since it was entered.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A child support order may be modified upon motion of either party after judgment. AS 25.24.170(a) provides that "any time after judgment the court, upon the motion of either party, may set aside, alter, or modify so much of the judgment as may provide for alimony, for the appointment of trustees for the care and custody of the minor children or for their nurture and education, for the care, nurture, and education of unmarried 18-year-old children of the marriage while they are actively pursuing a high school diploma or an equivalent level of technical or vocational training and living as dependents with a parent, guardian, or designee of the parent or guardian, or for the maintenance of either party to the action."
In the child support context, modification requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.170(b) further clarifies that "for the purposes of a motion to modify or terminate child support, the adoption or enactment of guidelines or a significant amendment to guidelines for determining support is a material change in circumstances if the guidelines are relevant to the motion." Alaska courts apply a presumption of a material change in circumstances when the support obligation calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) differs from the outstanding order by more than fifteen percent. This presumption is recognized in Alaska appellate decisions discussing the operation of the rule. See Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996); Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of child support in primary physical custody cases. Under that rule, the support award is determined by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by a specified percentage. For one child, the applicable percentage is twenty percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). The rule defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus enumerated mandatory and permissible deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Modification of a custody or support award must also serve the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified when a change in circumstances requires the modification and modification is in the best interests of the child. Alaska courts have consistently held that the primary purpose of Rule 90.3 is to ensure that support orders are adequate to meet children's needs, subject to the parents' ability to pay. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. BRANDON'S SUBSTANTIAL INCREASE IN INCOME CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES THAT PRESUMPTIVELY WARRANTS MODIFICATION.
The threshold question on a motion to modify child support is whether a material change in circumstances has occurred since the last order. In the present case, Brandon's income has increased from $52,000 per year to $78,000 per year, a gross increase of $26,000, or approximately fifty percent. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that when application of Civil Rule 90.3 to a parent's current income yields a support amount that is more than fifteen percent greater or lesser than the existing order, a material change of circumstances is presumed. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996); Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A), child support for one child is calculated at twenty percent of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Applying that percentage to Brandon's current gross income of $78,000, before mandatory deductions, yields a preliminary annual support figure of $15,600, or $1,300 per month. Even accounting for standard mandatory deductions such as federal and state income tax, Social Security, and Medicare tax as required by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), the resulting monthly obligation will substantially exceed $850 per month by a margin well above fifteen percent. The presumption of a material change in circumstances is therefore squarely triggered. Brandon bears the burden of rebutting that presumption, and no basis for rebuttal is apparent on the record presented.
The Alaska Supreme Court has further held that a court, upon finding even a single material change of circumstances, may reopen consideration of related support components, including expense allocations and other financial provisions. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). Accordingly, this Court is not limited to mechanically adjusting the base support figure. It may also address the allocation of the child's uncovered medical and educational expenses as part of a comprehensive recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3.
The facts here closely parallel those examined in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), where the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that a substantial discrepancy between a parent's reported income and the income on which the standing support order was based warranted modification, and that courts may impute income where a parent voluntarily reduces earnings. Although Brandon has not sought to conceal or minimize income in the present case, the Chapman decision underscores that courts must look to the full picture of a parent's financial circumstances, including total income from all sources as contemplated by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), in setting an appropriate support figure.
The prior support order of $850 per month was calibrated to an income base that no longer reflects Brandon's financial reality. Allowing that order to remain unmodified would deprive the child of support commensurate with her father's current earning capacity, contrary to both the letter and purpose of Civil Rule 90.3.
B. THE CHILD'S INCREASED FINANCIAL NEEDS, INCLUDING MEDICAL AND EDUCATIONAL EXPENSES, INDEPENDENTLY SUPPORT MODIFICATION.
Even setting aside the change in Brandon's income, the child's increased financial needs since 2021 provide an independent basis for modifying the existing order. The Alaska Supreme Court has long recognized that both a child's increased needs and changes in parental income are relevant considerations in support modification proceedings. Headlough v. Headlough, 639 P.2d 1010 (Alaska 1982). In Headlough, the court confirmed that in evaluating whether a support obligation should be increased, the court must consider not only the needs of the children but also the financial abilities of both parents.
The parties' daughter, now nine years old, has incurred medical expenses and educational expenses that were not contemplated at the time of the 2021 order. These costs fall disproportionately on Priya as the primary custodial parent. Under AS 25.27.060(c), a court in a proceeding where support of a minor child is at issue "may order either parent or both parents to pay the amount necessary for support, maintenance, nurture, and education of the child. under all circumstances" That provision expressly encompasses education-related costs and medical care, confirming that this Court has full authority to account for such expenses in a modified order.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E) recognizes work-related child care expenses for the subject children as a deductible component in calculating adjusted annual income, and the overall framework of the rule is designed to produce a support figure that reflects real costs of raising a child. The existence of unanticipated and ongoing medical and educational expenses reinforces the inadequacy of the current order and the need for upward modification.
C. MODIFICATION OF THE SUPPORT ORDER IS IN THE BEST INTERESTS OF THE CHILD.
Any modification of child support must serve the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.110(a). Here, the best-interests standard is plainly satisfied. The purpose of child support is to ensure that children benefit from both parents' financial resources, proportionate to each parent's ability to provide. Brandon's ability to contribute has increased by approximately fifty percent since the original order was entered. Holding Brandon to an obligation calibrated to a $52,000 income when he now earns $78,000 annually allows him to retain a windfall at the expense of his daughter's financial well-being.
Priya's income has remained essentially stable over the same period, increasing only marginally from $24,000 to $26,000. She continues to bear the day-to-day financial responsibilities associated with primary physical custody. Upward modification of the support order to an amount consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) would produce a fair and proportionate allocation of child-rearing costs between the parents, consistent with the child's best interests and with the equitable principles underlying Alaska's child support framework.
Because the original order has not been modified or adjusted at any point since 2021, and because the support amount recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) exceeds the current order by more than fifteen percent, this Court is presented with a straightforward case for modification. The evidence necessary to recalculate support, specifically Brandon's current income and applicable deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), is readily ascertainable and should be submitted in connection with this motion. The Court should enter a modified order reflecting Brandon's current adjusted annual income and directing appropriate allocation of the child's uncovered medical and educational costs.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Priya Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court grant her motion to modify the existing child support order. Specifically, Petitioner requests that the Court: (1) find that Brandon Nakamura's increase in annual income from $52,000 to $78,000 constitutes a material change in circumstances warranting modification under AS 25.24.170(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(a); (2) recalculate the child support obligation based on Brandon's current adjusted annual income in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A); (3) address the allocation of the child's uncovered medical and educational expenses as part of the modified order pursuant to AS 25.27.060(c); and (4) enter a modified support order that serves the best interests of the parties' daughter consistent with AS 25.20.110(a).
The existing order of $850 per month is no longer adequate, no longer equitable, and no longer consistent with Alaska law as applied to the current financial circumstances of both parties. Modification is warranted as a matter of law and equity, and the best interests of the child compel it.

III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts have authority to modify a child support order upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. Under AS 25.24.170, any time after judgment the court may, on the motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify so much of the judgment as provides for the maintenance of either party or for the care, nurture, and education of the minor children. AS 25.24.170 operates in conjunction with Civil Rule 90.3, which provides the computational framework for child support awards.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary physical custody case is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by a specified percentage: 20 percent for one child, 27 percent for two children, and 33 percent for three children. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008).
