Arndt v. Arndt, 777 P.2d 668 (Alaska 1989); Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013).
The primary purpose of Rule 90.3 is to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of the parents to pay. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). Trial courts have broad discretion in deciding whether and how to modify child support orders. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
Where unusual circumstances exist, Civil Rule 90.3(c) permits the court to vary the support award upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result if the award were not varied, provided good cause is shown. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) further recognizes that good cause may include a finding that unusual circumstances require variation of the award in order to award an amount of support that is just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. COLIN LARSEN'S SUBSTANTIAL INCREASE IN INCOME CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES REQUIRING UPWARD MODIFICATION OF CHILD SUPPORT.
The most fundamental basis for modification here is Colin's dramatic increase in income. At the time of the 2021 order, Colin earned approximately $62,000 per year. He now earns approximately $118,000 per year in his position with a North Slope oil contractor. This represents an increase of roughly $56,000 annually, an increase of nearly 90 percent. This is precisely the type of change that Alaska law recognizes as a material change in circumstances warranting modification.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary custody arrangement is based on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Applying the applicable percentage to Colin's current income of approximately $118,000, less allowable deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), yields a support obligation that is substantially greater than the existing $850 monthly order. The differential will far exceed the 15 percent threshold that triggers a presumption of a material change in circumstances, as recognized in Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008) and confirmed in Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996).
Colin's increased income is not a temporary windfall or a transitional circumstance. He is employed in an ongoing capacity as a North Slope oil contractor employee, a field known for stable, long-term employment. Alaska courts have consistently distinguished temporary income fluctuations from permanent changes that warrant modification. In Arndt v. Arndt, 777 P.2d 668 (Alaska 1989), the Alaska Supreme Court emphasized that a qualifying change in circumstances ordinarily must be more or less permanent rather than temporary. Colin's move to his current employer and the substantial salary increase that accompanied it is a permanent change, not a transient one.
Likewise, in Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013), the court addressed the significance of income changes and the propriety of using current income in calculating support. The lesson of Wilhour, read in Ashley's favor, is that where an obligor's income has measurably and durably increased, the court should apply that current income to the Rule 90.3 formula. Similarly, in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed a scenario in which a significant discrepancy between a prior support order and the obligor's actual income led the court to examine the obligation anew. The principle that support should reflect actual, current earning capacity is well established.
Colin's failure to seek voluntary modification after his income nearly doubled is itself telling. The existing order locks Ashley and the children into a support level calculated on less than half of Colin's current earning capacity. This Court should recalculate support based on Colin's current adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
B. THE SHIFT TO PRIMARY PHYSICAL CUSTODY WITH ASHLEY REQUIRES MODIFICATION OF THE CHILD SUPPORT FORMULA AND AMOUNT.
The 2021 support order was calculated under a shared custody framework reflecting roughly equal parenting time. The actual custodial arrangement has now changed fundamentally. Colin's North Slope rotation schedule keeps him away from Anchorage for extended periods, and the children now reside primarily with Ashley approximately 70 percent of the time. This shift moves the arrangement from shared physical custody into the primary physical custody category governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a) rather than any shared custody adjustment.
This change in custodial arrangement is independently sufficient to establish a material change in circumstances under AS 25.24.170, which authorizes modification of provisions for the care and nurture of minor children. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a significant change in child custody is among the clearest bases for revisiting a support order. Arndt v. Arndt, 777 P.2d 668 (Alaska 1989) (identifying a significant change in child custody as part of the constellation of changed circumstances warranting modification).
When one parent has primary physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(a) directs the court to calculate support by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage. Because the children now reside with Ashley approximately 70 percent of the time, Colin is properly characterized as the non-custodial parent for Rule 90.3(a) purposes. The formula must be applied accordingly. The current order was not calculated on this basis and therefore does not reflect the actual distribution of parenting responsibilities and associated costs.
Ashley bears the daily financial burden of housing, feeding, transporting, and caring for the children during the approximately 70 percent of time they are in her primary care. Colin's rotational schedule, while understandable as a function of his employment, shifts a disproportionate share of ordinary child-rearing costs onto Ashley. A support order that does not account for this shift is inadequate and should be modified.
C. THE YOUNGEST CHILD'S DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITY AND ASSOCIATED THERAPEUTIC AND EDUCATIONAL NEEDS CONSTITUTE AN ADDITIONAL AND INDEPENDENT BASIS FOR MODIFICATION, AND SUPPORT SHOULD BE VARIED TO ACCOUNT FOR THESE EXTRAORDINARY EXPENSES.
The youngest child's recent diagnosis of a developmental disability introduces an ongoing category of extraordinary expense that was entirely absent from the 2021 order. The child requires specialized therapeutic and educational services. These services carry costs beyond what ordinary child support calculations contemplate. This represents a material change in the needs of the child and provides an independent basis for modification under AS 25.24.170.
Under AS 25.27.060(c), in any proceeding where the support of a minor child is at issue, the court may order either parent or both parents to pay the amount necessary for support, maintenance, nurture, and education of the child. The court's authority to address the full scope of the child's needs is explicit in this provision. The specialized therapy and educational programming required by the youngest child's diagnosis falls squarely within the categories of nurture and education that AS 25.27.060(c) contemplates.
Beyond the standard Rule 90.3(a) calculation, this Court has authority under Civil Rule 90.3(c) to vary the support award where unusual circumstances exist that require variation in order to award an amount that is just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children. The rule provides that good cause may include a finding that unusual circumstances exist which require variation of the award in order to award an amount of support which is just and proper for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children. A child's diagnosis with a developmental disability requiring ongoing specialized therapy and educational intervention is precisely the kind of unusual circumstance that justifies a variation or supplemental award to cover those extraordinary expenses.
In allocating these costs, the Court should consider the disparity in the parties' incomes. Colin now earns approximately $118,000 annually while Ashley earns less than she did at the time of the original order due to her reduction in hours necessitated by the youngest child's care needs. Requiring Ashley, at her reduced income level, to bear an equal or disproportionate share of the extraordinary costs of the youngest child's disability-related services would produce manifest injustice within the meaning of Civil Rule 90.3(c). The Court should allocate the extraordinary therapeutic and educational expenses in a manner proportional to the parties' respective incomes and earning capacities.
In determining the best interests of the children and the proper level of support, the Court is directed by AS 25.24.150(c) to consider, among other factors, the physical, emotional, mental, and social needs of the child; the capability and desire of each parent to meet those needs; and other factors the court considers pertinent. Colin's substantially greater income equips him to bear a larger share of the youngest child's extraordinary expenses. The Court should order accordingly.
D. THE COMBINATION OF ALL THREE CHANGED CIRCUMSTANCES COMPELS MODIFICATION, AND THE COURT SHOULD RECALCULATE SUPPORT UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3 BASED ON CURRENT FACTS.
Each of the three material changes described above, considered independently, is sufficient to open the child support order for modification. Considered together, they present an overwhelming case for recalculation. The existing order of $850 per month was calculated based on: (1) Colin's income of $62,000; (2) a roughly equal custody split; and (3) no extraordinary child needs. All three of those predicate facts have now changed materially and permanently.
As the Alaska Supreme Court noted in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), where multiple material changes of circumstances have been alleged, a finding that one exists may be sufficient to allow the court to reopen the entire support issue, with the other changes bearing on the amount of support due. Here, all three changes bear directly on the amount of support that is just and proper, and all three point in the same direction: upward.
The recalculated support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) should be based on Colin's current adjusted annual income of approximately $118,000, less only those deductions authorized by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including mandatory tax obligations, mandatory retirement contributions, and other qualifying deductions. The applicable percentage should be applied to that adjusted income to yield the presumptive support amount. In addition, the Court should address the youngest child's extraordinary therapeutic and educational expenses as a separate component of the support order, allocated between the parties in proportion to their respective incomes pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(c).
Ashley respectfully submits that the modified support order should reflect all three components: (1) a recalculated base support amount under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using Colin's current income; (2) recognition of Ashley's primary physical custody status in the formula applied; and (3) a specific allocation of the extraordinary expenses associated with the youngest child's developmental disability and related services.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Ashley Larsen respectfully requests that this Court grant her motion to modify child support. The existing order of $850 per month was calculated under conditions that no longer exist. Colin Larsen's income has increased by nearly 90 percent to approximately $118,000 annually. The children now reside primarily with Ashley approximately 70 percent of the time, shifting the arrangement from shared to primary physical custody. The parties' youngest child has been diagnosed with a developmental disability that generates ongoing and substantial therapeutic and educational expenses not accounted for in the existing order.
Each of these circumstances constitutes an independent material change under AS 25.24.170 and Civil Rule 90.3. Together, they compel modification. This Court should recalculate the support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using Colin's current adjusted annual income, recognize Ashley's primary custodial status, and address the youngest child's extraordinary needs pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(c) and AS 25.27.060(c).
Ashley respectfully requests that the Court enter a modified child support order consistent with the foregoing, effective from the date of the filing of this motion.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0178)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Colby respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Since that order was entered, the circumstances of both parties and the children have changed substantially. Maria Colby has assumed primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, now exercising approximately 75 percent of the parenting time, while Marcus retains parenting time during alternating weekends and school breaks. Concurrently, both parties have experienced significant changes in their respective incomes: Maria's annual income has increased from approximately $42,000 to approximately $67,000, and Marcus's annual income has decreased from approximately $58,000 to approximately $44,000 as a result of a workplace injury. These combined changes, affecting both the custody arrangement and the financial circumstances of each parent, constitute a material change in circumstances warranting modification of the existing support order. Marcus asks the Court to recalculate child support in accordance with Alaska Civil Rule 983 and to enter a revised monthly obligation that accurately reflects the current parenting time division and each party's present earnings.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
In 2021, this Court entered a child support order based on a shared physical custody arrangement in which Marcus and Maria Colby divided parenting time equally between them. At the time of that order, Marcus earned approximately $58,000 per year as a licensed electrician, and Maria earned approximately $42,000 per year as a dental hygienist. Because the parties shared custody equally, child support was calculated under the shared physical custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b).
Following entry of the 2021 order, Maria relocated to Anchorage. By informal agreement of the parties, the children began residing with Maria the substantial majority of the time. The children now reside with Maria approximately 75 percent of the year and reside with Marcus during alternating weekends and school breaks, which constitutes approximately 25 percent of the year. No formal modification of the custody order has been entered by this Court to reflect this new arrangement.
In addition to the change in parenting time, both parties have experienced material changes in income. Maria received a promotion and now earns approximately $67,000 annually. Marcus, by contrast, suffered a reduction in work hours resulting from a workplace injury and now earns approximately $44,000 annually. Marcus's reduced income is not a voluntary or unreasonable choice but is the direct result of a physical injury limiting his working capacity.
These changes in custody and income have rendered the 2021 support order inaccurate and inequitable. Marcus now files this petition to modify the order so that it reflects the parties' actual circumstances.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska courts retain authority to modify child support orders upon a showing of changed circumstances. Under AS 25.24.170(a), any time after judgment the court may, upon motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify provisions of the judgment relating to the maintenance of minor children. The court's authority to modify custody and support arrangements is further established by AS 25.20.110(a), which provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified where the court determines that a change in circumstances requires modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child.
The procedural and computational framework for child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. Where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, Civil Rule 912(a) provides that child support is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage based on the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Where parents share physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides an alternative calculation that accounts for the incomes of both parents and the percentage of time each parent has physical custody of the children.
A material change of circumstances is presumed under Civil Rule 90.3 when support as recalculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. As recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), the party seeking modification must demonstrate that such a material change has occurred. Changes in income and changes in the custody arrangement each independently constitute grounds for modification. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), that a trial court does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3 using current income information as the appropriate baseline. Additionally, under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4), the court may calculate support based on a determination of potential income where a parent is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed, but no such finding is warranted here given that Marcus's income reduction results from a workplace injury beyond his control.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Justifying Modification of the 2021 Child Support Order.
The 2021 child support order was premised on two foundational assumptions: that the parties shared physical custody equally and that Marcus earned approximately $58,000 while Maria earned approximately $42,000 annually. Neither assumption remains accurate. The custody arrangement has shifted dramatically, with Maria now exercising primary physical custody and Marcus exercising only approximately 25 percent of parenting time. Both parties' incomes have changed substantially. Each of these changes, standing alone, would support modification. Together, they make modification not only appropriate but necessary.
Under AS 25.24.170(a), this Court retains ongoing authority to modify provisions of its prior judgment as they relate to the maintenance of minor children. Modification is appropriate where the existing order no longer reflects the actual financial and custodial circumstances of the parties. The change from a shared physical custody arrangement to a primary physical custody arrangement is precisely the type of changed circumstance that the modification framework is designed to address. As the Alaska Supreme Court made clear in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the distinction between shared physical custody and primary physical custody carries significant consequences for the applicable child support formula, because a parent with primary physical custody receives support calculated under the primary custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(a), while shared custody triggers the more complex formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b).
Here, because Maria now has the children for approximately 75 percent of the year, the existing shared custody order and the support calculation based on it no longer serve the interests of the children or accurately reflect the actual financial burdens each parent bears.
B. The Applicable Child Support Formula Is Civil Rule 90.3(a), Which Governs Primary Physical Custody Arrangements.
Because the children now reside with Maria approximately 75 percent of the time, and with Marcus approximately 25 percent of the time, this arrangement constitutes a primary physical custody arrangement rather than a shared physical custody arrangement. Civil Rule 90.3(a) therefore governs the calculation of Marcus's support obligation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), "a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody as defined by paragraph (f) will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." For two children, the applicable percentage is "27% (.27)." Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Marine v. Marine, 957 P.2d 314 (Alaska 1998), and reiterated in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), that a trial court does not abuse its discretion when it calculates child support by applying the Rule 90.3 formula to the non-custodial parent's current income. Marcus's adjusted annual income must be calculated by starting with his current gross income of approximately $44,000 and subtracting any applicable mandatory deductions as enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and any mandatory retirement contributions. Additional deductions authorized under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B) through (G) may also apply where documented.
The court in Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989), recognized that the distinction between primary and shared custody for purposes of Rule 90.3 turns on whether the custody arrangement specifies that a child resides with the non-custodial parent for at least the minimum threshold percentage of the year. Because the current informal arrangement gives Marcus approximately 25 percent parenting time, and because the existing formal order has not been updated to reflect this division, it is appropriate for this Court to enter a new order establishing Maria's primary physical custody and calculating Marcus's support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
C. Marcus's Reduced Income Is Not Voluntary Underemployment and Should Not Be Imputed Upward.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) allows a court to calculate child support based on a determination of potential income when a parent "voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed." However, this provision applies only where the parent's reduced income reflects a personal choice rather than genuine economic or physical limitation.
Marcus's income reduction from approximately $58,000 to approximately $44,000 per year is the direct result of a workplace injury that has curtailed his available work hours. This is not a voluntary reduction in earnings. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(B) directs the court to consider the totality of circumstances, including whether the parent's reduced income is temporary, whether it results from economic factors or purely personal choices, and the extent to which the children will ultimately benefit from the parent's decision. A workplace injury that physically limits a licensed electrician's available hours falls squarely outside the category of voluntary and unreasonable underemployment. Furthermore, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E) expressly provides that a determination of potential income may not be made for a parent "who is physically or mentally incapacitated." Marcus's injury-related reduction in income therefore warrants no upward imputation, and his actual current income of approximately $44,000 should serve as the basis for the support calculation.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), affirmed that a superior court properly sets child support based on the non-custodial parent's actual current income when that income reflects real and verifiable circumstances rather than a voluntary choice to earn less.
D. Maria's Increased Income Is Relevant to the Determination of Each Parent's Adjusted Annual Income and the Equitable Division of Child-Related Costs.
Although under a primary physical custody arrangement Maria's income is not used in the same direct computational fashion as it would be under a shared custody calculation, it remains relevant to the Court's overall determination of a fair and equitable support award, particularly as it relates to the allocation of healthcare costs and other child-related expenses under AS 25.27.060(c).
Under AS 25.27.060(c), the court shall allocate equally between the parents the cost of health care insurance for the child unless there is good cause to allocate the costs unequally, and shall likewise allocate equally the cost of reasonable health care expenses not covered by private insurance. Given that Maria now earns approximately $67,000 annually, a figure substantially higher than her income at the time of the 2021 order, this Court should ensure that any allocation of health insurance premiums and uncovered medical expenses reflects each parent's current financial capacity. Marcus's reduced income and Maria's increased income together create a significant shift in relative financial capacity that is relevant to a fair allocation of these costs.
Additionally, under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E), work-related child care expenses for the children who are the subject of the child support order may be deducted from the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Similarly, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(F) permits deduction of health insurance premiums paid by the parent for the parent only, subject to the ceiling of 10 percent of the parent's total income. These deductions, where applicable and documented, should be applied in calculating Marcus's adjusted annual income before the 27 percent multiplier is applied.
E. The Change from Shared to Primary Custody Constitutes a Material Change in Circumstances That Presumptively Requires Recalculation.
The shift from equal shared custody to a 75/25 primary custody division represents a fundamental change in the basis upon which the 2021 child support order was calculated. The original order applied the shared physical custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for the incomes and custody percentages of both parents. The appropriate formula going forward is Civil Rule 90.3(a), which applies exclusively to the non-custodial parent's income and produces a different result.
As recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), a material change of circumstances is presumed when recalculated support differs from the outstanding order by more than 15 percent. Given the change in both the applicable formula and the underlying income figures, the recalculated support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) will almost certainly differ from the current order by more than 15 percent, triggering the presumption of a material change in circumstances. Modification is therefore appropriate as a matter of law.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized in Rowen v. Rowen, 963 P.2d 249 (Alaska 1998), that the shared and primary custody formulas produce meaningfully different outcomes, and that application of the wrong formula to a custody arrangement constitutes legal error. Here, the continued application of the shared custody formula to what is now effectively a primary custody arrangement would result in an inaccurate and inequitable support obligation. This Court should correct the formula applied and enter a new support order accordingly.
F. Income Withholding Should Be Addressed in Any Modified Order.
Any modified support order entered by this Court should include an income withholding provision. Under AS 25.27.062(a), a court order providing for support must contain an income withholding order, and under AS 25.27.062(a)(2), where the support order is not being enforced by the agency and was issued on or after July 8, 1994, the income withholding order must provide for immediate income withholding. The inclusion of an income withholding provision in the modified order will ensure reliable delivery of support to Maria on behalf of the children and will protect the interests of all parties.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Marcus Colby respectfully requests that this Court grant his petition to modify the 2021 child support order. Specifically, Marcus requests that the Court enter an order that:
1. Finds that a material change in circumstances has occurred based on the substantial shift in physical custody from equal shared custody to primary physical custody with Maria and based on the significant changes in each party's annual income;
2. Recognizes Maria as the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children, with Marcus exercising parenting time of approximately 25 percent of the year;
3. Recalculates Marcus's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on his current adjusted annual income of approximately $44,000, without imputation of additional potential income, and applying the 27 percent multiplier applicable to two children;
4. Appropriately allocates health insurance premiums and uncovered medical expenses between the parties based on their current respective incomes under AS 25.27.060(c); and
5. Includes an income withholding provision consistent with AS 25.27.062.
Marcus Colby respectfully submits that the requested modification is consistent with Alaska law, supported by the changed circumstances of the parties, and in the best interests of the children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0179)
I. INTRODUCTION
Sarah Sutter respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order entered at the time of the parties' divorce in 2021. The current order was calculated using David Sutter's annual income of $52,000. David subsequently received a union promotion that increased his annual income to approximately $72,000, representing a substantial increase of roughly $20,000 per year. This increase triggers a presumptive material change in circumstances under Alaska law and Civil Rule 944, and warrants an upward recalculation of child support to reflect David's current earning capacity and the financial needs of the parties' two minor children. Sarah asks the Court to apply the applicable guidelines formula and enter a modified support order consistent with David's present income and the established custody arrangement.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties, David Sutter and Sarah Sutter, were divorced in 2021 following proceedings in this Court. As part of the divorce decree, the Court established a child support order based on David's then-annual income of $52,000 as a commercial electrician in Anchorage. At the time of the divorce, the Court awarded the parties joint legal custody of their two minor children and established that Sarah would have primary physical custody approximately seventy percent of the time, with David exercising parenting time the remaining thirty percent of the year.
Since the entry of the 2021 support order, David has received a union promotion. His current annual income as a commercial electrician is approximately $72,000. Sarah's annual income remains approximately $38,000 in her position as a medical billing specialist. David's income has therefore increased by approximately $20,000 per year since the existing order was entered. No modification of the support order has been sought or obtained since the original 2021 order was entered.
Under Civil Rule 90.3, a child support obligation in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by a fixed percentage based on the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Applying this formula to David's current income of $72,000 yields a substantially higher support obligation than that reflected in the existing order, which was based on $52,000. The difference between support calculated under the current order and support calculated at David's current income exceeds 15 percent, triggering a presumptive material change in circumstances. Accordingly, Sarah now petitions for upward modification of the child support order.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A final child support order may be modified upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.976(a) provides that "any time after judgment the court, upon the motion of either party, may set aside, alter, or modify so much of the judgment as may provide for alimony, for the appointment of trustees for the care and custody of the minor children or for their nurture and education, for the care, nurture, and education of unmarried 18-year-old children of the marriage while they are actively pursuing a high school diploma or an equivalent level of technical or vocational training and living as dependents with a parent, guardian, or designee of the parent or guardian, or for the maintenance of either party to the action. under all circumstances"
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3. In a case involving primary physical custody, the child support award is calculated as "an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." Civil Rule 90.3(a). For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2).
A material change of circumstances is presumed when support as recalculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the amount of the outstanding support order. This presumption is firmly established in Alaska case law. As the court addressed in Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005), the correct method for calculating child support for two children requires application of the 27 percent rate set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). Similarly, in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), the court confirmed that to trigger a modification in child support, the petitioning party must demonstrate a material change of circumstances, which is presumed if support recalculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order.
The Alaska Supreme Court has further recognized that a significant change in a parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances sufficient to support modification. In Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), the court recognized that shifts in the income level of one or both parents are among the most common and well-established forms of material change permitting modification of a child support order.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. DAVID'S INCREASED INCOME CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES WARRANTING UPWARD MODIFICATION OF CHILD SUPPORT.
The existing child support order was entered in 2021 and reflects a support obligation based on David's annual income of $52,000. David's income has since increased to approximately $72,000 per year following his union promotion. This increase of approximately $20,000 per year is not a minor or temporary fluctuation. It reflects a lasting, substantial change in David's earning capacity resulting from a career advancement in his trade.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), the support obligation for a non-custodial parent is calculated by multiplying his adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage. For two children, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) sets that percentage at 27 percent. Applying that formula to David's prior income of $52,000 yields an annual obligation of approximately $14,040, or about $1,170 per month. Applying the same formula to David's current income of $72,000 yields an annual obligation of approximately $19,440, or approximately $1,620 per month, before any applicable deductions are subtracted to arrive at adjusted annual income. The difference between these two figures exceeds 15 percent, triggering a presumptive finding of material change in circumstances, as recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), and consistent with Civil Rule 90.3.
The court in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), confirmed that when one parent holds primary physical custody, the non-custodial parent's support obligation is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a) and is determined by the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the specified percentage based on the number of children. In this case, David is the non-custodial parent, exercising parenting time approximately 30 percent of the year. Because he has parenting time of less than the threshold required for a shared custody calculation, Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation, and the formula is straightforward.
The court in Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013), emphasized that the superior court's determination of child support must conform to the analysis specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a), and that deviations from the mandatory formula require specific statutory or rule-based justification. No such justification exists here for maintaining the reduced order based on outdated income figures.
The Alaska Supreme Court's recognition in Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), that income changes are a recognized category of material change of circumstances is directly applicable here. David's $20,000 annual income increase is not a temporary fluctuation; it is the product of a formal union promotion and represents his current and foreseeable earning capacity.
B. THE COURT SHOULD CALCULATE DAVID'S SUPPORT OBLIGATION BASED ON HIS CURRENT ADJUSTED ANNUAL INCOME USING THE CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) FORMULA.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus certain mandatory and permitted deductions, including federal, state, and local income tax, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and other specified items. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A) through (G) sets forth the complete list of permissible deductions.
Sarah acknowledges that David is entitled to deduct mandatory union dues and other mandatory deductions in arriving at his adjusted annual income pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A). The precise adjusted annual income figure will depend on the actual deductions David is able to substantiate. Sarah requests that the Court direct David to provide complete and current income documentation, including pay stubs, W-2 forms, and documentation of any applicable deductions, so that the Court may calculate his adjusted annual income with precision.
Once David's adjusted annual income is established, the Court should multiply that figure by 27 percent in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to arrive at the annual child support award for two children, then divide by twelve to determine the monthly obligation. The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed this calculation method in Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005), holding that the 27 percent rate under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) is the required method for calculating child support for two children in a primary physical custody arrangement.
Sarah also notes that Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), confirms that when a party's income changes materially and a recalculation under Rule 90.3 would result in a more than 15 percent difference from the existing order, the court should proceed with modification. That case further illustrates that the court may consider all sources of income and, if appropriate, impute potential income where a parent's reported income does not reflect true earning capacity. While Sarah does not presently contend that David is underreporting income, she reserves the right to request imputation of potential income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) if discovery reveals that David has voluntarily limited his income or shifted compensation in a manner inconsistent with his demonstrated earning capacity.
C. THE MODIFIED SUPPORT ORDER SHOULD BE ACCOMPANIED BY A MANDATORY INCOME WITHHOLDING ORDER.
Alaska law requires that any order providing for child support include an income withholding component. AS 25.27.062(a) provides that any judgment, court order, or order of the agency providing for support must contain an income withholding order. Upon modification of the existing support order, Sarah requests that the Court include a conforming income withholding order requiring David's employer to withhold the monthly support obligation directly from David's wages and remit those funds to the Child Support Services Agency in accordance with AS 25.27.062(b).
An income withholding order will ensure consistent and timely payment of the modified support obligation, protect the children's financial interests, and reduce the likelihood of future arrearages. AS 25.27.900(2) defines arrearage as a debt that is past due and equal to at least one monthly obligation under the support order. To avoid accumulation of arrearages and the associated enforcement burdens, income withholding from the outset of the modified order is appropriate and required by statute.
D. THE MODIFIED SUPPORT ORDER SHOULD BE EFFECTIVE AS OF THE DATE OF THIS MOTION.
Under AS 25.24.170, the Court retains continuing jurisdiction to modify support orders. Modification of a child support order generally takes effect as of the date the motion to modify is filed. Retroactive modification to a date prior to the filing of the motion is prohibited under Alaska law, as recognized in Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013), where the court vacated a modification order in part because it improperly reached back to a period before the motion was filed. Sarah therefore requests that the Court make the modified child support award effective as of the date of the filing of this motion, consistent with Alaska law.
E. THE CHILDREN'S FINANCIAL NEEDS SUPPORT AN UPWARD MODIFICATION.
The purpose of child support is to ensure that both parents contribute to the financial needs of their children in proportion to their respective incomes and the custody arrangement in place. AS 25.27.060(a) provides that the court shall carefully consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet support obligations, the extent to which the parents supported the child before divorce, and the economic ability of the parents to pay after separation and divorce. David's income has grown substantially since the original support order was entered. Sarah's income of approximately $38,000 per year has remained relatively constant. The disparity between the parties' incomes has widened, and the current support order no longer reflects the proportionate contribution David is capable of making to the children's care. The children's daily expenses, including housing, food, clothing, health care, education, and extracurricular activities, are primarily borne by Sarah as the primary physical custodian. A support obligation calculated on a $52,000 income does not adequately reflect David's current ability to contribute to those expenses. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), recognizes that the guidelines formula under Civil Rule 90.3 governs the calculation of support obligations up to the income cap, and that the formula is designed to ensure proportionate contribution from the non-custodial parent. The upward modification Sarah seeks is consistent with that purpose and with the children's demonstrated financial needs.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Sarah Sutter respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that David Sutter's increase in annual income from $52,000 to approximately $72,000 constitutes a material change in circumstances warranting modification of the existing child support order;
2. Order David to provide complete and current income documentation, including pay stubs, W-2 forms, and documentation of all applicable deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), so that the Court may calculate his adjusted annual income;
3. Recalculate David's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) by multiplying his adjusted annual income by 27 percent as required by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) for two children, and divide the resulting annual amount by twelve to determine the monthly obligation;
4. Enter a modified child support order reflecting David's current income, effective as of the date of the filing of this motion;
5. Include a mandatory income withholding order in the modified support order as required by AS 25.27.062; and
6. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper in the interests of the parties' two minor children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0180)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Nakamura respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. The original order required Brandon Nakamura to pay $850 per month in child support, calculated on the basis of his then-annual income of $52,000 and a shared physical custody arrangement in which both parents exercised roughly equal parenting time with the parties' two minor children. Since that order was entered, material changes in circumstances have occurred on multiple fronts. Brandon's annual income has risen to approximately $74,000 following a promotion, while Marcus's annual income has fallen to approximately $38,000 due to a medical condition requiring him to reduce his working hours. Equally significant, the residential schedule has shifted substantially: the children now reside with Marcus approximately 70 percent of the time, converting what was a shared custody arrangement under the guidelines into a primary custody arrangement in his favor. These combined changes, affecting both the parties' relative incomes and the physical custody schedule, compel an upward modification of the existing child support obligation. Marcus requests that this Court enter a modified order requiring Brandon to pay approximately $1,400 per month, an amount that accurately reflects the current income disparity, the changed custody arrangement, and the financial needs of the children.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce decree, the superior court entered a child support order requiring Brandon Nakamura to pay Marcus Nakamura $850 per month. That amount was calculated based on Brandon's gross annual income of approximately $52,000 and a shared physical custody arrangement under which each parent exercised parenting time with the parties' two minor children for roughly equal periods of time, satisfying the definition of shared physical custody under Alaska Civil Rule 911(f).
Since the entry of the original order, the circumstances of both parties have changed materially. Brandon received a promotion and now earns approximately $74,000 per year, an increase of approximately $22,000 annually from his income at the time the order was entered. Marcus, by contrast, has experienced a significant reduction in income. Due to a medical condition that requires him to limit his working hours, Marcus now earns approximately $38,000 per year, a reduction of approximately $14,000 annually from his prior income level.
The parenting arrangement has also changed substantially. Brandon relocated to a different part of Anchorage for work. As a consequence of that relocation, the children have come to reside primarily with Marcus, who now exercises parenting time approximately 70 percent of the time. Brandon's parenting time has correspondingly decreased to approximately 30 percent of the time. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f), this arrangement no longer qualifies as shared physical custody and instead constitutes primary physical custody in Marcus's favor.
The existing order of $850 per month does not account for Brandon's increased income, Marcus's decreased income, or the change from a shared custody arrangement to a primary custody arrangement with the children residing predominantly with Marcus. Marcus now petitions this Court for an upward modification of child support to approximately $1,400 per month.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.977, a court may, upon motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify a prior judgment providing for the maintenance of minor children. Modification of a child support order is authorized when a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the prior order. AS 25.24.170(b) expressly provides that a material change in circumstances exists when modification of the order would result in a support amount that differs significantly from the currently ordered amount.
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 90.3, which establishes the framework for calculating support based on each parent's adjusted annual income and the physical custody arrangement. Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) governs the calculation of child support in cases of shared physical custody, while Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs calculation when one parent holds primary physical custody. When parenting time has shifted such that one parent now has primary custody, recalculation under the primary custody formula is required.
A material change in circumstances sufficient to justify modification of a child support order may arise from a change in a parent's income, a change in the physical custody arrangement, or both. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a substantial change in the parties' custody arrangement, from shared to primary custody, itself constitutes a material change in circumstances requiring recalculation of the child support obligation. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016). The court has further recognized that a change in income affecting the amount of support that would be calculated under the guidelines by at least 15 percent is presumed to constitute a material change in circumstances. Nicholas Ryan Dunn v. Dakota Christine Jones, 451 P.3d 375 (Alaska 2019). In determining whether and how to modify a support obligation, the court must consider the needs and financial abilities of both parents. Curley v. Curley, 588 P.2d 289 (Alaska 1979); Headlough v. Headlough, 639 P.2d 1010 (Alaska 1982).
When the supporting parent's income exceeds $138,000 annually, Civil Rule 90.3(c)(2) governs and allows the court to make an additional award only if just and proper. Brandon's income does not reach that threshold, and therefore the standard guideline calculations under Civil Rule 90.3(a) apply to this motion.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Has Occurred, Warranting Modification of the Existing Child Support Order.
Modification of a child support order requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.170(a). Three independent and compounding changes in circumstances have occurred since the entry of the 2021 order, each of which independently supports modification and which together make an upward modification plainly warranted.
First, Brandon's income has increased substantially. At the time the original order was entered, Brandon earned approximately $52,000 per year. He now earns approximately $74,000 per year following a promotion, an increase of more than 42 percent. This increase is substantial and well exceeds the threshold at which a presumption of material change arises. Nicholas Ryan Dunn v. Dakota Christine Jones, 451 P.3d 375 (Alaska 2019).
Second, Marcus's income has decreased materially. At the time of the original order, Marcus earned approximately $52,000 per year. He now earns approximately $38,000 annually due to a medical condition that requires reduced work hours. This reduction of approximately $14,000 per year represents a change of nearly 27 percent in his income, further widening the income disparity between the parties since the time the original order was entered. The court is required to consider the financial abilities of both parents when evaluating the need to modify support. Curley v. Curley, 588 P.2d 289 (Alaska 1979). Marcus's reduced earning capacity is a factor the court must weigh in determining the appropriate level of support, as the existing order fails to reflect the current economic reality of either parent.
Third, and perhaps most significantly from a guidelines standpoint, the physical custody arrangement has changed from shared custody to primary custody in Marcus's favor. The original order was based on a shared physical custody calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), which accounts for the fact that both parents bear direct expenditures on the children during their respective periods of custody. That premise no longer reflects reality. The children now reside with Marcus approximately 70 percent of the time and with Brandon approximately 30 percent of the time. Alaska Civil Rule 90.3(f) defines shared physical custody as the children residing with each parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. At exactly 70 percent primary time for Marcus, the arrangement now falls at the outer boundary of or beyond the shared custody definition, and the applicable calculation framework must be revisited accordingly. The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a shift from shared to primary custody constitutes a material change in circumstances requiring recalculation of the child support obligation. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016).
The combined effect of these three simultaneous changes, a large income increase for Brandon, a significant income decrease for Marcus, and a shift in the custody arrangement to primary custody in Marcus's favor, constitutes a material change in circumstances under AS 25.24.170(a) and requires reconsideration of the existing order.
B. The Modified Child Support Amount Should Reflect Brandon's Current Income and the Primary Custody Arrangement.
Having established a material change in circumstances, this Court must recalculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. Because the children now reside with Marcus approximately 70 percent of the time, the applicable framework is the primary custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a), rather than the shared custody formula that formed the basis of the original order.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support is calculated as a percentage of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income based on the number of children. For two children, the applicable percentage produces a guideline obligation that, when applied to Brandon's current income of approximately $74,000 per year, results in a monthly support obligation of approximately $1,400. This amount more accurately reflects Brandon's current ability to pay and the financial burden Marcus bears as the primary residential parent. The court is authorized and directed by AS 25.27.060(a) to carefully consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet their support obligations, and the economic ability of the parents to pay.
The requested modification to $1,400 per month is also consistent with the principle, recognized by the Alaska Supreme Court, that child support should reflect the needs of the children as well as the financial realities of both parents. Headlough v. Headlough, 639 P.2d 1010 (Alaska 1982); Curley v. Curley, 588 P.2d 289 (Alaska 1979). Marcus now bears the preponderance of the direct daily expenses associated with raising the two children, including housing, food, clothing, transportation, and other necessities. Brandon's income has grown substantially while Marcus's has declined due to circumstances beyond his control. The existing order of $850 per month, entered when incomes were comparable and parenting time was roughly equal, does not come close to reflecting the current state of affairs.
Where the guideline calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) would produce a significantly different result from the existing order, the court must apply the guideline amount unless good cause exists under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) to vary from it. No such variation is warranted here. To the contrary, the guideline amount serves the purpose of the support framework, which is to ensure that children benefit from the financial resources of both parents in a manner proportional to each parent's ability to contribute. Halvers v. Pruitt, 342 P.3d 932 (Alaska 2000) (addressing proper calculation of child support where there is a significant disparity between a parent's reported salary and actual income). The goal of the guidelines is to produce a just and proper amount for the parties to contribute toward the nurture and education of their children, and the requested modification accomplishes exactly that objective.
C. The Court Should Ensure That the Modified Order Accurately Reflects the Residential Schedule and Income of Both Parties.
When recalculating child support following a change in physical custody, the court must apply the formula that corresponds to the actual, operative custody arrangement. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018) (addressing proper identification and calculation of the applicable custody category for child support purposes). If the children reside with Marcus 70 percent of the time, the primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs. If the arrangement is treated as shared custody at the 70 percent boundary, the court should apply Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), which accounts for both parents' incomes and their respective percentages of parenting time. Under either calculation, the result under current income figures substantially exceeds $850 per month and supports the requested modification to approximately $1,400 per month.
The court should also take into account, when establishing the modified order, that Marcus's reduced income is attributable to a medical condition requiring reduced working hours, not to voluntary underemployment. The Alaska Supreme Court has addressed the significance of distinguishing between voluntary and involuntary reductions in income when calculating support obligations. Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013). Marcus's reduction in working hours is medically necessitated, not a voluntary choice, and imputing income to him at his prior earning level would be inappropriate under these circumstances. The court must take Marcus's actual current income of approximately $38,000 per year as the operative figure for any calculation involving his income.
The modification Marcus requests is grounded in the plain operation of the guidelines, supported by demonstrated material changes in both the custody arrangement and the parties' incomes, and is necessary to ensure that the children's financial needs are met in a manner that is equitable and proportional to both parents' current circumstances.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Marcus Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court enter an order modifying the existing child support order to require Brandon Nakamura to pay approximately $1,400 per month in child support, effective as of the date of the filing of this motion or such earlier date as the Court deems appropriate. This modification is warranted under AS 25.24.170(a) based on the material changes in circumstances that have occurred since the entry of the 2021 order, including Brandon's substantial increase in income, Marcus's medically necessitated decrease in income, and the shift from shared to primary physical custody in Marcus's favor. The requested modification is consistent with the guidelines set forth in Civil Rule 90.3, serves the best interests of the children, and reflects the current financial realities of both parties.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA

PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0181)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Priya Petrova respectfully requests that this Court modify the existing child support order entered in 2021, which currently requires Respondent Michael Petrova to pay $850 per month in child support. Two distinct and substantial changes in circumstances have occurred since that order was entered: Michael's annual income has increased from $62,000 to approximately $94,000, and the parties' custody arrangement has shifted from roughly equal shared physical custody to a schedule in which the two minor children reside primarily with Priya during the school week and spend only alternating weekends with Michael. Neither of these material changes has been captured in any court order. Because Alaska law requires that child support obligations accurately reflect current income and custody realities, Priya respectfully asks this Court to recalculate support under Civil Rule 982, enter a modified order reflecting Michael's substantially higher earnings, and formally recognize the de facto primary physical custody arrangement that has been in place since early 2023.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Priya Petrova and Michael Petrova divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the court entered a child support order requiring Michael to pay $850 per month. That calculation was based on Michael's annual salary of $62,000 as a commercial electrician, Priya's part-time income of approximately $24,000 per year, and a roughly equal shared physical custody arrangement for the parties' two minor children.
Since entry of that order, circumstances have changed materially in two respects. First, Michael accepted a supervisory position with an Anchorage electrical contractor and now earns approximately $94,000 per year, an increase of approximately $32,000 annually over his income at the time of the last order. Second, beginning in early 2023, the parties informally modified their custody schedule. The two children now reside with Priya during the school week and spend only alternating weekends with Michael. This arrangement places the children with Priya for the substantial majority of the year, well above the 70 percent threshold that defines primary physical custody under Alaska Civil Rule 936(f). This de facto change in the residential schedule has never been memorialized in a court order.
Priya continues to work part-time and earns approximately $27,000 per year, a modest increase from her income at the time of the original order. The current $850 monthly support obligation does not account for Michael's significantly higher income, does not reflect the current custody schedule, and no longer serves the best interests of the children.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a child support order upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.170 provides that "any time after judgment the court, upon the motion of either party, may set aside, alter, or modify so much of the judgment as may provide for . . . the appointment of trustees for the care and custody of the minor children or for their nurture and education." Additionally, AS 25.20.110(a) provides that "an award of custody of a child or visitation with the child may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification of the award and the modification is in the best interests of the child."
Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) establishes that a material change of circumstances is presumed when support as calculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. Once a material change is established, the court recalculates support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3. Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs cases of primary physical custody, providing that child support is calculated "as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2) under all circumstances." For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(b) governs shared physical custody calculations and applies only when a parent has custody for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that child support calculations must adhere to the framework established by Civil Rule 90.3. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016); Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). Courts have also recognized that a change in custody status, from shared to primary, alters the applicable formula and supports modification. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Based on Michael's Substantially Increased Income.
Michael's annual income has risen from $62,000 at the time of the original order to approximately $94,000 today, an increase of more than $32,000 per year. This represents a change of more than 50 percent in gross income. Under the original order, support of $850 per month was calculated based on the shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b). Recalculating under the primary custody formula applicable to the current de facto arrangement, and using Michael's current adjusted annual income, yields a monthly support obligation substantially greater than 15 percent above the existing order. This presumptive material change in circumstances satisfies the threshold for modification under AS 25.24.170 and AS 25.27.060.
In Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that a change in income that causes a more than 15 percent deviation from the existing support order constitutes a presumptive material change of circumstances warranting recalculation. The same principle applies here. Michael's income increase is not marginal. It reflects a sustained and voluntary career advancement, not a temporary fluctuation, and it has been ongoing since he accepted his supervisory role with the Anchorage contractor.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus enumerated mandatory deductions. For two children in the primary physical custody of one parent, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) specifies that "the percentage by which the non-custodial parent's adjusted income must be multiplied in order to calculate the child support award is . . . 27% (.27) for two children." Applying this percentage to Michael's adjusted annual income of approximately $94,000, and accounting for applicable deductions, yields a monthly child support obligation significantly greater than $850. The precise calculation will depend on Michael's verified adjusted annual income, which Priya respectfully requests the Court determine through disclosure of current income documentation.
The Alaska Supreme Court in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), confirmed that a court acts within its discretion when it bases a child support award on the obligor parent's actual gross income and applies the Civil Rule 90.3 formula to that figure. The same approach is warranted here. Michael's increased earnings capacity is not speculative. His employment with the Anchorage contractor at a supervisory level represents a documented and voluntary occupational advancement. The children are entitled to support that reflects their father's current ability to pay.
B. A Material Change in Circumstances Also Exists Based on the De Facto Shift to Primary Physical Custody.
In addition to the income change, the parties' custody arrangement has fundamentally changed. Since early 2023, the two children have lived primarily with Priya during the school week and have spent only alternating weekends with Michael. This schedule gives Michael physical custody for significantly less than 30 percent of the year, removing him from the shared physical custody category altogether under Civil Rule 90.3(f) and placing Priya squarely in the role of primary physical custodian.
Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) governs child support in shared custody cases, which are defined as arrangements in which each parent has the children for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. The alternating-weekend schedule currently in practice gives Michael the children for far less than 30 percent of the year. As a result, the shared custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(b) no longer applies, and the primary custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs. This change in custody classification is itself a material change of circumstances.
In Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that the applicable child support formula turns on the actual custody arrangement, specifically on whether each parent has the children for at least 30 percent of the year as reflected in the custody order. Here, the de facto custody schedule has departed significantly from the 2021 order. Even though no formal modification order has been entered, the court should give effect to the actual residential arrangement in calculating support, and should simultaneously enter an order reflecting the current schedule. The children's welfare is best served by ensuring that support obligations correspond to the parenting realities both parties have been living under for more than two years.
The change from a shared custody arrangement to what is functionally a primary custody arrangement also bears directly on the appropriate formula to apply. Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(C), the shared custody calculation yielded a net offset figure based on the incomes and custody percentages of both parents. That calculation is no longer appropriate when one parent has the children for well below 30 percent of the year. The correct calculation is now governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which multiplies Michael's adjusted annual income by 27 percent for two children. This shift in formula, combined with Michael's increased income, results in a substantially higher monthly obligation than the current $850 order.
C. Modification Serves the Best Interests of the Children.
Under AS 25.20.110(a), modification of a custody or support arrangement must be in the best interests of the child. Here, both components of Priya's requested modification, the upward income recalculation and the formal recognition of the de facto custody schedule, plainly serve the children's best interests. The children reside primarily with Priya and depend on her to meet their daily needs during the school week. The current support amount, calculated years ago based on lower incomes and an equal custody split, does not adequately account for the disproportionate financial burden now borne by Priya.
Michael's income has increased substantially, and he is fully capable of contributing more to the children's support. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997), recognized that child support determinations must account for the supporting parent's actual financial capacity and the children's standard of living. An upward modification to reflect Michael's $94,000 annual income is consistent with both the guidelines and the children's right to share in their father's financial success.
In addition, formalizing the current custody arrangement in a court order is in the children's best interests because it provides stability, clarity, and legal certainty regarding where the children reside and how parenting time is allocated. AS 25.20.110(a) requires the court to enter on the record its reasons for modification when a parent opposes it; Priya provides the factual and legal basis for that finding here through the documented change in the children's residential schedule since early 2023.
D. The Correct Child Support Amount Should Be Calculated Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Using Michael's Current Adjusted Annual Income.
The two-step analysis required in this case is straightforward. First, the Court should recognize that the current de facto custody arrangement qualifies as primary physical custody in Priya's favor, triggering Civil Rule 90.3(a). Second, the Court should apply the 27 percent multiplier to Michael's adjusted annual income, as required by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) for two children.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines the deductions available to reduce gross income to adjusted annual income, including mandatory taxes, Social Security contributions, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and certain voluntary retirement contributions up to 7.5 percent of total income. Priya respectfully requests that this Court order Michael to provide current income documentation so that his adjusted annual income can be precisely determined and the correct monthly obligation calculated. Priya estimates, based on publicly available wage information, that Michael's adjusted annual income after applicable deductions is approximately $82,000 to $86,000, yielding a monthly child support obligation in the range of approximately $1,845 to $1,935 per month, which represents a substantial increase over the existing $850 order.
In Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 525 P.3d 281 (Alaska 2025), the Alaska Supreme Court addressed a situation in which a party sought to modify child support based on income information reflected in tax returns, confirming that the court may rely on documented income evidence to determine the appropriate support level under Civil Rule 90.3. The same principle supports using Michael's current employment and salary documentation to anchor the recalculation here.
Priya further notes that if the Court finds Michael has taken steps to limit his reported income or has voluntarily reduced his earnings capacity in any respect, the Court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to impute potential income based on Michael's demonstrated earning capacity, employment history, job skills, and the prevailing wage levels in the Anchorage electrical trade.
V. CONCLUSION
The existing child support order of $850 per month no longer reflects the parties' actual financial circumstances or the children's residential arrangement. Michael's annual income has increased by more than $32,000, the custody schedule has shifted to place the children primarily in Priya's care, and more than three years have passed since the order was entered without any modification. Each of these facts independently supports a finding of material change in circumstances under AS 25.24.170, AS 25.20.110, and Civil Rule 90.3. Together, they compel an upward modification.
Priya Petrova respectfully requests that this Court: (1) find that a material change in circumstances exists based on Michael's substantially increased income and the de facto shift to primary physical custody; (2) formally recognize Priya as the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children consistent with the residential schedule in place since early 2023; (3) recalculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using Michael's current adjusted annual income of approximately $94,000; and (4) enter a modified child support order consistent with those findings, effective as of the date of this motion.
The children are entitled to support that reflects both parents' current financial realities and the actual division of parenting responsibilities. Justice and the guidelines both require a modification.

PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
