I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Okafor respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered at the time of the parties' 2021 divorce. The current order requires Jennifer Okafor to pay $650 per month in child support, an amount calculated on the basis of Jennifer's annual salary of $52,000 as a dental hygienist and Ashley's then-approximate earnings of $24,000 per year. Since the entry of that order, circumstances have changed materially for both parties. Jennifer has accepted a new position as a clinic supervisor earning $81,000 annually, representing a substantial increase in her income. Ashley, meanwhile, has reduced her working hours in order to serve as the primary caregiver for the parties' eight-year-old son, who resides principally with Ashley under the current custody arrangement. Jennifer's parenting time is limited to every other weekend and one evening per week, confirming Ashley's status as the primary physical custodian.
These changed circumstances warrant recalculation of Jennifer's child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which ties support to the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. The current order no longer reflects economic reality and, if left unmodified, would fail to serve the best interests of the child. Ashley respectfully requests that this Court exercise its authority under AS 25.24.170 to modify the existing support order and enter a new order consistent with the guidelines and the parties' present financial circumstances.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Okafor and Jennifer Okafor were divorced by order of this Court in 2021. At the time of divorce, the Court entered a child support order requiring Jennifer to pay $650 per month. That figure was derived from Jennifer's annual salary of $52,000 as a dental hygienist and Ashley's approximate annual earnings of $24,000 while working part-time.
The parties' eight-year-old son resides primarily with Ashley. Under the operative custody arrangement, Jennifer has parenting time every other weekend and one evening per week. Jennifer is therefore the non-custodial parent for purposes of Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Since the 2021 order, Jennifer accepted a new position as a clinic supervisor at a significantly higher salary of $81,000 per year. This represents an increase of $29,000 in gross annual income, more than a fifty-five percent rise over her income at the time the existing support order was established. Jennifer has not voluntarily notified the Court or Ashley of this income change, and no adjustment to the support order has been made.
Ashley, in turn, has further reduced her working hours to ensure adequate care for the parties' son, whose needs have grown as he has become more active in school and extracurricular activities. Ashley's reduced earnings increase her dependence on a support award that accurately reflects Jennifer's current income. The present monthly payment of $650 does not reflect the financial reality of Jennifer's elevated earning capacity, and the disparity between the existing order and a properly calculated guideline amount exceeds fifteen percent, thereby establishing a presumptive change in circumstances under Rule 90.3.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A. Modification of Child Support Orders
Under AS 25.24.950, a court may, upon motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify so much of a judgment as provides for the maintenance of either party or for the care and nurture of minor children. Alaska law further provides that the adoption of new guidelines or a significant change in income may constitute a material change in circumstances justifying modification. AS 25.24.170(b) specifies that a material change in circumstances is required as a predicate to modification, and courts look to whether a meaningful change in the financial condition of either party has occurred since the last order.
Alaska courts have recognized that a substantial increase in a non-custodial parent's income supports modification of an existing child support order. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016). Where the difference between the current order and the amount that would be required under the guidelines exceeds fifteen percent, a rebuttable presumption of a material change in circumstances arises under the framework of Civil Rule 90.3.
B. Calculating Child Support Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of child support in cases in which one parent has primary physical custody. The rule provides that the child support award shall equal the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which is twenty percent for one child. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). Adjusted annual income is defined as the parent's total income from all sources, minus mandatory deductions such as federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, as well as certain other allowable deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
Modification of an existing order to conform to guideline amounts is the default remedy when a material change in circumstances has been demonstrated. Corbeau v. Dietrich, 534 P.3d 403 (Alaska 2019).
C. Deviation from Guidelines Requires Clear and Convincing Evidence
Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) authorizes a court to vary the child support award calculated under the guideline formula, but only upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result from application of the formula. The rule further requires the court to specify in writing the reasons for any variation and to identify the amount that would have been required absent the variance. Good cause for deviation may include unusual circumstances that make the formula unjust. Christopher D. v. Krislyn D., 426 P.3d 1118 (Alaska 2018). The burden of establishing such unusual circumstances falls on the party seeking deviation. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Has Occurred
The threshold question in any modification proceeding is whether a material change in circumstances has taken place since the entry of the existing order. AS 25.24.920. Here, that threshold is clearly satisfied. Jennifer's annual income has increased from $52,000 to $81,000, a difference of $29,000, or more than fifty-five percent. This change is not minor or temporary; Jennifer holds a new supervisory position that carries this higher compensation on a salaried basis going forward.
The Alaska Supreme Court held in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), that courts should calculate child support based on the best available approximation of the parent's current and anticipated future income. Jennifer's current salary is the best available figure for this purpose and is substantially higher than the income figure used in the 2021 order. Where the properly calculated guideline amount differs from the existing order by more than fifteen percent, courts treat that disparity as presumptive evidence of a material change in circumstances. The gap here far exceeds that threshold.
In addition, Ashley's reduction in working hours, undertaken to provide primary caregiving for the parties' son, represents a concurrent change in the financial circumstances of the custodial household. Taken together, the increase in Jennifer's income and the decrease in Ashley's earnings create a significantly altered economic landscape from that which existed when the 2021 order was entered.
B. The Guideline Calculation Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Requires an Upward Adjustment
Civil Rule 90.3(a) establishes a straightforward formula for calculating child support in primary physical custody cases. The non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income is multiplied by twenty percent for one child. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A). Applying this framework to Jennifer's current salary of $81,000 requires computing her adjusted annual income by subtracting mandatory deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including federal income tax, state income tax, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax, as well as any applicable allowable voluntary retirement contributions not to exceed 7.5 percent of total income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B).
Assuming standard mandatory deductions and no extraordinary offsets, Jennifer's adjusted annual income will be materially higher than the income figure used to derive the existing $650 monthly order. Multiplying the resulting adjusted figure by twenty percent and dividing by twelve will yield a monthly obligation that substantially exceeds $650. Ashley respectfully requests that the Court direct both parties to submit updated Civil Rule 90.3 financial affidavits, commonly referred to as DR-305 forms, so that the precise adjusted annual income and the corresponding monthly support obligation can be determined with accuracy. See Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008) (discussing the use of updated financial affidavits to establish current income for purposes of Rule 90.3 calculations).
The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), underscores that a court conducting a modification analysis must examine all available evidence to arrive at the most accurate picture of the non-custodial parent's current income, including salary information from current employment. Jennifer's W-2 or current pay documentation reflecting her $81,000 salary will provide the appropriate evidentiary basis for this calculation.
C. The Court Should Decline to Deviate Downward from the Guideline Amount
Jennifer may argue for a deviation from the guideline amount based on the disparity between her income and Ashley's. Such an argument must fail under controlling Alaska precedent. Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) permits deviation only upon proof by clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would result from application of the guideline. In Christopher D. v. Krislyn D., 426 P.3d 1118 (Alaska 2018), the Alaska Supreme Court held that the superior court did not abuse its discretion by declining to find unusual circumstances warranting deviation simply because of an income disparity between the parties. The court observed that income disparity between divorcing or divorced spouses is not, by itself, an unusual circumstance justifying a departure from the formula.
In Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), the Alaska Supreme Court recognized that the Rule 90.3 formula is designed to produce a just result across the ordinary range of income situations. Deviation is reserved for genuinely unusual circumstances, not ordinary differences in earning capacity between parties. Jennifer's income of $81,000, while higher than Ashley's reduced earnings, does not bring Jennifer into the elevated income range governed by Civil Rule 90.3(c)(2), which applies to adjusted annual incomes exceeding $138,000. There is therefore no basis for departing from the standard twenty-percent formula applicable under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(A).
Skinner v. Hagberg, 183 P.3d 486 (Alaska 2008), reaffirms that any good cause variation requires the court to specify in writing the reasons for departure and the amount that would otherwise have applied. Were the Court inclined to entertain any request for deviation, Ashley respectfully submits that no such finding could be made on these facts, as nothing about Jennifer's transition from dental hygienist to clinic supervisor at a higher salary presents the kind of unusual circumstance that would make application of the formula unjust.
D. Income Withholding Should Be Ordered to Ensure Compliance
To ensure timely and consistent payment of any modified support obligation, Ashley requests that the Court include an income withholding order as required by AS 25.27.062(a). That statute mandates that any support order must contain an income withholding provision providing for immediate income withholding. An income withholding order will direct Jennifer's employer to withhold the support amount from Jennifer's wages and transmit those funds to the Child Support Services Division. AS 25.27.062(b). This mechanism protects Ashley and the parties' son from any future lapses in payment and eliminates the need for repeated enforcement proceedings.
AS 25.27.062(g) provides that an income withholding order has priority over all other attachments, executions, garnishments, or other legal process brought under state law against the same property, ensuring that the child's support interest is protected. Given that Jennifer's income increase was not voluntarily disclosed and no modification was sought by Jennifer, an income withholding order is a prudent and legally required component of the modified support order.
E. The Modification Should Be Retroactive to the Date of Filing
Ashley respectfully requests that the Court make the modified support obligation effective as of the date this motion to modify was filed. AS 25.27.200 directs that support amounts be established in conformity with applicable guidelines and standards. The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that while retroactive modification to a date before the filing of a motion is prohibited, modification to the date of filing is appropriate and is generally ordered when a material change in circumstances has been demonstrated. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). Jennifer has benefited from the lower support obligation during the period in which her income was substantially higher, and fairness to Ashley and the child requires that the adjusted obligation take effect without further delay from the filing date.
V. CONCLUSION
The undisputed facts establish that a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the 2021 child support order. Jennifer's annual income has risen by more than fifty-five percent, from $52,000 to $81,000, while Ashley's income has decreased as she devotes more time to primary caregiving for the parties' son. The existing monthly obligation of $650 no longer reflects the guideline calculation required by Civil Rule 90.3(a) and fails to meet the needs of the child in light of Jennifer's current earning capacity.
For all of the foregoing reasons, Ashley Okafor respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the 2021 support order under AS 25.24.170(a);
2. Order both parties to submit updated DR-305 financial affidavits reflecting current income and allowable deductions;
3. Calculate Jennifer's modified child support obligation pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a), applying the twenty-percent multiplier to Jennifer's adjusted annual income;
4. Decline to deviate from the guideline calculation absent clear and convincing evidence of manifest injustice under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1);
5. Include an income withholding order pursuant to AS 25.27.062 directing Jennifer's employer to withhold and remit the monthly support amount; and
6. Make the modified order retroactive to the date of the filing of this motion.
Ashley Okafor respectfully submits that granting this motion is both legally required and necessary to ensure that the parties' son receives the financial support to which he is entitled under Alaska law.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0183)
I. INTRODUCTION
David Larsen respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021, which requires Michael Larsen to pay $1,200 per month in child support. Two significant changes in circumstances have occurred since that order was entered. First, Michael has substantially increased his gross monthly income by accepting full-time employment as a petroleum equipment technician in Anchorage, raising his earnings from approximately $4,800 to $7,500 per month. Second, the actual parenting time distribution has shifted materially, with the two minor children now residing with David approximately 70 percent of the year, thereby transitioning the custody arrangement from shared physical custody to one that more accurately reflects primary physical custody in David's favor. Together, these changes compel an upward modification of child support under Alaska law and Civil Rule 90.3 to ensure the children receive support commensurate with both parents' current financial circumstances and the actual time the children spend in each household.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Larsen and Michael Larsen were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce decree, the Court entered a child support order requiring Michael to pay $1,200 per month. That order was based on Michael's income as a commercial fisherman, which generated approximately $4,800 in gross monthly income, and on a shared custody arrangement in which each parent had approximately equal parenting time with the parties' two minor children.
Following the divorce, Michael accepted a full-time position as a petroleum equipment technician in Anchorage. This career change substantially increased his gross monthly income to approximately $7,500, representing a significant departure from the income figure underlying the existing support order. Michael's annualized gross income under the current arrangement is approximately $90,000, compared to approximately $57,600 per year at the time the order was entered.
David continues to work as a dental office receptionist, earning approximately $3,200 per month, or approximately $38,400 per year. David's income has not materially changed since the original order.
In conjunction with Michael's relocation to Anchorage for employment, the actual parenting time arrangement has shifted substantially. The two minor children now reside with David approximately 70 percent of the year. This shift moves the arrangement outside the shared physical custody framework that formed the basis of the original child support calculation and instead reflects a primary physical custody arrangement in David's favor.
David now petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order upward to reflect both Michael's increased income and the actual distribution of parenting time, in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), an award of child support may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Separately, AS 25.24.170 provides that the court may, upon the motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify provisions of a prior judgment relating to the support of minor children.
Child support amounts in Alaska are governed by Civil Rule 90.3. In cases where one parent has primary physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(a) directs that the support award be calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a specified percentage: 20 percent for one child and 27 percent for two children. In cases where the parents share physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(b) provides an alternative calculation methodology that accounts for the parenting time each parent exercises and the income of both parents.
A material change in circumstances sufficient to trigger modification review may arise from a substantial change in a parent's income. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that courts do not abuse their discretion when child support is calculated in adherence to Civil Rule 90.3. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016). The Supreme Court has also addressed circumstances in which modification is appropriate when the Rule 90.3 formula, applied to updated income figures, yields a result that differs materially from the existing order. Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008). Furthermore, Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), confirms that a court should assess whether recalculation of child support under Rule 90.3 based on a parent's current, accurately reported income produces a result constituting a material change of circumstances warranting modification.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Substantial Change in Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification.
Modification of a child support order is warranted when the moving party demonstrates a change in circumstances that requires modification and that the modification is in the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.110(a). In the present case, two independent and overlapping changes in circumstances have occurred since the 2021 order, each of which independently supports modification, and the combination of which strongly compels it.
First, Michael's income has increased dramatically. At the time of the original order, Michael earned approximately $4,800 per month as a commercial fisherman. He now earns approximately $7,500 per month as a petroleum equipment technician, representing an increase of approximately $2,700 per month, or roughly 56 percent. This is precisely the type of material income change that courts consider when determining whether modification is warranted. In Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), the Alaska Supreme Court acknowledged that a recalculation of child support under Rule 90.3 reflecting a parent's significantly different income, where that recalculation yields more than a 15 percent change from the existing support amount, supports a finding of changed circumstances. Here, applying the Rule 90.3 formula to Michael's increased income yields a result substantially higher than $1,200 per month, as further demonstrated below.
Second, the actual parenting time distribution has changed materially. The original order was grounded in a shared physical custody framework in which each parent exercised approximately equal parenting time, which triggered the shared custody calculation methodology under Civil Rule 90.3(b). The children now reside with David approximately 70 percent of the year. A 70/30 parenting time split no longer qualifies as shared physical custody under the framework of Civil Rule 90.3(b). The arrangement is now more accurately characterized as one in which David has primary physical custody, triggering the primary custody calculation methodology under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Together, these two changes compel upward modification. AS 25.24.170 confirms the Court's broad authority to modify prior child support provisions, and AS 25.20.110(a) establishes that such modification is appropriate where circumstances have changed and modification serves the children's best interests. Providing child support that accurately reflects a parent's actual income and the actual time the children spend with each parent unquestionably serves the best interests of the children.
B. The Applicable Child Support Calculation Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Produces a Substantially Higher Obligation.
Because the children now reside with David approximately 70 percent of the year, the primary physical custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a) applies. That provision directs that the child support award be calculated as "an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." Civil Rule 90.3(a). For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Michael's gross annual income is approximately $90,000. To determine his adjusted annual income, the Court will subtract mandatory deductions as specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including federal and state income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and any other applicable mandatory deductions. After applying reasonable estimates of these standard deductions to a gross annual income of $90,000, Michael's adjusted annual income is expected to fall in the range of approximately $72,000 to $80,000, depending on the precise deductions established through his financial affidavit.
Applying the 27 percent multiplier for two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to an adjusted annual income of, for illustration, $75,000, yields an annual child support obligation of $20,250, or approximately $1,687.50 per month. Even at the lower end of adjusted income estimates, the resulting monthly obligation will substantially exceed the current order of $1,200 per month. The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that a court does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016). Here, strict adherence to the Rule 90.3(a) formula, applied to Michael's current income, compels a substantially higher monthly support award.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also recognized that where the obligor parent has elected to change employment or roles, and where that choice affects income, the court retains discretion to assess the income as reported or, where appropriate, to consider whether potential income should be imputed. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025). In this case, Michael's career change resulted in a significant income increase rather than a decrease, and his reported income of $7,500 per month directly supports a higher child support obligation. There is no basis for any downward deviation from Michael's actual current income.
C. The Income Withholding Provisions of Alaska Law Ensure Consistent Payment.
In the event the Court modifies the child support order, David respectfully requests that the Court include an income withholding provision in the modified order. AS 25.27.062(a) provides that a court order providing for support must contain an income withholding order. The statute further provides that such an income withholding order must, in certain circumstances, provide for immediate income withholding. AS 25.27.062(a)(2). An income withholding order will help ensure consistent and timely payment of the modified support amount, thereby serving the best interests of the children and minimizing the potential for arrears.
D. David's Lower Income Further Supports an Upward Adjustment.
David earns approximately $3,200 per month as a dental office receptionist, substantially less than Michael's $7,500 per month. The disparity between the parties' incomes is relevant to the Court's consideration of the appropriate child support amount. Under AS 25.27.060(a), the court is directed to carefully consider the need for support and the ability of both parents to meet their support obligations. The current support amount of $1,200 per month was calculated at a time when the income disparity was less pronounced and when Michael was not the de facto non-primary custodial parent. Now, with Michael earning nearly 2.3 times what David earns on a monthly basis, and with David bearing primary responsibility for the children's day-to-day needs approximately 70 percent of the time, the equities and the statutory framework both call for a higher support obligation from Michael.
Furthermore, the Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997), confirms that when calculating child support, courts are to apply the Rule 90.3 percentages to the non-custodial parent's adjusted income in a manner that reflects the children's actual needs and the supporting parent's ability to pay. The income data in the present case clearly establishes that Michael has the ability to pay a substantially higher amount, and that David and the children have a genuine need for additional support given the changed circumstances.
E. This Court Retains Jurisdiction to Modify the Existing Support Order.
This Court retains jurisdiction to modify the existing child support order. AS 25.25.205(a) provides that a tribunal of this state that has issued a child support order consistent with the law of this state has and shall exercise continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify its child support order where, at the time of the filing of the request for modification, this state is the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child for whose benefit the support order is issued. Michael resides and works in Anchorage, Alaska. David resides in Alaska. The children reside primarily with David in Alaska. Accordingly, this Court retains continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify the support order.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, David Larsen respectfully requests that this Court grant the motion to modify child support and enter an order that:
1. Finds that a material change in circumstances has occurred based on Michael Larsen's substantially increased income and the shift in the actual parenting time distribution to a primary physical custody arrangement in David's favor;
2. Recalculates Michael's child support obligation in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), using Michael's current adjusted annual income and applying the 27 percent multiplier applicable to two children, resulting in a monthly child support obligation substantially higher than the current $1,200;
3. Determines David's adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3 for purposes of any offset calculation the Court deems appropriate; and
4. Includes an income withholding order pursuant to AS 25.27.062 to ensure consistent payment of the modified child support obligation.
The proposed modification is supported by the evidence of changed circumstances, compelled by the Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines, and is in the best interests of the two minor children whose welfare this proceeding is designed to protect.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0184)
I. INTRODUCTION
Marcus Sutter petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Two material changes in circumstances have occurred since that order was entered. First, Brandon Sutter's annual income has increased from $52,000 to $84,000, a substantial rise that was not reflected in the original calculation. Second, the children's residential arrangement has shifted so that they now reside primarily with Marcus approximately 70 percent of the time, fundamentally altering the custody structure assumed when the original order was crafted. Because both changes are substantial and independently sufficient to justify modification, and because the revised calculation under Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 would produce a child support amount more than 15 percent greater than the outstanding order, this Court should grant Marcus's petition and recalculate child support in accordance with current law and the parties' present circumstances.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Marcus Sutter and Brandon Sutter were divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce decree, the superior court entered a child support order based on Brandon's annual income of $52,000 as a commercial fisherman and Marcus's annual income of $38,000 as a retail store manager. The original order was calculated under a shared physical custody framework reflecting a near-equal parenting time arrangement between the parties.
Since entry of that order, two significant changes have occurred. Brandon accepted a salaried position as a logistics coordinator earning $84,000 per year, a departure from his prior seasonal commercial fishing income of $52,000. Marcus's income has remained largely unchanged at approximately $40,000 per year.
In addition to the income change, the parties have informally modified their parenting schedule. The children now reside with Marcus approximately 70 percent of the time, making Marcus the primary physical custodian in functional terms. This shift from a near-equal parenting arrangement to one in which the children live with Marcus the substantial majority of the time represents a material departure from the custody structure on which the original child support calculation was premised.
Marcus now seeks a modification of the existing child support order to account for Brandon's substantially increased income and the children's current primary residence with Marcus.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A child support order may be modified upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. Under AS 25.24.170(a), after judgment a court may set aside, alter, or modify provisions of a judgment that address the maintenance of the parties or the care and custody of minor children. The statute authorizes modification any time upon the motion of either party.
Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 governs the calculation of child support in Alaska. Where one parent has primary physical custody, child support is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage set by the rule based on the number of children. Civil Rule 90.3(a). For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). A material change in circumstances is presumed when support as recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3 would be more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. See Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005); Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017).
The court may also base a child support calculation on a determination of a parent's potential income when a parent is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). A parent may be found voluntarily underemployed when the parent's current earnings reflect a decision to earn less than the parent is capable of earning. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(A). That provision is not at issue here, as Brandon's current salary of $84,000 reflects actual, documented employment income.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Based on Brandon's Substantially Increased Income.
The most straightforward basis for modification is the significant increase in Brandon's annual income. At the time of the original order, Brandon earned $52,000 per year as a commercial fisherman. He now earns $84,000 per year as a salaried logistics coordinator. This represents an increase of $32,000 in gross annual income, or approximately 61.5 percent above his income at the time the order was entered.
Alaska courts have recognized that a substantial change in the income of either party is a recognized ground for modification of child support. In Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that the 15 percent threshold test under Civil Rule 90.3 is the appropriate measure for determining whether a material change of circumstances has occurred with respect to child support. In Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005), the court similarly applied Civil Rule 90.3's formula to determine whether a change in a parent's income was sufficient to trigger a modification.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support in a primary custody case is calculated as the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Based on Brandon's current gross income of $84,000, even before accounting for all allowable deductions, the preliminary calculation demonstrates a support figure materially in excess of what was ordered in 2021 based on $52,000 in income. The difference between the calculation at $52,000 and the calculation at $84,000 greatly exceeds the 15 percent threshold that presumptively establishes a material change of circumstances. This Court should therefore find that a material change in circumstances exists based on Brandon's income increase alone.
B. A Material Change in Circumstances Also Exists Based on the Shift in the Children's Primary Residence.
Independent of the income change, the shift in the children's residential arrangement constitutes a separate and equally compelling basis for modification. The original child support order was calculated under a shared physical custody framework reflecting a near-equal parenting time split. The children now reside with Marcus approximately 70 percent of the time.
The distinction between shared physical custody and primary physical custody is significant under Alaska law and directly affects the child support calculation. In Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the Alaska Supreme Court explained that a parent has primary physical custody when the children reside with that parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of more than 70 percent of the year, and that shared physical custody exists when the children reside with a parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year. The court in Holmes further confirmed that the applicable child support formula, and thus the support amount owed, differs depending on which custody category applies, with primary physical custody cases governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a) and shared custody cases governed by a separate shared-custody formula.
Here, the children's current residential arrangement places Marcus at or approaching the threshold for primary physical custody. At 70 percent, Marcus is at the upper boundary of the shared custody range and approaching the primary custody threshold. Regardless of the precise label applied, the shift from a near-equal split to a 70-percent-with-Marcus arrangement represents a substantial departure from the custody structure on which the original order was premised. This shift directly affects both the appropriate formula to apply and the resulting support amount.
Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013), reinforces the importance of applying the correct Civil Rule 90.3 methodology to the actual custody arrangement in place at the time of modification. In that case, the Alaska Supreme Court vacated a child support modification order and remanded for recalculation because the superior court had not conformed its analysis to the requirements of Rule 90.3(a). The same principle applies here: the current child support order was calculated under a framework that no longer reflects the children's actual living arrangement, and it must be recalculated under the formula appropriate to their present circumstances.
The Alaska Supreme Court has further recognized that courts must examine the custody arrangement as it actually exists when calculating or modifying support. Gorton v. Mann, 281 P.3d 81 (Alaska 2012), illustrates that the percentage of time each parent actually has custody of the children is a controlling factor in the Rule 90.3 calculation. In Gorton, the court carefully examined the actual percentage of time each parent had custody and applied the appropriate formula based on those findings. This Court should do the same here.
C. The Combined Effect of Both Changes Requires Recalculation Under Civil Rule 90.3.
When both changed circumstances are considered together, the case for recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3 is compelling. Brandon's income has increased by more than 60 percent. The children's primary residence has shifted substantially in favor of Marcus. The original order reflects neither of these realities.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), a child support award where one parent has primary physical custody is calculated as the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Adjusted annual income is defined as total income from all sources minus the mandatory and authorized deductions specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1). These deductions include mandatory items such as federal, state, and local income tax; Social Security tax; Medicare tax; mandatory union dues; and mandatory contributions to a retirement or pension plan, as well as certain authorized voluntary contributions and other permitted deductions.
As illustrated in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), courts must carefully examine a parent's actual income, including all documented sources, when determining the appropriate child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3. In that case, the Alaska Supreme Court addressed how a parent's full income, as reflected in tax filings, must be accounted for in the Rule 90.3 calculation. Here, Brandon's income is straightforwardly documented: he earns an $84,000 annual salary as a logistics coordinator, which is his primary source of income and should form the basis of the adjusted annual income calculation.
Marcus respectfully submits that after accounting for allowable deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), Brandon's adjusted annual income will be substantially higher than it was at the time of the original order, and the resulting child support obligation, calculated at 27 percent of that adjusted income for two children, will far exceed the amount currently ordered. The modification requested is not a windfall for Marcus; it is the result that Alaska law requires when income increases significantly and the children's primary residence changes materially.
D. Modification Serves the Best Interests of the Children.
Any modification of child support must serve the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified when a change in circumstances requires modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Although AS 25.20.110 speaks primarily to custody modifications, the principle that child-related orders must serve the children's best interests pervades Alaska family law and applies with equal force to child support.
Alaska courts have consistently recognized that accurate, current child support awards are essential to the well-being of children. Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008), illustrates the importance of keeping child support orders current and accurate in light of changing circumstances, consistent with the requirements of Civil Rule 90.3. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), similarly reflects that the child support framework is designed to ensure that support levels accurately track the supporting parent's ability to pay.
Here, the children reside primarily with Marcus 70 percent of the time. Marcus bears the daily financial burden of housing, feeding, clothing, and otherwise caring for the children on a primary basis. The current child support order, calculated on an outdated income figure and a custody structure that no longer exists, does not adequately account for Brandon's current capacity to contribute to his children's support or for the financial responsibilities Marcus now shoulders. Modifying the order to reflect current realities directly serves the children's financial well-being and is consistent with the purposes underlying Civil Rule 90.3.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Marcus Sutter respectfully requests that this Court grant his petition to modify the existing child support order. Two independent and substantial changes in circumstances have occurred since the 2021 order was entered: Brandon Sutter's annual income has increased from $52,000 to $84,000, and the children's primary residence has shifted to Marcus approximately 70 percent of the time. Each change independently satisfies the material change of circumstances standard under Alaska law. Together, they require a comprehensive recalculation of child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a), using Brandon's current adjusted annual income and the applicable 27 percent multiplier for two children under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Marcus requests that the Court enter a modified child support order consistent with the results of that calculation, effective at the earliest date permitted by law.

III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170, a court may, upon the motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify a judgment that provides for the maintenance or support of minor children. Any such modification requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). Alaska courts have long recognized that a significant change in one or both parents' income may constitute a material change in circumstances sufficient to justify modification of a child support order. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997); Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989).
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of child support in cases where one parent is awarded primary physical custody. Under that rule, the support award is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a specified percentage. The percentage applied depends on the number of children subject to the order. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). A material change in circumstances is presumed when recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3 produces a support amount more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017).
The court may also consider whether a parent is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed, and if so, may impute potential income to that parent in calculating support. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). Additionally, the court retains authority to ensure that child support calculations accurately reflect each parent's total income from all sources, subject to the deductions specified in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1). Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025).

State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989).
Moreover, Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), confirms that a material change of circumstances is presumed when a recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3 produces a support obligation more than 15 percent greater than the existing order. As set forth in greater detail in Section IV.B below, the recalculated support obligation based on Wesley's current income is approximately $1,450 per month. This figure exceeds the existing $850 per month order by approximately $600, or roughly 71 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that a child support award in a case where one parent holds primary physical custody shall be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by the applicable percentage. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus specified mandatory and permissible deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, mandatory union dues, mandatory retirement contributions, and other enumerated items. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A)-(G).
Wesley's gross annual income is approximately $94,000. In that case, the Court stressed that child support calculations must accurately account for all sources of income available to the non-custodial parent, not merely W-2 wages. The Alaska Supreme Court's holding in Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013), further underscores that child support must be calculated in strict conformity with the analytical framework set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a). In that case, the Court vacated a modification order because the superior court's determination of the amount owed did not conform to the required Rule 90.3(a) analysis. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). Tomas requests that this Court conduct a thorough Rule 90.3(a) analysis on a complete income record so that the modified award is both legally correct and durable against future challenge.

Tomas respectfully requests that the Court take judicial notice of publicly available wage and salary information for construction project managers in the Fairbanks area to corroborate the income levels attributed to Wesley in this motion, to the extent such information is of a type subject to judicial notice under that rule. This information, combined with Wesley's own income documentation, will provide the Court with a reliable factual foundation for the Rule 90.3 recalculation.
V. CONCLUSION
The undisputed increase in Wesley Sutter's annual income from approximately $52,000 at the time of the 2021 order to approximately $94,000 today constitutes a material change in circumstances that clearly justifies upward modification of the existing child support obligation under AS 25.24.170 and Civil Rule 90.3. The recalculated monthly obligation of approximately $1,450, derived from application of the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula to Wesley's current adjusted annual income, exceeds the existing $850 order by more than 15 percent, establishing the presumption of a material change of circumstances as recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). The modification Tomas seeks is firmly grounded in Alaska statutory and rule-based authority, and it reflects the children's genuine and ongoing needs for housing, healthcare, and educational support.
For these reasons, Tomas Sutter respectfully requests that this Court enter an order: (1) finding that a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the 2021 child support order; (2) modifying the child support obligation to approximately $1,450 per month, calculated in strict conformity with Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on complete and verified income disclosure from both parties; (3) including a mandatory income withholding provision in the modified order as required by AS 25.27.062; and (4) granting such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper.

III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a child support order upon a showing of a material change of circumstances. AS 25.24.170(a) authorizes the court, upon motion of either party, to set aside, alter, or modify a judgment that provides for the maintenance of the parties or for child-related support. AS 25.24.170(b) further provides that a modification of child support may be made without an independent showing of a material change in circumstances when the existing order has not been modified or adjusted during the three years preceding the periodic modification, as necessary to comply with applicable federal law.
Alaska Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of child support when one parent holds primary physical custody, defining the award as an amount equal to the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a percentage determined by the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources, subject to specified mandatory and permissible deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits the court to calculate support based on the potential income of a parent who voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed.
A material change of circumstances is presumed when child support calculated under the applicable rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. This presumption is well-established in Alaska case law. In Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that the 15 percent threshold triggers the presumption of a material change in circumstances under Civil Rule 90.3. In Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), the Alaska Supreme Court applied this same framework in a modification proceeding, confirming that the petitioning party need only demonstrate that support calculated under the current guidelines exceeds or falls below the existing order by more than 15 percent to establish the presumption. In Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that changes in income and changes in custodial or visitation patterns may each independently constitute a material change in circumstances supporting modification.
The moving party must also demonstrate that modification serves the best interests of the children. AS 25.20.960 requires that, where a custody-related modification has already occurred, the court consider whether the modification of the corresponding support arrangements is consistent with the children's best interests.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A MATERIAL CHANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES EXISTS AND MODIFICATION IS WARRANTED.

This increase of approximately $32,000 represents a rise of more than 60 percent above the baseline figure used to set the existing order. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), child support for two children in a primary custody arrangement is calculated at 27 percent of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income. Applying this percentage to Wesley's current income produces a support obligation substantially greater than the amount currently ordered.
In Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), the Alaska Supreme Court confirmed that the court must apply the Rule 90.3(a)(2) formula to the non-custodial parent's current adjusted annual income and that a difference of more than 15 percent between the calculated amount and the existing order establishes a presumed material change of circumstances. The difference between support calculated on $84,000 in annual income at 27 percent and support calculated on $52,000 at whatever blended rate applied under the prior shared-custody framework far exceeds the 15 percent threshold. Modification is therefore presumed appropriate.
In Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996), the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that increases in a parent's income are among the paradigmatic circumstances triggering modification of child support. In Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), the Alaska Supreme Court similarly recognized that shifts in a parent's income level are a classic basis for a finding of changed circumstances. Wesley's income increase is not temporary or attributable to a one-time event; it reflects a sustained change in Wesley's professional role and compensation, and it is appropriate for the court to treat Wesley's current project manager salary as the operative income figure for purposes of calculating adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
In Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), the Alaska Supreme Court examined how courts should handle the income of a parent who may have stepped back from higher-earning responsibilities, and addressed whether imputation of potential income is appropriate when a parent's choices reduce reported earnings. Here, the opposite situation exists: Wesley's income has increased to a documented level, and no imputation is necessary. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f), a parent has primary physical custody when the children reside with that parent for more than 70 percent of the year as specified in the custody order. In Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the Alaska Supreme Court explained the relationship between physical custody classifications and the applicable child support calculation framework, confirming that shared-custody support under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) and primary-custody support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) rely on materially different formulas. Where, as here, the custody arrangement has shifted from a 50-50 shared schedule to one in which Tomas holds 70 percent of the custodial time, the entire framework for calculating support changes. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), the Alaska Supreme Court expressly recognized that a change in custodial or visitation patterns may constitute a material change of circumstances supporting modification of child support. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005), further establishes that the court must apply the correct Rule 90.3 methodology on remand or modification and may not apply a blended or improvised approach that does not conform to the formula specified by the rule. THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0187)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Petrova respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021, which currently requires Maria Petrova to pay $850 per month in child support. Since entry of that order, Maria has received two promotions and now earns approximately $94,000 per year, representing a substantial increase from the $62,000 annual income on which the original order was based. Meanwhile, Ashley continues to work part-time and earns $28,000 annually, and the children's childcare and extracurricular costs have risen considerably. The combination of Maria's significantly higher income and the children's increased financial needs constitutes a material change in circumstances under Alaska law, and the existing support amount no longer reflects the children's actual needs or the parties' current financial realities. Ashley therefore requests that the Court modify the order upward in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), the applicable formula for cases in which one parent holds primary physical custody.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Petrova and Maria Petrova divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the superior court entered a child support order requiring Maria to pay $850 per month. That figure was based on Maria's annual gross income of $62,000 and the custody arrangement in place at the time, which granted Ashley primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children. The custody arrangement reflected an approximately 80/20 split of physical custody, with Ashley providing the children's primary home environment.
Since the entry of the 2021 order, Maria has received two promotions and currently earns approximately $94,000 per year. This represents an increase of roughly $32,000 in gross annual income, or approximately 51.6 percent over her income at the time of the original order. Ashley's income has not increased meaningfully and remains at approximately $28,000 per year from part-time employment.
In addition to the change in Maria's income, the children's costs have risen substantially since 2021. Childcare expenses and extracurricular activity costs have both increased, placing a greater financial burden on Ashley as the primary custodial parent. The current monthly support payment of $850 no longer reflects what Civil Rule 90.3(a) would produce when applied to Maria's current adjusted annual income, and a recalculation under the rule yields a figure more than 15 percent greater than the existing order.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170(a), a court may, upon motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify the portion of a judgment that provides for child support. Modification of a child support order requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999). Under Civil Rule 90.3, a material change of circumstances is presumed when support calculated under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996); Kelly v. Joseph, 46 P.3d 1014 (Alaska 2002).
When one parent has primary physical custody, child support is governed by Civil Rule 90.3(a), which calculates the obligation by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by a specified percentage based on the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B); Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016); Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017).
A parent's adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) is the parent's total income from all sources minus mandatory deductions such as federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, mandatory union dues, and mandatory retirement contributions, along with other permitted deductions. The court may also consider work-related childcare expenses paid by the custodial parent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E).
Where an obligor parent has experienced an increase in income, the obligee parent and children are entitled to share in that increased earning capacity. As the Alaska Supreme Court has held, an obligor parent who experiences an increase in income cannot avoid paying additional support merely by contending that the children's current needs are being met at the existing level. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183. The governing principle of Civil Rule 90.3 is that as income available to both parents increases, the amount available to support children also increases. Id.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. MARIA'S SUBSTANTIAL INCOME INCREASE CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES.
The threshold question on a motion to modify child support is whether a material change of circumstances has occurred since entry of the prior order. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). A shift in one or both parents' income is among the most common grounds constituting such a change. Id. A material change of circumstances is presumed when support recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3 is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628; Kelly, 46 P.3d 1014.
Here, Maria's gross income has risen from $62,000 to approximately $94,000, an increase of approximately $32,000, or more than 51 percent. Applying the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula to Maria's current income would yield a child support obligation substantially exceeding 15 percent above the current $850 monthly payment, as demonstrated below. The presumption of a material change in circumstances is therefore triggered, and Maria cannot rebut that presumption by asserting that the children's needs are adequately met at the current support level. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183.
The Alaska Supreme Court has been clear on this point: the rule operates on the principle that as the income available to the obligor parent increases, the amount made available to support the children also increases. Id. Maria's two promotions and corresponding salary increase are precisely the type of factual change that courts routinely recognize as material. Bunn, 934 P.2d 753.
B. RECALCULATION OF CHILD SUPPORT UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(a) SUPPORTS AN UPWARD MODIFICATION.
Because Ashley holds primary physical custody of the two minor children and the custody arrangement is an 80/20 split, Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation of Maria's support obligation. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), the applicable multiplier for two children is 27 percent of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income.
To calculate Maria's adjusted annual income, the Court must begin with her total gross income of approximately $94,000 and subtract applicable mandatory deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including federal and state income taxes, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax, as well as any other mandatory deductions such as mandatory retirement contributions. The Court may also deduct voluntary retirement contributions up to the limits established in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B).
By way of illustration, assuming conservative mandatory deductions consistent with applicable federal and state tax obligations on a $94,000 gross income, Maria's adjusted annual income would be substantially higher than the $62,000 figure used in 2021. Even applying a modest effective deduction rate, the adjusted annual income remaining after allowable deductions would, when multiplied by the 27 percent factor prescribed by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), yield a monthly support obligation considerably greater than $850. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070; Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238. The Court is respectfully requested to conduct a full Rule 90.3(a) calculation at the evidentiary hearing using verified income documentation submitted by both parties.
Courts applying Civil Rule 90.3 do not vary from the formula's results without specific, articulated justification. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070. No such justification exists here. Maria has voluntarily advanced in her career and has increased her earnings substantially through two promotions. The children should share in the financial benefits of that advancement. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183. The Court should set Maria's new monthly support obligation at the amount calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) based on her current adjusted annual income.
C. THE INCREASED COSTS OF CHILDCARE AND EXTRACURRICULAR ACTIVITIES FURTHER SUPPORT MODIFICATION.
In addition to Maria's income increase, the children's associated expenses have grown since 2021. Childcare and extracurricular costs are relevant to the Court's overall assessment of the children's needs and are expressly recognized in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E), which permits work-related child care expenses to be deducted from the custodial parent's income for purposes of applying the shared income model underlying the rule's design. The increased costs borne by Ashley as the primary custodial parent further underscore the inadequacy of the current support order.
Evidence regarding the children's increased expenses is relevant under Alaska R. Evid. 401, which defines relevant evidence as evidence having any tendency to make the existence of any fact that is of consequence to the determination of the action more probable or less probable than it would be without it. The escalation of the children's needs and costs makes the inadequacy of the $850 order more probable and further supports the conclusion that the current order no longer serves the children's best interests.
Additionally, under AS 25.20.110(a), any modification of a custody or support arrangement must serve the best interests of the children. The children's best interests are directly implicated when an existing support order fails to keep pace with the obligor parent's substantially increased income and the children's own rising costs of care. An upward modification consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(a) would align the children's financial support with both the governing legal standard and the actual circumstances of the family.
D. THIS COURT HAS AUTHORITY TO MODIFY THE EXISTING ORDER AND SHOULD EXERCISE THAT AUTHORITY.
AS 25.24.170(a) authorizes this Court, upon motion of either party, to modify the portion of a prior judgment providing for child support. The petitioner bears the initial burden of demonstrating a material change in circumstances, which, as discussed above, is presumed here because the Civil Rule 90.3(a) calculation based on Maria's current income produces a result more than 15 percent greater than the current $850 order. Once that threshold is met, the Court proceeds to apply the rule's formula to determine the appropriate amount of support going forward.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that a court does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070. Adherence to the formula is the default, and departure requires explicit findings identifying unusual circumstances warranting variance. No such unusual circumstances are present here. Maria earns more than she did at the time of the original order. The children cost more to support than they did then. The law requires that the support order reflect these realities.
The Court should also take judicial notice, upon proper request, of any relevant, judicially noticeable facts concerning the parties' income or costs, to the extent permitted by Alaska R. Evid. 201(d), which provides that upon request of a party, the court shall take judicial notice of each matter specified in subdivision (b) if the requesting party furnishes sufficient information and has given each party notice adequate to enable the party to meet the request.
Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025) further illustrates that courts carefully examine an obligor parent's actual income, including examining tax returns and other financial documents, to ensure that child support calculations under Civil Rule 90.3 are grounded in verified earnings. In that case, the court was called upon to weigh an obligor parent's current salary against other sources of income reflected in tax filings. This Court should similarly require Maria to produce complete and current income documentation so that the Civil Rule 90.3(a) calculation can be performed accurately and equitably.
V. CONCLUSION
The record establishes that a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the 2021 child support order. Maria's gross annual income has increased by more than $32,000, from $62,000 to approximately $94,000, as a result of two promotions. Ashley continues to earn $28,000 per year while carrying the primary financial and custodial responsibilities for the parties' two minor children. The children's costs have increased substantially since the original order. Recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) at Maria's current income level will produce a monthly support figure more than 15 percent above the current $850 order, triggering the presumption of a material change in circumstances.
For all of these reasons, Ashley Petrova respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a material change in circumstances has occurred warranting modification of the 2021 child support order;
2. Order Maria Petrova to produce complete and current income documentation, including tax returns and pay stubs, sufficient to permit an accurate Civil Rule 90.3(a) calculation;
3. Recalculate Maria Petrova's monthly child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) based on her current adjusted annual income; and
4. Enter an amended child support order requiring Maria Petrova to pay the recalculated monthly amount, effective as of the date of this motion or such other date as the Court deems appropriate.

II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jacob Petrova and Colin Petrova divorced in 2021. At the time of divorce, the Superior Court entered a child support order requiring Colin to pay $850 per month. That order was based on Colin's annual income of $52,000, earned as a commercial electrician, and Jacob's annual income of $28,000, earned through part-time retail employment. The parties were awarded shared physical custody of their two minor children on a roughly equal basis.
Since the entry of that order, both parties have experienced significant changes in their financial circumstances.
