THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0190)
I. INTRODUCTION
Jacob Colby, petitioner and primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children, respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Since the entry of that order, respondent Wesley Colby has experienced a substantial increase in annual income, rising from approximately $26,000 per year to approximately $38,000 per year, an increase of approximately $12,000 annually. This significant change in Wesley's financial circumstances, combined with the children's growing educational and extracurricular needs, constitutes a material change in circumstances under Alaska law and warrants an upward modification of the current child support obligation. Jacob brings this petition pursuant to AS 25.24.934, AS 25.20.110, and Civil Rule 900(h), and asks this Court to recalculate Wesley's child support obligation in accordance with the formula established under Civil Rule 90.3(a) to ensure the children's financial needs are properly and adequately met.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jacob Colby and Wesley Colby are the parents of two minor children, currently ages 8 and 11. In 2021, this Court entered a custody and child support order granting Jacob primary physical custody of both children. Under that arrangement, the children reside in Jacob's home approximately 70 percent of the time, and Wesley exercises parenting time the remaining 30 percent of the time.
At the time the original child support order was entered, Wesley earned approximately $26,000 per year as a retail store employee. The existing support order was calculated based on that income figure using the applicable guidelines under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Since the entry of the 2021 order, Wesley has received a significant promotion within his retail employer and now holds the position of store manager. This promotion was accompanied by a substantial raise, increasing his annual gross income to approximately $38,000. Wesley's income has therefore increased by approximately $12,000 per year, representing a roughly 46 percent increase over the figure used to calculate the current support obligation.
Jacob currently earns approximately $72,000 per year as a licensed electrician in Anchorage. Jacob bears the primary financial burden of the children's daily care, housing, school expenses, clothing, and extracurricular activities, all of which have increased as the children have grown older. The children participate in extracurricular programs and require school-related expenditures that were not contemplated in the original order. The current child support obligation, calculated based on Wesley's prior income of $26,000, no longer reflects the parties' current financial realities and no longer adequately serves the children's needs.
Jacob now petitions this Court to modify the child support order upward to account for Wesley's increased income and to better ensure that the children's financial needs are met by both parents in proportion to their respective abilities to pay.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170, a court may, upon motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify a judgment insofar as it provides for the maintenance of minor children. Modification of a child support order requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) provides the standard for such modifications, stating that "a final child support award may be modified upon a showing of a material change of circumstances as provided by state law" and that "a material change of circumstances will be presumed if support as calculated under this rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order under all circumstances."
Once a material change of circumstances is established, the court calculates the modified support obligation using the formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a). For cases in which one parent holds primary physical custody, the child support award is calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which is 27 percent for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that trial courts hold broad discretion in deciding whether to modify child support orders, and that the primary purpose of Rule 90.3 is to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). The court has further recognized that a significant shift in a parent's income constitutes exactly the kind of factual change that may support modification of an existing order. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). Additionally, the court has recognized that a presumption of material change arises when recalculated support differs from the outstanding order by more than 15 percent. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996); Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. WESLEY'S SUBSTANTIAL INCOME INCREASE CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES WARRANTING MODIFICATION OF CHILD SUPPORT.
The threshold question in any modification proceeding is whether a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the existing order. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1); AS 25.24.170. The answer here is plainly yes.
At the time of the 2021 order, Wesley earned approximately $26,000 per year. He now earns approximately $38,000 per year, a gross increase of $12,000, representing approximately a 46 percent rise in his annual income. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized that a meaningful shift in a parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances justifying reconsideration of a child support obligation. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). The change at issue here is not minor or temporary; it reflects a permanent promotion to a higher-level position with a substantially increased salary.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1), a material change of circumstances is presumed when the recalculated support amount differs from the outstanding order by more than 15 percent. As demonstrated in detail in the following section, applying the Rule 90.3(a) formula to Wesley's current income produces a support obligation that exceeds the existing order by well more than 15 percent. Accordingly, the presumption of material change is triggered, and modification is appropriate as a matter of law. See Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017); Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996).
The Alaska Supreme Court's decision in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), further underscores that a demonstrated increase in income reflected in financial records, such as pay stubs or tax returns, is sufficient to trigger the court's recalculation of support under Rule 90.3. Wesley's income increase is verifiable through his employment records and W-2 documentation, which Jacob is prepared to request through appropriate discovery if not voluntarily provided.
B. THE RULE 90.3(a) FORMULA REQUIRES AN UPWARD MODIFICATION OF WESLEY'S CHILD SUPPORT OBLIGATION.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) sets forth the formula for calculating child support in cases involving primary physical custody. Because Jacob holds primary physical custody of the children, the applicable formula requires that Wesley's adjusted annual income be multiplied by 27 percent, the percentage applicable to two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
The adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) is calculated by taking Wesley's total income from all sources and subtracting mandatory deductions, including federal, state, and local income taxes, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax, as well as any other applicable deductions enumerated in the rule. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A). Based on Wesley's current gross annual income of approximately $38,000, his adjusted annual income, after standard deductions, will be determined at hearing with the benefit of his actual financial documents. Even using a conservative estimate of adjusted annual income at or near his gross figure, the resulting support obligation at 27 percent will meaningfully exceed the obligation calculated on his prior income of $26,000.
The prior support order was calculated on the basis of a gross income of $26,000. Using the same percentage of 27 percent, the prior order reflected an obligation proportional to that income. Wesley's income has now increased by approximately 46 percent. Applying Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) to his current income will produce a support obligation that is likewise substantially higher, comfortably exceeding the 15 percent threshold required to establish a presumed material change under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1). This result is entirely consistent with the Alaska Supreme Court's application of the rule in Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989), and Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005), both of which confirm that the Rule 90.3(a) formula must be applied consistently and faithfully to the non-custodial parent's actual current income.
Jacob does not seek any deviation from the formula. He asks only that the Court apply the guidelines as written to Wesley's current, verified income so that both parents contribute to the children's support in proportion to their actual financial capacity.
C. THE CHILDREN'S GROWING FINANCIAL NEEDS FURTHER SUPPORT AN UPWARD MODIFICATION.
Beyond the threshold question of material change, the children's actual needs provide additional grounds for the requested modification. As the Court recognized in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), the primary purpose of Rule 90.3 is to ensure that child support orders are adequate to meet the needs of children, subject to the ability of parents to pay. The children here are 8 and 11 years of age and are actively involved in school and extracurricular activities that generate ongoing expenses beyond basic housing and food costs.
Jacob bears the primary financial burden of these expenses because the children reside with him approximately 70 percent of the time. School supplies, fees, clothing, extracurricular program costs, and transportation expenses associated with the children's activities are incurred primarily within Jacob's household. The 2021 support order was not calculated with these current costs in mind, and the current order does not adequately apportion the children's financial needs between the parties.
Under AS 25.27.060(a), the court is directed to carefully consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet their support obligations, and the extent to which the parents supported the child prior to and after separation. Wesley's ability to contribute has increased substantially since 2021. His income has grown by 46 percent, while his parenting time obligations, at 30 percent, remain the same. Equity, the statutory framework, and the guiding principles of Rule 90.3 all counsel in favor of increasing his support obligation to reflect this changed reality.
D. INCOME WITHHOLDING SHOULD BE ORDERED TO ENSURE CONSISTENT PAYMENT.
Jacob respectfully requests that any modified support order include an income withholding provision pursuant to AS 25.27.062. Under AS 25.27.062(a), a support order must contain an income withholding order unless a specific exception applies. An income withholding order ensures timely and consistent payment of support by directing that amounts be withheld directly from Wesley's wages. This mechanism protects the children's financial stability and reduces the burden on both parties and the Court to enforce payment through subsequent proceedings. There is no basis on this record to exempt the modified order from the immediate income withholding requirement under AS 25.27.987.
V. CONCLUSION
For all of the foregoing reasons, Jacob Colby respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that Wesley Colby's substantial income increase, from approximately $26,000 to approximately $38,000 per year, constitutes a material change in circumstances under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) and AS 25.24.170;
2. Recalculate Wesley's child support obligation in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), applying the 27 percent rate to Wesley's current adjusted annual income as established at hearing;
3. Enter a modified child support order reflecting the upward adjustment in Wesley's support obligation, effective as of the date this motion was served on Wesley, consistent with Civil Rule 90.3(h)(2);
4. Include an income withholding provision in the modified order pursuant to AS 25.27.062; and
5. Grant such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper in the interests of the children's well-being.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0191)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Bergstrom ("Petitioner") respectfully petitions this Court for modification of the existing child support order entered approximately two years ago. The existing order was calculated using Respondent Jennifer Bergstrom's former annual income of $52,000, an income level that no longer reflects Jennifer's actual financial circumstances following a layoff and subsequent lower-paying re-employment at approximately $38,000 per year. Because Jennifer's income has decreased by more than $14,000 annually, and because the parties' two minor children have incurred increased financial needs in the areas of medical care and extracurricular activities, a substantial and material change in circumstances has occurred. Modification of the existing order is both legally compelled and necessary to serve the best interests of the parties' children. Petitioner accordingly requests that this Court enter a new support order calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a), using each party's current income and the existing custody allocation under which Ashley holds primary physical custody approximately 70 percent of the time.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Ashley Bergstrom and Jennifer Bergstrom are the parents of two minor children, currently aged 7 and 10. The parties have an existing custody arrangement under which Ashley exercises primary physical custody of both children for approximately 70 percent of the year. Jennifer has physical custody for the remaining approximately 30 percent of the year. Consistent with this arrangement, Jennifer is the obligor parent for purposes of child support.
Approximately two years ago, this Court entered a child support order based upon Jennifer's then-current gross annual income of approximately $52,000 per year. At that time, Jennifer was employed in a position reflecting that income level, and the support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) was appropriately grounded in that figure.
Since the entry of the existing order, Jennifer experienced a layoff from her prior position. Following her period of unemployment, she secured re-employment as an administrative assistant earning approximately $38,000 per year. This figure represents a reduction of approximately $14,000, or roughly 27 percent, from the income figure used to calculate the existing support obligation.
Ashley currently earns approximately $62,000 per year as a registered nurse in Anchorage. Ashley provides the primary day-to-day care for the two children, bearing the predominant share of expenses for food, clothing, shelter, medical care, and extracurricular activities. The children's financial needs have grown since the prior order was entered. Both children now participate in extracurricular activities that generate recurring costs. Additionally, the children have incurred ongoing medical and dental expenses that were not fully accounted for under the existing order.
The existing support order has not been modified or adjusted since it was entered approximately two years ago.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify an existing child support order upon a showing that a material change in circumstances has occurred. AS 25.24.170(a) authorizes the court, at any time after judgment and upon the motion of either party, to set aside, alter, or modify so much of a judgment as provides for the maintenance of either party or the care, nurture, and education of the minor children of the marriage. AS 25.27.190(e) further provides that modification of future periodic support payments may be ordered upon a showing of good cause and material change in circumstances.
For child support matters governed by Civil Rule 90.3, the Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a significant change in either parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances sufficient to justify modification. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). Specifically, Alaska courts have applied the principle that a change in income resulting in a difference of 15 percent or more from the support amount that would be produced under the current formula constitutes a material change. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
Once a material change in circumstances is established, the court calculates a new support obligation using the current income of both parents and the applicable custody arrangement. Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs cases in which one parent holds primary physical custody, defined as the child residing with that parent for more than 70 percent of the year. Under that rule, the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income is multiplied by the applicable percentage based on the number of children to determine the annual support obligation.
Potential income may be imputed to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). However, where a parent's reduction in income results from a layoff and subsequent re-employment at market-rate wages, imputation is generally not appropriate. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997).
The best interests of the child remain paramount in all support determinations. AS 25.24.150(c). The obligation of each parent to contribute to the financial support of the parties' children is not diminished simply because the children's existing needs are being met at a current level. State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification of the Existing Support Order.
The threshold question in any modification proceeding is whether a material change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the existing order. AS 25.24.170(b) provides that the adoption of guidelines or a significant amendment to guidelines constitutes a material change, but Alaska courts have more broadly recognized that a substantial shift in either parent's income satisfies this standard. In the present case, Jennifer's annual income has declined from approximately $52,000 to approximately $38,000, a reduction of approximately 27 percent. This reduction directly affects the support calculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that when application of the current guidelines formula to updated income figures produces a support amount that differs by 15 percent or more from the existing order, a material change in circumstances exists. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). Here, applying the Civil Rule 90.3(a) percentage for two children, which is 27 percent, to Jennifer's adjusted annual income of approximately $38,000 yields a result that is substantially different from the amount produced by applying that same percentage to her prior income of $52,000. The difference exceeds the 15 percent threshold recognized in Alaska case law. Modification is therefore warranted.
Additionally, the children's financial circumstances have evolved since the prior order was entered. Both children now incur ongoing extracurricular and medical expenses that were not fully reflected in the original order. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that as children's needs grow and as parental circumstances change, courts are obligated to ensure that support awards reflect those realities. Headlough v. Headlough, 639 P.2d 1010 (Alaska 1982). These increased needs independently support a finding of material change sufficient to justify modification.
B. The New Support Obligation Should Be Calculated Using Jennifer's Actual Current Income Under Civil Rule 90.3(a).
Because Ashley exercises primary physical custody of the two children for approximately 70 percent of the year, Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the support calculation. Under that rule, the annual support obligation is determined by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent, as set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) means the parent's total income from all sources minus mandatory deductions, including federal, state, and local income tax; Social Security tax; Medicare tax; mandatory union dues; and mandatory retirement contributions. Voluntary retirement contributions are also deductible, subject to the cap set out in the rule. Jennifer's adjusted annual income must be calculated based on her current gross income of approximately $38,000, reduced by her applicable mandatory deductions, to arrive at her adjusted annual income for support purposes.
The existing order was premised on Jennifer's prior income of $52,000. Using that figure today would produce a support obligation that does not reflect Jennifer's actual earning capacity or actual income, which is both inequitable and inconsistent with the requirements of Civil Rule 90.3(a). The Alaska Supreme Court has held that support obligations must be grounded in parents' current financial realities rather than in outdated figures that no longer correspond to present circumstances. Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013). Calculating Jennifer's obligation using her actual current income is therefore both legally required and equitable.
C. Imputation of Income to Jennifer Is Not Appropriate Because Her Reduced Earnings Result From Involuntary Layoff and Subsequent Market-Rate Re-Employment.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) authorizes the court to calculate support based on a determination of potential income when a parent voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed. However, this provision is not intended to penalize parents whose income has declined through no fault of their own. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that where a reduction in income results not from a voluntary personal choice but from economic circumstances such as a layoff, courts should not reflexively impute higher income to the obligor. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997).
In this case, Jennifer did not voluntarily reduce her income. She was laid off from her prior position and subsequently secured re-employment at the wage level available to her in the current Anchorage market for administrative assistants. Her current earnings of approximately $38,000 reflect market-rate compensation for her skills and position. There is no basis in the record to conclude that Jennifer is deliberately avoiding higher-paying work or that she is working below her capacity for personal reasons unrelated to economic realities. Under these circumstances, imputing Jennifer's prior income of $52,000 for support calculation purposes would be contrary to the governing rule and inconsistent with the Alaska Supreme Court's guidance in Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997).
To the extent Jennifer presents evidence that her reduction in income is only temporary, this Court should evaluate that claim carefully against the full record. The Alaska Supreme Court has noted that courts may examine whether a reduction in income is temporary in nature when determining whether to use a parent's current versus prior earnings. Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013). However, a bare assertion that income may recover in the future, unsupported by specific evidence, does not justify the continued use of an outdated income figure. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025). Because Jennifer's current employment appears to represent her reasonably available market-rate income, Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court use Jennifer's actual current income of approximately $38,000 in calculating the modified support obligation.
D. The Modified Order Should Account for the Children's Increased Medical and Extracurricular Expenses.
AS 25.27.060(c) requires that any support order address the health care needs of the children, including health insurance coverage and allocation of uncovered medical expenses. That statute provides that the court or agency shall allocate equally the cost of health care insurance for the child between the parents unless there is good cause to allocate the costs unequally, and that the court or agency shall allocate equally between the parents the cost of reasonable health care expenses not covered by private insurance unless there is good cause to allocate the costs unequally.
Both children have incurred ongoing medical and dental expenses not fully covered by insurance. Under AS 25.27.060(c), the court is required to address these expenses in any support order. Petitioner respectfully requests that the modified order include a provision requiring Jennifer to contribute her equal share of the children's reasonable uncovered health care expenses, consistent with the statutory mandate.
In addition, both children participate in extracurricular activities that generate recurring costs. While the Civil Rule 90.3(a) formula is designed to capture ordinary expenses associated with raising children, the court retains discretion under Civil Rule 90.3(c)(1) to vary from the formula in unusual circumstances. To the extent the children's extracurricular costs are substantial and ongoing, Petitioner may present evidence supporting a departure from the formula amount, or alternatively may request that the extracurricular costs be addressed as part of the overall support calculation.
The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently recognized that a child's right to support is commensurate with the parents' combined financial capacity, and that as circumstances change, the support award must be updated to ensure that the children's needs are adequately met. State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999). The children's increased financial needs since the prior order was entered, combined with the change in Jennifer's income, compel a comprehensive modification of the existing order.
E. The Modification Should Be Entered as a New Order Pursuant to AS 25.27.060 and Civil Rule 90.3(a), With an Income Withholding Provision.
Any new support order entered by this Court should contain an income withholding provision consistent with AS 25.27.062. That statute requires that any judgment or court order providing for support must contain an income withholding order, and provides for immediate income withholding where the support order is issued or modified on or after July 8, 1994. AS 25.27.062(a). Including an income withholding provision in the modified order will ensure consistent and timely payment of support to the benefit of the parties' children.
AS 25.20.110(b) further provides that in proceedings relating to custody and support, the court shall consider the past history of the parents with respect to compliance with child support payment provisions. Petitioner does not allege that Jennifer has willfully failed to comply with the existing order. However, given the changed financial circumstances on both sides, a modified order with built-in income withholding mechanisms will protect the children's financial interests going forward.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Ashley Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that a material change in circumstances has occurred based on Jennifer Bergstrom's substantial reduction in income from approximately $52,000 to approximately $38,000 per year, and the children's increased medical and extracurricular expenses;
2. Enter a modified child support order calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using Jennifer Bergstrom's current adjusted annual income of approximately $38,000 per year, applied at the 27 percent rate applicable to two children;
3. Decline to impute Jennifer Bergstrom's prior income, as her current earnings reflect the result of an involuntary layoff and subsequent market-rate re-employment rather than voluntary underemployment;
4. Include in the modified order a provision requiring equal allocation of the children's reasonable uncovered medical and dental expenses consistent with AS 25.27.060(c);
5. Include a mandatory income withholding provision in the modified order consistent with AS 25.27.062; and
6. Grant such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper in the best interests of the parties' minor children.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0192)
I. INTRODUCTION
Jacob Sutter brings this motion to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Two independent material changes in circumstances compel recalculation of the current support obligation. First, Brandon Sutter's annual income has increased from $52,000 to approximately $81,000, representing a rise of roughly 56 percent over his income at the time of the existing order. Second, the actual physical custody arrangement has shifted materially from the shared custody schedule reflected in the existing order, with the children now residing with Jacob Sutter approximately 70 percent of the time. Each of these changes, standing alone, constitutes a material change in circumstances warranting modification. Together, they demand that the court recalculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3 to reflect current financial and custodial reality. The children's right to adequate support from both parents depends upon orders that accurately reflect the parties' actual incomes and living arrangements. Jacob Sutter respectfully requests that this court modify the existing child support order accordingly.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jacob Sutter and Brandon Sutter divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce, the court entered a child support order for the parties' two minor children. That order was based on Brandon Sutter's annual income of $52,000 as a commercial electrician and Jacob Sutter's annual income of $38,000 as a retail manager. Because the parties shared physical custody of the two children on a roughly equal basis at the time, the court calculated support under the shared physical custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b).
Since entry of that order, two significant changes have occurred. First, Brandon Sutter has accepted a new position as a project supervisor at an annual salary of approximately $81,000. This increase of approximately $29,000 per year represents a rise of more than 55 percent over his 2021 income. Brandon's current income is substantially higher than the income figure on which the existing support order is based.
Second, and independently, the informal custody arrangement between the parties has shifted so that the children now reside primarily with Jacob Sutter approximately 70 percent of the time. Although no formal modification of the parenting plan has been entered by the court, this shift in the actual day-to-day living arrangement is well-established and ongoing. Jacob Sutter's income has remained relatively stable at approximately $40,000 annually.
Because the existing order was calculated under the shared custody formula based on outdated income figures and a custody arrangement that no longer reflects reality, a modification is necessary to serve the best interests of the children and to comply with Alaska's child support guidelines.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), a court may modify an award of custody or visitation if it determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. A court considering modification of a child support obligation must find a material change in circumstances as a prerequisite to recalculating the obligation. See AS 25.24.170(a).
Civil Rule 90.3 governs the calculation of child support in Alaska. Where one parent has primary physical custody, support is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which provides that the award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by a percentage determined by the number of children. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Where parents share physical custody, meaning each parent has the children for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year, support is calculated under the shared custody formula in Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), which takes into account the incomes of both parents and the actual percentage of custody time each parent exercises.
A material change in circumstances is presumed to exist when recalculation of support under Civil Rule 90.3 would produce an amount more than 15 percent greater or less than the current order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that retroactive modification of child support is prohibited, and that courts must perform the Rule 90.3 analysis correctly, including applying the proper formula for the custody arrangement actually in place. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). Courts have also confirmed that the distinction between primary and shared physical custody directly controls which formula applies and, therefore, directly affects the amount of the support obligation. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4), the court may calculate child support based on a determination of the potential income of a parent who voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed. Courts are also empowered to consider all sources of income and to make appropriate deductions in computing adjusted annual income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1).
The court is required to take judicial notice of any matter specified in Alaska R. Evid. 201(b) upon request of a party, provided that the requesting party furnishes sufficient information and has given each party notice adequate to enable the party to meet the request. Alaska R. Evid. 201(d).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. Brandon Sutter's Substantially Increased Income Constitutes a Material Change in Circumstances.
The existing child support order was premised on Brandon Sutter's annual income of $52,000. Brandon Sutter now earns approximately $81,000 annually in his position as a project supervisor. This increase of approximately $29,000 per year represents a rise of more than 55 percent. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), adjusted annual income is the parent's total income from all sources minus specific mandatory and permissible deductions. A straightforward application of the rule to Brandon's current gross income of $81,000, even after applicable deductions, will produce a support figure that is substantially higher than the amount calculated from his prior $52,000 income, and that difference will far exceed 15 percent of the current order.
As the Alaska Supreme Court recognized in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), a material change in circumstances is presumed when recalculated support under Civil Rule 90.3 differs from the existing order by more than 15 percent. Because Brandon Sutter's income has grown by more than half since the existing order was entered, this presumption is easily satisfied. The children are entitled to support that reflects their parents' current financial circumstances, and the existing order no longer accomplishes that objective.
Furthermore, the court in Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), recognized that courts must correctly apply the Rule 90.3 formula using current income data. Adherence to an outdated support figure, when a parent's income has materially increased, is inconsistent with the children's right to adequate support and with the purpose of the guidelines. Jacob Sutter respectfully submits that Brandon Sutter's current income of approximately $81,000 must serve as the basis for any recalculation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), because the parties have two minor children, the applicable percentage of the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income is 27 percent. Even applying conservative deductions, Brandon Sutter's adjusted annual income at $81,000 gross will result in a child support obligation significantly higher than that produced by his prior $52,000 gross income. Jacob Sutter requests that the court conduct the full Rule 90.3 analysis using current income documentation, which Brandon Sutter should be required to produce.
B. The Material Shift in Physical Custody Independently Constitutes a Material Change in Circumstances.
The existing child support order was calculated using the shared physical custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), based on the parties exercising roughly equal custody time. The actual custody arrangement has shifted materially. The children now reside with Jacob Sutter approximately 70 percent of the time. This means the arrangement no longer qualifies as shared physical custody under the applicable rules.
As the Alaska Supreme Court explained in Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018), a parent has shared physical custody when the children reside with that parent for a period specified in writing in the custody order of at least 30, but no more than 70, percent of the year. Where one parent has the children 70 percent of the time, the arrangement crosses the threshold from shared into primary physical custody. Under those circumstances, the correct formula is Civil Rule 90.3(a), not Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1). The formulas produce materially different results, and applying the wrong formula, as the current order effectively does, yields an inaccurate support figure.
Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(E) itself provides that failure to exercise sufficient physical custody to qualify for shared physical custody under the rule is grounds for modification of the child support order. Here, Brandon Sutter no longer exercises the level of custody time that formed the basis for the shared custody calculation in the existing order. The children reside primarily with Jacob Sutter. That shift, standing alone, is a sufficient ground for modification and for recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) rather than Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1).
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), if Jacob Sutter is recognized as the primary physical custodian of the two minor children, the court must calculate support as 27 percent of Brandon Sutter's adjusted annual income. At an adjusted annual income derived from $81,000 gross, this formula will produce a substantially higher monthly support obligation than the current order, properly reflecting both Brandon's increased earnings and Jacob's role as primary caregiver.
The court in Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013), vacated a support modification precisely because the lower court had failed to apply the Rule 90.3(a) analysis correctly. Jacob Sutter urges this court to avoid the same error by carefully applying the correct formula to the actual custodial arrangement in place, not the arrangement that existed at the time of the original order.
C. The Combined Effect of Both Changes Compels Immediate Modification.
Jacob Sutter submits that both changed circumstances exist simultaneously and that their combined effect makes the case for modification especially compelling. The existing order simultaneously understates the non-custodial parent's income and applies a formula designed for equal custody to a situation that is now one of primary physical custody with Jacob Sutter. The result is an order that systematically underestimates the support owed to the children.
Under AS 25.24.170(a), the court may, upon the motion of either party, modify so much of a prior judgment as relates to child support. Jacob Sutter brings this motion under that authority, supported by the material changes in circumstances detailed above. The modification Jacob Sutter seeks is consistent with AS 25.20.110(a), which requires that any modification be in the best interests of the child. Children benefit when the court's support orders accurately reflect the financial resources of both parents and the reality of how the children's time is distributed. Both factors now favor a higher support obligation from Brandon Sutter to Jacob Sutter.
As recognized in Richardson v. Kohlin, 175 P.3d 43 (Alaska 2008), the 15 percent threshold test under Civil Rule 90.3 is the standard benchmark for determining whether a material change in circumstances exists for purposes of child support modification. Here, the 15 percent threshold is satisfied by the income change alone, and independently satisfied by the custody shift alone. Taken together, the grounds for modification are overwhelming.
D. The Court Should Order Prospective Modification Effective as of the Date of This Motion.
Alaska law prohibits retroactive modification of child support. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). Jacob Sutter does not seek retroactive modification and understands that the modified support obligation will operate prospectively from the date of this motion or such other date as the court deems appropriate. Jacob Sutter requests that the court enter a new support order as promptly as practicable to ensure that the children receive the support to which they are entitled going forward.
The court should also note that AS 25.27.060(c) authorizes the court to order either parent or both parents to pay the amount necessary for support, maintenance, nurture, and education of the child, and AS 25.27.062(a) requires that any new support order contain an income withholding order to ensure consistent payment. Jacob Sutter requests that any modified order include the income withholding provision required by AS 25.27.062(a) so that compliance is assured.
E. The Court Should Take Judicial Notice of the Existing Order and Prior Income Findings.
Jacob Sutter requests, pursuant to Alaska R. Evid. 201(d), that the court take judicial notice of the existing child support order entered in 2021 and the income findings contained therein. Those findings establish the baseline from which the material change in Brandon Sutter's income is measured. Jacob Sutter has provided adequate notice of this request through the filing of this motion, and will furnish sufficient information to support the request at or before the hearing on this matter.
V. CONCLUSION
For all of the foregoing reasons, Jacob Sutter respectfully requests that this court enter an order granting the following relief:
1. Finding that a material change in circumstances has occurred based on Brandon Sutter's substantial increase in annual income from $52,000 to approximately $81,000;
2. Finding that a material change in circumstances has independently occurred based on the shift in physical custody, with the children now residing primarily with Jacob Sutter approximately 70 percent of the time;
3. Recalculating the child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using Brandon Sutter's current adjusted annual income and applying the 27 percent multiplier applicable to two children;
4. Entering a modified child support order effective as of the date of this motion, consistent with the prohibition on retroactive modification;
5. Including in the modified order an income withholding provision as required by AS 25.27.062(a); and
6. Granting such other and further relief as the court deems just and proper.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0193)
I. INTRODUCTION
Ashley Bergstrom, Petitioner and primary custodial parent, respectfully moves this Court pursuant to AS 25.24.170 and Civil Rule 90.3(h) to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. The current monthly obligation of $1,150 was calculated using income figures that no longer reflect the financial realities of either party. Since the entry of that order, Respondent Wesley Bergstrom has obtained employment as a petroleum equipment technician earning approximately $98,000 annually, an increase of nearly $37,000 from the $61,000 annual income on which the prior order was based. Simultaneously, Petitioner has incurred additional work-related childcare costs of approximately $800 per month attributable to her nursing shift schedule. These combined changes represent a material change in circumstances that presumptively triggers modification under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1). A support award recalculated under the Alaska Child Support Guidelines using the parties' current verified incomes would result in a monthly obligation that is more than fifteen percent greater than the existing order, thereby satisfying the threshold for modification as a matter of law. Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court set aside the existing support figure and enter a new order consistent with the Guidelines.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
The parties, Ashley Bergstrom and Wesley Bergstrom, are the parents of two minor children, ages seven and ten. The children reside with Petitioner Ashley Bergstrom as primary physical custodian approximately seventy percent of the time. Respondent Wesley Bergstrom exercises parenting time with the children the remaining thirty percent of the time.
The Court entered the most recent child support order in 2021. That order established a monthly child support obligation of $1,150 based on the financial circumstances of the parties at that time. At the time of the 2021 order, Respondent reported an annual income of approximately $61,000. Petitioner Ashley Bergstrom is employed as a registered nurse in Anchorage, Alaska, earning approximately $52,000 per year.
Since the entry of the 2021 order, Respondent Wesley Bergstrom has secured new employment as a petroleum equipment technician. His current annual earnings are approximately $98,000, reflecting an increase of nearly $37,000 per year over the income figure used to calculate the existing support obligation.
Additionally, Petitioner has incurred substantial new childcare expenses since the 2021 order was entered. Due to her rotating nursing shift schedule, Petitioner now pays approximately $800 per month in work-related childcare costs for the parties' two children. These expenses are directly attributable to her employment and were not reflected in the prior support calculation.
The combination of Respondent's significantly increased income and Petitioner's additional work-related childcare costs represents a fundamental change in the financial landscape of this case since the 2021 order was entered.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A child support order may be modified after judgment upon motion of either party where the circumstances warrant adjustment. AS 25.24.170(a) provides that "any time after judgment the court, upon the motion of either party, may set aside, alter, or modify so much of the judgment as may provide for alimony, for the appointment of trustees for the care and custody of the minor children or for their nurture and education, for the care, nurture, and education of unmarried 18-year-old children of the marriage while they are actively pursuing a high school diploma or an equivalent level of technical or vocational training and living as dependents with a parent, guardian, or designee of the parent or guardian, or for the maintenance of either party to the action."
Modification of a final child support award requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) provides that "a final child support award may be modified upon a showing of a material change of circumstances as provided by state law" and further that "a material change of circumstances will be presumed if support as calculated under this rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order."
Child support in a primary physical custody arrangement is calculated pursuant to Civil Rule 921(a), which provides that "a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody as defined by paragraph (f) will be calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2)." For two children, that percentage is twenty-seven percent. Civil Rule 909(a)(2)(B).
The adjusted annual income calculation allows for the deduction of work-related child care expenses for the children who are the subject of the support order, as expressly provided in Civil Rule 983(a)(1)(E).
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that shifts in one or both parents' income constitute material changes in circumstances sufficient to support modification. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). Moreover, Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989), confirms that a motion to modify child support is appropriately evaluated by applying the Civil Rule 90.3 formula to the parties' current financial circumstances to determine whether the resulting figure justifies departure from the existing order.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. RESPONDENT'S SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED INCOME CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES WARRANTING UPWARD MODIFICATION OF CHILD SUPPORT.
The existing support order of $1,150 per month was calculated in 2021 based on Respondent's annual income of approximately $61,000. Respondent now earns approximately $98,000 per year in his current position as a petroleum equipment technician, an increase of nearly $37,000 annually. This increase represents a change of more than sixty percent in Respondent's gross income since the last order was entered, and it constitutes precisely the kind of material change in circumstances that Alaska law recognizes as a basis for modification.
The Alaska Supreme Court held in Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), that changes in one or both parents' income may constitute a material change in circumstances sufficient to justify modification of a child support order. The principle is reinforced by Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), in which the court carefully examined the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income to recalculate the correct child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), affirming that current, verified income is the appropriate basis for any support calculation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1), a material change of circumstances is presumed when support recalculated under the Guidelines is more than fifteen percent greater than the outstanding order. Respondent's adjusted annual income, calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), must be multiplied by twenty-seven percent to arrive at the correct support figure for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Using Respondent's current gross income of approximately $98,000, and applying standard mandatory deductions, the resulting child support figure will substantially exceed $1,150 per month, satisfying the fifteen percent threshold as a matter of law and triggering the presumption of a material change in circumstances.
Petitioner respectfully submits that the Court should find that Respondent's income increase alone is sufficient to require recalculation and upward modification of the existing child support order.
B. PETITIONER'S ADDITIONAL WORK-RELATED CHILDCARE EXPENSES FURTHER SUPPORT MODIFICATION AND MUST BE INCORPORATED INTO THE GUIDELINES CALCULATION.
In addition to Respondent's income increase, Petitioner has incurred new and recurring work-related childcare costs of approximately $800 per month since the 2021 order was entered. These expenses are directly necessitated by Petitioner's rotating shift schedule as a registered nurse and would not be incurred but for her employment.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E) expressly provides that a parent's adjusted annual income is reduced by "work-related child care expenses for the children who are the subject of the child support order." The inclusion of this deduction in the Guidelines calculation serves the dual purpose of accurately reflecting the true economic burden carried by the primary custodial parent and ensuring that the child support award properly accounts for the full cost of the children's care.
The Alaska Supreme Court's analysis in Bergstrom v. Lindback, 779 P.2d 1235 (Alaska 1989), underscored that a trial court must properly account for work-related childcare costs when calculating adjusted annual income under Civil Rule 90.3. Failure to incorporate these verified expenses would result in an inaccurate Guidelines calculation and would understate the financial demands placed on the custodial parent. Tillmon v. Tillmon, 189 P.3d 1022 (Alaska 2008), similarly reflects that proper application of Civil Rule 90.3 requires that actual, reasonable childcare expenses be deducted from the applicable parent's income for purposes of calculating support.
The $800 per month in childcare costs, totaling $9,600 per year, constitutes a substantial recurring expense that was not contemplated by the 2021 order. Proper incorporation of this deduction will affect the adjusted annual income calculation and will produce a support award that more accurately reflects the financial circumstances of the parties and the needs of the children.
C. RECALCULATION OF CHILD SUPPORT UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3 IS REQUIRED UPON A FINDING OF MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES, AND THE RESULTING AWARD MUST REFLECT CURRENT VERIFIED INCOMES.
Once this Court finds a material change in circumstances, it is required to recalculate child support in accordance with the Alaska Child Support Guidelines. Civil Rule 90.3(a) establishes the mandatory framework: for a primary physical custody arrangement involving two children, the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income is multiplied by twenty-seven percent to arrive at the correct award. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
The court in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025), confirmed that a modification motion presenting evidence of a significant discrepancy between a parent's current income and the income underlying the existing order satisfies the fifteen percent threshold under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) and requires recalculation. The Alaska Supreme Court emphasized in that case the importance of using accurate, current income information in computing the proper support obligation, including consideration of whether income should be imputed where a parent has reduced earnings through personal choices.
In this case, no imputation issue arises. Both parties are fully employed and earning verifiable incomes. Respondent's current gross income of approximately $98,000 must be reduced by applicable mandatory deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A) to arrive at his adjusted annual income, which is then multiplied by twenty-seven percent pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). Petitioner's adjusted annual income of approximately $52,000, further reduced by $9,600 in annual work-related childcare costs under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E), properly frames her contribution to the children's support.
The resulting calculation, using current incomes and verified expenses, will produce a monthly child support figure materially greater than the existing $1,150 obligation. The presumption under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) is therefore triggered, and this Court must enter a new order consistent with the Guidelines. State, Child Support Enforcement Division v. Bromley, 987 P.2d 183 (Alaska 1999), confirms that the court may vary from the Guidelines formula only upon a showing of manifest injustice supported by clear and convincing evidence, a burden that Respondent cannot satisfy here where the Guidelines figure simply reflects his documented, substantial increase in earnings.
D. MODIFICATION SHOULD BE MADE EFFECTIVE AS OF THE DATE OF SERVICE OF THIS MOTION.
Civil Rule 90.3(h)(2) provides that a modification that becomes effective on or after the date a motion for modification is served on the opposing party is not considered a retroactive modification. Accordingly, Petitioner respectfully requests that any upward modification of child support be made effective as of the date this motion was served on Respondent. This ensures that the children benefit from the corrected support amount at the earliest permissible date and avoids any windfall to Respondent from delay in the proceedings.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Petitioner Ashley Bergstrom respectfully requests that this Court:
1. Find that Respondent Wesley Bergstrom's increase in annual income from approximately $61,000 to approximately $98,000 constitutes a material change in circumstances under Civil Rule 90.3(h)(1) and AS 25.24.170;
2. Find that Petitioner's additional work-related childcare costs of approximately $800 per month constitute a further material change in circumstances;
3. Order recalculation of child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a) using the parties' current verified incomes and Petitioner's documented childcare expenses;
4. Enter a new child support order consistent with the Alaska Child Support Guidelines, calculated at twenty-seven percent of Respondent's adjusted annual income pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), as adjusted by Petitioner's work-related childcare deduction under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E); and
5. Make the modified support order effective as of the date of service of this motion pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(h)(2).
The children deserve the benefit of a support order that reflects the current financial circumstances of both parents. The existing order, calculated on income data that is now more than three years old and that fails to account for Respondent's substantially higher earnings, no longer serves the children's best interests or the purposes of the Alaska Child Support Guidelines. Petitioner respectfully urges the Court to grant this motion in full.

PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
