I. INTRODUCTION
David Larsen, petitioner, respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered approximately three years ago. The prior order requires David to pay $850 per month in child support, an amount calculated when respondent Danielle Larsen earned only $24,000 per year in a part-time position. Since the entry of that order, Danielle has obtained full-time employment and received two promotions, increasing her annual income to approximately $38,000. Meanwhile, David continues to earn approximately $72,000 per year as a civil engineer and exercises physical custody of the parties' two minor children sixty percent of the time under the existing shared physical custody arrangement. Because Danielle's income has increased substantially, the current support obligation no longer accurately reflects the financial realities of either parent, and recalculation under the Alaska Child Support Guidelines is both necessary and appropriate. David therefore requests that the Court modify the child support order to reflect a recalculated obligation consistent with Civil Rule 906 and the current income of both parties.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David Larsen and Danielle Larsen are the parents of two minor children. Pursuant to a court order entered approximately three years ago, the parties share physical custody of the children on a 60/40 basis, with David exercising physical custody sixty percent of the time and Danielle exercising physical custody forty percent of the time. At the time the prior order was entered, Danielle was employed part-time and earned approximately $24,000 per year. Based on that income figure and the custody arrangement then in place, the Court ordered David to pay child support in the amount of $850 per month.
Since the entry of the prior order, Danielle has secured full-time employment and has received two promotions. Her annual income has risen to approximately $38,000 per year, representing an increase of approximately $14,000 annually, or roughly 58 percent above her income at the time of the prior order. David's income remains approximately $72,000 per year. The parenting time arrangement has remained the same, with David continuing to have physical custody of the children sixty percent of the time.
The substantial increase in Danielle's income, when applied to the Alaska Child Support Guidelines formula under Civil Rule 90.3, produces a child support obligation materially different from the current order of $850 per month. David brings this motion to conform the support obligation to the parties' present financial circumstances.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a child support award upon a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.24.927 provides that "any time after judgment the court, upon the motion of either party, may set aside, alter, or modify so much of the judgment as may provide for alimony, for the appointment of trustees for the care and custody of the minor children or for their nurture and education, for the care, nurture, and education of unmarried 18-year-old children of the marriage while they are actively pursuing a high school diploma or an equivalent level of technical or vocational training and living as dependents with a parent, guardian, or designee of the parent or guardian, or for the maintenance of either party to the action."
A material change in circumstances is presumed when the support obligation calculated under the Alaska Child Support Guidelines differs from the outstanding order by more than fifteen percent. Alaska courts have recognized that a significant shift in either parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances sufficient to support modification of a child support order. Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997). The adoption or enactment of guidelines, as well as significant changes in parental income, have been recognized as triggering grounds for modification. Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989).
Where shared physical custody exists, the Court calculates child support pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for the incomes of both parents and the respective percentages of time each parent exercises physical custody. The governing formula requires that the Court determine what each parent would owe the other under Civil Rule 903(a) assuming the other parent had primary custody, then adjust those figures by the percentage of time each parent has physical custody of the children, and ultimately calculate the net support obligation.
IV. ARGUMENT
A. DANIELLE'S SUBSTANTIAL INCREASE IN INCOME CONSTITUTES A MATERIAL CHANGE IN CIRCUMSTANCES WARRANTING MODIFICATION.
The threshold inquiry in any modification proceeding is whether a material change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the prior order. The Alaska Supreme Court has consistently held that a significant change in either parent's income satisfies this threshold requirement. In Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), the Court confirmed that changes in the level of a parent's income constitute a recognized basis for modifying a child support order. Danielle's income has increased from $24,000 per year to $38,000 per year, a change of approximately $14,000 annually. This increase of roughly 58 percent in Danielle's earned income is precisely the type of material factual change that the modification framework is designed to address.
Furthermore, AS 25.24.170(b) expressly provides that "the adoption or enactment of guidelines or a significant amendment to guidelines for determining support is a material change in circumstances if the guidelines are relevant to the motion." The Alaska Supreme Court applied this principle in Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989), where the Court held that the adoption of Civil Rule 90.3 itself constituted a material change in circumstances permitting recalculation of support. While the present motion is grounded in the change in Danielle's income rather than an amendment to the guidelines, the principle is instructive: the guidelines exist precisely to ensure that support obligations reflect current financial circumstances, and courts are authorized to modify orders when current incomes diverge materially from those upon which the original order was based.
The prior order was calculated using Danielle's income of $24,000 per year. Applying the guidelines to her current income of $38,000 per year, alongside David's income of $72,000 per year and the existing 60/40 shared custody arrangement, produces a support obligation that differs materially from the current $850 per month award. This differential meets the threshold for a presumption of material change in circumstances and warrants recalculation.
B. THE CHILD SUPPORT OBLIGATION MUST BE RECALCULATED UNDER CIVIL RULE 90.3(b) TO REFLECT THE SHARED PHYSICAL CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT AND THE PARTIES' CURRENT INCOMES.
Because the parties share physical custody, the Court must apply the shared physical custody formula set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(b). That rule provides that a child support award in a shared physical custody case "will be calculated by" first determining what each parent would owe the other under Civil Rule 90.3(a) if the other parent had primary custody, then multiplying those figures by the percentage of time the other parent will have physical custody, and then determining the net obligation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), each parent's adjusted annual income is calculated by subtracting mandatory deductions from total income. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2) then provides the applicable percentage multipliers. Because the parties have two children, the relevant percentage is 27 percent, as Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) specifies that the applicable percentage for two children is "27% (.27)."
Step one requires calculating what David would owe Danielle if she had primary custody. David's gross annual income is $72,000. Applying the 27 percent multiplier to his adjusted annual income (after applicable deductions) yields his hypothetical primary custody obligation. Step two requires calculating what Danielle would owe David if he had primary custody. Danielle's gross annual income is $38,000. Applying the 27 percent multiplier to her adjusted annual income yields her hypothetical primary custody obligation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(B), each parent's hypothetical obligation is then multiplied by the percentage of time the other parent has physical custody. David has custody sixty percent of the time, meaning Danielle's hypothetical obligation is multiplied by 0.60. Danielle has custody forty percent of the time, meaning David's hypothetical obligation is multiplied by 0.40.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(C), the parent with the larger resulting figure is the obligor, and the annual award equals the difference between the two figures multiplied by 1.5, provided that figure does not exceed the amount that would be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a) assuming primary custody.
When the formula is applied using Danielle's current income of $38,000 rather than the $24,000 figure used in the prior order, the resulting net child support obligation is substantially lower than $850 per month. The current order is therefore inconsistent with the guidelines as applied to the parties' present financial circumstances and must be modified. The Alaska Supreme Court in Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), confirmed that the adjusted annual income of each parent is calculated under Rule 90.3(a), and the applicable percentage for two children is the adjusted annual income multiplied by 0.27, before applying the shared custody formula. David respectfully requests that this Court apply these calculations to the current income figures and enter a revised support order.
C. EVIDENCE OF DANIELLE'S CURRENT INCOME IS DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE MODIFICATION DETERMINATION AND IS PROPERLY BEFORE THE COURT.
Danielle's current income of $38,000 per year, her full-time employment status, and her two promotions since the entry of the prior order are all directly relevant to the modification inquiry. Under Alaska R. Evid. 401, "relevant evidence means evidence having any tendency to make the existence of any fact that is of consequence to the determination of the action more probable or less probable than it would be without the evidence." Evidence of Danielle's increased income makes it more probable that a material change in circumstances has occurred and that the existing support order no longer reflects the guidelines calculation based on current financial realities. Accordingly, documentation of Danielle's current income, employment records, and pay history are relevant and properly considered by the Court in ruling on this motion.
D. THE PRIOR SUPPORT ORDER HAS NOT BEEN MODIFIED IN THREE YEARS, PROVIDING AN ADDITIONAL BASIS FOR MODIFICATION.
AS 25.24.170(b) further provides that "a periodic modification of child support may be made without a showing of a material change in circumstances if the child support order being modified on the periodic basis has not been modified or adjusted during the three years preceding the periodic modification." The prior order was entered approximately three years ago. David submits that this provision provides an independent, alternative basis for modification of the support order, apart from the substantial income change described above. Whether the Court proceeds on the basis of material change in circumstances or the three-year periodic review provision, the result is the same: recalculation of the child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3 using current income figures is authorized and appropriate.
E. INCOME WITHHOLDING SHOULD BE ADJUSTED TO REFLECT ANY MODIFIED ORDER.
Once a new support order is entered, the income withholding order must also be updated to reflect the revised obligation. AS 25.27.062(a) requires that any support order contain an income withholding provision, and the withholding order must be consistent with the support obligation established by the Court. David requests that any order modifying child support also include a conforming modification to the income withholding provisions to reflect the recalculated monthly obligation.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, David Larsen respectfully requests that this Court enter an order modifying the existing child support obligation. Danielle Larsen's income has increased by approximately 58 percent since the prior order was entered, constituting a material change in circumstances under AS 25.24.170 and the principles recognized in Bunn v. House, 934 P.2d 753 (Alaska 1997), and Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989). Recalculation of the child support obligation under the shared physical custody formula in Civil Rule 90.3(b), using the parties' current incomes and the existing 60/40 parenting time arrangement, will produce a monthly support amount materially different from the current $850 per month order. Additionally, the Court may modify the order on the independent ground that three years have passed without modification, as expressly authorized by AS 25.24.170(b). David requests that the Court enter a revised support order consistent with the Alaska Child Support Guidelines and adjust the income withholding provisions accordingly.

IN THE SUPERIOR COURT FOR THE STATE OF ALASKA
THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0195)
I. INTRODUCTION
This brief is submitted on behalf of Maria Nakamura, petitioner and mother of the two minor children at issue in this proceeding. Maria petitions the court for two forms of relief: first, formal recognition of the primary physical custody arrangement that has been in place as a matter of practice since the entry of the 2021 divorce decree; and second, an upward modification of the existing child support order to reflect both Tomas Nakamura's substantially increased income and the material change in the children's residential schedule. The existing order, entered in 2021, requires Tomas to pay $850 per month based on a shared physical custody calculation using his then-income of $52,000 per year. That order no longer reflects the reality of either parent's financial circumstances or the children's living arrangements. A modification of both custody designation and child support is warranted under Alaska law.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Nakamura and Maria Nakamura were divorced in 2021. The divorce decree incorporated a child support order requiring Tomas to pay $850 per month, calculated under a shared physical custody framework. At the time of the order, Tomas earned approximately $52,000 per year and Maria earned approximately $44,000 per year. The parties' two minor children, currently ages 7 and 9, were subject to an approximately equal parenting time arrangement at the time the support order was entered.
Since entry of the 2021 order, material changes have occurred on multiple fronts. Tomas has accepted a new position as a project manager and now earns $78,000 per year, representing a substantial increase of $26,000 annually from his income at the time of the existing order. Maria, by contrast, has reduced her work hours following the birth of a child from a subsequent relationship, and her annual income has declined from $44,000 to approximately $29,000.
Additionally, and critically for purposes of both the custody designation and the child support calculation, the parties have informally altered the children's residential schedule. The children now reside primarily with Maria. Tomas exercises parenting time on alternating weekends and one weeknight per week. This schedule, while practiced consistently by the parties, has never been reduced to a formal court order. No modification of the 2021 custody order has been sought or entered. Maria now petitions the court to formalize the current residential arrangement through a primary physical custody designation and to recalculate child support accordingly.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court may modify a child custody award, including provisions governing physical custody and child support, when there has been a change in circumstances and modification is in the best interests of the child. AS 25.20.941 provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child.
Child support in Alaska is governed by Civil Rule 964. Where one parent has primary physical custody, support is calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which sets the award as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a specified percentage based on the number of children. Where the parties share physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(b) applies a different methodology that accounts for both parents' incomes and the respective percentages of parenting time each parent exercises. The classification of the custody arrangement, whether primary or shared, is therefore determinative of the applicable calculation method.
A deviation of 15 percent or more from the existing support order, calculated using the correct methodology, generally constitutes a change of circumstances sufficient to support modification. The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized this threshold as a guideline for when modification of child support is appropriate, as discussed in cases such as Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016) and Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification of Custody Designation and Child Support
The threshold inquiry for any modification proceeding under AS 25.20.110(a) is whether a change in circumstances has occurred since the entry of the existing order. Here, the change is not merely incremental; it is substantial and multi-faceted. Tomas's income has increased by $26,000 per year, representing approximately a 50 percent increase from the $52,000 figure on which the existing order was based. Maria's income has decreased by approximately $15,000 per year, moving from $44,000 to $29,000. Most significantly, the children's actual residential arrangement has shifted from an approximately equal split to a schedule that places the children primarily in Maria's care, with Tomas exercising parenting time only on alternating weekends and one weeknight each week.
Each of these changes, considered independently, would likely satisfy the change of circumstances standard. Considered together, they compel modification. The existing order reflects a factual and financial landscape that no longer exists. Alaska courts have recognized that a parent's retirement and resulting change in both income and parenting time, even when not yet formalized by court order, can constitute the kind of changed circumstances that warrant modification. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016). The same logic applies with force here, where the departure from the court-ordered arrangement has been consistent and ongoing, not temporary or disputed.
B. The Children's Residential Schedule No Longer Qualifies as Shared Physical Custody, and Primary Physical Custody Should Be Formally Designated in Maria
Under Civil Rule 90.3, the distinction between primary and shared physical custody turns on the percentage of time each parent has the children pursuant to a written custody order. The shared physical custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) applies when the children reside with a parent for at least 30 but no more than 70 percent of the year as specified in a written order. The primary custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(a) applies when a parent has the children for less than 30 percent of the year under a written order.
In this case, the existing written order does not reflect the current residential schedule. The parties have informally modified the arrangement such that Tomas exercises parenting time only on alternating weekends and one weeknight per week. Calculated on an annualized basis, this schedule results in Tomas having physical custody of the children for substantially less than 30 percent of the year. Alternating weekends yield approximately 52 overnights per year, and a single weeknight per week yields approximately 52 additional overnights, for a combined total of roughly 104 overnights, or approximately 28.5 percent of the year. This falls below the 30 percent threshold for shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3.
The Alaska Supreme Court addressed a closely analogous transition in Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016), where a parent's relocation from Alaska effectively eliminated shared physical custody and resulted in the children residing with the other parent on a full-time basis. The court there recognized that the shift in the de facto residential arrangement, when combined with changed financial circumstances, supported both a change of custody designation and a corresponding modification of child support. This court should reach the same conclusion here. The informally altered schedule has been consistently practiced, is not disputed, and reflects the genuine residential reality for these children. Formalizing that arrangement through a primary physical custody designation in favor of Maria is both factually accurate and legally appropriate.
Maria respectfully requests that the court enter a formal order designating her as the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children, consistent with AS 25.20.110(a) and the best interests of the children. Such an order will also establish the correct framework for calculating child support going forward.
C. Child Support Should Be Recalculated Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Using Tomas's Current Income
Once the court designates Maria as the primary physical custodian, child support must be recalculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a), which governs primary physical custody arrangements. Under that rule, the annual child support award is calculated as the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage based on the number of children. For two children, the applicable percentage is 27 percent.
Tomas currently earns $78,000 per year. After applying the mandatory deductions permitted under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including applicable federal income and payroll taxes, his adjusted annual income will be determined by the court based on documentation submitted at hearing. Even using a conservative estimate of adjusted annual income, the resulting obligation will differ materially from the existing $850 per month order.
By way of illustration, if Tomas's adjusted annual income is calculated at approximately $65,000 after mandatory deductions, the Civil Rule 90.3(a) calculation for two children at 27 percent yields an annual support obligation of $17,550, or $1,462.50 per month. That figure represents a more than 72 percent increase from the existing $850 monthly obligation, well in excess of the 15 percent threshold recognized by Alaska courts as indicating a change of circumstances. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized that courts must apply the correct version of Rule 90.3 methodology and must recalculate support when both income and custody arrangements have changed materially. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025); Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016).
Maria acknowledges that the court will make final income determinations at hearing based on submitted financial documentation. She requests that the court order Tomas to produce current pay stubs, his most recent federal income tax returns, and any other financial records necessary to calculate his adjusted annual income with precision.
D. The Court Should Consider Both Parents' Incomes and the Shift in Financial Circumstances
While Civil Rule 90.3(a) focuses on the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income as the primary driver of the support calculation, the court retains authority under AS 25.27.060(a) to carefully consider the need for support, the ability of both parents to meet support obligations, and the economic circumstances of each parent following separation and divorce. Maria's income has declined significantly, from $44,000 to approximately $29,000 per year, reducing her capacity to independently meet the children's financial needs. Tomas's income, meanwhile, has increased substantially. The combination of these financial shifts reinforces the appropriateness of an upward modification.
Additionally, Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(E) permits a deduction from adjusted annual income for work-related child care expenses for the children who are the subject of the support order. To the extent Maria incurs child care costs for the parties' children as a result of her work schedule, those costs may be factored into the support calculation. The court should receive evidence at hearing regarding any such expenses.
The court is also directed under AS 25.27.060(c) to issue or review a medical support order, requiring health care insurance coverage for the children if such coverage is available to either parent at a reasonable cost. The parties should be prepared to address the availability and cost of health insurance at the modification hearing so the court may enter an appropriate medical support order consistent with this provision.
E. An Upward Modification Is in the Best Interests of the Children
The best interests of the children are the paramount consideration in any custody or support modification proceeding. AS 25.20.110(a). The existing support order of $850 per month was calibrated to a shared custody arrangement in which both parents bore roughly equal direct costs for the children's day-to-day care and in which Tomas's income was $26,000 lower than it is today. Under the current arrangement, Maria bears the primary financial burden of the children's daily care, housing, meals, clothing, school supplies, and extracurricular activities. The existing order leaves her substantially undercompensated for those costs, particularly given her reduced income.
A support award calibrated to Tomas's current income and to the children's actual primary residence with Maria will better serve the children's material needs and ensure that both parents contribute to those needs in a manner proportionate to their respective financial capacities. This is precisely the outcome that Civil Rule 90.3 is designed to achieve, and it is squarely consistent with the best interests standard that governs this proceeding. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018); Ferguson v. Ferguson, 195 P.3d 127 (Alaska 2008).
F. Modification Should Be Made Retroactive to the Date of Petitioner's Filing
Maria respectfully requests that the court make any modification of child support retroactive to the date of the filing of this petition. Alaska courts have recognized that retroactive application to the date of filing is appropriate where the petitioner promptly sought modification upon the occurrence of changed circumstances. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). Because the changes in income and residential schedule that form the basis of this petition have been ongoing, and because Maria has acted without undue delay in bringing this matter before the court, retroactive modification to the petition date is warranted.
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Maria Nakamura respectfully requests that the court:
1. Find that a material change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the 2021 child support order, satisfying the standard set forth in AS 25.20.110(a);
2. Enter a formal order designating Maria as the primary physical custodian of the parties' two minor children, consistent with the parties' actual and ongoing residential practice;
3. Recalculate child support under Civil Rule 90.3(a) using Tomas's current adjusted annual income of $78,000, less applicable mandatory deductions, and applying the 27 percent multiplier for two children;
4. Review and enter an appropriate medical support order pursuant to AS 25.27.060(c);
5. Make the modified support obligation retroactive to the date of this petition's filing; and
6. Grant such other and further relief as the court deems just and appropriate in light of the best interests of the children.

THIRD JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PETITIONER, Petitioner, vs. RESPONDENT, Respondent.
MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT
(doc-0196)
I. INTRODUCTION
Petitioner Tomas Nakamura respectfully moves this Court to modify the existing child support order entered at the time of the parties' divorce in 2021. That order required Respondent Michael Nakamura to pay $850 per month in child support, based on Michael's annual income of $62,000 and a shared physical custody arrangement affording each parent approximately equal parenting time. Since entry of that order, two material changes in circumstances have occurred. First, Michael has accepted a supervisory position with a regional contracting firm and now earns approximately $94,000 per year, a substantial increase over his income at the time of the original order. Second, the parties agreed to a modification of the parenting plan in early 2023, under which Tomas now exercises primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children. Together, these changes require recalculation of child support under Alaska Civil Rule 964. Tomas estimates that a proper calculation under the Rule 90.3 guidelines yields a monthly obligation of approximately $1,400, a figure far more than 15% above the current award and therefore presumptively constituting a material change in circumstances. Tomas respectfully requests that this Court enter a modified child support order consistent with the applicable guidelines.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Nakamura and Michael Nakamura were divorced by decree of the Superior Court in 2021. At the time of divorce, the court entered a child support order requiring Michael to pay $850 per month for the benefit of the parties' two minor children. That amount was calculated based on Michael's gross annual income of approximately $62,000, which he earned as a commercial electrician, and a shared physical custody arrangement under which each parent had approximately equal parenting time with the children.
Subsequent to the entry of the divorce decree and child support order, two significant changes have taken place. Michael has accepted a supervisory position with a regional contracting firm. In this new role, Michael earns approximately $94,000 per year, representing an increase of approximately $32,000 annually, or roughly 52%, over his income at the time of the original order. This increase in income is material and was not contemplated when the original child support obligation was established.
Additionally, in early 2023, the parties agreed to a modification of the parenting plan. Under the modified plan, Tomas assumed primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children. Michael continues to exercise parenting time, but no longer shares custody on an approximately equal basis as contemplated by the original order. The custody arrangement thus shifted from shared physical custody, governed by Civil Rule 90.3(b), to primary physical custody in favor of Tomas, governed by Civil Rule 934(a).
Tomas has remained employed part-time as a dental assistant and earns approximately $28,000 annually. As the primary physical custodian, Tomas bears the majority of the day-to-day financial responsibility for the children's care, maintenance, and education. The current child support order of $850 per month no longer accurately reflects the parties' respective financial circumstances or the current physical custody arrangement, and it is insufficient to meet the children's needs.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.24.170(a), a court may set aside, alter, or modify a judgment providing for child support upon the motion of either party at any time after judgment. Modification of a child support order requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. AS 25.27.190(e). Alaska Civil Rule 90.3 governs the calculation of child support in Alaska. Where one parent exercises primary physical custody, Rule 90.3(a) applies and child support is calculated as an amount equal to the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage, which is 27% for two children. Civil Rule 991(a)(2)(B). Where parents share physical custody on an approximately equal basis, Rule 90.3(b)(1) applies and a different formula is used to account for each parent's time with and expenditures on behalf of the children. Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1).
A material change in circumstances is presumed when child support as calculated under Rule 90.3 would be more than 15% greater or less than the outstanding support order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). A court does not abuse its discretion when it awards child support based on Civil Rule 90.3. Mitchell v. Mitchell, 370 P.3d 1070 (Alaska 2016). The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that Rule 90.3(a)(2) specifies the percentages by which a non-custodial parent's adjusted income must be multiplied to calculate child support, and that these percentages are mandatory in the absence of a recognized exception. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997). Modification of child support may be sought at any time upon a showing of material change in circumstances, and the enactment of a significant change in income or custody arrangements each independently supports such a finding. Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989).
Courts are also authorized to impute potential income to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). Additionally, child support calculations may take into account a court's finding regarding which parent's expenditures more accurately reflect the time each parent will spend directly supporting the children. Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1)(B).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Has Occurred Warranting Modification of the Child Support Order.
Two independent and significant changes in circumstances have occurred since entry of the original child support order in 2021. Each alone would be sufficient to support modification, and together they compel it.
First, Michael's income has increased substantially. At the time of the original order, Michael earned approximately $62,000 per year as a commercial electrician. He now earns approximately $94,000 per year in a supervisory capacity with a regional contracting firm. This is an increase of approximately $32,000, or more than 50%, over his prior income. Under the framework established by Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), a material change in circumstances is presumed when child support calculated under Rule 90.3 would be more than 15% greater than the current order. Recalculation of child support based on Michael's current income under Civil Rule 90.3(a), applied to a primary custody arrangement, yields an estimated monthly obligation of approximately $1,400. This figure is more than 64% higher than the current award of $850 per month, far exceeding the 15% threshold required to trigger the presumption of a material change in circumstances.
The Alaska Supreme Court confirmed in Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025) that a demonstration that a recalculation of child support under Rule 90.3 results in a more than 15% change from the current order satisfies the material change of circumstances threshold. That principle applies with equal force here. Michael's significant salary increase, standing alone, establishes a material change in circumstances under AS 25.27.190(e) and AS 25.24.170(a).
Second, the physical custody arrangement has changed from shared physical custody to primary physical custody in favor of Tomas. This change is independently significant because it alters the governing formula for calculating child support. The original order was based on shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(b), which accounts for the relatively equal time each parent spends with and directly expends money on behalf of the children. Now that Tomas exercises primary physical custody, Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs, and Michael, as the non-custodial parent, is obligated to pay a percentage of his adjusted annual income without the offsets that apply under the shared custody formula. This structural change in the applicable formula, combined with Michael's income increase, produces a dramatically different child support obligation than was contemplated by the original order. The modification agreed upon by the parties in early 2023 therefore constitutes a material change in circumstances separately warranting modification of the support order.
B. The Modified Child Support Obligation Should Be Calculated Under Civil Rule 90.3(a) Based on Michael's Current Income.
Because Tomas now exercises primary physical custody of the parties' two minor children, child support must be calculated under Civil Rule 90.3(a). That provision requires that the child support award be calculated as the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by 27% for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B). The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the percentages specified in Rule 90.3(a)(2) are mandatory and govern the calculation of support absent a recognized exception. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997).
Michael's gross annual income is approximately $94,000. From this figure, mandatory deductions must be subtracted pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including federal and state income taxes, Social Security tax, Medicare tax, and any other mandatory deductions applicable to Michael's employment. Voluntary contributions to tax-deferred retirement plans may also be deducted, subject to the cap in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B). After the applicable deductions are applied, Michael's adjusted annual income is then multiplied by 27%, as required by Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B), yielding the annual child support obligation, which is then divided into 12 equal monthly payments.
Based on Tomas's best estimate of Michael's adjusted annual income after mandatory deductions, the resulting monthly support obligation is approximately $1,400. This estimate is offered as a reasonable approximation pending the Court's receipt of complete financial documentation from Michael. Tomas respectfully requests that the Court order Michael to provide current income documentation and that the Court perform the Rule 90.3(a) calculation based on verified figures.
The Court should also note that Tomas earns approximately $28,000 per year as a part-time dental assistant. While Tomas's income is relevant under the shared custody formula in Civil Rule 90.3(b), it does not directly offset Michael's child support obligation under the primary custody formula of Civil Rule 90.3(a). The disparity in income between the parties further underscores the inadequacy of the current $850 per month order, which was set at a time when custody was shared and Michael's income was significantly lower.
C. The Modified Order Should Include an Income Withholding Provision.
Any modified child support order entered by this Court must include an income withholding order pursuant to AS 25.27.062. Under that statute, a judgment or court order providing for child support must contain an income withholding order requiring that the specified support amount be withheld directly from the obligor's wages and remitted to the appropriate agency. AS 25.27.062(a). This provision serves the important purpose of ensuring consistent and timely payment of support for the benefit of the children. An income withholding order issued under AS 25.27.062 has priority over all other attachments, executions, garnishments, or other legal process brought under state law against the same property. AS 25.27.062(g). Tomas respectfully requests that the modified order include an income withholding provision consistent with these requirements.
D. The Modification Should Be Effective as of the Filing of this Motion.
Under AS 25.24.170(a), the Court may modify a child support order at any time upon motion of either party. It is appropriate for the Court to make the modification effective as of the date of the filing of this motion. The changes in Michael's income and in the physical custody arrangement both occurred well before this filing. Tomas has borne the financial burden of primary physical custody since early 2023 on the basis of a child support award that was both factually and legally inadequate at the time the custody arrangement changed. Prompt modification is necessary to ensure that the children's financial needs are met going forward. Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989) (courts have authority to modify child support upon a showing of material change in circumstances, and such modification serves the best interests of the children).
V. CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, Tomas Nakamura respectfully requests that this Court find that a material change in circumstances has occurred by reason of both the substantial increase in Michael Nakamura's annual income and the change in physical custody from a shared to a primary custody arrangement in favor of Tomas, and that this Court enter a modified child support order calculated in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) reflecting a monthly obligation of approximately $1,400, subject to adjustment upon verification of Michael's complete income and deduction information, that the modified order include an income withholding provision pursuant to AS 25.27.062, and that the modified obligation be made effective as of the date of the filing of this motion. The children's financial well-being depends upon an order that accurately reflects the parties' current circumstances and the applicable law.

I. INTRODUCTION
Jennifer Whitfield respectfully petitions this Court to modify the existing child support order entered in 2021. Since the original order was entered, Tomas Whitfield's annual income has increased from $52,000 to $94,000, and Jennifer's annual income has decreased from approximately $18,000 to approximately $11,000 due to a documented medical condition. These changes in the financial circumstances of both parties constitute a material change of circumstances requiring upward modification of child support to serve the best interests of the parties' two minor children. A recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3 yields a monthly obligation substantially higher than the current $850 order. Jennifer therefore asks the Court to modify the existing order and to calculate a new support amount consistent with Alaska law and the Rule 90.3 guidelines.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Tomas Whitfield and Jennifer Whitfield divorced in 2021. At the time of the divorce decree, the superior court entered a child support order requiring Tomas to pay $850 per month. That figure was based on Tomas's annual salary of $52,000 as a warehouse supervisor and Jennifer's part-time annual income of approximately $18,000. The parties share physical custody of their two minor children on a roughly equal basis, with each parent having the children approximately 45 percent of overnights. The children reside primarily with Jennifer during the school week.
Since the entry of the original order, two significant financial changes have occurred. First, Tomas accepted a new position as a regional logistics manager earning $94,000 per year, representing an increase of $42,000 in annual gross income. Second, Jennifer has reduced her working hours because of a documented medical condition, and her annual income has fallen to approximately $11,000. Jennifer's reduced income is not the product of a voluntary or unreasonable decision but is instead attributable to a genuine medical limitation.
Under a recalculation using the Civil Rule 90.3 guidelines applied to the parties' current incomes and the existing custody arrangement, Jennifer estimates the new monthly obligation would be approximately $1,400. Jennifer now asks this Court to modify the order accordingly.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
Alaska Statute AS 25.20.110(a) provides that an award of child support may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Where a parent opposes modification and it is granted, the court must enter on the record its reason for the modification.
Alaska Statute AS 25.24.170(a) further authorizes the court, upon the motion of either party, to alter or modify so much of the judgment as may provide for the maintenance of either party or the care, nurture, and education of minor children. Under AS 25.24.170(b), a significant change in a parent's income constitutes a material change in circumstances for purposes of a motion to modify child support.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs child support calculations where one parent has primary physical custody. It provides that the award is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a specified percentage: 27 percent for two children. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources minus specified mandatory deductions. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits the court to calculate child support based on the potential income of a parent who voluntarily and unreasonably is unemployed or underemployed, but expressly prohibits such an imputation for a parent who is physically or mentally incapacitated.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that a modification of child support requires a showing of material change of circumstances, and that such a change is presumed where the recalculated support amount under Rule 90.3 is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). Courts have consistently applied the Rule 90.3 formula to determine child support obligations and have emphasized that trial courts must take all evidence necessary to accurately reflect the parties' economic reality. Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013). Retroactive modification of child support is prohibited, meaning the modification takes effect from the date of the motion or as otherwise ordered by the court. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change of Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification of the Child Support Order.
Under AS 25.20.110(a), the Court may modify a child support order upon a finding of a change in circumstances and a determination that modification is in the best interests of the children. Here, two independent and well-documented changes in financial circumstances have occurred since the 2021 order was entered: Tomas's annual income has increased by $42,000, and Jennifer's annual income has decreased by approximately $7,000 as a result of a documented medical condition. Either change alone would be significant; together they create a compelling basis for modification.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that a material change of circumstances is presumed when the support amount calculated under Rule 90.3 is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). Here, the current order is $850 per month. Jennifer estimates that a recalculation under Rule 90.3 based on the parties' present incomes yields a monthly obligation of approximately $1,400. That figure represents an increase of approximately 65 percent over the current order, which far exceeds the 15 percent threshold. The presumption of a material change of circumstances therefore applies, and modification is warranted.
B. Recalculation Under Civil Rule 90.3 Supports a Monthly Obligation of Approximately $1,400.
Civil Rule 90.3(a) provides that a child support award in a case in which one parent is awarded primary physical custody is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage specified in subparagraph (a)(2). The rule specifies that "the percentage by which the non-custodial parent's adjusted income must be multiplied in order to calculate the child support award is . . . 27% (.27) for two children." Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B).
Tomas's gross annual income is now $94,000. After applicable mandatory deductions under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), including federal and state income taxes, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax, his adjusted annual income will be substantially above the prior calculation base. Applying the 27 percent multiplier to Tomas's adjusted annual income yields a monthly obligation that Jennifer estimates at approximately $1,400. This Court should order the parties to submit updated financial affidavits and supporting documentation so that the exact adjusted annual income and corresponding support obligation can be calculated with precision.
The Alaska Supreme Court has held that in determining earning capacity under Rule 90.3, the court has discretion to choose the best indicator of future earning capacity based on the evidence before it, and that trial courts must take all evidence necessary to accurately reflect the parties' economic reality. Wilhour v. Wilhour, 308 P.3d 884 (Alaska 2013). Tomas's current salary of $94,000 as a regional logistics manager represents his actual, confirmed income from regular employment and is the appropriate basis for the recalculation.
The Alaska Supreme Court has also made clear that the Rule 90.3(a) formula must guide the calculation. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997); Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). The court's obligation is to follow the formula as written, and any deviation from it requires specific findings. No basis for deviation from the guidelines exists here; rather, strict application of the formula is appropriate given the straightforward nature of the parties' employment income.
C. Jennifer's Reduced Income Should Not Be the Subject of Income Imputation.
Tomas may argue that Jennifer is voluntarily underemployed and that potential income should be imputed to her under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4). That argument is without merit. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(E) expressly prohibits a determination of potential income for a parent who is physically or mentally incapacitated. Jennifer's reduction in working hours is the direct result of a documented medical condition, not a voluntary or unreasonable lifestyle choice.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4)(A) states that a parent may be voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed only when the parent's current situation and earnings reflect the parent's decision to not work or to earn less than the parent is capable of earning. Jennifer's documented medical condition prevents her from working at her prior capacity. Her current income of approximately $11,000 accurately reflects her actual earning ability at this time, not a strategic or voluntary reduction. Imputing income to her under these circumstances would be legally impermissible and factually unsupported.
D. Modification Is in the Best Interests of the Children.
Under AS 25.20.110(a), the Court must find that modification is in the best interests of the children. Here, that finding is clearly supported. The children reside primarily with Jennifer during the school week. Jennifer's reduced income, combined with Tomas's substantially increased ability to pay, means that the children's needs are not being adequately met under the current support amount. An upward modification in support will more accurately reflect the children's needs relative to the financial realities of both parents and will ensure that the children benefit from Tomas's increased earning capacity.
The Alaska Supreme Court has recognized that the purpose of the Rule 90.3 guidelines is to ensure that child support is calculated consistently with the parents' actual financial circumstances. Berkbigler v. Berkbigler, 921 P.2d 628 (Alaska 1996); Koller v. Reft, 71 P.3d 800 (Alaska 2003). Where, as here, one parent's income has increased substantially and the other parent's capacity to earn has diminished through no fault of her own, modification serves the best interests of the children by ensuring they receive adequate financial support from the parent best positioned to provide it.
E. The Court Should Implement Income Withholding to Secure Compliance with the Modified Order.
Once the Court enters a modified child support order, Jennifer respectfully requests that the Court include an income withholding provision. Under AS 25.27.062(a), a court order providing for support must contain an income withholding order, and under AS 25.27.062(a)(2), the income withholding order must provide for immediate income withholding where the support order is not being enforced by the agency and was issued on or after July 8, 1994. The existing and modified orders both fall within this category.
Additionally, AS 25.27.070(a) authorizes the court, on its own motion or motion of a party, to order either parent to assign to the custodian of the child that portion of salary or wages due currently and in the future sufficient to pay the amount ordered for the support, maintenance, nurture, and education of the child. An assignment order under AS 25.27.070 is binding upon Tomas's employer upon service of a copy of the order and has priority over any competing attachment, execution, or assignment unless otherwise ordered by the Court. AS 25.27.070(c). Including such a provision in the modified order will protect the children's interests by ensuring consistent and timely payment.
V. CONCLUSION
Jennifer Whitfield respectfully requests that this Court find a material change of circumstances based on Tomas Whitfield's increase in annual income from $52,000 to $94,000 and Jennifer's documented reduction in annual income from approximately $18,000 to approximately $11,000 due to a medical condition. Jennifer further requests that the Court recalculate child support in accordance with Civil Rule 90.3 based on the parties' current financial circumstances, that the Court find the recalculated amount to be in the best interests of the parties' two minor children, and that the Court enter a modified support order in the approximate amount of $1,400 per month, together with an income withholding order directed to Tomas's employer to secure compliance. Jennifer requests such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.

MOTION TO ESTABLISH OR MODIFY CHILD SUPPORT

I. INTRODUCTION
David Sutter respectfully moves this Court for modification of the existing child support order entered in 2021. Since that order was entered, two independent and substantial changes in circumstances have occurred. First, David suffered a significant reduction in income after losing his position as a civil engineer, and he now earns approximately $42,000 per year working as a contractor. Second, and equally significant, the parties' custodial arrangement has fundamentally shifted: the children now reside with David approximately 70 percent of the time, a figure that not only departs materially from the equal 50-50 schedule reflected in the 2021 order, but also crosses the legal threshold separating shared physical custody from primary physical custody under Alaska's child support guidelines. Concurrently, Sarah Sutter received a promotion and now earns approximately $98,000 per year as a hospital administrator in Anchorage. The current child support order no longer reflects the economic reality of either party, nor does it reflect the actual custodial arrangement under which David is raising these children. David therefore requests that the Court vacate the existing support obligation, recalculate support pursuant to Civil Rule 90.3, and enter a new order directing Sarah to pay monthly child support to David consistent with the applicable guidelines.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
David and Sarah Sutter are the parents of two minor children. In 2021, the Court entered a child support order premised on two factual conditions: the parties earned comparable incomes, and the children resided with each parent on an equal 50-50 shared custody basis. Those conditions no longer exist.
Since the 2021 order, David was laid off from his position as a civil engineer. He now works as a contractor earning approximately $42,000 per year, representing a significant reduction from his prior income. Sarah, by contrast, received a promotion to a hospital administrator position in Anchorage and now earns approximately $98,000 per year.
The custodial arrangement has changed as well. Sarah's increased work travel schedule has resulted in the children residing with David approximately 70 percent of the time. David is now the primary caregiver for the parties' two minor children, bearing the substantial majority of the day-to-day expenses associated with raising them. This 70-percent residential arrangement is not reflected in the operative 2021 order, which continues to govern the parties' support obligations as though custody remained equally divided.
David now earns less than half of Sarah's annual income, and he is providing primary care for the children more than two-thirds of the year. The combination of these changed circumstances renders the current support order inequitable and inconsistent with Alaska law.
III. LEGAL STANDARD
A court has broad authority to modify a child support order following its entry. Under AS 25.24.900, any time after judgment the Court may, upon the motion of either party, set aside, alter, or modify the portion of a judgment providing for the maintenance of minor children. Similarly, AS 25.20.110 provides that an award of custody or visitation may be modified if the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child.
For child support specifically, modification requires a showing of a material change in circumstances. Civil Rule 90.3 governs the calculation of child support in Alaska. Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), where one parent is awarded primary physical custody, the support award is calculated as an amount equal to the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent multiplied by a percentage based on the number of children. Where the parents share physical custody, Civil Rule 953(b) applies a distinct calculation that accounts for both parents' incomes and the percentage of time each parent has physical custody of the children.
A modification of child support is presumed to reflect a material change in circumstances when the recalculated amount under the rule is more than 15 percent greater or less than the outstanding support order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017). The Alaska Supreme Court has held that child support must be calculated based on current, actual income information, and a court may not rely on outdated income figures when a party has demonstrated a genuine reduction in earnings. Yerrington v. Yerrington, 933 P.2d 555 (Alaska 1997). Courts applying Civil Rule 90.3 focus on the children's needs and the parties' present financial circumstances, not those that existed at the time of the original order. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997).
IV. ARGUMENT
A. A Material Change in Circumstances Exists Warranting Modification of the Child Support Order.
David's motion satisfies the threshold requirement for modification of child support under Alaska law. Two independent and significant changes in circumstances have occurred since the 2021 order was entered.
First, David's income has decreased substantially. He was laid off from his civil engineering position and now earns approximately $42,000 per year as a contractor. This reduction is neither temporary nor voluntary. The Alaska Supreme Court has made clear that a genuine, substantial decline in a party's income constitutes a material change in circumstances warranting recalculation of child support. Yerrington v. Yerrington, 933 P.2d 555 (Alaska 1997). At the same time, Sarah's income has increased to approximately $98,000 per year following her promotion. The combined effect of these income changes means that the parties' economic positions are now markedly different from what they were when the 2021 order was entered.
Second, the physical custody arrangement has changed in a legally significant way. The 2021 order was premised on a 50-50 shared custody schedule. The children now reside with David approximately 70 percent of the time due to Sarah's increased work travel. Under Civil Rule 90.3(f), a parent who has the children for more than 70 percent of the year has primary physical custody, while shared physical custody exists when a parent has the children between 30 and 70 percent of the year. The shift from a 50-50 schedule to a 70-percent arrangement in David's favor represents a dramatic departure from the conditions underlying the existing order, and it directly affects which subsection of Civil Rule 90.3 governs the support calculation.
Taken individually, either of these changes would support a finding of material change in circumstances. Taken together, they compel it. The existing support order was calibrated to a factual picture that no longer exists. Because recalculation under Civil Rule 90.3 based on the parties' current incomes and the current custody arrangement will produce a support figure more than 15 percent different from the outstanding order, the material change in circumstances threshold is presumptively satisfied. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017).
B. Child Support Must Be Recalculated Under Civil Rule 90.3 to Reflect the Current Custody Arrangement.
The threshold question governing the applicable calculation method is whether the current custody arrangement qualifies as primary or shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(f). When David has the children 70 percent of the time, the children reside primarily with him, and the arrangement functions as primary physical custody in David's favor for purposes of the guidelines. This matters because Civil Rule 90.3(a) and Civil Rule 90.3(b) employ different formulas, and the distinction between primary and shared custody has a direct and significant effect on the calculated support obligation.
Under Civil Rule 90.3(a), where one parent has primary physical custody, the support award equals the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income multiplied by the applicable percentage. For two children, that percentage is 27 percent. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2). Applying that formula to Sarah's income of approximately $98,000 per year, after the mandatory and permissible deductions outlined in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1), the resulting support obligation would represent a substantial monthly payment from Sarah to David.
Even if the Court were to treat the current arrangement as shared physical custody under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1), because the children reside with David at or near the 70-percent threshold, the shared custody calculation would still result in Sarah owing support to David. The shared custody formula under Civil Rule 90.3(b)(1) calculates what each parent would owe the other assuming the other had primary custody, multiplies that figure by the percentage of time the other parent has the children, and then determines the net obligation by subtracting the smaller figure from the larger and multiplying by 1.5. Given the significant disparity between the parties' incomes and the significant disparity in the time each parent spends with the children, the result under either formula directs a support payment from Sarah to David.
The Alaska Supreme Court has confirmed that the custodial label assigned in an earlier order does not foreclose modification when the actual residential arrangement has materially changed. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). The operative custody schedule, not the schedule reflected in an outdated order, governs which formula applies for purposes of a modification proceeding. Charlesworth v. State, Child Support Enforcement Division Ex Rel. Charlesworth, 779 P.2d 792 (Alaska 1989). David therefore requests that the Court apply the formula that corresponds to the children's actual living arrangement as of the date of this motion.
C. The Court Should Calculate David's Adjusted Annual Income Using His Actual Current Earnings and Should Not Impute Additional Income.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) defines adjusted annual income as the parent's total income from all sources, less certain mandatory and permissible deductions. David currently earns approximately $42,000 per year as a contractor. This income reflects genuine market conditions following his layoff, not a voluntary or unreasonable choice to earn less than he is capable of earning.
Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) permits a court to impute potential income to a parent who is voluntarily and unreasonably unemployed or underemployed. However, that provision does not apply here. David's income reduction was involuntary, resulting from a layoff outside his control. He is actively employed as a contractor, earning income commensurate with available work in his field. The Alaska Supreme Court has cautioned that courts should not penalize a parent for an income reduction that is genuine and not a product of deliberate self-impoverishment. Flannery v. Flannery, 950 P.2d 126 (Alaska 1997). The totality of circumstances, including David's employment history, his field, and the circumstances of his layoff, does not support a finding that he is voluntarily and unreasonably underemployed. The Court should therefore calculate David's adjusted annual income using his actual earnings of approximately $42,000 per year.
D. The Court May, if Appropriate, Consider Potential Income Attribution with Respect to Sarah's Available Earning Capacity.
Sarah currently earns approximately $98,000 per year. Her income is the primary driver of the support obligation in this matter. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1) requires that Sarah's adjusted annual income be calculated by subtracting from her gross earnings the mandatory deductions enumerated in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(A), including applicable taxes, Social Security contributions, and Medicare tax. Any permissible voluntary deductions, such as retirement contributions not exceeding the cap set forth in Civil Rule 90.3(a)(1)(B), would also reduce her adjusted income. David requests that the Court require Sarah to submit a current Child Support Guidelines Affidavit reflecting her actual earnings, deductions, and benefits.
To the extent Sarah seeks to minimize her reported income through deductions or other means, the Court retains authority under Civil Rule 90.3(a)(4) to evaluate whether income should be imputed. The Alaska Supreme Court has held that courts should take a realistic view of a party's earning capacity and actual income in calculating support obligations. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025). David reserves the right to challenge any claims of deductions or reduced income that are not supported by adequate documentation.
E. The Existing Support Order No Longer Reflects the Children's Best Interests and Should Be Modified.
Child support calculations under Civil Rule 90.3 are grounded in the fundamental principle that children are entitled to share in the financial resources of both parents. The guidelines exist to ensure that support awards are proportional to parents' incomes and reflective of the actual custodial arrangement. Ronny M. v. Nanette H., 303 P.3d 392 (Alaska 2013).
The existing 2021 order was calculated on the premise of roughly equal incomes and equal parenting time. Neither of those premises remains accurate. David is now raising the children the substantial majority of the time, absorbing the lion's share of their daily living expenses, while earning less than half of Sarah's salary. Maintaining the current order under these circumstances would produce a result that is neither consistent with the guidelines nor in the best interests of the children.
Alaska law recognizes that the children's well-being is best served by a support award that accurately reflects the parents' present circumstances. Kelly v. Joseph, 46 P.3d 1014 (Alaska 2002). Because both the income disparity and the custodial shift are real, substantial, and documented, the Court should enter a modified support order directing Sarah to pay monthly child support to David in an amount calculated under Civil Rule 90.3 based on current incomes and the current custody arrangement.
F. Income Withholding Should Be Ordered Upon Modification.
Upon entry of a modified support order, the Court should also enter an income withholding order pursuant to AS 25.27.914. Under AS 25.27.062(a), a judgment, court order, or agency order providing for support must contain an income withholding order. Immediate income withholding is required unless one of the specific exceptions enumerated in AS 25.27.062(m) applies. No such exception is anticipated here. An income withholding order directed to Sarah's employer would ensure consistent and timely payment of any support obligation the Court may enter, protecting both the children and David from the disruption of irregular or missed payments.
V. CONCLUSION
David Sutter respectfully requests that this Court enter an order:
1. Finding that a material change in circumstances has occurred since entry of the 2021 child support order, based on the significant reduction in David's income, the significant increase in Sarah's income, and the material shift in the parties' custodial arrangement;
2. Calculating a modified child support obligation under Civil Rule 90.3, reflecting David's primary custody of the children approximately 70 percent of the time, David's adjusted annual income of approximately $42,000, and Sarah's adjusted annual income of approximately $98,000;
3. Directing Sarah to pay monthly child support to David consistent with the applicable guidelines for two children;
4. Entering an income withholding order pursuant to AS 25.27.062 to ensure timely payment of the modified support obligation; and
5. Granting such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper.

III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under AS 25.20.110(a), an award of custody or child support may be modified when the court determines that a change in circumstances requires the modification and the modification is in the best interests of the child. Similarly, AS 25.24.170(a) permits the court, upon motion of either party, to set aside, alter, or modify a judgment as it relates to the maintenance of minor children. Under Alaska Rule of Civil Procedure 90.3, child support is calculated based upon the adjusted annual income of the non-custodial parent when one parent holds primary physical custody, or by a formula accounting for the incomes of both parents and their respective percentages of custody when the parents share physical custody. Holmes v. Holmes, 414 P.3d 662 (Alaska 2018). A material change of circumstances is presumed when the support amount calculated under Civil Rule 90.3 would be more than fifteen percent greater or less than the existing order. Shanigan v. Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017); Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005).
Once a material change in circumstances is established, the court recalculates support using the formula appropriate to the current custody arrangement. Swaney v. Granger, 297 P.3d 132 (Alaska 2013). Where primary physical custody applies, Civil Rule 90.3(a) governs the calculation by multiplying the non-custodial parent's adjusted annual income by the applicable percentage for the number of children involved. Civil Rule 90.3(a)(2)(B) specifies a rate of twenty-seven percent for two children. Peter Chapman v. Julia Chapman, 563 P.3d 1155 (Alaska 2025).

Shanigan, 386 P.3d 1238 (Alaska 2017), and Hixson v. Sarkesian, 123 P.3d 1072 (Alaska 2005).
